en: The Śrī Padma Purāṇa,
Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa,
First Chapter.
Salutations to Śrī Viṣṇu,
who is as pure and white as the moon, whose waters produce foam from the agitation caused by the trunks of elephants and sea-monsters,
and who is resorted to by the foremost of Brahmins intent on vows and observances for the sake of attaining the state of Brahmā.

May the water from the lotus of Brahmā—the preceptor of the three worlds, adorned with a garland—purify you; water that is sanctified by his gaze, delightful with its expansive abundance, and the remover of all impurity.
(1) [Then] the great-minded one [approached] the son of Sūta, the disciple of Vyāsa, as he sat in a secluded place.
O dear one, you have heard from me the history named *Lomaharṣaṇa* composed by Ugraśravas;
having gone to the hermitages of the sages, tell them in detail, as requested, all the duties that you have learned from me in brief.
O son, all the Purāṇas have been narrated to you by me, having been obtained from Vyāsa;
they were told in detail by the Lord himself when he was questioned by the best of sages at Prayāga.
Thus questioned and instructed by the Lord who desires their welfare, those sages seeking dharma and desiring a sacred place, [beheld] that which has a beautiful nave,
divine form, truth as its movement, and auspicious prowess.
"O you who are free from sloth, this peerless wheel being turned, you shall attain that beneficial state by following behind it with disciplined conduct.
Wherever the rim of the turning Wheel of Dharma breaks, [there you shall find rest]."
"The region shall be considered holy," said the Lord himself.
Having spoken thus to all the sages, he once again vanished from sight at the place where the wheel fell apart upon the confluence of the whirlpools of the Gaṅgā.
"At that time, the Ṛṣis were performing a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) in Naimiṣa.
Go there and speak to them as they inquire about their doubts regarding dharma. Then Ugraśravas, wise and learned in knowledge, went to those bulls among sages.
Having approached them, greeted them, and paid homage with palms joined in reverence,
the wise one pleased those sages by prostrating himself. And those great-souled performers of the sacrifice, together with the members of the assembly, were likewise delighted.
Having gathered together, the sages offered him worship according to the prescribed rites and said:
"O Sūtaka, from where have you come? From which country have you arrived here? (13)
"O you who possess a splendor equal to the gods, tell me the reason for this in the scripture.
Sūta said: "I was indeed commanded by my father, the wise disciple of Vyāsa. (14)
Go and serve the sages; whatever they ask you, tell them that. "Tell me, O Blessed Ones, which story I should relate—whether it be a Purāṇa, an Itihāsa, or various kinds of Dharma. (15)
The best of sages heard those sweet words of his. Then, O Lomaharṣaṇi, having seen that learned man, the son of Vyāsa, so full of confidence, a desire arose in them to hear the Purāṇa.
At that sacrificial session, there was a head of the assembly named Śaunaka, an intelligent master of all scriptures and a teacher in the forest of wisdom;
having adopted that state of mind and desiring to hear the duties, he spoke to him.
O you of great intellect, the Blessed One, the supreme knower of Brahman, was begotten by you;
Vyāsa, the meaning of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, was properly served by you, and you milked from his mind that auspicious wisdom which rests upon the Purāṇas. 19–20.
O one of great intelligence, you have a desire to hear the ancient account concerning these foremost of Brahmins at this present time; it behoves you to cause it to be heard.
For all these high-souled men, belonging to various lineages, have assembled here.
"O exponents of the Veda, listen to your respective portions as declared in the Purāṇas.
When this long sacrificial session is completed, cause those sages to hear them; O high-minded one, you yourself relate the Padma Purāṇa to all."

"How did the lotus arise? How indeed did Brahmā come to be there? And how was the creation performed by him once he had arisen? Tell me that exactly as it happened. Thus questioned, he then replied to them with auspicious words.
The great seer, endowed with subtle reasoning, spoke thus:
"I am pleased and I am graced by you here for having urged me, who am a knower of the Purāṇas and devoted to all duties, to explain the meaning of the Purāṇas. (25-26)
I shall relate all of that to you exactly as it was heard and well-known;
One must maintain the lineages and offer praises to the great-souled ones.
Those who are seen as exponents of Brahman in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas have no authority whatsoever in the Vedas for a Sūta. 28–29.
While the sacrifice of the high-souled Pṛthu Vainya was in progress,
the Māgadha and the Sūta praised that lord of men; then, being pleased, a boon was granted to them by the high-souled king.
The Sūta and the Ayasūta, the Magadha and the Māgadha;
among these, one born from a *sūti* (a woman who has recently given birth) is known here as a Sūta, when the *Indra-sattra* is being performed and Bṛhaspati is conjoined with the planets. 31–32.
From that very Indra, this son was born of Bṛhaspati;

for the sacrificial oblation (havis) of the Guru, which had been mixed and consumed by the hand of the disciple, was born as a mixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara) through the downward and upward flow [of the fluids]. 33.
They were born from a Kṣatriya father and from the womb of a Brāhmaṇa woman.
Due to their similarity with the former [Kṣatriyas] and their difference from them, they are proclaimed as such;
for this is the intermediate duty of the Sūta, who lives by the profession of the field (charioteering).
"In this world, the right to study the Purāṇas has been ordained for Brāhmaṇas alone;
having seen this Dharma, I have been questioned by you, who are exponents of the Veda.
Therefore, O noble ones, I shall correctly proclaim the Purāṇa honored by the sages."
The mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs entered the lineage of Vāsava;
having been cursed by the Pitṛs, she was born within the womb of a fish as the cause for the holy birth of Agni from the fire-drill (araṇi).
From that [Veda], the great seer Parāśara, whose soul was purified, brought forth [the Purāṇa].
Having offered salutations to that Blessed One, the Truth, the Creator,
the Ancient Person who follows the word of Brahmā— 39.
To Viṣṇu, whose true self is the Śaṃsa [the Supreme], appearing in the guise of a human child—40—to him, as soon as he was born, the Veda approached in its entirety;
by churning that intellect as a churning-stick, he drew it forth from the ocean of the Śruti. 41.
The moon of the Mahābhārata has been brought forth to illuminate the world;
for if these three—the Bhārata, the Sun, and Viṣṇu—did not exist, what would be the condition of the world blinded by the darkness of ignorance? 42.
Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
For who else but the lotus-eyed one could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
Therefore, I have heard this Purāṇa from that teacher of Brahman.
From the Omniscient One, who is worshipped in all worlds and possesses radiant splendor, this ancient work was remembered by Brahmā as the first of all scriptures;
it is the most excellent for all worlds and the means for attaining all knowledge. 45.
The meritorious means for accomplishing the three goals of life, which extends to a hundred crores [of verses],
was brought forth by Keśava in the form of a horse from all the worlds without exception,
at the command of Brahmā. 46–47.

The Asura, having seized all the scriptures—including the Vedāṅgas, the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the extensive treatises on Nyāya—appropriated them for himself; [the Lord] then retrieved them at the beginning of the Kalpa from the ocean of water in the form of a fish. 48.
The omnipresent Lord, remaining within the waters, spoke all of this in its entirety.
Having heard it, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) declared it to the sages, and thus the origin of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa took place at that time. 49–50.
Then, seeing that the Purāṇa was not being grasped due to the passage of time,
the omnipresent Brahmā assumed the form of Vyāsa and, for the sake of its preservation in every age,
recited it in a measure of four hundred thousand verses during each Dvāpara Yuga.
Having divided it into eighteen parts, it was revealed in this world of mortals;
even today, its extent in the worlds of the gods is one billion verses, while here it has been set down in summary as four hundred thousand verses.
I shall proclaim this highly meritorious Purāṇa known as the Padma,
consisting of one thousand and fifty-five [verses] and divided into five sections (khaṇḍas).
Among these, the first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and after that follows the Bhūmikhaṇḍa.
After that follows the Svargakhaṇḍa, and then the Pātālakhaṇḍa;
fifth is the celebrated and excellent Uttarakhaṇḍa. Thus has this Great Lotus arisen, of which the entire world is composed.
Because it takes as its subject matter that account, it is therefore called the Pādma;
this Purāṇa is stainless and pure with the majesty of Viṣṇu,
which Hari, the God of gods, formerly narrated to Brahmā.

Whatever was previously declared by Brahmā to Marīci, that very same [teaching] Brahmā proclaimed in this world as the Pādma; and because it is the refuge of all beings, it is called the Pādma by the wise. (58–59)
The Pādma is recited here as consisting of fifty-five thousand [verses];
it is proclaimed in five sections (parvas) in brief, composed by Vyāsa.
Pauṣkara is the first section, wherein the Virāṭ himself was born.
The second section shall be the Tīrtha-parvan, which contains the accounts of all the hosts of holy fords (61).

The third section is the Grahaṇa-parvan, and the kings who gave abundant sacrificial fees are described therein; furthermore, the lineage history (vaṃśānucarita) is proclaimed as the fourth section (62).
The fifth is the principle of liberation (*mokṣa-tattva*), which is declared to be the totality of all principles.
In the *Pauṣkara*, creation is said to be ninefold, consisting of the creation of all [beings] by Brahmā,
as well as the creation of the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
In the second [chapter], the mountains, the seven islands, and the seven oceans;
in the third, the creation of Rudra and likewise the curse of Dakṣa;
and in the fourth, the origin of kings and the proclamation of all lineages.
O twice-born ones, I shall relate all of this—the final state of liberation and the proclamation of the scriptures of emancipation—within this Purāṇa.
This is a purifier, a treasury of glory, and it shall be exceedingly dear to the ancestors; it is eternally for the pleasure of the God, and it destroys the great sins of men.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Purāṇa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Two.
Sūta said:

Bow down to the Lord of all worlds and of the entire universe, who, as the knower of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), brings about this state of existence in the form of creation; he is the creator of the world,
the knower of the reality of the world, and the master of yoga who abides in yoga.
He created all beings, both stationary and moving.
Desiring to know the ancient accounts concerning that unborn one, the architect of the universe, the Lord of Consciousness, the witness of the worlds, I go for refuge to that omnipresent Sovereign.
Having offered salutations with a concentrated mind to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as to Indra, the world-protectors, and Savitṛ,
and to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the most eminent among sages; 4.
To him whose penance shone upon his face, who was born of Utathya and Ākṣuṣī,
to that venerable Vedavyāsa, the creator, the ancient Puruṣa, who follows the words of Bhṛgu— having bowed to him... (5-6)
Therefore, I heard from a knower of Brahman— an ancient teacher, omniscient, honored in all worlds, and radiant with splendor—
concerning that which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being.
It is certain that [the Unmanifest] creates everything from Mahat down to the specific elements (viśeṣa).
First, within the golden egg, there was the supreme birth of Brahmā;
the egg was enveloped by water, and the water by fire.
The wind is enveloped by space; the source of the elements (bhūtādi) is enveloped by that [wind];
and the Great Principle (mahat) is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Thus, the manifestation of the worlds has been described as being within the cosmic egg itself.
The manifestation of rivers and mountains is described;
a concise account of the Manvantaras and Kalpas is given; and the dissolution of the Brahma-tree and the creation of the progeny of Brahmā are described. 11–12.
The wandering through the kalpas, as well as the establishment of the world, the reclining of Hari upon the waters, and the lifting up of the earth once more; [these are described],
as well as the tenfold manifestation of births in Keśava due to the curse of Bhṛgu.

The arrangement of the Yugas and so forth, the classification of all the stages of life (āśramas), the division of the celestial abodes for mortals and those who travel to heaven, and the origin of both animals and birds have been fully described. 14–15.
Likewise, the acceptance of the Vedic study (svādhyāya) was conceived through such an indeterminate imagination;
furthermore, the secondary creations (pratisarga) of Brahmā are said to be preceded by his conscious intent.
The other three [ages] are not preceded by conscious intent; in that manner, he fashioned the worlds.
The origin of Bhṛgu and the others from the mouths of Brahmā;
the interval between two kalpas and the transition between two creations;
and the description of the creation of progeny by the sages, Bhṛgu and the rest. 17–18.
The Brahman-hood of the brahmin-sage Vasiṣṭha has been fully proclaimed, as well as the subsequent account of Svāyambhuva Manu;
and the creation of Nābhi and the high-souled Rajas has been described.
Therein is the description of the continents, oceans, and mountains (20).
The divisions of the continents and the inclusion of the oceans within the seven [great islands] are proclaimed, as well as those who dwell there according to their extent in yojanas (21).
His years, along with the rivers and mountains, the islands such as Jambūdvīpa and others, and surrounded by the seven oceans—
within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) are these worlds and the earth consisting of the seven islands. 22.

The movement of the sun and moon, as well as that of the planets and luminaries, is proclaimed through the power of Dhruva; likewise, the auspicious and inauspicious fortune of living beings [is known].
The solar chariot was fashioned by Brahmā himself according to his purpose.
The Lord has been conceived by him [as the axis];
from that [axis], the sun and other celestial bodies proceed; the movement of the chariots of the sun and others proceeds from Dhruva.
The Śiṃśumāra has been conceived, at whose tail Dhruva is situated.
At the end of manifestation comes dissolution, and at the end of dissolution comes manifestation.
It is not possible to describe in detail the [cycles] of the deities, the sages, Manu, and the host of ancestors; thus it has been stated in brief. 26–27.
Therein is the equal glorification of the past and future Manvantaras, as well as of the gods and lords of creatures by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
Pralaya is declared to be of three kinds: occasional (naimittika), elemental (prākṛtika), and absolute (ātyantika).
A threefold dissolution is ordained for all beings:
drought, the terrible fire of destruction from the sun, and the clouds that turn the world into a single ocean; such is the night of the Great Soul. 29–30.
The characteristics of the twilight periods have been indicated, as well as those of the Brāhma period in particular;
furthermore, there is a description of the seven worlds and of living beings. Here, I shall also proclaim the hells such as Raurava and others, which are for the wicked.
The determination of the transformation of all beings,
the secondary creation of Brahmā, the description of the universal dissolution, and the destruction of even the greatest beings in every kalpa— 32–33.
Having thoroughly understood and realized the impermanence of even the Brahman,
as well as the wickedness of enjoyments, the misery of saṃsāra,
the rarity of liberation, and the perception of faults through dispassion; 34.

Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest, the sattva is established in Brahman. Through the vision of non-duality, one becomes well-established; thereafter, one turns away from that [duality]. Then, transcending the threefold suffering, one is stainless and called Virūpa (the Formless).
"Having attained the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from any quarter.

Thus has the exposition of what is to be done been described as the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). In this [work], the transformations of the world—its creation and dissolution—are celebrated. (37)
The activity of living beings, the fruits of their actions,
the manifestation of Vasiṣṭha, and likewise the birth of Śakti, as well as his restraint from Saudāsa brought about by Viśvāmitra; 38–39.
And how the birth of the Lord Parāśara occurred from Adṛśyantī, and how the sage Vyāsa was born from the daughter of the Pitṛs,
as well as the birth of his wise son Śuka. 40.
Just as Parāśara harbored enmity toward Viśvāmitra,
so too was the fire prepared by Vasiṣṭha intended for the destruction of Viśvāmitra; yet it was digested by the powerful and wise Kaṇva for the sake of establishing peace.
O Brahmins, by the Lord who desires the welfare of the Brahmins, the one Veda consisting of four quarters was again divided into four by the Blessed Vyāsa out of grace toward all beings. 43.
Furthermore, the divisions of the branches were made by his disciples and grand-disciples. At Prayāga, the Lord himself was questioned by the best of sages,
and those sages, desiring righteousness, were instructed by Kṛṣṇa.
O best of the twice-born, all this— the unsurpassed system of the world for sages ever devoted to dharma— has been recounted according to its true nature,
just as it was formerly told by Brahmā to the high-souled Pulastya.
Then, at Gaṅgādvāra, this was proclaimed by Pulastya to Bhīṣma;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and the destroyer of all sins—
especially its recitation, hearing, and retention.
This Purāṇa,

which was formerly proclaimed in detail by Brahmā to the Brāhmaṇas, has been revealed in its proper sequence by Sūta; he who, having conquered his senses, studies it thoroughly, shall truly know one quarter of this [Veda].
By him, therefore, the Purāṇa has been studied; everything exists therein, of this there is no doubt.
(50) That twice-born who knows the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads, yet understands the Purāṇa as well—he is truly wise compared to that other. (51)
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me.
Having studied even a single chapter proclaimed by the Self-born himself, [one attains merit].
Having encountered calamities, one shall be liberated and attain whatever destination one desires. Since the Purāṇa was forgotten by Vasiṣṭha, he recited this supreme lineage from memory.
He who knows the etymological derivation of this [Purāṇa] is released from all sins.
The sages said to Sūta:
"How did the venerable seer Pulastya, the mind-born son of Brahmā, come into contact with Bhīṣma—he whose sight is difficult for men burdened by sin to obtain? (55)

"O Sūta, this is most wonderful! How was the great-souled sage propitiated by that Kṣatriya? Tell us that, O high-minded one; what kind of austerity did he perform, or what other restraint did he observe? (56-57)

The sage Brahmā spoke in such a way that he was satisfied; thus he related either a full chapter, or half a chapter, or the entire work in its entirety. In whatever place the venerable seer Pulastya was seen, [he related it] just as it was seen.
"O highly fortunate one, we are indeed eager to hear that from you.
Sūta said:
"There, the highly fortunate Gaṅgā, who brings benefit to the virtuous,"
Flowing forth with mountain-splitting force, purifying the world, Gaṅgā reached the great sacred ford of Gaṅgādvāra; there Bhīṣma, devoted to his ancestors,
remained for a very long time, intent on service and established in the great discipline of the noble ones.
For more than a hundred years, meditating with supreme concentration,
that great-souled one performed his ablutions three times a day and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods through the study of sacred texts.
As he was thus drawing himself up, the divine Grandfather Brahmā was pleased; he spoke to his son Pulastya, the best of sages:
"Go to Bhīṣma, the heroic Devavrata born of the Kuru lineage."
"O highly fortunate one, desist from your asceticism and declare the cause for it;
you stand here established in meditation, devotedly contemplating your ancestors.
Whatever desire is in his mind, fulfill that without delay."
Having heard the words of his grandfather, Pulastya, the best of sages,
then went to Gaṅgādvāra and spoke these words to Bhīṣma: "Choose a boon— may prosperity be yours— whatever resides in your heart."
"O Hero, the Grandfather, the Lord himself, was pleased by your austerity;
sent here by Brahmā, I shall grant you whatever boons you desire.
Having heard those words of his, which brought delight to his mind and ears, Bhīṣma—
Opening his eyes and seeing Pulastya standing before him,
he bowed down to that best of sages with a prostration of the eight limbs; having become prostrate, with his entire body touching the earth, he spoke.
Today is the fruit of my first endeavor; this day of birth is most auspicious, for your feet, which are worshiped by the world, have been beheld by me here.
This is the fruit of my penance that has been attained: that the Blessed One has been seen by me.
Having arrived at the riverbank as a special bestower of boons, he said: "This seat made of *bṛsī* grass has been prepared by me; please sit upon it, which is fashioned to grant comfort.
Then, with a vessel of *arghya* made of *pālāśa* wood, containing *dūrvā* grass, unbroken grains, flowers, and *kuśa* grass— 72–73.
"With mustard seeds, curd, honey, barley, and milk—
this is indeed declared by the sages of old as the eightfold offering (aṣṭāṅga-arha).
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor, [he performed the worship].
The venerable sage Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, sat down; filled with joy, he accepted the seat along with water for the feet and the vessel for the arghya offering,
being well-pleased by that display of virtuous conduct.
Pulastya said: "O lord of men, you are truthful, devoted to charity, true to your word,
modest, friendly, patient, and valiant in subduing your enemies."
You are a knower of dharma, grateful, compassionate, and pleasant of speech; you honor those worthy of honor, you are wise, devoted to Brahmanas, and affectionate toward the virtuous.
O Satvata, I am always pleased with you who are so intent on prostration.
"Speak, O highly fortunate one; I shall relate it to you.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, at what time did the all-pervading Lord Brahmā abide?"
Tell me, how did the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu formerly bring about the creation of the gods and others? How was Rudra created, and how were the ṛṣis and gods produced by that Great-Souled One? (80-81)
How is the earth, how is the sky, and how are these oceans?
How are the continents, the mountains, the villages, the forests, and the cities?
[Tell me] of the sages, the lords of progeny, and the eminent seven seers as well.
Tell me how the Blessed One formerly created the castes, the wind, their abodes, the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas;
or likewise the sacred fords, the rivers, and the sun and other planets and stars. (83-84)
Pulastya said: The Grandfather (Brahmā) is the supreme among the supreme, the Supreme Self;
he is devoid of form, color, and the like, and is free from all qualifications. 85
Devoid of all qualities—namely decrease, destruction, transformation, increase, and birth—it shines forth as absolute (kevala). Though it exists everywhere equally, it is considered incomparable. 86.
Meditating upon it as the form of Brahman, it is proclaimed by the wise;
it is that which is secret, supreme, eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable, and likewise exists in the form of Puruṣa and in the form of Kāla. 87–88.
Having bowed to him, I shall describe how the Lord of the World formerly performed the creation, O King, having arisen from his bed of lotus at the time of creation,
manifested through the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas).
The Great Principle (Mahat) is threefold— sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa—
and it is equal to the state of Pradhāna, being likewise enveloped by the seeds and other factors.
It is further divided as Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi, the latter being tāmasa.
This threefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born from the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva),
as were the five elements and the sense organs, together with the organs of action:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
I shall describe each one individually according to its own nature, in successive order.
First, space is merely sound; the source of the elements (bhūtādi) enveloped that space.
Then, space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch. 93–94.
This wind is powerful, and its quality is considered to be touch;
space, which consists of sound alone, enveloped the subtle element of touch. Then, undergoing transformation, the wind produced the subtle element of form.
That light, however, is said to have wind as its form and to possess the quality of that [wind] (96).
Wind, whose nature is touch, enveloped the mere form [of light];
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the mere quality of taste (97).
From that, the waters came into being; they enveloped the mere form (rūpa).
As the waters underwent transformation, they produced the mere quality of smell (gandha).
From that, the aggregate (saṃghāta) was born; therefore, smell is its quality.
They say the sense organs are composed of *taijasa* (fiery) matter, while the ten deities are *vaikārika* (pure).
The eleventh here is the mind, and these deities are remembered as being *vaikārika*.
Skin, eye, nose, tongue, and the ear as the fifth are the senses here.
Now, their respective functions are as follows: the apprehension of sound and so forth;

furthermore, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals as the fifth; and emission, manual skill, locomotion, and expression—these are their qualities, which arise from the opposite [of their objects]. 101.

Space, air, fire, water, and earth—these, O Hero, are endowed with successive qualities beginning with sound; they are known as the specific elements (viśeṣas) because they are respectively calm, terrible, and delusive. 102–103.

Having diverse powers and being separate, they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, failing to come together in their entirety. But having met through mutual conjunction and by relying upon one another, [they succeeded]. 104.
Having attained complete unity as a single aggregate of one hundred thousand parts (lakṣa),
and because they are presided over by the Puruṣa, as well as for the sake of favoring the manifest,
the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas indeed produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). 105–106.
Unfolding in that sequence, like a bubble upon water, Janārdana—who is unmanifest in nature—assumes a manifest form; there, Brahmā himself abides in the very form of Brahman. 107.
The Meru mountains became his umbilical cord, and the great mountains became his placenta (108).
The oceans were the amniotic fluid of that Great-Souled One;
therein were the continents and the seas, along with the collection of worlds including the luminaries (109).
Within that egg were born the heroes, gods, asuras, and humans;
it was surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, which were themselves enveloped by the principle of the origin of beings (bhūtādi),
and the egg was likewise surrounded by the mahat-principle with tenfold greater strength.
O King, the Great One (Mahat), together with all those [subtle elements], is enveloped by the Unmanifest (Avyakta);
joined with all these coverings and all the elemental beings,
it is like the seed within a coconut fruit surrounded by its outer husks.
He himself, as Brahmā, proceeds with the creation of the world;
and he protects that creation age after age, until the dissolution of the kalpa.
Thus, the one Lord Janārdana alone assumes these various designations.

O Indra among kings, that god is the enjoyer of beings, possessed of virtues, and of immeasurable prowess; at the end of the kalpa, he assumes a fierce form characterized by the excess of darkness (tamas) and, being most terrifying, devours all beings without exception. 114–115.
Having devoured all beings when the world has been turned into a single ocean,
he who assumes every form lies upon his serpent-couch;
and having awakened, he again effects creation while assuming various forms.
Through the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction, he is the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
As the Creator, he creates himself; as Viṣṇu, he protects that which is to be protected; and as the Destroyer, the Lord himself is also withdrawn.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
He alone is the Lord of all beings, the universal-formed, because He is imperishable.
Therefore, the creation and so forth, which abide within the elements, are His very own and serve as His benefactors.
He alone is the object of creation, and He is the creator of that creation; He alone is the protector, from whom all things are protected.
With His entire form manifesting through states such as Brahmā and others, He is Brahmā—the most excellent, the bestower of boons, and the one worthy of being sought.
120. Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Descent of the Purāṇa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 2.
The third chapter;
Bhīṣma said: Of the one who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and the Great Self—
"How indeed is Brahman's status as the creator of the world and so forth established?
Pulastya said:
"The powers of all entities are inconceivable and beyond the scope of [ordinary] knowledge."

Those powers of non-existence, beginning with creation, which belong to that Brahman, are said to have arisen; yet the wise man is declared to be eternally so by way of metaphor. By his own measure, his lifespan is recorded as a hundred years.
That which is called *tatpara* is proclaimed to be half of a *parārddha*.
Fifteen *kāṣṭhās* are said to constitute one *nimeṣa*, O best of kings;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* make one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute the measure of a *muhūrta*.

A human day and night is said to consist of that same number of muhūrtas. A month, consisting of two fortnights, contains that same number of days and nights. Six such months constitute an ayana; there are two ayanas, the southern and the northern, which together form a year.

The southern course is the night of the gods, and the northern course is their day. The period known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consisting of twelve thousand divine years, is called a Caturyuga; learn from me its divisions.

Those who know the past have stated that in the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, there are respectively four, three, two, and one thousand divine years. It is said that in each case, a period of a hundred years of the same measure precedes it as the "morning twilight" (saṃdhyā).

The period of twilight (*saṃdhyāṃśaka*) equal to that [period] follows immediately after each *yuga*. O best of kings, the time between the twilight and the period of twilight is to be known as the *yuga*, designated by the names Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth. (10)
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas;
a thousand such cycles, O King, are declared to be one day of Brahmā.
In one day of Brahmā, O King, there are fourteen Manus.
Listen now to their duration as determined by time:
the seven ṛṣis, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons, O King—these are all created at one and the same time and withdrawn in the same manner as before. (13)
The duration of a Manvantara, O King, is said to be seventy-one yugas plus a quarter;
by divine reckoning, it is recorded as eight hundred thousand years. (14–15)
O King, fifty-two thousand and thirty full crores more are reckoned by calculation;
likewise, O high-minded one, there are sixty-seven million others.
Twenty thousand years, without any addition, is the reckoning of a Manvantara by human years here; this period multiplied fourteenfold is known as a day of Brahmā. 17–18.
At the end of that [cycle], there is a dissolution known as the Brāhma-naimittika;
for then the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvas, is consumed by fire.
Afflicted by heat, the inhabitants of Maharloka depart for Janaloka.

When the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, lies upon the bed of the serpent, nourished by having swallowed the three worlds; that Lord of the universe, the pervasive one, is meditated upon by the Janas and the yogis. 20–21.
He creates [the world] again at the end of that night, which is of the same duration as that day;
thus is a year for Brahmā, and a hundred such years constitute the lifespan of that Great Soul. (22) Indeed, the supreme life-span of that high-souled one is one hundred years.
O sinless one, one *parārdha* of Brahmā’s lifespan has already passed;
at its conclusion occurred the great kalpa widely known as Pādma, O King, during this second *parārdha* that is currently unfolding. (23–24)
This first kalpa is designated as Vārāha; O great sage, tell me how that Lord named Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa created all beings at the beginning of that kalpa.
Pulastya said:
The Lord, the beginningless source of all, created living beings;
having risen from his sleep at night at the conclusion of the past kalpa, the Master [proceeded].
Thus Brahmā, his being overflowing with *sattva*, beheld the world as empty.
Perceiving the earth submerged within the waters during the deluge, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), having reflected upon it, desired to effect its rescue. (27–28)
Having recognized that form as Viṣṇu, he entered the bodies of the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, as well as the Boar-form, by his own splendor in order to bear the earth today;
assuming a form consisting of the Vedas and sacrifices for the maintenance of the world.
Then the firm-souled one, the soul of all, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati),
who supports the earth, entered that water which was the receptacle of waters. At that time, the Goddess beheld him who had arrived at the surface of Pātāla.
Having bowed down and become humble with devotion, the Earth, the bearer of wealth, offered praise.
The Earth said: "Salutations to you, the soul of all beings; salutations to you, the Supreme Self. (32)
"O Supreme Self, lift me up from this; I have arisen before you. Homage be to You, O Soul of the Puruṣa; homage be to You. 33.
Salutations to Him who is both Pradhāna and Vyakta, and who is Time and Being."
You are the creator of all beings, you are the protector, and you are the bringer of destruction. At the beginning of creation, you are the Supreme Brahmā who assumes the forms of Viṣṇu and Rudra;
and having consumed the entire world when it has been turned into a single ocean, [you remain]. 34–35.
O Govinda, you alone remain as that which is contemplated by the wise;
no one knows that supreme form of yours which transcends all. The denizens of heaven worship that form which you assume in your incarnations.
Desiring liberation, those who seek release attain that liberation by worshipping you, the Supreme Brahman. For who indeed shall obtain liberation without worshipping Vāsudeva?
You are the form that is perceivable by the mind, as well as that which is perceivable by the eyes and other senses.
Whatever is to be delimited by the intellect, all that is Your form;
I am composed of You, supported by You, created by You, and have taken refuge in You. Therefore, this world calls me "Mādhavī. 39.
Thus being praised by the Earth,
the glorious Earth-bearer, whose voice was like the sound of Sāman chants, roared with a deep, rumbling sound.
Then the Great Boar, whose eyes were like blossoming lotuses, lifted up the Earth with his tusk.
From the netherworld (rasātala), a great blue mountain-like mass resembling the petal of a blue lotus rose up.
As it rose, struck by the wind from his mouth, it made the sinless sages such as Sanandana—who were then dwelling in the world of Janaloka—once again the abode of purity. 41-42.
The waters, following the continuous sound produced by the wounds from the tips of his hooves, descend into the subterranean realm;
meanwhile, the mass of clouds moves all around him, driven by the wind of his breath. As he rises, having torn through the earth, the belly of that Great Boar remains wet with water.
Shaking their bodies composed of the Vedas, the sages dwelling within the pores of your hair attend upon you.

O Lord of lords, you alone are the Supreme Lord Keśava, the radiant one who wields the mace, conch, lotus, sword, and discus; you are the Lord who is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of all beings, and there is no other supreme state beyond you. 44–45.

The Vedas are your feet, the sacrificial posts are your tusks, the sacrifices and the scriptures are in your teeth, the fire is your tongue, and the darbha grass is your white body hair; O Lord, you alone are the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa).
The immeasurable space between heaven and earth is indeed your own body, O You of incomparable power.
O Lord, may you exist for the welfare of the entire universe, which is pervaded by you;
indeed, you alone are the Supreme Self, and there is no other, O Lord of the world. This is your majesty, by which this world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.

Those of dull intellect, perceiving this entire world— which is in its true nature pure consciousness— as being of the nature of material objects, wander in the flood of darkness. But those who know wisdom and possess pure minds perceive this entire world [in its true nature].
O Supreme Lord, they behold your form as consisting of pure consciousness;
O Soul of all beings, be gracious toward this world. O Immeasurable One, O Lotus-eyed One, lift up this earth that is submerged! 51.
"O Blessed One, O Govinda, having risen up, you have covered this earth; O Lord, for the sake of the world, perform that which brings welfare to all beings.
While being thus praised, the Supreme Self, the Uplifter of the Earth, [acted]. 52–53.

He quickly lifted up the earth and placed it upon the great ocean; there it remained like a massive ship upon a flood of water. Then, having made the earth level, he arranged the mountains across the world.
Having divided the earth accordingly into its seven continents, the beginningless Blessed One, the Supreme Person,
then fashioned the four worlds, beginning with Bhūr, exactly as before.

This very thing was previously demonstrated by Brahmā and Viṣṇu when the God of gods was pleased: "O Lord, you are the Supreme Person; this world must be supported and protected with effort by both you and me. 57.

"O Lord, those leaders of the Asuras to whom a boon has now been granted by me must be slain by you out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. I shall perform the work of creation, and that creation must be protected by you, O Lord. (58-59)
When he had spoken thus, the all-pervading Viṣṇu created the gods and others;
from him there appeared, without prior conscious intent, that which consists of darkness (tamas):
namely, darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhasaṃjñaka).
As the Great-Souled One meditated, the creation remained in five states, unmanifest both internally and externally, with its nature concealed and consisting of immobile beings;
therefore, this is called the primary (mukhya) creation, while that which follows is the secondary (amukhya). 61–62.
Seeing that creation to be unsuccessful, the Lord intended another creation; as he was meditating upon it, a creation with downward-streaming currents (tiryaksrotas) emerged.
Because its activity proceeded sideways, it is therefore known as tiryaksrotas.

These are known as the beasts and so forth; they consist mostly of darkness (tamas), lacking knowledge, following wrong paths, and regarding their own ignorance as knowledge. They are full of egoism and self-conceit, and are of twenty-eight kinds.
All of them were internally luminous, yet they were mutually obstructed by one another.

Considering even that state to be ineffective, he meditated upon something else; thus there arose the third, the *ūrdhvasrotas* (the upward-streaming), which was characterized by *sattva* and moved upwards. 65–66.
Abounding in happiness and joy, unobstructed both internally and externally,
and luminous within and without, they are therefore known as the "Upward-streamers" (ūrdhvasrotas).
This third creation, belonging to those whose souls are contented, is remembered as the divine creation (devasarga).
When that creation was completed, Brahmā then felt satisfaction; however,
realizing that those beings produced at the beginning of the primary creation were ineffective for his purpose, he then meditated upon another, superior creation that would be effective.
As he was thus meditating with true intent, there then emerged from that Unmanifest the "downward-streaming" (arvāksrotas) progenitor; because they proceed downward,
they are therefore called the downward-streaming ones.
Abounding in light and tejas, yet dominated by tamas and excessive rajas, they are therefore full of suffering and act repeatedly [in such ways].
Humans, however, possess light both externally and internally; they are the seekers (sādhakas). 71–72.
The fifth is the creation of favor (*anugraha-sarga*), which is established in four ways:
through error (*viparyaya*), attainment (*siddhi*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and contentment (*tuṣṭi*). Furthermore, they do not know the past or the present [of this creation]. 73.
The sixth creation is said to be that of the beings beginning with the Bhūtas (the elemental spirits).

They are all possessors of property, they are characterized by a strong sense of individual ownership, and they are to be known as those whose nature is driven by ritual injunctions and the chanting of prayers. 74–75.
Thus, O best of kings, these six creations have been described here:

the first is the creation of the Mahat; the second is that of Brahmā; the third is that of the subtle elements (tanmātras); and the fourth is indeed remembered as the creation of the gross elements (bhūtas). 76.

The third creation, however, is known as the Vaikārika, which is the creation of the senses. Thus, this Prākṛta creation has arisen preceded by intelligence. The fourth is the Mukhya creation; the "Mukhyas" are remembered as the stationary beings (plants).

The collection of those with horizontal currents is called the animal realm; thereafter, the sixth creation is remembered as that of the upward-streaming beings, the gods. Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is human.
The eighth is the Anugraha creation; it is both Sāttvika and Tāmasa.
These five are known as the Vaikṛta creations, while three are known as the Prākṛta creations.
The ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation, which is both Prākṛta and Vaikṛta.
Thus have been described to you the emanations of Prajāpati,
both primary and secondary, which are the fundamental causes of the world.
What else do you wish to hear concerning the Lord of the Universe as he creates?
Bhīṣma said:
"The creations of the gods and others, as well as those of the Preceptor, have been told by you in brief.
O best of eminent sages, I wish to hear them from you in detail."
Pulastya said:
"All of them are conditioned by their actions, both auspicious and inauspicious; indeed, when released from that manifestation, they are withdrawn during the dissolution."
O King, the fourfold classes of beings, beginning with the gods and ending with the immobile, were born as mind-born (mānasa) offspring of Brahmā while he was performing creation;
thereafter, the fourfold [beings] consisting of gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans [were produced]. 85–86.
Desiring to create these waters, he united himself with his own self;
from that Prajāpati, whose soul was liberated, there were born evil-minded beings. First, from the loins of him who desired to create, the Asuras were born.
Then, O Indra among kings, she abandoned that body which consisted of the syllable *mā* and was of a wicked nature; once that body was cast off by her, it became the night.
Desiring to create while residing in another body, the gods then attained great joy.
O King, when that body, which was predominantly composed of *sattva*, emerged from the mouth of Brahmā, it was cast aside;
thus, the day became characterized by *sattva*.
Therefore, the Asuras are powerful at night, while the Devas are powerful by day.
Then he took up another body consisting solely of the quality of *sattva*.
As he regarded it as his father, the Pitṛs (Ancestors) were born from him;
having thus produced the Pitṛs, that Lord then cast off even that body.
Then that twilight, which exists as the interval between day and night, was cast off;
thereafter, he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas.
O best of the Kurus, humans were born from that [body] in which the quality of rajas predominated.
Prajāpati also, through his swift continuity, produced that first subtle-bodied one;
she became Jyotsnā (the Moonlight), who is designated as the morning twilight (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*).
With the arrival of Jyotsnā, human beings and likewise the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) become strong.
O Indra among kings, from that twilight they indeed arise;
O Lord, these four—the moonlit night, the day, and the two twilights—are the bodies of Brahmā, which are supported by the three qualities (guṇas). 96.

From that, he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas (rajo-mātrātmikā). Then hunger arose in Brahmā, and by that [hunger] he was provoked to anger. Emaciated by hunger, the Blessed One then created darkness. 97–98.
Desiring to devour Virūpa, they rushed toward that Lord;
because he said to them, "Protect me," they then became Rākṣasas. Others said, "Let us eat him," and they became Yakṣas.
Seeing them, the hair of Brahmā fell off in great terror;

being severed from the head, they climbed back onto it again. Because of their slithering (sarpaṇa), they became serpents (sarpas), and because of their being severed (hīna), they are known as *ahis*.
Then, by the enraged Vaisravana, beings of a wrathful nature were emanated;
they were fierce, flesh-eaters, and tawny-brown in color.
At that very moment, Gandharvas were produced from him as he consumed the flesh. 102.
Drinking [the essence], they were born as speech; therefore, they became the Gandharvas.
(103) Having created these, the Lord Brahmā, impelled by that power, then created other birds according to his own will from his own vital energy. (104)

From his shoulders and chest he created the *cakravāka* birds, and from his mouth he created goats; from his belly Prajāpati created cows and buffaloes; and from his feet he created horses, elephants, donkeys, gayals, and deer. (105)

O best of kings, at the beginning of the Kalpa, during the onset of the Tretā Yuga, camels, mules, ruddy oxen, and other species, as well as plants bearing fruits and roots, were born from his body hair. 106–107.

Having properly created the animals and the plants, he then employed them in the sacrifice: the cow, the goat, the buffalo, the ram, as well as the horse, the mule, and the donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn from me those that are wild. 108.108-109ab.
Wild beasts, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys as the fifth, birds; (109) camels are the sixth class of animals, while reptiles are the seventh.
[They correspond to] the Gāyatra, the Ṛgveda verses, the Trivṛt-stoma, and the Rathantara-sāman. (110)
From his eastern mouth, he fashioned the Agniṣṭoma as the first of sacrifices,
as well as the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the fifteen-fold Stoma; likewise,
from his southern mouth, he brought forth the Bṛhat Sāman and the Uktha.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāmāni, Jagatī, Chandas, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa, the Atirātra,
as well as the twenty-onefold Atharvaṇa and the Aptoryāma.
From his northern mouth he created the Ānuṣṭubh and the Saverāja meters;
from his limbs were born various beings of high and low degree. Having created the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans, Prajāpati—
Then again, from that very same resolve, the Grandfather (Brahmā) created Yakṣas,
Piśācas, Gandharvas, as well as hosts of Apsarases, Siddhas, Kinnaras, Rākṣasas, lions, birds, beasts, and serpents.

Then the Lord Brahmā, the omnipresent creator of the beginning, created all this— the imperishable and the perishable, the stationary and the moving. Whatever actions those beings had undertaken in a previous creation, [those he assigned to them].
Those very same [qualities] they attain as they are created again and again—
whether violent or non-violent, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false;
permeated by those [past tendencies], they enter them, and therefore that which is pleasing to each person becomes their preference.

That Lord himself ordained the diversity and the specific application of the senses, their objects, the elements, and bodies; as well as the names and forms of beings and the expansion of their activities. 120.
From the words of the Vedas alone, he first created the gods and others;
the names of the sages, exactly as they are heard in the Veda, and those of others as well, he fashioned according to their fitness and their respective functions. 121–122.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons are seen again and again in their succession,
so too do these very same states of being appear at the beginnings of the Yugas; in this manner,
He repeatedly performs such a creation at the start of every Kalpa.
Desirous of creating and endowed with power, he was impelled by the creative power.
Bhīṣma said:
You have described the one who flows downwards, namely the human being.
O Brahman, tell me in detail how Brahmā created the darkness (Tamas),
and how he created those of his own kind and their qualities, O great sage;
let that which is remembered as the duty of the Brāhmaṇas and the others be told.

Pulastya said: O best of the Kurus, as Brahmā was previously meditating upon the principle of goodness (sattva) while desiring to create progeny, beings characterized by an abundance of goodness were born from his mouth. 127

O best of the Kurus, other creatures were created by Brahmā from his chest, being permeated by *rajas*; likewise, others were produced from his thighs, being permeated by both *rajas* and *tamas*. Furthermore, other progeny were created by Brahmā from his feet.
All of them were dominated by *tamas*, and from that [state] arose this fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*):
O best of kings, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras emerged respectively from the feet,
thighs, chest, and mouth.

O Great King, Brahmā created all this—the fourfold caste system (cāturvarṇya)—as the supreme means for accomplishing sacrifice. Through sacrifice, the gods are nourished; through the release of rain, human beings are sustained.
From this sacrifice of dharma, the causes of auspiciousness flourish;
they are accomplished by men who are always devoted to virtuous deeds, who are free from contrary conduct, who are righteous, and who walk upon the path of the good. 132–133.

O King, O Lord, men attain heaven, liberation, or human status; indeed, O Sovereign, those beings created by Brahmā for the establishment of the fourfold order go to whatever place they desire. 134. The subjects were created by Brahmā for the arrangement of the four castes.
O best of kings, their conduct was perfectly pure;
they dwelt wherever they pleased, free from all afflictions, with purified inner hearts and cleansed by the performance of pure dharma. (135–136)
When their minds are purified and Hari is established within their pure hearts,
they perceive the pure knowledge called Brahman, by which that state is attained.
Then, he who is the soul of time is said to be the abode of Viriñca (Brahmā).
O Indra among the lords of gods, demons, and men, this cycle of existence is exceedingly terrible, possessing very little essence;
it is the seed of unrighteousness, arisen from darkness and greed, and the means for the successive progression of passion and the other afflictions. (138–139)

Then, O King, that innate perfection (sahajā-siddhi) does not arise for them to any great extent; rather, the other eight perfections, such as subjugation (vaśya) and so forth, come into being. When all those [perfections] have waned and their transgressions are increasing, [the innate perfection remains].

Then those creatures became afflicted by the suffering of being overcome by pairs of opposites (dvaṃdva). Consequently, they constructed fortresses: those in trees, on mountains, in water, as well as desert forts, cities, and settlements such as mountain villages (khārvaṭaka). 141–142.
O Great-Minded One, having constructed houses in those cities and other places according to the proper method for the sake of pacifying afflictions such as cold and heat,
they then established this gatekeeper against cold and the like for those subjects.
Thereafter, they established the means of livelihood (vārtā), consisting of the manual skills born of labor.
These included rice, barley, wheat, millet, sesame, priyaṅgu, kovidāra, koradūṣa, and cīnaka.
Māṣa, mudga, āmala, niṣpāva, kulattha, aḍhaka, caṇaka, and śaṇa— these seventeen are recorded as the varieties of cultivated herbs,
O King. (146) Thus ends the enumeration of the species of cultivated plants, O King.
There are fourteen sacrificial plants, both cultivated and wild:
rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, with *priyaṅgu* as the seventh, and *kulattha* as the eighth. (147–148)
O King, śyāmāka, nīvāra, vartula, sagavedhuka, veṇuyava, and likewise markaṭaka— these fourteen medicinal plants are recorded as being both cultivated and wild. 149.
In this same way, they are likewise the supreme cause for the accomplishment of sacrifice.
These, together with sacrifice, are the ultimate cause for all creatures;
therefore, the wise who know the higher and the lower perform sacrifices.
O best of kings, the daily performance of sacrifices brings benefit to men who act with a desire for results; yet,
O high-minded one, for those [who have attained liberation], this drop of worldly existence has been brought to an end by Time.

O best among the upholders of dharma, he established the boundaries for the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) according to their respective places and qualities, as well as the duties of all the worlds that properly observe their dharma. 153–154.
O King, the station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battles;
and the station of the Maruts is for Vaiśyas who follow their own duty.
The station that is ordained for the eighty-eight thousand ascetics of the Gāndharva and Śūdra castes who abide in service, and for those whose vital seed is drawn up (celibates),
is the very same as that of the students dwelling with their preceptors.

That which is remembered as the abode of the seven sages is likewise that of the forest-dwellers; for householders it is the station of Prajāpati, while for renunciants it is known as the station of Brahmā.
For yogis, it is the immortal station, the supreme state of Brahman.
For those yogis who are single-minded, ever-exerting, and meditative—those wise ones behold that supreme abode which they see.
The planets, such as the moon and the sun, go to and return from it. (159–160)
Even today, those devoted to Nārāyaṇa do not return [to rebirth];
[they avoid] Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the terrible Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci.
This place is declared to belong to those who revile the Veda, those who obstruct sacrifices, and those who abandon their own duty.
Then, as he meditated, mental offspring were born from him. 162–163.
Together with the instruments residing in the body that had arisen from that very body, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged from the limbs of that wise one—
those very ones whom I have previously described.
From the gods down to the immovable beings, all remain within the sphere of the three qualities (guṇas).
Thus were the beings, both immovable and moving, created; yet when all these offspring of the wise one did not multiply, [he reflected]. 165–166.
Then he created other mind-born sons who were like himself: Bhṛgu, Māṃ, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these were his mind-born sons.
These nine Brahmās have reached this certainty regarding the Purāṇas:
"Those such as Sanandana and others who were previously created by the Creator do not create living beings in the worlds, being indifferent toward the procreation of offspring. (168-169)
For all those who had arrived were free from passion and devoid of envy;
when they thus showed such indifference,
a great wrath arose in the high-souled Brahmā, capable of consuming the three worlds.

From his anger, that light arose, blazing with garlands of flames; it then began to burn the entire triple world. From his forehead, which was inflamed with rage and furrowed by a frown, [that light emerged].
Then Rudra was born, possessing a body as fierce and immense as that of the midday sun, with a form that was half-woman and half-man;
having said to him, "Divide yourself," Brahmā then vanished.
Thus addressed, he manifested both femininity and masculinity;
that Lord divided his masculine form into eleven parts—
both gentle and fierce— and likewise manifested his feminine form with peaceful aspects.
And he divided himself manifoldly into dark and white forms.
The Lord, Svāyambhuva Manu, took that woman Śatarūpā— whose impurities had been washed away by ascetic penance— as his wife. And from that Puruṣa, the goddess Śatarūpā gave birth [to offspring].
In ancient times, the Prajāpati Dakṣa gave his daughter Prasūti to Priyavrata and Ākūti to Uttānapāda;
he took Ākūti as his wife, and from her was born Sadakṣiṇa.
Then, from that couple, the highly fortunate Putra-yajña was born. From the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of that sacrifice, twelve sons were born,
who are known as the Yāma gods in the period of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
Likewise, at his birth, Dakṣa produced twenty-four daughters; hear their names correctly from me:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā. (182)

The Lord Dharma accepted Buddhi, Lajjā, Śānti, Ṛddhi, and Kīrti as his thirteenth wife; these were the daughters of Dakṣa. From among them, eleven beautiful-eyed daughters remained unmarried. (183-184)
Khyāti, Satya, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Sannati,
Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā;
Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and likewise the sage Aṅgiras.
O best of kings, I, Pulaha, Kratu— the most excellent of sages—
as well as Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Agni, and the Pitṛs, respectively,
accepted the daughters beginning with Khyāti from the two sages.
Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; Lakṣmī to Bala; Niyamā to Dhṛti;
Tuṣṭi to her son Saṃtoṣa; Puṣṭi gave birth to Lobha;
Medhā to Śruta; Kriyā to Daṇḍa; and Vinayā to Naya. 188.
Bodha gave birth to Buddhi, as well as Lajjā, Vinaya, and Vapus as her sons;
Vyavasāya was born from Ekṣema, and Śānti gave birth to Kṣema.
Sukha, Ṛddhi, Yaśas, and Kīrti—these are the sons of Dharma. 189–190.
From Kāma, Hiṃsā (Violence), the wife of Adharma, gave birth to Nandīputra (Joy-son) and Harṣa (Delight), who were the grandsons of Dharma; from them was born Anṛta (Untruth).
Furthermore, Nikṛti (Deceit) was their daughter, and from those two were born Bhaya (Fear) and Naraka (Hell).
Thus, Māyā and Vedanā formed a pair, a couple.
From those two was born Māyāmṛtyu, the destroyer of beings; and from Vedanā, moreover, Duḥkha was born from Raurava. 192–193.
Death, disease, old age, sorrow, thirst, and anger were born;
these are all known to be characterized by suffering and are all defined by unrighteousness (adharma). They have no wives nor sons, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
O son of the best of men, these forms of Brahmā are indeed fierce; they constantly bring about the dissolution of this world. I shall now describe the creation of Rudra, just as Brahmā performed it.
At the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord was meditating upon a son equal to himself, there appeared from him a youth with matted hair, blue and red in hue.
O best of kings, he then cried out with a beautiful voice and ran about.
"What are you crying for? the god asked him in reply.
Then he replied to Prajāpati, "Give me a name. [The god said:
"Because of your crying (*rodana*), you shall be named Rudra; do not cry, maintain your fortitude. 198–199.
Thus addressed, the Lord wept seven times;
thereafter, he gave him seven names,
and he established eight abodes for the eight forms.
Then, O King, the Grandfather spoke to Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva:
"The sun, water, earth, fire, wind, and space... (201-202)
The initiated Brāhmaṇa [is] Soma;
thus, in this manner, that Rudra obtained Satī as his wife.
Due to Dakṣa’s wrath, she abandoned her own body.
O best of kings, she became the daughter of Himavat through Menā;
and the blessed Lord Bhava, having requested her again, married her.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were the sons of Dakṣa’s daughter, and Khyāti gave birth to the sons of Bhṛgu.
"And Śrī, who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods.
(206) Thus ends the third chapter in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Four.
Bhīṣma said:
"I have heard that Lakṣmī was born from the Ocean of Milk;
how is it that you say she was born from Khyāti as the daughter of Bhṛgu?"
How did the auspicious daughter of Dakṣa abandon her body, and how was the birth of Umā from the womb of Menā brought about?
For what purpose was the daughter of Himavat made the wife of the God of gods?
And then the Blessed One spoke to me regarding the conflict with Dakṣa.
Pulastya said:
O protector of the earth, listen to this which I have been asked by you here.
This glorious account was heard by me from my grandfather:
Durvāsas, the son of Atri, while wandering over this earth,
saw a beautiful garland of fragrant flowers in the hand of a Vidyādharī.
"O Brahmin, I shall place this upon my mass of matted hair"—
thus was she questioned by that ṛṣi; and then,
O King, filled with joy, she gave that garland to him.
Having taken it, he bound that garland of heads upon himself for a very long time.
Shining like a mad ghost, the Brahmin spoke this:
"This is a Vidyadhara maiden with full and elevated breasts."
The mind of even a wise man, when it encounters one endowed with beauty, ornament, and grace, undergoes agitation; therefore, let me go elsewhere, displaying my own excellence. 9.
Let me go elsewhere, displaying my own excellence.
Having spoken thus, O lord of kings, he wandered over the earth.
He beheld Śakra, the lord of the inhabitants of heaven, the sovereign of the three worlds and husband of Śacī, shining resplendent as he was mounted upon Airāvata.
Taking that garland from his own head, which was frequented by wandering, intoxicated bees, the sage cast it toward the King of the Gods like one who is mad.
Having taken it, the King of the Gods placed that garland upon the head of his elephant.
Like the Gaṅgā on Kailāsa, that garland of pearls shone like the moon; then the elephant,
its eyes blinded by rut, having smelled the fragrance of the saugandhika flowers, took up that garland with its trunk and cast it down upon the surface of the earth.
Then the venerable Durvāsas, the bull among sages, became enraged;
O Indra of kings, being angry, he spoke these words to the king of the gods:
"O Vāsava, you whose soul is corrupted by the intoxication of power, you are exceedingly arrogant!"

"Since you do not welcome this garland, the abode of glory, given by me; therefore, O fool, the splendor of the three worlds shall go to its destruction. Because this garland given by me has been cast down upon the earth by you. (16–17)

"Therefore, the three worlds shall become bereft of prosperity when he becomes enraged, for at his wrath the entire world of mobile and immobile beings trembles with fear. Yet you, O King of the Gods, out of excessive pride, treat me with contempt."
Maheṃdra, having quickly descended from the shoulder of his elephant, sought to propitiate the sinless sage Durvāsas;
and being thus propitiated by him with prostrations preceded by humble entreaties, [the sage was appeased]. 19–20.
"O Śatakratu, I shall not forgive you; what is the use of saying more?
Having said this, the brahmin departed, and the king of the gods likewise set out again for Amarāvatī, mounting the elephant Airāvata.
From that time forward, the three worlds were bereft of prosperity.
Those skilled in policy ceased to act, ascetics abandoned their penances, and gifts were no longer bestowed; the world had become as if destroyed.
Thus, in this utterly destitute triple world devoid of sentient beings,
the Daityas and Dānavas exerted their strength against the gods.
Having been defeated by the Daityas, the thirty deities, headed by Indra, went for refuge.
Led by the Fire-god, the gods reported everything exactly as it had been told to the illustrious Grandfather; Brahmā then spoke thus to the Asuras and,
accompanied by the gods, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having gone there, the Grandfather spoke to the Blessed Vāsudeva:
"Arise quickly, O Viṣṇu, and act for the welfare of the gods!
Without you, all have been defeated by the Dānavas again and again."
Thus addressed, the lotus-eyed Puruṣa, the Supreme Person,
having beheld the gods with their unprecedented forms and appearances, said to them: "O gods, I shall provide an augmentation of your splendor."
"O gods, I declare what must be done by you: having gathered all the medicinal herbs together with the Daityas, bring them to the Ocean of Milk;
making Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope," 30.
"O gods, churn the nectar while I stand as your helper!
And having first addressed the sons of Diti there with conciliatory words, you shall become sharers in the fruit of this undertaking. (31-32)
Whatever nectar (amṛta) is produced there in that ocean while it is being churned,
by drinking it you shall become powerful immortals;
likewise, I shall act in such a way that the enemies of the gods [are defeated].
"The gods shall not obtain the nectar; they will share only in suffering.
Having been addressed thus by the God of Gods, all those deities then entered into an alliance with the asuras and strove diligently for the sake of the nectar.

Having gathered all medicinal herbs and cast them into the waters of the Ocean of Milk— which possessed the pure white luster of an autumnal cloud— the gods, Daityas, and Dānavas made Mount Mandara their churning stick and Vāsuki their rope.
Then, O Indra among kings, they began to churn the nectar with speed;
all the gods stood together at the tail, while the Daityas were placed by Viṣṇu at the front part of Vāsuki’s body. 37–38.
O you of immortal luster, by that breath of his and by fire,
the splendor of all those asuras was struck down, and they became devoid of energy. Then, by that very wind from his mouth, clouds were produced.
Then, as they rained down upon the region of the tail, the gods were refreshed.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, and Mahādeva of great splendor, both residing upon the back of Viṣṇu, [were present]. 40–41.

Taking Mount Mandara with his two arms like a lotus, O scorcher of foes, and having fashioned it into a chain, he seized Mount Mandara and stood in the midst of the forces of both the gods and the dānavas.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord Hari himself took the form of a tortoise;
with another portion of his splendor, Hari strengthened the gods.
Then, as that Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and the Dānavas, 43–44.
Formerly, Surabhi, who is worshipped by the gods, became the vessel for the sacrificial oblation; at that time, O high-minded one, both the gods and the Dānavas experienced great joy.
With their minds entirely captivated, they all remained with their eyes fixed in a trance.
Then, as the Siddhas were reflecting in their minds, "What is this?",
the goddess Vāruṇī appeared, her eyes rolling from intoxication,
stumbling at every step from that whirlpool.
"Let the Dānavas seize me, this goddess who bestows self-confidence, while I am clad in a single garment, my hair disheveled, and my eyes fixed with passion.
Thinking her to be impure and intoxicated by wine, the Asuras then abandoned her.
The Daityas seized it; at the conclusion of that seizure, it became the Surā.
During the churning, the Pārijāta tree—the celestial Nandana tree—arose, as did hosts of Apsarases endowed with beauty, generosity, and other virtues. 49–50.
Then sixty crores were born, common to both gods and demons;
all of them had previously performed meritorious deeds common to all. Thereafter, the cool-rayed moon appeared, bestowing joy upon the gods.
The Lord Śaṅkara requested the Moon, saying, "O God, let him become the ornament for my matted locks;
there is no doubt that this Moon has been accepted by me.
Brahmā also gave his consent for the Moon to serve as an ornament for Hara.
Then, the terrifying Kālakūṭa poison emerged;
by that very poison, all the Dānavas, along with the gods, were afflicted. Mahādeva, having taken it up at will, drank that poison.
From his drinking, Maheśvara was born as Nīlakaṇṭha at that time.
Then, from the remainder of the milk-ocean after it had been drunk, Dhanvantari himself arose, wearing white garments. 55–56.
Then, holding a water-pot filled with nectar, he arose; and by the sight of the King of Physicians, they became composed in mind. Then a horse was produced, as well as the elephant Airāvata.
Then, from that water, the goddess Śrī arose, seated upon a fully blossomed lotus of shimmering luster and holding a lotus in her hand;
the great sages, filled with joy, praised her with the Śrīsūkta.
The Gandharvas, headed by Viśvāvasu, sang before her,
while the hosts of Apsaras, led by Ghṛtācī, danced there;
and the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, presented their waters for the purpose of her ritual bath.
Taking pure water contained in golden vessels brought by the elephants of the quarters,
they bathed the Goddess, the Great Sovereign of all worlds;
and Kṣīroda himself presented her with a garland of unfading lotuses.
Viśvakarman gave her ornaments and adorned her limbs;
she was bathed, wearing divine garlands and garments, and embellished with jewelry.
Indra and the other hosts of immortals, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents [were there].
The Dānavas, the great Daityas, and the Rākṣasas, along with the Guhyakas, all desired the maiden; thereupon Brahmā said:
"O Vāsudeva, you alone must accept her, for she has been given by me."
"Both the gods and the Dānavas are forbidden from entering here;
however, I am pleased with you for this act of selflessness.
O Goddess, that Śrī was told by Brahmā: 'Go to Keśava.'"
"Having obtained a husband given by me, rejoice for eternal years!
(67) As all the gods looked on, she went to the chest of Hari;
then, having reached the chest, she spoke these words to the God: (68)
"O God, I am never to be abandoned; always acting according to your command, I shall dwell upon the chest of the one who is beloved by the entire world.
Thereupon, the gods were looked upon by her as she remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
O King of kings, Lakṣmī suddenly attained supreme bliss, while the Daityas,
who were averse to Viṣṇu, fell into great agitation; thus were the Dānavas, led by Vipracitti, abandoned by Lakṣmī.
Then those Daityas, possessed of great prowess and filled with sin, seized the bow from the hand of Dhanvantari and took that nectar.
But Viṣṇu, resorting to the form of a woman, tempted them with his illusory power (māyā).
Having arrived, the Dānava said: "Let one water-pot be given to me;
having come under your control, I shall remain in your house.
Having seen that woman, endowed with beauty and the most beautiful in the three worlds, [he spoke].
Those whose minds were struck by greed, longing for his beautiful form,
then saw him standing before them after he had given the nectar to them.
Having taken that nectar from the Dānavas, he then bestowed it upon the gods.
Then the hosts of gods, headed by Śakra, drank that respective nectar.
The Daityas, with their weapons and swords raised, rushed toward them;
but once the nectar had been drunk, the Daitya army was then defeated by the powerful [gods].
Being struck down, they fled in all directions and entered the netherworld (Pātāla).
Then the gods, filled with joy, prostrated before the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
and returned to heaven as they had before.
From that time forward, those Dānavas became lustful toward women;
however, being cursed by Kṛṣṇa, they went down to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Then the sun, with its radiant luster, proceeded upon its own path.

The Lord Hutāśana blazed forth with intense and beautiful radiance, and at that time, a mind devoted to the dharma of all beings arose. The three worlds, endowed with prosperity, were protected by Viṣṇu.
Then the gods were addressed by Brahmā, the sustainer of the world:
"For the sake of your protection, Viṣṇu has been appointed by me, as well as the Lord of Umā, the Lord of the Gods; these two shall provide for your security and well-being."
"Since these two, who grant boons, are constantly being worshipped by you and bring about your welfare,
they shall therefore always remain secure and bestow blessings upon you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One departed for his own destination.
When the Grandfather of all the worlds had vanished from sight,
and when Śakra had gone to the world of the gods, the two deities Hari and Śaṅkara reached their own respective abodes— Hari his realm and Śaṅkara Kailāsa— at that very moment.
Thus, while the three worlds were protected by the King of the Gods, the highly fortunate Lakṣmī was born from the Ocean of Milk;
she has now been born again as Khyāti from Bhṛgu, and she is eternal.
O Great King, Śrīsahasra was born together with the great seer Bhṛgu;
he previously established a city by his own name on the bank of the river Narmadā, with the approval of Brahmā. 88–89.
Lakṣmī, together with her own city and its key, went to the world of the gods; having returned there, she then made this request:
"When I repeatedly entreated him, the city was not given out of greed. (90)
"From the presence of Bhṛgu, I did not obtain Keśava;
however, my city has been seized by my father who has overcome me. You yourself must wrest that city from his hand and bring it back. (91-92)
Having gone there, the lotus-eyed Lord, the wielder of the discus and the mace, spoke conciliatory words to Bhṛgu: "Entrust the girl to the city;
let the key and the lock be released by my grace. 93.
Enraged, Bhṛgu said to him: "I shall not surrender that city;
O Keśava, I myself requested this city from Nala-lakṣmī, and I will not give it up, O Blessed One. Thus he spoke with contempt. 94-95.
The god spoke to him again, "Hand over that city to Lakṣmī;
however, O great sage, you must by all means abandon it at my word.
Thereupon, Bhṛgu, overcome with anger, spoke to Keśava.
"O Madhusūdana, because you have now oppressed your wife Māṃsā through partiality, you shall obtain ten births in the world of men;
you will experience sorrows due to separation from your wife. (97–98)
Thus did Bhṛgu, exceedingly enraged, pronounce a curse upon him;
and furthermore, a curse was given to him by the high-souled Viṣṇu:
"O bull among sages, you shall not obtain the joy derived from offspring."
Having pronounced the curse upon that Ṛṣi, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Then, having seen the lotus-born one, Lord Keśava said this:
"O Blessed One, this Bhṛgu, your son, is exceedingly prone to anger."
"Without cause, I have been cursed by him: 'Therefore, you shall obtain ten births in human form and experience manifold sufferings;
moreover, there shall be the agony born of separation from your wife, which destroys both strength and manliness. (102)
"Having abandoned this world, I shall lie in the great ocean;
yet, in all matters concerning the work of the gods, you must perform the invocation once again.
To the god who was speaking thus, Brahmā, the preceptor of the worlds, then [replied]. (103–104)
For the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, he performed this hymn of praise:
"O Keśava, this world was created by you; it emerged from the lotus at your navel, and there I was born—thus I am subject to your will. (105)
O Lord, you are the protector of all worlds and the creator of the universe;
the three worlds must not be abandoned by you—this alone is my boon.
For ten births among men, [act] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
"You yourself are not capable of acting as the agent, nor even of bestowing a curse. Who is this Bhṛgu, and how could he possibly curse you, O Janārdana?
Always honor the Brahmins; the Brāhmaṇas themselves are your own body. 107-108.
"O Lord, resort to yogic sleep; sleep in the Ocean of Milk. At the time for action, O Mādhava, I shall awaken you again.
Blessed One, let this [work] first be augmented by your power. (109)

"Śakra, the performer of all tasks and slayer of enemies, shall carry out your command while protecting the three worlds through a portion of your own self. Thus praised, Viṣṇu then spoke these words to Brahmā.

"O Lord, I shall do all this that you command me; I did not even know that the god Brahmā had become invisible. When the god Viṣṇu had thus departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [reflected].
Furthermore, the Lord, the source of the worlds, brought about the creation once more.
Seeing him, Tārada, the best among those skilled in speech, spoke these words:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet."
By touching the earth, which pervades everything, he stood ten fingers' breadth above it.
Since whatever has been and whatever is yet to be all originates from you,
therefore this entire universe has arisen and will arise from you, O Father.
