From you was born the sacrifice in which all is offered, the speckled butter, and the two kinds of sacrificial animals; from you arose the Rig-verses and the Sama-chants. From you were born the sacrifices, and from you came horses and elephants.
Cows were produced from you; from you were born the wild animals.
From your mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born; from you the Kṣatriyas arose. The Vaiśyas were born from your thighs, and the Śūdras emerged from your feet.
From your eyes the sun was born, from your ears the wind, and from your mind the moon; from the internal cavities of your body the vital breath (prāṇa) arose, and from your mouth fire was born.
From your navel the atmosphere emerged, and from your head the sky came into being.
The directions arose from your ears and the earth from your feet; all this has come into being from you.
Just as a vast banyan tree is contained within a tiny seed, so too did you, who have become the seed, create the entire universe. 120–121.
Just as a banyan tree arises from the production of a seed-sprout and attains vast expansion,
so too does the world expand from your creation. For indeed,
just as no other bark is seen apart from the leaves of a plantain tree, [so is the world not distinct from you].
Thus, this entire universe is seen as nothing other than residing within You, O Lord.
That power called *hlādinī* resides in You alone, existing as Your inseparable companion; yet in You, who are devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), it is mixed with both delight and affliction.
Salutation to You who exist as separate beings, as a single being, and as all beings; You are the manifest, the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, the Virāṭ, and likewise the Samrāṭ.
You are in everything, You are the being of all beings, You are the All, and You assume every form.
Everything has arisen from you; therefore, salutations to you, the soul of all.
(126) Since you are the soul of all, O Lord of all, and abide within all beings, what then can I say to you? You know everything that resides in the heart. (127)
"O Lord of the World, this desire of mine has been made fruitful by you; it has been well-tapped and fully realized that you have been seen. 128.
Brahmā said:
"O son, that this fruit of my asceticism has now been seen by you is indeed the case; for the sight of me, O Nārada, never occurs in vain. Therefore, choose a boon according to your own desire."
"O Father, everything is accomplished once you have come within the range of my vision.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, you abide in the heart of everyone."
"O Lord, what is there that you do not know in your mind regarding that which I desire? O All-pervading One, I have seen the creation exactly as it was fashioned by you;
therefore, curiosity has arisen in me upon seeing the gods, sages, and demons. (131-132)
Pulastya said:
Brahmā, the divine lord of heaven, was pleased with Nārada’s father;
he granted a boon to Nārada, saying, "You shall be the most excellent among sages. 133
By my grace, you shall become one who delights in the playful tales of the Kalpa age;
your movement shall be unimpeded through the celestial realms and down to the netherworld (rasātala). With the sacred thread as its cord, it shall hang like a yogic belt.
O sinless Nārada, you shall always obtain delight among the kings on the islands, as well as in the presence of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Śakra, [carrying] an umbrella, a lute, and ornaments. 135–136.
"You are indeed the teacher of the social classes (varṇas); I have granted this boon to you. O son, remain in heaven as you desire, being served by the gods.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Origin of Lakṣmī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
In the fifth chapter,
Bhīṣma said:
"How did the virtuous and auspicious daughter of Dakṣa abandon her body?"
For what reason was Dakṣa’s sacrifice destroyed by Rudra?
O Brahman, this is my curiosity: how did the illustrious Maheśvara, the enemy of Tripura, come under the sway of anger?
Pulastya said:
In ancient times, at Gaṅgādvāra, Bhīṣma Dakṣa commenced a sacrifice;
there were gathered the hosts of gods and asuras, the ancestors, and the great ṛṣis.
All the gods, together with Vāsava, as well as the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Suparṇas, and likewise the creepers and medicinal herbs, assembled there filled with joy;
so too did the venerable Kaśyapa, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Pracetas, Aṅgiras, and Vasiṣṭha of great asceticism—
having prepared a level altar there, he established the Cāturhotra sacrifice;
Vasiṣṭha was the Hotṛ priest there, and Aṅgiras was the most excellent Adhvaryu.
Then Bṛhaspati was the Udgātṛ priest, and Nārada was the Brahman;
while the sacrificial rites were underway and the fires were being offered into,
all the Vasus and the twelve Ādityas arrived.
The Aśvins, the Maruts, and likewise the fourteen Manus [were present]. Thus, when the sacrifice had commenced and the fires were being offered oblations,
there appeared that supreme and auspicious abundance consisting of various kinds of food and edibles.
Having surveyed the ground on all sides for ten yojanas,
a great sacrificial altar was constructed there by all those who were assembled;
and having seen all the gods, headed by Śakra, at that sacrifice, the auspicious Satī [was moved].
Then she spoke these conciliatory words to Prajāpati.
Satī said:
"The king of the gods, Śatakratu, has mounted Airāvata."
Accompanied by his wife Śacī, the performer of a hundred sacrifices (Indra) has arrived and taken up residence here;
he is seen together with his wife Dhūmorṇā, the lord of the unrighteous who, through righteousness, is the punisher of sinners. 12–13.
The divine Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures and the sustainer of the world,
arrived here at the pavilion with his wife Gaurī;
likewise, the god who is the sovereign of all Yakṣas and the son of the sage Viśravas [Kubera] arrived.
Accompanied by his wife Ātvi and Sahadevī, the Lord of Wealth has arrived;
he who is the mouth of all the gods, who dwells within the bellies of all living beings, and for whose sake the Vedas were produced—he, that very one, has come to this sacrifice. 15–16.
Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, was appointed as the guardian of the western quarter;
he came here along with his wife to this sacrifice,
for he was created of old by Brahmā as the bestower of life in this world.
Accompanied by a group of forty-nine known as Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna, that god Vāyu, who is Prajāpati himself, arrived at the sacrifice. 18–19.
He who is the presiding lord over the twelve suns, the eyes of this world, who protects the three worlds, and who is the supreme refuge of the gods;
he who is indeed the lord of the ages, of the yugas, and of the days.
The Lord of Saṃjñā, the Sun, the purifier of the world, has arrived here;
born of the lineage of Atri, he is a king among the twice-born, possessed of great fame, and the lord of the world who generates joy for the eyes upon the surface of the earth. 21–22.

The Lord of herbs and also of all creepers, as well as the Moon, the lord of the stars, has arrived here with his wife; O Śaśin, [you too have come]. The eight Vasus have arrived together, and the two Aśvins have also come.
The trees and forest lords, the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, the vidyādharas, multitudes of bhūtas, vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
piśācas of fierce deeds, and others who take away life; 24–25.
The rivers, the streams, and the oceans; the islands along with the mountains;
the domestic and wild animals;
whatever is animate and whatever is inanimate—[all these were created by] the blessed Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and others.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Sanaka, and the other great sages;
the meritorious royal sages and all the kings upon the earth;
as well as the members of the social orders and the stages of life—all those who perform their respective duties.
What is the use of saying more here? This creation of Brahmā has arrived here; these are my sisters, nephews, and brothers-in-law, all together with their wives, sons, and kinsmen.
All of them were honored by you with gifts, honors, and hospitality;
all those who were invited were treated with respect. Yet, in my mind, only the Blessed Lord, my husband, has truly arrived here. (30–31)
"Without him, all this appears to me as if empty;
yet I think that your husband has been invited by me, but perhaps he has been forgotten by you. Please tell me everything."
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words spoken by her, Dakṣa Prajāpati [regarded her] as being filled with affection for her husband and dearer to him than his own life.
"Let this virtuous girl, devoted to her husband, be placed upon your lap"—
so he spoke with a profound demeanor to that highly fortunate woman, a devoted wife who desired the welfare and pleasure of her husband, "Listen, my child, to the truth as it is. 34-35.
For this reason, he has been invited here by his father;
carrying a skull-bowl as his vessel, wearing a skin, his body smeared with ashes,
bearing a trident, shaven-headed, and naked, he always delights in the cremation ground.
He constantly wipes all his limbs with ashes;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and draped with an elephant hide;
a garland of skulls rests upon his head, and a khaṭvāṅga staff is held in his hand. 38.
Having bound a serpent upon his waist and likewise a circle of serpents around his neck, and having made Vāsuki— the king of serpents— his sacred thread,
he wanders constantly over the earth in this form.
Naked hosts of nāgas, piśācas, and many multitudes of bhūtas were there;
the Lord, three-eyed and bearing a trident, was always devoted to song and dance, and likewise constantly performed various loathsome acts. 40–41.
"How can there be shame for me in the presence of the gods?
What kind of garment does he not deserve as his dwelling? (42) Thinking thus, out of shame for these faults and for the sake of the worlds, I [concealed myself].
"O daughter, I did not summon him for any other reason;
rather, upon the completion of this sacrifice, having performed worship together with you,
you shall bring back your husband, the Three-eyed One, along with you."
"I shall also perform the highest worship for the three worlds with due honors.
All this has been told to you as the great cause of my distress;
you should not feel any resentment in this matter, for everyone deserves their own portion.

"O daughter, whatever kind of auspicious or inauspicious karma was performed by you in other births, such is the fruit you experience here in this birth. Do not grieve; enjoy the fruit of what was done in the past."
Seeing her supreme prosperity, endowed with beauty, good fortune, and splendor—
her form, radiance, charm, lovely ornaments,
birth in a great lineage, and an exceedingly beautiful body— (48)
O lady of virtuous vows, these things are to be obtained by men through their past merits;
do not revile yourself, nor your fortunes, O lady of virtuous vows. For who is capable of bestowing the fruit ordained by destiny? 49–50.
There is no one at all who is powerful, nor anyone who is ignorant, nor anyone who is wise; both wisdom and power arise solely from past karma.
These gods have reached heaven and remain there, shining for a long time.
"Whatever merit has been earned by these through their religious merit and austerities in various sacred fields, they are the sharers of the fruit thereof.
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous woman was then filled with rage toward Bhīṣma.
Reproaching her father with eyes reddened by anger, she said: "It is exactly as you have stated before me, O father:
every person partakes in merit, and through merit one attains prosperity. (54)
Through merit one obtains birth; through merit enjoyments are established.
Therefore, this Lord of all worlds, the most excellent of the excellent, has by his wisdom bestowed these abodes upon everyone. 55–56.
Even the tongue of Brahmā, the Creator, would not be capable of describing the qualities of that God; indeed, it is impossible to proclaim the glory of that Supreme Lord.
His ashes, bones, and skull-caps, as well as his dwelling in the cremation ground, [are likewise beyond description].
All the serpents, beginning with Gonasā, have been made into his ornaments.
The hosts of bhūtas and pretas, as well as piśācas and guhyakas, belong to him;
he is the creator, the ordainer, and the protector of the quarters.
"O Rudra, by your grace Purandara attained heaven;
if divinity resides in Rudra, and if Śiva is omnipresent,
then by that truth, may Śaṅkara destroy your sacrifice."
"If I have performed any austerity or practiced any dharma,
may that sacrifice be worthy of peace through the fruit of that dharma, provided that I am dear to the Lord and provided that he will deliver me."
"By this truth, let this pride come to an end.
Having said this, he resorted to yoga and, with the splendor residing within his own body,
he then consumed himself along with the gods, asuras, and pannagas.
When the hosts of Gandharvas and Guhyakas asked, "What is this?", she,
being enraged, then cast off her body on the bank of the Gaṅgā; that sacred ford named Saukaṅka is located on the western shore of the Gaṅgā.
Having heard the news that Rudra had been praised, he became deeply distressed at the loss of his wife;
while the gods looked on, the resolute one resolved to destroy the sacrifice. Ten million Gaṇas were commanded, as well as the Grahas and Vaināyakas.
And the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* were present for the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having gone there, all the gods were defeated and destroyed by them. When the sacrifice was slain, Dakṣa thereafter became devoid of enthusiasm and devoid of effort.
Approaching the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, he spoke in terror: "O Lord, I did not recognize you as the sovereign master of the gods of gods.
You are the supreme lord of this world; all the deities have been conquered by you."
O Great Lord, have mercy and turn back all the Gaṇas—
those various and terrible hosts adorned with diverse ornaments, possessing various faces, teeth, and lips, and brandishing various weapons. 70–71.
Adorned with masses of matted hair bitten by various lords of the *nāgas*,
they were fierce, striking with terrible blows, possessed of intense and haughty pride, capable of assuming any form at will, lovely, and endowed with the fulfillment of every desire. 72.
By yogis who have attained mastery through yoga, possessing irresistible and fierce powers;
with matted hair like trembling manes, mouths grinning fiercely with fangs, and the skillful swelling of temples like the lordly elephants—those who possess the bodies of lions. (73–74)
Some, with splendors like lamps flickering from the intense heat of their breath,
wearing various variegated garments and possessing the steady gait of noble steeds; some uttering the cries of deer, tigers, and lions, and wearing the skins of hyenas.
With serpent-garlands, bracelets, and sacrificial threads as their ornaments;
bearing tridents, swords, and spears; holding axes and darts in their hands;
and grasping thunderbolts, saws, bows, and the staff of Death as weapons in their palms.
Surrounded by the hosts of Gaṇeśvaras, who were exceedingly difficult to overcome— like the sun surrounded by planets— the sacrifice, having been destroyed, went to heaven;
and Śaṅkara, assuming the form of a deer, was filled with fear.
Salutations to the god who has the luster of a conch shell, to the one with a bull as his vehicle, to the one who is the moon, and to the end-maker of sacrifices and time;
salutations to the one whose garment is the skin of the directions, and salutations to you of fierce splendor. 79–80.
Salutations again and again to Brahmā, to the one whose body is Brahman, to the one who is devoted to Brahman, and to the immeasurable;
salutations to Girīśa, to Sureśa, and to Īśāna. (81) Salutations to Rudra, to the one who is like a thunderbolt, to Śiva, and to Krathana.
Salutation to the lord of the Suras and Asuras, to the lord of those who have gone beyond; 82.
Salutation indeed to the smoke-colored, the fierce, the deformed, the sacrificer, the one of terrible form, to the thousand-eyed Virūpākṣa, the auspicious-eyed one. 83.
Salutations to the shaven-headed one, to Caṇḍamuṇḍā, to the bearer of the excellent Khaṭvāṅga, to the one whose form is the Kavya, to the Havya, and to the destroyer of all;
salutations to Rudra, who is exceedingly compassionate toward his devotees and who is praised through recitation. 84.

Salutations again and again to the one who assumes forms that are deformed, beautiful, and perfectly formed; to the five-faced one, the one with an auspicious face, and the one with a moon-like countenance;
salutations to the giver of boons, the one worthy of boons, to the Tortoise, and to the Deer.
Salutations again and again to the one who bears playful locks of hair and the crescent moon,
to the one whose name is the universe, to the universe itself, and to the Lord of the universe. O Three-eyed One, slayer of Tripura, may protection be granted to us.

O Maheśvara, [this was said] by one who had surrendered through the states of speech, mind, and body. (88) Thus praised then by Dakṣa, who had fallen into distress, the God was then intensely propitiated by this divine hymn. (89)
"O Prajāpati, I have bestowed upon you the entire fruit of sacrifice;
for the fulfillment of all your desires, you shall obtain the unsurpassed fruit.
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, he then bowed down to the Lord of the Gods.
While the hosts of Gaṇas were looking on, he went to his own abode.
At that time, the god remained at Gaṅgādvāra, overwhelmed by grief for his wife, brooding over that chaste lady: "Where has my beloved gone? (91-92)
While he was overcome by grief, Nārada appeared in his presence; for that Satī, the wife of the Lord of Gods who was as dear to him as his own life, had passed away—
she who was the daughter of Himavat, born from the womb of Menā.
She, who knew the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, assumed another body. Having heard of her, the God beheld her as she had descended through meditation;
then, having made himself fulfilled, the God remained there.
The queen, having reached the bloom of youth, was married once again;
thus indeed, O Bhīṣma, has been told how the sacrifice was destroyed in the past. 96.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 5.
The sixth chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
[Regarding] the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas...
"O Guru, tell me this origin in detail according to the prescribed rule.
Pulastya said:
"The creation of the ancestors is said to have arisen from resolve, sight, and touch."
After Dakṣa Prācetasa, creation arose from sexual union; hear now,
O Kaurava,
exactly how he brought it about when he was creating the hosts of gods, sages, and serpents.
At that time, the world did not increase due to the practice of sexual union;
then Dakṣa begot thousands of sons upon his sixty daughters.
Seeing those illustrious ones desiring to create various offspring, [he was filled with joy].
Nārada spoke to the Haryaśvas, the sons of Dakṣa, who had assembled there:
"O best of sages, having ascertained the entire extent of the earth, both above and below, then proceed with the creation in detail."
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions;
even today, the oceans and rivers have not returned.
When the Haryaśvas had perished, Dakṣa Prajāpati once again—
The Lord produced a thousand sons from Vīriṇī alone;
they were all together in the work of creation, the Śabalāśvas.
Then the sage Nārada spoke again to those who had followed him, just as before.

"Having learned the entire extent of the earth, you shall then return and carry out the creation once again in its full detail. Following those words, they then departed along that very path, accompanied by their brother.

From that time forward, the younger brother who desires the path [of his elder] becomes a seeker of suffering; therefore, one should avoid him. Furthermore, Prajāpati created sixty daughters among them as well.
Then Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot offspring upon Vīriṇī;
he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two he gave to the son of Bhṛgu, and two to the wise Kṛśāśva;
and two indeed he bestowed upon Aṅgiras. Listen now in detail to the names of those mothers of the gods and the expansion of their progeny from the beginning.
Aruṃdhatī, Vasu, Jāmi, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and the beautiful Viśvā—
these are declared to be the wives of Dharma; learn now of their sons from me.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas, and from Sādhyā were born the Sādhyas. From Marutvatī were born the Marutvats, and likewise from Vasu were born the Vasus.
From Bhānu were born the Bhānus, and from Muhūrtā were born the Muhūrtajas.
To Lambā was born the one named Ghoṣa; to Nāgavīthī was born Jāmī;
and Arundhatī gave birth to him who was born from the surface of the earth.
To Saṃkalpā was born Saṃkalpa; do you, O Vasu, support this creation.
If these luminous ones, O gods, pervade all directions, they are declared to be the Vasus; hear their names:
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, and Anala. (20–21)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
The four sons of Āpa were Śrānta and Vaitaṇḍa, as well as Apiśānta, Muni, and Babhru; they were the ones authorized for the protection of the sacrifice.

From Dhruva was born a son, Varcas, who was born from Soma. Draviṇa and Havyavāha are remembered as the two sons of Dharā. From him [Varcas] were born Prāṇa, Ramaṇa, and Śiśira, who endure until the end of the kalpa.
Then Manohara had Udhava as his son, and Śiva had sons who were the offspring of Hari.
Śiva obtained a son named Manojava, who grants a course of movement that is imperceptible.
Then Anala obtained sons whose qualities were predominantly like those of fire.
Among them were Śākha and Viśākha, who were the offspring of Svayambhū through the Kṛttikās; therefore he is remembered as Kārttikeya.
The son of Pratyūṣa was the sage Ṛbhu, and his name was Devala.

Viśvakarman, the son of Prabhāsa, was a master craftsman and lord of creatures; he was the architect for the thirty gods in the construction of palaces, mansions, gardens, statues, ornaments, and the like, as well as in the making of tanks, groves, and wells.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Tharavata; Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Asureśvara;
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita. 29–30.
These are declared to be the eternal Rudras, the eleven lords of the hosts.
Of these mind-born ones, who bear the excellent trident,
eighty-four crores are considered their imperishable sons.
In all directions, the lords of the Gaṇas provide protection.
These indeed are the sons and grandsons born from the womb of Surabhi;
I shall now describe the sons, grandsons, and others of Kaśyapa through his various wives.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā,
Kadrū, and Khasā— likewise Muni; learn from me now of their excellent sons.
The Tuṣita gods belong to the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu;
and in the interval of Vaivasvata, twelve Ādityas are recorded:
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu—
these are remembered as the thousand-rayed Ādityas who arose from Āditya.
Born from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, they were the sons of Aditi.
The sons of the sage Kṛśāśva are remembered as the divine weapons (Devapraharaṇas).
O dear one, these hosts of gods arise in every Manvantara and likewise dissolve at the end of every Kalpa.
We have heard that Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyakaśipu and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa. Similarly, four sons were born to Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Saṃhlāda, and Hlāda;
the sons of Prahlāda were Āyuṣmān, Śibi, and Vāṣkali, while Virocana was the fourth, who obtained Bali as his son. 41–42.
O King, Bali had a hundred sons, of whom Bāṇa was the eldest; they were Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Vivasvān, Aṃśu, Tāpana,
Nikumbha, Gurvakṣa, Kukṣi, Bhauma, and Bhīṣaṇa.
Thus there were many others; Bāṇa was the eldest and superior in qualities.
Bāṇa, however, possessed a thousand arms and was endowed with the excellence of all weapons;
he had propitiated Śiva through austerity, and the wielder of the trident dwells in his city.
He who was the Sārthya of the wielder of the Pināka bow attained the state of Mahākāla;
Hiraṇyākṣa’s son was named Andhaka by name, as well as Bhūtasaṃtāpana and Mahānāga. 46.

From these were born seventy-seven crores of sons and grandsons, who were exceedingly strong, possessed of massive bodies, diverse forms, and great majesty. Danu obtained one hundred sons from Kaśyapa, who were arrogant due to the boons they had received.
Among them, the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti became the leader;
likewise there were Śakuni with sixteen heads, Śaṅkuśirodhara,
Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapila, and Vāmana.
Marīci, Māgadha, Hari, Gajaśiras, Nidrādhara, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatakratu,
Indramitra-graha, and likewise Vajranābha. (50–51)
Ekavastro, Mahābāhu, Vajrākṣa, Tāraka,
Asiloman, Puloman, Vikurvāṇa, the great Asura,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and others such as these were the sons of Danu.
Svarbhānu had Suprabhā as his daughter, and Śacī was the daughter of Puloman.
Upadānavī was the wife of Maya, as were Mandodarī and Kuhū.
Śarmiṣṭhā and Sundarī were the daughters of Vṛṣaparvan, and Caṇḍā was also his [daughter]. 53–54.

Pulomā and Kālakā, both daughters of Vaiśvānara, were the wives of Mārīca; they were both highly virtuous and possessed many offspring. In former times, there were sixty thousand Dānavas born of them.
In ancient times, Mārīca begot the Paulomas, Kālakhañjas, and Kālakeyas;
they were inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura, incapable of being slain by men, having obtained boons from the Four-faced One (Brahmā), yet they were eventually destroyed by Vijaya.
Vipracitti begot nine sons upon Siṃhikā;
these thirteen were indeed the nephews of Hiraṇyakaśipu:
Kaṃsa, Śaṅkha, O King of kings, Nala, and Vātāpi.
Ilvala, Namuci, Khasṛma, and likewise Añjana; Naraka, Kālanābha, and Paramāṇu as well;
and the famous Kalpavīrya, who increased the lineage of Danu. 59–60.
In the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhlāda were the Nivātakavacas,
who were invincible to all the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
those who, relying on their strength, were slain by Arjuna on the field of battle.
From the seed of Mārīca, Tāmrā gave birth to six daughters:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugṛdhī, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci.
According to dharma, Śukī gave birth to parrots and owls.
Śyenī gave birth to hawks and Bhāsī to kites and crows; Gṛdhri gave birth to vultures, Sugṛdhri to pigeons and other birds,
and Śuci gave birth to swans, cranes, ducks, and water-fowl.
These sons of Tāmrā have been described; now listen to those of Vinatā:
Garuḍa, the best of birds, and Aruṇa, the lord of winged creatures, as well as their daughter Saudāminī, who is renowned in the sky. 65-66.
Both Saṃpāti and Jaṭāyu were the two sons of Aruṇa;
Saṃpāti’s son was Vabhru, who was swift and highly renowned.
Jaṭāyu’s sons were Karṇikāra and Śatagāmin, both of whom were famous.
The progeny of those birds, consisting of sons and grandsons, became innumerable.
In ancient times, Surasā gave birth to a thousand serpents with a thousand heads,
and the virtuous Kadrū likewise obtained a thousand.
O subduer of enemies, among them twenty-six are renowned as the principal ones:
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Śaṅkha, Airāvata, and Kambala; Dhananjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, and Takṣaka.
Elāpatra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Balāhaka;
Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, and Śubhānana; Śaṅkharoman, Canahuṣa, Uramaṇa, and Paṇina. 71–72.
Kapila, Durmukha, and likewise those headed by Patañjali— all of them had infinite sons and grandsons;
for that [lineage] which had previously been mostly consumed in the palace of Janamejaya [had now flourished again].
She gave birth to a host of Rākṣasas named Krodhavaśās.
A million of those fanged creatures perished at the hands of Bhīmasena.
[He also slew] the fanged ones, jackals, crows, and others, as well as the female buffalo-cows and the female boars.
In ancient times, Surabhi gave birth to a triad from Kaśyapa:
a multitude of sages for the sages, as well as a multitude of apsarases;
likewise, Ariṣṭā gave birth to many kinnaras and gandharvas.
From Irā, he produced all grasses, trees, creepers, and shrubs (77).
From Khaśā, he brought forth yakṣas and rākṣasas by the millions;
these are the descendants of Kaśyapa by the hundreds and thousands (78).
In this Manvantara, the creation of Bhīṣma is recorded as occurring during the Svārociṣa period;
thereafter, Diti, who knew the dharma and was beloved by the immortals, gave birth to forty-nine Maruts from Kaśyapa. 79.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seven. Bhīṣma said:
"How were the sons of Diti born as the Maruts, beloved of the gods?
And why did they attain such unsurpassed friendship with the gods, despite being their rivals?
Pulastya said:
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when her sons and grandsons had been slain by the asuras, she, afflicted with grief,
came to this most excellent world at the great sacred site of Puṣkara, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī.
Diti, the mother of the Daityas, being devoted to the propitiation of her husband, performed severe penance for the sake of the sages; observing excellent vows,
she subsisted on fruits and practiced austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
For more than a hundred years, she remained overwhelmed by old age and grief;
then, having performed austerities, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and the others:
"Tell me, sirs, the means for the destruction of my sorrow for my son."
The sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, spoke of the vow of the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, which bestows the fruit of good fortune both in this world and the next;
by the grace of which she became free from the grief for her son.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brāhmaṇa, I wish to hear about the vow of the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, by which Diti obtained forty-nine sons once again. 8.
Pulastya said:
Listen now from me in detail to this very same vow which was previously narrated to Aditi by Vasiṣṭha and the others. 9.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the full moon day, one who is observant of vows should place an unblemished jar filled with white rice,
likewise provided with various fruits and stalks of sugarcane.
Covered with a pair of white garments and smeared with white sandalwood paste,
and provided with various kinds of food offerings along with gold according to one's means,
one should place a copper vessel filled with molasses upon it. 11–12.

Therefore, one should place Brahmā above [the image] within the hollow of a golden lotus; to his left, one should place Sāvitrī together with Śarkarā. One should offer perfumes and incense to those two and cause songs and instrumental music to be performed.

In the absence of that [image], how should one act? Just as the Grandfather (Brahmā) did for the lotus, one should fashion an auspicious image called Brahmā made of jaggery and worship the Lotus-born One with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds. 14–15.

Having worshipped the two feet with "Obeisance to Brāhmā," the two shanks with "Obeisance to the Bestower of Good Fortune," the pair of thighs with "Obeisance to Viriñci," and the waist with "Obeisance to Manmatha";
[one should worship] the belly with "Obeisance to Svacchodara" and the chest of Vidhi with "Obeisance to Atandraya."

"Salutation to the one whose face is a lotus," [he should say] to the mouth; "Salutation to the one whose hands are the Vedas" to the two arms; "Salutation to the Soul of All" to the head, and he should also worship the lotus.
Then, at dawn, he should present that water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should devoutly feed a Brāhmaṇa, while one should oneself eat without salt;
with devotion, one should perform a circumambulation and recite this mantra:
"May the Blessed One, the Grandfather of all the worlds, be pleased here. (19)
That bliss which is designated as existing within the hearts of all the worlds—by this method, one should perform everything month after month;
fasting on the full moon day, one should worship the imperishable Brahman. 20–21.
Having consumed a single fruit, he should sleep upon the ground during the night; then,
in the thirteenth month, he should give a bed equipped with all its furnishings along with a cow of ghee to Viriñca.
Having fashioned Brahmā out of gold and Sāvitrī likewise out of silver,
the creator of the world, who is of the nature of the lotus, should receive Sāvitrī; and having worshipped the Brahmin together with his wife with devotion, using garments and ornaments.
One should give gifts such as the relinquishment of one's power (śakti) and say, "May [the deity] be pleased.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with white sesame seeds while reciting the names of Brahmā.
Likewise, the knower of dharma should likewise offer oblations of cow’s ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer a gift of wealth and a garland of flowers according to one's ability.
Whoever performs this rite on the full moon day, even if it be a woman,
becomes liberated from all sins and attains identity with Brahman.

He who remembers that Brahmā— who is known as Viṣṇu, the Great Lord whose essence is bliss— certainly attains excellent sons in this world and good fortune. One who seeks happiness should remember the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the form of Kāma.
Having heard this, Aditi performed everything in its entirety.
Due to the greatness of the vow, Kaśyapa returned with supreme joy and created Karkaśā once more, endowed with beauty and grace.
They gratified him with excellent boons, and he chose a most excellent boon:
"I choose a high-souled son of great luster, capable of slaying Śakra and the destroyer of all the immortals. 31.
Kaśyapa spoke these words to Indra, the powerful slayer:
"O auspicious one with beautiful breasts, I shall grant you this; however, let this be done today: perform the Āpastamba sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son. (32-33)
"O auspicious one, having touched your breasts, I shall then conceive a fetus;
O Goddess, there will be a noble child who shall be the slayer of Śakra. Then she performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, which was superior even to that of Indra.
"O Indra, become our enemy!"—thus he quickly offered the oblation.
The gods, Daityas, and Dānavas repeatedly turned their faces away;
then Kaśyapa placed the embryo in Aditi and spoke to her again.
Your face resembles the moon, your breasts are like bilva fruits,
your lips have the hue of coral, and your complexion is exceedingly beautiful.
O large-eyed one, having seen you, I forget my own lovely body.

Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, this embryo must be placed by you with your own hand upon your breasts; for, O fair-faced one, without any effort on your part, this embryo must be nurtured within you for a full hundred years while you dwell in the forest of penance.
O woman of excellent complexion, she who is pregnant must never eat during the twilight hours;
she must never stand nor walk at the roots of trees. She must not sit upon household implements such as the pestle, the mortar, and so forth.

One should not plunge into water, and one should avoid an empty house (41). One should not stand upon anthills, nor should one be troubled in mind; one should not scratch the ground with one's nails, nor upon charcoal or ashes (42).
One should always remain vigilant, avoid physical exertion,
and must not sit upon frost, charcoal, ashes, bones, or skulls.
One should also avoid quarreling with people in the world, as well as the anointing of the limbs with oil.

She should not remain with her hair disheveled, nor should she ever be impure (44). She should never sleep with her head toward the north, nor with her head toward the foot of the bed; nor should she be without clothing, nor agitated, nor have wet feet (45).
She should not utter inauspicious speech, nor should her laughter be excessive;
she should always perform worship for her elders and remain intent on auspiciousness.
She should perform her bath with water infused with all medicinal herbs.
Having performed her protective rites, intent upon service, speech, and worship,
she should remain with a serene countenance, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband; she should never, under any circumstances, speak ill of her husband.
"I am emaciated and weak, and old age has come upon me; my breasts have shifted from their place and my face is wrinkled and sagging.
You should never say such things about me to her. 49.
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Having been told "So be it" by her once more, he vanished right there while all beings were looking on.
Then she remained there, acting according to the instructions spoken by her husband.
Then, having learned of this, Indra also approached the side of Diti;
leaving the abode of the gods, he remained there, desiring to serve her.
Seeking a vulnerability in Diti, the subduer of Pāka became intent on finding an opening.

Internally distracted by contrary thoughts, yet outwardly speaking with a serene countenance, he performed his own auspicious duties as if unaware of them. Then, at the end of a hundred years— actually three days short of that— (he passed away).
Having achieved their purpose, they were filled with joy and wonder;
without having washed their feet,
they lay down with their hair disheveled, overcome by the weight of sleep as if their heads were turned toward the other direction.
Then, having found that opportunity and entered within, Śacīpati,
the lord of the thirty gods, split that embryo into seven parts with his thunderbolt.
From that, seven Kumāras were born, possessing the splendor of the sun.

As those seven children cried out, Hari, like the wielder of the thunderbolt, cut each one of them into seven pieces again— those who were crying even after being restrained by the water of the Dānava. Furthermore, he cut them while they remained within his stomach.
Thus becoming forty-nine in number, they roared most fiercely.
Indra restrained them, saying again and again, "Do not roar! Then the slayer of Vṛtra reflected with this thought.

"By the greatness of what karma have these been restored to life? Having understood this fruit of the full-moon day through its connection with merit, or perhaps it has come about from the worship of Brahmā. (61)
Struck by the thunderbolt, they met their destruction;
yet even as one, he attained multiplicity because he was hidden within the belly [of Viṣṇu].
"Surely these are not to be slain; therefore, let them become gods," [he thought]. 62–63.
"Since you wept (*arudan*) when told by Māra that you were born from a womb, therefore, by this name, may you be called Maruts and be partakers of happiness.
Then, having propitiated her again, the Lord of Gods said to Diti, "Forgive me."
"Having relied upon the science of statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), this evil deed was committed by me.
Having made the host of Maruts equal to the gods, the lord of the immortals placed Diti along with her sons in a celestial chariot and ascended to heaven.
Consequently, all the Maruts became partakers of sacrificial portions;
they did not reach unity with the Asuras, and therefore they are beloved by the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Brahmā, you have described to me in detail the primary creation (ādisarga) and the secondary creation (pratisarga); now tell me who their presiding lords were.
Pulastya said:
When Pṛthu was consecrated as the sovereign lord of the entire earth,
he likewise appointed Soma as the lord of medicinal herbs, sacrificial vows, and ascetic penances—
Soma who is the golden-wombed source of the expanse of constellations, stars, brahmins, trees, shrubs, and creepers.
He made Varuṇa the lord of the waters, Vaiśravaṇa likewise the sovereign of riches and kings;
he made Viṣṇu the overlord of the Ādityas, Agni the lord of the Vasus, and Dakṣa the overlord of the Prajāpatis; and he made Śakra the sovereign of the Maruts. (70–71)
Then [he saw] Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas; Yama, the lord of the Pitṛs;
the king of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Paśus, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and Vetālas; Śūlapāṇi (Śiva); Himavat, the lord of mountains; and the ocean, the sovereign of rivers.
Furthermore, he made Citraratha the lord of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras.
He appointed the serpent-lord Vāsuki of fierce valor as the sovereign of the serpents, and he made the elephant-lord named Airāvaṇa the ruler of the world-elephants that guard the directions.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) formerly consecrated Suparṇa as the lord of winged creatures, Uccaiḥśravas as the king of horses,
the lion as the king of beasts, the bull as the lord of cows, and the Plakṣa tree as the sovereign of all forest trees;
he then consecrated these once more as the rulers of all the directions.
Then he consecrated the guardian of the eastern quarter by the name Suvarman, the banner of his enemies;
thereafter, the Lord of the Cosmic Egg made Śaṅkhapada the sovereign of the south; and he made Saketumat the lord and guardian of the western direction. 76–77.
He made Hiraṇyaroman the lord of the northern quarter, the Prajāpati and son of Megha;
even today, the lords of the quarters constantly carry out his command for the protection of the world.
By these four, the king named Pṛthu was consecrated as the first ruler upon the earth.
In the interval between the ages known as Cākṣuṣa, they established this [Manu] on earth by the name Vaivasvata;

and when that interval had passed and the one called Vaivasvata began again, he— the son of the Solar lineage— became the Prajāpati of all this moving and unmoving world, marked with his own distinctive signs.
Pulastya said: [I shall describe] all the Manvantaras, the deeds of the Manus, the duration of a Kalpa, and its creation in brief. 81.
Listen with a single-minded and serene soul, O descendant of Kuru:
in a former age, during the interval of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were the Yāma gods;
and previously, there were the seven sages who are remembered as Marīci and the others.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vibhu, Savana,
Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Bhavya, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu—
these ten were the progenitors of the lineage of this Svāyambhuva Manu. 83–84.
Having brought about the dissolution at the end of each cycle of creation, they went to the supreme state.
Thus has the Svāyambhuva Manvantara been described; hereafter follows the Svārociṣa.
The sons of Svārociṣa were four, possessing the splendor of gods.
Nabhas, Nabhasya, Prabhṛti, Bhāvana, Kīrtivardhana,
Datta, Agni, Cyavana, Stambha, Prāṇa, Kaśyapa,
and Arvā-Bṛhaspati were the seven sages (Saptarṣis). 86–87.

Then, during the Svārociṣa interval, the gods were known as the Catuṣitas; Haviṣmān, Indra, Sukṛta, Mūrti, Āpaḥ, Jyotis, and Atharvan are recorded [as the seven Ṛṣis]. At that time, the seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were the Prajāpatis.
This second Manvantara has been described;
hereafter, I shall further proclaim another auspicious Manvantara.
Therein, the one named Uttama-Manu begot ten sons.
Iṣa, Ūrja, Tanūja, Śuci, Śukra, as well as Madhu, Mādhava, Nabhasya, and Nabhas;
Sahas and Sahasya—of these, the latter is the most excellent, the increaser of fame. 91.
The Bhānavas were the gods there, and the Saptarṣis (Seven Seers) are remembered as the Ūrjas. Kaukabhiṇḍi, Kutuṇḍa, Dālbhya, Śaṅkha, Pravāhita,
Miti, and Saṃmiti— these seven are the augmenters of yoga.
The fourth Manvantara, renowned by the name Tāmasa,
had Kapi, Pṛthu, Agni, Akapi, and Kavi; likewise, there were seven sages known by the names Janya and Dhāman.
And those groups of deities belonging to the *sādhya* class who were mentioned within the *tāmasa* [section]—[they are as follows]:
Akalmaṣa, Tapodhanvin, Tapomūla, Tapodhana, Taporāśi, Tapasya, Sutapasya, and Parantapa. (95–96)
All the sons of Tāmasa were increasers of their lineage;
ten in number. Now hear likewise of the interval of the fifth Manu, Raivata:
Devabāhu, Subāhu, Parjanya, Samaya, and Muni.
Hiraṇyaroman, Saptāśva—these seven are remembered as the Ṛṣis.
The gods are remembered as Bhūtarajas and likewise Prakṛti; also Avaśa, Tattvadarśin, Vītimat, Havyapa, and Kapi. 98–99.
Mukta, Nirutsuka, Satva, Nirmoha, and Prakāśaka—endowed with the power of dharma and vigor—these ten were the sons of Atri.
Bhṛgu, Sudhāmā, Viraja, Sahiṣṇu, and likewise Nārada [were the sons of Aṅgiras]. 100.
Vivasvat was the name of the [seventh] Manu, and there were seven other great sages (saptarṣis). During the interval (antara) of Cākṣuṣa, the gods known as the Lekhas were renowned;
the inhabitants of heaven (tridivaukasas) are also separately celebrated as the Vibhus. 101–102.
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had arrived, the fifth generation of gods appeared;
likewise, the ten sons of Cākṣuṣa, beginning with Ruru,
have been mentioned by me previously in the lineage of Svāyambhuva.
The period between the Cākṣuṣa and this [Vaivasvata] has been described by me to you. Now I shall declare the seventh, which is called Vaivasvata;
[the sages of that period were] Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Gautama. 104–105.
Bhāradvāja, the yogi Viśvāmitra, and the powerful Jamadagni— these seven are currently those great ṛṣis;
having established the order of dharma, they proceed to the supreme state.
I shall now proclaim the future interval of the Manu Sāvarṇya.
Aśvatthāman, Śaradvān, Kauśika, Gālava, Śatānanda, Kāśyapa, and Rāma are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis). 107–108.
Dhṛti, Varīyān, Yavasu, Suvarṇa, Dhṛtivarī, Variṣṇu, Vīrya, Sumati, Vasu, and the powerful Śukra—
these are proclaimed as the sons of the future Manu, Arkasāvarṇi. 109.
Raucya and others are likewise proclaimed as Manus.
The son of Prajāpati Ruci shall be named Raucya; similarly, the son of Bhūti shall be named Bhautya. 110–111.
Then Tushita, the son of Brahmā, is remembered as the Manu Sāvarṇi;
likewise, Ṛbhu, Ṛtadhāman, and Viṣvaksena are the Manus.
Thus have the past and future Manus been fully described.
O lord of men, this entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, is pervaded by these for a thousand yugas of years. Having brought forth all this within their respective intervals,
when the dissolution of the kalpa occurs, they are liberated along with Brahmā.
"At the end of these thousands of yugas, Brahmā and the others perish again and again; thereafter, O King, they shall indeed attain union with Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Manvantaras," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eight.
Bhīṣma said:
It is heard that in ancient times, the earth was enjoyed by many kings.

Why was the designation "pārthiva" (earthly) applied due to its connection with the earth (*pṛthivī*), and why is it called "pṛthivīka" due to its connection with *pṛthivī*? For what purpose was that technical term for the earth established?
And why is this name "gauḥ" (cow) used for the earth? Tell me this.
Pulastya said: In the former Kṛta Yuga, there was a Prajāpati named Aṅga;
he married the daughter of Mṛtyu, who was exceedingly ill-favored.
In ancient times, there was a lord of the earth named Sunītha; his son was named Vena, who was devoted to unrighteousness, lustful, powerful,
and a perpetrator of injustice against the world, seizing the wives of others.

Then, for the sake of his success and for the sake of the world, he was entreated by the great seers; yet, being of impure soul, he did not grant them safety. Thereupon, afflicted by the fear of a kingless state, they slew him with a curse.

The sinless Brahmins churned his body with force; from that body being churned, various Mleccha tribes were produced. Those born from the portion of the mother’s body had a luster like black collyrium.
Through the union with a portion of his father, there was born a righteous son who performed dharma;
he emerged from the right hand, equipped with a bow, arrows, and weapons, consisting of divine splendor, and adorned with jeweled armor and armlets. 8–9.
Pṛthu himself became known by that name, and he was born as Viṣṇu;
having performed very difficult austerities, he was consecrated by the Brahmins,
and as a lord, he attained sovereignty over everything through a boon from Viṣṇu.
Seeing the surface of the earth devoid of Vedic study, the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and all righteousness, he of immeasurable prowess prepared to pierce it with an arrow out of anger; thereupon,
the Earth assumed the form of a cow and endeavored to flee.
Then Pṛthu, with his bow and arrows, followed behind her; standing in one place, he said, "What shall I do? (13) Pṛthu also spoke these words: "O lady of excellent vows, grant me what I desire."

"Quickly for the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. "So be it," the earth replied; and King Pṛthu milked her, making Svāyambhuva Manu the calf and placing his own hand as the milking vessel.
That food became milk by which the subjects live;
then the sages milked Soma as the calf, Vācaspati became the milker, the Veda the vessel, and austerity the essence. 16.
Then the gods milked the Earth; Marut was the milker.
Indra became the calf, and the milk that emerged was vigorous strength.
The vessel for the gods was made of gold, and likewise, that of the ancestors was made of silver.

Antaka became the milker, Yama was the calf, and Svadhā was the milk; the hole [of the earth] was the vessel, and Takṣaka was the calf of the Nāgas. Then, Viṣa was the milk, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra again became the milker.
This [earth] was milked by the Asuras using an iron vessel for the purpose of afflicting their enemies;
O child, Māyā was the calf and Virocana was the milker, by whom that illusion (māyā) was set in motion. 20–21.
O Lord of the Earth, in ancient times, the Yakṣas, desiring invisibility, milked the earth using Viśvāvasu as the calf and Maṇimān as the vessel;
and the hosts of Pretas and Rākṣasas milked it for marrow and copious blood.
Raupyanābha became the milker and Sumālī the calf.
Then the earth was milked again by the Gandharvas along with the hosts of Apsaras;
having made Citraratha the calf, they drew forth perfumes from the lotus-petals. (23-24)
Then the milker named Vasuruci, a master of the Atharvaveda,
milked the earth through the mountains for various kinds of jewels;
and the mountain Meru, the milker, milked the earth for divine medicinal herbs.
There, Himavat became the calf, while the vessel was made of stone.
The Earth was the cow whose milk was trees, which sprout again even when cut;
the Sāla tree, dense with flowering groves, milked her into a vessel of Palāśa leaves.
Then, O dear one, the Plakṣa tree became the calf, the lord of all trees and forests.

In this manner, the earth was likewise milked by others according to their desires—longevity, wealth, happiness, and sovereignty over the earth while ruling the kingdom. 28. While Pṛthu was governing the realm, [these were obtained].
While he ruled the vast kingdom, there was no poverty, nor disease, nor lack of wealth, nor any evildoer; there were no calamities and no violence,
and the people were constantly joyful, free from suffering and grief.
With the tip of his bow, he of great strength pushed aside the lords of mountains and leveled the circle of the earth out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
There were no cities, villages, or fortresses, nor were there men bearing weapons.

Where people die in misery and there is no respect for the treatises on worldly affairs (artha-śāstra), yet men solely devoted to righteousness (dharma) govern the kingdom separately; and where the worthy recipients have been described, and the milk is as it was yours. 32–33.
Whatever each person has a taste for, that was given to them by me, who understand;

thus, O illustrious one, everything regarding sacrifices has been explained to you by me. (34) Since, O high-minded one, the Earth attained the status of being Pṛthu’s daughter, [she is called] Pṛthivī.
Because of her following that path, she is known as Pṛthivī by the wise.
Bhīṣma said: O Brāhmaṇa, tell me the entire Solar dynasty (Ādityavaṃśa) in its proper sequence.
O knower of truth, you ought to describe the lineage of Soma exactly as it is.
Pulastya said:
In ancient times, Vivasvat was born from Kaśyapa and Aditi.
He had three wives: Saṃjñā, Rājñī, and Prabhā.
Of them, Rājñī, the daughter of Raivata, gave birth to a son named Revata; Prabhā gave birth to Prabhāta; and Saṃjñā likewise gave birth to Manu, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Yama and Yamunā were born as twins;
then, unable to endure the effulgent form of Vivasvat,
she produced from her own body a blameless woman.
The beautiful woman named Chāyā, who was the very embodiment of the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, stood before him and said, "What shall I do? He replied to her as she stood there,
"O fair-faced one, you must serve that husband of mine."
"Protect these children of mine with maternal affection.
Having said, "So be it," that lady of excellent vows went toward Kāma. The god also, out of respect, desired her, thinking, "She is Saṃjñā."
He begot Sāvarṇi Manu, who was the very embodiment of Manu;
and because of his similarity in color (savarṇa) to Vaivasvata Manu, he was called Sāvarṇi.
Then, in due order, he begot sons from Tapatī, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ.
The Sun-god then begot this woman named Saṃjñā in Chāyā;
at that time, Manu felt greater affection for his own son [Yama] than for Chāyā. The former Manu did not tolerate this, and Yama became overwhelmed with anger.
Then, raising his right foot, he threatened him:
"May this shadow become possessed of worms; may this one foot become a source of flowing pus and blood. (46-47)
Afflicted by his father’s curse, Yama reported to him:
"O Lord, I have been cursed for no reason by my mother in her anger;
in my childhood, I once raised my foot against her."
"O Lord, although she was being restrained by Manu, she nevertheless bestowed a curse upon me.
For the most part, she is not our mother, because of her lack of affection toward us.
Then the god spoke again to Yama: "What shall I do, O high-minded one?"
If, due to happiness, there were no suffering for anyone, or if the continuity of karma were unavoidable even for one in the state of existence (bhava),
what then could be said of other sentient beings?
A cock will devour a worm at your feet.
"And this foot shall become both lame and beautiful.
Having been told this, he was comforted and performed intense penance at the holy site of Puṣkara, subsisting on fruits, foam, and air out of a sense of detachment.
Having propitiated the Grandfather (Brahmā) for ten thousand years,
the Lord of Gods, the Lotus-born One, was satisfied by the power of his asceticism;
he chose the status of a world-protector as well as the imperishable realm of the ancestors.

Thus, O sinless one, he obtained from the Lotus-born Lord the guardianship of the worlds, as well as sovereignty over the ancestors and over dharma and adharma, for the purpose of examining this world which consists of both dharma and adharma. (55–56)
Then Vivasvat, having learned of that conduct and activity of Saṃjñā,
went into the presence of Tvaṣṭṛ and spoke to him with anger. Thereupon, Tvaṣṭṛ addressed him with these words, preceded by consolation:

O Lord, O dispeller of darkness, unable to endure your intense splendor, she assumed the form of a mare and came here into my presence; however, O Lord of Heaven, she was turned back by me out of fear of you.
"Since you have come here without my knowledge and without asking me for permission, it does not behove you to enter my abode.
Having been addressed thus, the blameless woman departed quickly for the desert region.
"Having assumed the form of the submarine fire (*baḍabā*), I am now established within the element of earth.
Therefore, grant me your favor; if I am worthy of your grace, I shall withdraw this radiance of yours by placing the sun within a yantra."
"O Lord, I shall create a form that brings joy to the worlds.
Having been told "So be it" by the Sun,
Śiva caused the Sun to whirl and separated his brilliance, fashioning it into the discus of Viṣṇu.
He also fashioned for Rudra a trident and for Indra another weapon, a vajra; moreover,
he created a peerless and great form consisting of a thousand rays, capable of destroying Daityas and Dānavas, with the exception of Tvaṣṭṛ’s own son.
No one was able to behold that form of the Sun’s feet again; even today, no one anywhere should cause those feet to be made [as images]. He who does so is most sinful and attains a censured state.
One incurs the disease of leprosy, known as suffering, in this world.
Therefore, one who desires merit, pleasure, and wealth should never have the feet of the wise God of Gods made upon various pedestals or in any [other] shrines. 67–68.
Then the Blessed One, the lord of the immortals, having gone to the world of Bhūr,
being afflicted by desire, sought after her like the sun with its face turned toward her,
endowed with a great horse-form and splendor.
Overwhelmed by fear and agitated by the mental agitation caused by that perception, she released [the seed] from her nostrils out of the suspicion that it was another man;
from that seed, the two Aśvins were born—so we have heard. (70–71)

Because he had heard of the two Dasras, the Nāsatyas born from the tip of the nose, he recognized that god after a short time and attained supreme satisfaction. (72) Filled with joy, he returned to heaven in a celestial chariot together with his wife.
Even while he was Sāvarṇi Manu, he continued to perform austerities on Mount Meru until today;
by the power of his penance, Śani attained equality with the other planets,
and Yamunā and Tapatī likewise became rivers once again.
Likewise, Viṣṭi, who is of a terrible nature, is established as Time itself.
Furthermore, Vaivasvata Manu had ten sons of great strength;
among them, Ilā was the first, who was produced through a sacrifice for obtaining a son.
Ikṣvāku, Kuśanābha, Ariṣṭa, and Dhṛṣṭa;
Nariṣyanta, Karūṣa, and the mighty Śaryāti;
Pṛṣadhra, and then Nābhāga—all these were divine-human beings.
Having first consecrated his righteous son Ila, Manu went once again to Puṣkara, that forest of asceticism, for the sake of performing penance.
Then Brahmā, the bestower of boons, arrived there for the purpose of granting him success.
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one; choose whatever you desire," [he said].
Then he spoke to that lotus-eyed, lotus-born, all-pervading Lord:
"May all the kings on earth in my lineage be endowed with righteousness. 79-80.
"O Lord, O Lotus-born one, by your grace may we become sovereigns.
Having said, "So be it," the Lord of Gods vanished right there. Then, having returned to Ayodhyā, he established himself as before.
Then once, having mounted his chariot, the son of Ilā and Manu set forth for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, wandering over this earth which was mostly devoid of people,
subduing all the kings of the various islands.
Then the powerful one, drawn by destiny, went to the great forest of Śiva known as Śaravaṇa, which was filled with wish-fulfilling trees and creepers,
where the Lord of Gods, Soma, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, delights.
There, in the Aśoka grove, Umā made a covenant:
"Whatever being shall come to our forest bearing a male name, all of them within a radius of ten yojanas shall attain womanhood. 85–86.
King Ajāila, unaware of the agreement, went to the Śaravaṇa forest and suddenly attained womanhood; in an instant, he became a mare.
All that had been done for his manhood was then forgotten within his female body. 87.
There appeared a woman with full, high, and firm breasts;
with elevated hips and loins, eyes as long as lotus petals, a face like the full moon, slender, graceful, and dark-eyed. (88–89)
She had full, elevated, and long arms, dark curly hair, fine body hair, a beautiful face, and spoke with soft, faltering words;
she was of a dark-gold complexion, with slender, copper-colored nails. 90.
Possessing eyebrows like a bow, moving with the grace of a swan, that beautiful woman wandered through this forest and thought:
"Where are my two brothers? Or where is my brother here?"

"Whose husband was I given to? How many years have I spent on this earth?"—while she was thus reflecting, that woman of excellent complexion was seen by the son of Soma, whose mind was captivated by her beauty. (93)
Then Budha, afflicted by desire, made an effort to obtain her;
he assumed a distinguished appearance as a shaven-headed ascetic, carrying a water-pot, a book, a bamboo staff, a sacred grass ring, and a small hoe. 94–95.
O Brahman, assuming the form of a twice-born man, wearing a topknot and earrings,
and accompanied by young students carrying sacrificial wood, flowers, kuśa grass,
and water, he searched for him with time and then summoned Satī to that place.
Concealed within a grove of trees outside the forest, he suddenly became filled with agitation as if possessed by a haunting presence:
"Having abandoned the service of the *agnihotra* fire, where have you gone from my home? (97-98)
"This is the time for retiring; it is now passing away. Come, come, O lady of broad hips! For what reason are you so bewildered?
99 "This is the evening hour for retiring here."
"Having performed the smearing [of the floor], decorate my house with flowers.
She replied, "O ascetic, I have forgotten everything—myself, you as my husband, and my family; forgive me, O sinless one."
Budha said to that slender woman: "O lady of excellent complexion, you are Mīlā;
and I am known as Budha, a man of many sciences who is called 'the Lustful One' (Kāmuka).
My father was born into a family of radiant splendor and was a lord among Brāhmaṇas."

At his command, she entered the palace of Budha, which was filled with jeweled pillars and fashioned through divine illusion; staying in that residence, she considered herself to have achieved her purpose. 103–104.
Oh, what conduct! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what wealth! Oh, what noble lineage! Oh, what supreme loveliness belongs both to me and to this husband of mine!
She took delight with him in the land of Ilāvṛta for a very long time.
Just as in a palace of Indra filled with every luxury, [he remained] there.
(106) Then, searching for the king, his human brothers, led by Ikṣvāku, arrived at the vicinity of the Śara forest. (107)
Then they all saw that unsurpassed mare standing before them, shining with the rays emanating from the gems on her saddle-cloth;
having recognized her, they were all filled with wonder. 108.
This horse of that great-souled one was named Candraprabha;
for what reason did it assume the excellent form of a mare?
Then they questioned their own priest, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa.
"O best among those who know yoga, what is this? he asked in wonder.
Vasiṣṭha, having seen everything with the eye of meditation, replied:
"Long ago, in the Śaravaṇa forest, an agreement was made by the beloved of Śambhu."
Any man who enters here shall attain womanhood;
even this horse has attained womanhood along with the king, just as Ila became a man like Sudhanvan.
In that very manner, they should exert effort after propitiating the wielder of the Pināka bow;
then those men went to where the god Maheśvara was,
and they praised Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord with various hymns.
The two of them said: "Enough! This is our established rule; what else could it be now? Whatever fruit may come from Ikṣvāku’s horse-sacrifice, that shall belong to us both;
the heroic Kiṃpuruṣa will undoubtedly become ours. (115-116)
Having said "So be it," all those sons of Vaivasvata departed;
having performed the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), they subsequently became *kimpuruṣas*.
For one month the hero was male, and for another month he again became female.
While residing in the abode of Budha, Ilā became pregnant;
she gave birth to a son endowed with manifold virtues.
Having procreated Puru through Budha, she returned once more to heaven.
Then that region known as Ilāvṛta became the land of Ilā; there arose King Aila, born of the lunar and solar lineages, who increased his dynasty.
Thus, Purūravas became the progenitor of the lineage of Pūru.
Likewise, Ikṣvāku is declared to be the lord of men belonging to the solar dynasty (Ādityavaṃśa). Ila, who is also called Sudyumna, attained the state of being Kimpuruṣa;
furthermore, three invincible sons were born to Sudyumna. 121–122.
Likewise, Utkala had Utkaḷā as his kingdom, and the heroic Dhṛtāśva had Gayāpura; the southern region was known as the domain of Dhṛtāśva,
along with the Kurus.
Having consecrated his son Purūravas upon the throne,
he then went to Ilāvṛta to enjoy [itself], subsisting on divine fruits for a year;
Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, obtained the Middle Country.
The son of Nariṣyanta was the very powerful Śuka. From Nābhāga came Aṃbarīṣa; and Dhṛṣṭa had three sons:
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Svadharma, and the heroic Raṇadhṛṣṭa.
The daughter of Śaryāti was named Sukanyā, and Ānarta had a son, the powerful Rocamāna. There was a country named Ānarta, and its capital city was Kuśasthalī.
To Rocamāna were born two sons, Revanta and Raivata; and Kakudmin was another name for the eldest of his hundred sons.
His daughter Revatī became the renowned wife of Rāma.
From Karūṣa were born many Kārūṣas, renowned upon the earth.
From the killing of a cow by Pṛṣadhra, a Śūdra was born due to his teacher’s curse.
The sons of Ikṣvāku were named Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka.
There were fifty excellent sons, and they had fifty sons in turn; those best of kings were born to the north of Meru. Furthermore, there were forty-eight others who were among that hundred.
And those kings are proclaimed as being to the south of Meru.
From Jyeṣṭha was born a son named Kakutstha, who was Suyodhana;
his son was named Pṛthu, and Viśva was the son of that Pṛthu.
Ārdra was his son, and from him Yuvanāśva was born; Yuvanāśva’s son was the heroic Śāvasta, by whom,
O lord of men, Śravastī was built in the land of Aṅga.
From Śāvasta was born Bṛhadaśva, and from him came Kuvalāśva.
In ancient times, having slain the demon Dhundhu, he attained the name Dhundhumāra.
Three sons were born to him: Dṛḍhāśva and Ghṛṇi, and another.
The renowned Kapilāśva was the powerful son of Dhundhumāra; Pramoda was the son of Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son. Nikumbha was the son of Haryaśva, and from him Saṃhatāśva was born.
Akṛtāśva and Oraṇāśva were both sons of Saṃhatāśva. From Oraṇāśva was born Yuvanāśva, and from him came Māndhātṛ. Purukutsa and the king Dharmasētu were the sons of Māndhātṛ.
The renowned and powerful Mucukunda was a friend of Śakra; he was the son of Purukutsa, the invincible lord of the Narmadā.
Saṃbhūti was his son, and from him Tridhanvan was born.
The son born to Tridhanvan was known as Trayyāruṇa. His son was named Satyavrata, from whom Satyaratha is recorded to have descended. His son was Hariścandra, and from Hariścandra came Rohita.
From Rohita, Vṛka was born; from Vṛka, Bāhu was born;
Sagara was his son, a king most devoted to righteousness. Sagara also had two wives: Prabhā and Bhānumatī.

Formerly, the Aurva fire was propitiated by those two out of a desire for sons. Aurva, being pleased with them, granted an excellent boon according to their wish: one [wife] requested sixty-one thousand sons, while the other requested a single son.
Prabhā took the progenitor of the lineage as her son, while Yādavī and Prabhā gave birth to many sons; Bhānumatī bore one son, Asamañjasa.
Then Yādavī gave birth to sixty thousand sons.
When the earth was scorched by Viṣṇu during his search for the horse,
Aṃśumat, renowned by the name Asamañjas, became his son.
Dilīpa was his son, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha.
By whom the Bhagirathi Ganga was brought down after performing austerities;
his son was known as Bhagiratha, and [Bhagiratha's] son was the famous Nabhaga.
From Nabhaga was born Ambarisha, and from him Sindhudvipa arose.
Tasya had a son named Ayutāyu; from him was born Ṛtuparṇa.
His son was Kalmāṣapāda, who is remembered as Sarvakarmā. Anaraṇya was his son, and Nighna was his son. 151–152.
Two sons were born to Nighna: Anamitra and Raghu, the best of the Raghus.
O King, Anamitra went to the forest for the sake of destroying his enemies. From Raghu was born Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa likewise came Aja.
From Aja was born Dīrghabāhu, and from him came Prajāpāla;
from him was born Daśaratha, who had four sons,
all of whom were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and Rāma was the eldest among them.
Likewise, he was the end-maker of Rāvaṇa and the increaser of the Raghu lineage; Vālmīki, the best of the Bhṛgus, composed his life story.
His son, named Kuśa, was the enhancer of the Ikṣvāku family.
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son. Nala was born from Niṣadha, and Nabhas was born from him.
From Nabhas came Puṇḍarīka, and after him came Kṣemadhanvan. (157–158)
His son was the heroic and majestic Devānīka;
his son was Ahīnagu, and after him came Sahasrāśva. Then followed Candrāvaloka, and from him was born Tārāpīḍa.
His son was Candragiri, and his son was Candra. From him was born Śrutāyu, who was cast down to earth in Bhārata.
Two Nalas are particularly renowned in his lineage. 160–161.
Likewise, Vīrasena’s son, the lord of men Nala;
these were kings of great liberality in the lineage of Vivasvat. Thus, those born of the Ikṣvāku dynasty have been proclaimed primarily. 162–163.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Solar Lineage," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Nine.
Bhīṣma said:
"Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme lineage of the ancestors, specifically that of Ravi, Śrāddhadeva, and Soma. Pulastya said:
"Indeed, I shall describe to you the most excellent lineage of the ancestors.
In heaven, there are seven groups of ancestors; three of them are formless (amūrta), while four possess forms (mūrtimant). All of them are possessed of immeasurable splendor."
The formless hosts of Pitṛs belong to Vairāja Prajāpati;
those groups of gods who worship them are renowned as the Vairājas,
and they are those very ones who, having fallen from yoga, attained the eternal worlds.
Furthermore, at the end of a Brahma-day, those who discourse on Brahman are born again;
having regained that same memory, they attain the unsurpassed Yoga and Sāṃkhya,
and through Yoga they reach perfection from which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to find.
Therefore, funeral offerings (śrāddhas) should be given by donors only to yogis.
Among these, the mental daughter of Himavat is considered their wife;
Maināka was his heir, and Krauñca was his son.
By him, Krauñcadvīpa was remembered as the fourth, endowed with stability.
Then Menā gave birth to three daughters who were possessed of yoga:
Umā, Ekaparṇā, and Aparṇā, all of whom were devoted to rigorous vows.
One [daughter] was given by Himavat to Rudra, another to Bhṛgu, and another to Jaigīṣavya—
these young women, who surpassed all the worlds in asceticism.
Now listen as I relate that which is celebrated throughout the world concerning the ancestors.
The worlds known as Somapatha, Nāmayatra, and Mārīcanandana exist there,
where the Pitṛs reside, whom the gods fully honor. They are renowned as the Agniṣvāttas, where the performers of sacrifices dwell.
To them was born a daughter of excellent complexion named Acchodā.
There, a lake called Acchoda had been created by her ancestors in ancient times. Then Acchodā performed divine penance for a thousand years.
The ancestors, being pleased, arrived indeed intending to grant a boon; all of them bore divine forms, wearing celestial garlands and unguents.
All were preeminent and powerful, resembling the god whose weapon is the flower (Kusumāyudha).
In their midst, beholding a man named Āvasu, that woman,
afflicted by the god of love and seeking a boon, chose him as her consort;
yet, having fallen from yoga, that beautiful lady was led astray by his infidelity.
Previously, she had descended to the surface of the earth before the one who touches the food (the Moon);

Because she was beloved by the ancestors, she made whatever was given to them inexhaustible. With her face cast down, dejected and ashamed due to the exhaustion of her asceticism, she prayed to the ancestors for the restoration of her own prosperity.
Then, while she was feeling ashamed before her fathers,
those illustrious ones, beholding her future and your divine purpose, spoke these words to that ascetic woman with voices auspicious with grace.

O woman of excellent complexion, whatever is performed by the wise with a divine body, the fruit of that very action is experienced by them; for actions bear fruit immediately in the state of divinity, and after death in the human state. 21–22.

Therefore, having performed virtuous deeds, you shall obtain that fruit after death; in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from the womb of a fish. However, due to your transgression against the ancestors, you will enter a miserable lineage.
Therefore, you will certainly become the daughter of King Vasu.
In your state as a maiden, you will again attain those celestial worlds that are difficult to reach;
and by the power of Parāśara, you will obtain one son.
Moreover, on the island abounding in jujube trees, your son will divide even Bādarāyaṇa— who possesses the Vedas— into many parts.
Furthermore, there were two sons of Śaṃtanu, who was a portion of the Ocean, born of a woman of the Pūru lineage.
"Vicitravīrya shall be his son, as will King Citrāṅgada. Having produced these two sons as *kṣetraja* offspring for that wise man,
you shall once again go to the world of the ancestors on the day of the Proṣṭhapadā constellation during the Aṣṭakā rites."

In this world, you shall be known by the name Satyavatī; likewise, in the world of the ancestors, you shall be the Aṣṭakā rite, which eternally bestows long life and health and grants the fruit of all desires. In the next world, you shall become a river.
"The most excellent river of meritorious waters in the worlds, named Acchodā"—
having been addressed thus by those hosts of attendants, she vanished right there.
As for her, she experienced the fruit of her misconduct which was previously described by me.
And on another day, those of great splendor dwell in the world named Vibhrāja, where the ancestors who are firm in their vows reside as Barhiṣads;
there, thousands of celestial chariots are yoked upon the sacred grass.
There stand the wish-fulfilling trees that grant fruits;
there the givers of ancestral offerings rejoice in halls of prosperity—those who are the hosts of Dānavas, Asuras, Gandharvas, and Apsarases. 33–34.
Those hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, as well as the deities of heaven,
the sons of Pulastya by the hundreds, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga—
those high-souled and most fortunate ones who grant fearlessness to their devotees— worship him. 35.
Among these, the daughter of Pīvarī, known as Mānasī and renowned throughout the heavens, was a Yoginī and the mother of Yogas; she performed most severe penance.
The Blessed One became pleased with her, and she then chose a boon from him. 36-37.
"O best of speakers, if you are pleased with me, O God, grant me a husband who is endowed with yoga, handsome, and has conquered his senses.
The God replied, "When Śuka becomes the son of Vyāsa, he shall be yours."
That virtuous woman shall become the wife of that teacher of yoga,
Bhavitrī; and that daughter of yours, Kṛttikā, shall then become a yoginī named Sātvatī and be given in marriage to the lord of the Pañcālas.
The mother of Brahmadatta is remembered as Yogasiddhāntā;
Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, and Śambhu will be his sons.
Even while in celestial chariots enriched with all desires, they shall remain pure.
How much more so, then, those faithful Brahmins who possess devotion and are endowed with ritual action?
For them, the daughter named Gau shines in their minds; she is the beloved wife Sukanyā, the increaser of the fame of the Sādhyas.
In the world within the solar orb, there is a place named Marīcigarbha where the ancestors— the sons of Aṅgiras, who are rich in oblations—
reside; there, the best of Kṣatriyas come to offer śrāddha at the sacred ford.

Indeed, they were the fathers of kings who bestow the fruit of enjoyment in heaven. Among them was a daughter born of their mind, renowned by the name Yaśodā; she was the excellent wife of Śuṣmāṇa and the daughter-in-law of Pañcajana.
Then his mother, the great-grandmother of Bhagīratha and daughter of Dilīpa,
[attained] those worlds called Kāmadughā, which bestow the fruit of the enjoyment of all desires;
there her sons, the Pitṛs known as Susvadhās, reside.
In the worlds of the Ājyapās, belonging to Kardama Prajāpati, the Vaiśyas who are the heirs of the elder brother of Pulaha cause them to prosper;
there, all those who have performed śrāddha rites behold them simultaneously upon arrival. 48–49.
Even mothers, brothers, fathers, sisters, friends, relatives, and kinsmen—
seen and experienced thousands of times over tens of thousands of births—
even for these, Virajā was an unknown daughter born from their minds. (50)
She was the co-wife of Nahuṣa and likewise the mother of Yayāti;
later, she became Aṣṭakā and, having gone to the world of Brahmā, remained there as a virtuous being.
These three groups have been described; now I shall speak of the fourth.
The worlds named Sumanas are situated above the world of Brahmā;
there the ancestors of the Somapās dwell eternally (53). All of them are remembered as embodiments of Dharma, existing beyond even Brahmā.
At the end of the dissolution, those yogis who have attained the state of Brahmā,
having performed all the acts of creation and so forth, now remain within his mind;
and among them, there is a daughter named Narmadā, a river flowing with water.
Purifying all beings, that river flows toward the western ocean;
knowing that from it all human beings were fashioned during the creation of progeny, people always perform śrāddha rites with a sense of dharma. 56.
Through his grace alone, there shall be a continuous flow of yoga for those who give at all times.
Furthermore, in the primary creation of the ancestors, the śrāddha was thus ordained;
for all of them, the vessel should be made of silver or associated with silver. 57–58.
Having first offered the *svadhā* invocation, one always gratifies the ancestors;

however, the wise should perform the act of satiation (*āpyāyana*) for the *āgnīdhra* and the *somapa* [deities]. In the absence of fire, however, it may be done in the hand of a Brahmin or even in water.
In the ear of a goat, in the ear of a horse, in a cow-pen, or near a Śiva-liṅga—these are praised as pure places for the ancestors. Furthermore, the southward direction is recommended;
likewise, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), water, sesame seeds, and the arrival [of the guest] are essential.
Meat from the rhinoceros, as well as food consisting of śyāmāka, śāli rice, barley,
nīvāra, mung beans, sugarcane, and white flowers and fruits—
these are always beloved and highly praised by the ancestors in this world.
