I shall now describe the items to be avoided at a Śrāddha: Darbha grass, black gram, sixty-day rice, cow’s milk, honey, and clarified butter;
as well as weapons, and likewise lentils, hemp, flat beans, kidney beans, and horse-gram. (63–64)
The lotus, bilva, arka, dhattūra, pāribhadra, and ṭarūṣaka should not be offered in rites for the ancestors; likewise, goats and sheep [should not be offered].
So too, kodrava, dāru, varaṭa, kapittha, madhuka, and atasī [are forbidden].
These too should not be given to the ancestors by one desiring prosperity. He who gratifies the ancestors with devotion, they in turn gratify him;
the ancestors bestow upon him nourishment, personal health, offspring, and the fruit of his desires.
Furthermore, the rite for the ancestors (pitr-kārya) is superior even to the rite for the gods;
it is traditionally taught that the nourishment of the ancestors precedes that of the deities.
They are quick to grant grace, free from anger, unattached, and firm in their friendship.
The Pitṛs (ancestors) are peaceful-souled, devoted to purity, always speaking kindly, attached to their devotees, bestowers of happiness, and deities on the sacred festival days.
Among those who offer oblations, the Sun is remembered as the presiding deity of the Śrāddha.
Thus has this entire glorification of the lineage of the ancestors been told; it is meritorious, purifying, conducive to health, and should always be recited by men.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard all this once more, supreme devotion arose [in her] regarding the time for the *śrāddha*, the ritual procedure, and the *śrāddha* itself;
as well as which twice-born men are to be fed at the *śrāddhas* and which twice-born men are to be excluded from the *śrāddhas*.

At what part of the day should one begin the Śrāddha for the ancestors? O best among the knowers of Brahman, how does the food offered in the Śrāddha proceed? By what rite should it be performed, and how does it gratify those ancestors? (73–74)
Pulastya said:
One should perform the śrāddha rite day after day with food and water,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
The śrāddha is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and for the fulfillment of desires (kāmya).

First, I shall describe the daily rite, which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana). One should know that the pārvaṇa rite, performed on the lunar festival days (parvan), is likewise without the deity (adaivata).
O Lord of the Earth, listen with care: the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha] is said to be of three kinds.
O King, hear now those who are to be appointed for the Pārvaṇa: one who maintains the five fires, a Snātaka, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, and one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas. 77–78.

A learned scholar of the Vedas (*śrotriya*), the son of a learned scholar, proficient in the words of the injunctions, omniscient, possessing the Vedas, a minister, endowed with knowledge, lineage, and noble family; one who has performed the *Trināciketa* and *Trimadhu* sacrifices, and established himself in other sacred scriptures. (79)
One who knows the Purāṇas, a knower of Brahman, devoted to Vedic study, intent on silent recitation (japa),
a devotee of Brahman, devoted to the ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava—
a Brāhmaṇa whose soul is established in yoga, who has conquered his self, and who is of virtuous character— (80-81).
These should be honored with effort; now hear those who are to be avoided:
an outcast, his son, a eunuch, a slanderer, one who is deformed, and one who is diseased—82. All these must be excluded at the time of the śrāddha by those who perceive the dharma.
On the previous day or on the following day, one should invite those who are disciplined.
Once invited, the ancestors approach those twice-born guests in the form of wind; they follow them as they move and wait upon them as they sit.
Touching the right knee and lowering the left, he should invite them, saying:
"In this śrāddha rite, you must remain free from anger, devoted to purity, well-bathed, and exponents of the Veda,
just as I myself shall be."
Having completed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), one who maintains the sacred fires should perform the rite known as tarpaṇa; likewise,
when the moon is waning, he should perform the Śrāddha called Piṇḍānvāhāryaka on a site smeared with cow dung that slopes toward the south.

One should begin the *śrāddha* with devotion either in a cow-pen or near water; one who maintains the sacred fire should offer the ancestral oblation (*pitrya*) as a sacrificial pap (*caru*) or with handfuls of groats (*saktu*).
Reciting "I offer this to the ancestors," he should place everything toward the south.
Then, having performed the sprinkling of clarified butter, one should make three offerings (nirvāpa) in front.

(89) Those [offerings] should be made one span (vitasti) long and four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) wide; and one should prepare three ladles (darvī) made of khadira wood and adorned with silver. (90)
A vessel one *ratni* in measure, exceedingly smooth, with a handle shaped like a hand;
water-pots made of bell-metal, a stirring-spoon, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass;
vessels for sesame seeds, fine garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments.

He should bring everything slowly to the right, keeping his left shoulder uncovered (apasavya). Having thus brought all that inside the northern part of the house, he should prepare a maṇḍala on ground smeared with cow dung and sprinkled with cow urine.
Having saluted them again and again, he should wash the feet of the Brahmins with water containing raw rice grains and flowers, using his right hand for the right foot and his left hand for the left.
Once they are seated upon their seats provided with Darbha grass according to the prescribed rules, [he should proceed].
Having seated the Brahmins who have sipped water, he should address them with mantras.

(95) He should feed two at the rite for the gods and three at the rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two; even a wealthy person, being wise, should not make the gathering too large here. (96)
Having first offered [the oblation] to the gods, the wise should then honor the Brahmins with the *argha* offering and other honors;

then, permitted by the Brahmins, the Brahmin should perform the rite in the fire according to the rules, having performed it entirely according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. 97.
The wise man should perform the act of satiation (*āpyāyana*) with the portions for Agni and Soma.
O best of the twice-born, that very fire which was brought forward into the *dakṣiṇāgni* is [the same];
then, having removed the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), he should perform the sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*) and other rites. 98–99.
All this should be performed by one who knows [the ritual] while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
Having obtained [the site], he should especially prepare the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and offer water;
he should pour out the water with vessels for water using his left hand.
One who is free from envy and disciplined should give everything with effort.
Having carefully drawn the lines, one should perform the pouring of water for washing (avanejana) while facing south; then, having indeed placed the darbha grass, one should proceed. 101–102.
Having placed each individual piṇḍa upon all the darbha grass in sequence,
he should then offer [libations] upon the darbha grass while reciting the names and lineages (gotra).
He should wipe that hand upon those darbha grasses for the sake of the "smear-partakers" (lepabhāgin).
In that same manner, one should perform the recitation (japa) and again the ritual rinsing (pratyavanejana).
Having offered water along with salutations, perfumes, incense, worship, and so forth,
one should thus invoke all of that by means of the Vedic mantras as prescribed.
One who maintains only the single sacred fire (ekāgni) should likewise offer the oblation with water using a ladle;

then, having done so, the wise man should offer kuśa grass to the ancestors. Thereafter, he should perform the rites of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and so forth, including the invocation (āvāhana) and the dismissal (visarjana).
Then, having taken portions from the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in due order for all his mothers,
the man, having first caused those same Brahmins to rinse their mouths, should always feed them the desired, pure food while describing its qualities. 107–108.
Remembering Nārāyaṇa Hari, one should avoid being overcome by anger;
having ascertained that they are satisfied, one should again perform the scattering of food (vikira) for all castes.
Having set aside a portion of the food along with water and sesame seeds, one should cast it upon the ground.
Once they have sipped water, one should again offer water along with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should perform the entire rite of pronouncing "svadhā" over the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). One should conclude [the rite] beginning with the deities; otherwise, the śrāddha will be ruined. 110–111.
Having dismissed the Brahmins after bowing to them and circumambulating them, the man,
with his face turned toward the southern direction and intent upon his ancestors, should say:
"May our donors prosper, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
"May faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give;
may our food be abundant, and may we receive guests; may there be those who ask of us, but may we never have to ask anything of anyone. (113-114)
This is declared for one who maintains the sacred fire; however, the *anvāhārya* rite of the *parvan* is performed just as when the moon wanes, and it is likewise prescribed in other cases.
One should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to cows, horses, or Brahmins, or even into the fire or into water.
Or he should scatter it on the edge of the mound, or he should cause water to flow over it.
Then, with humility, he should have his wife eat the middle piṇḍa, saying:
"O ancestors, bestow a fetus that increases the lineage of sons. (116-117)
One should remain until the extinguishing of the fires, or until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
then, having concluded the rites for the ancestors, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Afterwards, being peaceful and accompanied by loved ones, one should eat what was offered to the ancestors.

Furthermore, one who performs a *śrāddha* or eats at a *śrāddha* should always avoid these: eating a second time, traveling on foot, riding in a vehicle, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, reciting the Vedas, quarreling, and sleeping during the day. (119–120)
By this procedure, one should always perform the Śrāddha for the three groups [of ancestors] during the dark fortnights whenever the moon is situated in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus;
wherever the rite consisting of Sapindīkaraṇa is to be offered.
In this matter, one who maintains the sacred fire should always give according to this procedure.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which was declared by Brahmā:
the Śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
During the solstices and the equinoxes, on the new moon day, during the sun’s passage into a new sign, on the new moon, the Aṣṭaka days, and the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight;
during the lunar mansions of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; and upon encountering a worthy Brāhmaṇa.
On the day of Gajacchāyā, during Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti; on the third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika, the fifteenth of Māgha,
and the thirteenth of Nabhasya.
These are indeed remembered as the Yugādis (beginnings of the ages), which are beneficial for the ancestral rites (pitṛpakṣa);
likewise, a wise person should offer śrāddha at the beginning of the Manvantaras and other such times.
Also, on the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja and the twelfth day of Kārttika;
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada;
the new moon of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh of Pauṣa; the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh of the month of Māgha. (128–129)
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the full moon of Kārttika, the full moon of Phālguna, and the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha—
these are the beginnings of the Manvantaras, which cause what is given on them to become inexhaustible.
A self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors here;
by him a Śrāddha is performed for a thousand years—this is the secret that the ancestors declare regarding fasts on the full moon of Vaiśākha, as well as festivals and the Mahālaya rite. 131–132.
A wise person should offer the śrāddha at sacred fords, shrines, cow-pens, islands, gardens, or houses, in secluded places that have been smeared with cow-dung.
On the previous day and on the following day, he should invite Brahmins who are self-disciplined.
One should feed two who are endowed with virtue, conduct, and good qualities, and possessed of noble lineage, youth, and beauty, at the rite for the gods;
three at the rite for the ancestors; or one at each of the two.
Even if one is very wealthy, one should not perform an elaborate feast.
Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, preceded by the offering of a seat,
one should fill two vessels and place them upon *darbha* grass purifiers. One should pour water with the mantra "śanno devī" and likewise offer barley with the mantra "yavo'si."
Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with perfumes and flowers, one should assign them [to their places].
Having invoked them with the two verses beginning with "viśvedevāsaḥ," one should scatter barley grains, [reciting]:
"Thou art barley, the king of grains; thou art the offspring of Varuṇa, mixed with honey. (137–138)
The dispeller of all sins, the purifier praised by the sages—
having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should offer the *argha* water with the mantra "yā divyā.
(39) Having worshipped and offered the perfumes and other items, one should commence the *pitṛyajña*.
Having first prepared the darbha seats and so forth, one should worship three vessels.
Having first placed pavitra-strainers in them, one should pour water with the mantra "śanno devīḥ.
Then, one should place sesame seeds with the mantra "tilosi," followed by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. 140–141.
One should likewise prepare a vessel made of wood, or again one made of leaves, or one of silver, or even one originating from the ocean.
A vessel of gold, silver, or copper is said to be suitable for the ancestors.
Even the mere mention of silver, as well as its sight and gift, [is beneficial].
For these ancestors, even water given with faith in silver vessels accompanied by silver leads to inexhaustible results. 144
Even today, silver is included among the vessels for the ancestors because it originated from the eye of Śiva; it is the most excellent and is beloved by the Pitṛs. 145.
Thus, having consecrated the vessels according to one's availability, one should remain free from envy.

Having placed darbha grass in his hand while reciting the father's name and lineage with the words "yādivyeti," and having been told again by those [brahmins], "So be it," he should then invoke the ancestors with the two ṛg verses beginning with "uśantas tvā" and "āyantu naḥ. (146–147)
Having offered the *arghya* water with the mantra "yā divyā," one should then present the perfumes (*gandha*) and other offerings;
having first given a seat consisting of a cloth followed by *darbha* grass, one should place it upon the vessel for the ancestors and then set it face down to the north.
Having placed [the vessel] with the mantra "pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi," one should serve the food.
Therein, too, one who is free from envy should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) first;
then, having taken [the food] with both hands, one should serve it. 149–150.
With the mantra "uśantas tvā," one should especially offer darbha grass held in the hand,
along with various vegetables and diverse edibles endowed with excellent qualities; likewise,
food accompanied by fresh curd, cow's ghee, and sugar.
The Lotus-born One has declared that one satisfies all the ancestors for one month with the meat of fish,
for two months with the meat of deer, for three months with the meat of the antelope, for four months with the meat of sheep, and for five months with the meat of birds. (152–153)
With the meat of a boar, there is excellent satisfaction for six months;
likewise with the meat of the seven metals and with that of a goat for eight months; and with the meat of a spotted deer, satisfaction lasts for nine months indeed.
They are satisfied for ten months with the flesh of boars and buffaloes;
for eleven months with the meat of rabbits and tortoises; and for a full year with cow’s milk or milk-rice (pāyasa).
They are satisfied for fifteen months by the meat of the common pig (saukara), while the satisfaction from the meat of the Vārdhrīṇasa lasts for twelve years; furthermore,
there is indeed infinite satisfaction from the Kālaśāka vegetable and the meat of the rhinoceros (khaḍga).
Whatever cow’s milk mixed with honey, curd, or milk-rice (pāyasa) is offered,
the ancestors— the deities of old— declare that it becomes inexhaustible.
One should cause the recitation of the ancestral Vedic study (svādhyāya) and all the Purāṇas.

One should recite, according to one's ability, the various hymns dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka (the Sun), and Rudra, as well as the Indra-sūkta, the Soma-sūktas, and the Pāvamānī verses; furthermore,
the Bṛhat, Rathantara, Jyeṣṭhasāman, and Atharva-raiva.

In the same manner, he should recite the Chapter on Peace (Aśāntikādhyāya), the Madhu Brāhmaṇa, and likewise the Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa, as well as whatever else may cause delight to the Brahmins and to himself; all of that he should proclaim. (161–162)

O King, the study of the *Bhārata* should be performed, for it is most dear to the ancestors; and when the Brahmins have finished eating, one should bring food, water, and other offerings from all social classes (varṇas) with great care. (163)
One should scatter food remnants on the ground before those who have finished eating:

"May those beings in my family who were cremated by fire, as well as those not yet cremated, be satisfied by what is given upon this earth; and being satisfied, may they attain the supreme goal. (164-165)

May this food, given on earth for the satisfaction of those who have neither mother nor father, nor kinsmen, nor friends, nor even sustenance, and who died uninitiated or were abandoned by their families— may it go to them from wherever they may be, for the sake of their spiritual union (yoga). 166.
The scattering of food (vikiro) upon the darbha grass is the seat for those who are entitled to the remnants.
Having known them to be satiated, one should offer water once over the scattered food; likewise, the surface of the ground should be smeared with cow dung, urine, and water.
Having carefully placed the darbha grass with their tips pointing south according to the prescribed rule, a person should,

in accordance with the regulations for all castes, offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) like those in the Pitṛyajña, preceded by the ritual sprinkling (avanejana) and the utterance of the names and lineages.
Having spoken thus, having offered flowers and other items, and having performed the ritual rinsing (pratyavanejana),

one should know that for the mother, just as for the fathers, the rite must be performed according to the rules with the sacred grass (darbha) in hand, circling three times clockwise while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) with the left hand.
The wise man should perform the lighting of the lamp and the worship with flowers in that same manner;

likewise, having sipped water (ācamana) at the end, he should offer water once for each [deity]. Then, he should offer flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and finally the water for inexhaustibility (akṣayyodaka).
One should give [the gift] along with sesame seeds, mentioning the name and lineage, and offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
One should give cows, land, gold, garments, auspicious items, and beds— whatever is desired by the Brahmins, as well as for oneself and for one’s father.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should bring satisfaction to the ancestors;
then, after giving water for the *svadhā* invocation to the ancestors and the Viśvedevas,
the wise man should likewise receive blessings from the twice-born.
"May the ancestors be non-terrible; may they be peaceful," thus addressed again by the twice-born;
"May the lineage likewise increase," and being answered by them in turn, "So be it," he should perform the recitation for well-being after respectfully lifting the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
The remnants of the meal should remain until the dismissal of the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—such is the established rule of dharma.
The remnants that have fallen upon the ground belong to one who is straightforward and free from deceit.
They declare that the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for that group of servants is their allotted portion.
O lord of men, this nourishment was ordained of old by the ancestors for those who have not observed vows, for those without sons, and even for women. 179–180.
Then, standing before that place and taking up a small water-vessel,
he should dismiss [the deities] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while muttering the mantra "vāje vāje.
He should perform a circumambulation outside and follow [them] for eight steps.

Accompanied by his circle of kinsmen and joined by his sons and wife, having returned and prostrated, he who knows the mantras should then attend to the fire and perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the daily bali offering.

Then, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, he should eat together with his servants, sons, kinsmen, and guests; all that which has been partaken by the ancestors [should be eaten]. (184) Even one who is uninitiated (anupanīta) should perform this on all festival days (parvan).

This common Śrāddha, O King, bestows the fruits of all desires; even one who is separated from his wife, or one living in exile, or even a Śūdra, may perform it with devotion according to this rite, provided he does so without mantras. 185.
The third type, the *ābhyudayika* or *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, is prescribed [for occasions such as]:
festivals, joyful ceremonies, sacraments, sacrifices, marriages, and other auspicious events.
First the Mothers are to be worshipped, and immediately after them, the Fathers.
Then, O Great King, one should offer the piṇḍas for the maternal grandfather and likewise for the Viśvedevas,
with a clockwise ritual procedure using curd, unbroken rice, fruits, and water; facing eastward, one should present both the previous and the ancient piṇḍas.
Saying "It is prepared," one should offer the *arghya* water for prosperity in pairs.
The twice-born should be honored in pairs with garments, ornaments, clothing, and so forth.
The *tilaka* rite should be performed with barley, and that should be done for all in successive order.
One should cause the best of the twice-born to recite all auspicious hymns;
likewise, even a Śūdra should always perform the ordinary *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and various acts of giving with the mantra of obeisance (*namaskāra*).
191. A wise man should indeed perform these gifts with the *namaskāra* mantra.
"The Lord, the Master, has declared that for a Śūdra, charity is the foremost duty,
because through charity, the attainment of all desires arises for him.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of General Prosperity," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Tenth Chapter.
Pulastya said:
Thereafter, I shall describe the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, as it was formerly declared by Brahmā.
If the father must perform the funeral rites for his deceased sons, the period of impurity is as follows:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) is ordained to last ten days; for Kṣatriyas it is twelve days, and for Vaiśyas it is indeed a fortnight.
For a Śūdra, impurity lasting ten days is prescribed for sapinda relatives; for those below the tonsure ceremony, it is one night, and beyond that, it is remembered as three nights.
In the case of birth as well, it shall be exactly the same for all castes at all times.
After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
One should perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased for twelve days;
that is declared to be his provision for the journey, as it brings him great satisfaction.
Since the deceased is led to the city of the departed after twelve days,
and the son and wife remain beholding him at home for twelve days, therefore milk should be placed in the open air for ten nights.
For the sake of pacifying all burning afflictions and destroying the fatigue of the journey;
then, on the eleventh day, a person should feed eleven brahmins, beginning from the time the period of impurity (sūtaka) regarding their lineage and so forth has ended. 7–8.
On the second day, one should again perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite in the same manner, according to the rules;

it is devoid of the invocation (āvāhana), the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and the deities (daiva). Only one purifier (pavitra), one water-offering (argha), and one funeral cake (piṇḍa) are prescribed.
One should say, "May it attend upon [the ancestors]," and afterwards, the water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) should be given.
One should say "Svasti" when the water is poured into the hands of the Brahmins, and at the conclusion, "May you be delighted.
Those who know the Vedas understand that the remaining rites here also should be performed as previously described.
One should perform all this according to this procedure every month;
at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), on the second day, one should give a distinctive bed, as well as a golden man accompanied by fruits and garments. 12.
Having honored a brahmin couple adorned with various ornaments and having seated them upon a bed, he should then offer the *madhuparka*—
consisting of curd and milk— in a silver vessel. 13–14.
Having taken a small amount from the forehead bone and having mixed it, one should,
endowed with devotion to the ancestors, cause a Brāhmaṇa couple to drink it. This very procedure is observed by the best of the twice-born in the Pārvatīya region.
Therefore, that bed, being defiled by a woman in her courses and unfit to be accepted by the best of the twice-born,
requires a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once it has been taken;
for in both the Vedas and the Purāṇas, such a bed is everywhere censured.
All those who take [such a bed] become destined for hell;
those who, being ignorant, touch a bed woven with a net of wealth and used by a husband and wife—all of them go to hell. 18.
One should not eat at a *navaśrāddha*; having eaten there, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Out of devotion to the ancestors, sons should always perform these rites;
they should also perform the *vṛṣotsarga* (the rite of releasing a bull) and give away an auspicious tawny cow (*kapilā*).
O best of men, a water-pot filled with food, edibles, and fruits should be given for a year, preceded by water and sesame seeds; thereafter,
when the year is complete, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite shall take place.
Since after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite the deceased partakes in the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha],
the householder should then perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha, preceded by the deities, during rites such as those for prosperity (*vṛddhi*). 22–23.
One should invoke the ancestors there, designating the deceased (preta) separately;
one should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds.
For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the contents of the preta-vessel into the vessels of the ancestors.
In that same manner, being intent on the ancestors, he should then mentally conceive four pindas;
with the two verses beginning "yesamānāḥ," he should divide the food into three parts.
According to this procedure, he should first cause the arghya water to be offered.

Then, having attained the status of a father, he at that time becomes the fourth among those such as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs and attains supreme immortality. After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, offerings are given to him separately.
That piṇḍa must be given specifically to those among the paternal ancestors to whom it belongs.
From that time forward, one should perform the Śrāddha with three piṇḍas on occasions such as the Saṃkrānti and eclipses; however, on the anniversary of death, the Ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed.

One who performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) while neglecting [the *pārvaṇa*] will always cause the laughter of the ancestors and likewise bring about the destruction of his brother.
A man of equal status who performs the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of death goes to hell.

Since the liberation of the deceased occurs when there is a union with the state of heaven, the giver of the śrāddha who knows the ritual rules should then perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food). He should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) with that [raw food] and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) with that very same substance. 31–32.
When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed after three months, one month, or three years,
then at that time, by the power of time, he shall be released from bondage. Even though liberated, he attains a share in the merit through the cleansing with *kuśa* grass.
The three beginning with the fourth [descendant] are partakers of the lepa (the smearings of the funeral cake); they are the partakers of the piṇḍa (the funeral cakes).
The giver of the piṇḍa is the seventh among them; thus, there are seven generations of sapindas.
Bhīṣma said:
How are the *havyas* (offerings to the gods) and *kavyas* (offerings to the ancestors) given here by people in this world?

By whom are they generally said to receive them in the world of the ancestors? Whether a twice-born man eats [the food] among mortals or whether it is offered into the fire—[how does it reach them]? 35–36.
"How do the pretas, who are of both auspicious and inauspicious nature, consume that food?
Pulastya said:
"The ancestors are of the nature of the Vasus, and the grandfathers are the Rudras. (37)
"The great-grandfathers are likewise the Ādityas"—this is the Vedic revelation;
for it provides the names and lineages of the ancestors for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
Through devotion, one may thus perceive the true essence of the Śrāddha through its mantras.
The Agniṣvātta and other ancestors are established as the presiding deities over them;
their names and lineages serve as the designations for those beings who are being born, and this [offering] which has arrived is worthy of pleasing the living beings. 39–40.

If one's father, mother, or preceptor, through the influence of their past actions, attains a divine state, then the food [offered] to them becomes nectar and follows them even in that divine condition. If they are in the state of a Daitya, it takes the form of enjoyment; if in the state of a beast, it becomes grass.
The food of a *śrāddha* ceremony attends upon one even in the state of a serpent in the form of wind;
it becomes drink in the state of a Yakṣa, and likewise meat in the state of a Rākṣasa; it becomes drink in the state of a Dānava, and blood-water in the state of a Preta.

For those who possess human status along with various enjoyments such as food and drink, there arises the power of pleasure toward a beloved woman; for others, there is the power of eating, the power of giving, as well as wealth, beauty, and health. (44)
This is declared to be the flower of the Śrāddha, and its fruit is union with Brahman.
O King, when the hosts of ancestors are pleased, they bestow longevity, sons, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and likewise sovereignty. 45–46.
It is heard that the sons of Kauśika attained liberation from the city [of rebirth] and,
through five successive births, reached the supreme state of Brahman.
Bhīṣma said:
"How, O Kauśika, did the heirs attain the unsurpassed yoga? Through how many connections of births does the destruction of karma occur? Pulastya said:
The great ṛṣi named Kauśika, whose nature was dharma, dwelt in Kurukṣetra;
learn from me now of his sons by name and by deed:
Svasṛpa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, and Kavi. 49.
At that time, there were those who were corrupt in speech, those who remained devoted to their fathers, and the disciples of Garga.
When their father passed away, a severe famine occurred for them,
along with a great drought that struck fear into all the world.
"Those whose wealth is their asceticism protect cows such as Gargā and Vanedogdhṛ;
we, however, being greatly oppressed by hunger, shall eat this Kapilā cow.
While they were thus contemplating this sin, the younger brother spoke briefly.
If she must necessarily be employed in the form of a *śrāddha* offering,
then by being employed in that *śrāddha*, her sin will certainly perish.
Thus permitted by his younger brothers, he then acted according to the wishes of his father.

Having concentrated his mind on the *cakra* and partaken of that [food], the giver of the *śrāddha* should then again assign two brothers for the gods (*daiva*) and three others for the ancestors (*pitrya*) in due order;
likewise, he himself should designate one as the guest (*atithi*).
Remembering the *śrāddha* rite with the syllable "ca" as the mantra, he remained devoted to his ancestors. Then, having arrived free from suspicion, they reported it to the Guru:
"The cow has been killed by a tiger; let this calf be accepted. (56–57)
Thus, having consumed that cow, those seven ascetics,
relying on the power of the Vedas, fearlessly performed cruel deeds.
Then, in the course of time, they perished and became hunters in Daśapura.

Having been imbued with the disposition toward their ancestors, they attained the recollection of their former births (jātismaratva). There, perceiving dispassion (vairāgya), they righteously cast off their lives at the edge of the sacred ford (tīrtha) by means of fasting (anaśana), while remaining unobserved by the world.
Having assumed the forms of deer on Mount Kālañjara,
they attained the yoga of realized wisdom and abandoned their own bodies; then, with minds born of world-weariness, they died by leaping down.
From the Mānasa lake, seven yogins were born as rākṣasas:
by name and by deed, they were all Sumanas, Kusuma, Vasu, Cittadarśin, Sudarśin, Jñāta, and Jñānapāraga. 62–63.
Devoted to their eldest brother, these seven were the most excellent and purifiers through yoga;
however, three among them became fallen from yoga due to their wavering minds.
Seeing that Aṇuha shining resplendently accompanied by women, [they were filled with envy].
One among those water-dwellers, born of the Pāñcāla lineage, possessed of great strength and prowess, sporting with various enjoyments and having abundant forces and vehicles,
became desirous of sovereignty. (65–66)
A brahmin who was devoted to his father, performed ancestral rites, and was affectionate toward his elders,
as well as two other ministers with vast armies and vehicles— those two best of the twice-born, seeing him, desired the office of minister in that mortal realm.
The sole son of Vibhrāja became known as Brahmadatta; likewise, there were two sons of ministers, Puṇḍarīka and Subālaka.
Brahmadatta was consecrated in the excellent city of Kāmpilya.
The King of Pañcāla was valiant, devoted to the ancestral rites, and affectionate toward his father;
at that time, he was a knower of yoga and one who understood the minds of all living beings.
At that time, the King had a wife who was the daughter of Sudeva.

In former times, there was a woman renowned by the name Sannati, who was the daughter of Kapila; because she was appointed to perform the ancestral rites, she became a knower of Brahman (brahmavādinī).
With her, the prince ruled over the entire kingdom together with his ministers.
Once, while the king was in the company of that woman, having gone to a garden,
he saw a pair of insects engaged in a love-quarrel;
the female ant was facing downward, while the male insect stood before her.
With his limbs tormented by the five arrows [of love], he spoke with a faltering voice:
"There is no woman like you anywhere in the world; you have slender waists, broad hips, large eyes, and a most graceful gait. (74-75)
With a face resembling the color of gold and a beautiful smile, her countenance appears as sweet as molasses and sugar;
she says: "When I have eaten, you shall eat; likewise, when I have bathed, you shall bathe. (76)
"While I am away you are dejected, and when I am angry you are trembling with fear.
For what reason, O auspicious one, do you remain with your face cast down? She said to him, blazing with anger: "What are you saying, O rogue? (77-78)
"O Manmatha, you have indeed consumed the powder of the sweetmeat even while leaving me aside; having bypassed me, you gave it to another woman.
The ant said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, O beautiful woman, you ought to forgive this one offense of mine, committed toward another through my resemblance to you.
I shall not do so again; thus [I speak], O lady of beautiful breasts, free from anger."
"I touch your feet with truth; be gracious to me who am prostrate before you. O lady of beautiful hips, if you are angry, death will stand before me;
but if you are pleased, O lovely-thighed one, all my heart's desires will be fulfilled."

"O lady of beautiful hips, drink deeply and always from my mouth, which resembles the full moon and tastes like the essence of nectar, for I am ever attached to you. Thinking this, O auspicious one, you must always show compassion toward me."
Having heard these words, she then became filled with faith. Then, in order to delude her, he transformed himself into an ant;
Brahmadatta, having understood all of this, laughed and said: (84–85)
"Through the power of his previous karma, he possessed knowledge of the cries of all sentient beings.
Bhīṣma said: "How did King Brahmadatta become a knower of all sounds? (86)
"And furthermore, there was once a group of four *cakravāka* birds somewhere; tell me that, O Knower of All, and who among them was the one of excellent vows?
Pulastya said:
In that very city, O King, there were born four sons of an aged Brahmin who was a wise knower of his past lives:
Dhṛtimān, Tattvadarśin, Vidyāvarṇa, and Tapodhika. (88–89)

"O sons, because of their names and their actions, they shall indeed become very poor. Then, O twice-born ones, the thought of performing ascetic penance arose in those best of the twice-born, and they said, "We shall attain supreme perfection."
Having heard those words of theirs, Sudaridra, who was performing great austerities, spoke in a piteous voice: "What is this, my sons? "This is unrighteousness, father," they replied to him. 91-92.

"Having abandoned your aged father, who is poor and lives in the forest, where indeed will your dharma be now, having forsaken both him and your own refuge? They replied, "We have provided for your livelihood; listen to your father's words."

"O King, this is the vow: he who recites it at dawn shall receive abundant wealth and thousands of villages. Furthermore, those Brahmins who are in Kurukṣetra and those who are in the city of Daśapura—" 94-95.
"Having become deer at Kālañjara and cakravāka birds at Lake Mānasa," having said this to their father, they went again to the forest for the sake of penance (96).
O King, even though he was old, that virtuous twice-born man departed to achieve his own purpose.
In ancient times, Aṇuha, the lord of Pañcāla, known as Vaibhrāja,
being desirous of a son, propitiated the omnipresent Grandfather, the lotus-born Lord of the gods, by devoting himself to rigorous vows. (97-98)
Then, after a long time, his grandfather was pleased and said, "O King, choose a boon, whatever is desired in your heart; may it be well with you.
Aṇuha replied:
O Lord of Gods, grant me a son of great strength and prowess,
one who has mastered all branches of knowledge, who is righteous, the best among yogis,
and who understands the cries of all living beings— grant me such a son, a true yogi. 100.
"So be it," the Supreme Lord, the Soul of the Universe, said to him;
while all beings were looking on, he vanished right there.
Then, a powerful son named Brahmadatta was born to him. 101–102.
Compassionate toward all sentient beings, surpassing all sentient beings in strength, knowing the cries of all sentient beings, and the Lord of the lords of all sentient beings—
then that yogic soul arrived as an ant.
Where that pair of insects remained sporting, Sannati,
having seen him laughing and greatly amazed,
and suspecting something, questioned that lord of men. 105.
Sannati said:
"O King, why has this sudden, excessive laughter occurred?
I do not know the cause of your laughter, since it was produced by you at an improper time. (106)
The son of Rājaputra spoke thus: "O fair-faced one, this speech of the ant arose from passion and was unpleasant; O lady of pure smiles, there is no other cause whatsoever for this laughter. (107)
She reflected on that; then the goddess said: "This of yours is false. I alone am laughed at here; I shall not live with you now.
How can a mortal understand the chatter of an ant, except for a god? (108-109)
"Therefore, I alone have been laughed at by you today; what more than this could there be?
Then the king, rendered speechless and desiring to know the truth of Hari's words, remained for seven nights observing a vow, free from all impurity.
At the end of his dream, Brahmā spoke to him; wandering through the city at dawn, he said, "O best of the aged twice-born, your beloved shall know everything.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished, and at dawn the king departed from the city.
As he was departing accompanied by his ministers and his wife, he saw an elderly Brahmin approaching before him, speaking as he came. (113) The Brahmin said:
"The foremost of the Yavyas dwell in Kurujāṅgala; the Dāśas in Dāśapura; the Mṛgas on Mount Kālañjara; and the seven Cakravākas are the Siddhas who reside on Lake Mānasa.
Having heard these words of his, he fell down, overcome with grief.
Those two sons of the best of the three mantrins attained the memory of their past births.
Bābhravya, however, was the author of the Kāmaśāstra; he was known as Bālaka and was celebrated throughout the worlds as Pañcāla, a knower of all scriptures.
Puṇḍarīka also, though virtuous in nature and a promoter of the Vedas and scriptures,
having become one who remembered his former births, fell down before him out of grief; we two, too, fallen from our state through the bondage of karma born of desire, were lamenting.
Having lamented thus at length, those three, who had mastered the yoga of weapons,
marveled again and again at the greatness of the śrāddha; and having praised him, they gave him wealth along with many villages.
Having dismissed that aged brāhmaṇa who was filled with the gift of wealth,
the king consecrated his own son, named Viṣvaksena, who possessed the marks of royalty, upon the throne.

Then, in that lake of Mānasa, all those foremost of yogins—Brahmadatta and the others—were devoted to their father, free from envy, and full of joy; and a prostration occurred, as it were, shown by me to you. 121–122.
"O King, all this fruit of yoga which is now perceived—'so be it,' the King replied, welcoming him from the front. 'By your grace alone is all this fruit thus obtained by me. (123-124)
Then, all those forest-dwellers, having resorted to yoga,
attained the supreme state through the aperture of Brahma by the power of their asceticism.
Thus [are obtained] life-span, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness.
When satisfied, the ancestors bestow sons and sovereignty upon men. O King,
a wise man who causes this majesty of the ancestors to be heard by the twice-born, or who hears it himself, or even recites it, [attains great merit].
For more than a hundred crores of kalpas, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.
127. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Ancestors," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eleven.
Bhīṣma said:
At what part of the day should one who performs a śrāddha perform the śrāddha?
And at which sacred fords (tīrthas), O twice-born one, does a performed śrāddha yield great fruit?
Pulastya said:
There is a sacred ford named Puṣkara, which is remembered as the most excellent of all,
standing like the fulfilled desire of all the foremost of the twice-born.
There, what is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted becomes certainly infinite;
it is eternally dear to the ancestors and highly esteemed by the sages. Likewise, there are the Nandā and Lalitā, as well as the auspicious holy site of Māyāpurī.
Likewise, O King, is the station of Amitrapada, and beyond that is the supreme Kedāra. They call Gaṅgāsāgara auspicious, for it consists of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Similarly, there is the Brahmasaras and the auspicious waters of the Śatadru.
The sacred ford named Naimiṣa bestows the fruit of all holy places; there,
at Gaṅgodbheda on the Gomatī, the eternal Lord Yajñavarāha and the trident-bearing God of gods appeared.
Where that gift of gold was given by Hara, who has eighteen arms;
and where, in ancient times, the rim of the Wheel of Dharma became worn out—
that is this Naimiṣa forest, frequented by all sacred fords.
There, one who beholds the God of gods and Varāha becomes purified in soul and shall go to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
Kokāmukha is a supreme tīrtha, and the path of Indra is also seen there.
Moreover, there is the Pitṛ-tīrtha of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
situated in the Puṣkara forest is that Lord, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
where the vision of Viriñci is supreme and bestows the fruit of liberation.
The place named Kṛtaṇāma is of great merit and the destroyer of all sins, where Janārdana himself appeared as the primordial Nārasiṃha;
there is also the Ikṣumatī river, which brings auspiciousness to the ancestors. 12.
The ancestors are eternally gratified at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Kurukṣetra is a place of great merit where even the path [to heaven] is visible;
even today, it is a sacred ford for the ancestors that bestows the fruits of all desires.
O lord of men, there is the sacred ford known as Pitṛtīrtha, famous as Nīlakaṇṭha;
likewise the meritorious Bhadrasaras and Lake Mānasa;
as well as the Mandākinī, the Acchodā, the Vipāśā, and the Sarasvatī.
Likewise, Sarvamitra-pada, Vaidyanātha which yields great fruit (16),
the Kṣiprā river, the Puṇya [river], the auspicious Kālañjara,
Tīrthodbheda, Harodbheda, Garbhabheda, and Mahālaya (17).
O blessed lady, the great sages have declared that Bhadreśvara, Viṣṇupada, and Narmadādvāra are equal to Gayā in terms of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
These are sacred sites for the ancestors and destroyers of all sins.
Even for people who merely remember them, [what merit shall they gain], let alone those who offer ancestral rites (śrāddha)?
Oṃkāra, Pitṛtīrtha, the Kāverī with its Kapila waters, the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka—[these are the holy places]. 19–20.
Bathing and other rites performed there shall yield twice the merit of Kurukṣetra.
That place is renowned as Śuklatīrtha, and Someśvara is a supreme holy site;
it removes all diseases, is meritorious, and its fruit is more than ten million times greater.
During the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), the giving of gifts, burnt offerings (homa), and even during Vedic study, the name of the trident-bearing God of gods was present;
his incarnation known as Rocamāna appeared in the auspicious abode of the Brāhmaṇas. 22-23.
Jātataḥ, Sumahāpuṇya, as well as the river Carmaṇvatī, Śūlatāpī, Payoṣṇī, and likewise the confluence of the Payoṣṇī;
Mahauṣadhī, Cāraṇā, and Nāgatīrtha-pravartinī.
The Mahāveṇā river is meritorious, as is the Great Śāla;
likewise the Gomatī and Varuṇa, and the supreme holy site of Hautāśana; also Bhairava, Bhṛgutuṅga, and the unsurpassed Gaurī-tīrtha. 25–26.
The holy site named Vaināyaka, the unsurpassed Vastraśvara, as well as the one called Pāpahara, the meritorious river Vetravatī,
the great Rudra, the great Liṅga, and the great river Daśārṇā. 27.
The Śatarudrā, the Śatāhvā, as well as the city of the Pitṛs;
likewise the Aṅgāravāhikā, and the two rivers Śoṇa and Gharghara; the meritorious river Kālikā and the auspicious river Pitarā. 28–29.
These are also praised as sacred fords (tīrthas) for bathing and giving gifts;
the Śrāddha performed at these is recorded to yield infinite fruit.
[There are] the Śatāvaṭānadī, the Jvālā, and likewise the Śaradvīca river.
Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and likewise the northern Sarasvatī; the river named Mālavatī, as well as Girikarṇikā, and the Dhūtapāpa tīrtha on the southern ocean. 31–32.
Gokarṇa, Gajakarṇa, and likewise the auspicious Cakranadī;
Śrīśaila, Śākatīrtha, and thereafter Nārasiṃha; Maheṃdra, and likewise the meritorious Mahānadī.

Even among these, it is traditionally held that food given with faith always yields infinite fruit (34). Merely by sight, the holy Tuṅgabhadrā river and likewise the Cakrarathī are indeed immediate destroyers of sin (35).
There is Bhīmeśvara, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Kāverī, and the river Añjanā;
the holy Godāvarī river, the three junctions of the day (Trisaṃdhyā), and the supreme,
perfect Tīrtha named Traiyambaka, which is saluted by all sacred fords.
There, the Lord Bhīma himself, the three-eyed one, has set;
at all these places, a funeral offering (śrāddha) bestowed becomes ten-millionfold in merit.
Even by mere remembrance, O King, sins depart in a hundred ways. (37-38)
Śrīparṇa, the holy Acanadī, the unsurpassed Vyāsatīrtha,
as well as Matsyanadī, Kārā, Śivadhārā, and likewise the famous Bhavatīrtha and the eternal Puṇyatīrtha. 39.
Likewise, there is the meritorious Rāmeśvara, Veṇāpura, and Alampura;
the famous Aṅgāraka, Ātmadarśa, and Alambuṣa;
as well as Vatsavrāteśvara and the supreme Gokāmukha. 40–41.
Govardhana, Hariścandra, Puraścandra, Pṛthūdaka,
Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, as well as the Kadalī river;
these are the names, and likewise the one joined with Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa).
Indranīla, Mahānāda, and likewise Priyamelaka—
these too are always highly recommended for the śrāddha, since it is taught that the presence of all the gods resides within them. 43–44.

A gift given to all of these would yield a hundred million times more merit than the merit of the Bāhudā river; likewise, there is the auspicious Siddhavaṭa, the Pāśupata tīrtha, and the Paryaṭikā river. 45.
A śrāddha offered at all of these [sites] yields a hundred times ten million-fold merit.
Likewise, there is the Pañcatīrtha, where the river Godāvarī flows with a thousand liṅgas, carrying water to both her right and left sides. 46–47.
That supreme abode of joy belonging to Jamadagnya is the Tīrtha where the river Godāvarī flows out of fear of Pratīka;
There, the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and the offering of fire results in merit exceeding a hundred crores;
likewise, there is the supreme Sahasraliṅga and Rāghaveśvara.
In ancient times, Śakra went there to the meritorious Indrakālānadī. 49–50.
Having slain his enemy Namuci, he attained heaven through austerity;
a śrāddha offered there by men shall yield infinite fruit.
There is also the sacred ford named Puṣkara, and likewise Śālagrāma.
Śoṇapāta is renowned, where indeed Vaiśvānara resides;
likewise there is the Sārasvata Tīrtha and the Svāmitīrtha. There is also the holy Malada river, as well as the Kauśikī and Candrakā. 52–53.
Vidarbhā, Vegā, Payoṣṇī, Prāṅmukhā, Aparā,
Kāverī, Uttarāṅgā, and likewise the Jālandhara mountain— 54.
At these shrāddha-tīrthas, a śrāddha performed attains infinity.
Lohadaṇḍa, as well as the Tīrtha of Citrakūṭa;
the divine, all-pervading bank of the Gaṅgā, and likewise the auspicious bank of that river; Kubjāmraka, as well as the Tīrtha of Urvaśī and the sandy bank (pulina) [of the same]. 55–56.
The Saṃsāramocana Tīrtha and likewise the Ṛṇamocana;
at these ancestral Tīrthas, one attains infinite fruit from a Śrāddha. Also, the Aṭṭahāsa Tīrtha and likewise Gautameśvara.
Likewise, there is the Avasiṣṭhatīrtha and the Bhārata thereafter;
then Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, and likewise Haṃsatīrtha, as well as the famous Piṇḍāraka and Śaṅkhoddhāra. 58–59.
Bhāṇḍeśvara, Bilvaka, and the Nīla mountain,
as well as Badarītīrtha, the lord of all lords of holy places (tīrthas),
and the holy place called Vasudhārā, and likewise Rāmatīrtha. 60.
Jayaṃtī, Vijayā, and likewise Śuklatīrtha—those who offer śrāddha at these places go to the supreme state. There is also the holy site named Mātṛgṛha, as well as Karavīrapura. 61–62.

At that place, which is the lord of all lords of sacred fords (tīrtha) named Saptagodāvarī, a śrāddha ceremony should be offered by those desiring infinite fruit. Gayā is meritorious among the Kīkaṭas, and the Rājagṛha forest is meritorious.
May the holy hermitage of Cyavana and the ever-purifying river go again and again to the holy gratification of the senses,
where the Gāthā proclaimed by Brahmā dwells. 65.
"One should desire many sons, so that at least one might go to Gayā,
or perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull. This verse circulates in sacred fords and shrines.
O King of Men, all these people have gathered together proclaiming:
"Will there be any son born in our lineage who will go to Gayā and, having gone there, satisfy those seven ancestors before him as well as seven after him? (67-68)
This ancient Vedic revelation applies likewise to maternal grandfathers:
"The son who, having gone to the Gaṅgā, shall cast a heap of bones there, and shall offer even seven or eight handfuls of water with sesame seeds [attains the highest goal]. (69)
He will also perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) at the three forest hermitages:
first at Puṣkarāraṇya, then at Naimiṣa,
and having reached Dharmāraṇya once again, he will devoutly offer the śrāddha.

At Gayā, on the Dharmapṛṣṭha, at the lake of Brahmā, and likewise at the Vaṭa tree of Gayāśīrṣa, what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. He who, while traveling, performs the ancestral libation (nivāpa) and continues along his path, [attains the same merit].
He quickly leads even his ancestors dwelling in hell to heaven. O King of men, no one in his lineage shall ever become a ghost;
through the offering of the piṇḍa, even those who have attained the state of a ghost attain liberation.

If one who holds a copper vessel in his hand offers water at the root of a mango tree, the mango trees are watered and the ancestors are satisfied; thus, it is well known that a single act serves a twofold purpose. No other gift is superior to the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā.
Even by the offering of a single funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), those who go to liberation remain satisfied.

The lords of sages declare that the gift of grain and likewise the gift of wealth are preeminent; they say that what is given by men at the sacred sites of Gayā is the most excellent cause for merit. (76–77)
Those who, with their whole being, behold that great mountain and great river with devotion, having gone there mentally to the south or the north,
and having bowed to the foremost of the twice-born, have attained the fruit of their birth.

Whatever an immortal desires, he obtains that without a doubt. This collection of sacred fords has been described by me only in brief; even the Lord of Speech would not be able to describe it in detail, much less a mortal man.
Truth is a sacred ford (tīrtha), compassion is a sacred ford, and the restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
even within the home of those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, tranquility is declared to be a sacred ford.
Whatever śrāddha is performed at these sacred fords is held to yield ten million times the merit.
That śrāddha which is performed at Gayā bestows liberation;
therefore, one should diligently perform the śrāddha at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
The morning time consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration.
Midday consists of three muhūrtas; after that is afternoon;
and evening consists of three muhūrtas—one should not perform a śrāddha at that time. This period is named Rākṣasī and is forbidden for all ritual acts.
The muhūrtas of the day have been explained as being five, ten, and three at all times.
Among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called *kutapa*;
for from that point, the sun always begins to diminish in its course from midday.
Therefore, an undertaking there that yields infinite fruit is distinguished;
[the following eight are traditionally remembered]: a sword, a vessel, a kutapa blanket, a Nepalese woolen rug (naipālaka), gold, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and an eighth, a daughter's son.
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because it causes torment to such [a person], these eight are therefore renowned as "Kutapas.
From the Kutapa Muhūrta upwards, for a period of four Muhūrtas— (88–89)
The recitation of the *svadhā* is prescribed for five *muhūrtas*;
likewise, *kuśa* grass and black sesame seeds produced from the body of Viṣṇu— these,
the wise declare, are the characteristics and the proper time for the *śrāddha*.
Those dwelling at a sacred ford (tīrtha) should offer a handful of sesame seeds and water at the edge of the water.
A śrāddha performed at home with darbha grass in hand will become meritorious,
purifying, life-prolonging, and the destroyer of all sins.
This glorification of the holy places and the Śrāddha rites was indeed spoken by Brahmā;
the man who hears it or even recites it becomes endowed with prosperity. Furthermore, at the time of a Śrāddha, this should be recited by those residing at the holy place.
This is considered the means for pacifying all evils and destroying misfortune (94). This is a purifier, a treasury of glory, and a destroyer of great sins;
those who know it declare that this greatness of the śrāddha is honored by Brahmā, Arka, and Rudra (95).
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Section on Śrāddha," in the first book, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twelve. Bhīṣma said:
"O expert in this matter, tell me how the Lunar dynasty (Soma-vaṃśa) was born,
and who were the kings who became its banners and increasers of fame?
Pulastya said:

Long ago, at the beginning of the process of creation, Atri was first commanded by Brahmā; subsequently, that powerful sage performed austerities for the sake of creation. O Blessed One, when [he attained] Brahman, which bestows bliss and destroys all affliction—
Having established peace within his own mind regarding that which transcends the senses— the inner realm beyond Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Sūrya— Atri remained steadfast in self-restraint;
indeed, the majesty of asceticism brings about supreme bliss.
Because the Lord of the Lineage (Brahmā) established himself there together with Soma,
and having seen him, [the Lord] spoke to Soma, therefore the All-pervading One became Soma. Then, water born from Atri flowed forth from his two eyes.

Illuminating the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, with its moonlight, it [the light] entered the quarters of the sky there in the form of women, who were filled with desire; that [light],
born of Atri, remained within their wombs.
Then, being unable to bear [the embryo], the quarters of space discharged it; thereupon,
the four-faced Brahmā, taking that embryo and unifying it, made it into a youth, a man bearing all weapons.
Having placed him upon a chariot consisting of the power of the Vedas, the Lord, the Grandfather, led him to his own world.
Then it was proclaimed by the Brahman-sages: "May he be our master."
As he was being praised by the sages, gods, gandharvas, and likewise by the apsarases, there arose a vast and extraordinary difference;
from the expansion of his splendor, a multitude of celestial medicinal herbs appeared upon the earth.
Its radiance is always greater than that [of the sun] at night;
because of this, Soma became the Lord of Herbs and is indeed counted among the twice-born, for he is the essence residing in the Vedas, which is this auspicious orb.

It wanes and waxes always during the bright and dark fortnights; and Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave twenty-seven daughters endowed with beauty and charm and great luster to him. 14. These maidens were possessed of form and grace, and were highly resplendent.
Then, for ten thousand times a thousand years,
the cool-rayed moon, intent solely on meditation upon Viṣṇu, performed penance;
thereupon the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari was pleased with him.
"Choose a boon," said Janārdana, the Supreme Self.
Thereupon Soma chose a boon: "May I perform sacrifices in the world of Śakra;
may the enjoyers [of the offerings] be present in my own abode."

"O Lord, may Hara, the wielder of the trident, be our protector and guardian among the fourfold classes of gods, including Brahmā and the other hosts of deities at the Rājasūya sacrifice. Having been told "So be it," Viṣṇu caused the Rājasūya to be performed.
Trita was the Hotṛ, Bhṛgu the Adhvaryu, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) the Udgātṛ;
Hari himself became his Brahman, acting as the supervisor.
All the gods were the Sadasyas; such is recorded as the procedure for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Likewise, the Vasus, the Adhvaryus, and the Viśvedevas were present. By that [sacrifice], the three worlds were bestowed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Then Soma attained a sovereignty difficult to attain, honored by the Creator.
Having then attained the status of the sole lord of the seven worlds through his own ascetic power, he once beheld her in a garden, adorned with ornaments of many flowers—
her limbs exceedingly delicate even while gathering blossoms, and weary from the burden of her large hips and breasts.

Afflicted by love, the lord of the stars seized Tārā— his wife, who was as enchanting as the arrows of the bodiless god of love, with her long and beautiful eyes— by the hair on a secluded spot of ground; she too, tormented by desire, took her pleasure with him, her mind entirely captivated by his form and splendor.
Having sported for a long time, the Moon then took Tārā and went from there to his own home;

yet even in his own home, he who was enamored of Tārā found no satisfaction in the arrival of pleasures. Bṛhaspati, consumed by the fire of separation from her, became single-mindedly intent on her alone.
The Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) was unable to cast a curse upon him, nor could he harm him by various means such as mantras, weapons, fire, or poisons,
nor even through diverse rites of sorcery. Then,
tormented by the god of love on account of his wife, he entreated that god Soma.
Though he was being entreated, Indra, deluded by the power of passion, did not give his wife to Bṛhaspati;
then Maheśvara, along with the four-faced Brahmā, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the world-protectors, [intervened],
yet when Indra would not give her up by any means, Śiva became overcome with wrath.
He who is celebrated on earth as Yajñavāmadeva, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by many Rudras;

then that Lord of the Mountain, the wielder of the Pināka bow, accompanied by his disciples and bound by affection for Bṛhaspati, the enemy of Tripura, went forth, attended by the lords of beings and the Siddhas.
Blazing with a special luster from the fire of his battle-sacrifice, his face formidable with the fire of his third eye,
and possessing a fierce form, he went together with sixty-two Gaṇeśvaras;
accompanied by many Gaṇas, he followed the lords of the Yakṣas who were stationed upon their chariots.
With one hundred thousand Vetālas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kinnaras, and likewise with ten million Padmas,
and with thirty-one lakh chariots, Soma also went there with his wrath increased;
he was joined by the armies of the Nakṣatras, Daityas, and Asuras, possessing the augmented splendor of Śanaiścara and Aṅgāraka.
Likewise, the seven worlds—including the earth, the mountains, the islands, and the oceans—were seized by fear;
and the wielder of the Pināka bow, having grasped his blazing weapons and the vast fire, approached Soma himself.
Then there occurred that great battle between the two terrifying and formidable armies of Soma.

Increasingly intense, characterized by sharpness and preeminence, and having the singular form of a blazing fire, the two armies brought their entire forces to destruction with one another through fierce and keen weapons;
those blazing weapons fell, utterly consuming the earth and the netherworld (pātāla). 36–37.

Out of anger, Rudra released the head of Brahmā, and Soma likewise discharged the Soma-missile of unfailing potency; by the falling of those two, there arose terror for the oceans, the earth, and the intermediate space.
Then, beholding that fierce battle which had commenced for the destruction of the worlds, even the Grandfather (Brahmā) [intervened].
Then, having entered, he somehow restrained him along with the gods: "O Soma, why do you cause the destruction of people without cause? This improper act must not be done by you;
for it was for the sake of abducting another's wife that you waged this most terrifying war."
"You shall become an evil planet among people; you are a sinner who has consumed fire from its very mouth.
O Vākpati, honoring these words of mine, hand over this wife of yours.
(41) "So be it," said the moon-crested Lord, and having thus become pacified, he withdrew from the battle.
Then Bṛhaspati, having taken Tārā, departed; and Rudra, being delighted, went to his own home.
Pulastya said:
Then, at the end of a year, [a son] resembling the twelve Ādityas was born.
Wearing divine yellow garments and adorned with celestial ornaments,
Kumāra emerged from the womb of Tārā, radiant as the sun;
he was a learned scholar, conversant in all treatises on every subject, and the founder of the science of elephant-lore.
This son of the Moon, renowned as the royal physician, is known as Budha because he is the son of King Soma;
indeed, this powerful one eclipsed all the splendors of the people. 45.

Then Brahmā and the other gods, together with the celestial sages, arrived there at the house of Bṛhaspati for the birth-ceremony festival; those gods then asked Tārā, "By whom was this young boy born?"
Then, filled with shame, that excellent woman said nothing to them; though questioned again and again, she remained bashful. After a long time, she spoke to Soma, and then the Moon took the son.
He gave him the name Budha and bestowed upon him sovereignty on the earth.
Then, having performed the consecration, the omnipresent Lord Brahmā, accompanied by the celestial sages (brahmarṣis), granted him a place among the planets. 49-50.
While all beings were looking on, he vanished right there;
and in the womb of Ilā, that wise one begot a most righteous son who,
by his own splendor, performed more than a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Known as Purūravas, he was honored by all the worlds. Having propitiated the Grandfather (Brahmā) on a beautiful peak of the Himavat mountains,
O King, he then attained sovereignty over the worlds and became the lord of the seven continents.
The Daityas, headed by Keśin, entered his service, while Urvaśī, infatuated by his beauty, became his wife;
he [ruled] over the earth with its seven continents, including its mountains, forests, and groves. 54.
Protected by him who desired the welfare of the entire world through righteousness,
fame was carried by yak-tail whisks and even his own body-servants;
then, by the grace of Brahmā, Indra granted him half of his throne.
He protected virtue, wealth, and pleasure by means of virtue alone;
then Virtue, Wealth, and Pleasure, filled with curiosity, came to see him,
desiring to know how he looked upon them all equally.
Then, with devotion, he offered them water for the hands and feet and other honors;
having brought three divine seats adorned with gold and seated them there, he performed worship once again, though slightly more extensive than before.
Both of them, Kāma and Artha, went before the king in great anger.
Artha gave him this curse: "Through greed, you shall meet your destruction.
Kāma also said: "In the Gandhamādana mountain, you shall become insane."
"By resorting to Kumāravana and because of your separation from Urvaśī,
you shall become long-lived and righteous," said Dharma; "O Indra among kings, your lineage shall endure as long as the moon and stars."

It will increase a hundredfold and shall not perish on earth; for sixty years, this madness born of desire for Urvaśī shall persist. Before long, even the Apsaras as his wife will come under his control.
Having spoken thus, they all vanished; then the king enjoyed his kingdom (verse 64).
Day after day, Purūravas would go to see the lord of the gods;
once, having mounted his chariot, he traveled through the southern sky with one who moves in the heavens (verse 65).
Together with Śakra, he then beheld Citralekhā and Urvaśī being carried away through the sky by Keśin, the lord of the Dānavas;
having defeated him in battle by raining down various weapons.
Formerly, even Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, was defeated by him in battle; he entered into friendship with him and gave him Urvaśī.
From that time forward, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) maintained that state of friendship.
The wielder of the thunderbolt, being highly pleased, said to Purūravas, who surpassed all the world: "Let this very [sāman] be brought forth.
For the sake of pleasing Purūravas, she sang that great narrative.
The ceremony known as Lakṣmī-svayaṃvara was inaugurated by Bharata.
He commanded Menakā, Urvaśī, and Rambhā, saying, "Dance! There, Urvaśī danced with rhythmic measure in the form of Lakṣmī.
Seeing Purūravas, she danced, tormented by desire,
forgetting all the gestures previously instructed;
Bharata, out of anger at her separation from him on the earth, cursed her.
For fifty-five years you shall become a creeper;
then Urvaśī approached him and made him her husband for a long time.
At the end of his experience of that curse, Urvaśī united with the son of Budha.
He begot eight sons; learn their names from me:
Āyu, Dṛḍhāyu, Vaśyāyu, Balāyu, Dhṛtimān, Vasu, Divyajāyu, and Śatāyu—all of whom possessed divine strength and vigor.
Āyu’s son was Nahuṣa, and likewise Vṛddhaśarman;
Raji, Daṇḍa, and Viśākha were five heroic great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
A hundred sons were born to Raji, renowned as the Rājeyas.
Raji, being free from sin, propitiated Nārāyaṇa;
Viṣṇu, gratified by his asceticism, granted a boon to the lord of the earth:
"At that time, he shall be victorious over gods, asuras, and humans. (78)

Then a terrible war between the gods and the asuras took place for three hundred years; neither Prahlāda nor Śakra was victorious over the other. Thereupon, the four-faced god Brahmā was questioned separately by both the gods and the asuras.
"Which of these two shall be victorious? he asked. "Wherever you prevail," the king replied. "Then, being sought for victory, become my ally," [Indra] said.
"If you become our lord, O Daityas, then that is sufficient. 81.
That which had not been undertaken by the Asuras was then undertaken by the gods: "Become our lord, you who destroy the hosts of enemies.
Thereupon, all those who were to be slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi) were destroyed.
Then Indra, pleased by that deed, attained the status of his son;
having given the kingdom back to Indra, Raji departed for ascetic penance.
At that time, the kingdom was forcibly seized from Indra by the sons of Raji.

The share of the sacrifice as well as the kingdom were taken by those endowed with the qualities of ascetic power and strength. (85) Thereupon, Śakra, fallen from his kingdom and oppressed by the sons of Raji, spoke dejectedly to Vācaspati: "I am afflicted and tormented by the sons of Raji. (86)
"O Bṛhaspati, Lord of Wisdom, exert yourself for my sake, who am oppressed, so that I may obtain the kingdom which is the rightful share of one skilled in policy.
Thereupon, Bṛhaspati made Śakra proud with power.

Having gone there, Bṛhaspati, though a knower of dharma, performed rites for the pacification of the planets and for prosperity, and while adopting the religion of the Jina which is outside the Vedas, he deluded the sons of Raji. 88–89.
The Lord of Wisdom, having recognized those who had fallen away from the three Vedas as being outside the Vedic fold and possessed of fallacious reasoning,
struck all those excluded from the Dharma with his thunderbolt.
I shall now declare the seven righteous sons of Nahuṣa:
Yati, Yayāti, Śaryāti, Uttara, Para, Ayati, and Viyati; these seven were the increasers of his lineage. 91–92.
Even while in his youth, Yati became a yogi and a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa);
Yayāti, however, always took refuge solely in dharma and ruled the kingdom. Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, was his wife.
And Devayānī, the daughter of Bhārgava, who was firm in her vows, [was also there].
I shall now declare by name the five heirs of Yayāti: Devayānī gave birth to Yadu as her son, and also to Turvasu.
Likewise, Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to sons from the enamored Pūru: Yadu, Pūru, and Bharata; these were the ones who increased their respective lineages.
(96) O King, I shall now describe the lineage of Pūru, in which you yourself were born.
From Yadu were born Vajra, and there [were born] Balarāma and Keśava for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden and for the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas;
and five sons of Yadu were born who were like the sons of gods. 97–98.
Sahasrajit’s eldest son was Kroṣṭu; [his sons were] Nīla, Añjika, and Raghu.
Sahasrajit’s heir was the king named Śatajit. And Śatajit had three heirs who were supremely righteous.
Haihaya, Haya, and likewise Tālahaya;
the heir of Haihaya was Dharmanetra, who was promised [the throne]; Kunti was the son of Dharmanetra, and Saṃhata was his son. 100–101.
The heir of Saṃhata was the king named Mahiṣmān;
the son of Mahiṣmān was the powerful Bhadrasena, who became the king in Vārāṇasī, as has indeed been mentioned previously. 102.
Bhadra’s son was the unrighteous one named Durdama. Durdama’s son was the heroic Bhīma, whose name was Dhanañjaya.
Dhanañjaya indeed had four sons who were world-renowned. 103–104.
Kṛtāgni, Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtadharma, and likewise Kṛtaujas was the fourth; and from Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna, a king who possessed a thousand arms and ruled over the seven continents. 105.
For ten thousand years, that lord of the earth performed difficult austerities; Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, who was born of Atri,
and Puruṣottama granted him four boons.

Previously, that best of kings possessed a thousand arms; yet for one contemplating unrighteousness, even fear and its prevention [were required]. Having conquered the earth through battle, he indeed obtained power through righteousness.
Even death while engaged in battle would be better for him than anything else.
By this means, this earth— with its seven continents, its cities and towns,
and surrounded by the seven oceans— has been conquered through the kṣatriya code of conduct.
A thousand arms were born to that wise one who so desired; all the sacrifices of that mighty-armed hero were accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
All his sacrificial stakes were made of gold, and all his altars were made of gold.
They were attended by all the gods, adorned and stationed in their celestial chariots, as well as by gandharvas and apsarases who served them constantly;
and at whose sacrifice the gandharva Nārada sang this verse: 112–113.
Having beheld the greatness of the royal sage Kārttavīrya, he thought:
"Surely, other kings shall follow the path of Kārttavīrya through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, and sacred learning. (14)
Traversing the seven islands with speed like the wind,
that lord of men became a universal monarch (cakravartin) over the earth consisting of the seven islands for eighty-five thousand years.
He himself became the cowherd; he indeed became the guardian of the field; through his yogic power, he became Parjanya as rain, and Arjuna [the white one];
he who, with his thousand arms, had skin hardened by the striking of bowstrings.
He shone with a thousand rays like the autumnal sun.
This one of great splendor was not among men in Māhiṣmatī;
he indeed possessed the speed of the ocean during the rainy season. 118–119.
The lord of the earth sports against the current for his own pleasure;
by him sporting, the Narmadā—garlanded with waves—is approached apprehensively, her rows of waves appearing like frowning brows. 120.
Thus, as he plunged into the great ocean within the lineage of Manu,
he drew up its force with his hand to please his beloved; and so the great ocean was agitated by his thousand arms.
The great asuras dwelling in the netherworld remained motionless and devoid of activity,
startled by the agitation of her thighs and fearing the production of the nectar of immortality; likewise, the great serpents bowed with their heads held steady.
This archer discharged arrows toward Rāvaṇa. This archer, having seized his bow, forcibly bewildered the lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, along with his army, using five uplifted shafts.

Having conquered and bound him, they brought him to Hiṣmatī and imprisoned him there; then, O King, I went before him and, establishing friendship with that monarch, I caused my grandson Arjuna to be released. 126.
The sound produced by the bowstrings of those thousand arms was like the roar of the sacrificial fire when it has been kindled at the end of an eon;
oh, the power of destiny and the prowess of Bhārgava, since he severed them! 127–128.
In battle, his thousand arms were like a grove of golden palm trees—Arjuna, whom the powerful Vasiṣṭha, filled with rage, had cursed, saying:
"O horse, since you have burned my famous forest here! (129)
Therefore, another will destroy that evil deed you have committed.
Having severed your thousand arms and having violently crushed you,
that powerful ascetic Brahmin of the Bhṛgu lineage shall indeed slay you.
Due to the curse of a sage, that wise king became devoid of offspring;
however, he had one hundred sons, five of whom were great chariot-warriors (mahārathas), skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and possessed of great strength. (132)
Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭa, and Vaikarṣṇa; Jayadhvaja, Saivakartṛ, Avanti, and Rasapati;
and the son of Jayadhvaja was the exceedingly powerful Tālajaṅgha.
He had hundreds of sons known as the Tālajaṅghas;
among those high-souled Haihayas, there were five clans:
the Vītihotras, the Sañjātas, the Bhojas, and likewise the Avantyas. (135)
The Tuṇḍakeras were valiant, and they are celebrated as the Tālajaṅghas.
Vītihotra’s son was the powerful one named Ananta;
his son was Durjaya, the subduer of enemies.
O Great King, while protecting his subjects with righteousness and sincerity,
