there was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms; by him,
with his bow, the earth as far as the ocean was conquered.
If a person rises at dawn and recites his name,
there shall be no loss of wealth for him, and he shall recover whatever has been lost;
so too for one who recounts here the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya.
"According to how one has sacrificed and according to how one has given, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Glorification of Yadu's Lineage," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirteen.
Pulastya said:
O Indra among kings, hear from me the lineage of Kroṣṭu, which possesses the most excellent men;
in whose family was born Viṣṇu, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
To Kroṣṭu was born a son named Vṛjinīvan, who was highly illustrious.
His son was Svāti, and his son was Kuśaṅku.
To Kuśaṅku was born a son named Citraratha.
There was a universal monarch (cakravartin) renowned as Śaśabindu.
Regarding him, this genealogical verse was sung in ancient times: "Śaśabindu had a hundred sons, and for each of those hundred sons there were a hundred [descendants]. 3–4.
To those wise ones of beautiful form, possessing abundant wealth and splendor,
and who were the leaders of a hundred [clans], there were four of great strength known as Pṛthusāhvā:
Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthutejas, and Pṛthūdbhava.
Those who know the Purāṇas proclaim that King Śaśabindu was of vast fame and great intelligence, and that he possessed supreme renown;
from him were born sons, among whom Uśanas, the scorcher of enemies, was foremost.
And the son of that Uśanas was Śineyu, the most excellent of beings;
Śineyu’s son was he who was known as Rukmakavaca. Having slain Rukmakavaca in battle, that expert in warfare—
Having conquered this earth with various arrows,
the archer king performed the horse sacrifice and gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmins; from him, who wore golden armor and was the slayer of enemy heroes, were born Parāvṛt and Paravīra-han.
From him were born five sons of great heroism and prowess:
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari.
The father established both Parigha and Hari in Videha.
Rukmeṣu became the king, and likewise Pṛthu was the one who took refuge in gold. Expelled from the kingdom by those two, he lived below the bowstring in a hermitage.
While staying in that peaceful hermitage, he was awakened by a brāhmaṇa.
Taking up his bow, the bannered and chariot-borne hero went to another region; alone on the bank of the Narmadā, he was utterly emaciated by his circumstances.
Having gone to Mount Ṛkṣavanta, he sat down, free from all other concerns.
Jyāmagha’s wife was Śaibyā, who had been married to him while she was still a maiden.
Although the king remained childless, he did not seek another wife;
instead, he achieved victory in battle and obtained a daughter there. 15–16.
Out of fear, he said to his wife, "O lady of pure smiles, this is your daughter-in-law.
Having spoken thus, he asked her, "Whose daughter-in-law is she?
The king replied:
"Whosoever shall be born as your son, she shall become his wife.
Through her severe asceticism, that maiden gave birth to a son, Vidarbha, who was fortunate; and Śaibyā, having reached maturity, [became his wife].
Then the two learned Kratha and Kauśika were born of the princess as her daughter-in-law; subsequently,
Vidarbha begot a third son, Lomapāda, who was supremely righteous,
heroic, and skilled in battle.
Babhru was the son of Lomapāda, and Dhṛti was his son.
Cedi was the son of Kauśika, and from him the Caidya kings are said to have descended. Kratha was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his son.
From Kunti was born Dhṛṣṭa; from Dhṛṣṭa was born the powerful Sṛṣṭa. The son of Sṛṣṭa was the righteous Nivṛtti, the slayer of enemy heroes.
The son of Nivṛtti was Dāśārha, who was known by the name Vidūratha.
Bhīma was the son of the descendant of Daśārha; from Bhīma, Jīmūta is said to have been born.
Vikṛti was the son of Jīmūta, and his son was Bhīmaratha. Now, it is said that Navaratha was the son of Bhīmaratha as well.
His son was Daśaratha, and Śakuni was his son. From him came Karaṃbha, and from him Devarāta was born. From Devarāta was born King Devakṣatra, who was of great fame.

Born like one from the womb of a god, the son of Devakṣatra was named Madhu, possessed of great splendor; he is remembered as the Kuruvaṃśa of Madhu. From Kuruvaṃśa was born a powerful son, Puruhotra.
Aṃśu was born of Draupadī, the princess of Vidarbha, by Puruhūta.
Vetrakī became the wife of that Aṃśu, and of her was born Sātvata, who was endowed with goodness and increased the fame of the Sātvatas. 28–29.
Having understood this creation of the great-souled Jyāmagha,
one who possesses progeny attains union with the wise King Soma. Kausalyā gave birth to sons endowed with strength, the Sātvatas.
Listen now to their four lineages in detail:
Bhajamāna had a son named Bhāja born of Sṛñjayī; from him, the Bhājakas were born through the daughter of Sṛñjaya. (31–32)
The two wives of that Bhāja gave birth to many sons:
Nemi, Cakru, Kaṇa, Vṛṣṇi, and Parapurañjaya.
Because they were born from Bhajamāna, they are remembered as the Bhājakas.
Devāvṛdha, named Pṛthu, was a nourisher of friends;
he was childless and performed supreme austerity, desiring, "May a son endowed with all virtues be born to me. (34-35)
Then, having joined Kṛṣṇa and touching the water of the Parṇāśā river,
the river attained his presence through that contact with its waters. As he was performing auspicious rites, the river then grieved for him.
With his mind overwhelmed by anxiety, he then reached this conclusion:
"I shall become a woman and go [to him], so that a son such as this may be born to her; therefore, today I shall become the giver of a son to her. (37-38)
Then, having become a maiden and assuming a most excellent form, she informed the king; thereupon, the king desired her. Then, in the ninth month, that best of rivers gave birth.
The supreme Babhru, endowed with all virtues, was born as his son from Devāvṛdhā.
Regarding this lineage, those learned in the Purāṇas are heard to say that they proclaim the qualities of that great-souled Devāvṛdha.
Babhru was the best among men, equal to Devāvṛdha among the gods;
he had seventy-six thousand and one hundred sons,
all of whom attained immortality through Babhru and Devāvṛdha.
The wise Bhoja, devoted to sacrifice, charity, and austerity, dedicated to Brahman, firm in his vows,
handsome, and possessed of great luster, begot four sons upon Mṛtakāvatī, the daughter of Śarakānta. (43–44)
Kukura was born from Bhajamāna; Śyāma was the son of Kambalabarhiṣa.
Vṛṣṭi was the son of Kukura, and Dhṛti was the son of Vṛṣṭi.
Kapotaroman was his [Dhṛti’s] son, and Tittiri was his [Kapotaroman’s] son.
He had many sons, among whom there was indeed a learned son named Nari. His other name was celebrated as Candanodakadundubhi. His son was Abhijit, and from him Punarvasu was born.

For that best of men, being childless, was formerly impelled by the sages and joyfully performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son. While he was moving about in the midst of it, [a voice] arose from the center of the assembly hall.
Andha, however, was learned, a knower of dharma, a performer of sacrifices, and a donor of wealth; he was Punarvasu.
O best among the wise, it is said that this Vaso had a pair of children, Arijit—namely Āhuka and Āhukī, both of whom were renowned. 49–50.
And in this regard, they cite these verses, which are full of intense emotion,
concerning the quivers, the trailing shafts,
the armor, and the chariots— ten thousand chariots with a roar like thunderclouds. (51)
Neither those who speak untruth, nor the Bhojas, nor those who do not give a thousandfold at sacrifices; neither the impure, nor the ignorant—none became superior to the Bhoja.
Having reached the beloved state of Āhuka, this is what is called his lineage.
Āhuka also gave his sister Āhukī to the people of Avanti; and Āhuka’s daughter gave birth to two sons who were equal to the offspring of the gods:
Devaka and Ugrasena.
And the sons of Devaka were born, equal to the gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita.
To Vasudeva, he gave their seven sisters as wives.
Devakī, Śrutadevā, Yaśodā, Śrutiśravā,
Śrīdevā, Upadevā, and Surūpā as the seventh—
these are the seven daughters of Ugrasena; among them, Kaṃsa was the eldest.
Nyagrodha, Susunāman, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, and Subhū;
another was Rāṣṭrapāla, as well as Baddhamuṣṭi and Samuṣṭika.
They had five sisters: Kāśā, Kāñcanamālā, and likewise Kaṃsavatī.
Surabhī, Rāṣṭrapālī, Cakrā, and Kaṅkā were his excellent wives;
Ugrasena, along with his offspring, was declared to have been born from Kukura. Bhajamāna’s son was Vidūratha, a preeminent chariot-warrior.
Rājādhideva was the heroic son of Vidūratha. Two sons were born to Rājādhideva, both esteemed as heroes and devoted to the vows of the Kṣatriya: Śoṇāśva and Śvetavāhana.
The five sons of Śoṇāśva were heroes skilled in warfare:
Śamīcara, Rājaśarman, Nimūrti, Śatrujit, and Śuci.
Pratikṣatra was the son of Śamī, and Pratikṣatra’s son was [Śūra].
Pratikṣatra’s son was Bhoja, and Hṛdīka was his son.
Hṛdīka had ten sons of terrible prowess;
Kṛtavarman was their eldest, and Śatadhanvan was the most excellent among them.
Devārha, Subhānu, Bhīṣaṇa, Mahābala, Ajāta, Vijāta, Karaka, and Karaṃdhama;
the learned son of Devārha was born as Kaṃbalabarhiṣ. 65–66.
From him were born two sons, Asamaujas and Samaujas; though their father had no other sons, these two were born with equal vigor.
The three sons of Samaujas were renowned and supremely righteous.
Sudaṃśas, Suvaṃśas, and Kṛṣṇa were his younger brothers by name. He who constantly recites this lineage of the Andhakas obtains for himself a vast lineage and progeny thereafter.
Gāndhārī and Ādrī were the two wives of Cakroṣṭu.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sunītra, who was devoted to his friends;
and then Ādrī gave birth to the son Yudhājit, as well as Devamīḍhuṣa.
Anamitra and Śini were the two who bore the marks of the five [great sacrifices].
Anamitra’s son was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons:
Prasena, who was of great heroism, and Śaktisena.
The Syamantaka, the unsurpassed jewel of Prasenajit,
was universally recognized as the king of all jewels upon the earth;
having placed that gem upon his chest, he shone exceedingly.

For the sake of the king, Śauri requested that most excellent jewel; though Govinda was capable of obtaining it, he did not take it. Once, having gone out on a hunt, Prasenajit was adorned with that gem.
He heard the sound of "billa" uttered by some creature;
then, having entered the cave,
Prasena encountered the bear, and likewise, the bear encountered Prasena.
Having encountered one another with a desire for mutual victory, they fought;
then the bear, having killed Prasena, took that jewel.
Hearing that Prasena had been killed, Govinda became apprehensive.
Surely Prasenajit was killed by Satrājit, his brother, along with other Yādavas and Govinda, on account of the jewel.
Prasenajit, adorned with that precious gem, had gone into the forest.
Seeing that he was not abandoning the syamantaka jewel, Keśava struck him down;
because he did not hand it over, he became his enemy. This is the report made by Satrājit, which has become famous everywhere.
Then, after a long time, having gone out again for a hunt,
Govinda arrived by chance near the entrance of the cave.
Thereupon, that powerful king of bears made a sound just as he had done before.
Having heard the sound, Govinda entered with sword in hand and beheld Jāmbavān, the immensely powerful king of the bears;
then Hṛṣīkeśa quickly approached that bear with great speed.
Seeing Jāmbavanta thus engaged in the capture [of the jewel], and beholding Viṣṇu in his Vaiṣṇava form through his deeds, the king of the bears, his eyes bloodshot with anger,
quickly offered praise with the Viṣṇusūkta.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, offered him a boon.
Jāmbavān said:
"I desire that my death from you by the blow of the discus be auspicious."
"This maiden is my daughter; may she obtain you as her husband.
This jewel which I obtained after killing Prasenajit—O Lord, let it be taken by you; this jewel is here. 87-88.
Thus addressed, the mighty-armed Keśava, having accomplished his task, slew Jāmbavanta with his discus and then took the maiden. Thereafter, he gave this jewel-gem to Satrājit.
Because Janārdana was tormented by that false report regarding what he had received from the King of the Bears in the presence of all the Yādavas,
all those Yādavas then spoke to Vāsudeva.
It was in our minds that Prasenajit had been slain by you;
however, each of Satrājit’s ten beautiful wives bore him one hundred and one sons who were renowned for their truthfulness.
Vikhyāta, Mahāvīrya, and Bhaṅgakāra were his elder brothers.
Satyā, Vratavatī, and Svapnā gave birth to sons for Bhaṅgakāra;
and the powerful Śinīvāla begot them as princes.
Abhanga and Yuyudhana were born, and Śini became his son; from him came Yugandhara, whose hundred sons are celebrated.
He who was known by the name Anamitra was indeed born of the Vṛṣṇi lineage.
From Anamitra was born Śini, the joy of the Vṛṣṇis;
and from Anamitra was also born the Vṛṣṇi hero Yudhājit. He had two other heroic sons, Vṛṣabha and Citra.
Ṛṣabha took as his blameless wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
and Jayanta obtained Śubhā Jayantī as his wife. From Jayanta and Jayantī, a son was subsequently born.
From him was born Akrūra, who was a constant sacrificer, exceedingly wise, learned, and fond of guests.
From Akrūra were born Sudakṣa and Bhūridakṣiṇa, as well as Ratnakanyā and Śaibyā; Akrūra obtained her [Śaibyā] as his wife. 99–100.
He begot eleven sons of great strength:
Upalaṃbha, Sadālaṃbha, Utkala, Āryaśaiśava, Sudhīra, Sadāyakṣa, Śatrughna, and Vārimejaya. 101.
Dharmadṛṣṭi, Dharma, Sṛṣṭimat, and Mauli likewise—
these were all born as the protectors of the jewels.
From Akrūra and Śūrasenā were born two sons who brought joy to their lineage.
Devavān and Anupadeva were born, both highly esteemed by the gods;
from Aśvinī, three or four sons were born: Pṛthu, Vipṛthu, Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa. (104)
Riṣṭanemi, Suvarcā, Sudharmā, Mṛdu, Abhūmi, Bahubhūmi, Śraviṣṭhā, and Śravaṇā—these two are females.
The wise man who knows this false accusation against Kṛṣṇa [attains success]. 105–106.
Because he could not be approached by anyone with a false accusation,
the son of Ikṣvāku begot a son who was heroic, wonderful, and Mīḍhuṣa.
From Mīḍhuṣa and Bhojā were born ten heroic sons.
The mighty-armed Vasudeva was born first, followed by Ānakadundubhi; then Devabhāga, and again Devaśravas,
as well as Anāvṛṣṭi, Kuni, Nandi, and Sakṛdyajña.
Śyāmā, Śamīkā, Saptākhyā, Pañcacūḍā, and Varāṅganā;
Śrutakīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutadevī, Śrutaśravā, and Rājādhidevī—these five were the mothers of heroes. (110)
Śrutadevī bore to Vṛddha a king of the Kārūṣas.
To Śrutakīrti, from Kaikeyī, was born King Saṃtardana;
and to Śrutaśravas, the son of the Caidya, Sunītha was born.
Born of Rājādhidevī through Dharma and free from fear, that hero was bound by friendship; he gave Pṛthā to Kuntibhoja.
Thus, she who was named Kuntī was the sister of Vasudeva, known as Pṛthā.
Kuntibhoja gave that blameless woman to Pāṇḍu as his wife.
For the sake of Pāṇḍu, that queen, the daughter of a charioteer, gave birth to sons who were great car-warriors like gods; Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma, and Vṛkodara was born from Vāyu.
And Dhanañjaya, whose prowess is equal to Śakra, was born from Indra;
he is a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) born from three persons through three portions, the performer of the gods' work and the slayer of all the Dānavas. (116)
Even the Dānavas who were incapable of being slain by Śakra were killed by him;
having regained his splendor, he was established in heaven by Śakra.
We have heard that he begot the two Aśvins upon Mādravatī.

Nakula and Sahadeva, endowed with beauty and the quality of goodness, obtained as their wives Rohiṇī and Pauravī, the two daughters of Anaka-dundubhi; and from Rohiṇī, he (Anaka-dundubhi) obtained his beloved son Rāma, as well as Sāraṇa, who was dear to her feet.
Durdhara, Damana, Piṇḍāraka, and Mahāhanu—120.
Now, the new-moon day (Amāvāsyā) will belong to Devakī;
on that day, the mighty-armed one was formerly born as Prajāpati. 121.
Anujātā, Kṛṣṇā, Subhadrā, Bhadra-bhāṣiṇī, Vijaya, Rocamāna, Stuvardhamāna, and Devala—
these high-souled ones were all born of Upadevī. 122.
Bṛhaddevī gave birth to the high-souled Agāvaha.
From Bṛhaddevī, Mandaka by name was born himself;
she bore as her seventh son Remanta, the son of Devakī.
Formerly, while wandering in the forest during his stay with Śrutadevī, Śauri begot an elder son named Kauśika upon a Vaiśya woman— a highly fortunate seeker who was undefeated in battles. (125)
King Śrutadhara took Saugandhā as his wife;
their son was the powerful Kapila, the offspring of Vasudeva, who became the first among men to wield the bow and to cause them distress. 126–127.
Saubhadra and Abhava were both great beings;
Devabhāga’s son was Prastāva, who is remembered as wise. Bāhudeva was the first among the learned, and Śravas was most excellent. (128)

From that [Ikṣvāku], Śatrughna was born, who had turned back his enemies and was renowned for his mental fortitude; he was the glory of the Ikṣvāku lineage, like water to a virtuous woman. To Gaṇḍūṣā, Kṛṣṇa, being pleased, granted a hundred offspring.
Both Raṃtipāla and Caraṃti, the two sons of Nandana, were highly fortunate, heroic, and possessed of great strength, along with Sacandra. Furthermore,
there were four sons of Śamīka who were valiant and exceedingly powerful.
Viraja and Dhanu were the sons of Vyoma, and Sṛñjaya was the son of Dhanu.
Vyoma was childless; however, Sṛñjaya had a son named Dhanañjaya, who upon his birth attained the status of a Bhoja and the rank of a royal sage (rājarṣi). 132–133.
The person who constantly recites or hears the account of Kṛṣṇa’s birth and exaltation is forever liberated from all sins. Now, the god Mahādeva was formerly Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati.
For the sake of dwelling among gods, humans, and even non-humans, the lotus-eyed one was born of Devakī by Vasudeva through the power of austerity;
he appeared with four arms, possessing a divine form and being the refuge of all people. 135–136.
Seeing the god marked with the Śrīvatsa and endowed with all auspicious signs, Vasudeva said to him: "O Lord, please withdraw this form;
I am afraid of Kaṃsa, O God, and therefore I speak thus to you."
"My six sons, excellent and of terrible prowess, have been slain by him.
Hearing Vasudeva's words, Acyuta withdrew his form; then Śauri, taking leave of him, led him to the house of Nandagopa.
Having given him [the child], he said to the cowherd Nanda, "Let him be protected";
therefore, every auspiciousness shall belong to the Yādavas.
This embryo of Devakī, however, will slay Kaṃsa.
Until then, there shall be great insecurity on earth, bringing a heavy burden;
he will slay all those wicked kings when the battle of the Kauravas occurs and all the kṣatriyas have assembled.
This god himself will act as Arjuna’s charioteer;
having rid the earth of the kṣatriyas until only a remnant remains, he will enjoy it. He will also lead the entire Yadu clan to the world of the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
Who is this Vāsudeva, and who is the illustrious Devakī? And who is the cowherd Nanda, and who is Yaśodā of great vows?
"She who nourished Viṣṇu and who bore him as her mother," she said. Pulastya said: "She who gave birth to the embryo and who reared him."
That Puruṣa was Kaśyapa, and Aditi is remembered as his beloved wife.
Kaśyapa was a portion (aṃśa) of Brahmā, and likewise Aditi was a portion of the Earth.
Nanda was declared to be Droṇa, and Yaśodā became Dharā.
Then the mighty-armed one fulfilled the desires of Devakī which she had previously cherished for that Great Soul before his birth;
not long after, the Great God entered a human body.
Deluding all beings through his yogic power,
the Lord Viṣṇu entered the Vṛṣṇi clan; for when dharma and sacrifice had perished,
he appeared to establish dharma once more and to destroy the asuras.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Satyā, Nāgnijitī, as well as Sumitrā, Śaibyā, Gāndhārī, Lakṣmaṇā,
Subhīmā, Mādrī, Kauśalyā, and Vijayā. 151.
In this manner, Rukmiṇī gave birth to sixteen thousand such goddesses; now hear of the sons she bore, who were skilled and wise:
Cārudeṣṇa, a hero in battle, and Pradyumna of great strength. 152–153.
Sucāru, Cārubhadra, Sadaśva, Hrasva, and the seventh, Arugupta; Cārubhadra, Cāruka, Cāruhāsa, Kaniṣṭha, Kanyā, and likewise Cārumatī. 154.
To Satyabhāmā were born Bhānu, Bhīmaratha, Kṣaṇa, Rohita, Dīptimat, Tāmrabandha, and Jalandhama;
and to them were born four younger sisters. 155–156.
To Jāmbavatī was born a son named Sāmba, who was exceedingly handsome;
he was indeed the author of the Saura Śāstra and of the Pratimā-mandira.
By that high-souled one, the establishment of Mūlasthāna was also performed.
The God of gods, being pleased, destroyed his leprosy.
Sumitra and Cārumitra were born of Mitravindā; and Mitrabāhu and Sunītha were born of Nāgnajitī. 158–159.
Behold these thousands of sons and others;
likewise, there were eighty thousand sons of Vāsudeva.
And the heir of Pradyumna, born of the princess of Vidarbha, was the most excellent in intelligence.

Aniruddha, Uraṇa, Yoddhāja, Jajñeśya, and Mṛgaketana—these were born [to him]. Kāmyā obtained Itarasthin as her son from Sāmba. The five supreme gods are proclaimed to be of the nature of *sattva*. 161–162.
There were thirty million great-souled Yādava heroes, along with six million valiant and mighty men;
all of them were portions of the gods, born here endowed with great splendor.
The Asuras, who were slain in the war between the gods and the Asuras, were indeed possessed of great strength;
having been born here among human beings, they oppress all men.
For the sake of their eradication, [the Lord] was born in the lineage of Yadu.
Among the hundred clans of the high-souled Yādavas,
Viṣṇu was their leader and remained established in the position of sovereign;
all the Yādavas prospered while abiding by his command.
Bhīṣma said:
"The seven ṛṣis, Kubera, the yakṣa Maṇidhara,
as well as Sātyaki, Nārada, Śiva, and Dhanvantari."
Why have the primordial god Viṣṇu and these deities been born together upon the earth? How many future incarnations will there be for this Great Soul? (168–169)

For what purpose is he born here among all the various fields? For what reason has Viṣṇu appeared here in the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans? Tell me again and again, as I ask you, that which concerns human beings.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O King, I shall declare a most profound secret:
how Viṣṇu, possessing a divine body, is born here among human beings. 171
When the end of the age has arrived and time has become lax, the Lord Hari,
the Sovereign, is born among gods, asuras, and humans.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was a Daitya who ruled over the three worlds.
And when the three worlds were again presided over by Bali, there was a supreme friendship between the gods and the asuras;
for ten full cycles known as yugas, the world remained undisturbed. 173–174.
While they remained obedient to his command, Bali himself was bound by the gods and asuras;
this crushing conflict has now fully unfolded, a most terrible and great destruction of both gods and asuras. (175)
"And for the purpose of establishing the order of dharma among human beings here, he was born;
this occurred on account of Bhṛgu’s curse, brought about by the gods and asuras.
Bhīṣma said:
"How did Hari assume a body for the sake of the gods and asuras?
O observer of virtuous vows, tell me that account of the gods and asuras exactly as it occurred.
Pulastya said:
For the sake of their victory, indeed, there shall be most terrible battles.
Two pure incarnations are recorded for each Manvantara;
listen briefly to their intended names.
The first was Nārasiṃha, and the second was Vāmana;
the third was Varāha, and the fourth was the Churning for the Nectar (Amṛtamanthana). The fifth was the most terrible battle, namely the Tārakāmaya war. 180.
The sixth is indeed named Āḍīvaka, and the seventh is Traipura;
the eighth is Andhakavadha, the ninth is Vṛtraghātana;
Dhvaja is the tenth among them, and after that is Hālāhala. (181–182)
Among them, the twelfth was the famous and terrible Kolāhala; likewise,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was destroyed by Narasiṃha,
and in ancient times, Bali was bound by Vāmana during his conquest of the three worlds.
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in single combat by the gods;
the ocean, situated therein, was split asunder by the boar with his tusks; and Prahlāda was conquered in battle by Viṣṇu during the churning for the nectar of immortality.
Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was constantly intent on slaying Indra;
however, by Indra’s prowess alone he was struck down during the Tārakāmaya war.
Unable to withstand the three cities of the Asuras, even the gods were powerless against them.
Having been deluded by the enemy of the Asuras when the nectar was drunk in the form of a cow, the deceased Asuras could not be revived again and again;
for all the Dānavas had already been slain by Tryambaka throughout the three worlds. 187–188.
The Asuras, Piśācas, and Dānavas were slain by gods, humans, and Pitṛs alike during the slaughter of Andhaka;
Vṛtra, joined by the Dānavas, was killed amidst a terrible clamor.

Then, while he was being struck down by Mahendra with Viṣṇu as his ally, Vipracitti, who was skilled in yoga, concealed himself through illusion; having entered [his body] for a moment with the thunderbolt, he killed him along with his followers. 190–191.
The Daityas and Dānavas were all assembled together;
these twelve battles between the gods and the Asuras occurred,
causing the destruction of both gods and Asuras, yet for the welfare of all creatures.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu shone for an arbuda of years;
furthermore, possessing the sovereignty over the three worlds, he remained for seventy-two million and eighty thousand additional years.
In turn, Bali became king for seventy billion,
sixty thousand, and twenty million years; such is the duration of time proclaimed for Bali’s exercise of royal authority.
For that duration, Prahlāda remained at ease together with the Asuras;
these highly powerful Asuras were to be understood as intent on victory, [thinking], "This triple world is being protected by Mahendra without any agitation. (196–197)
All this was incomplete, even up to ten thousand years,
for the three worlds were obtained by Indra only in turn.
Then, abandoning the asuras, the sacrifice went to the gods.
When the sacrifice had gone to the gods, the sons of Diti spoke to Kāvya.
The Daityas said:
"The kingdom has been seized by Maghavan; having abandoned the sacrifice, it has gone to the gods."
"We are unable to remain here; let us enter the netherworld (rasātala).
Thus addressed, he spoke to those dejected ones, consoling them with his voice:
"Do not fear, O Asuras; I shall support you by my own splendor."
Whatever exists upon the earth— both mantras and medicinal herbs— all that which resides within me shall indeed be present in you gods, even if it be but a quarter-part.
And all of that, which has been sustained by me, I shall bestow for your sake.
Then, seeing those gods held in check by the wise Kāvya,
the deities, deeply agitated and desiring to seize him, consulted together:
"This Kāvya is indeed forcibly turning all of us away from our purpose."
"Come, let us go quickly so that he may not cause our downfall;
having forcibly conquered the remaining ones, we shall send them to Pātāla. Then the gods, filled with fury, approached the Dānavas.
Then, being tormented by them, they fled toward Kāvya himself.
Then, seeing those gods pursued by the deities and fleeing for their protection, Kāvya gathered those gods who were being oppressed by the suras for the purpose of guarding them.
Seeing Kāvya standing there, the gods abandoned their apprehension; then Kāvya, reflecting upon the beneficial words of Brahmā,
spoke to them while recollecting past events.
The entire three worlds were carried away by Vāmana in three strides. Bali was bound, Jambha was slain, and Virocana was killed;
twelve great asuras were destroyed by the gods in battles.
By various means, the majority have been slain, primarily those who were the leaders;
only a few of you remain, and it is my opinion that there is no more battle.
You must be guided by policy and employed through strategic means as time passes.

"I shall go to Mahādeva for the sake of mantras that bring victory. Then, having obtained from Maheśvara those mantras which are irresistible, we shall fight with the gods once more; thereafter, you shall indeed attain victory."
Then, having reached an agreement, those Asuras said to the gods:
"We shall all lay down our weapons, divest ourselves of armor, and be without chariots;
we shall likewise perform penance, clothed in bark garments."
Then, having heard those words of theirs spoken with truth, all the gods turned back, freed from fever and filled with joy;
when the Daityas had laid down their weapons, the Asuras then desisted.
Then Kāvya said to them:
"O Dānavas, established in penance, free from arrogance, and endowed with ascetic power, wait for me while I am at my father’s hermitage; I shall accomplish your purpose in due time."
Aiming at those asuras, Kāvya sought refuge with Mahādeva.
Śukra said:
"O God, I desire the mantras that exist with Bṛhaspati."
"For the defeat of the gods and for the victory of the asuras.
Having been addressed thus, the god said: "O Bhārgava, perform this vow for a full thousand years: with your head downward, inhale the smoke of chaff."
"If it is for your welfare, O Bhadra, then you shall obtain the mantras.
Having thus granted his permission with "So be it," Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, touched the feet of the god and spoke these words: "Very well."
"O Lord, I am performing the vow commanded by you, O Master. Thus instructed by the God of gods, the sage Bhārgava performed it.
Then, when Śukra had departed for the welfare of the asuras, [the battle resumed].
The poet, for the sake of the meaning of the mantras, practiced celibacy under Maheśvara;
having understood that through his intellect, he then attained the bliss of the Vairāja state.
At that moment, in this vulnerability, the gods, out of indignation, rushed toward them.

Seeing the gods once again equipped with armor and weapons, led by Bṛhaspati, all the hosts of Asuras seized their own weapons and suddenly sprang up in terror, addressing them with these words: ||| 225-226 ||
The Daityas said: "O gods, while our preceptor has undertaken his vow and we have laid down our weapons, you have come here seeking to slay us after having granted us your promise of safety. (227)
Having abandoned all weapons out of indignation and resentment,
we stand here wearing bark and black antelope skins, inactive and without possessions; we shall not be able to conquer the gods in battle by any means whatsoever.
"Without fighting, we shall seek refuge with the mother of Kāvya;
we shall inform her of this distress until our preceptor returns. And once the planet Śukra has departed, we shall fight, girded with our weapons."
Having spoken thus to one another, they, being terrified, sought refuge with Kāvya’s mother; she then granted them freedom from fear, saying:
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas!"
"Stay in my presence;
you need not fear. Having seen those Asuras protected by her, the gods then attacked them by force, without considering their relative strength.
Then, seeing those asuras being bound by the gods,
the goddess became enraged and said to the gods, "I shall now delude them with sleep.
Having gathered all the necessary materials, she then dispatched Sleep.

Then the goddess, a woman rich in asceticism, joined with yoga, paralyzed him by her power. Seeing Indra thus paralyzed, the gods fled in terror like those who are bewildered upon seeing Indra brought under control.
When the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra.
Viṣṇu said: "Enter me; may it be well with you; I shall protect you, O best of gods. (237)
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu.
Seeing him protected by Viṣṇu, the Goddess, filled with rage, spoke these words:
"O Maghavan, together with Viṣṇu, I shall burn you by force."
"While all beings look on, let the power of my asceticism be seen.
Overcome by her, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, became [afflicted].
Then Viṣṇu spoke to Indra: "How may we both be released together? 239–240.
Indra said, "Kill her, O Lord, before she consumes us;
I am especially overwhelmed by her, so kill her, kill her without delay!
(241) Then Viṣṇu, having observed them, became intent upon the difficult task of slaying the woman.
Then the Lord quickly perceived that Śakra had fallen under her influence.
Thereupon, Viṣṇu, having understood the cruel intent of that goddess, became filled with haste and, overcome by fear, acted with speed. 242–243.
Enraged, he took up a discus and severed his head out of fear;
seeing that terrible slaughter of a woman, the lord Bhṛgu became furious. Then, indeed, Viṣṇu was cursed by Bhṛgu for the killing of his wife.
Bhṛgu said: "Since you, through ignorance of dharma, have slain a woman who should not be killed,
therefore you shall enter among human beings seven times."
Then, because dharma had been repeatedly destroyed by that curse,
he was born here among humans for the sake of the welfare of the world;
and having thus addressed Viṣṇu, he himself took up that head.
Then, having brought his body back and taken it by the hand, Bhṛgu said this:
"O Goddess, you have been struck down by Viṣṇu; I shall now restore you to life. (248)
"If this entire dharma has been known by me, or even practiced, by that truth may you live, if what I say is true.
Then, having sprinkled her with cold water, he said, "Live! Live! (249).

Then, as soon as that [mantra] had been uttered and the goddess was restored to life, all living beings, seeing her as if risen from sleep, exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! on every side upon beholding her.
Thus was the goddess drawn back by Bhṛgu at that time, while the gods looked on; it was indeed like a marvel. With an unperturbed mind, Bhṛgu restored his wife to life once again.
Having seen this, Indra found no peace due to the fear of Kāvya;
then Indra remained awake and spoke thus to Jayantī.
Desiring a reconciliation, Pākaśāsana addressed these words to his own daughter.
Indra said:
"This son of Kavi indeed observes a terrible vow that is devoid of Indra; because of that, O daughter, I have been made deeply agitated by your wise resolve. (255)

"O daughter, serve him with all those various services that are pleasing to his mind, remaining untiring, in such a way that this twice-born man may be satisfied. Go; you have been given to him, so exert yourself for my sake."
Having been addressed thus, Jayantī took her father’s words to heart and went to where he was performing his formidable penance;
and seeing him drinking the smoke of chaff with his face turned downwards, she approached.
Seeing that purifying Kāvya standing firm, being struck down by the yakṣa Kuṇḍadhāra,
striving in his effort, exhausted in the destruction of his enemies, and reduced to a state of weakness; 259.
Then she carried out the words spoken by her father exactly as instructed;
praising him with agreeable words, the sweet-spoken woman served him at the proper times by massaging his limbs and providing pleasant sensations to his skin.
For many years, he spent his time mostly in worship, conforming to the practice of his vows;
when that thousand-year period of the terrible smoke-vow was complete,
Śiva became pleased and then offered him a boon.
Maheśvara said:
"This vow has been performed by you alone and by no one else;
therefore, indeed, by means of your austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength,"
By your splendor alone, you shall overcome all the asuras. O Brahmin, O descendant of Bhṛgu, whatever power resides in me, I shall bestow it all upon you;
but you must not speak of this to anyone.
What is the use of much speaking? You shall be invincible.
Having bestowed those boons upon that descendant of Bhṛgu again and again, he granted him the lordship over subjects, the lordship over wealth, and indeed invincibility.
Having obtained these boons, Kāvya’s hair stood on end with joy;
having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, the blue-and-red Ishvara,
he, endowed with wisdom, then bowed before him with palms joined in reverence.

Then, when the god had vanished, he said this to Jayantī: "Whose daughter are you, O blessed one? Why are you alone, and why are you sorrowful while I am sorrowful? Endowed as you are with great ascetic power, for what purpose do you seek to conquer me?"

"O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion, I am pleased by this devotion that is unwavering, by your humility, self-restraint, and affection. What do you desire, O lovely woman? What wish of yours is set forth?"
"Today I shall accomplish that for you, even if it be very difficult to perform.
Having been addressed thus, she said to him: "O Brahmin, you ought to know what I intend to do; tell me exactly as it is."
Having been addressed thus, he looked upon her with his divine eye and said to her:
"O fair-hipped one, O beautiful woman, you desire to have union with me here for a hundred years,
unseen by any living beings."
"O Goddess, O blue-lotus dark one, O worthy one with pure eyes, since you thus choose these desires, O goddess of sweet speech,
let it be so; let us go to my home, O intoxicated beauty."
Then, having returned home with Jāyantī,
the descendant of Bhṛgu, firm in his vows, lived for a hundred years with that goddess, invisible to all beings through his power of illusion (māyā).
Knowing that Śukra had returned having accomplished his purpose, all the sons of Diti,
joyful and desiring to see him, went to his house. When they arrived, however, they did not see their preceptor, for he was concealed by illusion.
And not having understood his true nature, the Guru did not come.
(279) Thus they all returned to their own abodes just as they had come;
then all the hosts of gods, having gone to Aṅgiras, said to him: (280)
"O Blessed One, go to the abode of the Dānavas; having deluded that army there, bring it quickly under your own control. Viṣaṇa said to those gods, "I shall go even thus."
Having gone there, the lord of the Dānavas, Prahlāda, was rendered helpless;
Śukra remained there and performed the duties of the family priest for more than a hundred years, until Uśanas arrived at that time.
Then the sons of Danu saw Bṛhaspati in the assembly;
they wondered, "Uśanas is here alone; what has this second one come here for?
There will surely be great curiosity here, and a firm conflict is certain."
"What will this world say? What will this man standing at the gate say?
And what will this preceptor seated in the assembly hall say to us?"—as the sons of Danu were thus conversing, the poet arrived.
Seeing Bṛhaspati seated there, wearing his own natural form, he spoke these words in anger: "O Preceptor of the Gods, why have you come here?
Is it right for you to delude my disciples?"
Those fools do not know you, for they are certainly deluded by your māyā.
O Brahman, this assault upon the disciples of another is not fitting for you;
go to your own celestial realm, and there you shall abide in righteousness.

"O Brahmin, this disciple of mine was previously killed by the foremost of the Dānavas while seeking knowledge; your son is not fit for this path here. Having heard those words of his, the Guru smiled and spoke.

There are thieves on earth who steal the wealth of others; but such as these, who steal one's very form and body, have never been seen before. In ancient times, Indra incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin by slaying Vṛtra.
"By you, the doctrine of the Lokāyatas has been disregarded;
I know you to be Bṛhaspati, the divine preceptor of the Āṅgirasas.
Let all these Dānavas now behold you who have arrived here assuming my form. (293)
"Having been brought here by the machinations of Viṣṇu, he is capable of deluding you;
therefore, bind him with chains and cast him into the salt ocean.
Śukra then spoke again to the gods, placing his priest at their head.

"O Dānavas, deluded by this [deceit], you will surely go to your destruction! O lord of the Dānavas, I have been deceived by that evil-souled one. For what reason were you abandoned by him, and another made his priest?"
This very Bṛhaspati is the preceptor of the gods and the son of Aṅgiras (297).
You have been deceived, there is no doubt, for the sake of the welfare of the inhabitants of heaven;
therefore, O illustrious one, abandon him who brings victory to the side of the enemy (298).

O Lord, out of fear of being instructed, I had previously entered the midst of the waters; there I was swallowed by Mahādeva Śambhu. While I remained within his belly, a full hundred years indeed passed.
"From my belly, I was emitted by you through the penis in the form of semen. The God, the Giver of Boons, said to me, "O Śukra, choose a desired boon.
O King, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, was thus entreated for a boon by me.
"O Śaṅkara, by your grace, may all those excellent objects desired by my mind remain present within my thoughts. "So be it," said the God; thus sent forth, I have come into your presence.
At that time, Bṛhaspati was present here as their priest.
"O Lord of the Dānavas, what I have said is true; behold it!
Having been addressed thus, Bṛhaspati then spoke these words to Prahlāda.
"I do not know this man who speaks thus, O King; he is a Dānava wearing my form, come here for the sake of deceiving you. Then all those Dānavas cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (305).
"Let him be our priest, whoever he may be, whether he be old or young.
"We have no need for him; let him go back the way he came!
Thus Kāvya, filled with anger, cursed the assembled lords of the Dānavas. 306–307.
Just as I have been abandoned by you, so too shall I soon behold all of them— bereft of fortune, deprived of life, living in misery,
and having fallen into a most terrible calamity in every respect. (308)
Having spoken thus, Kāvya departed from that place for the penance grove by chance.
After Śukra had gone there, Bṛhaspati remained in that spot,
staying for some time while protecting the Dānavas.
Then, O Lord of Men, after a great deal of time had passed, all the Dānavas gathered together and questioned their preceptor:
"In this essence-less cycle of existence, grant us some knowledge. (311)
"By whose grace, O observer of excellent vows, may we attain liberation?
Then the preceptor of the gods, who had assumed the form of Śukra, replied:
"This very same intention that you have expressed was previously my own as well."
"O Daityas, becoming pure and concentrated together for a moment, I shall indeed speak that knowledge which bestows liberation.
This is the Vedic revelation known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma. (314)
Due to the displeasure of Vaiśvānara, that which causes suffering to living beings here [occurs]. Those sacrifices and śrāddhas performed by the base, who are intent on their own worldly interests—
those Vaiṣṇava dharmas and those likewise established by Rudra [are rendered fruitless].

How will Rudra, who is accompanied by his unrighteous wife and whose nature is primarily characterized by violence and harmful acts, attain liberation—especially he who is surrounded by hosts of spirits and adorned with bones?
317. Furthermore, he is encircled by multitudes of elemental beings and likewise decorated with bones.
In this world, neither heaven nor liberation exists; indeed, people suffer in vain. How can Viṣṇu, who is established in violence, attain liberation?
Brahmā, whose nature consists of the quality of passion (rajas), subsists upon his own creation.
Furthermore, there were celestial sages and others who adhered to the Vedic school;
they were always cruel, prone to violence, eaters of meat, and doers of evil.
These gods, however, were drinkers of wine, and these [others] were eaters of meat, even though they were Brāhmaṇas.
By this dharma alone, how shall one go to heaven, and how shall one attain liberation?

Whatever action there is, such as sacrifices and the like prescribed by the Smṛti, as well as ancestral rites (śrāddha) and so forth—in those, there is no final liberation, for this Vedic revelation is heard regarding them: [321-322]
If heaven is reached by performing a sacrifice, killing an animal, and creating a mire of blood, then by what means is hell reached? (323) If,
by one person eating here, satisfaction were to arise in another;
One should perform the *śrāddha* for one who is traveling abroad, but one must not bring food for them to eat.
O Danavas, those Brahmins who travel through the sky by eating meat have fallen;
for them there is neither heaven nor liberation, nor even this world. 324–325.
Life is desired by every living being once born;
how then could a wise person eat flesh that is like his own flesh?
(326) And how is it that these creatures, born from a womb, resort to that very same womb?
"O Lord of the Dānavas, how will they go to heaven by means of talk about sexual intercourse?
Where purity is achieved through earth and ashes, what kind of purity could that possibly be?
O Dānava, behold this world as it truly is—how utterly perverse it has become!"
After the discharge of feces and urine, there must be purification of the penis and the anus. O King, it is not possible to purify the mouth with earth or water;
how then could the anus and the penis be purified after eating or while eating? (328–329)
In the same way, purification is performed for this contrary state;
wherever washing is prescribed, they perform it with that very thing.
In ancient times, Soma went away after having abducted Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati.
Budha was born as his son; then Guru took her back. Śakra himself seized Mahalyā, the wife of the sage Gautama by name—behold what kind of dharma this is! 331-332.
This world and whatever else is seen here yields only evil;
such is the nature of dharma in this state—what, then, is considered the ultimate truth?
Speak, O Lord of the Dānavas! Speak further, for I shall tell you more.
Having heard the words of the Guru, which were endowed with the ultimate truth, the Dānavas, filled with curiosity and secluded there from the ocean of worldly existence, said: The Dānavas said:
"O Guru, initiate all of us who have surrendered to you and remain here with devotion, so that by your command we may never again fall into delusion;
for we are utterly disenchanted with this worldly existence which bestows only sorrow and confusion. (335-336)
"O best of Brahmins, you have rescued us all from the well by pulling us out by our hair; to which deity should we go for refuge?
O high-minded one, reveal the divinity to whom we may surrender. (337)
Through remembrance, fasting, meditation, and likewise through concentration,
as well as when offerings and worship are performed, liberation is attained.
We, however, being detached from our family, do not strive for it further here.
Thus concealed by those bulls among the Danus, the Guru was addressed by them:
"How shall I accomplish this task?
How am I to make these sinners dwellers of hell?"
"Because they are outside the Vedic revelation, they are a mockery and a cause of laughter for the three worlds.
Having spoken thus, O King, Adhiṣaṇa meditated upon Keśava;
and Janārdana, perceiving that which he had thought, [assumed] the delusion of Māyā.
Having produced this, he gave it to Bṛhaspati, saying:
"This Māyāmoha shall delude all those Daityas;
together with you, he will [delude] all those who have been cast outside the path of the Vedas. (343)
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One vanished.
Then, while the Asuras were intent on their ascetic penance, he assumed the form of Māyāmoha;
approaching them, Bṛhaspati spoke.
"Out of affection for you and pleased by your devotion, I have come here;
I am this naked, shaven-headed yogi who carries peacock feathers.
When the Guru had spoken thus, Māyāmoha then spoke these words:
"O lords of the Daityas, speak! You who are established in asceticism, do you desire the fruits of penance for the sake of this world or for the sake of the next?
The Dānavas said:
"Austerity practiced for the sake of obtaining the dharma of others is not considered [true austerity] by us; why then has this been undertaken? What is intended there?
The Digambara replied:
"Follow my words if you desire liberation.
All this of the Arhatas is an unobstructed gateway to liberation; this Arhat-dharma is the means to liberation, and there is nothing higher than this. (349–350)
"Remaining right here, you shall attain both heaven and liberation"—
with many such words, O Daityas, you were excluded from the path of the Vedas by that Māyā-moha, who is devoid of the vision of liberation.
"This is for the sake of Dharma, this is for the sake of non-Dharma; this is real, this is unreal.
"This leads to liberation, this does not bestow liberation. "This is the ultimate truth, this is exceedingly the ultimate truth, and yet this is not [the ultimate truth]. (352–353)

"This is to be done; this is not to be done; this is clear, but that is not"—thus, through the delusion of *māyā*, they utter various such declarations of meaning: "This is the dharma of those who go naked; this is the dharma of those who wear many garments. (354)

Then all the Daityas were told, O King, "You have been made to abandon your own duties; therefore, you ought to follow my dharma. Because they were told this and resorted to that dharma, they became Ārhata-s (Jainas). 355–356.
Having abandoned the path of the Three Vedas, those asuras were made to be deluded by illusion (māyā); they became absorbed in that [illusion], and likewise others were awakened by them.
By them others were [deluded], and by those others yet others, and by these mutual [influences] still more.

"Salutation to the Unstruck Sound (Ahaṃta)," thus saying, all those who maintained fixed doctrines were abandoned by those Daityas within a few days; consequently, the Triple Veda (Trayī) was mostly lost.
Then [the Lord], wearing red garments, with eyes that had conquered illusion and delusion, appeared once again.
Going to other asuras as well, he spoke these sweet words:
"If you desire heaven, or furthermore, if you desire nirvāṇa, then enough with these wicked practices such as animal sacrifice; listen! (360)
"Understand that this entire world without exception consists of consciousness alone;
comprehend my words correctly, for thus it has been declared here by the wise: this world is without foundation, consisting of nothing other than the proliferation of delusive cognition. (361–362)
Those whose minds are excessively corrupted by passion and other defilements wander through the perils of existence;
for them, he spoke various kinds of words joined with liberation. In whatever manner he taught the Dharma, they abandoned it in that very same way.
O King, some revile the Vedas, others the gods,
while still others revile the entire collection of sacrificial rites and the twice-born;
yet these words do not withstand logical reasoning, for sacrifice results in the dharma of violence.
The wise consider offerings burnt by fire to be fruitless;
if it is claimed that an animal slain in a sacrifice attains heaven, why is one's own father not killed there by the sacrificer? 366.

If another person has already eaten, a man’s satisfaction does not arise [from the offering]. One should perform the *śrāddha* for one who is traveling; travelers do not suffer. Having attained the status of a god through many sacrifices, he enjoys [the fruit] with Indra.

If you consider wood such as the *śamyā* to be better [than a leaf-eating animal], then let it be understood that those words are to be distrusted by people; disregarding them for the sake of your own welfare, may what has been spoken by me be pleasing to you. 369.
"For great asuras do not fall headlong into the words of an authoritative teacher.
[Indra said: "A statement that is logical should be accepted by me and by others like you.
The Dānavas said:
"All of us have taken refuge in you through our devotion to the teaching of reality. O Lord, if you are pleased now, grant us your grace;
let us gather all the necessary materials for the initiation. (371-372)
"By your grace, liberation shall quickly come into our hands.
Then Māyāmoha spoke to all those asuras: "He has indeed sought refuge in my teaching; he is my preceptor of foremost intellect. (373)
"O best of beings, at my command he will grant initiation to you. O Brahmin, initiate these sons of mine at my word.
When their delusion had departed, those Dānavas spoke these words to Bhārgava: 374–375.
"O highly fortunate ones, receive the initiation that liberates from all saṃsāra.
"So be it," said Uśanas to the Daityas, "let us go to the Narmadā. Ho there! Cast off your garments; I shall cause you to undergo the initiation."
Thus, those Dānavas were addressed there by the wise Bhṛgu, the descendant of Aṅgiras, who appeared in a terrifying form;
he told those gods-dressed-in-leaf-garments that their banner should be a peacock feather and their beautiful garland a string of guñjā berries.
Then, having given [the gifts], he performed the shaving of their heads;
for the plucking out of hair is indeed the supreme means for accomplishing dharma.
By the shaving of his hair, the god Dhanada became the lord of riches.
By constantly wearing this dress, they have attained supreme accomplishment (siddhi).
Indeed, thus was eternity obtained; so the Arhat himself declared of old:
"In this world, divinity is attained by men through the plucking out of their hair. 380–381.
Therefore, what should one not do? For it bestows great merit;
indeed, such a desire of the gods has arisen in this world of humans:
that [this teaching] might exist in this land of Bhārata-varṣa within a family of lay disciples (śrāvaka) at the time of birth. 382.
"Let us indeed apply ourselves to austerity by first plucking out our hair;
let the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras likewise be placed before us, and let the Lord of Serpents provide a shade that reveals the path of meditation. 383-384.

For one who praises the Arhat with the recitation of mantras, heaven is already within reach; liberation will surely follow—what need is there for further deliberation? (385) When shall I, filled with indignation, become as radiant as the sun or fire?
Having thus recited [the mantra] without passion and likewise performed the five ancillaries (pañcāṅga),
those of meritorious deeds who die from the exhaustion of time while practicing austerity have their heads shattered by a stone. 386–387.
"When will it be that we shall dwell in a lonely forest,
and our disciples, with concentrated minds, shall whisper into our ears? O Sage, you must go where the path to liberation lies."
"Those states which have been attained, which lead to higher existence and provide sustenance—these must be abandoned by him; this is indeed the word of the Truthful One (the Buddha).
Likewise, through our asceticism and various observances," (389–390)
Go to that supreme state, the path of liberation which the wise,
endowed with austerity and practicing penance, find through a spirit of devotion— wherein there is restraint of the senses and constant compassion for all beings. 391.
That alone is called the dharma of austerity; everything else is a mere mockery.
Having understood this, O noble one, you must attain the supreme state—the goal which the Tīrthaṅkaras have reached and which the yogis have attained.
In this way, the gods, vidyādharas, and mahoragas of old,
contemplating their desires and longings day and night, [attained their goals]; for if you have indeed renounced worldly existence, let there be no further longing.
Abandon your wives, who are the bolts barring the path to heaven! How can you serve that womb from which your father came? And how can living beings eat flesh that is like their own flesh? 395–396.

Then all those formidable Dānavas spoke these words to their preceptor: "O highly fortunate one, initiate us who stand before you as embryos. Having done so, the priest addressed them with a solemn agreement.
"You must never perform prostrations to other deities (398).
When food is offered in a single place, it should be eaten with palms joined together;
the water placed there should be free from hair and insects (399)."
"O Lord, one should act with equal regard toward the pleasant and the unpleasant; never should anything be done that is marred by partiality. You must eat according to this conduct;
act accordingly, and you shall all be partakers of liberation together."
Having spoken thus and having made those bulls among Danavas take their oaths, O King, Bṛhaspati went to the world of the gods, the inhabitants of heaven;
there he reported all that had been done by the Dānavas.
Then those Asuras arrived and dwelt near the Narmadā; seeing those Dānavas there deprived of Prahlāda, the King of the Gods was delighted and spoke these words to Namuci: 403.
"The King of the Gods, being joyful, then addressed Namuci with these words."
Hiraṇyākṣa, Yajñahana, Dharmaghna, Vedanindaka;
the Rākṣasa Krūrakarman, Praghasa, and likewise Vighasa; as well as Muci, Bāṇa, and also Virocana.
Seeing Mahiṣākṣa, Bāṣkala, Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍaka,
Rocamāna, the exceedingly fierce one, and Suṣeṇa, the best of the Dānavas,
as well as others, he then spoke to those lords of the Dānavas.
Indra said:
"O lords of the Dānavas, you were born as kings and have ruled the kingdom in Triviṣṭapa;
how is it that now this vow, which destroys the Vedas, has come to pass?"
"You have begun to act like naked ascetics carrying shaven heads and water-pots, and bearing peacock banners; how is it that you remain thus?
The Dānavas said:
Having abandoned all asura-nature, we abide in the dharma of the sages. We perform actions that increase righteousness toward all living beings;
O Śakra, enjoy the entire sovereignty of the three worlds and depart.
Having said "So be it," Maghavan returned once more to Triviṣṭapa.
Thus, all those best of Dānavas were deluded by Bhīṣma and the priest;
having reached the river Narmadā, they remained there.
Having learned this, Śukra informed them all of the events;
then they once again set their cruel minds upon seizing the three worlds.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Account of the Incarnation," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fourteen. Bhīṣma said:
How was Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, born from three persons?
How is Karṇa proclaimed to be the son of a charioteer born of a maiden?
What was the nature of their relationship from birth?
Tell me that, for my curiosity is great; you ought to explain it to me.
Pulastya said: In ancient times, Brahmā, overcome by great anger, cut off his faces;
sweat then arose on his forehead, and taking it up, he struck it upon the ground.
From his sweat was born Kuṇḍalin, a hero equipped with a bow and great quivers, clad in a thousand coats of mail; he said, "What shall I do?
To him, Viriñca spoke, pointing out Rudra by his power.
"Let this evil-minded one be slain so that he is not born again.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Maheshvara, with arrow in hand and a most fierce gaze, raised his bow and set out from behind.
Seeing that most fierce man, the three-eyed Lord was terrified;
he then fled with speed and went to the hermitage of Viṣṇu,
crying out, "Save me, save me, O Viṣṇu, from this man, O slayer of enemies!"
"O Lord of the World, act in such a way that this evil man, created by Brahmā in the form of a barbarian and terrifying, does not kill me in his anger.
Then Viṣṇu, having deluded that man with the sound of the syllable "Huṃ," [acted accordingly]. 8–9.
Invisible to all beings, the Lord whose self is yoga and who perceives the universe,
Keśava comforted Virūpākṣa when he arrived there.
Then, having been seen by the god Viṣṇu, he prostrated himself upon the ground.
Viṣṇu said: "O Rudra, you are my grandson; what desire of yours shall I fulfill?
Having seen the god Nārāyaṇa, he said, "Give me alms."
Having displayed before him a skull blazing with intense splendor,
Viṣṇu beheld Rudra with a skull in his hand and thought: "Who else would be a suitable recipient for this alms-offering at this moment?"
Thinking, "He is worthy," the moon-crested Lord offered his right arm; he pierced it with an exceedingly sharp trident.
Then, a stream of blood flowed from the arm of the Lord.
Having the appearance of molten gold and fashioned like a flame of fire,
it fell into the midst of the skull, directed by Śambhu from his nose;
straight, impetuous, and fierce, it touched the sky with speed.
Fifty yojanas in length and ten yojanas in width,
this [city] flowed from the arm of Hari for a thousand divine years;
for such a duration of time, that Lord, acting as a mendicant, accepted alms.
Then Nārāyaṇa gave [the skull] into the excellent Kapāla vessel;
thereafter, Nārāyaṇa spoke these supreme words to Śambhu: "Is the vessel full or not? Then indeed, O Lord, the Supreme One [spoke].
Having heard the speech of Hari, which resounded like a water-bearing cloud, Hara—
whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and who is adorned by the moon upon his crest— fixed his gaze upon Janārdana with his three eyes from within his skull-bowl.
Tapping with his finger, he said, "The skull is full. Hearing those words of Śiva, Viṣṇu withdrew the stream;
then, as Hari watched, the Lord [poured] blood from his own finger.
For a thousand divine years, he churned [the ocean] with his glances;
as it was being churned, there then gradually arose a mass of blood and bubbles, and after that, the diadem-wearing god appeared, equipped with his bow.
A man resembling fire was seen upon the skull, his shoulders like those of a bull, wearing a pair of quivers and finger-guards.
Upon seeing him, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these words to Rudra: 24–25.
Then, having heard the words of Hari, the Lord Bhava, who had manifested as a man from the skull, said to him, "O All-pervading One, listen:
this person named Nara is the best among those who know the supreme weapons."
"Because you have spoken thus, he shall be called Nara;
therefore, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa will become renowned in this age for their deeds in battle, for the sake of the gods, and for the protection of the worlds. (27-28)

From him shall be born a son named Nārāyaṇa Saravona; that one of great splendor will provide you assistance in the slaying of the asuras. Furthermore, he will become a sage who is victorious in the world through the examination of knowledge.
This divine fifth head of Brahmā is preeminent in splendor.
From the blazing arm of Brahmā, from the blood of your [severed] arm, and from the fall of my gaze—these are the three splendors that have come forth. (30–31)
Born from their union, he will conquer his enemies in battle;
others who are otherwise invincible shall become slayable by him. He shall be a source of terror even to Śakra and the immortals.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu remained there, and Hari was then filled with wonder.
Placing his joined palms upon his head, the fierce and noble-minded one then praised Hara and Keśava right there where they stood within the skull.
"What shall I do? he asked; having said this, he stood bowed down.
To him, the illustrious Hara spoke, empowered by his own splendor through Brahmā: "A man has been created by me; with bow in hand, you must destroy him."
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara took the two hands of the man who was praising him with joined palms;
lifting them out from the skull-cup, he spoke these words again. (36–37)
"This is that very fierce being whom I have described to you;
he has been cast into a deluding sleep produced by Viṣṇu’s *huṃkāra*. Awaken him quickly! Having said this, Hara vanished.
In the very presence of Nārāyaṇa, this Nara struck him with his left foot, and that exceedingly powerful one rose up once more;
then a great battle took place between those two, who were dripping with sweat and blood.
The entire surface of the earth resounded with the sound of their drawn bows;
the armor of the sweat-born one was pierced by the blood-born one.
Thus, for two divine years, the battle continued between those two as they met in combat.
O King, as the two born of sweat and the one born of blood fought on,
having seen the two-armed one born of blood and the one born of sweat joined together,
Vāsudeva reflected and went to the supreme abode of Brahmā.
Madhusūdana spoke these words to Brahmā with agitation:
"O Brahmā, today this sweat-born [being] has been struck down by the blood-born.
Hearing this, the agitated Brahmā addressed Madhusūdana.
"Let this son of mine live! he cried at that birth.
Then Viṣṇu, being thus pleased, said to him, "It shall be so. Having gone to their hermitage, He restrained them both and spoke to them.

"In another birth, when a great battle occurs at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, I shall unite you two there. Having been thus summoned by Viṣṇu, the Lord of Planets and the Lord of the Gods—
"By my command, these two—Uttama, Mauna, Raukma, and Drauṇi—are to be protected.
This one, born from the sweat of the thousand-rayed Sun, is his own portion [incarnated] upon the surface of the earth;
he is to be brought down at the end of the Dvāpara age for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods. 48–49.
In the lineage of Yadu, there will be a hero named Śūra, possessed of great strength;
his daughter, named Pṛthā, peerless in beauty on earth, a highly fortunate woman, shall be born for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. 50.
Durvāsas, however, will grant him this collection of mantras.
O Goddess, by means of this mantra, whoever invokes the Lord with devotion,
through His grace, he shall have a son for you.
O Vibhāvasu, having seen you rise, she will be filled with desire and, while remaining in her menses and overcome by anxiety, she must be approached.
From her womb shall arise this son of Kuntī, born out of wedlock (Kānīna).
"He shall be a son for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the God of gods.
Having said "So be it," the Sun, a mass of splendor, spoke:
"I shall procreate a son who will be born of Kānīna and proud of his strength."
By my grace, the entire world shall speak of this Viṣṇu, whose ears are like those of a horse, as one of purified soul among the Brahmins; indeed,
there is nothing whatsoever in the world that Keśava cannot give away.
"And may you bring him forth with such power as this by my word.
Having spoken thus to the high-souled god Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of Dānavas, the thousand-rayed Sun vanished right there.
When the sun, the stealer of waters, had gone beyond the range of sight, he, with a delighted mind, spoke thus even to Vṛddhaśravas:
"This man, by my grace, has arisen from the blood of the thousand-eyed one."
"At the end of the Dvāpara age, you must be proclaimed on this earth as one born from my own portion.
O highly fortunate one, when the illustrious Pāṇḍu obtains Pṛthā as his wife, and also Mādrī, O highly fortunate one, he will then go to the forest. (60-61)

While he is dwelling in the forest, a deer will deliver a curse to him; by that, having developed dispassion, he will go to Śataśṛṅga. Desiring sons born from his wife, he will speak to her regarding the sacred field.
Then, not desiring [anything else], she will say to the husband of Kuntī:
"O King, I do not desire sons from a mortal man by any means; O lord of men, I desire sons through the grace of the gods."
"O Śakra, Kuntī is praying that a man should be born from you;
therefore, O Lord of Śacī, act according to my word.
Then the Lord of the Gods, being distressed, spoke these words to Viṣṇu.
When this twenty-fourth cycle of Yugas in the current Manvantara had passed,
he descended into the Raghu lineage and took birth in the house of Daśaratha for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the peace of the dwellers of heaven.
"O Lord, while you were wandering in the forest in the form of Rāma for the sake of Sītā, my son was slain by you, the son of the Sun, acting for the benefit of Sugrīva,
the lord of the monkeys named Vālin. (68)
"Tormented by this suffering, I shall take a human son.
To Indra, who refused to accept this and argued for another reason,
Hari spoke to Śunāsīra regarding the removal of the earth's burden.
O Lord, I shall descend into the world of mortals for the sake of destroying the son of the Sun and for the victory of your own son;
I shall also act as the charioteer and bring about the destruction of the Kuru lineage.
Then Śakra became delighted by those words of Viṣṇu;
accepting Nara with joy, he praised your truthful speech.
Having thus granted the boon and sent him away, the Lord Acyuta himself departed.
Having gone there, the lotus-eyed one spoke again to Brahmā:
"O Lord, this entire triple world, with its moving and non-moving beings, was created by you; we two are merely your assistants in the performance of this task."
O God, you do not realize that after having yourself performed [this act], you seek to undo it. This loathsome deed was committed by you while desiring to kill this Śambhu;
indeed, a man was created by you out of anger toward the God of gods. 75–76.

O Grandfather, perform the supreme expiation for this most grievous sin; O God, maintain the three sacred fires and perform the Agnihotra sacrifice in a holy pilgrimage site, a sacred region, or even in the forest.
"Perform the sacrifice together with your own wife through our acceptance;
O Lord of the World, all the gods, as well as the Ādityas and Rudras, will carry out your command, for you are our sovereign. (78-79)
The Gārhapatya fire is one, the Dakṣiṇāgni is the second, and the Āhavanīya is the third; arrange these in the three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Worship me, the Self, in the circular pit, and then in the one shaped like a bow.
O God, having produced fires through asceticism at the four corners with the names of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and having attained supreme prosperity,
you shall extinguish those fires after offering oblations for a thousand divine years.
Nothing else is recited here as being more purifying than the Agnihotra;
through the well-performed Agnihotra, the twice-born become purified on this earth.
These very paths to the world of the gods have been shown by the Brāhmaṇas.
A single fire must always be maintained by a twice-born householder;
without the fire, the state of a householder cannot be attained here by a twice-born man.
Bhīṣma said:
This man named Dhanurdhara who has emerged from the skull—
was he born from Mādhava, or rather by his own karma, or was he produced by Rudra, or perhaps intentionally? (85–86)
O Brahman, this Hiraṇyagarbha is born from an egg and possesses four faces;
how did his fifth face, which is so wondrous, arise?
For sattva is not seen in rajas, nor is sattva ever found in rajas.
"How did the Lord Brahmā, established in goodness (sattva), assume that mudrā?
By what deluded soul was it sent to kill Hara?
Pulastya said:
Maheśvara and Hari alone abide upon the true path;
for those two great-souled ones, there is nothing unknown, whether accomplished or unaccomplished.
The fifth face of the high-souled Brahmā was situated above.
Then Brahmā became deluded, augmented by the quality of rajas;
thereafter, he thought that this creation had been brought forth by some other power, [thinking]:
"There is no god other than me by whom this creation was set in motion."
Abounding with Sahadevas, Gandharvas, beasts, birds, and wild animals—
thus the deluded Viriñci became five-faced once again;
his eastern face was the originator of the Ṛgveda.
His second face was the originator of the Yajurveda;

the third [was for] the Sāmaveda, and the fourth for the Atharva. [He taught] the Vedas along with their limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas), the Itihāsas, the secret doctrines (rahasyas), and the compendiums (saṃgrahas). 94.
Having studied the Vedas with his fifth mouth and upward-looking eyes,
all the gods and asuras were eclipsed by the brilliance of that face of wondrous luster,
just as lamps lose their light at the rising of the sun.
Even in their own cities, they moved about distracted and full of anxiety; no one else was taken into account by them, as they cast down others with their brilliance.
They did not go forward, nor did they look ahead, nor did they approach anyone.
All the gods, terrified and deprived of their luster, regarding themselves as if overcome, approached the great lord Brahmā, the lotus-born,
and all those deities consulted together for their own welfare. 98-99.
"Let us go for refuge to Śambhu; by his splendor, may this [world] be freed from its lack of luster.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all beings, O Maheśvara; salutations again and again! (100)
"O Source of the World, You are the Supreme Brahman;
You are the eternal refuge of all beings and the cause of all worlds, together with Viṣṇu.
Thus was He praised by the gods, sages, ancestors, and demons.
Having vanished, he spoke these words: "O gods, grant what is desired.
The gods said:
"O Lord, having granted us a direct vision, grant us whatever we desire."
"Show us compassion and let a boon be granted to us as well.
Whatever great heroism, splendor, vitality, and prowess we possessed, all of that has been swallowed up by Brahmā through the brilliance of his five-month-old son. (103-104)
"O Lord, by your grace, may all our splendors return;
O Maheśvara, act so that we may become as we were before.
Then, with a gracious countenance, he was saluted by the gods.
There, Brahmā, his intellect deluded by the egoism born of passion (rajas), wandered about. 106.
Praising the Lord of the gods, they gathered around him and sat down;
yet Brahmā, shrouded in rajas, did not recognize Rudra when he had arrived. 107.

Then the Soul of the Universe, the Creator of the Universe, and the Sustainer of the Universe— who illuminates the world with a splendor surpassing that of thousands of millions of suns— became visible,
along with the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the entire assembly of gods seated there. 108.
Approaching the supreme Brahmā, Rudra said:
"Oh, how your face shines with exceeding splendor! Having spoken thus, the moon-crested Lord let out a loud roar of laughter.
With the tip of the nail of his left thumb, he severed the fifth head of Brahmā as easily as a man might pluck the core of a plantain tree with his fingernails.
Once severed, that head then remained resting in the hand of Bhava.
Standing in the midst of the circle of planets like a second moon, Maheśvara danced with a skull held aloft,
appearing like Mount Kailāsa with the sun resting upon its peak.
When he had spoken thus, the gods were delighted; they praised that bull-bannered god of gods, the one with matted hair (Kapardin), with various hymns of praise. 114.
The gods said:
Salutations always to the Skull-Bearer, the slayer of Mahākāla;
to him who is endowed with sovereignty and wisdom, and who bestows all portions.
115. Salutations to the one who delights in joy and play, and who consists of all the gods.
Because you are the agent of the destruction at the end of the age, you are indeed remembered as Mahākāla.

You are the destroyer of the afflictions of devotees; therefore, you are called Duḥkhānta (the End of Suffering). You bring about the welfare of your auspicious devotees; therefore, you are remembered as Śaṅkara (the Beneficent One).
"Since you have severed the head of Brahmā and carry his skull-cup, O Lord, you are Kapālī;
being thus praised, may you be gracious today. 118. Thus praised, Śaṅkara, with a pleased soul, dismissed the gods.
The Blessed One remained right there, filled with joy, in his own celestial abodes (119).
Then, having understood the intention of Brahmā and the birth of Vīra,
he acted according to the words of Śironīra for the sake of pacifying the wrath of the worlds (120).
Then, placing his joined palms to his head and bowing down to that Prajāpati, the supreme Brahman and treasury of splendor, he praised him in this manner with the Nirukta,
Sūktas, and secret doctrines as expressed in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. 121.
Rudra said:
"Obeisance to you, the immeasurable, the supreme self beyond the highest;
you are the source of wonders and an inexhaustible treasury of splendors. (122)
O you who arise from victory, you are the essence of all existence, the creator of creation, O one of great splendor!
123 Salutations to you whose face is turned upward; salutations to you who are the essence of purity (*sattva*) and the essence of the earth.
Salutations to you who recline upon the waters, who are born from the waters, and whose abode is the waters! 124
O Grandfather Jayadeva, whose eyes are like the blossoming petals of a water-born lotus,

I was indeed created by you in the past for the sake of creation, O Lord; I am the constant consumer of the oblations of sacrifice, the one who presides over the limbs of the sacrifice— salutations to you!
O you who have a golden womb, a lotus-womb, and the womb of the gods; O Prajāpati!
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, and you are the *svadhā* offering, O Lotus-born One. By the word of the gods, O Lord, my head has been severed by me.
"I am overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin; protect me, O Lord of the World!
When addressed thus, Brahmā spoke these words to the God of Gods.
Brahmā said:
The divine Lord Nārāyaṇa will purify you;
He is worthy of being glorified by you, the blessed one, and He is to be worshipped by me as the all-pervading Lord Himself. Indeed, you have surely been meditated upon by that Lord Viṣṇu.
Because devotion has arisen in them, the thought to praise me has occurred to you.
By the severing of your head, you have become a *kapālin* (skull-bearer), the one who brings about the destruction of the moon;
O you of great splendor, you are the deliverer of hundreds of millions of Brahmins. 130–131.
One should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa; nothing else exists [as a substitute].

Sinners, the cruel, slayers of Brāhmaṇas, and evildoers are not to be spoken to; those who perform Vedic sacrifices improperly and those established in wrong actions are not to be addressed by any means whatsoever.
If one has seen them in that manner, one should likewise gaze at the sun;
O Rudra, if there has been contact with their limbs, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
In this way, one attains the purification previously observed by the wise.
"You are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin; therefore, perform this vow. Once the vow has been completed, you shall again obtain many boons.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed, and Rudra did not perceive him.
Then Viṣṇu himself meditated upon him through the path of contemplation—
upon the eternal God of gods, the bestower of boons, who is accompanied by Lakṣmī.
With an eight-limbed prostration, the three-eyed God of gods [was thus honored].
Having become prostrate, he praised the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace.
Rudra said:
"I praise Viṣṇu, the nectar of the lineages, the ancient one, higher than the highest, possessed of infinite prowess. (138)
