I constantly remember the eternal Puruṣa, the most excellent Nārāyaṇa, who is peerless and ancient; higher than the highest, the first-born, of fierce speed, profound, and the foremost among those of deep intellect. I bow to that Lord Hari, the Ruler, the abode higher than the highest, and the supreme light.

I praise Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is pure, who is both transcendent and immanent, the supreme abode, the Lord of the transcendent and the immanent, the vast Puruṣa. He created this entire world as the subtle one who is both transcendent and immanent; because he is eternally present, may that Puruṣa, the Pradhāna, the peaceful Pradhāna, be my refuge. 140–141.
I eternally praise the auspicious Nārāyaṇa, the stainless, the ancient, the Viṣṇu who is higher than the highest and the shoreless shore;
the primordial lord of the earth, the foremost among those possessed of wisdom, and the supreme embodiment of fortitude, forbearance, and peace—
him of great majesty, with a thousand heads and many feet.

I praise Nārāyaṇa, the supreme lord beyond the succession of lords, who has infinite arms, eyes like the moon and sun, and who is both the perishable and the imperishable; he who sleeps upon the ocean of milk, who is unattainable even by the gods, who abides within the three creations, whose eyes are the three fires, who is perceived through the three principles, who is the dissolution of the three, and who possesses three eyes. 143–144.

I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the immeasurable one, who was white in the Kṛta age, red in the Dvāpara, and black in the Kali age; I then bow to Him who created the Brahmins from His very mouth, the Kṣatriyas from the space between His arms, the Vaiśyas from the pair of His thighs, and likewise the Śūdras from the tips of His feet. 145.
I bow to Him who has the universe as His body, the Ancient One, higher than the highest, who has reached the further shore, and who is immeasurable.
I bow to Him whose form is subtle, whose form is great, whose form is knowledge, and who is formless—
the armor of all the gods, whose eyes are like the petals of a lotus.
They bow down to the Supreme Lord, the lord of gods, who has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and mighty arms; who stands pervading the entire universe—
the eternal Viṣṇu, the victorious one, the refuge and the protector worthy of seeking shelter.
I bow to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who resembles a dark blue cloud;
I bow to Hari, who is pure, omnipresent, eternal, whose form is like space, who is ancient, and who is liberated from both existence and non-existence. 149–150.
"O Acyuta, I do not see anything here that is distinct from you;
I behold all this, both the moving and the unmoving, as consisting of you alone.
While Rudra, the supreme lord, was speaking thus—
When he had spoken thus, Sanātana, who is himself higher than the highest, appeared before his sight.
With the discus in his hand and seated upon Garuḍa, illuminating the mountain like the sun, he rose up.
"Choose a boon," said Sanātana; "I am here as your boon-granting deity, come to grant you a boon. (152-153)
Thus addressed repeatedly, Rudra spoke: "O Lord of Asuras, your purity shall become unsurpassed;
for no other supreme remover of this sin is seen except you.
My body, overwhelmed by the slaughter of a Brahmin, has turned black."

"The odor of a corpse is upon my limbs, and these ornaments are of iron. O Janārdana, how can this form of mine become such as yours? O Mahādeva, what shall I do so that I may regain my former body? (155-156)
"By your grace, may that come to pass; tell me this, O Acyuta.
Viṣṇu said: "The murder of a Brahmin is supreme, fierce, and the greatest bestower of all suffering. (157)
One should not even mentally entertain the thought of this sin;
by your own words, this conclusion has been made known.
Now, O mighty-armed one, act according to what was spoken by Brahmā.
Rub all your limbs with ashes three times a day on your body;
wear bones upon your crest, your ears, and your hand.
For those who act in this manner, O Rudra, no suffering shall ever occur.

Having thus instructed him, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign Rudra, accompanied by Lakṣmī, vanished from that place; he did not know that [the world] had been paralyzed. Wandering this earth with a skull in his hand, the Lord of Gods [continued his journey].
Together with Himavanta, Maināka, and Meru;
Kailāsa, the entire Vindhya range, and the great mountain Nīla; as well as Kāñcī, Kāśī, Tāmraliptā, Magadha, and Āvilā. 162–163.
Vatsagulma, Gokarṇa, as well as the Northern Kurus, Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and the region of Hairaṇyaka; Kāmarūpa, Prabhāsa, and the Mahendra mountain.
Overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin, he wandered about and found no refuge.
Filled with shame, always beholding the skull held in his hand, he shook his arms repeatedly and was driven to distraction again and again. 165–166.
When he shook his hands and the skull fell away, the thought arose in him: "I shall now observe this vow;
let all [the food] come from my own path to this twice-born man. (167)
Having meditated thus for a very long time, the god wandered upon the earth. Having reached Puṣkara, he entered an excellent forest,
filled with various trees and creepers and resounding with the cries of various wild beasts.

The ground was adorned with flowers that seemed as if they had been intentionally placed there by a wise hand, and it was perfumed by a gentle breeze carrying the fragrance of the heavy burden of tree blossoms;
likewise, it was filled with various scents and other flavors from fruits, both ripe and unripe.
He entered the thicket of trees, greeted by the fragrance of their blossoms.
(171) "If I worship here with devotion, Brahmā will grant me a boon.
By the grace of Brahmā, the desired knowledge of the *Pauṣkara* was attained. (172)
Thus, as Rudra of immeasurable splendor was thus meditating— [he who is] the destroyer of sin, the pacifier of the wicked, and the increaser of nourishment, prosperity, and strength—
Brahmā, the lotus-born, arrived there, delighted by his devotion.
Raising up the prostrate Rudra once more, the Guru said:
"I have been propitiated by you through the performance of divine vows and observances, and by your extreme faith born of a longing for a vision of me."
Human beings as well as deities behold those established in the vow;
by their will, I grant whatever boon is most excellent. Since this vow has been practiced for the sake of accomplishing all desires, [I grant it].
"With my inner self satisfied by the states of mind, speech, and body, I shall grant you whatever desire you wish for; speak, O Lord, as you desire. Rudra said:

O Blessed One, this alone is a most excellent and great boon, that you, the creator of the world and the one worshipped by the world, have been seen; salutations to you! [This was achieved] through a great sacrifice, performed over a long period of time. (178–179)

"O Lord of Gods, this skull was seen by you through penance that cost you your very life; O All-pervading One, it has fallen from your hand. O Lord, this conduct of yours causes shame even to the sages and is indeed contemptible."
"By your grace, this Kāpālika vow has been performed; it is accomplished for me who has sought refuge.
Now let this great vow be declared here. Tell me in which holy place I should cast this [skull]. (181–182)
"By what means may I become purified among the sages of cultivated souls?
Brahmā said: "There is an ancient abode of the Blessed One called Avimukta. (183)
There, the holy ford (tīrtha) named Kapālamocana shall come into being; there I shall be stationed, as will you and Viṣṇu as well.
Upon seeing you there, even those who are great sinners [shall be purified].
They enjoy their desired pleasures, purified within my abode.
Varaṇā and Asī are two rivers dear to the gods;
in the sacred field between them, one should meditate at some point. 185–186.
This is the most excellent of holy fords (tīrthas) and the most excellent of sacred fields (kṣetras).
Those men who serve this field until the fall of their bodies go, upon death, to heaven by means of a swan-vehicle, free from all fear. 187.
"A field measuring five *krośas* has been given by me to you.
When the Gaṅgā comes from the midst of that field to the Lord of Rivers, then, O Rudra, this city shall become a great place of merit. (188-189)
The meritorious Gaṅgā flows northward, and the Sarasvatī flows eastward;
yet the river Jāhnavī, though facing north, travels with such speed that she covers a yojana in an instant.
There, indeed, all the gods together with Vāsava and myself were present.
"Go to that hermitage and release the skull there.
Those who go to that sacred ford (tīrtha) and satisfy their ancestors with funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and śrāddha rites, their world in heaven shall be imperishable. (191-192)

A man who bathes at the great sacred ford (mahātīrtha) in Vārāṇasī is liberated; by merely going there, he is released from the sins committed during seven lifetimes. That sacred ford is proclaimed to be the most excellent of all sacred fords.
There, living beings who have bowed down to you give up their lives;
O Rudra, having reached your presence, they rejoice together with you.
Furthermore, whatever gift is given there by one of self-restraint, O Rudra— (194–195)

For that person of purified soul, there shall be a great fruit; those men who perform the restoration of cracked parts on his own body, having reached the world of Rudra, always rejoice in happiness. 196.
There, for embodied beings who possess devotion to Rudra, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings yield infinite fruit;
and by offering a lamp there, a person gains the eye of knowledge. 197–198.
He who purchases and liberates a bull that is free from physical defects, young, gentle, and handsome, goes to the supreme state;
together with his ancestors, he attains liberation—of this there is no doubt. 199.
Now, what is the use of saying more? Whatever is performed there by men with a view toward the dharma of action, that shall yield infinite fruit;
that is considered the supreme tirtha on earth, the cause of both heaven and liberation. 200–201.

O Rudra, those devotees who, being solely intent on you, go with devotion to the sacred ford of Vārāṇasī and achieve the means for infinite fruit through bathing, recitation, and likewise fire-offerings—
those devotees who meet their death there, of this there is no doubt. (202)

The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas as the great-grandfathers; such is the Vedic revelation. O sinless one, the threefold rule for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) has thus been declared by me.
Those who have come here must always perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for humans;
likewise, the offering of rice-balls should be performed there with devotion by one's own sons. Such good sons indeed become the bestowers of happiness upon their ancestors.
I have described this sacred ford (tīrtha) to you, which grants liberation even by its mere sight. Having bathed in its waters, one is released from the bondage of birth;
O Rudra, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin there at ease. 206–207.
"Stay here with your wife, for you have been granted by me, Avimukta.
Rudra said:
"Whatever holy places exist upon the earth, in those I shall dwell together with Viṣṇu. (208)
"I abide by what has been spoken by you; this boon has been chosen by me. I am Deva, Mahādeva, who must always be propitiated by you. And I shall grant you a boon with a satisfied inner self. (209)
"And I shall grant to Viṣṇu the boons desired in his mind.
Among all the gods and the sages of purified soul, I alone am the giver and I alone am the one to be entreated; no other should be thought of in any way. (210-211)
Brahmā said:
"O Rudra, I shall do exactly as you have spoken in these auspicious words;
Nārāyaṇa will carry out everything according to your speech, without a doubt. (212)
Having thus dismissed Rudra at that time, Brahmā vanished.
Having gone to Vārāṇasī, Mahādeva established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Rudra's Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, what was done by Brahmā when he sent [him] to the city of Vārāṇasī?

O Sage, what deeds were performed by Janārdana and by Śaṅkara? How was that sacrifice performed by him, and at which sacred site? Tell me all about those members of the assembly and the officiating priests.
"Who were the gods satisfied by him? This is a great curiosity of mine.
Pulastya said: "The city of Śrīnidhāna is on the peak of Mount Meru, adorned with jewels. (3)
It was an abode of many wonders, crowded with numerous trees,
variegated by diverse minerals, and as pure as clear crystal;
it was enriched by the beauty of canopies of creepers and resounded with the cries of peacocks.
It was crowded with herds of elephants terrified by the roar of the king of beasts;
it was cooled by the showers of spray rising from the falling waters of mountain torrents;
and it was variegated by the clear drinking pools formed where masses of trees were struck down by the wind.
The entire forest was perfumed with the excellent fragrance of musk;
travelers and Vidyādharas slept there, exhausted from their dalliances in the vine-cottages;
and it resounded with the sweet melodies sung by throngs of Kinnaras.
Therein was the abode named Vairāja belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, whose entire grounds were beautified by manifold arrangements;
it resounded with the sweet melodies sung by celestial maidens.
Adorned with garlands of blossoms produced from the *pārijāta* tree,
variegated with many colors arising from the mass of jewel-rays, it was beautified by millions of erected pillars and graced with spotless mirrors. 10.
It was made radiant by the playful grace of the dancing postures of the apsarases;
it resounded with the collective sounds produced by many musical instruments; it was endowed with rhythmic timing and tempo, and adorned with numerous songs and instrumental performances.
The assembly hall named Kāntimatī bestows happiness upon the gods;
it is joined by throngs of ṛṣis, frequented by multitudes of sages, resounded by the chanting of the Sāman hymns of the twice-born, and bestows bliss. 13.

Seated there, the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather, intent upon the twilight rites, meditated upon the Supreme God by whom this world was created. As he was meditating, the thought arose in him: "How shall I perform the sacrifice?"

"In what place on the surface of the earth should a sacrifice be performed by me? Is it Kāśī, Prayāga, Tuṅgā, Naimiṣa, or likewise Śṛṅkhala? Or is it Kāñcī, Bhadrā, Devikā, Kurukṣetra, or the Sarasvatī? (16)
Prabhāsa and other such sacred fords (tīrthas) exist here in the center of this earth;
whatever holy fields and meritorious tīrthas exist here in every direction, as well as others on the surface of the world created by Rudra at my command. 17–18.

Just as I am established as the primordial god among all gods, so too do I make this one supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) the first of its kind. Wherever I have arisen, that lotus was born from the navel of Viṣṇu.
"The sacred site is called Puṣkara by the sages who recite the Vedas. As the Prajāpati Brahmā was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind: "I shall go now to the surface of the earth."
Having first reached the summit of that mountain, he entered its most excellent interior,
which was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
resounded with the cries of various birds, and teeming with herds of various wild animals.
It perfumed the gods and asuras with the fragrances of the abundant blossoms of the trees;
its ground was adorned with flowers that seemed intentionally placed there, possessing various scents and tastes, both ripe and unripe, produced by the six seasons. 23–24.
With fruits rich in the beauty of gold, enchanting to the sense of smell and the eye,
the wind— as if out of favor— casts away the withered leaves, grass, dry wood, and fruits that have grown there. (25)
The wind, carrying the fragrance of various clusters of flowers, blew coolly over the sky, the earth, and all directions; it was filled with lush,
green, and unblemished forests that were teeming with trees and free from insects.
It was adorned with various kinds of trees possessing lofty peaks—
some healthy, beautiful to behold, well-rounded, and some radiant—
which appeared on all sides like the family of Brahmins surrounded by officiating priests.
The trees, covered with sprouts resembling [precious] minerals, look beautiful;
like men of noble birth enveloped by their own flawless virtues, they seem to touch one another as their peaks are shaken by the wind. 29–30.
In some places, the Nāga trees, adorned with flower-branch ornaments, seem to smell one another as they bear blossoms and the filaments of the vānīra reeds;
they shine like eyes with flickering pupils and black irises.
In some places, *karṇikāra* trees with peaks laden with flowers shone like pairs of couples; and rows of *sinduvāra* trees, with the profusion of their abundant blossoms, appeared like brides.

In various places, the forest deities appear as if personified, resplendent with flower-ornaments like *kundalatā* vines; they shine upon the trees in every direction, raised aloft like young moons. 34.
In certain forest regions, the flowering Sarja and Arjuna trees shone like men clad in garments of washed silk; likewise, the trees were entwined by flowering Atimuktaka creepers. 35-36.
With their branches entwined with one another, the *sāla* and *aśoka* trees shone like beloved women embracing their husbands,
as if with hands touching hands like friends who have met after a long separation. (37)
The jackfruit trees, saralas, and arjunas, bowed down by the weight of their fruits and flowers,
seemed to honor one another with their blossoms and fruit,
as those trees with arms like *sāla* trunks were embraced by the force of the wind. 38-39.
Having approached the world that has arrived nearby, they stand forth as if through their own splendors;
indeed, having reached the month of Vasanta, they vie with men for the sake of supreme beauty by means of their clusters of flowers. 40.
With their peaks adorned with the beauty of flowers and shaken by the wind,
the trees— like joyful men with garlands decorating their crests— seemed to dance as rows of blossoms were cast from the tips of their branches by the breeze. 41-42.
In some places, trees covered by creepers bent with their own flowers appear like beloved human beings dancing;
they shine like the sky in autumn, variegated by clusters of stars. 43.
Or rather, at the tops of the trees, flowering *mālatī* creepers shine like crests fashioned by some conscious intelligence;
the green trees, possessing the luster of gold, are laden with both fruit and flowers.

In the gathering of the virtuous, men seemed to display their friendship; likewise, bees from all directions, tawny with the pollen of flower filaments, seemed to proclaim the victory of the kadamba flower. 46.
In some places, those intoxicated by the wine of flowers fall here and there;
in others, like male cuckoos with their beloveds in the thickets of trees, pairs of parrots resembling śirīṣa flowers are seen together. 47–48.
The peacocks with their variegated plumage, well-attended by their companions, utter diverse songs like honored Brahmins;
even at the edges of the forests, they dance and appear as beautiful as dancers. 49.
Flocks of birds warbling and crying out in various notes made that forest, already beautiful, even more delightful;
it was filled with herds of various animals and always resounded with the joyful calls of birds.

That forest was equal to the Nandana grove, increasing the delight of the mind and the sight; the Lord, born from the lotus, beheld that supreme forest with a gentle gaze as if it were reflected in a mirror, as if purifying it.
Having seen the Tathāgata in that manner, all those rows of trees offered abundant flowers with devotion to Brahmā;
and the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), having accepted the flowers from the trees, [bestowed them]. 53–54.
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you, O trees," he said to them.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, all the trees, free from restraint, spoke with palms joined in reverence after bowing to Viriñca (Brahmā).
O Giver of Boons, O God who is affectionate toward those who have sought refuge, 56 remain ever present right here in this forest, O Blessed One;
this is our supreme desire, O Grandfather—salutations to you! 57
O Creator of the Universe, if you dwell in this forest of the Lord of Gods, then for us who have sought refuge with our whole being and desire the supreme boon,
let there be no need for millions of other boons; let this alone be granted.
"By its proximity to the sacred fords (tīrthas), this shall become a great and preeminent place.
Brahmā said:
"This shall be the most excellent and meritorious of all sacred fields."
They are always endowed with flowers and fruits, and possess eternally stable youth; they travel at will, assume forms at will, and bestow desired forms and fruits;
they appear according to the desires of men, blazing with the perfection of the asceticism of those mortals.
"By my grace, you shall be endowed with supreme glory. Thus did Brahmā, the bestower of boons, favor the trees.
Having remained there for a thousand years, he cast a lotus (puṣkara) upon the earth.
The earth fell down, and the surface of the underworld trembled violently;
the oceans, with their agitated waves, helplessly overstepped their shores as if struck by Indra’s thunderbolt, while the forests of tigers and serpents were likewise shattered.
The peaks of mountains by the thousands were shattered,
and the celestial chariots of the gods and siddhas, as well as the cities of the gandharvas, shook, wandered, fell, and entered the surface of the earth.
Doves fell from the sky, appearing as if they were clusters of hollows;
the intensely bright suns became obscured by masses of stars. By that great sound, the world was rendered mute, blind, and deaf.
The entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, became utterly agitated;
the bodies and minds of all the gods and asuras grew faint, and they could not comprehend what this was or why it had occurred.
Maintaining his composure, he looked everywhere for Brahmā;
yet, not seeing him, he wondered where Brahmā had gone. Why did the earth tremble? What was the cause of this portentous omen? 69–70.
Viṣṇu went there where the gods were stationed; having prostrated, those inhabitants of heaven spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, tell us, what is this appearance of omens and portents?"
By him who was joined with the law of time, the three worlds were shaken;
at the end of that kalpa, when the oceans had broken their bounds, did the four elephants of the quarters remain immovable or did they tremble? (72-73)

O Blessed One, there is no purposeless arising of sound from the waters of the seven oceans that have suddenly overflowed; for whatever kind of sound has not been remembered [before], it neither existed nor will exist. 74.
"By which fierce wheel the three worlds have been thrown into turmoil;
whether this sound, O Blessed One, is auspicious or inauspicious for the inhabitants of the three worlds and the dwellers of heaven—if you know it, tell us what this is. (75-76)
Thus addressed, Viṣṇu, impelled by the Supreme Being, spoke:
"Do not fear, O all you Maruts; listen here to the cause.
Having understood it with certainty, I shall tell you exactly as it is."
The Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, holding a lotus in his hand,
settled upon a region of the earth that was a mass of merit, in order to perform a sacrifice on a mountain slope in an exceedingly beautiful forest. (78–79)
The lotus fell from his hand onto the surface of the earth,
and its great sound was that by which you were all shaken;
there he was, greeted by the fragrance of the flowers from the multitude of trees.
Then the Blessed One, having graced that forest filled with deer and birds,
chose to dwell there for the sake of blessing the world; he designated that sacred ford as Puṣkara and that field as Vṛṣabha.
"O you who act for the welfare of the worlds, go there together with me and propitiate Brahmā, whom the Blessed One has created;
being worshipped, the Blessed One will grant excellent boons."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, together with those gods and Dānavas,
went to that forest region where the lotus-born Brahmā resided;
they were joyful, their minds satisfied, and they were warbling like the song of the cuckoo.
They entered the forest of Brahmā, which was auspicious and radiant with heaps of flowers;
it was frequented by all the gods and resembled the Nandana grove.
Abounding in lotuses, deer, and blossoms, that very firm forest shone brilliantly at that time.
Then, having entered the forest adorned with every kind of flower, the gods wandered about, desiring to see the deity, thinking, "The god is here!
Thus all those gods, together with Vāsava, searched for him everywhere.
The swift-moving gods did not see the end of that wondrous forest while searching for the deity; then Vāyu was beheld by them. He said to Brahmā: "You shall not see him without ascetic penance."
Then, undaunted, they searched again and again on that mountain slope— on the southern, the northern,
and in between; keeping the words of Vāyu in their hearts, Vāyu spoke to them once more.
The threefold means of perceiving this Viriñci are always declared to be faith, knowledge, austerity, and yoga;
through these, yogis behold the Lord both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). 92.
The ascetic perceives the entire [manifested] reality, while the man of knowledge perceives the supreme partless [Brahman].
Once higher realization has arisen, one of dull faith does not perceive it;
however, yogis behold Brahman swiftly through supreme devotion. 93–94.
This Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, who is free from change, is to be beheld;
you, who are ever-yoked in devotion, should perform penance with body, mind, and speech toward the Grandfather (Brahmā), intent upon his propitiation—may prosperity be yours. 95.
"96–97. 'I must grant my vision at all times to those twice-born devotees who have received the Brāhmī initiation.
Having heard these words of Vāyu and realizing that they were for his own benefit,"
Then those whose minds were permeated by the desire for Brahman spoke to the Lord of Speech:
"O Knower of Wisdom, bestow upon us the Brahma-initiation.
Desiring to quickly initiate the immortals with the Brahma-initiation, he [Vācaspati] acted accordingly.
The Guru initiated them according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas. With humble attire and bowed down, they attained the status of disciples;
having obtained the grace of Brahmā, they were taught the knowledge known as Pauṣkara.
Dhiṣaṇa, the best of Adhvaryu priests, performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites;
having fashioned a lotus rich with lotus-stalks through the ritual application of the Padmadīkṣā, the sage, impelled by the desire of the gods, showed favor to those deities.

To those discerning ones, Bṛhaspati, the noble-minded and high-souled one who knew the application of the Vedic injunctions, gave initiation after casting aside all astonishment; and having consecrated a single fire for the inhabitants of the three heavens, he [performed the rites]. 102–103.

Being pleased, the descendant of Aṅgiras gave him that which is declared in the Vedas—the Trisuparṇa, the Trimadhu, and the purifying Pāvamānī—as well as all other recitations and such; he of noble intellect taught them all. 104.
The bath performed with the mantra beginning "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" is declared to be Brāhma;
it destroys sin, pacifies evil, increases nourishment, prosperity, and strength, grants success and fame, and annihilates the impurities of the Kali age. 105–106.

Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the Brāhma-bath; doing so, they should be silent, self-controlled, initiated, and have their senses subdued. All should carry a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), have their girdles loosened, and wear rosaries of beads.
Carrying staffs, clad in bark garments, and exceedingly adorned with matted locks (108),
they were devoted to the practice of bathing and to sitting in meditation, maintaining diligent concentration;
having yoked their minds to Brahman, they desired only restricted food (109).
Abstaining from seeing, conversing with, associating with, or meditating upon [others],
all of them maintained such vows and performed their ablutions at the three times of day,
endowed with supreme devotion and according to the highest ritual procedure.
After meditating for a long time, those whose minds were fixed on divine knowledge—
whose single-minded purity had been incinerated by the fire of meditation on Brahman— beheld the Blessed One appearing within the range of their vision. (111–112)
Sustained by his splendor, their minds became bewildered;
then, summoning their fortitude, they devotedly worshipped their chosen deity according to the prescribed rites,
with joyful hearts and focused intent through the yoga of the six-limbed Veda.
With their heads bowed and palms joined in reverence, they touched the earth with their foreheads and praised the Lord, the creator of the universe and the sustainer of all beings.
The gods said:
With well-restrained minds, we pay homage to Brahmā, the embodiment of Brahman, who is devoted to Brahman and unconquered;
salutations to the one who bestows the Vedas upon sacrifices, the compassionate deity toward the worlds, whose very form is the creation. 115–116.
Salutations to the one who is compassionate toward his devotees, who is praised by the Vedas and their recitations, whose own form consists of many forms, who assumes hundreds of forms,
the Lord of Sāvitrī, and the Lord of Gāyatrī. 117.
Salutation to the one seated on a lotus, who is the lotus itself, whose face is like a lotus;
118 to the giver of boons, who is worthy of the best gifts, who is the tortoise and the deer; to the one endowed with matted hair and a crown, and who holds the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles. 119
Homage to him who has the deer-mark and the nature of a deer, the leader of the Dharma;
homage again and again to Viśva by name, to the All, and to the Lord of the All.
O Leader of the Dharma, you ought to provide us with protection even greater than this.
"O Grandfather, we have taken refuge in you through our speech, mind, and body.
Thus praised by the gods at that time, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, said:
"I shall grant [your request]; very well. For the sight of me is never in vain for you."
"O sons, speak what you desire; I shall grant you excellent boons.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the gods spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, this very thing is already a great boon, more than sufficient for us today."
"O Lord, this auspicious sound produced by you as you cast down the lotus—why was the earth shaken and the worlds thrown into agitation?
This cannot be without purpose; O God, let the reason for it be told. (124-125)
Brahmā said:
"This lotus has indeed been deposited by me for your benefit and for the protection of the gods; hear now the reason for this."
This Asura Vajranābha, the snatcher of the lives of the ignorant,
remains stationed there, having seized the very foundation of the netherworld (rasātala),
knowing that you have arrived while remaining in penance with your weapons laid aside.
That man of evil conduct desired to kill even the gods, including Indra;
his destruction was brought about by me through the falling of a lotus,
for he was arrogant with the power of his kingdom and sovereignty, and thus he was slain by me.
"In this world, may those Brahmins who are devoted to their vows and have mastered the Vedas never fall into an evil state,
but instead attain a happy rebirth.
[May this apply] to gods, Dānavas, humans, serpents, and Rākṣasas."
"O dwellers of heaven, I am impartial toward the entire multitude of living beings.
For your benefit, this wicked one was slain by me with a mantra;
by the sight of my lotus-like face, he has attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds."
"Because I have released the lotus, this place shall become known on earth as Puṣkara;
it will be a great, purifying, and merit-bestowing tīrtha, proclaimed as a source of merit for all living beings upon the earth. (133)
O God, you have indeed shown favor to us devotees who desire devotion.
O sinless one, Mahākāla has come to this forest at my request; for it was requested by the trees that he dwell there eternally. 134-135.

O gods, as you perform penance, great knowledge has been revealed to you; now, for your own sake and for the sake of others, take it to heart. You must manifest yourselves upon the earth, assuming various forms.
A man who hates a wise Brahmin is surely afflicted by sin alone;
he shall not be released from that sin even in hundreds of millions of births.
One should neither kill nor defile a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Because when one [such a person] is slain, ten million are considered killed,
therefore, one who is endowed with faith should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has reached the end of the Vedas; for him, it becomes as if ten million Brāhmaṇas have been fed— of this there is no doubt.
He who gives alms sufficient to fill the bowl of ascetics is liberated from all sins and shall not fall into an evil state of existence;
for I am the eldest, the most excellent, and the grandfather of all the gods.
Likewise, the one who possesses knowledge—free from the sense of "mine" and without possessions—is always worthy of worship.
For the sake of liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra, this vow protected by Brahman has been proclaimed by me for the sake of the twice-born as the cause of non-rebirth. 142.
He who, having undertaken the Agnihotra sacrifice, abandons it because his senses are unsubdued, quickly goes to the Raurava hell, led there by the servants of Yama.
He who engages in frivolous debate regarding the course of worldly life performs a base deed.

One with a mind full of passion, a lover of the erotic arts, fond of women and wealth, eating alone, a consumer of very sweet foods, engaged in agriculture, trade, and service; one who is ignorant of the Vedas, a reviler of the Vedas, and one who consorts with the wives of others. 145.

By even conversing with one who is corrupted by such defects as these, a man shall go to hell; so too for one who violates virtuous vows, who is discontented, whose mind is divided, who is evil-minded, and a doer of sin. 146–147.
"One should not touch this by bodily contact; having touched it, one becomes pure through bathing.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Brahmā, together with those immortals, established the sacred field (kṣetra); I shall describe that to you exactly as it happened.
To the north of the river Candrā and extending eastward as far as the Sarasvatī, and to the east of the Nandana grove as far as the entire Kalpa forest including Puṣkara—
this is indeed the sacrificial altar (vedī) fashioned by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, for the sake of sacrifice. (149-150)
The eldest should be known as the first tīrtha, which purifies the three worlds; it is renowned as having Brahmā as its presiding deity, while the middle one likewise belongs to Viṣṇu,
and the youngest has Rudra as its presiding deity— thus he made them, beginning with that of Brahmā.
This is the primordial, supreme, and secret field recited in the Vedas. In the forest named Puṣkara, the Lord Brahmā is personally present;
indeed, grace has been bestowed by Brahmā himself upon this portion of the earth. 152–153.
For the sake of favoring all the brahmins who dwell upon the earth,
he had an altar fashioned from gold and ending with diamonds, made of desirable materials, with a floor variegated with jewels and rendered most beautiful in every way. 154.
There the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, rejoices;
likewise do the two gods Viṣṇu and Rudra, the Vasus, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the celestial dwellers along with Mahendra.
This truth has been declared for the sake of favoring the world,
following the sequence of the Saṃhitās with mantras according to the prescribed rites.
Those Brahmins who study the Vedas and are devoted to service toward their guru [attain this].
"All those who have been empowered by him dwell in the vicinity of Brahmā.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, by what rite should men [practice] at Puṣkara in the forest?"

Those dwelling in this sacred field who desire to attain the world of Brahmā—whether they be men or women, or those belonging to any caste or stage of life—what must they practice while residing here? Tell me all of this. (159–160)
Pulastya said:
Men and women residing according to their caste and stage of life should dwell there, devoted to the practice of their own duties and free from hypocrisy and delusion. 161
"By those devoted to Brahman, who have conquered their senses through deed, mind, and speech;
who are free from malice, noble-minded, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
Bhīṣma said:
"What must a man do to be called a devotee of Brahman in this world through his actions? And what kind of people are remembered as devotees of Brahman among men? Tell me.
Pulastya said:
Devotion is declared to be threefold, arising from mind, speech, and body; it may be worldly, Vedic, or likewise spiritual (ādhyātmikī).
That which consists of meditation, concentration, and the recollection of the meaning of the scriptures by means of the intellect—this is spiritual devotion. 164.
That which causes delight to Brahman is called mental devotion (mānasī-bhakti).

Vocal devotion (vācikī-bhakti) is desired to consist of the recitation of mantras, prostrations, contemplation on the fire-sacrifice (agni-śrāddha) and other rites, and the performance of essential prayers (jāpya). 165–166.
By those disciplined in vows and fasts who restrain their minds and senses,
by ornaments rich in gold and gems, as well as by the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances, by the Brahma-kṛcchra fasts, and by other auspicious vows; 167.
Physical devotion has been described as threefold for the twice-born:
[it consists of offerings] consisting of cow-ghee, milk, and curd; jewel-lamps and water with *kuśa* grass;
and various perfumes, garlands, and minerals that have been prepared. 168–169.
With incense of ghee and guggulu, fragrant with black aguru,
with ornaments rich in gold and gems, and with variegated garlands; with dance, instrumental music, song, and offerings of all kinds of jewels.

The worship performed by men with various kinds of food, edibles, meals, and drinks, dedicated specifically to the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), is considered worldly devotion (*laukikī bhakti*). Devotion performed through the application of Vedic mantras and sacrificial oblations is considered Vedic devotion (*vaidikī bhakti*).

The Agnihotra sacrifice should be performed on either the new moon or the full moon day; the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), the offering of the puroḍāśa cake, the preparation of caru oblations, the iṣṭi, the dhṛti, the drinking of soma, and all sacrificial rites are highly commended.
The recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the study of the Saṃhitās, when performed according to the prescribed rules with devotion, is considered Vedic practice.
[One should worship] fire, earth, wind, ether, water, the moon, and the sun. (174–175)
O King, every action performed with a specific purpose has Brahman as its deity;
however, spiritual devotion to Brahman is twofold and established in this way.
One is known as Sāṃkhya, and the other arises from Yoga; hear now the distinction between them.

The twenty-four principles, beginning with *pradhāna*, are enumerated as seventeen; they are insentient and are objects of experience. The twenty-fifth principle is the *puruṣa*; the *puruṣa* is sentient, the experiencer, and not the agent of that action.

The Self is indeed eternal and imperishable, the presiding controller and the instigator; it is the unmanifest, the eternal Puruṣa, the cause, and the Grandfather (Pitāmaha). In truth, there is the creation of the principles (tattva-sarga), the creation of states (bhāva-sarga), and the creation of the elements (bhūta-sarga).
Number, enumeration, the primary, and that which consists of qualities; similarity, measurement, sovereignty, the primary, and the dissimilar;
causality, Brahman-hood, and desirability—this is what is being described. (180–181)

This difference is stated: that the Pradhāna is the object of being employed, whereas the Brahman-Puruṣa is the agent; yet in all cases, the Brahman-Puruṣa is also non-agency [in the sense of not undergoing transformation].
This similarity is stated: that the Pradhāna possesses consciousness.
The differentiation of the principles (tattva), the fact that karma alone is the cause of the principles,

the purpose, the application, and the sovereignty according to the enumeration of the principles— these are declared by the wise who investigate the meaning, having reached a firm conclusion, as being existent. 183–184.
Having heard the equipment for reality, the enumeration of reality according to its true nature, and even that which exceeds the reality of Brahman, the wise know reality.
This devotion, established by the Sāṃkhya authors, has been made spiritual by the virtuous.
Listen also to the devotion toward the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) of those who possess yoga-born devotion:
one who is constantly intent on breath-control (prāṇāyāma), possessed of meditation, with senses restrained;
one who subsists on alms, or observes vows, having withdrawn all his senses.
One should perform the mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) by meditating upon Prajāpati seated in the center of the heart-lotus, with a red face and beautiful eyes,
his countenance radiant on all sides, wearing the sacred thread and reaching down to his hips. 188.
He has four faces and four arms, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The perfection born of yoga and mental concentration is considered the supreme devotion to Brahmā.
He who possesses such devotion toward the Lord is called a devotee of Brahmā.
And hear, O Indra among kings, the mode of life for those residing in the sacred field,
which was previously declared in detail by the Lord himself in the presence of all, including the Brahmins headed by Viṣṇu. 191.
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, unattached and without possessions;
devoid of affection even for their circle of kinsmen, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
they grant fearlessness to all beings through their various constant activities.
Constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), dedicated to supreme meditation,
performers of sacrifices, ever pure, and intent on the duties of ascetics;
they were knowers of the rules of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, knowers of dharma, and free from doubt.
Those Brahmins residing in the sacred field who perform sacrifices according to this rite—
listen to the true fruit for those who die in the Pauṣkara forest:
they attain the imperishable union with Brahman (Brahmasāyujya), which is very difficult to reach.
Having attained that which grants freedom from rebirth and abandons the cycle of return, they have established themselves in the knowledge of Brahman;
for others who dwell in the stages of worldly life (*prapañca-āśrama*), there is a return once more. (197)
Relying upon the rules of the householder's life and always devoted to the six duties,
he who offers oblations properly according to the ritual with mantras consecrated by sacrifice attains superior fruit, freed from all suffering. (198–199)
Moreover, his movement throughout all the worlds is never obstructed;
mounted upon a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot, shining like the rising sun, he travels together with his retinue by means of divine sovereign power.
Surrounded by thousands of women, moving at his own will and dwelling wherever he pleased, he wandered through all the worlds as he desired, irresistible,
most desirable to men, the wealthiest, and the highest in all dharmas. 201–202.
Falling from heaven, he shall be born into a great family, handsome,
a knower of dharma, devoted to dharma, and one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge;
likewise, through celibacy and service to his guru.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas, subsisting on alms, with senses conquered,

constantly engaged in the vow of truth, and remaining vigilant in his own duties— he [should dwell] in a place where all desires are fulfilled and which does not depend upon any specific objects of desire.
Unobstructed by his celestial chariot, which was like the sun without a second,
there were hosts of Guhyakas known as Brahmās who were highly esteemed,
possessed immeasurable strength and sovereignty, and were worshipped by gods and Dānavas. 206.
Endowed with power equal to theirs and possessed of complete equality,
he becomes one whose weapons are not restricted among gods, dānavas, and mortals,
for thousands of crores of years and hundreds of crores of years.

Thus, endowed with sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; having dwelt there with such splendor, when he eventually falls from that state, he is born again in the celestial realms by virtue of his own deeds. 209–210.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest and established himself in the stage of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*), he dwells there through the study of the Vedas; even if he dies while staying there,
having died, he goes by means of a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*) through his own spiritual power.
With a radiance like that of the full moon, he is as pleasing to behold as the moon itself;
having reached the world of Rudra, he rejoices together with the Guhyakas and attains great sovereignty as the lord of the entire universe. 212–213.
Having enjoyed [bliss] for thousands of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
then, having eventually descended from that world of Rudra,
he remains there eternally joyful, having experienced happiness free from all ailment.
He is born into a great and divine family among the twice-born;
or, among humans, he becomes a virtuous soul, handsome, a lord of speech, one whose form is desirable to women, a powerful master of great enjoyments. 215–216.
Following the conduct of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), avoiding cultivated herbs,
his movement through all worlds is never obstructed.
Subsisting on withered leaves and fruits, he may eat flowers, roots, and water.
He should live by means of subsistence such as gleaning grains like pigeons, using a stone for grinding, or using his teeth as a mortar; he should wear clothes of rags or bark,
have matted hair, bathe at the three periods of the day, abandon all faults, and carry a staff.

Whether he be one devoted to the *kṛcchra* vow, or even another such as a *śvapaca*, or one who sleeps in water, performs the five-fire penance (*pañcatapas*), or immerses himself in clouds during the rains,
or likewise sleeps upon the ground covered with insects, thorns, and stones— 220.
Delighting in standing and the heroic posture (vīrāsana), sharing [his food] with others, firm in his vows,
eating forest herbs, granting fearlessness to all beings,
constantly devoted to the acquisition of dharma, he has conquered anger and subdued his senses.

O Bhīṣma, listen also to the destination of that sage who dwells here at Puṣkara, a devotee of Brahman, an inhabitant of the sacred field, who has renounced all attachments, whose delight is in the Self, and who is free from longing.

Resplendent in the sky like a second moon, the devotee of Brahmā travels in a celestial chariot that moves at will and is adorned with pillars and altars shining with the brilliance of the rising sun.
Accompanied by hosts of gandharvas and apsaras skilled in song, instrumental music, and dance,
and joined by celestial nymphs, he remains there for hundreds of millions of years;
unhindered, he goes to the world of whichever deity he desires.
By the grace of Brahmā alone, he shines resplendent here and there;
even when fallen from the world of Brahmā, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu,
and falling from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Falling from that very place, he is born in the continents,
as well as in the heavens and other realms, having enjoyed desired pleasures;
and after enjoying sovereignty there, he is subsequently born again among mortals.
A king, or a prince, or one who is born wealthy and happy;
handsome, fortunate, beloved, renowned, and permeated by devotion—whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those dwelling in the countryside. 230–231.
O King, those who were devoted to their own duties, well-behaved, long-lived,
entirely devoted to Brahman, and intent on showing grace to all beings,
dwelt at the great sacred field of Puṣkara as seekers of liberation. 232.
Upon death, they go to the abode of Brahmā in beautiful celestial chariots that travel at will, assume any form at will, and resound with the songs of throngs of Apsarases.
Or else, he who offers his own body as an oblation into a perpetually blazing fire [attains the same].
The great being who meditates upon Brahmā shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
for him, the world of Brahmā is imperishable and eternal, along with its splendors.
He becomes preeminent in all worlds, delightful, and the accomplisher of his desired aims. (235)
O Bhīṣma, for those high-souled ones who cast off their lives in the waters at the highly meritorious Puṣkara, there is an imperishable world of Brahmā;
they behold the Lord himself, the destroyer of all suffering.
The Śūdra men who died by fasting in the Puṣkara forest go to the god Rudra, who is joined by all the immortals and accompanied by the hosts of Viṣṇu;
from there, they travel in celestial chariots yoked with swans and radiant as the sun.
Rich with various jewels and gold, firm and perfumed with fragrances; possessing other incomparable qualities, resounding with the songs of apsarases;
adorned with banners and flags, and echoing with the sounds of various bells.
Endowed with many wonders, skilled in the arts of play, radiant, perfected in virtues, and borne by excellent peacocks— those wise men,
having died, take delight in the world of Brahmā.
Having dwelt there for a long time and enjoyed pleasures as desired,
that mortal who has returned to the human world is born into a wealthy family as an enjoyer of luxuries.
Furthermore, the man who prepares a fire-pit of dried cow-dung in the Puṣkara forest [attains the same].
Having abandoned all worlds, he goes to the world of Brahmā; he shall dwell in the world of Brahmā until the end of the kalpa. Indeed, he does not see a mortal suffering on account of his own karmas.
His movement is unimpeded across, upwards, and downwards;
he is worthy of worship in all worlds, spreading his fame, self-controlled, wise in the rules of right conduct, and captivating to all the senses. 245–246.
Skilled in dance, instrumental music, and song, he was handsome and pleasing to behold;
his flowers never withered, and he was adorned with divine ornaments.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, his hair was dark and curled.
Not low-born, with beautiful waists, and filled with every kind of good fortune;
endowed with all sovereign qualities and exceedingly proud of their youth, the women stationed there serve him and delight him upon his bed. 248–249.
Awakened by the sounds of lutes and flutes,
he enjoys the great festival-happiness that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to attain,
through the grace of Brahmā, the God of gods, the performer of auspicious deeds. 250.
Bhīṣma said:
Their conduct was the highest dharma, and they were devoted to the duties pertaining to their station;
they were intent on the practice of their own specific duties, having conquered anger and subdued their senses.
"It is not surprising in my opinion that they go to the world of Brahmā;
without doubt, O twice-born ones, they also go to other worlds even without the Padma fast and likewise without [other] observances. (252–253)
O Brahmin, women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts,
the mute, the dull-witted, the blind, and the deaf— those who are devoid of austerity and self-restraint—
attain their respective states by remaining at Puṣkara.
Pulastya said: O Bhīṣma,
women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, cattle, birds, and wild animals—
those who die at Puṣkara go to the world of Brahmā.
With bodies of divine form, they ascended celestial chariots of radiant luster,
256 equipped with divine arrays, possessing excellent golden banners, and adorned with stairways of gold and diamond and pillars of jewels. 257
Abounding in the enjoyment of all desires, traveling at will and assuming forms at will, rich in various flavors, and accompanied by thousands of women,
those great-souled ones go to the world of Brahmā or to other worlds as they desire.
Even those who have fallen from the world of Brahmā proceed in due course to the continents; there, as a virtuous twice-born man, he becomes wealthy in a great and extensive family.
As for those who have entered the wombs of animals—snakes, insects, and ants—[they likewise attain their goal]. (259–260)
Those born from land, water, sweat, eggs, sprouts, or wombs—
whether with desire or without desire— who die in Puṣkara or in the forest,
ascend in celestial chariots originating from the sun and proceed to the world of Brahmā.
In this most terrible Kali age, when living beings are impelled by sin,
dharma and heaven cannot be attained by any other means than this: those men who dwell at Puṣkara, devoted to the worship of Brahmā.
In the Kali age, those who have achieved their purpose find it easy, while others suffer in vain;
for whatever sin a man commits at night through his five senses,
by action, mind, or speech, he remains subject to the power of desire and anger.

Having reached Puṣkara at dawn while it is still possessed of water, and having approached the Grandfather (Brahmā) after becoming pure, one is liberated from that sin; this applies from the rising of the sun until its upward disappearance [behind the western mountain]. 265–266.

By contemplating the yoga of Brahman known as Mānasa, one removes sin; having seen Viriñci at midday, a person is liberated from evil. (267) Even if one should commit sin with the senses from midday until sunset, [it is destroyed by this].
By merely seeing the grandfather [Brahmā] at the time of twilight, one is thus liberated.
(268) Even while enjoying all objects of the senses such as sound and the rest according to his desire, he who dwells at Puṣkara devoted to Brahman remains established in austerity. (269)

Those men of virtuous deeds who dwell in Puṣkara, eating food seasoned with the taste of sweet delicacies while staying in the midst of the Puṣkara forest, are considered equal to those who subsist on air alone, even though they eat three times a day. (270)
"O venerable ones, it is by the power of this sacred field that such great enjoyments are obtained.
Just as there is no other body of water equal to the great ocean, so too no other holy ford (tīrtha) exists that is equal to Puṣkara. (271-272)
There is no sacred ford (tīrtha) superior in qualities to the Puṣkara forest;
now I shall describe the others who are established in this field, including all the gods such as Indra and Viṣṇu. 273.
The elephant-faced Kumāra moves like the sun with his chariot;
likewise, the goddess Śivadūtī and Kanyākṣemaṃkarī are always present.
For those who perform worship through virtuous deeds, there is no need for austerities or restrictive observances.
Even after performing great acts such as vows and fasts elsewhere,
if a twice-born man remains here in the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara forest, free from worldly exertion, he attains the fulfillment of all his desires while always residing right here.
The grandfather’s equal, supreme, and imperishable station [is attained] in twelve years during the Kṛta age, in one year during the Tretā,
in one month during the Dvāpara, O Bhīṣma, and in a single day and night during the Kali age. 277–278.

"The fruit is obtained in this world by those dwelling at sacred fords (tīrtha) in this field"— this is what was previously told to me, O Brahmins, by the God of gods. There is no field superior to this upon the surface of the earth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in this forest.
Whether a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant, all who act according to what has been prescribed attain the supreme goal. 280–281.
He who practices the dharma of even a single stage of life according to the rules,
free from desire and hatred, is exalted in the hereafter.
This ladder with four rungs has been established here by Brahmā.
Relying upon this ladder, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), free from malice and skilled in the matters of dharma and worldly purpose, should dwell for at least a quarter of his life with his teacher or with the teacher’s son.

One who desires to study should learn from a teacher beyond the mere performance of ritual duties; when summoned, he should provide the sacrificial fees and take refuge with the teacher. He should sleep later and rise earlier than his teacher in the teacher's house.
Whatever must be done by the disciple— such as service and other duties— he should perform all of that, thinking "it has been done," and then remain at his side as a servant,
performing everything and being skilled in all tasks. (286–287)
Pure, skillful, endowed with virtues, and having conquered his senses, he should look at the teacher with his eyes without distraction and speak the desired answer.
He should not eat while the teacher has not eaten, nor drink while he has not drunk.
One should not remain standing in that manner, nor should one go to bed while still asleep.
With both hands turned upward, one should gently touch the feet;
one should press the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand.
Having saluted his guru, he should speak, pronouncing his own name:
"O Blessed One, I shall do this, and this also has been done by me.
Thus, having informed him of everything, he should offer the gift to the guru.
And all that has been performed should again be reported to the teacher.

Regarding those fragrances or flavors which the religious student (brahmacārī) does not enjoy, it is the settled rule in the dharmas that he may enjoy them after his formal graduation (samāvartana). 292–293.

Whatever rules have been stated in detail for those who do not practice celibacy, the devotee and disciple of the guru should observe them all according to his ability; he alone, having rendered service to please the guru, [attains success]. 294.
In non-rural hermitages alone, the disciple should abide through his actions; likewise, O twice-born one, having studied the Vedas, the Vedānta, the various branches of the Vedas,
and the meaning of the Vedas from the mouth of the guru, he should subsist on alms and sleep upon the ground.

Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru according to his capacity— one-fourth of what is required for the Vedic vows— he should perform the *samāvartana* ceremony according to the prescribed rule.
Then, accompanied by noble persons endowed with righteousness, he should invoke and worship the sacred fires (*agni*).
During the second portion of his life, one should live as a householder (gṛhamedhī).
Four modes of livelihood for householders were previously established by the sages:
the first is that of one who possesses a granary of grain (kusūladhānya), and the second is that of one who possesses a jar of grain (kuṃbhīdhānya). 298–299.
The third [mode of life] is called "no-provision-for-tomorrow" (aśvastanī), and the fourth is the "pigeon-like" (kāpotī);
among these, each subsequent one is superior in terms of dharma and is the best for conquering the world. One [householder] subsists by the six duties, while another proceeds with three.
And by these two alone does the twice-born man become established as a true knower of Brahman.
They declare that there is no greater sacred ford than the vow of the householder;
he should not cook food for his own sake, nor should he slaughter an animal in vain.

Whether it be a living being or a non-living thing, one should perform sacrifices with consecrated materials; one should never sleep during the day, nor ever during the first or last watches of the night.
One should not eat at improper times, and one should not speak untruth here in this world.
Furthermore, no Brahmin should dwell in one's house without being honored while eating;

likewise, guests who are the conveyors of offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) must be honored—those who are purified by Vedic knowledge and vows, who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), and who have mastered the Vedas. 304–305.

Those who live by their own prescribed duties, who are self-controlled, active in their rites, and ascetic—for them, the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) are ordained for the sake of honoring;
[but not for one] who has departed from his own dharma and who has fallen away from his own duty. 306.
For one who has abandoned the *agnihotra* sacrifice, for one who acts falsely toward his teacher, and for one who is intent on untruth, there is no entitlement to the two rites;
however, a share of all beings remains here for them. 307–308.
In the same manner, the householder should give to those who have not yet cooked; he should always be one who eats the remains (vighasa) and always one whose food is nectar (amṛta).
The remnant of a sacrifice is nectar; such a meal is equal to the sacrificial oblation (havis).
He who eats what remains after others have eaten is called a "consumer of vighasa" (vighasāśin).
He should be devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, diligent, and one who has thoroughly subdued his senses;
he should eat together with the officiating priest, the family priest, the teacher, maternal uncles, and guests.

One should not engage in disputes with the elderly, children, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends; nor with one's mother, father, son-in-law, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants. (312)
By resolving these contradictions, one is liberated from all sins.
By conquering these, one undoubtedly conquers all the worlds;
for the teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā, and the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati.

The guest is the lord of all the worlds; the officiating priest is the refuge of the Vedas and their master; the son-in-law is among the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen are those related through the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
relatives and blood-kin are on the earth; and the maternal uncle and mother are likewise there. (315)
The elderly, children, and the sick, as well as those who possess power in the sky;

the family priest, the world of sages, and the lords of the worlds; those who have taken refuge there, the Sādhyas, and the world-protectors; the lord of the Aśvinīs, the physician, and his brother, the lord of the Vasus—316–317.

Candra is the wife of Lokeśvara; his daughter is among the Apsarases in their abode; his eldest brother is equal to his father; his wife, son, and his own body [are his]; the scribes and the group of slaves, and his daughter, are most wretched. 318. Kāyastha. Dāsa-varga. Duhitā. Kṛpaṇa. Parama.
Therefore, one who is reviled by these [critics] should always endure it without feverish distress.
A wise man, devoted to the duties of a householder, established in dharma, and having conquered fatigue, should not undertake many tasks; being possessed of dharma, he should undertake only a little.

There are three modes of life for householders; they say that among these, each successive one is superior for the sake of the highest good, as is the system of the four stages of life (cāturāśramya). Furthermore, whatever observances have been prescribed, all of them must be performed by one who desires to prosper.
In that kingdom where these people dwell— those who store grain only in jars, those who gather gleanings, and those who follow the pigeon-like mode of life— that kingdom prospers;
it purifies ten generations of ancestors before and ten generations after.
One who practices this very mode of life of a householder, free from the distress of worldly attachment,
shall attain a destination equal to that of the worlds of the Wheel-bearers (cakradharas);
or rather, this is ordained as the destination for those who have conquered their senses.
This is the ladder established by Brahmā for householders of self-restraint who dwell in the heavenly world;
having ascended this second stage in due order, one who is liberated from it is glorified in the heavenly world.
I shall speak of the third stage as well; listen to the forest-dweller's order of life (*vānaprastha-āśrama*).
When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, and [sees] the offspring of his offspring, he should then take refuge in the forest.
Listen, O auspicious Bhīṣma, concerning those who dwell in the forest hermitage (vānaprastha) being weary of the householder's vows— those who take refuge in all the worlds as their very self,
who have desisted from worldly life through initiation, and who reside in sacred lands. 228–229.
Endowed with the power of wisdom, possessing truthfulness, purity, and forbearance,
he should spend the third part of his life in the forest-dweller stage (vānaprastha),
serving those same sacred fires and worshipping the gods.
One who is fixed in their diet and devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu—
then for such a person, all sacrificial elements, including the Agnihotra, as well as uncultivated rice, barley, nīvāra grain, and the remnants of offerings (vighasa), are [sufficient]. 231–232.

In summer one should consume food fit for sacrifice (haviṣya); these four modes of subsistence are prescribed even during the five months of the rainy season. Among those in the forest-dwelling (vānaprastha) stage of life, some are eaters of what is obtained immediately, while others store up provisions for a month.
Some store provisions for a year, and others for twelve years,
for the sake of honoring guests and for the performance of sacrificial rites; they live under the open sky during the rains and take refuge in water during the winter.
In summer they perform the penance of the five fires; in autumn they subsist on nectar-like food; they roll upon the ground and stand even on their tiptoes.
They remain in standing and sitting postures, and likewise in various bodily positions.
Some used their teeth as mortars, while others used stones for grinding;
some drank boiled barley-gruel during the bright fortnight, while others drank it during the dark fortnight, or ate according to the traditional rules.

Some, firm in their vows, subsist according to the rule on roots alone, others on fruits alone, and still others on water alone; these and various other initiations belong to those high-minded ones who uphold the Vaikhānasa vow. 339.

And the fourth dharma, that of the Upaniṣads, is considered common [to all]. During that very age, O Tāta, the other [stages], namely the forest-dweller and the householder, proceed constantly among the Brahmins who perceive the meaning of all things. (340-341)
Agastya, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), Madhucchandas, Gaveṣaṇa, Sāṃkṛti, Sadiva, Bhāṇḍi, Yavaprotha, Atharvaṇa,
Ahovīrya, Kāmya, Sthāṇu, Medhātithi, and Budha. 342.
Manovāk, Śinīvāka, Śūnyapāla, and Kṛtavraṇa—
these wise men, through their ritual acts, attained heaven;
they were seers who perceived dharma directly, as were the groups of Āyāvaras.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Gods, those sages of fierce austerity, who perceive the subtleties of dharma, took refuge in the protection of the Brahmins;
having cast aside all latent illusions, they took refuge in the protection of the Brahmins.
Then those groups of ascetics, who were unassailable and free from the influence of the stars, appeared as they had departed [from their former state].
Wasted by old age and afflicted by disease,
they proceeded from the stage of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha) to the final remaining stage of life (the fourth āśrama).

Performing sacrifices immediately, having offered all his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasa-dakṣiṇā*), being a self-sacrificer with a mind devoted to Soma, sporting in the Self and taking refuge in the Self; having established the sacred fires within himself and renounced all worldly attachments— 348.

One should always perform sacrifices and rites here that yield immediate results; for those who constantly sacrifice, the sacrifice proceeds within the self. One should properly abandon the three fires within the self by means of the self in an instant.
Whatever he may obtain, he should eat that without disparaging it; or, devoted to the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vānaprastha-āśrama*), he should cast off his hair, body hair, and nails.
Purified by his actions, he goes immediately from one stage of life (*āśrama*) to the next.
If a twice-born man goes forth into the homeless life after granting fearlessness to all beings,
his worlds will be full of splendor after death, and he attains infinity.
Possessed of excellent conduct and character, with his impurities removed, he does not strive for anything either here or hereafter.
One whose peace and conflict arise from a state free of anger and delusion, who remains like a neutral observer through self-reflection,
who is not distressed by what happens to himself or to others, whose heart is empty of his own scriptures and free from self-delusion— such a person,
devoted to dharma and having conquered the senses, may move about as he pleases, performing the sacrifice of the Self, without doubt. 354.

Beyond this, hear now the description of the fourth and supreme stage of life (āśrama), which is presided over by the most excellent and abundant virtues, transcends the [other] three stages, is declared to be the highest goal, and is the ultimate refuge;
having attained the refinement resulting from these two preceding stages, one proceeds beyond them. 355–356.

Listen with a one-pointed mind to that which is the task for the sake of the Supreme Self: having donned the saffron robe, he who proceeds toward the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), through the three stages of the spiritual orders (*śreṇī*). 357.
Listen now to how one should live after renouncing through that cultivation: "One should practice dharma alone, without companions, for the sake of perfection.
He who wanders alone, seeing clearly, neither abandons nor is abandoned. (358-359)
Without fire and without a fixed dwelling, he should enter a village for the sake of alms; the sage, endowed with pure intent,
should not provide for the morrow and should eat light food, restricting his diet and consuming it only once a day.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, tattered rags, solitude, and equanimity toward all beings— this much is the characteristic of a mendicant,
into whom words enter like waters reaching the ocean.
They do not go again to the state of being a speaker; he should dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
He should never look upon nor hear anything that is unfit to be spoken to anyone, especially regarding Brahmins; this must never happen under any circumstances.
One should always speak only that which is agreeable to a brāhmaṇa;
one should remain silent during his censure, thereby performing a remedy for oneself.
By whom alone is the sky always made as if full? (By the wind. 365-366.
The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa by whom emptiness is fully pervaded.
(366) The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa by whom [the body] is covered with anything at all, by whom it is fed with anything at all, and who sleeps anywhere whatsoever. (367)
The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who is afraid of the people of this world as if of enemies, and of his friends as if of hell, and of women as if of wretches;
who neither exults when honored nor desponds when dishonored. (368)
The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa who grants fearlessness to all beings.
He should neither rejoice in death nor rejoice in life;
he should simply await his time, just as a farmer awaits the instruction [of the season].
One whose mind is unassailed, who is self-controlled, whose intellect is likewise unshaken, and who is liberated from all sins— such a person goes from here to heaven.
Since he grants fearlessness to all beings, he receives fearlessness from all beings.
For one who is liberated from the body, there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever.
Just as all other footprints of those who walk upon the earth are eclipsed by the footprint of an elephant, so too are all [other] cognitions eclipsed within the mind [of the liberated].
Thus, in non-violence, both dharma and wealth flourish greatly;
for he who practices violence remains eternally subject to death, whereas one who is non-violent is consequently possessed of perfect fortitude and restrained senses. (374)
He who is a refuge for all beings attains the unsurpassed goal.
For the wise man who is thus satisfied with wisdom and free from fear, death is no longer a superior state; he attains immortality. 375–376.
The sage who is liberated from all attachments, who abides like space,

who acts for the pleasure of Viṣṇu, and who is peaceful— the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa. (377) He whose life is for the sake of dharma, and whose dharma is solely for the sake of delight [in the divine].
The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who seeks merit not for the sake of day and night rituals;
who has desisted from all worldly undertakings, who offers neither salutations nor hymns of praise, and who, though his actions have ceased, remains undecayed. 378–379.

All beings delight in happiness, and all sufferings become intense for them; one who feels weariness born from the production of their existence should perform actions with faith. For the gift of fearlessness to all beings here surpasses all other gifts.
He who first offers an oblation with a sharp-edged vessel attains infinite fearlessness for his progeny.
He offers the oblation with an upturned mouth and attains infinite support on all sides;
through the contact of its limbs, he has indeed reached this entire Vaiśvānara world. 381–382.
That which extends a span's length and flows into the heart—into that, the self-sacrificer offers with the vital breath (prāṇa).
That Agnihotra offering becomes established in the Self within all worlds and all deities. Those who know that golden, threefold deity as the ordainer, they know him as the supreme reality.
Honored among all beings, those gods who are capable attain immortality.
He who knows everything—the Vedas, that which is to be known, the entire ritual procedure, etymology, and the supreme truth—within the Self of the body; all these [gods] constantly attend upon him.
He who knows that golden one, unattached to the earth and the heavens, immeasurable,

moving clockwise within the circle of the sky in the southern atmosphere, with blazing rays, revolving and turning back— possessing six fellies, twelve spokes, and three joints— [he indeed knows the Self]. 386.
That *Kālacakra* (Wheel of Time), whose mouth encompasses the entire universe, is hidden within the cave of the heart;
from it one attains grace, the body of the world, and all the realms here.
For by satisfying the gods within that [cakra], one becomes eternally liberated in this very life. 387–388.

Therefore, he is eternally composed of splendor and is ancient; he exists in the world for the sake of purpose, and from him living beings do not experience fear. He who never trembles before living beings, who is beyond reproach and does not reproach others—he alone, O Brahmin, should regard himself as preeminent. 389.
One whose delusion has been subdued and whose impurities removed does not seek gain either in this world or the next.

Free from anger and delusion, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with grief abandoned and both alliance and conflict departed, free from blame and praise, and indifferent to the pleasant and unpleasant, the mendicant wanders like one who is truly detached.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dwelling in a Sacred Place," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixteen. Bhīṣma said:

O Brahmin, this supreme majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha) which has been described—how did that ford come to exist upon the earth through the falling of the lotus? And by whom was it established there: by the Blessed Viṣṇu or by Śaṅkara?
O tiger among sages, recount all that was done;
how indeed was the sacrifice caused to be performed there by the omnipresent Lord?
Who were the members of the assembly, who were the officiating priests, and which Brahmins had assembled there?
What were the portions of that sacrifice, what was the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), what was the altar, and what was its measurement? And what was performed there by Viriñci?
Who was the one to be worshipped by all the gods, who is recited everywhere in the Vedas?
Meditating upon his own desire, the Creator performed a sacrifice.
Just as that lord of gods was indeed undecaying and immortal,
so too is the heaven of that god seen to be imperishable.
Furthermore, heaven was granted by that Great-Souled One to other gods as well;
likewise, the Vedas and medicinal herbs were produced for the sake of the Agnihotra sacrifice,
and all other animals upon the earth exist for the purpose of sacrifice.
"This was created by this Blessed One"—such is the Vedic revelation.
Having heard what you have spoken here, I have a great curiosity regarding that single desire for which it was intended, its fruit, and the underlying intention. (8–9)
He has indeed performed a sacrifice; you ought to praise it all.
She who was Śatarūpā is here called Sāvitrī. She is declared to be the wife of Brahmā and the mother of the ṛṣis.
Brahmā,

the beloved of Brahmā, begot Sāvitrī as his lawful wife; she gave birth to the seven sages beginning with Pulastya, the Prajāpatis beginning with Dakṣa, and the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, thus becoming a mother of sons.

How did he abandon his virtuous wife— who was devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, firm in her vows, and sweetly smiling— and take another? What was her name, what were her deeds, and whose daughter was she, O Lord?
"By whom was she seen, O King, and by whom was she pointed out to him? What is the form of that Goddess who deludes the mind, seeing whom the Lord of Gods fell under the sway of Kāma? (14–15)
O Sage, she surpassed Sāvitrī in both complexion and form;
she was the one who deluded the Lord, the all-pervading Sovereign of all worlds, so that the God took that woman as his wife, the most beautiful in the world. 16.16–17a.
Proclaim everything exactly as this sacrifice proceeded.
Having seen her by the side of Brahmā, what did Sāvitrī do? At that time, Brahmā engaged in amorous dalliance with Sāvitrī.
