Even though the Sāvitrī had been addressed by Brahmā with words full of censure at that time, she spoke again; you ought to relate everything. What was done there by you—was it anger, or perhaps forgiveness?
Whatever was done there, whatever was seen, and whatever has been told by me here— 20—
I wish to hear in full detail all the deeds of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), as well as the entire procedure for the ritual and the supreme method of sacrifice. 21.
The sequence of the rites, the commencement,
the office of the Hotṛ priest, the portion for the Hotṛ, and how the first draught was offered—
how did the Lord Viṣṇu provide assistance, by whom, and of what kind?
You ought to explain that which was done by the immortals. Having abandoned the world of the gods, how did you come to the mortal realm?
And [how did you maintain] the Gārhapatya fire according to rule, as well as the Anvāhāryapacana and Dakṣiṇa fires?
He likewise established the Āhavanīya fire, the altar, the *sruva* ladle, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *sruk* ladle, and the *āvabhṛthya* water; indeed,
he arranged the three fires that carry the portions of the oblation.

He made the Asuras eaters of *havya* (oblations) and the Pitṛs eaters of *kavya* (funeral offerings). For the sake of their shares in the sacrificial rites, he created, according to the rules of sacrifice,
the sacrificial posts, the fuel, the *kuśa* grass, the *soma*, the strainers, and the enclosing sticks.
Just as Brahmā performed the sacrificial rites,
so too did he shine forth in ancient times through his supreme office (*pārameṣṭhya*) and ritual action.
Moments (*kṣaṇa*), eye-blinks (*nimeṣa*), units of time (*kāṣṭhā*), divisions of time (*kalā*), and the three periods of time (*traikālya*) likewise [arose].

The muhūrtas, lunar days (tithis), months, days, and likewise years; the seasons and the conjunctions of time; the threefold measure of ancient times; lifespan, fields, decline, characteristics, and physical excellence—these were [established]. 29–30.
The three castes, the three worlds, the threefold knowledge, the three fires,
the three times, the three actions, the three castes, and the three qualities— these supreme worlds were created by the Creator, as were others by one of limited intellect.
He is the destination of those endowed with dharma and the destination of those who commit sinful deeds;
he is the source of the fourfold varna system and the protector of the fourfold varna system;
he is the knower of the four Vedas and the one who takes refuge in the four stages of life (āśramas). 32–33.
He who is heard of as the supreme light, he who is heard of as the supreme austerity, he who has declared that which is beyond the beyond, he who possesses the supreme Self;
he who is the bridge for all bridges of the worlds, and the pure one among those whose deeds are pure.
He who is the object of knowledge for those who know the Vedas, the Lord of those whose nature is power; he who is the vital breath of all beings, the fire for those possessing the luster of fire;
he who is the mind of human beings, and the asceticism of the ascetics. (35-36)

The Grandfather of the worlds, creating all these—including those who follow the discipline of the Vinaya, those whose conduct is guided by reason, and even those who possess splendor—desired to know the course of sacrifice; how was the mind directed toward sacrifice? 37.
O Brahman, this is our doubt; this is our supreme doubt:
Brahmā is recited by both gods and Daityas as a supreme marvel, yet he is said to be such in reality because his actions are themselves marvelous. 38–39.
Pulastya said: "This burden of questions you have posed regarding Brahmā is indeed great;
nevertheless, I shall speak according to my ability—listen to that supreme glory."
To him who has a thousand faces, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet,
a thousand ears, a thousand hands, and is imperishable; to the Lord who possesses a thousand tongues, a thousand [forms], and a thousand supreme [powers].
He who bestows thousands upon thousands, the thousand-eyed and thousand-armed, the imperishable;
he who is the oblation, the act of pouring, the sacrificial offering, and the priest himself;
as well as the vessels, the purifiers, the altar, the initiation, the sacrificial porridge, and the ladle.
The *sruk* ladle, the *soma*, the *avabhṛtha* bath, the *prokṣaṇī* water, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
the wealth, the *adhvaryu* priest, the *sāmaga* singer, the learned *vipra*, the *sadasyas*, the sacrificial seat,
the assembly, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), the *kuśa* grass, the *darvī* spoon, the *camasa* cups, and the *ulūkhala* mortar. 44.
The sacrificial hall (prāgvaṃśa), the sacrificial ground, the Hotṛ priest, and the binding;
those that are short and those of excessive measure, as well as those of standard measurement; expiatory rites, sacrificial oblations, sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila), and likewise Kuśa grass. 45–46.

The wise learned in the Vedas declare him to be the mantra, the sacrifice, the oblation, the portion for the fire, and Bhava himself; he who eats first, who consumes the burnt offering, whose rays are auspicious, and who wields uplifted weapons—he is the eternal Lord of Sacrifice. 47.

O Great King, you have asked about this meritorious and divine narrative; for what purpose the Blessed Brahmā performed a sacrifice upon the earth for the benefit of gods and mortals, and for the prosperity of the worlds. 48–49.
Brahmā, as well as Kapila and Parameṣṭhin,
the gods, the seven ṛṣis, and the highly illustrious Tryambaka;
Sanatkumāra of great majesty, Manu the high-souled, and the blessed Prajāpati.
The Ancient God, whose splendor was like a blazing Vaiśvānara fire, spoke thus:
"In former times, while that lotus-born one was sleeping within his hollow, it was there in the lotus that the gods and the hosts of ṛṣis were born. (51-52)

This manifestation of the Great-Souled One known as Pauṣkaraka is narrated here as an ancient account, which is well-harmonized with the Vedas and the Smṛtis. Indeed, Varāha, the mouth of the Śruti, manifested from Viriñcin.
For the sake of assistance, the best of gods assumed the form of a boar;
he established the vast holy site of Kokāmukha at Puṣkara,
he whose feet were the Vedas, whose tusks were the sacrificial posts, whose hands were the rituals, and whose mouth was the sacrificial altar.
Agni-jihva (fire-tongued), Darbha-roma (darbha-haired), Brahma-śīrṣa (Brahma-headed), Mahā-tapas (of great austerity),
Aho-rātra-īkṣaṇa (having day and night as eyes), Divya (divine), Vedāṅga (the limbs of the Vedas), Śruti-bhūṣaṇa (adorned with the Vedas),
Ājya-nāsa (having clarified butter for a nose), Sruva-tuṇḍa (having a sacrificial ladle for a snout), and Sāma-ghoṣa-svana (whose great sound is the chanting of the Sāmaveda). 56.
He was composed of truth and righteousness, glorious, and honored for his prowess in action;

he was firm with penance as his nails, had the sacrificial animal as his origin, and took the form of a sacrifice; he had the Udgātṛ priests as his intestines, oblations as his testicles, and the great medicinal herbs as the seeds of his fruit.
He has the wind as his inner self, the mantras as his limbs, and is firm; he has the waters as his buttocks, Soma as his blood, and the Vedas as his shoulders.
He is the fragrance of the oblation, the carrier of offerings to gods and ancestors, and possesses great speed.
His body is the eastern hall of the sacrifice, he is radiant, and he is honored by various initiations.
The yogi is the great sacrificial session (mahāsatra) whose heart is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
he is the beautiful Upākarma sacrifice, adorned with the whirlpools of the Pravargya rite.
Accompanied by his consort Chāyā, he stands as lofty as Mount Maṇiśṛṅga.
Then Hari, the upholder of the earth, whose very self is for the welfare of the entire world, lifted the earth with his lower fang and brought it back to its own place; thereafter,
because of supporting the earth, he attained nirvāṇa.
In this manner, in ancient times, the earth submerged in the waters of the ocean was lifted up by Varāha at Puṣkara, who, seeking the welfare of Brahman,
was himself enveloped by tranquility and self-restraint while standing upon the tip of his divine tusk.
Together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and deities;
with the Rudras, the Viśvāsahāyas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras;
and with the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the earth, the rivers, and the oceans.

The glorious Brahmā, the preceptor of the moving and the unmoving, and the best among the knowers of Brahman, spoke these words: "O Lord, this holy site of Kokāmukha must always be protected and kept secret by you; O Makha, protection must be provided here."
"O Blessed One, I shall do exactly so," he said to Brahmā;
then Brahmā spoke again to the god Viṣṇu, who stood before him:
"You are indeed my supreme god; you are indeed my supreme teacher."
O best of gods, you are the supreme abode for Śakra and the others;
O you with eyes like full-blown, stainless lotuses, bring about the destruction of the faction of our enemies, so that the Dānavas may be utterly destroyed by means of sacrifice. (69–70)
Therefore, you must act accordingly; salutations to you who are bowed down to.
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of Gods, cast away your fear; I shall bring the Dānavas to their end."
"And those who create obstacles nearby—the Yātudhānas as well as the Asuras—I shall slay them all; remain in peace, O Grandfather.
Having spoken thus, he stood there, prepared to provide assistance.
Auspicious winds blew and the ten directions became clear;
the luminaries shone with beautiful radiance and circumambulated the moon; the planets ceased their eclipses and the oceans became tranquil.

The earth was free from dust, the waters bestowed complete delight, the rivers followed their own courses, and the oceans were not agitated; the senses of men and their inner selves became auspicious. (75)
The great seers, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud;
during this sacrifice, while the oblations were being cooked, the fires became auspicious, and the people, whose conduct was righteous and who followed the established dharma, were joyful in heart.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu, whose promise is true, regarding the destruction of the enemy,
the gods then arrived along with the Dānavas and Rākṣasas;
all the Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas also came there in succession.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, and hosts of Vidyādharas;
the trees and medicinal herbs— whatever exists here and whatever does not— were brought from all directions by the wind at the command of Brahmā.
Having reached the Sacrifice Mountain, all the gods stood to the north, facing the direction of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while they were stationed at the boundary mountain;
likewise, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and sages who have mastered the Vedas were there as well. 81.
In that great sacrifice, all the hosts of gods, the dānavas, and the throngs of asuras stood there, stationed in the western direction,
having cast aside their resentment and being well-pleased with one another.
They all attended upon the sages and likewise served the Brahmins;
the ṛṣis, the brahmarṣis, the twice-born devarṣis,
and the most eminent rājarṣis arrived from every direction.
And who will be the one to whom the sacrificial oblation is offered in this rite?
(85) There, animals and birds have come desiring to see it, as well as Brāhmaṇas and all the social classes in their proper order, desiring to eat. (86)
Varuṇa himself gave the jewel, and Dakṣa himself gave the food;
having come from his own world, Varuṇa cooked the prepared food himself.
Vāyu [provided] the various types of food, and the Sun, the cooker of essences, [provided] the juices.
Bṛhaspati is the giver of intelligence and the moon who ripens the food;
the Lord of Wealth is the giver of riches and the overseer of various garments;
Sarasvatī is the mistress of rivers, along with the goddess Gaṅgā and the Narmadā. 88–89.
And whatever other holy rivers there are, as well as wells and reservoirs, ponds, lakes, various pools, principal springs, and numerous natural excavations made by the gods; ||| 90 ||
All reservoirs of water, including the seven oceans—

consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water— as well as the seven worlds together with the nether regions (pātāla), the seven continents, and their cities, [are all contained therein]. 91–92.
Trees, creepers, grasses, vegetables, and fruits;
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—these beings possess physical forms, as do the treatises on dharma. 93.
The Vedabhāṣyas, the Sūtras, and whatever was created by Brahmā—
whether formless, extremely subtle, or manifest as all that is visible— were likewise present during that sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā). 94–95.
There, in the presence of the gods and in the assembly of the sages,
the eternal Viṣṇu stood at the right side of Brahmā,
while the Lord Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow and the bestower of boons, stood at his left side.
The high-souled one also performed the selection of the officiating priests there:
Bhṛgu was chosen as the Hotṛ, Pulastya as the excellent Adhvaryu, Marīci as the Udgātṛ, and Nārada was appointed as the Brahmā priest. (97–98)

Sanatkumāra and others who were members of that assembly were the Prajāpatis; Dakṣa and others were the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. And in the presence of Brahmā, the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) was performed. 99.
Adorned with garments and ornaments provided by Vaiśravaṇa,
the twice-born priests— four, two, twelve, and sixteen in number— were decorated with rings, bracelets, and crowns. 100–101.
Honored by Brahmā with prostrations, they were all addressed: "All of you must show favor toward her in this sacrifice here. O twice-born ones, she is my wife Sāvitrī; you are my refuge."
Having summoned Viśvakarman, the shaving of Brahmā’s head—
which had been ordained for the sacrifice— was performed by the best of the twice-born; likewise, garments made of *ātasa* wool were provided for the couple by the brahmins.
Those Brahmins made the heavens resound with the sound of the Veda; and those Kṣatriyas stood there armed, protecting this world. There, the Vaiśyas prepared various kinds of food.

Then, having prepared food and edibles endowed with an abundance of flavor, the Lord Prajāpati, the creator of beings, seeing what had never been heard of before nor seen before, was pleased; the omnipresent creator gave the name "Prāgvāṭa" to those Vaiśyas. 106–107.
"In this world, service to the feet of the twice-born must always be performed by Śūdras;
namely, washing their feet, eating their leftovers, and wiping them clean. At that time, they did so there, and Pitāmaha spoke further to them.
"For the sake of service, you have been placed by me in the fourth quarter.
Service must be rendered to the three [classes]—the twice-born, the kṣatriyas, and those such as yourselves who are kinsmen. Having spoken thus, Brahmā acted accordingly. 109–110.
Mādhava established Śakra as the guardian of the gate, Varuṇa as the giver of flavors,
Vaiśravaṇa as the bestower of wealth, Pavana as the giver of fragrance,
Sūrya as the creator of light, and he himself remained in the position of sovereign lord.
Soma, the bestower of Soma, was situated on their left side.
His wife, a most excellent woman who was a mother, was highly honored;
summoned by the Adhvaryu priest, she came with haste, saying, "Come, O Goddess! (112-113).
All the fires have been kindled and the time for initiation has arrived;
yet, due to her feminine nature, she has not come, being preoccupied with the preparation of ornaments. Indeed, no decoration whatsoever has been made here at the door by me.
No variegated paintings have been made on the walls, nor has the svastika design been drawn in the courtyard;
furthermore, no washing of the vessels has been performed here, and yet Lakṣmī—who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa—has not arrived even now. 115–116.

Svāhā is the wife of Agni; Dhūmorṇā is the wife of Yama; Vāruṇī is likewise the wife of Varuṇa; Gaurī is the wife of Vāyu; Suprabhā is the wife of Soma; Ṛddhi is the wife of Vaiśravaṇa; and Gaurī, the beloved of the world, is the wife of Śambhu.
Medhā, Śraddhā, Vibhūti, Anasūyā, Dhṛti, Kṣamā, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Nandā, and other such maidens arrived;
as did Indrāṇī, the wife of Indra, and Rohiṇī, the beloved of the Moon. 119–120.
Arundhatī, the wives of Vasiṣṭha and the Seven Sages, Anasūyā the wife of Atri, and other women here— brides,
daughters, female friends, and sisters as well. 121.
"All those women have not yet arrived; I, however, have remained here for a long time. I will not go alone as long as those women have not come.
Go and tell Brahmā: 'Wait for a moment.'"
Accompanied by all of them and moving with haste,
O high-minded one, surrounded by all the gods, you shall attain supreme splendor,
and so shall I; of this there is no doubt.
While she was speaking thus, the Adhvaryu priest left the Brahman and arrived [at the scene].
Sāvitrī was distracted, O Lord, being occupied with household duties; "As long as my friends have not yet arrived, so long shall there be no arrival for me. 125–126.
"Thus addressed by me, O Goddess, even time itself passes away;
therefore, O Grandfather, do whatever you deem appropriate now.
Being thus addressed, Brahmā was then somewhat filled with anger.
"O Śakra, quickly bring another wife here for my sake, so that the sacrifice may proceed and not be delayed by the lapse of time;
act swiftly and bring some woman here. (128-129)
"Until the completion of my sacrifice, do not set your mind upon me;
I shall release you again here at the conclusion of the rite.
Thus addressed, Śakra then went throughout the entire surface of the earth.
All those women whom he saw were the wives of others;
they were Ābhīra maidens, rich in beauty, with fine noses and lovely eyes—neither goddesses, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor Pannagas. 131–132.
There was no other maiden like that beautiful woman;
he beheld her of exquisite limbs as if she were another goddess Śrī herself, who, by the perfection of her beauty, seemed to contract the very power of the mind’s activity. 133.
Whatever exquisite object was obtained anywhere, that slender-limbed woman regarded as superior when it was attached to her own body; seeing her, he thought: "If this were a maiden... (134-135)
"Therefore, there exists no other god on earth who has performed such merit as I have;
this jewel among women is she, for whom the Grandfather (Brahmā) feels affection. If he were indeed filled with passion, then this labor of mine would bear fruit. (136)
He beheld her, bearing with her limbs— her hair, cheeks, eyes, and lips— a radiance resembling blue clouds, gold, lotuses, and coral,
like a newly blossomed bud upon the tree of the god of love. 137–138.

How indeed could the Creator have created such a woman, seeing that her form was so ill-proportioned? She must have been fashioned by him while his heart was consumed by the fire of love, with its mass of flames like the rays of the sun;
for if she were conceived by his own intellect, it would be the ultimate proof of his supreme skill.

As I behold these two breasts with their lofty peaks, a happiness arises within me; who, indeed, would not experience this in their heart? Though this lower lip clearly has a body overcome by passion (or stained red), it is no wonder. 140–141.
Nevertheless, even while she acts thus, she bestows nirvāṇa upon him;
for even curled locks, though they possess crookedness, grant happiness when worn.
Even a fault appears as a virtue when it rests upon great beauty. (142)
Those who know what is beneficial declare that the consciousness of emotion (bhāvacaitanya) arises from a cause when these two [earrings], which adorn the eyes, reach as far as the ears;
for by means of the ornaments on the ears, the eyes [are reached], and these two ears are [the source of] the eyes. 144.
There is no room here at all for earrings or collyrium;
it is not fitting that they should cause a division within the heart by their side-glances. How is it that those who are related to you here must partake in such suffering?
Any transformation produced by natural qualities attains the state of being most beautiful; yet,
this wealth of theirs was seen even by hundreds of aged eyes— the Creator has displayed the very limit of his skill in the production of such beauty.
She captivated the minds of these men with her affectionate gestures and playful charms;
as he reflected thus, his body— its luster stolen by her form— became covered with incessantly rising horripilation.
Beholding her, who possessed the luster of fresh gold and whose eyes were as long as lotus petals, the noble one thought:
"Among the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, nor among various other beings seen by me, has such an abundance of beauty ever been observed. (149-150)
"Whatever object exists within the three worlds, having taken the most excellent of each of those, the Creator fashioned her form and established its stability.
Indra said:
"O lady with beautiful brows, tell me from where you have come to this Kāśī;
for what reason do you stand alone in the middle of the street? And as for these ornaments set upon your limbs that you wear..."
These are not ornaments for you; indeed, they are ornaments for these [others].
O fair-eyed one, neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman, nor a Kinnara woman has ever been seen before like you. 153-154.

Although I have spoken thus many times, why do you not give me an answer? Then that cowherd girl, overcome with shame and trembling, spoke to Śakra: "O Hero, I am a cowherd girl; I sell such dairy products here."
"Here is pure butter, and here is curd with its whey;
O scorcher of foes, whether you desire curd, buttermilk, or even the liquid essence, tell me what you want and take as much as you wish. (156-157)
Thus addressed, the demon Āśaka then seized her firmly by the hand and led that large-eyed woman to where Brahmā was stationed.
As she was being led away by him, she cried out to her father and mother.
"O father! O mother! O brother! This man is carrying me away by force.
Or rather, if there is something I must do, ask my father; he will surely give me to you—this is spoken as the truth. (159–160)
Who would not desire a husband for his daughter who is devoted and affectionate? O lover of righteousness, there is nothing at all that should not be given by my father;
propitiate him with your head bowed low, and being satisfied, he will grant it.

"If I were to give myself away without knowing my father's mind, my great merit would surely perish; therefore, I do not seek to please you. But if my father gives me to you, O dear one, I shall become subject to your will. (162-163)
Being addressed in this manner, Śakra was unable to speak;
placing her before Brahmā, he said to him, "O powerful one, for his sake I have brought here,
O large-eyed one of excellent complexion, this woman who is pure."
Having seen that cowherd girl of golden complexion and great luster, he considered her to be Kamalā herself;
she had eyes like lotuses and a full chest resembling a wall of refined gold. 165–166.

Seeing him, whose thighs were rounded like the trunks of intoxicated elephants and who possessed the luster of red, elevated claws, she too considered herself to be moving according to her heart's desire;
for her mind appeared to have arrived with the thought that he was the means to attain that goal.
Even the daughter of the cowherd considered herself to possess the power of generosity, thinking:
"If he desires to take me away so persistently because of my beauty, then there is no woman on earth more fortunate than I. (168–169)
"By him I have been brought here; whatever comes within the range of his sight, if he abandons me, death will follow, but if he does not abandon me, there will be the happiness of life.
Yet, because of this humiliation, fie upon my form that brings only suffering! (170)
Even she who is seen with the eye through her grace is fortunate, of this there is no doubt; how much more so she who would embrace him?
For the entire world-form, though existing as distinct entities, has resorted to his movement. 171–172.
The Creator has displayed all that beauty gathered in one place here;
the god of love is its worthy likeness, and the splendor of the god of love is the likeness of her.
Yet this grief has been cast aside; neither father nor mother is the cause of it.
Since he does not take this [gift] from me, nor does he speak even a little to me;
because of his remembrance [of her], death born of grief will overcome him. Yet, though she is innocent, such a state has quickly come upon his wife.

While she was gazing at his face, which possessed the luster of a pure lotus for the sake of adorning the jewels upon her breasts, my mind became absorbed in meditation; yet, had you not highly esteemed me through the contact of the touch of her body? 176.
"Touching my body, you have now attained the state of a dancer; alas, you have achieved the highest goal!
Or rather, there is no fault in this for you, for you are one who acts according to his own whim.
You have surely been robbed of your memory; protect your beloved Rati! 177-178.
By this form in which he appears even superior to you,
my entire treasure of the jewel of my heart has been firmly stolen. From where does that splendor seen upon his face come, [which surpasses] even that of the moon?

Nevertheless, she should be beheld in those specific places by those desiring spiritual perfection.

I shall now describe before you those belonging to the stages of the objects of meditation (smartavyābhūmikā). O auspicious one, among the most excellent of holy places, there is the one named Sāvitrī at Puṣkara;
in Vārāṇasī, she is Viśālākṣī, and in Naimiṣa, she is Ligadhāriṇī.
At Prayāga she is Lalitādevī; at Gandhamādana she is Kāmukā;
at Mānasa she is Kumudā; likewise, she is Viśvakāyā in the sky; at Gomatī on Mount Gomanta she is Gomatī; and on Mandara she is Kāmacāriṇī. (184–185)
Madotkaṭā is in Caitraratha, Jayantī in Hastināpura, Gaurī in Kānyakubja, Rambhā on the Malaya mountain,
Kīrtimatī in Ekāmraka, and Viśvā as well as Viśveśvarī likewise [are there]. (186)
Karṇikā is at Puruhasta; Mārgadāyikā is at Kedāra (187).
Nandā is on the back of the Himavat mountain; Bhadrakālikā is at Gokarṇa;
Bhavānī is at Sthāṇvīśvara; and Bilvapatrikā is at Bilvaka (188).
On Śrīśaila are Mādhavī and Bhadrā, and likewise Bhadreśvarī;
on Jayāvarāhaśaila are Kamalā and Kamalālayā (189);
at Rudrakoṭi are the Rudrāṇīs, and likewise Kālī at Kālañjara.
At Mahāliṅga she is Tuṅgakapilā, and at Karkoṭa she is Maṅgaleśvarī (190).
At Śāligrāma she is Mahādevī, and at the Śiva-liṅga she is Jalapriyā;
in Māyāpurī she is Kumārī, and likewise Lalitā in Saṃtāna (191).
Utpalākṣī is at Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣī at Mahotpalā, Maṅgalā at Gayā, Vimalā at Puruṣottama,
Amoghākṣī at Vipāśā, and Pāṭalā at Puṇyavardhana. (192)
Nārāyaṇī is on Supārśva, while Bhadra-sundarī is on Trikūṭa (193). On Vipula is she named Vipulā, and Kalyāṇī is on Mount Malaya;
Koṭavī is at Koṭitīrtha, and Sugandhā is in the Mādhavī forest (194).
She is Kubjā at Amraketri, Gaṅgādvāra at Trisaṃdhyātuga, Haripriyā at Śivakuṇḍa, Anandinī at the bank of the Devikā,
Rukmiṇī at Dvāravatī, and likewise Rādhā in Vṛndāvana. 195.
Devakī is in Mathurā, while Parameśvarī is in Pātāla;
likewise, Sītā is at Citrakūṭa, and Vindhyavāsinī is on the Vindhya mountains; Ekavīrā is on the Sahya mountain, and Candrikā is in Hariścandra.
Mṛgāvatī is at the Ramaṇārāma-tīrtha on the Yamunā;
Mahālakṣmī is at Karavīra; Rumādevī is at Vināyaka; Aroga is at Vaidyanātha; and Maheśvarī is at Mahākāla. 198.
Abhayā resides at Abhayāpuṣpatīrtha, Amṛtā in the cave of the Vindhya mountains;
Māṇḍavī is the goddess at Māṇḍavya, Svāhā in the city of Māheśvara; Pracaṇḍā is at Vegala, and Caṇḍikā is at Marakaṇṭaka. (199–200)
At Someśvara she is Varārohā; at Prabhāsa she is Puṣkarāvatī;
at the Sarasvatī river she is Devamātā; she stands on the bank at Pārāpāra as Piṅgaleśvarī; at Mahālaya she is Mahāpadmā; and at Payoṣṇī she is Piṅgaleśvarī.
Siṃhikā is at Kṛtaśaucetuka, Kārtikeyī at Tuśaṅkarī; Lolā is at Utpalāvartaka, Subhadrā at the confluence of the Sindhu;
Lakṣmī is at Umāsiddhavana, and Anaṅgā at Bharatāśrama. 202–203.
Jālandharī is at Viśvamukhī, Tārā on Mount Kiṣkindha, Puṣṭi in the Devadāru forest, and Medhā in the region of Kashmir.
Bhīmādevī is on the Himādri mountain, and likewise Catuṣṭi at Vatreśvara. 204.
At Kapālamocana is Śraddhā; at Mātākāyāvarohaṇa [is Śraddhā];
at Śaṅkhoddhāra is Dhvani; likewise at Piṇḍāraka is Dhṛti; and at Kālāñjara, on the banks of the Candrabhāgā, is Acchodā, the bestower of success (siddhi). 205–206.

In Veṇā she is Amṛtādevī, in Badarī she is Urvaśī, in Oṣadhī she is Auṣadhī, in Uttarakuru she is Kuśodakā, in Kuśadvīpa she is Manmathā, in Hemakūṭa she is Kumudā, and in Satyavādin she is Satyavādinī. (207)
She is like the *aśvattha* tree at the place of worship; she is the treasure in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa (208).
She is Gāyatrī at the mouth of the Veda, and Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva; likewise, she is Indrāṇī in the world of the gods, and Sarasvatī in the mouth of Brahmā (209).
In the solar orb she is the mother named Prabhā, and likewise the Vaiṣṇavī;
among chaste women she is Arundhatī, and among beautiful women she is Tilottamā.
In Citra she is the power (Śakti) of all embodied beings, known as the Brahma-kalā.

Out of devotion to you, I have proclaimed this supreme one hundred and eight names; this collection of one hundred and eight sacred fords (tīrthas) has also been declared. Whoever recites or even hears this is liberated from all sins.
That best of men who, having performed his ablutions at these sacred fords (tīrthas), beholds [the deity],
shall be liberated from all sins and dwell in the city of Brahmā for a kalpa.
Furthermore, he who recites the hundred eight names in the presence of Brahmā—
On the full moon day or the new moon day, a man shall have many sons;
furthermore, by giving gifts of cows, performing śrāddha rites daily, or while engaged in the ritual worship of the gods, one who listens [to this] attains the Supreme Brahman. 214–215.
To Viṣṇu who was thus praising her, Sāvitrī, firm in her vows, said: "O son, you have been perfectly praised by me; you shall be invincible.
In your incarnations, together with your wife, you shall be beloved by your father and mother."
And having come here, O Yama, one who praises me with this hymn shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme abode.
Go now to the sacrifice of Viriñca and bring it to completion, my son.

"At Kurukṣetra and Prayāga, I shall become the giver of food and remain near my husband; I will fulfill what you have spoken. Having been addressed thus, Viṣṇu departed from the excellent assembly of Brahmā.
When Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī spoke these words:
"O sages, listen to my words in the presence of your husband; for I am pleased and ready to grant a boon, which I shall now declare. (220–221)
Those men who, filled with devotion, worship Brahmā,
for them there shall be clothing, wealth, grain, wives, happiness,
and riches; likewise, there shall be uninterrupted happiness in their home, along with sons and grandsons.
Having enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] for a very long time, he will in the end attain liberation.
Pulastya said:
Having established Brahmā with all efforts according to the prescribed rites, [he shall proceed].
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit of that merit which one obtains:
whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas, one shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten millionfold through this consecration. 224–225.
O lord of men, having observed the fast on the full moon day with devotion, the man who worships Viriñci according to this rite,
O mighty-armed one, attains the state of Brahmā on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Viriñci and Vāsudeva, especially along with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), [should be worshipped].
In the month of Kārtika, the chariot procession (rathayātrā) of the Lord is proclaimed;
by performing it with devotion, human beings attain the state of the world of Brahmā.

O King of kings, O scorcher of foes, on the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, one should cause the four-faced Lord Brahmā, together with Sāvitrī, to circumambulate the entire city by way of the main road, accompanied by various musical instruments.
O King, having caused the deity to circumambulate the city and its surroundings,
and having first fed the Brāhmaṇas and worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī, one should place the Lord upon the chariot amidst the sounds of auspicious musical instruments.
Having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī at the front of the chariot according to the prescribed rites,
and having caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers and performed the *puṇyāha* ceremony,
one should place the deity upon the chariot and observe a vigil (*prajāgara*).

Having kept a vigil with various kinds of spectacles and abundant offerings for the slayers of Brahmins, O King, one should, at dawn, feed the Brāhmaṇas with many kinds of edible foods according to one's capacity.
O King, O mighty-armed one, having worshipped the fire according to the rules with the Ajana-mantra,
using clarified butter, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa), and having caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious blessings according to the prescribed rites, O King.
Having proclaimed the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*), one should cause that chariot to be paraded through the city (236). Brahmā’s chariot should be paraded by Brahmins learned in the four Vedas—
by Rig-veda chanters, Atharva-veda priests, heroic Sāman-chanters, and likewise by Adhvaryu priests (237).
One should cause that chariot of the God of gods, the foremost of the asuras,
to circumambulate the entire city by way of the smooth path. O hero, a chariot should not be driven by a Śūdra who desires his own welfare.
O King, a wise monarch should not mount the throne except for the *bhojaka*.
O King, he should place the Gāyatrī on the right side of Brahmā, the *bhojaka* on the left side, and set the lotus in front. 239–240.
Thus, having paraded the chariot clockwise throughout the entire city of the hero with the sounds of musical instruments and the abundant blasts of conchs,
the wise man, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), should re-establish the deity in its own place.
Whoever undertakes such a pilgrimage, or whoever beholds [the deity] even with devotion,
or whoever pulls the chariot, shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
and he who offers a lamp on the new moon day of the month of Kārttika [shall likewise attain that goal].

One who performs the rite for Brahmā in the hall shall go to the supreme state; he who honors himself with perfumes, flowers, and new garments on that first day of the lunar fortnight shall likewise go to the abode of Brahmā.
This is a highly meritorious guest, the promoter of King Bali’s reign;
she is eternally dear to Brahmā and is celebrated as Bāleyī.
Whoever worships Brahmā on this day should especially worship his own self as well.

O mighty-armed one, the first day (Pratipad) of the month of Caitra is a meritorious and most excellent occasion; it is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor. On that day, O best of men, even if one has touched an outcaste (śvapaca), he who performs an ablution [is purified].

O King, tiger among the Kurus, no misfortune whatsoever, nor mental anxieties or physical ailments, shall befall one who has bathed; therefore, one should perform the bath. For that is a divine lustration ceremony (nīrājana) which destroys all diseases. 248–249.

O King, descendant of the Kuru lineage, one should cause all cattle, such as cows and buffaloes, to be driven forth; with all those [animals] and with garments and other items, one should place the archway (toraṇa) outside. Furthermore, one should provide food for the Brāhmaṇas.
O descendant of Kuru, O King, these three lunar days were indeed proclaimed of old:
in the month of Kārttika, in the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise in the month of Caitra. O King, on the lunar day of Kārttikeya, bathing and giving gifts yield a hundredfold merit.
Gāyatrī, who bestows auspiciousness upon King Bali and brings benefit to all animals, spoke; she repeated the words that Sāvitrī had addressed to the Lotus-born One. 253.
"Indeed, Brahmins will never perform worship [of me] on their own;
however, those who, having heard my words, perform such adoration, shall enjoy pleasures here in this world and partake in liberation in the hereafter. (254)
Having recognized this supreme vision, the Lord, being pleased, grants a boon:
"O Śakra, I shall grant you a boon for the suppression of enemies in battle;
at that time, Brahmā, having gone to the abode of the enemy, will deliver you. (255-256)
"You shall regain your lost city and attain supreme joy from the destruction of your enemies;
a great kingdom free from thorns shall belong to you in the three worlds. O Viṣṇu, when you take an incarnation in the mortal world,"

"The supreme sorrow arising from the abduction of your wife and other causes, which you could not endure with your brother, shall end when you have slain the enemy; you will regain your wife in the presence of the gods, and having taken her back and ruled the kingdom once more, you will go to heaven. (258–259)
For eleven thousand years you shall dwell again in heaven; your fame shall be vast in the world, and you shall possess the affection of the people.
The worlds of those who belong to your lineage shall endure, being well-established.
By you, in the form of the divine Rāma, human beings have been delivered.
Then Gāyatrī, the bestower of boons, replied to Rudra: "Even when their bodies have fallen, those men who perform worship [to you]... (261-262)

Those who are purified, performers of meritorious deeds, and partakers of the heavenly world— such a goal they do not attain through the Agnihotra sacrifice or oblations poured into the fire as they do by worshipping you,
O Bali.

Those who, having risen early in the morning, shall always worship you on the banks of the Gaṅgā with bilva leaves will become partakers of the world of Rudra. And even though you have attained the state of being a devotee of Śarva, you shall remain a purifier of worldly existence.
When you are pleased, all the gods are pleased; of this there is no doubt.

Since the oblation is offered by the gods through your mouth, when you are pleased, they are certainly pleased and partake [of it]; there is no uncertainty here, according to the words spoken in the Vedas. 266.
He spoke this to all those Gāyatrī-brāhmaṇas:
"Having performed acts of propitiation for you, men shall all go to the station known as Vairāja at all sacred fords; of this there is no doubt. (267-268)
By giving various kinds of food and manifold gifts,
and by providing satisfaction at the śrāddha rites, they became gods among gods; indeed,
the inhabitants of heaven [dwell] within the mouths of those who are the best of brāhmaṇas.
And the ancestors shall quickly partake of the sacrificial oblation (havis) and the ancestral offering (kavya).
For you are indeed capable of sustaining the three worlds, there is no doubt;
and by means of a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma), you all shall become purified.
O best of the twice-born, by bathing specifically at Puṣkara and reciting the Mother of the Vedas (Gāyatrī),
you shall not incur the faults resulting from accepting gifts;
moreover, all the deities will be pleased by the gift of food at Puṣkara.
By feeding a single Brahmin, one shall obtain the fruit of feeding ten million;
all men who give wealth into your hands shall be freed from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and other evil deeds they have committed or are about to commit. 273–274.
By my recitation performed three times, he is to be worshipped;
even a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin perishes at that very moment. [Sins] born over ten lifetimes and those committed in the past over a hundred [lifetimes] are likewise destroyed.

The Gāyatrī destroys sin when recited three thousand times during the three junctions of the day. Knowing this, you shall always remain pure; my words are infallible. You will attain [this state], there is no doubt, and no further deliberation is required in this matter.
Having especially recited [the mantra] together with the three-measured *praṇava*, all are purified; of this there is no doubt, having recited me along with the head [of the mantra].
I abide as the eight-syllabled one, and by me indeed is this world pervaded.
I am the mother of all the Vedas, adorned with all their words.
O best of the twice-born, by chanting me with devotion, you shall attain perfection; through my recitation, preeminence shall belong to you all.
A self-controlled Brahmin who knows even just the essence of the Gāyatrī is better than this uncontrolled man who, though knowing the four Vedas, eats all things and sells all things;
for the curse of the Sāvitrī was uttered upon the Brahmins by the Sadasya.
"Whatever is given and whatever is offered here shall all be inexhaustible.

O best of the twice-born, I have granted this boon to him: 'O Brahmins devoted to the *agnihotra*, you who perform the fire-oblation at the three periods of the day, [shall receive these rewards]. 282–283.
They shall go to heaven along with twenty-one generations of their lineage; such is the supreme boon of Gāyatrī from Śakra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Pāvaka, Brahmā, and the Brāhmaṇas.
Having given that [gift] at Vaipuṣkara, she went to the side of Brahmā.
Then the Cāraṇas related the cause of Lakṣmī’s curse,
having learned of the individual curses of all the young women.
And Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, granted a boon to Lakṣmī:
"Always performing all actions without reproach, you shall be beautiful with wealth; you will shine, there is no doubt, bestowing affection upon all. (287)
"O daughter, all those who have been looked upon by you shall partake of merit;
but all those who have been abandoned by you shall be partakers of suffering. O lovely-faced one, their birth, lineage, character, and even their dharma [are of no consequence]. (288-289)
They shall shine in the assembly and be seen by the kings;
moreover, those best of the twice-born will fulfill their requests. They show them kindness, saying, "You are our brother, our father, and our teacher."
"Even my kinsmen are not a doubt [to me]; I cannot live without you.
When you are seen, my vision becomes clear and beautiful; my mind is exceedingly pleased—I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth. (291-292)
Those virtuous people who have been looked upon by you with such words will hear them and bring joy to the people.
O Indra, having attained the position of Indra, Nahuṣa will see you and make a request of you.
"O Sage, surely this sinner has been struck down by your glance because of the words of Agastya. Having attained the state of a serpent, he will surely entreat you;
'I am ruined through my pride, O Sage, be my refuge. (294-295)
Having felt compassion in his mind at these words of the king, the venerable ṛṣi will speak these words:
"O delighter of your lineage, a king shall be born in your family. (296)
Upon seeing him wearing the form of a serpent, he will indeed break the curse; then,
having abandoned your state as a serpent, you shall go again to heaven with your husband, who has performed the horse sacrifice, to the celestial realm once more.
"O beautiful-eyed one, you shall obtain this through my gift of grace.
Pulastya said:
"Then all the wives of the gods were addressed by her with words of satisfaction."
"Even for those deprived of offspring, there shall be no sorrow. Then Gaurī, who is indeed Gāyatrī, being thus awakened,
that high-minded lady, filled with satisfaction, granted boons and increased [their strength].
Desiring the completion of that sacrifice, the beloved of Brahmā,
Gāyatrī— the mother of the Vedas and the bestower of boons— was seen by Rudra; having prostrated before her, he then offered this hymn of praise.
Rudra said:
"Salutations to you, O Mother of the Vedas, purified by the eight-syllable mantra; O Gāyatrī, who delivers one from distress, and likewise the sevenfold Vāṇī. (303)

All hymns of praise, all treatises, and likewise all songs; all syllables as well as their grammatical characteristics (lakṣaṇas); all commentaries and other scriptures, and whatever other rules there may be—304.
You are all the syllables; O Goddess, salutations to you!
(305) You are white and possess a white form, with a countenance equal to the moon, bearing two massive arms as tender as the interior of a plantain tree. (306)
Holding a deer-horn in one hand and a stainless lotus in the other,
she was clothed in silken garments and a red upper robe;
her chest was adorned with a necklace as radiant as the rays of the moon.
You are beautifully adorned with ears filled with divine earrings;
you shine with a face that has become a rival to the moon,
and you are graced by a most pure crown and a well-bound mass of hair.
Her two arms were like the coils of serpents and served as ornaments for heaven; her breasts were beautiful, divine, round, and possessed symmetrical nipples.
With her exceedingly radiant hips, she was proud of the beauty of the three folds of skin.
The goddess has a navel situated at the center of her waist, which is deep and auspicious to behold;
she possesses broad hips and beautiful buttocks, O lady of excellent countenance; likewise, she has a pair of well-formed, rounded thighs, and well-developed knees and feet.
"O bearer of the three worlds, through your truthful prayer on this earth, you shall become a highly fortunate one, a giver of boons, and possessed of excellent complexion;
and having performed a pilgrimage to Puṣkara, you will behold me."
"On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, you shall receive the foremost worship.
And those men who, knowing your power, shall offer you worship—for them, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to obtain, whether in terms of sons or wealth. (314-315)
For those submerged in wildernesses, or in the forest, or in the great ocean,
or for those obstructed by bandits, you are the supreme refuge of men.
You are success, prosperity, fortitude, fame, modesty, knowledge, humility, and intelligence.
You are the twilight night, the radiance, and sleep; you alone are the Night of Time (Kālarātri). You are Ambā, the mother of Kamalā, Brahmāṇī, and the observer of celibacy (Brahmacāriṇī);
you are the mother of all the gods and the supreme woman, Gāyatrī.
You are Jaya and Vijaya, you are Puṣṭi, Kṣamā, and Dayā; you are Sāvitrī’s younger sister and are always active within the Grandfather (Brahmā).
You possess many forms, universal forms, beautiful eyes, and you are a celibate student of the Veda.
O large-eyed one, you possess beautiful form and are the protector of your devotees. O Mahādevī of lovely countenance, your residence is in holy cities, hermitages, forests, and groves. (320–321)
In all the stations of Brahmā, Sāvitrī stands to the left of Brahmā, while Pitāmaha Brahmā himself is in the middle; to his right is the sacrificial altar (antarvedī),
which is the sacrificial fee for both the sacrifices and the officiating priests.
You are indeed known as the success (*siddhi*) of kings, born from the ocean at the proper time;
you are considered the supreme splendor of the initiation for those practicing celibacy (*brahmacārin*);
you are the goddess of light among the luminaries, and Lakṣmī abiding in Nārāyaṇa. 323–324.
For sages, perfection lies in forbearance; for the stars, Rohiṇī;
at royal gates, in sacred fords, and at the confluences of rivers, as well as on the full moon day when the moon is full, the intellect finds its steadiness in policy and patience. (325)
O Goddess Umā, you are heard of as the most excellent among women;
you are the beautiful gaze of Indra, the companion of the thousand-eyed one;
you are the righteous intellect of the sages and the supreme refuge of the gods.
You are the furrow for farmers and the earth for all living beings; you grant women freedom from widowhood and bestow wealth and grain.
When worshipped, you shall pacify disease, death, and fear.

"O bestower of auspiciousness, you shall become a goddess who grants all desires when you are well-worshipped on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika. Whoever reads this hymn or hears it repeatedly,"
"A man shall obtain the accomplishment of all his goals; there is no doubt in this matter.
Gāyatrī said: "It shall be exactly so, just as you have spoken, my son. (331)
"You shall exist together with Viṣṇu in all places.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon Gāyatrī in the Dispute with Sāvitrī," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The eighteenth chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, I have heard this most wonderful account in its true essence.
The consecration of Gāyatrī was likewise performed by Sadasyavrata;
as well as the conflict with Sāvitrī and the bestowal of the curse,
and how the Goddess was glorified by Viṣṇu in all her stations.
O Gāyatrī, O friend, O Raudrī, O you who are praised by us, O lady of excellent complexion— having heard that description of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) in detail,
my hair stands on end with joy and my mind has become tranquil.
Upon hearing this, there was indeed supreme joy and great curiosity.
Then the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having performed that supreme hymn of praise with devotion by the wife of Brahmā, placed her upon the mountain.
Viṣṇu spoke these words, which bestow contentment and nourishment,
to Śrīmatī, Hrīmatī, and the goddess Īśvarī:
"O Brāhmaṇa, this very [truth] has been heard by me as it issued from your mouth."
O Blessed One, you ought to relate in due order all that occurred in the northern region and everything that was done in that place;
by hearing it, the purification of my body will come to pass, of this there is no doubt.
Pulastya said:
O King, listen to this wondrous account of how it was previously performed when that supreme Lord Parameṣṭhin was sacrificing at Puṣkara. 9.
In the beginning of this Kṛta Yuga, when the Grandfather was performing a sacrifice,
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and the Prajāpati Dakṣa likewise offered their salutations.
Shining and adorned with all ornaments,
hosts of Apsarases danced before Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods; then, in the sky,
they greeted him with the musical instruments of the Gandharvas.
Together with many Gandharvas, Citraratha sang,
as did Mahāśruti, Citrasena, Ūrṇāyu, Anagha,
Gomāyu, Sūryavarcas, and Somavarcas, O Kaurava. 13.
Yugapa, Catṛṇāyu, Candra, and Citraratha; the thirteenth was Śāliśiras, Parjanya was the fourteenth,
Kali was the fifteenth, and Tāraka was the sixteenth here.
Hāhā, Hūhū, the Gandharva Haṃsa, and the one of great splendor—
these divine Gandharvas sang before the Lord.
Likewise, the celestial Apsarases danced before that Lord.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga;
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya—these are the twelve Ādityas, blazing with radiant splendor. (17–18)
The lords of the gods paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā) there,
as did Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and the highly illustrious Nirṛti;
as well as Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
O lord of the people, Bhava, Viśveśvara, and Kapardin; Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and the blessed Rudra— all these were stationed there,
as were the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the mighty Maruts.
The Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
so too did the great nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, the serpents headed by Vāsuki, Kāśyapa, Kambala, and the mighty Takṣaka. 22–23.
By this [means], the great-souled ones stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, the mighty Garuḍa, Vāruṇi, and Aruṇi—the sons of Vinatā—stood there in attendance. 23–24.
And the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, accompanied by all the great sages, came to the world and spoke to the Teacher of the World:
"O Lord of the Universe, all this is pervaded by you; it was created by you."
"Therefore, you are Lokeśvara; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! Command what must be done by me here and what task remains to be performed.
Thus spoke the Lord, the Master, together with the celestial sages.
Having paid homage to Brahmā, the lord of the asuras, whose birth is unmanifest,
Brahmā remained there, illuminating the quarters with his splendor,
his chest covered by the Śrīvatsa mark and shining with a golden thread. 28.28–29a.
Resembling a celestial sage, glorious, self-born, the creator of beings; pure-haired, broad-chested, the Lord consisting of all splendor;
the goal of those of virtuous conduct, and the inaccessible path for those of sinful deeds. 29–30.
The great-souled ones perfected in yoga know this supreme world,
whose eightfold sovereignty they call the best of the gods; having attained that eternal state, O brahmins, those who are self-controlled and desire liberation [abide there].
Thus, those purified by yoga are liberated from both birth and death.
That which all those dwelling in the various stages of life (āśramas) call "austerity" is practiced by them as they observe their vows with restricted diets and undertake difficult penances.

He who is proclaimed as "Yonaṃta" by all yogis, along with Śeṣa and other supreme beings, possesses a thousand heads and red eyes; he who is worshipped as "Yajña" by the best of Brahmins desiring heaven.
The glorious, peerless, and singular poet has his course through various places (35). He knows that God, the Knower, the bestower of sacrificial portions—
the God whose eyes are the bull, fire, sun, and moon, and whose body is the ether (36).
Seeking refuge, O Blessed One, we take shelter of that God, the worthy protector, the refuge, the God who is the source of the existence of all gods;
the creator of the sages and the worlds, the Lord of the Suras. 37.

For the sake of the gods' pleasure and for the maintenance of the entire world, he established the *kavya* appropriate for the ancestors and the supreme *havya* for the deities; I bow to that best of gods by whom all this was set in motion. 38-39.
Just as the supreme deity Parameṣṭhin, sacrificing with the three sacred fires,
had previously performed the creation of the sacrifice according to the original creation,
so too did Brahmā act once more through Ananta, the sustainer of the worlds.
Then the venerable Grandfather (Brahmā), though aged yet possessed of wisdom and an inconceivable soul, arrived at the sacrificial enclosure while being attended;
it was filled with wealthy officiating priests and guarded by members of the assembly.
Then, as Viṣṇu, the all-powerful one, took up his bow, the hosts of Rākṣasas stood before the kings of the Daityas and Dānavas;
and he quickly reflected upon himself by means of his own self.
Having reflected upon the sacrifice according to its true nature, the Lord, who is the eternal sacrifice itself, caused the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) there;
and Bhrigu and others, who were experts in the performance of sacrificial rites, became the ṛtvijas.

They heard the meritorious syllables proclaimed by the foremost of the Bahvṛcas, as well as the sacrificial science and the Vedic science of those who knew the padapāṭha and kramapāṭha, during that extensive ritual performed there by the best of sages.
It resounded with the voices of the supreme sages;

likewise, it was filled with the sounds of twice-born brahmins who were experts in the arrangement of sacrifices, masters of phonetics (śikṣā), knowers of the etymological definitions of words, and proficient in all branches of learning.

O Indra among kings, they saw there many eminent brahmins who were experts in Mīmāṃsā and the logic of scriptural statements, who moved about in various directions, who were self-restrained and firm in their vows, and who were devoted to the practice of recitation and fire-offerings.
Standing upon that sacrificial ground was Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds;
the glorious teacher of gods and asuras, being served by gods and asuras alike, while there the lords of creatures waited upon him, the sovereign lord.
Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Marīci—the best of the twice-born—as well as Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Atri, Gautama, and Nārada;
[and] knowledge, the mind, the atmosphere, wind, fire, water, and earth. 52.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell; the primary matter and its modifications, as well as whatever other great cause exists;
and the four Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan. (53–54)
Grammar, phonetics, etymology, ritual manuals, and prosody;
Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Mīmāṃsā, and likewise mathematics; together with the knowledge of elephants and horses, and accompanied by history (Itihāsa). 55.

Adorned with these primary limbs (aṅgas) and secondary limbs (upāṅgas), all the Vedas together with the syllable Om attend upon the Great-Souled Grandfather (Brahmā). Tapas, Vrata, Saṃkalpa, and Prāṇa likewise attend him. 56–57.
These and many others— purpose, virtue, desire, hatred, and joy— were constantly present before the Grandfather (Brahmā),
as were Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Saṃvarta, and Budha.
Śanaiścara, Candra, Rāhu, and all the other planets likewise;
the Maruts, Viśvakarman, and the Pitṛs as well, O Bhārata;
and both the Sun and the Moon attend upon Brahmā. (59–60)

O Lord of the people, the *gāyatrī*, the *durgataraṇī*, the sevenfold speech (*saptavidhā vāṇī*), all the syllables, as well as the constellations, all the commentaries, and all the scriptures constitute his body. 61.
The moments, instants, and muhūrtas, as well as days and nights, the half-months and months, and all the seasons likewise,
wait upon the Great-Souled Brahmā together with the gods.

And other excellent goddesses were there: Hrī (Modesty), Kīrti (Fame), Dyuti (Splendor), Prabhā (Radiance), Dhṛti (Fortitude), Kṣamā (Forgiveness), Bhūti (Prosperity), Nīti (Policy), Vidyā (Knowledge), Mati (Intellect), Śruti (Revelation), Smṛti (Tradition), Kṣānti (Patience), Śānti (Peace), Puṣṭi (Nourishment), and Kriyā (Action). 64.
And all the divine Apsarases, experts in dance and song— indeed,
all those Mothers of the Gods— wait upon Brahmā.
Also present are Vipracitti, Śibi, Śaṅku, Aya, and likewise Śaṅku.
Vegavān, Ketumān, Ugra, Sogra, Vyagra, Mahāsura,
Parigha, Puṣkara, Sāmba, Aśvapati, Prahlāda, Bali, Kumbha, Saṃhrāda, and Gaganapriya.
Anuhrāda, Hariharavarāha, Kakuśa, Rāja,
Yonibhakṣa, Vṛṣaparvan, Aligabhakṣa, or Kuru,
Niḥprabha, Saprabha, Śrīmān, and likewise Nirūdara. (68–69)
Ekacakra, Mahācakra, Dvicakra, Kulasaṃbhava,
Śarabha, Śalabha, Krapatha, Krāpatha, Kratha,
Bṛhadvānti, Mahājihva, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahādhvani. (70)
Dīrghajihva, Ugrakṣaṇa, Mṛḍakāya, Mṛḍapriya;
Vāyu, Gariṣṭha, Namuci, Śambara, Vijvara, Vibhu; Viṣvaksena, Candrahartṛ, and Krodhavardhana. 71–72.
Kālaka, Kalakānta, Kuṇḍada, Samarapriya, Gariṣṭha, Variṣṭha, Pralaṃba, Naraka, Pṛthu,
Indratāpana, Vātāpī, Ketumān, and Baladarpita.
Asiloman and Suloman, Bāṣkali, Pramada, and Mada;
Sṛgālavadana and Keśin, as well as Śarada; Ekākṣa, Rāhu, Vṛtra, and Krodhavimokṣaṇa. 74–75.
These and many other Dānavas, increasing in strength, waited upon Brahmā and then spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, we were created by you; the three worlds belong to us through you."

"O Blessed One, we have been made superior even to the best of the excellent gods, the Asuras. O Grandfather, what shall we do here at your sacrifice? Tell us what is beneficial for us; we are capable of accomplishing whatever task is required. (77-78)
"What is the use of these wretched deities born from the womb of Aditi, all of whom have been slain and forever defeated?
You are the grandfather of us all, together with the gods."
Furthermore, upon the completion of your sacrifice, there will undoubtedly be a conflict with us regarding Śrī, along with the gods;
for now, let us all, together with the Dānavas, observe the situation.
Pulastya said:
Having heard their arrogant words, the highly illustrious Lord Janārdana, together with Śakra, spoke this to Śambhu. 82
"O bulls among men, Rudra has arrived here to create obstacles;
though invited by Brahmā, they are striving for the sake of creating hindrances. However, we must practice forbearance until the sacrifice is completed."
"O Lord, once this sacrifice is completed, you must act so that the earth is cleared of Dānavas for the sake of the gods' victory, both for Śakra here and for me as well. (84-85)
The Maruts have been appointed as the servers for the twice-born;
taking whatever wealth belongs to the Dānavas, let us sacrifice it here while the Brahmins have arrived and the people here are in distress. 86.
"Established with a neutral disposition, we shall cause destruction for him.
While Viṣṇu was speaking thus, Brahmā addressed these words to him:
"These sons of Danu are enraged; they desire to provoke you. 87-88.
"O Bhava, you must not show anger toward Rudra and the gods;
for when the end of the Yuga has arrived and the sacrifice has reached its conclusion,
I have sent you here, as well as these bulls among men."
"Indeed, peace or even war must be made with all of them at that very time.
Pulastya said:
Then the Lord Brahmā himself spoke these words again to those Dānavas.
"O Dānavas, do not oppose me in any way regarding this sacrifice.
You must always remain in a state of friendship toward us for the sake of our purpose.
The Dānavas said:
"O Grandfather, we shall carry out all this instruction of yours;
there is no fear for those gods who are our younger brothers.
Pulastya said:
Having heard this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was then highly pleased with them.
While they stood there for a moment, ten million sages arrived,
having heard of the sacrifice of the Grandfather and the worship being offered to them by Keśava.
Then the god who wields the Pināka bow offered them seats;
Vasiṣṭha, urged by Brahmā, offered them the arghya water. Having then given the cow and the arghya, and having inquired after their imperishable welfare, he [continued].
"Having established your residence at Puṣkara, you may stay," he said.
Then all those sages, wearing matted hair and deerskins,
adorned that best of lakes just as the gods adorn the Ganges.

Some were shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes, while others wore long beards; some had sparse teeth, and others had flattened eyes. Some had large bodies with thin bellies, and others had squinting eyes. 98.
Some had long ears, some were earless, and others had their ears severed; some had long foreheads, some were foreheadless, and they were all shrouded in sinews and skin;
even the bellies of those sages of purified souls protruded outward. 99–100.

O tiger among men, having seen the Puṣkara tīrtha blazing on all sides, the high-souled Vālakhilyas and others who subsist by grinding with stones stood upon its bank out of a desire for that sacred site. 101.
Others were those who used their teeth as a mortar, while others were constant washers;
some subsisted on air, some on water, and others on leaves; they were engaged in various observances and likewise slept on the bare ground. 102–103.
Having seen their faces in this lake, they instantly became beautiful;
then, wondering "What is this?", they looked at one another. [They realized:
"In this sacred bathing place (tīrtha), there is such beauty of face through the mere sight of it."
Having given it the name "Mukhadarśana," those ascetics, purified by their baths and observances of discipline, then became handsome;
they were born resembling the sons of gods, endowed with incomparable qualities. 105–106.
All those forest-dwellers, standing there looking magnificent, O best of men,
immediately divided the sacrificial ground by means of their sacred threads alone;
they offered the agnihotra oblations and performed various rites.

Reflecting thus, O Indra among kings, those twice-born ones, whose sins had been burnt away by their penance, said, "We shall not go to another holy place; this lake, in its state of seniority, shall be known by the name Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara. Thus did the twice-born give it that name. 108-109.
There, seeing many hunchbacks standing near the holy ford (tīrtha),
the people who had gathered there were struck with wonder. Having given gifts and various vessels to the twice-born, they remained.
Having heard that the Sarasvatī flows eastward, the twice-born arrived, desiring to bathe;
they were accompanied by various groups of brahmins at the excellent tirtha of the Sarasvatī,
which was filled with *badara*, *iṅguda*, *kāśmarya*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *vibhītaka* trees.
It was likewise filled with *pauloma* trees, *capalāśa*, *karīra*, and *pīlu* trees,
as well as *dhanvana*, *syaṃdana*, *kapittha*, *karavīra*, *bilva*, and *āmlātaka* trees growing at the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) along the Sarasvatī. 113.
It was adorned with clusters of *atimuktaka* and *pārijāta* flowers,
abounding in groves of *kadamba* trees, and enchanting to all living beings;
it was frequented even by those who subsist on air, water, fruits, and leaves, as well as by those who use their teeth as mortars.
Likewise, it was surrounded by the most eminent sages, headed by Aśmakuṭṭa;
it resounded with the sound of Vedic recitation and was crowded with hundreds of herds of deer; and it was exceedingly graced by those who were non-violent and devoted to dharma.
The rivers named Suprabhā, Kāñcanākhyā, Prācīnandā,
and Viśālakā flow there through five streams into Puṣkara while the Grandfather (Brahmā) resides upon the surface of the earth. 117–118.

In that vast sacrificial enclosure, where the twice-born and others had arrived with welcome, while the proclamations of "Auspicious Day" resounded far and wide and the gods were engaged in their observances,
the deities themselves were occupied in that sacrificial rite.

And there, O Great King, while his grandfather was initiated and performing that sacrifice which fulfills all desires, whatever objects were conceived in his mind— those pertaining to dharma and artha as well— were likewise attained.
O Indra among kings, the twice-born attended upon him here and there;
the gods and Gandharvas sang, the hosts of Apsaras danced,
and they readily played divine musical instruments.
Because of the perfection of that sacrifice, even the gods were satisfied;
they attained the highest wonder, let alone those of human birth.
While the Grandfather (Brahmā) was thus engaged in the sacrifice at Puṣkara, [the gods were amazed].
O Indra among kings, the ṛṣis, being pleased by that, spoke to Sarasvatī, who was named Suprabhā and was also known as Sarasvatī.
Having seen that Sarasvatī flowing with great velocity, all those sages [spoke].
Illumining the Grandfather (Brahmā), they highly esteemed that sacrifice.
Thus, this best of rivers, the Sarasvatī, manifested at Puṣkara for the sake of the Grandfather and for the satisfaction of the wise.
O Indra among kings, the Sarasvatī— known by the names Puṇyapāvanī, Pañcasrotas, Sarasvatī, Suprabhā, and indeed Sarasvatī—
is where peaceful sages dwell, proclaiming various sacred recitations.
When they had arrived, those sages remembered the Sarasvatī.
That illustrious great river, pleased by their devotion, stood facing the eastern direction as she was meditated upon by the sages who were performing the sacrificial session (sattra).

O Great King, listen to this other supreme wonder on earth: we have heard that the Brahmin Maṅkaṇaka was wounded by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, yet Sarasvatī, who is worthy of being venerated by sages and known by the names Prācī, Pūrvā, and Avahā, [healed him].
131. We have heard that the Brahmin Maṅkaṇaka was wounded by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass.
O King, from his wound, vegetable juice indeed flowed forth.
Seeing that vegetable juice, he was overcome with joy and began to dance;
then, as he danced, everything both stationary and moving [began to dance].

The entire world, deluded by his splendor, began to dance, O King, along with Indra and the other gods and the sages rich in asceticism. Thereupon Brahmā was petitioned: "Act in such a way that he does not continue to dance."
O King, Rudra was thus commanded by Brahmā for the sake of the sage:
"You ought to speak in such a way that this Bhīma does not dance.
Having gone there and seen the sage exceedingly overcome with joy, Rudra—
"Oho! O bull among Brahmins, for what reason do you dance?
As you dance, the entire world dances as well. Thus forbidden by him, that best of sages continued dancing and replied: 137.
"By this [dance], he was restrained; yet the best of sages, indeed, continued dancing and spoke:"
The sage said:
"O God, do you not see that vegetable juice is flowing from my hand?
Seeing that, I began to dance, overcome with great joy."
Laughing, the God spoke to that sage who was deluded by passion: "O Brahmin, I feel no wonder at this which I behold here. Thus addressed by Mahādeva, O Kaurava, that best of sages—
While meditating, O Indra among kings, he thought, "By whom have I been forbidden? and likewise struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger.
Thereupon, O King, something as white as snow emerged from the wound in the ashes.
Seeing that, he was overcome with shame and, falling at his feet, said:
"O Rudra, I consider nothing else to be greater than you;
O wielder of the trident, you are the refuge of the moving and unmoving world. (142-143)
The wise declare here that all this was created by you,
and at the end of the eon, everything enters back into you alone.
You cannot be fully known even by the gods, so how could it be possible for me?
All the gods, including Brahmā and the others, are seen within you;
you are everything to the gods, both their creator and their instigator.
By your grace, all the gods here become free from fear from any quarter.
Having praised Mahādeva in this manner, the ṛṣi bowed down and said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, my ascetic merit shall not diminish here.
Then the God, with a pleased mind, spoke again to that ṛṣi.
"O Brahmin, by my grace, may your ascetic power increase a thousandfold.
I shall always remain here with you, like the eastern direction itself, especially in this most meritorious field of Sarasvatī. (148-149)
O Nata, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain for one in this world or the next who casts off their body on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī;
even if they are intent on recitation on the eastern bank, they shall not die again here.
Having bathed there, he shall obtain the abundant fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Emaciating his own body through restraints and fasts,
that ascetic subsisted on water, air, and leaves.
Likewise, he who sleeps on the bare ground and that best of the twice-born who performs other various observances and vows—
he, with his body purified, attains the supreme abode of Brahman. (153)
Whatever gold, even the measure of a sesame seed, is given at that sacred ford, it shall be equal to the gift of Mount Meru; so Prajāpati declared of old.
Furthermore, those men who shall perform the śrāddha ceremony at that sacred ford—
Those men who offer a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) at this auspicious tirtha of the ancestors shall go to heaven accompanied by twenty-one generations of their kin;
and having been delivered here by their own son, they shall go to the world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, those who do not desire food proceed upon the path of liberation (157).
Listen now to how the ancientness of Sarasvatī truly came to be; in former times, Sarasvatī was proclaimed by all the gods, including Vāsava (158).
"You must proceed to the shore of the western salt ocean;
having led this submarine fire there, cast it into the sea. When this is done, all the gods shall be freed from fear. (159)
Otherwise, the submarine fire will consume them with its own heat.
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, protect these gods from this imminent danger; be the bestower of fearlessness to the deities, like a mother.

When she had been addressed thus by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, the goddess said: "I am not independent; let my father, the self-ruling lord, be asked. I am a maiden who has observed her vows and am always obedient to his command."
"Without my father's command, I will not go anywhere, even for a single step; therefore, O Lord, consider some other means.
Having understood his intention, they gathered together and spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).

"O Grandfather, it is impossible for anyone else to lead [her] away, except for your own daughter, the maiden Sarasvatī, who is free from any perceived fault; having brought that woman of excellent complexion, place her upon your lap. 165.
Having affectionately smelled her head, he then spoke to Sarasvatī:
"O Goddess, the gods have told me that you are virtuous; speak to that illustrious lady.
Take him and cast him into the salt waters of the ocean."
Having heard her father’s words, the maiden, like a kurarī bird separated from its mate, wept that very day with a distressed mind.
Her face, with eyes clouded by tears of grief, was beautiful to behold.
Likewise, that white lotus, though blooming, was sprinkled with drops of water;
seeing it in such a state, all the gods, led by Pitāmaha, fell under the sway of grief. 169–170.
Then, steadying her heart which was tormented by grief, the Grandfather said to her: "Do not weep; you have no fear.
Through my power, you shall obtain honor."
"O son, take the fire and cast it into the midst of the saltless ocean.
Thus addressed, that young girl, her eyes clouded with tears, bowed to the Lotus-born One and said, "I am going. 172–173.
"Do not fear," they said to her again, and her father likewise spoke thus; casting off her fear with a joyful heart, she stood ready to depart.
At the moment of her departure, there was the sound of conchs and dundubhi drums.
The world was filled with the auspicious sounds of benedictions;
the blessed lady wore white garments, was adorned with white sandalwood paste, and was decorated with a pearl necklace as radiant as an autumn lotus. 175–176.
With a face like the full moon and eyes as long as lotus petals, she filled the ten directions with her auspicious fame, which was like that of the Lord of the Gods;
having emerged from his heart by her own splendor, she illuminated the entire world. 177.
As she was following her, Gaṅgā spoke to that woman of excellent complexion: "I shall see you again; to what place shall I go, O friend?
Thus addressed, Gaṅgā replied with sweet words.

O auspicious one, as soon as you see me in the eastern direction while surrounded by the gods, you shall attain my sight; then, O lady of radiant smiles, turn your face toward the north and abandon your grief.
I am facing north due to my merit, while you, O Sarasvatī of excellent vows, face east.
There, by bathing and giving gifts, one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices; likewise, whatever is constantly offered to the ancestors through the performance of *śrāddha* becomes inexhaustible.
Those men who shall perform this will be liberated from the three debts and shall proceed upon the path to liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
(183) Then Gaṅgā said to her: "May we meet again."
"Go to your own abode, O blessed one; I am to be remembered by you, O sinless one.
Yamunā likewise departed, as did Gāyatrī, the charming Sāvitrī, and all her friends, having sent their companion away. 184–185.
Then, having dismissed those gods, that wise Sarasvatī became a river and appeared at the hermitage of Uttaṅka; there,
beneath a Plakṣa tree, she cast off her body.
While the illustrious gods were looking on, that tree then descended;
it is the form of Viṣṇu, praised by all the gods, and must be constantly served by the twice-born for the sake of fruit, being of great majesty. 187–188.
Spread with many branches like another four-faced Brahmā,
the various voices of twice-born ones who had entered the crevices of its hollows as well as of gods with impassioned hearts were heard there. 189.
The lord of the forest, though not yet flowering, appeared as if in full bloom;
that best of rivers shone with auspicious, parrot-green flowers clinging to its branches like jasmine and campaka, and with fragrant ketaki blossoms. 190–191.
With its *kokilābhis*, *māleva*, and *phenaka* flowers in bloom,
she was like the Gaṅgā with Hara, or indeed like the Sītā with Plakṣa.
Then, standing upon the water there, she spoke to the Lord Janārdana.
"Hand over that fire; I shall carry out the command of the gods.
When she was addressed thus by Viṣṇu, she replied at that time: "He must not be burned; you yourself must abandon this king of fires."
"O auspicious one, in order to lead the *vāḍava* fire to the western ocean, proceed in this manner; then, O auspicious one, you will reach the Pañca [river].
Then, having placed that *vāḍava* fire within a jar of white gold (*śātakuṃbha*), he—
Govinda offered [it] into the vast belly of Sarasvatī. Having taken that, the lady of beautiful hips went facing westward;
by means of her power of invisibility, that great river reached Puṣkara.
On that boundary mountain, the pure river was born;
there is the vast Puṣkara forest frequented by gods and Siddhas, where the Grandfather performed his sacrificial session. 198.
This great river has come for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the foremost sages.
Indeed, she has emerged having inundated all those sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) wherein the oblation (*homa*) was performed by Viriñci. 199–200.
In that field, the highly meritorious Puṣkara-sā arose;
therefore, its filling was proclaimed by Vāyu, the life-force of the world. That meritorious great river, having reached that holy field, became known as Puṇyā.

The goddess Sarasvatī, who dwells there, is the destroyer of the sins of mortals. (202) Those of virtuous deeds who behold Sarasvatī situated at Puṣkara do not see that most terrible downward state of existence. (203)

Furthermore, the man who performs his bath there with a state of meditative absorption (bhāva) reaches the world of Brahmā and rejoices together with Brahmā. He who gives delightful curd to a Brāhmaṇa there—
He too, having reached the world of Agni, enjoys most splendid pleasures. Furthermore,
he who with devotion gives an excellent garment to a twice-born man shall obtain ten times the fruit of the gift of fine clothing.
Having bathed in the Jyeṣṭha-kuṇḍa and offered libations to the ancestors,
a man of pure intellect delivers all of them from even hell;
for he has reached the holy Sarasvatī in this sacred and purified ancestral field.

What else would a man desire? The son of Brahmā declared that whatever fruit one obtains by bathing in all the holy fords (tīrthas), a mortal may obtain all of that by bathing but once in the Jyeṣṭha-kuṇḍa. 208–209.
What is the use of saying much more here? He by whom this triad—[the right] field, the sacred ford, and the auspicious state—is attained, has attained the supreme goal.
Having bathed and offered oblations at the proper time, in the [right] field, and likewise at the sacred ford, those three [attain that goal].
He who bestows wealth upon a twice-born man enjoys infinite happiness.
