O Moon-Adorned One, during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, in Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and at the proper time in Kurujāṅgala— 211–212.

"O twice-born one, among all those sacred fords (tīrthas) mentioned by the lords of sages in these fields, the Grandfather (Brahmā) has declared this one to be the most meritorious. Having bathed in the central pool on the full moon day of Kārttika, whatever man [performs this]..."
He who bestows wealth shall also attain the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
(214) Likewise, having bathed here with concentration even at the Kaniṣṭhaka pool,
he who gives even a single Śālika bird of beautiful form to a Brahmin— (215)
A person who departs [to that place] quickly reaches the delightful world of Agni;
accompanied by twenty-one generations of their kin, they enjoy great fruit there.
Therefore, with every effort, one's resolve to go there should be firm.
A person should perform auspicious deeds for the sake of attaining Puṣkara.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest where the Sarasvatī flows toward the east, one should cultivate a mind characterized by mindfulness,
auspicious recollection, wisdom, intelligence, discernment, and supreme compassion.
These six synonyms of Sarasvatī have been proclaimed;
from that time onwards, wherever that Sarasvatī became eastward-flowing,
those who stand upon the banks and behold the water situated there [attain merit].

They too obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. (220) Furthermore, any man who descends there and performs a ritual bath while endowed with meditative concentration shall indeed become an attendant of Brahmā. (221)
Even a man who honors the ancestors there with vegetables and the like attains vast enjoyments through the very power of those ancestors. Furthermore,
those men who perform the śrāddha ceremony there according to the prescribed rule—
By this, they lead their ancestors even from hell, which is a giver of suffering, to heaven.
Their ancestors are satisfied by him who, having bathed there, offers them pure water mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds. (223–224)
Of all sacred fords (tīrthas), this alone is remembered as the most preeminent;
therefore, it is renowned on earth as the primordial tīrtha among all tīrthas, established as a treasury of sport for both dharma and liberation. 225.
Furthermore, Sarasvatī joined with this [river] to become even more virtuous;
it is the bestower of all four goals of life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—
and those men who enter its waters here for the destruction of their impurities [attain these].
The wise have said that for them, the fruit shall indeed be equal to the gift of a cow through mere happiness; likewise, it is equal to the gift of gold.
By means of libations and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), even those situated in the hells [are uplifted].
The ancestors go to heaven, delivered there by their son. Furthermore,
those people who drink the water of the Sarasvatī at Puṣkara attain imperishable worlds praised by Brahmā and Viśveśa.
The Sarasvatī at Puṣkara has become a ladder to heaven;
that great river can be reached by meritorious men and is frequented here and there by sages who know the true essence of dharma. 231.
Therefore, the goddess Sarasvatī is pure everywhere and established on all sides;
yet at Puṣkara she is especially purified, for she is the most holy of the holy.
The meritorious river Sarasvatī is easily accessible and remains present throughout the world.
Difficult to attain even at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, or Puṣkara, that sacred site has been ordained on earth as the most excellent of all holy places;
it is the means for accomplishing all four goals of life: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Having reached the Prācī Sarasvatī, if one seeks another sacred ford, he is like one who, casting away the nectar held in his own hand, desires poison.
Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as being at Jyeṣṭha and Madhyamā at the center of Prayāga. 235–236.
Then the wise man should proceed clockwise around the youngest [of the three];
one should bathe at all three of these and also perform circumambulation. He who offers water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors [attains great merit].
The ancestors, being pleased, bestow upon him immeasurable fruit once again.

He who, having bathed and remaining constantly self-restrained, should then behold the Grandfather (Brahmā) through both the direct and reverse orders, as well as in their separated and combined forms. 238–239.
One who desires the world of Brahmā should bathe daily at Puṣkara;
there are three white peaks and three springs.
These are well-known as the Puṣkaras, yet we do not know the reason for that.

The Kanīyāṃsa, Madhyama, Tṛtīya, and Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara—these are the names of the peaks, and they are auspicious sources of flowing water. By the mere resolve for them, a man obtains the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. 241–242.
Whoever should cast off their body there attains liberation without a doubt;
being self-restrained and purified, one who bathes in that place should give an auspicious cow consecrated with mantras to a brahmin, and thereby attains worlds that grant liberation. 243.
What need is there for much speaking on this matter? For even at night, he who bathes and bestows wealth upon a supplicant enjoys infinite happiness;
therein, the most excellent sages praise the gift of sesame seeds.
A bath is always prescribed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; he who, being self-restrained, offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) here with oil-cake or molasses,
goes to the world of the ancestors.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest, the Sarasvatī again vanished from there; she proceeded toward the west,
and not very far from that Puṣkara, she became most beautiful.
Having reached the date-palm forest, adorned with fruits and flowers,
and having dwelt there, the Goddess [proceeded] further to the grove of Munis, which is delightful,
strewn with blossoms of all seasons, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
The Nandā, the best of rivers, renowned throughout the three worlds,
is filled with pure water and abounds with fish, crocodiles, and large fish.
Sūta said:
Then Devavrata said: "O Brahman, what other river is superior to her? This is my curiosity: why is the Sarasvatī called by the name 'Ānandā'?
What is the true nature of this best of rivers, and for what reason was she created?"
When this had been said, Pulastya began to relate to Bhīṣma this ancient account known as the Nandana, saying:
"There was once a king named Prabhañjana who constantly observed the vows of a Kṣatriya."
The exceedingly powerful one set out into that forest to hunt deer;
then, he saw a doe standing within a thicket and pierced her, who was directly in front of him, with a very sharp arrow.
Having surveyed all directions and seen him with the arrow in hand, she said:
"O fool, what is this difficult deed you have done?
I am standing here with my face turned downward, ready to offer my breast to my son."

"O King, I have previously heard it said that one should not kill such a deer as this—one pierced by the greed for flesh, yet fearless within; one drinking while its fawn is hidden, and approaching for secret mating. (257-258)
"Because you struck with an arrow like a thunderbolt this innocent woman who had come to the forest while nursing her suckling child,
therefore you too, O evil-minded one, shall attain the state of a flesh-eating beast."
"Assume the form of a tiger in this forest thick with thorns.
Upon hearing these words of the curse, the king, standing before her with his senses distressed, spoke to that doe with palms joined in reverence.
"O blessed lady, you who are intent on providing the breast-milk here for your son, you have been struck down by ignorance; be gracious through excellent meditative concentration.
When shall I cast off this tiger-form and regain my human state?"
"O deer, I desire liberation from such a curse.
When he had spoken thus, the deer addressed him with these auspicious words:
"O King, at the end of a hundred years, when the cow has arrived, there shall be release from the curse. (263-264)
Upon reaching the conclusion of his conversation with Nandā, as soon as the words were spoken by the doe, the king then became a tiger;
endowed with claws and fangs as weapons, he assumed the form of a most terrifying tiger.
There he remained subsisting by killing four-footed beasts and even the two-footed creatures dwelling there, as they were brought to him in due course by time;
in this manner, a hundred years passed for him in that forest.
"Self-reproaching as I eat the flesh of deer, when shall I again attain such a human state? I shall not commit any despicable act that causes one to fall into a lower birth. (268)
For those who, driven by intense greed, run about hunting,
there comes a calamitous encounter with humans that brings fear and causes me great distress upon seeing deer together with men. (269-270)
"Though born into a family of the virtuous, I have been rendered sinful by my own evil deeds; though born sinless, I have been brought to a state of corruption—behold the reversal of time!
Therefore, I possess no merit, for even this single act of violence is censurable."
"By this [action], suffering is obtained and liberation will not come to pass.
How shall my liberation occur? How can she truly become a deer?
While he was dwelling in that forest in this manner, a hundred years passed by.
Because of the need for fodder and water for the cows that had arrived at Gokula, the cow-pen was established there;
it stood near the forest, filled with the sound of churning. 274.
That forest was filled with intoxicated cowherds and even with trees;
it resounded with the sound of flutes at night and brought auspiciousness to the gopīs.
While he was thus dwelling in the midst of that grove of date palms, (275–276).
Joyful, contented, well-nourished, and full of bliss, she was known by the name Vaināman;
she was the foremost of the herd of cows, white in color, with a flowing udder, a long snout, well-proportioned limbs, beautiful form, and thin skin. (277)
With a blue throat, an auspicious neck, and a sweet voice like a row of bells (278),
she moves fearlessly at the head of her entire herd; having gone to a secluded place, she grazes on grass alone according to her pleasure (279).
There, on the bank of the river, is another mountain named Rohita, which is covered with various desirable plants and fragrant trees, frequented by wild animals,
and filled with many caves, ravines, and caverns. 280.
To its northeast, in a region filled with terrible grass, narrow, impassable, and difficult to traverse, hair-raising and fearsome,
teeming with deer and lions and inhabited by many beasts of prey.
In this fortress, dense with thickets of creepers and trees and resounding with the howls of hundreds of jackals, there dwells a terrifying being in the form of a man, a source of fear;
he has shoulders smeared with the blood of leopards and possesses formidable fangs and claws as his weapons. 283.
There was a virtuous soul named Nanda, who was devoted to the welfare of the cowherds;
he protected his wealth of cattle with long grasses whose tips were uncut.
Having strayed from the herd, she [the gopī] followed after him out of a desire for grass.
As they were walking, a cow appeared before the tiger;
the leopard rushed toward them and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (286) "O cow, you have been ordained as my food today, and here you are, come of your own accord!"
Having heard the harsh and hair-raising words of the leopard,
the cow, drenched in affection, remembered her calf— Bhadra— who was endowed with a white form and possessed a luster like the moon; and she spoke with words faltering from emotion.
Nanda, who was devoted to her son, was burning with grief for her son;
weeping piteously and despairing of seeing her son again, she was deeply distressed. Then Dvipin saw that cow crying out in extreme misery.
He spoke these terrible words: "O cow, why do you weep?
By fate you have been brought here comfortably; you are my food by chance. Whether you weep or whether you laugh, your life shall remain yours. (290-291)

"What is ordained is being experienced in this world; you, O wish-fulfilling cow, have arrived of your own accord. Death has been ordained for you this very day; why do you grieve in vain? (292) To them, the leopard asked again, "For what reason were you weeping?"
"Tell me truly, O lord, this great wonder that has arisen within me.
Having heard the tiger's words, Nanda then spoke these words: "O Lord, you who can assume any form at will, you ought to forgive me; salutations to you!"
Having encountered you, no protection remains for the world;
I do not grieve for the sake of life, for death must be attained by me.
For indeed, death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died.
Therefore, O Lord of Beasts, I grieve for this unavoidable matter;
since it is certain that even all the gods must inevitably die against their will,
I alone, O tiger, do not grieve for my own life.
However, out of affection and the sorrow of my wretched state, I wept; there is a burning anguish in my heart, which you ought to hear.
O lord of beasts, when I had reached the first stage of life, I gave birth.
This beloved first-born son of mine is but a child;
he is my calf still drinking milk and does not yet even smell the grass.
Bound in the cowherd’s fold, he gazes at me, afflicted by hunger. (299–300)
I too grieve for him; how will my son live?
Driven by affection for my son, I desire to give him my breast to suck. Having let the calf drink from my breast and having licked its head, [I shall follow].
Having entrusted her to her friends and instructed them on what was beneficial and harmful, he said, "I shall return again; you may eat as you please.
Hearing these words of Sanandā, the lion spoke once more: (302-303)
"What is to be done by your son? Do you not perceive that death is coming? All beings tremble and die upon seeing me; yet you, overcome with pity, keep crying out, 'Son! Son! (304)

Neither a son, nor asceticism, nor charity, nor mother, nor father, nor a guru is able to protect a man who is tormented by Time. How then can you go to Gokula, which is crowded with the community of cowherd women? 305–306.

Resounding with the bellowing of bulls, adorned with young calves, it is the ornament of the world of the gods; there is no doubt that it is equal to heaven. It is eternally joyful, divine, and worshipped by all the gods.
That which is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things; that which is the holy ford of all holy fords and the supreme among the blessed;
endowed with every excellence, it is the great abode of the Lord. (308-309)
That land of all sacred fords (tīrthas), which is proclaimed as the unsurpassed heaven on earth,
is where misfortune (alakṣmī) is struck down by the sound of the churning of the cowherd women, by the lowing of calves,
and by the "hum" sound of the cows.
Where the calves uttered plaintive "hum" sounds out of longing for their mothers; where it was protected by heroic cowherds who had exerted themselves in wrestling matches;
and which resounded with singing, dancing, conversation, and the joyful sound of clapping hands.
The cow-pen appeared like a lake with its calves standing here and there, bellowing on all sides, as if with moving lotuses;
it was the abode of prosperity, gentle, and crowded with joyful and well-nourished people. 313. I beheld that lovely sanctuary of Lakshmi, teeming with contented and robust folk.
"Having seen the likeness of Goloka, how will you return? O blessed lady, these five elements are drinking your blood;
I shall not make these insatiable elements desist by mere words."
Nanda said:
"O Lord of Beasts, listen to my words as I speak thus regarding my first-born calf;
for I have seen my friends, my young son, and the cowherds who are his protectors. (316)

Having addressed the cowherd women, and especially my mother, with oaths, he said: "I shall return; if you do not release me, let there be whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, or in the slaying of one's mother or father. (317)
May I be tainted by that sin of hunters, of barbarians, and of those who administer poison to kings, if I do not return here again.
(318) May I be tainted by that sin of hunters, of barbarians, and of those who administer poison to kings, if I do not return here again. (319)
"May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return here, [the sin] of those who would create obstacles for cows or strike one while she is sleeping. Furthermore, may I be tainted by the sin of one who,
having given his daughter once, desires to give her a second time."
"May I be stained by his sin here, if I do not return again—
[the sin] of that man who yokes oxen unfit for the task to a difficult path,
or he who creates an obstacle while this story is being told. (321-322)
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again,
should my friend who has come to my house depart disappointed; may I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again.
"By these terrible sins, I shall return again.
Having understood this conviction, the leopard spoke these words once more.
The tiger said:
"O Dhenuka, confidence has been born in us through your oaths.
Perhaps you think, 'This fool has been deceived by me,' yet even in this matter some will say that there is sin in an oath."
"In matters concerning women, arrows, marriages, and likewise the release of cows,
when the loss of life has occurred, you must not place your trust [in them].
In this world, there are some atheists who are fools yet consider themselves learned."

Those men of base character, whose minds are shrouded by ignorance and who are unskilled in the scriptures, will instantly cause the minds of others to whirl like those mounted on a wheel through their accounts of fallacious reasoning and sophistry, thereby deluding them. (328-329)
Highly skillful people display even falsehoods as truths,
just as those skilled in the art of painting show depressions and elevations on a level surface.
Generally, when people have achieved their own ends, they consider themselves benefactors.

Seeing the depletion of her milk, a calf abandons its mother; I do not see anyone in this world who returns a favor for what has been done. For when everyone’s purpose has been accomplished, their inclination turns toward something else.

In former times, oaths were made by sages, gods, asuras, and humans to one another for the sake of accomplishing their goals; we honor those very oaths today. One who swears even by truth in the presence of the gods, fire, or a guru—

King Vaivasvata cuts away half of that person's dharma. (334) Let not such a thought occur to you; he has been deceived by these oaths. You yourself have revealed everything; now do as you wish. (335)
Nanda said:
"O great virtuous one, it is exactly so; who is capable of deceiving you? He who intends to deceive another has already deceived himself. (336)
The female leopard said: "O cow, you who are so fond of your calf, go see your son; let him drink from your udder and lick your head. (337)
"Having seen your mother, brother, friends, kinsmen, and relatives,
place truth alone before you and return quickly. Having thus made this oath, that cow indeed became a speaker of truth.
Permitted by the lord of beasts, she who was devoted to her son departed;
with a face filled with tears, miserable, trembling, and deeply distressed, uttering cries of "Ha! Ha!", she fell into an ocean of grief.
Seized by the trunk and foot in the midst of the water,
she was unable to be rescued; lamenting again and again,
she reached Gokula situated on the bank of the Harinī river.
Hearing the calf crying out, she ran toward him; and having approached that young calf,
whose eyes were clouded with tears, the calf,
reaching his mother, questioned her anxiously.
"I do not perceive any composure, nor do I observe any fortitude today;
your gaze appears agitated and you seem exceedingly terrified.
Nanda said:

"O son, drink from my breast if you ask for the reason; I am unable to explain it to you—satisfy yourself as you desire. O son, this is the final time that a mother’s sight shall be difficult for you to obtain."
"Having drunk only this one day today, whom will you drink tomorrow at dawn? O son, I have come here under solemn oaths that I must depart after leaving you;
the life of a tiger, emaciated by hunger, must be given [as food]. (346-347)
Having heard the words of Nandā, Vatsa spoke these words;
Vatsa said:
"I shall go there where you wish to go. (348)
"Even my death would be praiseworthy, without a doubt, if it were together with you;
for I, being afflicted, must die alone without you. O mother, if a tiger should kill me while we are together in the forest,"

"The destination of those devoted to their mothers will certainly be mine; therefore, I shall surely go with you, there is no doubt. Or else, O Mother, you may stay, provided that my oaths remain true."
What is the purpose of life for one separated from his mother?
For me, who am constantly without a protector in the forest, who will become my protector?
There is no kinsman equal to a mother for children who live on milk.
There is no protector equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother.
There is no affection equal to a mother; there is no face equal to a mother. There is nothing equal to a mother, both in this world and in the next. (353–354)
Such indeed is the supreme dharma ordained by Prajāpati; those sons who always abide by it attain the highest goal.
Nanda said:
"O son, death has been ordained for me alone; you shall not come [to die].
Nor can this death of yours be brought about by the death of another living being.
This is the final, supreme message from your mother."
"Stay here at my word; thereafter, you must again perform service.
Whether moving through water or on land, do not commit any negligence, O dear one.
Through negligence, all beings perish; of this there is no doubt. (357-358)
One should never act with greed even toward a blade of grass situated in a precarious place;
for through greed comes the destruction of all, both in this world and in the next.
O son, those deluded by greed enter the ocean and the forest.
Even a learned man may commit an extremely terrible misdeed out of greed.
Through greed, negligence, and misplaced trust—by these three, the ruin of men occurs.
Therefore, one should not succumb to greed, nor be negligent, nor place undue trust.

One must always exert effort to protect oneself from all predators, as well as from the perils of barbarians, thieves, and the like; even when living together with animals of sinful birth, one must guard oneself. (362)
"O son, knowing that they are perverse and lack a steady mind,
you must not place your trust in clawed beasts, rivers, horned animals, those who bear weapons, women, or servants. (363-364)
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place excessive trust even in the trustworthy;
for danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots.
One should not trust even one's own body when it is strong yet the mind is fearful.
They will say that [the cow] is excessively hidden, asleep, or intoxicated through negligence.
(366) Fragrance must always be diligently smelled everywhere; cows see by means of scent, and kings see by means of the eyes of their spies. (367)
One should not remain in this terrible forest; one should contemplate the Dharma alone. You must not feel agitation, for death is certain for everyone.
Just as a certain traveler stands taking refuge in the shade of a tree, so do all beings abide for a time before departing.
Just as one who has rested goes forth again, so too is the meeting with living beings.
Since the entire world is constantly subject to the cycle of birth and death, why do you alone grieve therein?
Therefore, cast off your sorrow and follow my words.
Smelling her son on the head and licking his crown,
she was overcome with great grief; her eyes clouded with tears,
she sighed long and hot breaths again and again like a female serpent.
Seeing the world as empty because it was bereft of her son, she felt as if she were sinking;
standing there like one mired in a great quagmire, the sorrowful mother lamented and spoke these words once more to her son.
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no happiness equal to that of a son; there is no joy equal to that of a son; there is no attainment equal to that of a son.
For one without a son, the world is empty; for one without a son, there is no happiness in the home.
Through a son one obtains the world; without a son, one goes to hell. (375) The world speaks these words: "Sandalwood is indeed cool," yet the embrace of a son's body is cooler than sandalwood. (376)
Having thus described the virtues of her son and looking again and again at her own mother and her friends, the gopīs, she asked in great haste:
"As I was walking at the head of the herd, a lion pounced upon me."
"O Muktāhā! By these oaths, I shall indeed go there once more—to see my son, my mother, my friends, and Gokula;
having come here by means of truthful speech, I shall surely return there again. (378-379)
"O Mother, forgive all this that I have done through my ill-behavior and so forth;
he is but a child, your grandson—what else can I say in this matter?
O Vipulā, O Caṃpakā, O Mother, O Bhadrā, O you who take pride in your fragrance!"
O Vasudhārā, Priyā, Nandā, Mahānandā, and Ghaṭasravā!
O highly fortunate ones, please forgive whatever unpleasant thing has been said by me, whether out of ignorance or knowledge, and whatever else has been done by me. 381–382.
All of you, endowed with every virtue, mothers of the entire world,
who are eternally the givers of all things— protect my young child!
Protect my little son, who is helpless, impaired, and miserable.
"O sisters, you shall protect me, who am tormented by grief for my mother;
since you will protect me, who am helpless and without a protector, like a son, forgive me, O highly fortunate ones, and I shall depart, relying upon truth."
"O friends, no great anxiety should be felt regarding this first-born child by any means; for death stands before him already.
Having heard these words of Nanda, the mother and her friends were filled with sorrow.
They fell into a state of extreme despondency and, filled with astonishment, said this:
"Oh, what a great marvel! That you, O Nandā, who speak the truth, have prepared to carry out this terrible command of the tiger!"
Having deceived [him] with oaths and truthful words, one should destroy the great danger with effort; one must not go there under any circumstances.
One should not go even with Nanda, for unrighteousness would be committed by you. 389.

"That one abandons one's own young son and proceeds out of greed for the truth"—regarding this, a verse was formerly proclaimed by the seers who discourse on Brahman: "When the loss of life has occurred, there is no sin in oaths. (390-391)
Where the preservation of the lives of living beings would result from speaking an untruth,
there that untruth shall be truth, and even truth becomes untruth. This applies likewise in the case of women, at weddings, and for the release of cows.
In the case of the ruin of Brahmins, there is no sin in [taking] oaths.
Nanda said:
"For the sake of protecting the lives of others, I shall indeed speak a false word."
I would not venture to speak for my own sake under any circumstances, even for the sake of my life.
(394) Alone one is joined [to suffering] in the womb, and likewise at death and at burial;
alone one experiences pleasure and pain. Therefore, I speak the truth. (395)
The world is established in truth, and Dharma is established in truth;
by his word of truth, the ocean does not overstep its bounds.
Having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali took refuge in the netherworld (Pātāla).
Though Bali was bound by deceit, he did not abandon his word of truth.
Though the lord of mountains grew and rose up with its peaks,
Vindhya, remaining steadfast in truth, did not overstep the restriction.
Heaven, liberation, and hell are established upon truthful speech;
he who violates his word has destroyed everything.
He who represents himself as one thing when he is otherwise is a thief of the self.
What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self? Having destroyed myself by my own hand, I shall go to a terrible hell;
King Vaivasvata cuts away half of its merit.
Having bathed in the lake of forgiveness— a pure sacred ford with unfathomable waters— one is liberated from sin and attains the supreme goal.
When a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were weighed on a scale, [truth outweighed them].
Truth indeed excels even a thousand horse-sacrifices (403).
Truth is heard to yield excellent fruit; it is supreme, free from afflictions and the like, the proximity of the virtuous, the family-wealth of the good, and the fruit of all stages of life.
"Since he has departed for heaven after attaining that [state], how is it that he is abandoned by the people here at this gathering? Speak the truth daily; this must certainly be so.
The friends said:
Rejoice, for you are worthy of salutation by all the gods and asuras alike,
since you are casting off your life-breaths— which are so difficult to abandon— with such supreme goodness. O auspicious one, what more can we say of you, who uphold the burden of dharma?
"By this renunciation, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that cannot be attained.
Indeed, we see that through this renunciation there shall be no separation from our son; for a woman of virtuous mind, no calamities ever exist anywhere. (406-407)
Having seen all the cowherd women and having circumambulated Gokula,
she set out toward Nanda, again taking leave of the gods, the trees,
the earth, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and the Moon.

Having prostrated again and again, he made a request to all the deities of the ten directions, the trees, the constellations, and the planets; likewise to the Siddhas who had taken refuge in the forest and to all the forest deities. 409–410.
May the Campaka, Aśoka, Punnāga, Sarala, Arjuna, and Kiṃśuka trees protect my son as he wanders through the forest;
may all you trees listen to my distressed message.

"Protect this young calf, who wanders alone and piteously in the rugged forest; guard this child out of affection as if he were your own biological son— he is bereft of mother and father, helpless, and dejected in mind."
As my son wanders upon this ground, crying out in great misery, as he laments here in the vast forest,
overcome by intense grief and afflicted by hunger and thirst— 414.
"To you who are solitary and empty, beholding the entire world as empty;
while you wander, its protection must be performed with compassion"—having thus instructed him out of love and affection, Nandā fell under the sway of maternal affection. (415–416)

Blazing with the fire of grief and deprived of the sight of her son, she wandered like a female cakravāka bird separated from her mate, fallen from the tree of her life; blind and devoid of vision, she stumbled at every step.
She went back again to that place where that flesh-eater sat,
his mouth gaping wide, with sharp fangs, and terrifying; meanwhile, her son Vatsa, with his tail held high, was moving with great speed.
Having arrived at the front of her mother, she stood before the lion;
then, seeing her son arrived and death standing before her,
and beholding the tiger, the cow spoke these words:
"O lions, lords of beasts, I have gone; I abide in the vow of truth and dharma.
Now, satisfy yourselves as you desire with my flesh. Satisfy all living beings and drink my blood."
"Since she has died, let us eat this child.
The panther said, "Welcome to you, O auspicious one; O cow, you are a speaker of truth. 423
"For those who possess truth, nothing inauspicious ever occurs anywhere.
O Dhenuka, you previously spoke the truth regarding our return; because of that, curiosity has arisen in me as to how he might come back again."

"I have sent you back again for the purpose of testing your truthfulness; otherwise, having reached me alive, how would you have departed? And that curiosity which has arisen in us is my own search for the truth."
Therefore, by this truth, O auspicious one, you have now been declared my sister by me; your son is my nephew,
for I am one whose actions are most virtuous and who has bestowed spiritual instruction upon you.
The world is established in truth, and dharma is established in truth.
By truth, the cow releases her stream of milk, dear as a sacrificial oblation. That cowherd is most blessed who lives upon your milk.

O auspicious one, those regions of earth, along with their grasses and creepers, are blessed; they are fortunate and have achieved their life's purpose, for by them alone has a meritorious deed been performed— those who drink your water have attained the very essence of birth.
Having gained confidence in the Lord of Beasts, he attained the highest astonishment:
"This is indeed a refusal shown to us by the gods;
it is true that having seen the beloved cows, my desire is only for life. (431-432)
I shall perform that deed by which I may be released from this sin;
thousands and hundreds of living beings have been devoured by me. Having seen such truth regarding the cow, what destination shall I now attain?
"I am a sinner, of evil conduct, cruel, and a slayer of living beings.
Having committed such a most dreadful deed, to what worlds shall I go?
I shall go to holy pilgrimage sites and perform the purification of my sins."
"Having ascended a mountain I shall cast myself down, or I shall enter the fire;
for the sake of purifying myself from sin, I must perform penance by means of a cow.
Therefore, instruct me in brief, for this is no time for prolixity. (436)
The cow said:
"They praise austerity in the Kṛta age, and knowledge alone in the Tretā; they say sacrifice is the way in the Dvāpara, but in the Kali age, charity alone."
Of all gifts, this alone is the single most excellent:
the granting of fearlessness to all beings; there is no gift superior to this.
He who bestows fearlessness upon all creatures, both moving and stationary, [attains the highest reward]. (438–439)
Freed from all fears, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
There is no gift equal to non-violence; there is no austerity equal to non-violence.
Just as every other footprint is encompassed within the footprint of an elephant, so too are all virtues contained within non-violence.
O Vyāghra, all dharmas are indeed dissolved through non-violence (ahiṃsā).
The shade of the tree of yoga destroys the threefold affliction;
its flowers are dharma and knowledge, and its fruits are heaven and liberation.
For one scorched by the threefold suffering, this tree of union with the Shadow is remembered;
having attained supreme nirvāṇa, one is no longer afflicted by sufferings.
Thus, this supreme welfare has been proclaimed to you in brief. 443.
"You already know all this; you are merely questioning me.
The leopard said:
"In the past, I was cursed by a doe and have remained here in the form of a tiger."
Consequently, everything regarding the slaughter of living beings has been entirely forgotten by me;
yet, through your company and your instruction, memory has arisen once more.
And you too, by this truth, shall go to the supreme goal.
Therefore, O auspicious one, I ask you again this single question that dwells in my heart; for more than a hundred years have passed while I have been reflecting on it,
O beautiful lady of heaven, through the power of your good fortune.
"The establishment of Dharma has been made, firmly rooted in the path of the virtuous.
O auspicious one, O lady of excellent vows, tell me, who am ignorant, what is your name?
Nanda replied:

"Why do you remain standing here with the thought 'I shall now devour him,' while being addressed as 'Nandana' by your master who has brought you joy? Upon hearing that name, Prabhajana was released from his curse. 449–450.
Having regained his kingship and being endowed with strength and beauty,
in the meantime Dharma, knowing her to be truthful,
arrived there to see her and spoke to that milch-cow.
"O you whose vows are true, I am Dharma, come here emboldened by your asceticism. Choose a boon, may prosperity be yours; choose indeed the most excellent boon.
Thus addressed, Queen Nandā requested a boon from him.
"By your power, I, along with my sons, am going to the supreme abode.
May this auspicious ford become a bestower of dharma for sages; and let this river be known by my name as the Sarasvatī named Nandā. (454)
"O Lord of Gods, because of the granting of this boon, this is what has been requested by me.
Pulastya said:
"At that very moment, the Goddess went to the auspicious abode of those who possess truth."
Prabhañjana also obtained that kingdom previously acquired;
Nandā went to heaven after reaching the Sarasvatī river named Nandrā, and for that reason she is called Nandāsarasvatī by the wise. 456–457.
Furthermore, Sarasvatī emerged from that forest known as Kharjūra and flowed again toward the south, flooding the surface of the earth;
even a man who merely approaches her without uttering her name [is purified].

While living, he attains happiness, and upon death, he becomes a sky-walker (khecara). Those men who perform auspicious deeds and cast off their bodies there become happy people, kings of the Vidyādharas.
For men, the Sarasvatī is a ladder to heaven; by bathing in and drinking from it,
those who perform their ablutions there on the eighth day with well-concentrated minds,
having died, reach heaven and rejoice in great delight.
There, Sarasvatī always bestows good fortune upon women;
even by fasting on the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā), one becomes a recipient of good fortune.
By merely beholding her there, one is liberated from the accumulation of sins.
Those men who touch it should also be known as lords among sages;
by the gift of silver, a man becomes handsome.
This river, endowed with both holy and unholy waters, is the daughter of Brahmā.
The river named Nandā, having flowed out extensively toward the south,
went not very far from there and then turned back;
from that time forth, that goddess has remained manifest by her own power.
On its meritorious banks are holy fords and shrines frequented on all sides by sages and perfected beings;
in all of them, the Sarasvatī becomes the cause of dharma.

By bathing, drinking, or giving gold in the Mahānadī river, and by giving gifts of gold, land, or cows at the Nanda-tīrtha, men who have bathed produce inexhaustible fruit for their great prosperity. (468–469)
The lords of sages declare that the gift of grain and likewise the gift of wealth are highly praised;

whatever is bestowed by men at those sacred fords is ordained as the most excellent cause of dharma. Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever, being self-restrained, should diligently undertake a fast unto death there—

Having attained union (sāyujya) at the sacred fords (tīrthas), he enjoys the fruit as he desires in the abode of Brahmā. Furthermore, whatever beings— whether stationary or moving— die in his vicinity, they too, by the exhaustion of their karma, shall forcibly and suddenly obtain the fruit of that sacrifice which is otherwise so difficult to attain.

Therefore, for those men whose minds are afflicted by the sufferings of birth and so forth, Sarasvatī—the giver of the fruits of dharma—should be served with all their soul and with great effort as a river that yields the fruit of merit.
(473) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Nandā and Prācī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. (18)
Chapter Nineteen.
Bhīṣma said:
"I have heard the supreme majesty of Puṣkara and the Nandā."

When ten million sages arrived at Puṣkara, they all attained handsome forms simply by beholding your face; I have heard all of this. Now, tell me about those sacrificial threads with which they were honored.

How was the classification of the sacred fords (tīrthas) made by those great-souled ones? Furthermore, which sacred fords were established in the hermitage by the great seers (maharṣis)? Previously, Viṣṇu set foot upon Yajñaparvata.

There, five holy bathing places (tīrthas) were created by those highly venomous Nāgas. By whom was the step-well for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) previously constructed? How did the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī come to flow upon the earth facing northward?
"How should a pilgrimage be performed during a period of three dry years by Brahmins learned in the Vedas, and what fruit arises from it? Tell me that.
Pulastya said:

This great burden of questions has been devised by you; therefore, with a one-pointed mind, listen to this which yields great fruit for the seekers of truth. (7) He whose hands, feet, and speech are well-restrained—
One who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown enjoys the fruit of a true pilgrimage site (sat-tīrtha).
One who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is content with whatever comes,
and who has turned away from egoism enjoys the fruit of a true pilgrimage site.
O Indra among kings, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.
O best of the Bharatas, this is the supreme secret of the sages.
Formerly, O Great King, at that sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
ten million ascetics of fierce penance gathered there;
relying upon the sight of his face, they remained at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara.
Having attained supreme beauty, those best of sages were delighted;
filled with great joy, they longed for a vision of Brahmā.
Having divided the non-sacred space and remaining devoted to worship, they stood there. Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), being pleased with them,
approached them upon seeing the honor shown by those wise ones, having formed a group of ten million.
"From this day forward, there shall be an increase in your merit.
Whatever man comes here and first bathes a limb of his in the water for the sake of beauty, [he shall obtain it], for beauty has been brought about by this sacred ford."
There is no doubt that it will exist within a circle extending for one yojana.
Its width is half a yojana and its length is indeed one and a half yojanas;
such is the measurement of this sacred ford (tīrtha) established by ten million sages.

O Indra among kings, O subduer of enemies, by merely going to Puṣkara, a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. The highly meritorious Sarasvatī has entered Jyeṣṭha-Puṣkara.
O Indra among kings, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Brahmā and the other gods, sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas go there;
one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution there.
One then obtains the merit of a horse-sacrifice (Gomedha) and uplifts one's entire lineage;
such was the classification of the sacred fords (tīrtha) established by those great sages. Having fully gratified the ancestors and the gods, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed there, a mortal becomes as stainless as the moon;
he attains the world of Brahmā and proceeds to the supreme goal.
This sacred ford (tīrtha) of the God of gods is renowned throughout the three worlds in the realm of men. 23–24.
O lord of the earth, the famous Puṣkara, which destroys great sins,
is the presence of ten thousand times ten million holy sites during the three periods of the day, O delighter of your lineage.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts,
as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, are eternally present there, O Lord; for it is there that the gods, Daityas, and Brahman-sages have performed austerities.
Endowed with great merit through divine yoga and great kingship,
even the high-minded person who merely desires the Puṣkara lakes in their mind is purified of all sins and rejoices in the heights of heaven.
O great king, at that sacred ford the Grandfather (Brahmā) always dwelt with supreme delight, honored by both gods and dānavas;
and at Puṣkara, O great king, all the gods, preceded by the sages, [resided].
Having attained perfection and being endowed with great merit,
those who perform an ablution there while devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods—
the wise declare that such an act is ten times more meritorious than a horse sacrifice.
If one residing in the Puṣkara forest feeds even a single Brahmin,
by that food a crore [of ancestors] become honored and gratified; through that deed, O Bhīṣma, he rejoices both here and in the hereafter.
Whatever one maintains oneself on— whether vegetables, roots, fruits, or anything else— that one should give to a Brāhmaṇa with faith and without malice;
by that alone, a wise man shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
O best of kings, whether one be a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra,
[one should go] to the meritorious lake of the Grandfather (Brahmā) known by the name Puṣkara,
which indeed bestows merit upon the Vaikhānasa Siddhas and sages.
Today we have reached the Sarasvatī, most meritorious and vast ocean, where the primordial god, the great yogi Madhusūdana, resides;
he is renowned by the name Ādivarāha and is worshipped by the thirty deities. 37.
Those of low caste who have gone to the ancestral ford (Paitāmaha-tīrtha) do not enter a base womb after bathing at that ford of the Great-Souled One;
this is especially true for him who goes to Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika.
We have heard that for him, the fruit of that [act] becomes inexhaustible;
O Kaurava, he who remembers the Puṣkara lakes with palms joined in reverence at dawn and dusk has, as it were, performed ablutions in all sacred fords.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth—
all this perishes merely by bathing at Puṣkara,
just as the Grandfather (Brahmā) is the foremost among all the gods. 41–42.
In that very same way, Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having seen it, one who is self-controlled and pure at Puṣkara for ten years obtains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
But he who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice for a full hundred years, or dwells for even a single *kārttikī* day at Puṣkara—it is exactly equal.
At Puṣkara, the fire-oblation is difficult to perform; at Puṣkara, austerity is difficult to practice.
Giving gifts at Puṣkara is difficult, and residing there is even more difficult.
A Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, having gone to Jyeṣṭha-Puṣkara, becomes a partaker of liberation through bathing, and a savior of his ancestors through the performance of Śrāddha. 46.
Even a Brahmin who merely utters the name [of this place] and performs his twilight devotions there for twelve years— by him the twilight devotions have indeed been performed;
of this there is no doubt, as was declared of old by the Self-born One.

The fault described by Sāvitrī does not arise in that family where a wife gives water from a copper vessel to her husband as he performs his twilight devotions; indeed, such water goes to heaven like a pearl. 49.
Having reached the world of Brahmā, he remains there for a day of Brahmā (50).
Even though he has come alone, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) should be worshipped in due order with water from a lotus, or else with water placed in a vessel (bhṛṅgāra) (51).

O best of kings, for him who performs the libations to the ancestors while his wife stands nearby, facing the southern direction, the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra shall undoubtedly be as if performed for twelve years.
The supreme satisfaction of the ancestors is accomplished for twelve years;
through the offering of the *piṇḍa* at the *śrāddha*, one attains infinity for a thousand *yugas*.
For this very purpose, indeed, the wise take a wife.
"Having gone to the sacred ford (tīrtha), we shall indeed bestow morsels of food upon them preceded by a śrāddha;
their sons, wealth, grain, and lineage shall become uninterrupted—of this there is no doubt. Thus spoke the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O King, listen with a focused mind as I describe the hermitages to you;
here is the hermitage established by Agastya, which is equal to the abodes of the gods.

In ancient times, there was here an hermitage of the seven ṛṣis, esteemed by the gods; likewise, there was the supreme abode of the Brahman-ṛṣis and the Manus. And on the slope of the Sacrificial Mountain lies the delightful city of the Nāgas.
I shall relate in brief the power of the great king Agastya, whose soul was immeasurable; listen with a well-composed mind.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there were Dānavas, O Bhīṣma, who were intoxicated by war.
The hosts known as the Kāleyas, who were exceedingly terrible, having taken refuge with Vṛtra, prepared to slay the gods. Thereupon, the gods, greatly agitated, approached Brahmā.
To all those who were praised with palms joined in reverence, Parameṣṭhin spoke thus:
"O gods, everything that you desire to accomplish is known to me;
I shall declare the means by which you will slay Vṛtra."
There is a great ṛṣi of noble intellect, renowned as Dadhīci;
go to him all together and request a boon from him.
That righteous-souled one will grant it with a well-pleased inner heart.
"You all, desiring victory, must speak together with one voice:
'Give us your own bones out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds.
He will cast off his body and give you his own bones."
"Let a great, formidable, and firm vajra be fashioned from her bones—
a divine weapon known as the thunderbolt (aśani) that slays the great enemy.
With that very vajra, Śatakratu shall indeed slay Vṛtra.
"All this has been related to you; therefore, let everything be carried out.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then took leave of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and, placing Śatakratu (Indra) at their head, went to the hermitage of Dadhīci.
On the far bank of the Sarasvatī, the place was covered with various trees and creepers,
resounded by the humming songs of bees as if by singers of the Sāmaveda,
and filled with the cries of jīvañjīvaka birds mingled with the calls of male cuckoos.
With buffaloes, boars, sṛmaras,
and even yaks (camaras) roaming here and there, free from the fear of tigers;
and with female elephants and male elephants whose temples and faces were flowing with rut.
It resounded on all sides with the playful cries of peacocks,
and it echoed with the great roars of lions and tigers;
it was also filled with peacocks perched within the caves and mountain clefts.
Resounding with the most delightful sounds in those various groves,
they arrived at Dadhīci’s hermitage, which was as renowned as heaven itself;
there they beheld Dadhīci, whose splendor was equal to the sun.

O King of the Asuras, having saluted and prostrated before his feet— which were blazing with splendor and possessed four arms— they all requested a boon, exactly as had been instructed by the Supreme Lord.
Then Adhīci, being highly pleased, spoke thus to those best of gods:
"O gods, I shall do whatever is desired by you today; I shall even cast off my own body.
Having spoken thus to them, that most excellent of the twice-born then suddenly gave up his life-breaths.
The gods and the Asuras took his bones as required for their respective purposes.
Then, appearing joyful in their desire for victory, the gods approached Tvaṣṭṛ and spoke of that matter.
Having heard their words, Tvaṣṭṛ, appearing joyful and purified, applied himself with great effort.
Having fashioned a vajra of exceedingly fierce power and taken up that weapon, he spoke joyfully:

"With this most excellent of weapons, O God, reduce the fierce enemy of the gods to ashes today! Then, having slain the foe along with his hosts, may you, dwelling in heaven, happily rule over the entire three worlds."
Thus addressed by Tvaṣṭṛ, Purandara, being delighted and composed, took up the thunderbolt.
Then, equipped with the thunderbolt and honored by the gods, he advanced toward Vṛtra, who stood encompassing both heaven and earth.
It was protected on all sides by the massive-bodied Kālakeyas, who stood with weapons raised like mountains with peaks;
then a battle broke out between the gods and the Dānavas.
For a moment, O best of the Bharatas, there arose a great and terrifying sound that struck fear into the world—
produced by the swords raised and brandished by the arms of heroes,
and by bodies being torn asunder. 84-85.

As their heads fell from the sky to the surface of the earth, the world appeared as if covered by palm trees, O lords of the earth; those Kāleyas, clad in golden armor and armed with iron clubs, [fell]. 86.
