Then the thirty gods retreated like trees consumed by fire.
Unable to withstand the force of those swift ones as they rushed forward together, the gods, though united, could not endure it; broken, they fled in fear. 87–88.
Seeing them fleeing in fear and Vṛtra growing in power, the thousand-eyed Purandara was overcome by a great dejection.
Seeing Śakra thus possessed by dejection, the eternal Viṣṇu [intervened].

He bestowed his own splendor upon Śakra, increasing his strength. Seeing Śakra thus nourished by Viṣṇu, all the hosts of gods as well as the pure Brahman-sages then contributed their respective splendors. 90–91.
Strengthened by Viṣṇu along with the deities and the highly blessed sages, Śakra became powerful. Knowing that the lord of the gods was thus established in strength, Vṛtra let out a great roar.
By his roar, the earth, the quarters, the sky, the heavens, and the mountains— all trembled.
Then Mahendra, greatly distressed upon hearing that most terrible and immense sound,
submerged in fear, swiftly released his great thunderbolt indeed upon his head.

Struck by Indra’s thunderbolt, he fell with a great roar, wearing a golden garland, like a magnificent great mountain released from the hand of Viṣṇu before Mount Mandara. When that foremost of Daityas was slain, Śakra, overcome with fear, fled to enter the ocean.
And he did not see the thunderbolt released from his own hand, nor Vṛtra, who had been slain by fear.
Then all the gods, along with the sages, were delighted and overjoyed, and they praised him;
meanwhile, the gods quickly gathered and struck the remaining Daityas, who were tormented by the slaughter of Vṛtra.
Then, being pursued by the gods, those great asuras, possessing a speed equal to the wind,
entered the ocean in their affliction by fear; and having entered that immeasurable sea,
which was crowded with fish and filled with jewels, they then held a consultation together.
There, some among them, firm in their resolve and contemplating various means,
being afflicted by fear and tormented by the divine hosts, set their minds upon the destruction of the three worlds.
As they contemplated there, a terrible thought arose within them due to the onset of the time of dissolution.
"Those who are endowed with knowledge and austerity—their destruction must first be accomplished.
For all the worlds are sustained by austerity; therefore, hasten to bring about the decay of austerity! 101.
Whosoever there are upon this earth who are ascetics, knowers of dharma, and possessors of that [knowledge],"

"Let their slaughter be carried out quickly; for once they are destroyed, the world will be ruined. (102) Thus, with their minds set on this course, all were exceedingly delighted at the prospect of the world's destruction;
they took refuge in the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, which possesses great waves and is a mine of jewels. (103)
Having reached the ocean, that reservoir of waters belonging to Varuṇa,
the Kāleyas assembled for the destruction of the three worlds. Enraged during the night, they then devoured those sages.
In the hermitages and in the sacred sanctuaries that exist—
specifically in the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha— one hundred and eighty-eight brahmins and other ascetics were devoured by those evil-minded ones in the forest.
Having gone to the holy hermitage of Cyavana, which was frequented by the twice-born,
they ate the fruits and roots consumed by hundreds of sages;
thus spending their nights there, they entered the ocean during the day.

Having gone to the hermitage of Bharadvāja, twenty self-controlled celibates who subsisted on air and water were then destroyed by the Dānavas for the sake of food. In this manner, the Dānavas continued to slay the sages in succession.
At night, relying on the strength of their arms, they roamed about; after a long time, they indeed slew many hosts of sages.
O lord of men, they did not recognize them as humans.
The world became devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, with the performance of sacrifices and festivals lost;
it was listless, O lord of men, oppressed by the fear of the Kali age.
Thus did those human beings waste away, O ruler of men.
Terrified and intent on saving themselves, some fled in the ten directions; other brahmins scattered in all directions,
while others, agitated by fear, gave up their lives out of terror.
There, certain great archers, heroes exceedingly proud of themselves,
exerted the utmost effort in searching for the Dānavas;
yet they did not follow them once they had taken refuge in the ocean.

When he was born, the world attained supreme tranquility and reached its very dissolution; yet, O lord of men, as the rites of sacrifice and festival perished, the gods became exceedingly distressed. 116. They arrived [in that state], O ruler of men.
Having assembled with Mahendra, they both performed a consultation; placing the unconquered Nārāyaṇa of Vaikuṇṭha at their head,
the gods then spoke together to Madhusūdana.
O Lord, you are our creator, protector, and sustainer of the universe;
by you this entire world was created—whatever moves and whatever does not move.
O lotus-eyed one, in ancient times the earth was submerged in the ocean by you.
Assuming the form of a boar, you lifted up the earth for the sake of the world.
Long ago, O Puruṣottama, the first Daitya of great prowess, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
was destroyed by you after you assumed the body of a man-lion.
The great Asura Bali, who was invincible to all beings,
was cast down from the three worlds by you after you assumed the form of a dwarf. Furthermore,
there was the Asura renowned as Jambha, a wielder of a mighty bow.
The cruel one who caused the disturbance of the sacrifice was struck down by the immortals.
Such are their deeds, the number of which is unknown;
O Madhusūdana, you are the refuge for us who are terrified with fear. 123–124.

Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, we inform you for the sake of the world: protect the worlds, the gods, and Śakra from this great fear. By your grace, all four classes of living beings continue to exist.
Human beings become healthy through offerings to the ancestors and the gods, and the denizens of heaven are sustained by oblations to the gods;
thus do the worlds proceed, mutually dependent upon one another.
Through your power, they remain free from anxiety, being protected by you alone.
And this supreme terror has come upon the worlds;
we do not know by whom these Brāhmaṇas are being slain at night. When the Brāhmaṇas are destroyed, the earth itself shall go to ruin.
"O mighty-armed Lord of the Universe, by your grace and protected by you, may all the worlds never meet with destruction. Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, everything that causes the destruction of my subjects is known to me.
I shall also tell you; listen with your anxieties dispelled.
There are groups of beings known as the Kālakeyas, who are exceedingly cruel. (130-131)
Seeing Vṛtra slain by the wise thousand-eyed Indra,
they entered the abode of Varuṇa to preserve their lives;
having entered the formidable ocean, which was crowded with various kinds of crocodiles.
"O sages, you destroy the multitude of nights here for the sake of the world's destruction;
yet it is not possible to bring the oceans to an end while they remain. Therefore, let your minds consider how the ocean might be destroyed. (133-134)
Having heard these words uttered by Viṣṇu,
the gods approached Parameṣṭhin and went to the hermitage of Agastya.
There they beheld the high-souled son of Varuṇa, blazing with splendor.
He was being worshipped by sages like the Grandfather (Brahmā) by the gods;
they approached that high-souled son of Mitrāvaruṇa, the supreme one,
who was vigilant and a mass of asceticism through his own performed deeds.
The gods said:
"In former times, you were the refuge of the worlds when they were oppressed by Nahuṣa;
that thorn of the worlds was deprived of his sovereignty over the gods for the sake of the worlds. (138)
"O best of mountains, out of anger you have grown so great that you do not cease increasing; yet, O Vindhya, you shall not grow further as long as you do not transgress my word.
While the world is shrouded in darkness and all creatures are tormented by death," (139) [the gods spoke].
Having come to you alone as our protector, we have attained supreme bliss.
For us, who are terrified by fear, you are eternally our refuge; therefore, we now entreat you for a boon, for you are indeed the giver of boons. 140–141.
Bhīṣma said:
"For what reason did the Vindhya mountain suddenly grow while overcome with anger?
I wish to hear this in detail, O great sage. (142)
Pulastya said: The sun circumambulates Meru, the king of mountains, the great mountain of gold, from its rising to its setting.
Seeing him then, the Vindhya mountain spoke to the Sun:
"Just as Meru is constantly circumambulated by you,
O Bhāskara, so do you perform a circumambulation of me."
Thus addressed, Sūrya then replied to the Lord of Mountains:
"O Mountain, it is not by my own will that I cause you to be circumambulated;
this is the path ordained for me by Him who created this world."
Thus addressed, O scorcher of foes, that mountain suddenly grew in wrath and desired to block the path of the sun and the moon.
Then all the gods together with Indra approached that great king of mountains.
Then they tried to stop him as he was springing up, but he did not heed their words.

Thereupon, those gods went together to the sage Agastya, who resided in his hermitage, the most eminent among ascetics and observers of dharma, and possessed of most wonderful and radiant power; and they spoke to that noble one.
The gods said:
"O King of Mountains, this Vindhya, driven by the power of anger, obstructs the path of the sun and moon as well as the course of the stars. (150)
"O Lord of Sages, no one else is capable of restraining him.
Having heard those words of the gods, the Brahmin went to the mountain Vindhya;
having approached him who stood there respectfully, he spoke to the Vindhya.
"O best of mountains, I desire a path granted by you; I shall go toward the southern direction on some business. Until my return, please wait for me. (152-153)
"O Lord of Mountains, therefore grow according to your desire once you have ceased [your expansion].
Pulastya said:
"Even today, Vāruṇi does not turn back from the southern region. (154)

All this has been related to you exactly as the Vindhya mountain ceased to grow through the power of Agastya, concerning which you questioned me. Furthermore, O King, I have told how the Kāleyas were destroyed by all the gods.
"Having reached the gateway of Agastya, listen to what I say: (156) Having heard the words of the gods, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa said:
'For what purpose have you come? What boon do you desire from me? (157)"
Thus addressed by him, the gods then spoke to that sage:
"O divine sage, O high-souled one, we desire one wonderful boon: drink up the ocean entirely. "If it is so desired by you, O great rishi, let the great ocean be drunk up in its entirety."
"Therefore, we shall destroy the army of the enemies of the gods, which is accompanied by Sānubaṃdha and known as Kāleya.
Having heard the words of the thirty [gods], the sage said, "So be it; I shall fulfill your desire, which will bring happiness to the worlds."
Having spoken thus, O observer of noble vows, he then went to the ocean, the reservoir of waters, together with the gods and sages perfected by austerity;
likewise, men, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kimpuruṣas [accompanied him].
Desirous of seeing that wonder, they followed the high-souled one.
Then, together with him, he beheld the ocean with its terrifying roar, as if dancing with its waves and leaping about with the wind.
Seeming to laugh with its masses of foam as it tumbled through the caves,
the river was crowded with various crocodiles and filled with flocks of diverse birds; there,
the gods, along with Agastya, Gandharvas, and great serpents, [beheld it].
The highly fortunate sages approached the great ocean.
Having reached the sea, the venerable sage Vāruṇi spoke to the assembled gods and those sages who had gathered there.
Desiring to cross the ocean, Agastya, the best of sages, said:
"For the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall drink this abode of Varuṇa.
Whatever must be performed by you, let that be arranged quickly."
Having spoken these words, Maitrāvaruṇi, standing at the front, angrily drank up the ocean while all the world looked on;
and seeing the ocean being thus drunk up, the gods, including Indra, were struck with wonder.
They were filled with supreme wonder and honored him with hymns of praise:
"You are our protector, the creator, and the sustainer of the worlds;
by your grace, may the entire universe attain prosperity. (170)
Being honored by the thirty gods while the chief Gandharvas sang, and being showered with divine flowers, that Great-Souled One rendered the great ocean waterless.
Seeing the great ocean made waterless, all the gods were exceedingly delighted.

Taking up their excellent divine weapons, those of undaunted spirit struck down the Dānavas. Being slaughtered by the high-souled, mighty, and roaring gods who were endowed with great speed, the Dānavas were then unable to withstand the force of those powerful and high-souled inhabitants of heaven.
Being thus assailed by the gods, O Bhārata, the Dānavas, who uttered terrifying roars, waged a most tumultuous battle for about a moment.
Previously, they had been consumed by the ascetic power of sages whose souls were purified.
Exerting themselves to the utmost of their power, they were slaughtered by the gods;
adorned with golden neck-ornaments and wearing earrings and armlets,
those slain ones shone greatly like *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Then some of the remaining Kāleya demons, the best of the Asuras,
having torn through the goddess Earth, took refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
Seeing the Dānavas slain, the gods [approached] the bull among sages.
They praised him with various words and spoke these words:
"O illustrious one, by your grace, great happiness has been attained by the worlds;
and by your splendor, the Kāleyas of terrible prowess have been slain. (178-179)
"Fill this great ocean of the Brahmins, the sustainer of the world;
release again into it that water which was drunk by you.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the bull among sages, replied.

"That water has turned to ice; let another means be devised by you who have exerted yourselves for the purpose of filling the ocean. Having thus heard the words of the great seer of purified soul, [the gods spoke]. 181-182.
The gods, both astonished and dejected,
took leave of one another and, having bowed down to that bull among sages,
O great king, all the subjects departed as they had come.
Together with Viṣṇu, the thirty gods followed the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Consulting one another for the purpose of filling the ocean, they all, with palms joined in reverence, spoke regarding the filling of the sea. 184–185.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke to those who had assembled:
"Go, all you gods, according to your desire and as you wish.
After a long period of time, these atoms will return to their primordial nature."
"Making his kinsmen the reason, the great king Bhagīratha will once again fill the ocean with the flood of the Gaṅgā. Thus were the gods and the best of sages dispatched by Brahmā.
The Blessed One, being pleased, said to Agastya, the best of sages: "O Sage, let the work of the gods—the destruction of the Dānavas—be accomplished by you;
for I am indeed gratified that the gods have been rescued by you."
"Whatever desired boon you seek, that I shall grant to you.
Thus addressed, Agastya then replied with a prostration: "O God of gods, while remaining here, this task has been accomplished by me."
"O Blessed One, let this hermitage of mine become the most excellent among all hermitages;
as you have spoken, so shall it be—of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā said:
Those men who, having completed their pilgrimage at Puṣkara, come here and perform bathing,
libations to the ancestors and the gods, and worship of the deities in these sacred pools— this entire act brings about imperishable merit.
Then, taking various kinds of *arghya* offerings, as well as *śaṣkulī* cakes and *apūpa* cakes,
they shall give them to the foremost of the twice-born; by that, their ancestors will remain satisfied in heaven until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*).
He who gratifies a sage with bulbs, roots, and fruits,
having reached the abode of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣisthāna), rejoices for eternal years;
he who, having ascended Mount Yajña, beholds the emergence of the Gaṅgā.

The celestial river flows northward toward Puṣkara. Whoever performs an ablution here, being devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, shall undoubtedly obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. 197–198.

O Lord of Sages, he who feeds even a single Brahmin has fed ten million; furthermore, food and drink given here become inexhaustible. Whatever desire one may have, all of that shall be fulfilled for him.
A man who has merely bathed here on earth does not enter a new womb;
O best of sages, this shall undoubtedly become the supreme station among all stations and the most excellent sacred ford among all sacred fords, as granted by me. 200–201.
"Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth—
all of this perishes for one who has merely bathed right here.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, [departed].
Having taken leave of the sage Agastya, the best of sages, he departed.
O scorcher of foes, Agastya remained there in his own hermitage.
Thus has the origin of Agastya’s hermitage been recounted to you. 203–204.
O descendant of Kuru, I shall now proclaim the hermitages of the seven ṛṣis:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Gautama, Sumati, and likewise Sumukha. (205)
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, Pratardana, Raibhya, Bṛhaspati, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu,
Durvāsas, Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava.
Uśanas, Bharadvāja, the sage Yavakrīta, Sthūlākṣa, Sakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kṛta,
Nārada, Parvata, Svagandhi, and the twice-born Cyavana. 208.
Tṛṇa, Ambu, Śabala, Uddhavya, Śatānanda, Kṛtavraṇa,
Jamadagni, Rāma, Aṣṭaka, and others such as these, as well as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana accompanied by his sons and disciples; 209–210.
Having reached Puṣkara, the ascetics, endowed with compassion and bound by their observances, stayed in the hermitage of the Seven Sages;
they were characterized by benevolence, victory, fortitude, austerity, truth, forgiveness, and straightforwardness.
Compassion, charity, and recitation—these are established as the foundation for all.
Knowing that whatever action is performed here is experienced there in the next world, the sages, devoted to the supreme goal, understand it to be thus. 212–213.
Neither atheists nor those who do not restrain their senses go there; nor do the cruel, the malicious, the ungrateful, or the arrogant.
Rather, those who possess the splendor of truth, the brave, the compassionate, and those devoted to forgiveness [go there].

Those who have performed sacrifices, those whose nature is sacrificial, who are free from exertion and free from affliction, who are devoid of possessiveness and devoid of egoism— they go there to Puṣkara.
For those high-souled ones, there shall be neither disease, nor old age, nor death.
There, deluded men whose nature is directed toward sense-objects do not enter,
for they are afflicted by lust, greed, pride, arrogance, anger, and delusion;
whereas those who regard honor and dishonor as equal, who are free from the pairs of opposites, and whose senses are restrained, do enter.

And those who are devoted to the yoga of meditation go to Puṣkara. Those twice-born ones who dwell in the hermitages as prescribed, following the rules as stated, attain worlds of great splendor. 218–219.
Those who do not harm living beings by deed, thought, or word;
who are exceedingly compassionate, always speaking kindly;
who are constantly devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice and ever honoring guests—(they go there). 220.
Constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and always intent on ritual bathing,
they look upon the wives of others as their own mothers, sisters, or daughters, being forever free from desire.
Those who do not become angry when reviled, nor harm others even when harmed, being equal in suffering and happiness, great-souled ones with conquered senses—
they all perceive this, for they formerly wandered this earth. (223)
While they were contemplating the eternal world of Brahmā through meditative absorption,
there once occurred a great drought; indeed, at that time,
the entire world there became afflicted by hunger and was reduced to a state of extreme distress.
Then, in that world devoid of food, those who desired to preserve their own lives took up a dead child and, overcome by distress, began to cook it.
Thereupon, she attended to the distressed sages there for their benefit.
Seeing this, the king, afflicted by despair, then spoke these words:
The King said:
"Accepting gifts is seen as an irreproachable means of livelihood for Brāhmaṇas."
Therefore, O best of sages, accept from me these boons:
villages, rice, barley, juices, jewels, gold, cows, and milch-cows; O twice-born ones, cook all that meat for me. 228–229.
The sages said:
"O King, accepting gifts is terrible; it has the taste of honey but is like poison.
Knowing this, why do you attempt to entice us? (230)
An oil-presser is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-distiller is equal to ten oil-pressers;
a prostitute is equal to ten liquor-distillers; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes.
A tavern-keeper who causes ten thousand slaughterhouses to operate is equal to all of them combined.
Therefore, the acceptance of gifts from that king is as terrible as that [sin].
A Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by greed, accepts gifts from such a king,
is cooked in the terrible hells beginning with Tāmisra.
"Therefore, O King, go; may it be well with you. Let this be given away along with the gift to others. Having spoken thus, they departed for the forest.
Then, by the king's command, the ministers went there.
They scattered udumbara fruits filled with gold upon the ground;
then, while searching for food, they also picked up those udumbara fruits, but Atri declared that they should not be taken once their heaviness was recognized. 235-236.
Atri said: "We are not of deluded understanding, nor are we of dull intellect; we recognize these as made of gold, for we are awakened and possess knowledge. (237)
This very thing brings pleasure to the wealthy in this world, but after death it results in a state of limited splendor;
therefore, one who desires infinite happiness should certainly not accept this. (238) A *niṣka* multiplied by a hundred and accompanied by a thousand—
And he who should receive [gifts] from another attains the most sinful state.
Realizing that the rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women found on this earth are surely not sufficient for even one person, one should practice tranquility.
Vasiṣṭha said: He who has an accumulation of austerities and he who has an accumulation of material goods—the accumulation of austerity alone is superior to the accumulation of wealth. 241
As one renounces all accumulations, misfortunes come to an end;
for no one who possesses accumulations is seen to be free from misfortune.
To the extent that a Brahmin does not accept improper gifts, [to that extent he is free from harm].
For through contentment with suchness (*tathātā*), the splendor of Brahman increases.
He weighed possessionlessness and sovereignty on a scale;
possessionlessness was found superior even to sovereignty for one who has realized the Self.
Kaśyapa said:
This great accumulation of wealth is a misfortune for a brāhmaṇa;
for a twice-born man, deluded by the power of wealth, falls away from his highest good.
The attainment of wealth leads to delusion, and the lack of delusion leads to hell.

Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon from afar that wealth which is called a source of misfortune; for him whose pursuit of wealth is for the sake of dharma, the absence of such pursuit is superior.
Indeed, it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off;
that dharma which is accomplished through wealth is proclaimed to be perishable.
That renunciation for the sake of others is imperishable and characterized by liberation.
Bharadvāja said:
The hair of an aging man decays, and the teeth of an aging man decay;
yet the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay even as one ages.
The eyes and ears grow old, but craving alone remains free from decay.
(250) Just as a needle-bearer draws a thread through cloth with a needle, so too is the thread of saṃsāra drawn through by the needle of craving. (251)
Just as the horn of a ruru deer grows as its body grows, so too does craving—which is shoreless, difficult to satisfy, and brings forth hundreds of sufferings—increase;
it is full of unrighteousness, and therefore one should utterly abandon it. 252.
Gautama said:
Who, being contented, is unable to transcend even [the world of] fruits?
One who is greedy plunges into perils through the fickleness of the senses.
For one whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere;
for him whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is as if covered with leather.
That happiness which belongs to those of peaceful mind, satisfied by the nectar of contentment—[no wealth can equal it]. (254–255)
How can there be contentment for those greedy for wealth who run hither and thither?
Discontent is the supreme misery; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, a person seeking happiness should remain constantly contented.
Viśvāmitra said: "If the desire of one who longs for an object is fulfilled according to his wish,
then another desire pierces him even more deeply, like an arrow."
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more.
A man who, out of delusion, longs for desires does not attain happiness. 258–259.
Like a partridge moving toward the shade of a tree that serves as a hawk’s lair,
he who enjoys this earth bounded by the four oceans,
yet remains indifferent to stone and gold alike, is a king whose purpose has been truly fulfilled.
Jamadagni said:
Even one who is capable of receiving gifts does not accept them; he attains those eternal worlds belonging to those whose nature is to give.
A Brahmin who desires wealth from a king should be pitied by the great seers.
That fool of deluded soul does not perceive the fear of torments in hell;
even if he is capable of receiving gifts, he should not be addicted to accepting them.

Through the acceptance of gifts, the spiritual luster (*brāhma-tejas*) of Brahmins is extinguished; yet for those who are capable of receiving but have desisted from accepting, that luster remains. Whatever worlds belong to those who give, those very same worlds belong to those who do not accept.
Arundhatī said:
Just as the lotus fiber constantly enters the water,
so too does craving— which is without beginning or end— always enter the body.

"That thirst which is so difficult for the foolish to abandon, and which does not decay even as one decays—that very thirst is a disease that ends only with life; for him who abandons it, there is happiness.
Thus spoke the Cāṇḍāla.
"O Great Lords, because I am afraid of both Ugra and the others, and because I am like one who is weak before those who are stronger, for that reason I am indeed afraid. Thus spoke Paśusakha.
"Whatever wise men, who are ever devoted to dharma, practice—
that alone should be done by a learned man desiring his own welfare. Having said this, he indeed cast away those fruits containing gold within them.
All those sages of firm vows departed elsewhere; then,
as they were wandering about, they reached Madhyama Puṣkara and suddenly beheld a wandering mendicant who was a friend of Śunaḥśepa.
Accompanied by him, they went there into another part of the forest and beheld a supreme lake, a reservoir surrounded by lotuses;
having settled on the bank of the lake, they reflected upon their auspicious course.
Then all the sages spoke together to Śunaḥsakha, who was hungry, saying, "O friend, what is the nature of the sensation of hunger? To them,
they [the sages] replied collectively to the wandering mendicant Śunaḥsakha.
The sages said:
Though she was afflicted by spears, swords, maces, discuses, javelins,
and arrows, even that [affliction] was overcome by the pain of hunger.
Even that hunger produced by diseases such as asthma, leprosy, consumption, tumors, fever, epilepsy, and colic becomes no more than a slight affliction.
[They appear] with golden armlets, bracelets, crowns, and radiant earrings.
Those men who remain there do not shine when hungry,
just as the sun’s rays draw up water that has fallen upon the earth;
in the same way, the channels born of the body are dried up by the digestive fire.
He does not hear, nor does he smell; he does not see with his eyes.
278 The deluded one is burned, wasted away, and parched, afflicted by hunger.
He does not go to the east, nor to the south, nor to the west, nor even to the north. 279
One overcome by hunger finds neither what is below nor what is above;
indeed, in hunger, muteness, deafness, dullness, lameness, and boundless ferocity increase. 280.
Afflicted by hunger, he abandons his father, mother, sons, wife, daughter, as well as his brother or kinsmen;
he does not properly worship his ancestors, nor the gods, nor likewise his teacher.

Even when sages have approached him, one overcome by hunger finds nothing; such are the conditions for embodied beings who are destitute of food. Therefore, one should bestow food in this manner, endowed with faith.
Having become Brahman, he then rejoices together with Brahman.

Furthermore, whoever gives well-prepared food to a twice-born man day after day, and whoever recites this "Gift of Food" (annadāna), especially during a śrāddha ceremony, [attains the same reward]. 284–285.

Having become single-minded on the new moon day when the moon has waned, he who always causes [this] to be heard during a śrāddha rite that is complete and free from injury to living beings—his ancestors remain satisfied for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt. (286)
One who gives food standing near a deity or a twice-born man is liberated (287).
Whether awakened or heedless, whether approached incidentally or even devoid of devotion, one who listens is liberated from sin (288).

Brahmins endowed with generosity are happy and partakers of the Dharma; self-restraint (dama), tranquility (yama), and discipline (niyama) have been proclaimed by those who perceive the true meaning of reality. For Brahmins, in particular, self-restraint is the eternal Dharma.
Self-restraint increases one's splendor; it is pure and supreme.
Through self-restraint, a person becomes free from sin and radiant.
Whatever observances exist in this world, and whatever dharmas follow from auspicious causes, [all arise from self-restraint].
Even the fruit of all sacrifices is surpassed by this;
for austerity, sacrifice, and likewise charity proceed from self-restraint alone.
What is the forest to one who is unrestrained, and what is a hermitage to one who is restrained?
Wherever a self-controlled person may dwell, that is a forest and a great hermitage.
For one endowed with good character and conduct, whose senses are restrained and who abides in uprightness,
what need is there for formal stages of life?
Even in the forest, faults arise for those possessed by passion; even at home, the restraint of the five senses is penance.
For one who engages in blameless action and from whom passion has turned away, the home is a grove of asceticism (tapovana).
For those whose lives are earned through righteous deeds and dharma, and who always find contentment and delight in their homes—

Liberation belongs to those who have conquered their senses, who are fond of guests, and who remain steadfast in dharma even within the home; it does not belong to one devoted solely to the science of grammar, nor to one intent on attachment to the castes,
nor to one preoccupied with food and clothing, nor to one intent on adopting the worldly conduct of the masses.
For one who is solitary in conduct, firm in his vows, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind is absorbed in internal yoga, and who is eternally non-violent, liberation is certain. Furthermore, the self-controlled man sleeps happily and wakes up happily.
He whose mind awakens to equanimity toward all beings travels happily on the great path by means of that self which is well-disciplined, not by chariot, nor by elephant.
Hari, when touched, would not act [to harm], nor would a serpent even when greatly provoked,
nor an enemy who is constantly enraged, just as the Self (ātman) when devoid of pride.
They say "restraint" and "self-control," but the Self indeed is called restraint.
He by whom this very self is mastered is indeed distinguished from Yama;
he who is called "Yama" is merely that [self], yet people tremble at him in vain.
For what can Yama do to one by whom this very self has been mastered? (302–303)
There is constant fear of flesh-eating beings and of those who are unrestrained;
for their restraint, the rod of punishment was created by the Self-Existent One.
The rod protects all beings; the rod guards the subjects.

The rod indeed restrains the most wicked, or it is itself invincible. Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes, and bringing fear to all beings, the rod is the ruler of men; upon it dharma is established.
Now, among all the stages of life (āśramas), self-restraint (dama) alone is the highest vow.
I shall describe those signs by which one is celebrated as "self-restrained" (dānta):
freedom from miserliness, absence of harshness, contentment, and proper conduct. (307)

Reverence for the teacher, freedom from envy, worship [of the gods], compassion toward all beings, and absence of backbiting— these six are declared by the sages of tranquil intellect to be self-restraint (dama). Furthermore, O King, both dharma and liberation, as well as heaven, are dependent upon compassion.
He who is not agitated by dishonor and does not exult in honor,
being steadfast in both sorrow and joy, is celebrated as "the peaceful one" (śānta).
Indeed, the peaceful one sleeps happily and wakes up happily.

Therefore, one should remain superior; by showing contempt, one perishes. One who has been insulted should never contemplate that person's sin, even while observing his own duty, he should not disparage the duty of others.
One should know oneself and not reproach others for their faults—
whether they be deficient in mantras, rituals, or even by birth.
Self-restraint covers all such deficiencies, just as a cloth covers a defective limb.
Those who study this without understanding its meaning do not truly know it;
for this is the root of all that is heard, and this is the eternal dharma.
Indeed, he who weighs his own self against gold on a scale does not weigh the Self.
One who possesses steadfastness is truly renowned, not one who is deluded by wealth;
among all religious observances, self-restraint alone is the supreme goal.
(316) Even if a twice-born man studies the six auxiliary branches of the Vedas and knows the true meaning of the Vedas, [he is not truly learned if he lacks restraint].

One who is devoid of self-restraint does not attain the state of being worthy of worship. (317) The Vedas do not purify one who is lacking in self-restraint, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences;
likewise, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, noble lineage, birth, and ritual bathing at sacred fords are all rendered useless. (318)
The knower of yoga should find satisfaction in insult as if it were nectar; the twice-born man should always loathe honor as if it were poison.
Through insult, austerity increases; through honor, austerity perishes.
A Brahmin who has been honored and worshipped departs like a cow that has been milked;
yet, just as a cow is replenished again by means of grass and water,
so too is the twice-born one restored through recitations and burnt offerings.
In this world, there is no friend equal to the reviler, for he takes away one's misdeeds and gives back one's own good deeds.
One should not revile those who revile; one should turn back one's own anger.
Having fully restrained that self, he sprinkles himself with the nectar of immortality.
(323) A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude, lack of worldly concern, and celibacy—these lead one to the supreme goal. (324)
Having completely conquered desire and anger, what will one do in the forest? Indeed, the Veda is maintained by practice, the family by character,
mantras by virtues, and anger by goodness of heart.

The hero who restrains the anger that has arisen within himself and conquers it through non-anger—who on earth is equal to him? He who remains steadfast, having subdued the anger that has arisen within him. (326–327)
The man who sits within this, considering it to be the most excellent reality,
is this eternal mass of Brahman, the secret of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Indeed, that which I have described to you at great length is the very rule of Dharma.
The worlds of those who perform sacrifices are one thing, and the worlds of those who practice austerities are another;
yet different are the worlds of those who possess forgiveness—they are indeed most highly honored. There is but one fault among the forgiving, and a second does not exist.

When people consider one who is endowed with forgiveness to be powerless, this should not be regarded as a fault; for forgiveness is the strength of those possessed of wisdom. He who understands tranquility is honored for his sacrifices and charitable works.

Whatever one mutters, offers in sacrifice, or worships while possessed by anger—all that perishes for him like water from a broken jar. Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this meritorious chapter on self-restraint (dama), [attains the highest goal]. 332–333.
Having boarded the ship of the True Dharma, he shall cross over all difficulties;
the twice-born man who constantly causes this meritorious chapter on self-restraint to be heard attains the world of Brahmā and never falls from it again.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be held fast:
one should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself; one should regard the wives of others as one's own mother and the wealth of others as a clod of earth. (335-336)
He who sees all beings as himself truly sees;
for his cooking is for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and his very life is for the sake of others.
This indeed constitutes his entire wealth, just as gold is the essence of all minerals.
"O King, by studying that which is for the welfare of all beings, one partakes of immortality. Having thus spoken the entirety of the dharma, they,
together with the friend of the dog, all sat down upon the bank of the lake.
Beholding that vast lake covered with lotuses and water-lilies,
they descended into it and, having gathered bundles of lotus stalks, cast them upon the shore of the lake and performed the meritorious water-rites.
Then, having emerged from that water and gathered together,
they saw these lotus stalks and spoke these words.
The sages said:
"By whom have the lotus stalks been taken away from us, who are tormented by hunger and burdened by evil karma,
by that cruel man desiring food?"— fearing this, those best of the twice-born questioned one another. 342-343.
O King, they all made a firm resolve regarding the path of Śiva.
Kaśyapa said:
"Let him seize everything everywhere and let him commit the misappropriation of trusts. (344)
May he who steals lotus stalks become a false witness;
may he who steals lotus stalks practice dharma through hypocrisy and serve the king;
may he who steals lotus stalks eat honey and meat.
"Let him always speak untruth, let him indulge in sensual objects, let him give away his daughter for a bride-price, and let him who steals lotus stalks commit such theft.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Let him who steals lotus stalks engage in sexual intercourse out of season, let him indulge in sleeping during the day;
let him who commits such theft become a guest for one another in a village where a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman resides in a single well. 347–348.
"May he who commits the theft of lotus stalks attain the same world as that [deity].
Bharadvāja said:
"May he be cruel toward all, and may I also be filled with pride. (349)
One who is envious and slanderous, one who commits theft of lotus stalks, one who reviles when reviled, one who strikes when struck,
and one who sells liquids that are not liquids— these commit the theft of lotus stalks.
Gautama said:
"May he who steals lotus stalks always eat the food of a Śūdra and, upon encountering a guest, practice partiality in his cooking. (351)
"Let him proclaim his taking of what was given; let him be content with another's wife;
let him eat his favorite food all alone—he who commits the theft of lotus stalks.
Viśvāmitra said:
May he be constantly devoted to sensual desires and engage in sexual intercourse even during the day;
may he be a perpetual sinner, stealing lotus stalks, speaking slander against others, and consorting with the wives of others. 353–354.

He who delights in reviling others and commits the theft of lotus stalks is a person of evil intellect who treats his mother and father with contempt. He who, harboring a hostile intent toward his mother, commits the theft of lotus stalks [is likewise such a person].
"May he eat the food cooked by others, may he serve another man's wife,
may he be a seller of the Vedas, and may he commit the theft of lotus stalks.
Jamadagni said:

Let the householder study the Vedas according to the rules and be hospitable toward guests; let him speak the truth constantly, and let him who commits theft perform penance;
let him offer oblations into the fire according to the injunctions and perform sacrifices perpetually. (358–359)
"May he who steals the lotus stalks go to the abode of Brahmā.
The sages said: "This which has been made a solemn oath is indeed pleasing to the twice-born. (360)
"O friend of Śunaḥ, you have committed the theft of the lotus stalks for all of us.
Śunaḥsakha said:
"O twice-born ones, these lotus stalks were indeed hidden by me. (361)

"O best of sages, know me to be Vāsava, desiring to hear the Dharma from you. Because of our lack of greed, imperishable worlds have been won by us; ascend these celestial chariots, let us go to the abode of the Thirty-three."
Then those great sages, experts in speech, having recognized Purandara, spoke these words to Purandara:
"That man who, having come here, enters the middle Puṣkara... (363-364)
Having fasted for three nights, one shall certainly obtain the fruit;
for forest-dwellers, this is remembered as being equivalent to a twelve-year initiation.
One shall obtain its entire fruit here, of this there is no doubt.
He does not fall into an evil state of existence, but rejoices together with his own kinsmen. Having reached the abode of Viriñci, he remains there for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Pulastya said:
Delighted by Indra, they then went to the third heaven (Triviṣṭapa).
Though they were thus enticed here by various kinds of temptations, they did not yield to greed; therefore, they went to Triviṣṭapa.
Whoever should constantly hear this auspicious account of the sages' conduct is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world. 369.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Seven Sages," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 19.
Chapter Twenty. Bhīṣma said:
This story is most wonderful, beautiful, and destructive of sins.
Tell me in detail and according to the truth as I ask you:
the majesty of the middle [caste] as proclaimed by the sages,
the fruit of food that has been described, and the majesty of self-restraint.
O great sage, tell me how Viṣṇu set foot there, and how the birth of the youngest [brother] occurred exactly as it was.
Pulastya said:
O descendant of Bharata, in a former age of the Rathaṃtara, there was a king named Puṣpavāhana,
renowned throughout the worlds and equal to the sun in splendor;
he was gratified by the four-faced Brahmā on account of his ascetic penance.
O King, he was given Kamalālaṅkā and Kāñcanadatta, which could be traveled at will;
and he constantly wandered as he pleased through the world of the seven continents.
At the beginning of the kalpa, however, that island was equal to that of the dweller of Puṣkara.
Therefore, it is called Puṣkaradvīpa because it is honored by the world;
that very lotus was given as his vehicle by Brahmā,
and for that reason the gods and demons call him Puṣpavāhana.
There was nothing in this triple world comparable even to that king seated upon the Brahma-lotus.
Then, by the power of the king's asceticism, his queen— worshipped by thousands of women—
became known as Calāvaṇyavatī, who was as beloved to him as Pārvatī is to Bhava.
He had ten thousand sons who were righteous-souled and skilled archers;
beholding those sons of his again and again, the king was filled with wonder.
He addressed these words to Pracetasa, the foremost of sages and a venerable guest who had arrived:

O Lord of Sages, why was such sovereign splendor—consisting of worship by immovables, gods, and mortals, and resembling that of the Lotus-born Brahmā—granted to me by the Creator, who was satisfied by my meager penance? And why was the lotus-abode given to me, into which even hundreds of millions of kings, accompanied by their ministers, elephants, chariot-arrays, and retinues, have entered? (11–12)
It is not perceived where it has gone, for it is inaccessible even to the rays of the moon, the sun, and the hosts of stars moving through the sky.
Therefore, what other deed, such as dharma and the like, was performed by one born from the womb of a mother that transcends all people?
O Pracetas, tell me all of that—whether by me, by my sons, or even by this virtuous wife.
He too then spoke, having perceived what was concealed by a previous birth: "O Lord of the Earth, listen to this account of its wondrous cause.

Your birth occurred even in the family of a hunter; you were born indeed as one who daily commits terrible sins. Furthermore, your body was entirely adorned with foul-smelling joints of the limbs of men, with impure substances, and with deformed nails."

At that time, neither her friends, nor her sons, nor her kinsmen, nor even her sister or mother—who were so highly esteemed, most beloved, and standing before her—could protect her; yet this beautiful woman remained facing her husband, the lord of the earth. Then, for the sake of food, there occurred a most terrible drought lasting for many years.
When he was oppressed by hunger and had not obtained any food such as wild fruits to eat,
he then beheld a great lake abounding in lotuses with its banks covered in mud;
having taken many lotuses from there, he went to the city named Vidisha.
At that time, you wandered throughout the entire city all day long to obtain the price for it, yet no buyer at all was born among the lotuses; you were utterly exhausted and tormented by hunger.
(19) Then, together with your wife, you sat down in the courtyard of a certain house.
Then, during that night, he heard the sound of auspicious music;
accompanied by his wife, he went to where that auspicious sound was coming from.
There, he beheld the image of Viṣṇu situated in the center of a maṇḍala.
Having observed the Dvādaśī vow for twelve years, the courtesan Anaṅgavatī, upon the completion of that vow on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha,
offered a mountain of salt and a bed furnished with all its accessories to her preceptor.
Having respectfully adorned Hṛṣīkeśa with golden ornaments, she was then seen by the two of them, and this thought occurred to them:
"What is the use of these lotuses? It is better that Viṣṇu be adorned [with these]."
O Lord of Men, at that time such devotion arose between the husband and wife; through that occasion, they worshipped Keśava and the Salt-Mountain (Lavaṇācala),
and the bed was honored on all sides with heaps of flowers.
Then, being pleased with them, Anaṅgavatī commanded, "Let three hundred measures of grain and three palas of gold be given.
However, because they were supported by their great resolve (*mahāsattva*), those two did not accept it. (26–27)
O King, Anaṅgavatī again brought four kinds of food for them and said, "Let this food be eaten.
But that too was rejected by the two of them, who said, "O fair-faced one, we shall eat tomorrow."
"By this incidental connection, O lady of firm vows, may fasting and the playing of musical instruments bring us auspiciousness.
O Goddess, we two have been most sinful since birth; through our association with you, let there be at least a trace of dharma here in your house. (29-30)
Thus, the vigil was performed by the two of them on that occasion;
and in the morning, she gave a bed, a salt-mountain,
and a village to her preceptor with devotion, as well as twelve villages to the Brahmins.
Cows adorned with garments and ornaments and accompanied by gold,
as well as food, were given to friends, allies, the poor, the blind, and the wretched;
and having honored that hunter couple, they were dismissed.
O Lord of Men, having been born as a hunter together with his wife, you have now become a king because of that worship of Keśava at the Puṣkara grove; for you,
whose every sin has been destroyed, this is the temple of Puṣkara.
O King, because of the greatness of that truth and his austerity free from greed,
the four-faced Lord of the World, being well-pleased, granted you a vehicle that travels at will; therefore, O Indra among kings, take refuge in Puṣkara.
"O Indra among kings, having undertaken this twelfth-day vow of Vibhūti for a kalpa, you will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
Having said this, the sage vanished right there.
And King Puṣpavāhana performed it again exactly as instructed.
O King, for one who practices this in whatever manner possible, there shall be the perfection of the vow after twelve *dvādaśīs* have passed in time, O monarch. (38–39)
O King, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the gods and the Brahmins according to one's capacity:
cows are to be given for the eldest [rite], excellent land for the middle, and gold is to be given for the youngest; this is remembered as the prescribed dakṣiṇā.

The first has Brahmā as its presiding deity, the second likewise belongs to Viṣṇu, and the third has Rudra as its deity; thus the three gods are established in the three [sections]. Whoever recites or even listens with devotion to this [work] which tears away the impurities of people, [attains merit]. 41-42.
And with a mind full of faith, he dwelt in the world of the gods for as many years as there are hairs on the body.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme vow among all vows, which was taught by that Rudra as the destroyer of great sins. 43.
Having performed this for a year by night, one should give half a cow along with two garments to a householder;
furthermore, one should give a golden discus and trident to a Brahmin. He who performs such meritorious deeds rejoices in the world of Śiva.
This very vow, which destroys even great sins,
consists of passing a year while eating but one meal a day and giving away a cow together with a bull;
by giving a cow made of sesame seeds, one attains the abode of Śaṅkara.

O Rudra, this vow named [after you] destroys fear and sorrow. He who, eating only at night on alternate days, offers a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar at the conclusion of the month, along with a bull— 47-48.
This is remembered as the Nīla-vrata, which leads one to the world of Viṣṇu;
a man should avoid oil-baths for four months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
and by giving food and household utensils as a gift, he goes to the abode of Hari.
That which brings joy to the people is here called the Prītivrata for men. Having avoided honey during the month of Madhu (Caitra), one should give curd, milk, ghee,
and sugarcane products, as well as fine garments, together with a vessel of juice.
Having worshipped a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," this is the vow known as Gaurī-vrata, which bestows the world of Bhavānī.
Having performed the fast at night on the thirteenth day of the month beginning with Puṣya, and then again...
One should give an Ashoka tree made of gold, ten fingers in height, joined with sugarcane and accompanied by a garment to a Brahmin, saying, "May Pradyumna be pleased.
Having resided in the city of Viṣṇu for a Kalpa, O King, one shall thereafter be free from sorrow.
This is known as the Kāmavrata, which eternally destroys grief. He who, during the vow beginning in the month of Āṣāḍha, avoids eating fruit,
and upon the conclusion of the Cāturmāsya, [offers] a jar filled with ghee and jaggery—

On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should again present a golden [image] to a Brāhmaṇa; he attains the world of Rudra. This is remembered as the Śiva-vrata. He who avoids flowers during the months of Hemanta and Śiśira [is likewise blessed].

Having prepared three flowers made of gold according to one's means on the full moon day of Phālguna, one should offer them at the two junctions of time (dawn and dusk); may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
By giving these, one goes to the supreme abode; this is remembered as the Saumya-vrata.
He who avoids salt on the third lunar day of the month beginning with Phālguna,
and at the end of the year gives a bed and a house equipped with household utensils, having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased," [attains great merit].
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgyavrata.
Having observed silence during the twilight hours, at the conclusion of the year, a man should offer a jar of ghee, a pair of garments, sesame seeds, and a bell to a Brāhmaṇa.
One goes to the world of Sarasvatī, from which a return to this world is difficult to obtain.
This [world] named Sārasvata bestows knowledge of forms and names.
Having worshipped Lakṣmī on the fifth lunar day, a man should observe a fast.
At the end of the year, one should give a golden lotus together with a cow; such a person goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, and Lakṣmī shall be theirs in birth after birth.
This is the vow known as Lakṣmī-vrata, which destroys misery and grief.
Having performed the smearing of the ground before Śambhu and Keśava,
one should further give a cow and a water-pot for as long as a year;
such a person shall be a king for ten thousand births and thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
This is known as the *āyur-vrata*, which bestows all desires;
having prostrated before the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā with a one-pointed mind,
a man free from envy should observe a single meal a day for one year.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple accompanied by three cows;
he who gives a golden tree shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
This is known as the Kīrti-vrata, which bestows the fruits of prosperity and fame. 68–69.
Having performed a bath with clarified butter for Śambhu or Keśava,
and having fashioned a circle of cow-dung with unbroken grains and flowers,
at the conclusion of the year, one should offer a golden lotus accompanied by a sesame-cow.

One should give a trident eight finger-breadths long; such a person is glorified in the world of Śiva. Now, the Sāma-vrata is described here: having taken a single meal on the ninth lunar day, one should [honour] maidens according to one's ability.
Having fed [the Brahmins], one should give them a golden tunic and seven horses; by giving a golden lion to a Brahmin, one shall go to the abode of Śiva.
For a hundred million births, one will be handsome and undefeated by enemies.
This is called the Vīravratam, which bestows happiness upon men.
(74) Filled with compassion, one should offer water for four months beginning with Caitra;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot along with food and clothing. (75)
One who offers a vessel of sesame seeds and gold is honored in the world of Brahmā;
this vow of bliss, which generates prosperity at the end of a kalpa, is called the Ānanda-vrata.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for a full year, [one attains this].

At the end of the year, one should again give a cow accompanied by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) to a Brahmin, as well as a conch; he goes to the state of Śaṅkara and becomes a king at the end of the kalpa. This is remembered as the Dhṛti-vrata.
Having avoided meat throughout the duration of his vow, a man should, at its conclusion, give a cow;
likewise, he should give a golden deer, and he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
This is called the Ahiṃsā-vrata (the vow of non-violence); by it, one becomes a king at the end of a kalpa.
Rising at dawn and having performed his ablutions, he should worship the couple (the Sun and his consort).
Having fed them according to his ability with garlands, garments, and ornaments, he shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a kalpa; this is known as the Sūryavrata.
A man who bathes every morning during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
and having given a meal to a brāhmaṇa on the full moon day of Kārtika, becomes a giver of cows;
he indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu— this is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vrata.
One should avoid flowers and clarified butter from the winter solstice until the summer solstice.
At the end of that period, by giving flowers, food, and a cow made of ghee, along with ghee and milk-rice to a Brahmin, one goes to the abode of Śiva. 83–84.
This is known as the vow of conduct (*śīlavrata*), which bestows the fruit of virtuous character and health;
he who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*) for an entire year on the fifteenth day [of every fortnight],
should at the end of the year perform a *śrāddha* and give five milch cows.
He who gives saffron-colored garments along with water-pitchers goes to the world of Viṣṇu and delivers a hundred ancestors;
O Indra among kings, this is remembered as the Pitṛvrata, which lasts until the end of the kalpa.
He who offers a lamp at the twilight hours should use ghee and avoid oil.
At the end of the year, he should give a lamp, a discus, a trident, gold, and a pair of garments to a Brahmin; such a man shall become radiant with splendor.
One attains the world of Rudra; this is known as the Dīptivrata.

Having consumed cow-urine and barley-gruel on the third lunar day of the month of Kārttika and so forth, one should observe the night-vow (nakta) for one year; at the end of the year, one becomes a giver of cows.
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
This is the vow known as Rudra-vrata, which always brings about auspiciousness;
he who avoids perfumes and ointments for four months [attains this]. 91-92.
One should give oyster-shell scent and unbroken grains, along with two white garments, to a Brahmin;
one attains the station of Varuṇa—this is remembered as a firm vow.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should avoid flowers and salt, and then become a giver of cows.
Having become one who is like Viṣṇu’s abode and remaining so, one shall become a king here on earth.
This vow, named Śānti, bestows the fruits of peace, fame, and desire;
it consists of making a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) accompanied by a heap of sesame seeds.
Having become a giver of other [gifts] with clarified butter, he should satisfy the fire and the virtuous twice-born;
having honored the Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments, he should say,
"May the Soul of the Universe be pleased," according to his ability, offering at least three palas.
On an auspicious day, one should give [this gift]; others attain the state of Brahman, which is freedom from rebirth (97).
This is known as the Brahma-vrata, which bestows the fruit of Nirvana upon men;
and he who gives a "two-faced" cow, endowed with all abundant qualities (98).
He who observes a milk-vow for one day attains the supreme state;
this is indeed known as the Suvrata vow, from which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to obtain.
Having remained for three days observing the milk-vow, he obtains a golden wish-fulfilling tree.

Having given [this] for one year, along with a *prastha* of rice according to one's capacity, one goes to the abode of Brahmā; this is remembered as the Bhīma-vrata. He who, having fasted for a month, gives a beautiful cow to a Brahmin, [attains the same]. 100–101.
One who observes this Bhīmavrata attains the station of Viṣṇu; it is thus remembered.
Having fashioned an image of the Earth out of gold weighing more than twenty palas, one should give it as a gift.
Remaining for a day under a vow of milk, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This is declared to be a bestower of wealth, following one after another for seven hundred kalpas. Furthermore, in the month of Māgha or Caitra, one should offer a cow made of jaggery;
by performing the Guḍavrata on the third lunar day, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī. 103–104.
This is indeed the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), which produces supreme bliss:
he who observes the fast for a fortnight and gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin attains the world of Brahmā, highly honored by gods and asuras. (105)
At the end of the eon, one shall become a sovereign king; this is remembered as the *Prabhā-vrata*.
By eating only one meal a day for a year and giving vessels of food and water, one shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is remembered as the *Prāpti-vrata*. 106–107.

He who gives a cow at the end of the year on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina attains the city of Indra; this is called the Sugati-vrata (the vow of a good rebirth). He who provides fuel to a Brahmin during the four seasons beginning with the rainy season [attains merit].
And at the end, the giver of a cow with ghee goes to the Supreme Brahman.
(109) The vow named Vaiśvānara destroys all sins; one who eats only at night on the eleventh lunar day should offer a discus. (110)
Having completed it at the end of the year, one shall attain the golden foot of Viṣṇu;
this vow known as Kṛṣṇavrata bestows a kingdom at the end of the kalpa.
Eating only milk-rice, one should, at the conclusion of the year, give a pair of cows to a Brahmin.
One shall dwell in the world of Lakṣmī for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Devī-vrata.
On the seventh lunar day, one who eats only at night should, upon completion, give a milch cow;
he attains the world of the Sun—this is remembered as the Bhānu-vrata.
On the fourth lunar day, one who eats only at night should likewise give a pair of cows along with gold at the conclusion [of the vow].
This is known as the Vaināyaka vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Śiva.
He who, having renounced large fruits during the Cāturmāsya, gives them to a twice-born man...
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should likewise give a pair of cows made of gold to Kārtikeya.
This is known as the Saura-vrata (the Sun-vow), which bestows the fruit of the world of the Sun.
O King, he who completes twelve Dvādaśīs by means of fasting [attains this].
A man should worship Brahmins according to his ability with cows, garments, and gold;
he attains the supreme state. This is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vrata.
On the fourteenth day, one should eat only at night, and at the conclusion of the year-long vow, he should gift a pair of cows.
One attains the state of Śiva; this is known as the Traiyambaka vow.
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man.
They say this is the Varavrata, which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā. 118–119.

Having reached Āsīṃsā, he who gives a milch cow shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa; this is remembered as the mantra-vow (mantravrata). At the end of the year, having renounced mouth-perfumes, he should become a giver of a cow.

One attains the world of Varuṇa; this is called the Vāruṇa-vrata. He who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should offer a golden moon; this is declared the Candra-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the lunar world. 121–122.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who performs the penance of the five fires at the end [of the day] and gifts a golden cow goes to heaven;
this is remembered as the Rudra-vrata on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
One should perform this ritual once on the third lunar day in a temple of Śiva.
The Bhavānī-vrata, which concludes with the gift of a cow, is now described.

On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, one should wear wet clothes at night and become a giver of a cow; having worn [these] for two days, one becomes a king on earth—this is the Pavana-vrata. 124–125.
Having fasted for three nights, one should give a beautiful house on the full moon day of Phālguna;
one attains the world of the Sun—this is remembered as the Dhāma-vrata.
Having fasted, one should worship a married couple at the three junctions of the day with ornaments.
By giving this, one attains liberation; this is remembered as the vow of liberation (mokṣavrata).
Having given a vessel of salt on the second day of the dark fortnight to the Moon, and at its conclusion giving a cow to a Brahmin, one goes to the abode of Śiva. 127–128.
O Indra among kings, he who, at the conclusion [of the rite], gives bell-metal, fine cloth, and likewise a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), as well as a cow, goes to the abode of Śiva.
At the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings; this is remembered as the Somavrata.
One who eats only one meal a day throughout the various lunar phases (pratipad) and completes the vow is granted its fruit;
he attains the station of Vaiśvānara. This is known as the Śikhivrata.
A golden chariot weighing more than two palas and yoked with a pair of horses [is the reward]. 130–131.
Having observed a fast, one should give [this gift]; he shall dwell for a hundred kalpas among the gods, and at its conclusion, he shall become a king of kings—this is remembered as the Aśvavrata.
Likewise, one should again give a golden chariot yoked with two elephants.

A lord of the earth may dwell in Satyaloka for even a thousand kalpas; having returned here to this world, he becomes [a king]. This is remembered as the Karivrata. On the tenth day, one who eats only one meal and, upon its completion, gives ten cows [attains this].
One who gives a golden lamp shall become the lord of the Brahmāṇḍa;
this is known as the Viśvavrata, which destroys great sins.
Furthermore, he who performs the gift of a maiden at Puṣkara during the month of Kārttika [shall attain the same].
Endowed with twenty-one virtues, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
There is no gift anywhere superior to the gift of a daughter in marriage;
this is especially so at Puṣkara, and particularly on the full moon day of Kārttika.
One should give to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite; for them, there shall be no destruction in this world.
Having fashioned an elephant out of sesame paste and endowed it with jewels, those men who bestow it upon a Brahmin while standing in the midst of water [attain great merit].
And for them, there shall be an imperishable world until the dissolution of all beings (bhūtasaṃplava).
Whoever recites or even hears of this unsurpassed Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata shall become the lord of the Gandharvas for a hundred Manvantaras.

O King of Kings, this merit-bestowing Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata, which is beneficial to all people, has been described to you today; if you wish to hear more, O best of the twice-born, listen to what must be performed. Purity and the purification of one's inner disposition do not exist without bathing.
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, bathing is prescribed first.
One should perform the bath with water either drawn from a source or not drawn, and the wise knower of mantras should designate the sacred site (*tīrtha*) using the root mantra. (142–143)
The root mantra is proclaimed as "Namo Nārāyaṇāya.
Holding darbha grass in his hand, having sipped water according to the rules, being self-controlled and pure, [he should prepare] a square area measuring four cubits on all sides. 144.
Having prepared [the vessel], the wise man should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras:
"You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, you belong to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is your deity; protect us from that sin which extends from birth until the end of death. 145–146.
Vāyu declared that there are thirty-five million tīrthas;
O Jāhnavī, they exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
Among the gods, your names are Nandinī and Nalinī.
Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, Asitā;
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, and likewise Lokaprasādinī; Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī. 148–149.
One should recite these names of merit at the time of bathing; then the Ganges, which flows through the three paths, becomes present there.
[This should be done] with the hands joined together, over which the mantra has been recited seven times.
One should pour water over the head three, four, five, or seven times;
likewise, one should perform a bath with clay after addressing it according to the prescribed rite:
"O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, and traversed by Viṣṇu! (151-152)
O Earth, take away this sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me;
you were raised up by the thousand-armed Kṛṣṇa in the form of a boar. Obeisance to you, the source of all worlds, O virtuous Goddess Araṇi.
Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having sipped water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule,
one should rise and put on two pure, bright garments;
then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the sake of nourishing the three worlds.
First, one should satisfy Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Prajāpatis,
the gods, the yakṣas, as well as the hosts of nāgas, gandharvas, and apsarases;
the cruel serpents, the suparṇas, the trees, the jambhakas, and others.
Likewise, for the Vidyādharas and the cloud-bearers who travel through the sky,
and for those living beings who are without support and devoted to virtuous dharma— for their nourishment, this water is offered by me. (157–158)

Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavīta) for the gods, one should then become one who wears it around the neck (nivītī) and offer libations with devotion to humans, as well as to the sons of the sages and the sages themselves:
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana; 159.
May Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha likewise always attain satisfaction through the water offered by me.
[May they do so] along with Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
He should satisfy Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada, as well as all the divine and brahminical sages, with water mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and resting his left knee upon the ground, he should proceed.

Likewise, one should devoutly gratify the Agniṣvāttas, the Saumyas, the Haviṣmats, the Ūṣmapās, the Sukālins, the Barhiṣads, and the Ājyapas with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste. 163–164.
Then, with darbha grass in hand, one should satisfy one's own ancestors according to the rite—namely the father and others by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfathers.
Having satisfied them with devotion according to the rule, one should recite this mantra: 165.
"May those who were my kinsmen or non-kinsmen in this life, or who were my kinsmen in another birth—may they all attain complete satisfaction; and may those who desire our water [also find it].
Having sipped water according to the proper rite, one should duly draw a lotus in front."
One should diligently offer the *arghya* with raw rice grains, water, flowers, sesame seeds, and red sandalwood, while reciting the names of the Sun:
"Salutations to you of universal form; salutations to you who possess the form of Viṣṇu. (168)
"Salutations to you, the god of all gods; be gracious to me, O Bhāskara. Salutations to you, O Divākara; salutations to you, O Prabhākara.
Having thus paid homage to Sūrya and having circumambulated him three times, [he should proceed].
Having seen and touched a golden image of the twice-born (Brahmā) marked with the sign of a bird, one should go home;
thereafter, one should worship the meritorious image situated in one's own house. Following that, one should provide a meal, beginning with the twice-born.
By this method, all the sages attained perfection. 172.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Twenty-one.
Pulastya said: In former times, during the Bṛhat-kalpa, there was a lord of men named Dharmamūrti,
who was a friend of Śakra and by whom thousands of Daityas were slain.
By whose splendor the moon, the sun, and others have their radiance eclipsed by the hundreds, and by whom the dānavas have been utterly defeated;
who, though a human, is unconquered and assumes whatever form he desires at will.
His wife was Bhānumatī, a virtuous woman who was the most beautiful in the three worlds;
with a form like that of Lakṣmī, she surpassed the celestial beauties and was the king’s chief queen, dearer to him than his own life.
Surrounded by ten thousand women, he shone like the goddess Śrī;
even by ten million kings, he was never equaled.
Once, while seated in his assembly hall, he questioned his own domestic priest.
Overcome with wonder, he bowed down to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, and asked:
"O Blessed One, by what dharma does my unsurpassed prosperity arise,
and from what cause does this vast and supreme luster always reside within my body?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
Formerly, there was a courtesan named Līlāvatī who was devoted to Śiva;
by her, a mountain of salt was gifted at Puṣkara on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight. 8.
Then, along with the gods of the golden trees, that goldsmith Śūdra became a performer of rites according to the proper injunctions;
he was a servant in the household of Līlāvatī, by whom golden objects were fashioned.
O King, those trees with golden flowers were endowed with great beauty and were beautifully fashioned by one possessed of faith;
knowing it to be for the sake of a righteous act, no wages were accepted. (10-11)
O King, those golden trees were set ablaze by their wife,
and even in the house of Līlāvatī,
service such as the attendance upon the twice-born was performed by them without guile.
O sinless one, after a long time, that prostitute Līlāvatī was liberated from all her sins and went to the abode of Śiva;
as did that goldsmith, who, though poor, possessed great virtue.
Having now taken priceless jewels from a courtesan,
he has become the lord of the seven continents, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns—
by whom golden ornaments were fashioned for a goldsmith. (15)
"Because this Bhānumatī has been properly kindled by you as your wife,
you shall therefore be unconquered in the worlds of men, endowed with health, good fortune, and immovable prosperity; therefore,
O King, you too should here perform the rites for the Mountain of Grain and the others according to the prescribed injunctions."

Pulastya said: Having honored Vasiṣṭha’s words with "So be it," he whose form is the embodiment of dharma gave all those mountains of grain and other offerings according to the prescribed rites; then, being worshiped by the gods, he departed for the world of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva). 18.
If one should behold these [scriptures] being brought forward, touch them as they are presented here by men,
or hear them with devotion and apply one's mind to them, even such a person, freed from sin, goes to heaven.
By reciting the *Śailendra* [hymns], which shatter the fear of worldly existence, a human being attains the pacification of evil dreams.

What indeed could one do, even by making a gift of all the lords of mountains, that would equal the act of one who, with a perfectly tranquil mind, performs this [fast] for the sake of the bull among kings?
Bhīṣma said:
Is there any vow or fast capable of uprooting the accumulation of grief caused by separation from what is desired?
On this ground which brings about the stability of liberation, it also effects the destruction of a person's fear of worldly existence.
Pulastya said:
This which you have asked is dear to the world, yet difficult even for the gods to attain because of its greatness.
Nevertheless, O Indra, because you are my devotee, I shall describe to you this secret vow among gods and men,
the meritorious Viśokadvādaśī-vrata in the month of Āśvayuja. On the tenth day, the wise man, having eaten light food, should begin it with self-restraint.
Facing either north or east, having first performed the cleansing of the teeth, and having properly worshipped Keśava on the eleventh day while remaining without food,
and having likewise worshipped Śrī according to the rules, he should resolve: "I shall eat on the following day."

Having slept according to this rule, one who rises in the morning should perform a bath with all medicinal herbs and with water mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Wearing white garlands and garments, he should worship the Lord of Śrī with blue lotuses.

Salutations to Viśokāya for the feet; salutations to Varadāya for the shanks; likewise, salutations to Śrīśāya for the knees and to Jalaśāyine for the thighs. Salutations to Kandarpāya for the private parts; salutations to Mādhavāya for the hips.
"To Dāmodara" [he should offer] to the belly, and "to Vipula" to the sides;
"to Padmanābha" to the navel, and "to Manmatha" to the heart; "to Śrīdhara" to the chest of the Lord, and "salutation to Madhubhid" to the two hands. 28–29.
Salutations to Vaikuṇṭha for the throat; salutations to Padmāmukha for the face; salutations to Aśokanidhi for the nose; and salutations to Vāsudeva for the eyes.
Salutations to Vāmana for the forehead, and again to Hari for the eyebrows.
"Salutation to Alakamādhava, to the one whose crown is the universal form (Viśvarūpin). Salutation to the Soul of All; may this head be yours.
Having thus worshipped Govinda with incense, garlands, and ointments, [he should proceed]. 31-32.
Then, having prepared the mandala, one should fashion a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with clay— quadrangular, one cubit (aratni) in size,
sloping slightly toward the north, smooth, pleasing, and surrounded on all sides by a triple enclosure.
The parapet (vapra) should be three finger-breadths in height, and its width twice that, at two finger-breadths;
above the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), there should be a wall eight finger-breadths high.
One should place an image of Lakṣmī upon the sun [disk] using river sand.
On the sacrificial ground, the wise man should worship Lakṣmī situated in the center of the solar disc, saying:
"Salutation to the Goddess, salutation to Peace, salutation to Lakṣmī, salutation to Śrī;
