salutation to Contentment, salutation to Nourishment, salutation to Creation, salutation again and again to Vision. (36)
"O Viśokā, for the destruction of sorrow and suffering; O Viśokā, you who grant boons! May there be Viśokā for my prosperity, and Viśokā for the attainment of all perfections.
Then, having enveloped the Sun with white garments, one should worship him with fruits. 37–38.
With various kinds of edible foods and a golden lotus, the wise man should place water with *darbha* grass into silver vessels.
Then, he should cause dances and songs to be performed throughout the entire night.
When three watches of the night have passed, the person should rise from there and, having approached the couples of Brahmins,
should worship them according to his ability with garments, garlands, and ointments— either three couples or one.
The places where He reclines are worthy of worship; "Salutations to the One Who Sleeps upon the Waters.
Then, when the night vigil has been performed with song and instrumental music, one should perform the ritual bath at dawn and worship a married couple.
One should feed [the Brahmins] according to one's capacity, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth (43).
Having heard the Purāṇas with devotion, one should spend that day [in this manner]. One should perform everything in this manner month after month (44).
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a cow made of molasses, provided with pillows, a comfortable seat, and beautiful coverlets;
[doing so] so that Lakṣmī may never leave you, O Lord of Men.
Likewise, may there always be for me beautiful form, health, and freedom from sorrow.
(46) Just as misfortune never arises anywhere when one is separated from the Lord, so may there be for me freedom from grief and supreme devotion to Keśava. (47)
With this mantra, one who desires prosperity should offer a bed accompanied by a cow made of jaggery, along with the Sun together with Lakṣmī.
[One should also offer] blue lotuses, karavīra flowers, or unfading saffron.
The *ketaka*, *sindhuvāra*, *mallikā*, *gandhapāṭalā*,
*kadaṃba*, *kubjaka*, and *jātī*— these are always praised.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Lord of Sages, please explain the ritual for the gift of a cow made of molasses (guḍadhenu).
What is its form, and by what mantra should it be given? Let that be told here.
Pulastya said:
I shall now describe the form and the fruit of the rite for the "Jaggery-Cow" (guḍadhenu),
which destroys all sins.
One should place upon the ground a black antelope skin measuring four cubits, with its neck pointing toward the east.
On ground smeared with cow-dung and strewn everywhere with darbha grass, one should likewise prepare a small deer-skin and a calf.
One should fashion the cow, along with her calf, out of clay, facing the east.

The best *guḍadhenu* (sugar-cow) should always consist of four *bhāras*; one should make the calf with one *bhāra*. The middling [cow] is recorded as being made with two *bhāras*, while the calf for that should be half a *bhāra*. The smallest, however, consists of one *bhāra*.
The calf should be one-fourth [the size] of the cow, according to the owner's wealth;
both the cow and the calf should be fashioned and clothed in fine white garments. Their ears should be made of mother-of-pearl, their feet of sugarcane, and their eyes of pure pearls.
They possessed networks of veins like white threads and were covered with white blankets;
their cheeks and backs were copper-colored, and their hair was as white as chowries; they had pairs of eyebrows like coral and were endowed with breasts of fresh butter. 57-58.
Equipped with a pair of golden eyes and pupils of sapphire-blue, having tails of fine linen and bronze milking-vessels, they were bright, exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with golden horns, and possessed hooves richly decorated with silver. 59.
Two caskets for fragrant scents, filled with various fruits, should be prepared;
having arranged them in this manner, one should likewise worship them with incense and lamps.
Whatever Lakṣmī belongs to all beings, and whatever resides among the gods—61.
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin—
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu and Svāhā in the sacrificial fire.
May she who is the power of the Moon, Sun, and Indra, as this boon-granting cow, be mine.
"Since you are the self-nature of the foremost of the ancestors (Svadhātman) and the Svāhā of those who consume the sacrifice,
O cow who removes all sins, therefore grant me prosperity. Having thus addressed that cow, one should present her to a Brāhmaṇa.
This procedure for all cows is recited; however,
O lord of men, I shall describe the nature and the names of those ten cows that are recited as the destroyers of sin.
The first is the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu), and then the second is the ghee-cow (ghṛtadhenu). The third is the sesame-cow (tiladhenu), and the fourth is that named water (jalanāmikā).
The fifth is the milk-cow (kṣīradhenu), and likewise the next is the honey-cow (madhudhenu).
The seventh [cow] is the sugar-cow (śarkarā-dhenu), the eighth is fashioned from curd (dadhi), the ninth is the milk-cow (rasa-dhenu), and the tenth exists according to its own form.
For the milk-cows, there should be jars; for the others, there are heaps of grain.
Some men here also desire a golden cow; other great seers likewise [desire one] with ghee and oils. The procedure for this shall be the same, and those very same accessories are prescribed.

Accompanied by the invocation mantras, they should always be offered on every festival day according to the śrāddha rite; they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. In this context of the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu), all of them have been described by me to you.
Bestowing the fruits of all sacrifices without exception, removing all sins, and auspicious—
since the Viśoka-dvādaśī vow is the most excellent among vows, the guḍadhenu (molasses-cow) is highly praised here as an integral part of it. 72–73.

On the auspicious solstices and equinoxes, as well as during the Vyatīpāta yoga, gifts such as the "jaggery-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others should be given; likewise on lunar nodes (uparāga) and other festival days.
This auspicious Viśoka-dvādaśī is the remover of all sins.
By fasting on this day, a man attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; in this world, he gains good fortune, long life, and health,
and at the time of death, he attains the city of Viṣṇu through the remembrance of Hari.
O King, for nine thousand and eighteen billion eons, one who knows the Dharma shall never experience sorrow, suffering, or misfortune;
and the same applies to any woman who observes this Viśoka-dvādaśī.
She too shall obtain that same fruit as those who are constantly devoted to dance and song.
For he who recites thus, "In this world, the dance, song, and instrumental music of Hari are infinite," and he who hears it correctly here— [shall attain the infinite].
Or, whoever beholds the worship of the enemy of Madhu, Mura, and Naraka,
or even bestows wisdom upon people, dwells in the world of Indra for one kalpa and is honored by the hosts of gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme majesty of giving—
that which is inexhaustible in the other world and honored by the hosts of gods and sages."
Pulastya said: O best of kings, I shall describe the gift of Meru in ten ways (81),
by giving which one attains infinite worlds honored by the gods.

The fruit that one enjoys here by studying the Purāṇas, the Vedas, performing sacrifices, and visiting sacred shrines— that same fruit is not obtained merely by having studied them or performed them. Therefore, I shall describe the gift [of land] according to the sequence of the mountains.

The first is the mountain of grain (dhānya-śaila), the second is the mountain of salt (lavaṇācala), the third is the mountain of molasses (guḍācala), and the fourth is the golden mountain (hemaparvata).
The fifth shall be the mountain of sesame seeds (tila-śaila), and the sixth is the mountain of cotton (kārpāsa-parvata). 84.
The seventh is the mountain of ghee, and the eighth is likewise the mountain of jewels (85).
The ninth is similarly made of silver, and the tenth is the mountain of sugar.
I shall describe the ritual procedure for these in due order and according to the rules (86).
On the solstices, on auspicious days, during Vyatīpāta, at the end of the day (Dinakṣaya), on the third day of the bright fortnight, during an eclipse, at the waning of the moon,
or again on the twelfth day during marriages, festivals, or sacrifices— 87.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under an auspicious constellation according to the prescribed rite (88),
the mountain of grain and other such gifts should be offered on the full moon of Kārttika, at Puṣkara in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
or at sacred fords, temples, cow-pens, or the courtyards of dwellings (89).
One should devoutly construct a pavilion that is square, facing north,
auspiciously sloping toward the northeast, or facing east, according to the prescribed rules;
on the ground smeared with cow dung, one should spread *kuśa* grass.
In the center of that, one should construct a mountain accompanied by supporting peaks (viṣkaṃbha).
Here, a mountain made with a thousand *droṇas* of grain is considered the best;
one with five hundred is middling, and one with three hundred is the lowest. 91–92.
Mount Meru should be made of great rice-grains, with three golden trees joined at its center;
furthermore, O best of the twice-born, its summit should be placed in the sky, and it should be adorned in many ways.
Its four peaks should be of silver, and its hip-regions should also be of silver.
To the east it was joined with pearls and diamonds;
to the south with agate and rubies (padmarāga); to the west with emeralds and sapphires; and to the north with beryl and topaz.
It was surrounded on all sides by pieces of sandalwood and coral, entwined with creepers, and enriched with pavements of pearls. 94–95.

There, Brahmā, Viṣṇu the Blessed One, Purāri (Śiva), and even the Sun-god shall be golden; likewise, the mountain caves shall be covered with sugarcane groves, and there shall be streams of ghee-water in all directions. A row of clouds shall appear like white garments in the east, and yellow ones in the south.

Then, one should place variegated garments to the west and thick red cloths to the north (97). Having established the eight world-protectors, headed by Mahendra, in their proper order starting from silver [images],
there should be various groves on all sides, as well as delightful garlands and ointments (98).

Having thus arranged a white canopy above, adorned with unfading flowers of five colors, one should place the foremost mountain of the immortals and the great supporting mountains of Meru in their respective order;
then, on the four sides, one should establish [the deities] occupying a fourth part [of the space], enriched with flowers and ointments.
To the east, Mount Mandara should be situated, adorned with many fruits and shining with a golden Kāma tree;
to the south, Gandhamādana should be placed, consisting of heaps of wheat and possessing silver, joined with a golden Yajñapati, a Mānasa lake, a Vastra tree, and silver forests. (100–101)
One should cause that [shrine] to be fashioned with flowers so that it has the golden banyan tree as its crest and shines with a golden banner;

likewise, having made it possessed of a radiant canopy of silver and honeyed *bhadrasarasā* wood, then a fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed by four eminent brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and Purāṇas, self-controlled, and of irreproachable conduct and appearance. 103–104.
To the east, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit; it should be offered oblations of sesame, barley, ghee, fuel-sticks, and kuśa grass.
At night, a vigil should be kept with unrestrained songs and music. Now I shall describe the invocation of the mountain deities:
"O you who are the treasury of the abodes of all the hosts of gods, O divine mountain, quickly destroy whatever is adverse within our homes! 105.
Bestow security and grant me unsurpassed peace, for you have been fully worshipped by me with supreme devotion.
You alone are the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
you are the seed consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest. Therefore, protect me, O Eternal One! 106–107.
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors, of the Universal Form,
and of the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, therefore grant me peace.
Since your head is never empty of the immortals and their consorts, [grant me peace].
"Therefore, deliver me from this ocean of suffering and saṃsāra.
(109) Having thus worshipped Meru, one should also honor Mandara, [saying]: "O Mountain, because you possess the Caitraratha grove and the Bhadrāśva forest," (110)
O Gandhamādana, shine brightly upon this Mandara mountain and quickly become a source of joy; since you are the crest-jewel of Jambūdvīpa,
adorned by the hosts of Gandharvas, may my fame therefore be firm.
Since you possess the splendor of Ketumāla, Vaibhrāja,
and Hiraṇmaya, as well as the beauty of the Aśmaka forest, may my prosperity be firm;
and since [you possess the splendor] of Uttarakuru and the Sāvitra forest, [may my prosperity be firm].
"May the glory of King Supārśva protect me eternally from decay. Having thus addressed them all, at the clear dawn,
he should bathe and give the middle of the best of mountains to the preceptor.
O King, one should give the supporting mountains (*viṣkaṃbha-parvata*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in due order.
Twenty-four cows, or twelve, O Ruler, should be given according to one's capacity; or seven or eight, or five, if one is lacking in means. (115–116)
Even a single Kapila cow that yields milk should be given to the Guru;
this same rule is prescribed for all mountains without exception.
Those very same mantras are prescribed for the worship, and those very same ritual implements are prescribed.

The performance of the fire-oblation (homa) for all the planets, the world-protectors, and Brahmā and the others, is prescribed on the mountains using their respective mantras. One should always observe a fast; however, if one is incapable, eating only at night (nakta) is permitted. 119.

O King, listen now in due order to the ritual procedure for all the mountains, as well as the mantras used in their donation according to the specific fruit obtained from each mountain. (120) Since food is declared to be Brahman, and food is proclaimed to be the vital breaths;
From food all beings arise; by food the world grows.
Since food itself is Lakṣmī and food itself is Janārdana, therefore protect us, O best of mountains, in the form of this mountain of grain. 121–122.
Whoever gives a mountain made of grain according to this rite is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred *manvantaras*,
shining resplendent amidst throngs of celestial nymphs and *gandharvas*.
O best of kings, by means of a celestial chariot he goes to the heights of heaven;
when his karma is exhausted, he obtains a kingdom here on earth—of this there is no doubt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of salt.
By the giving of which a man attains a world endowed with auspiciousness, the best salt-mountain (lavaṇācala) should be made with sixteen droṇas;
the middling is with half of that, and the lowest is recorded as being with four [droṇas]. 126.
One who is destitute of wealth should have [the structure] made according to his capacity, extending beyond seven *droṇas*.
He should separately construct the supporting mountains (*viṣkambhaparvata*) with a fourth part [of the size].
He should always perform the ritual procedure for Brahmā and the other deities as previously described.
In the same way, one should construct the abodes of all the world-protectors (lokapālas) made of gold, including lakes, forests, trees, and other such features;
one should also perform a vigil here— now learn the mantras for the gift-offering.
O best of mountains, protect me who am in distress by being of the nature of that salt-flavor which is endowed with the essence of auspiciousness;
for all other flavors are intense only when devoid of salt.
Since you are eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, therefore become a bestower of peace; since you were born from the body of Viṣṇu and are the increaser of health,
therefore, in the form of a mountain, protect us from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Whoever should give a mountain of salt according to this rite shall dwell in the world of Umā for a kalpa, and thereafter attain the supreme goal.
Hereafter, I shall describe the excellent mountain of jaggery.
By the gift of which a man, honored by the gods, attains heaven:
the best [gift] is considered to be ten bhāras, the middling five bhāras,
the lowest three bhāras, and one with limited wealth may give half of that.
In the same manner, one should perform the invocation, worship, golden trees, and the adoration of the gods;
likewise, the supporting mountains, the years, the forest deities, the fire-oblation, the vigil, and the consecration of the world-protectors. 136–137.
One should fashion [the mountain] like a mountain of grain and recite this mantra:
"Just as Janārdana is the foremost among the gods, the soul of all, so is the Sāmaveda among the Vedas and Mahādeva among yogins. (138)

Just as the *praṇava* is among all mantras, and Pārvatī is among women, so too is sugarcane juice always the most excellent among all tastes. Therefore, may this mountain of jaggery grant me supreme prosperity. (139–140)

Since you have been fashioned as a mountain of jaggery by Pārvatī, who bestows good fortune, and since you are her very abode, therefore protect me at all times. (141) He who should give a mountain made of jaggery according to this rite—
Being honored by the Gandharvas, he is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Furthermore, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he becomes the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with long life and health, and unconquered by his enemies.

Now I shall describe the supreme Suvarṇācala, which removes all sins, by the gift of which men go to the abode of Vaiśravaṇa. The best [weight] is one thousand palas, and the middling is five hundred.

Half of that is the minimum; likewise, even a man of small means, free from envy, should give more than one *pala* according to his capacity. O best of kings, he should arrange everything else just as in the case of the mountain of grain. 145–146.
In the same manner, one should present the supporting mountains to the officiating priests [with the mantra]:
"Salutations to you, the seed of all things; salutations indeed to you who contain the Veda within. Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect me, O mountain. (147)
Since you are the offspring of Agni and since you are the son of the Lord of the World, therefore protect us,
O best of mountains, in the form of the Golden Mountain.
Whoever should give a mountain of gold according to this rite— 149.
One goes forever to the supreme world of Brahmā, the source of bliss; there one shall remain for a hundred kalpas, and from there one attains the highest goal. 150.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the ritual procedure for the Tila-śaila (the mountain of sesame seeds) according to the rules.
By the gift of which a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu.

O Indra among kings, a mountain of sesame seeds is declared to be "excellent" when consisting of ten droṇas, "middling" when five are remembered, and "inferior" when three; thus is the mountain of sesame proclaimed. 151–152.
As before, I shall describe all the rest, including the Viṣkambha mountains and so forth; O best of kings, I shall now proclaim the mantra for the gift,
since [these mountains] arose from the sweat of Viṣṇu’s body during the slaying of Madhu.
Sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and mung beans—therefore, be the bestower of peace.
Since sesame seeds alone provide protection during offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya and kavya), O Lord of Mountains, grant us prosperity; salutations to you, the Mountain of Sesame.

Having thus addressed [the recipient], he who should give this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds goes to the realm of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to obtain. Furthermore, a mountain of cotton is considered excellent here when made with twenty bhāras.

The medium [gift] is said to consist of ten [bhāras], and the inferior is considered to be five. A person of modest means should give according to his capacity, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth; O best of kings, everything else should be prepared just as in the case of the mountain of grain.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should give [the gift] and recite this:
"Since you alone are always the protection for the worlds here, O Reed of Cotton (kārpāsādrena), salutations to you; be the destroyer of the multitude of my sins."
He who should give this king of mountains made of cotton in the presence of Śarva shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter he shall become a king here on earth.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of ghee.
Ghee is full of splendor, meritorious, and the destroyer of great sins.
A Ghee-mountain made with twenty jars of ghee is considered the best;
one with ten is declared middling, while one with five is remembered as the lowest.
Even one with little wealth may perform this according to the prescribed method here;
likewise, one should fashion the supporting mountains using a fourth part [of the materials], and place vessels of rice upon the jars. 163–164.

One should have them constructed closely joined and not too high, otherwise it would lack beauty; one should wrap them according to the injunction with white cloths, sugarcane stalks, fruits, and so forth.
All the ritual procedures here are recited just as they are for the Mountain of Grain (*dhānyaparvata*).
Having first performed the acceptance [of the offerings], the worship of the gods with oblations for the welfare and prosperity [of the recipient],

and when the night has turned to dawn, one should, with a tranquil mind, present the supporting mountains (*viṣkaṃbha-parvata*) to the preceptor and likewise to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). 166–167.
Since ghee is produced from a combination [of ingredients] within the essence of nectar,
may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be pleased here by this ghee-flame;
since Brahman, consisting of light, is established in ghee.
Therefore, O Supporter of the Earth, protect us by means of this form of the mountain of ghee.
By this rite, one should offer the unsurpassed mountain of ghee;
even one joined with great sins attains the world of Śambhu. 169–170.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, and surrounded by apsarases, siddhas, and vidyādharas,
he shall wander together with his ancestors until the dissolution of all beings.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Jewel Mountain (Ratnācala).
This mountain is considered unsurpassed when it consists of a thousand pearls;
the medium one has five hundred, and the inferior one is recorded as having three hundred.

The supporting mountains (viṣkaṃbha-parvatas) should be on all sides, each being one-fourth [the size of the central mountain]. To the east, they should be made of diamond and gomedaka; to the south, they should be made of sapphire (indranīla). Gandhamādana should be fashioned by the wise as being endowed with topaz (puṣyarāga).

To the west, one should place a vast mountain mixed with lapis lazuli and coral; to the north, one should likewise arrange [mountains] made of rubies and gold. In all other respects here as well, one should prepare everything according to the procedure for the mountain of grain.

In the same manner, having performed the invocation (āvāhana), one should worship the trees and the golden deities with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings; at the time of radiance, there should be the dismissal (visarjana).
As before, one should recite this mantra to the preceptor and the officiating priests (ṛtvij): [177]
Just as all the hosts of gods abide within all jewels,
you are eternally composed of jewels; therefore, O Great Mountain, protect us, for by the gift of jewels, Janārdana attains satisfaction.

Therefore, O Mountain, protect us through the grace of this worship mantra. He who gives a mountain made of jewels according to this rite goes to the world of Viṣṇu, honored by the Lord of the Immortals.
O lord of men, he shall dwell there for more than a hundred kalpas;
endowed with beauty, health, and virtue, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed by him here or in another world— [it shall be destroyed]. (181-182)
All that [sin] goes to destruction, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed silver mountain (Rūpyācala), by the gift of which, O best of men, a person goes to the world of Soma. 183.
A superior silver mountain is made with ten thousand palas;
the middling is said to be with five thousand, and the inferior is recorded as being with half of that.
One who is unable [to afford more] should always have it made with at least twenty palas, according to their capacity.
In the same manner, one should fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkaṃbha-parvatas) with a fourth part [of the measurement];
as before, one should construct Mandara and the other mountains according to the prescribed rule using silver. Likewise, the wise man should have the world-protectors (lokeśas) made of gold.

The mountain of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Arka (the Sun) should be made of copper; that of Indra should be made of gold. For the others, it should be silver, and for the remaining mountains, it should be gold.
One should perform the remaining rites as before, such as the fire-oblation (homa), the night vigil (jāgaraṇa), and so forth.

In the same manner, at dawn, he should give a mountain of silver to his preceptor, and mountains of the [other] supporting peaks to the officiating priests, having honored them with garments and ornaments.
Reciting this mantra, free from envy and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should make the gift. (189)

"Since silver is beloved by the ancestors, as well as by the Moon and Śaṅkara, may it therefore protect us from the ocean of worldly existence and sorrow. Having thus dedicated [the merit], he who should give an excellent mountain of silver— 191.

That wise man obtains the fruit of ten thousand times ten thousand cows; honored by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases, he shall dwell in the world of Soma until the dissolution of all beings.

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme mountain of sugar (śarkarācala), by the gift of which Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra are always pleased. With eight bhāras of sugar, the great mountain becomes excellent. 193–194.
The middling [type] is said to consist of four [loads], while the inferior is recorded as consisting of two loads.
One who possesses little wealth may construct the Viṣkambha mountains with one load or even half a load; a person should make them using a quarter-measure. 195.
Everything should be well-equipped with golden garments, just like the mountain of grain (dhānyaparvata). On top of Meru, three golden trees should be placed there:
the Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpa tree. 196–197.
One should place these three trees upon the summit of all [mountains]:
the *haricandana* and the *santāna* on the eastern and western sides respectively;
they are to be placed on all mountains, but especially on the mountain of sugar (*śarkarācala*). (198)
On Mount Mandara, the god Kāmadeva shall always face the west;
on the peak of Gandhamādana, Dhanada (Kubera) shall face the north;
and on Mount Vipula, Haṃsa, the embodiment of the Vedas, shall face the east.

On the Supārśva mountain, however, it should be made of gold, facing the south, and with all the rites such as the invocation and the sacrifice performed just like those for the Mountain of Grain (Dhānyaparvata).
Then, one should give the best middle mountain to the preceptor.
To the officiating priests, he should recite these four mantras for each mountain:
"This supreme Mountain of Sugar, which is the essence of the nectar of good fortune, therefore, O Lord of Mountains, may you always be a cause of joy. (202-203)
O Hill of Sugar, protect us—you who arose from those droplets that fell upon the earth while the gods were drinking nectar;
you, moreover, who emerged from the center of the bow of the God of Love. 204.
"May we be saved from this great ocean of saṃsāra by that Great Mountain.
A man who gives a mountain of sugar according to this rite, being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Brahmā. 205–206.
Having ascended a vehicle resembling the moon and sun, he shall rise together with his dependents to the world of Viṣṇuprabha in heaven;
thereafter, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Endowed with long life and good health, for as long as three hundred thousand births,
one should provide food according to one's ability on all mountains without stinginess;
and with their permission, one should personally consume food that is free from pungent salts and salt.
One should cause all the mountain accessories to reach the abode of a Brāhmaṇa. All this unsurpassed gift of a mountain has been narrated to you; O King, ask me whatever else may please you.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, please describe some vow that effects one's crossing over the ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra) and bestows the fruits of heaven and health."
Pulastya said: I shall proclaim the solar dharma known as Kalyāṇa-saptamī,
as well as Viśoka-saptamī and Phala-saptamī.
One should observe Śarkarāsaptamī as well as Kamalasaptamī,
Mandārasaptamī, Ṣaṣṭhīsaptamī, and Śubhasaptamī;
all these are declared to yield meritorious fruits and are honored by both gods and sages.
I shall describe their ritual procedure correctly and in due order:
when the seventh day of the bright fortnight coincides with a Sunday, that day is called Kalyāṇinī and is also designated as Vijayā.
In the morning, one should perform a bath in a river with cow’s milk.
Wearing white garments, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with unbroken grains (akṣata), facing east, with a circular pericarp in the center similar to it. (216–217)

One should install the Lord of Gods on all sides in sequence with flowers, unbroken rice, and water; first with "To Tapanaya" or "To Mārtaṇḍāya," then in the south with "To Divākara," and in the southwest with "To Vidhātre."

In the west, [one should worship] with "Salutation to Varuṇa" and "Salutation to Bhāskara"; in the northwest (Anila), with "Salutation to Vikartana. On the eighth petal, [one should worship] with "Salutation to Deva.
At the beginning, the end, and the middle, let there be salutation to the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Having worshipped with these mantras ending in salutations,
one should worship with devotion upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using white garments, fruits, edibles, incense, garlands, and unguents, as well as jaggery and salt.
Then, having dismissed the eminent brahmins with the *vyāhṛti* mantras,
one should devoutly gratify them according to one's ability with molasses, milk, ghee, and other offerings.
One should present a vessel of sesame seeds and gold to a brahmin.
Having slept according to such a rule, one who rises in the morning,
having performed his ablutions and recitations, should eat ghee and milk-rice together with Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and free from the "cat-vow" (hypocrisy). 224.
One should offer a vessel of ghee, a golden coin, and a water-pot filled with water, saying:
"May the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, the Sun, be pleased here. By this rite, one should perform everything month after month. 225–226.
Then, in the thirteenth month, he should give thirteen cows—
milch cows with golden horns, adorned with garments and ornaments;
even if he is destitute of wealth, he should give at least one, provided he is free from envy.
One should not harbor deceit or guile, for through delusion one falls downward. He who performs the Kalyāṇasaptamī according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
In this world, infinite longevity, health, and sovereignty are born;
this [vow] removes all sins and is worshipped by all the deities. It pacifies all evils and is always the Auspicious Seventh Day (Kalyāṇa-saptamī). 230.
Whoever hears or even recites this auspicious Saptamī, which bestows infinite fruit, shall be liberated from all sins.
O best of kings, I shall likewise describe the Viśoka-saptamī.
By fasting on this day, a man never experiences grief here;
having bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
and having first cleaned his teeth, he should take his meal consisting of *kṛsara*.
Having observed the vow of fasting, he should sleep at night while remaining celibate (234).
Then, having risen at dawn, performed his ablutions and recitations, and become pure,
he should fashion a golden lotus and worship it with the mantra "Arka-āya" (235).
O Āditya, just as the world is always rendered free from sorrow by you alone through the red karavīra flower and a pair of red garments,
so too may there be freedom from sorrow for me, and devotion to you in every birth.

Having thus honored [the deity], one should devoutly worship the twice-born on the sixth day. Having personally consumed cow's urine and arisen, having performed his daily rites, he should diligently honor the Brahmins, providing them with vessels of molasses.
One should offer a pair of fine garments and a lotus to a Brāhmaṇa; having eaten food free from oil and salt on the seventh lunar day while observing silence,
one who desires prosperity should thereafter listen to the Purāṇas.
By this procedure, one should perform everything for both parties until the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus.
One who, free from stinginess regarding wealth, performs the Viśoka-saptamī according to this rite by giving a bed with its furnishings and a milk-yielding tawny cow, attains the supreme goal.
For as long as a hundred times ten million, up to the peak of thousands of births,
he shall remain free from sorrow, exempt from disease and misfortune;
whatever desire he may wish for, that he attains in its full abundance.

He who performs [this rite] without desire attains the Supreme Brahman; and he who recites or even hears this Saptamī known as Viśokā, having reached the world of Indra, shall never again be subject to suffering anywhere.
I shall now proclaim another [vow], named Phala-saptamī.
By fasting on this day, a man becomes liberated from sins and attains heaven.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the fifth lunar day, one should observe the vow with self-restraint.
Having fasted on the sixth lunar day and having had a golden lotus fashioned,
one who knows the Dharma should give it, together with sugar, to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family; and having fashioned a golden image of a single fruit, he should likewise give it.
At the time of the two twilights, one should give [gifts] with the thought, "May the Sun be pleased with me.
Having honored the Brahmins according to one's capacity on the seventh lunar day and having partaken of a meal of milk, one should observe the renunciation of fruits until the Kṛṣṇa-saptamī arrives.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rules and in this very sequence,
one should likewise give a golden fruit accompanied by a golden lotus, joined with a vessel of sugar and provided with a garment and a garland. 251.
Having fasted on both seventh lunar days (ubhayasaptamī) for a year according to this very procedure, one should recite the Sūrya-mantra in sequence:
Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śukra, Hari, and Śiva. (252–253)
"May the glorious Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Varuṇa be pleased"—
reciting one name each month on the seventh lunar day, he should perform this while practicing the renunciation of fruits every fortnight.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments.
One should give a jar of sugar accompanied by a golden lotus and fruit, [with the prayer]:
"May the desire of your devotees never be fruitless. 255-256.
Likewise, may there be the attainment of infinite fruit for me in birth after birth;
whoever performs this Phala-saptamī, which bestows infinite fruit, shall deliver twenty-one generations of men, both past and future. (257)

Whoever hears or even reads this shall become a partaker of auspiciousness; with a soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun. Whatever [sin] such as the drinking of liquor has been committed here or in the hereafter— 258–259.
All that perishes for one who performs the Phala-saptamī;
likewise, I shall describe the Kalmaṣa-nāśinī Śarkarā-saptamī, by which infinite longevity, health, and sovereignty are produced. (260)
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mādhava, one who is firm in his vows, having bathed in the morning with white sesame seeds and being adorned with pure garlands and unguents,
should draw a lotus with a pericarp using saffron upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
In that [image], one should offer perfumes and flowers with the mantra "namo bhagavate sūryāya" (or "namo 'stu savitre"),
and place a water-pot together with a vessel of sugar,
having adorned it with white garments, white garlands, and white unguents.
One should worship [the deity] with golden flowers while reciting this mantra:
"Since you consist of the universal Veda and are recited within the Vedas, and since you alone are the very essence of immortality, therefore grant me peace. (264-265)

Then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should sleep on the ground at its side; he should remain there reciting the Saura-sūkta and listening to the Purāṇas. When a day and night have passed, he should then perform his daily obligatory rites on the eighth lunar day.
One should offer all of that to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas (267).
One should feed as many Brāhmaṇas as one is able with sugar, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa);
or else, remaining silent, one should eat oneself without oil or salt (268).
By this rite, one should perform everything month after month;
at the end of the year, [one should provide] a bed accompanied by a jar of sugar,
along with all household utensils and likewise a milch cow.
One who possesses the means should give a house equipped with all household utensils;
having prepared it, one may give it for a thousand niṣkas, or for a hundred, or for ten, or for three, or even for a single niṣka. 270–271.
One should offer a lotus according to one’s own capacity, reciting the mantra as before; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for by doing so, one incurs faults.
From the mouth of the Sun-god as he drinks the nectar, drops of ambrosia fall.
From that [earth], rice, mung beans, and sugarcane sprouted upon the ground; from that [sugarcane] came the juice of sugar-candy, which was the essence of nectar.
Because it was desired by the Sun, it became the sacred substance for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
This Śarkarāsaptamī bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha),
pacifies all evils, and increases one's sons and grandsons;
he who performs it with supreme devotion goes to the Supreme Brahman.
He shall dwell in heaven for one kalpa and thereafter attain the supreme state. O sinless one, whoever hears this, remembers it, recites it here,
or even bestows their attention upon it, shall be honored by the gods and the lords of sages in the city of the immortals.
Hereafter, I shall describe the Kamala-saptamī,
by the mere recitation of which the Sun-god is pleased in this world.
On the Amala-saptamī of the spring season, one who has bathed well with white mustard seeds [should proceed].
Having placed a beautiful golden lotus within a sesame-seed vessel and having covered it with a pair of garments, one should then worship it with perfumes and flowers, saying:
"Salutations to you who hold a lotus in your hand; salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe. (279-280)
"Obeisance to you, O Divākara; obeisance to you, O Prabhākara.
Then, at the time of the two watches [of the day], having honored a Brahmin with garments, garlands, and ornaments, one should give him a water-pot.
According to one's capacity, one should give away a tawny cow (kapilā) after adorning it according to the prescribed rite.
Then, when a day and night have passed, on the eighth lunar day, one should feed the twice-born according to one's means; thereafter, one should eat meatless food, avoiding oil.
By this procedure, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight month after month,
one should perform everything with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth. At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should give cows that yield milk along with gold according to one's ability, as well as vessels,
seats, lamps, and other desired household articles.
Whoever performs the Kamala-saptamī rite according to this procedure [attains the supreme goal].
He attains infinite prosperity and rejoices in the world of the Sun (Sūryaloka). Having gone separately to each of the seven worlds in every kalpa,
surrounded by celestial nymphs (apsaras), he thereafter attains the supreme goal.
Whoever should behold this, hear it for a moment, recite it with devotion, or bestow their attention upon it,
shall attain stainless prosperity here and go to the world of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which destroys all sins.

One should observe the meritorious Mandāra-saptamī, which grants all desires. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, a wise man should eat light food; then, having used a tooth-stick, he should fast on the sixth day.
Having fully honored the Brahmins, one should pray to Mandāra at night;
then, having risen at dawn and performed his bath, he should feed the twice-born according to his ability and offer eight mandāra flowers.
Likewise, one should fashion a very beautiful golden image of a man holding a lotus in his hand (293).
Having fashioned a lotus with black sesame seeds in a copper vessel with eight petals,
one should worship it with golden mandāra flowers, saying "To Bhāskara," in the east (294).
Likewise, with the word "namaskāra," one should offer [oblations] to Sūrya on the western petal; similarly to Arka in the south, and to Aryaman in the southwest (nairṛta);
to Vedadhāman in the west, and to Caṇḍabhānu in the northwest (vāyavya).
Having worshipped Pūṣan to the north, one should worship the next with "To Ānanda" (296).
Then, having placed the Puruṣa in the pericarp and also in the Sarvātman,
one should surround him with white garments, edibles, garlands, fruits, and so forth (297).
Having thus worshipped, he should again give all of that to one learned in the Vedas;
then, remaining silent and facing the east, the householder should eat food without oil or salt.
By this procedure, he should perform everything every month on the seventh lunar day.
One should perform this for as long as a year, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
At the conclusion of this very vow, one who desires prosperity should place [the image] upon a water-pot and give it away along with cows, according to one's means.
Homage to Mandāranātha and to the abode of Mandāra!
O Lord, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra. Whoever performs the Mandāra-saptamī according to this rite, [attains the supreme goal]. 301.
Free from sin and full of happiness, that mortal rejoices in heaven for a kalpa. 302.
Carrying this lamp that dispels the terrifying darkness of the mass of clouds of sins, a man shall not stumble while traversing the night of saṃsāra. 303.
Whoever reads or even hears this Mandāra-saptamī, which bestows the fruits of one's desired objects, shall also be liberated from sins. Now, I shall describe another auspicious Śubha-saptamī.

By fasting on this day, a person is liberated from the flood of disease and grief. Having performed the ritual bath and recitation in the month of Āśvayuja, being pure and having caused the Brahmins to recite [the scriptures], one should then commence the auspicious Saptamī vow. (305–306)
One should worship Kapilā with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
I bow to her who is born from the Sun and is the abode of the entire world—O auspicious and blessed one, I [worship] you for the purification of my own body. 307.
Then, having prepared a prastha of sesame seeds together with a copper vessel,
as well as a golden bull likewise provided with cloth, garlands, and molasses, along with a pillow, a resting place, and a seat; 308–309.
At both times of day, one should offer various kinds of fruits and foods combined with ghee and milk-rice, saying, "May Aryaman be pleased.
Having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should sleep on the bare ground upon a layer of grass.
Then, when morning has dawned, one should satisfy the twice-born with devotion.
According to this rite, a man should always, month after month,
give a bull made of gold along with two garments, and likewise a cow produced from gold.

At the end of the year, one should give a bed provided with sugarcane stalks and molasses, along with a prastha of sesame seeds in a copper vessel and a golden bull, to a knower of the Vedas, saying: "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased."
The wise person who performs the Śubhasaptamī according to this rite shall possess pure fortune and stainless fame in birth after birth,
being honored by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas in the abode of the gods.
Having become the Lord of the Gaṇas, he shall dwell until the dissolution of all beings;
and having descended at the beginning of the Kalpa, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents,
[freeing himself] from a thousand murders of embryos and a hundred murders of Brahmins.
This auspicious Saptamī, when recited, is capable of destroying [all sins].
(317) Whoever reads this, hears it for even a moment, or even sees it being given away incidentally—his body liberated from all evil—he attains the status of a leader among the Vidyādharas. (318)
"Whatever man performs this Saptamī vow for seven years, joined with its sevenfold ritual, he shall successively become the sovereign of the seven worlds and attain the supreme abode of Murāri.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puṣkara," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 319. Chapter 21.
The twenty-second chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
"The world of the earth (Bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (Bhuvarloka), the world of heaven (Svarloka), as well as Maharloka and Janaloka."
Austerity and truth— these seven are proclaimed as the worlds of the gods.
How, however, may there be sovereignty over all of them in turn,
as well as auspicious form, long life, and health in this world?
"O Brahmin, honored by the gods, how may vast prosperity be attained?
Pulastya said: "In ancient times, on the surface of the earth, the Fire-god was together with the Wind."
Commanded by Indra for the destruction of the enemies of the gods,
he then burnt thousands of Dānavas;
among them were Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, and Parāvasu.
But Virocana and Saṃhrāda departed;
they entered the interior of the ocean and established their residence there. Being powerless, they too were disregarded by Agni and Māruta.
From that time forward, O gods, having oppressed all the sages along with humans and serpents, they would enter the waters again.
Thus, O heroes, five and seven thousand yugas passed.
"O King, by the strength of their water-fortress, they oppress the three worlds.
Therefore, O Lord of the Immortals, command Agni and Vāyu once again so that this ocean may be dried up without delay. 8-9.
"Since this ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, is the refuge of our enemies,
therefore let it be brought to dryness by you two this very day.
Then those two spoke to Śakra, the slayer of Maya and Śambara.
O Indra, this destruction of the ocean is unrighteous;
since it would result in the total annihilation of the great multitude of living beings, therefore, O Purandara, resort to another means.
"O most excellent one, how can he deserve destruction, when even within a single *yojana* there dwell hundreds of millions of living beings?
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods (Indra), his eyes bloodshot with anger, [spoke].
Out of anger, the thief of speech spoke these words to the two immortals, Agni and Māruta:
"Immortals never incur a connection with merit or demerit;
yet you two, being especially high-souled, stand [in such a position]."

O Vibhāvasu, because of my ignorance, you have been treated by me as an equal to the wind; therefore, becoming intent on the vows of a sage and having taken up this body, enter a womb devoid of the knowledge of the scriptures on Dharma and Artha.
Therefore, you shall take birth in the world in human form with a single body, equal to Māruta;
for even while in human state, you dried up [the ocean] with a mere mouthful.
"O Vahni, you shall become the ocean; then you will attain divinity.
Due to this curse from Indra, the two of them fell instantly to the surface of the earth. Thereafter, they obtained birth from a water-jar (kumbha) within their bodies.
From the power of Mitra and Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha was born as their son.
Then Agastya, the best of sages, became possessed of fierce asceticism;
he was the brother of this [Vasiṣṭha], and that sage was the younger brother of Vasiṣṭha.
Bhīṣma said: How were Mitra and Varuṇa remembered as his parents? Tell me now how Agastya’s birth from the jar occurred. 22
Pulastya said: In ancient times, the Purāṇa-Puruṣa Viṣṇu, having become the son of Dharma on Mount Gandhamādana, performed extensive penance. 23.

Fearing his ascetic power, Śakra dispatched both Mādhava and Aṅga, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, for the purpose of creating obstacles; yet when Hari [was not moved] by their singing, instrumental music, and amorous gestures and coquettish charms, 24.
It was impossible for Kāma and Madhu to lead him into delusion.
Then the host of Kāma, Madhu, and the women fell into despondency;
the best of men exerted himself to agitate their thighs.
He brought forth a woman who could enchant even the three worlds;
both the gods and the asuras were utterly infatuated by her.
Then, in the presence of the apsaras and the gods, Hari spoke.
She shall become famous in the world by the name Urvaśī.
Then, having been summoned by Mitra who was desiring her, Urvaśī was told, "Delight me," and she replied, "So be it."
Then, as the lotus-eyed woman was departing for the world of the Sun, she was intercepted by Varuṇa from behind, who addressed her with these words:
"O Lord, I was chosen first by Mitra; the Sun is my husband."
Varuṇa said, "Entrusting your heart to me, you may go.
When she had departed, Mitra replied, "So be it," and then pronounced a curse:
"Go this very day to the world of mortals, to the son of the daughter of Soma."
"Since you have committed this false act by saying 'serve me,' therefore,
O best of sages, semen has been cast into the water-jar by Varuṇa and Mitra;
from that, two such excellent sages were born."
In ancient times, a king named Nimi was playing at dice with women.
In the meantime, Vasiṣṭha, born of Brahmā, arrived;
the sage cursed the king because he failed to offer him worship.
"Be bodiless," thus was the sage cursed by him as well;
and due to their mutual curses, the two splendors became bodiless and went to Brahmā, the Lord of the World, in order to have their curses removed.
Then, O King, by the command of Brahmā, the blinking of the eyes of all living beings ceased for the sake of his rest;
and Vasiṣṭha likewise remained within that water-pot as before.
Born from that [fire], he became the most excellent of sages, the tranquil-souled Agastya, possessing four arms and holding a rosary and a water-pot;
he dwelt in a certain region of the Malaya mountain according to the Vaikhānasa ordinances.
Accompanied by his wife and surrounded by sages, he performed most difficult austerities.
Then, after a long time, seeing the world oppressed by Tāraka and the other demons, he drank up the ocean with great wrath.
Then Śaṅkara and all the others became granters of boons to him;
both Brahmā and the Lord Viṣṇu approached to bestow boons. "Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever is desired by you, O sage," they said.
Agastya said:
"For twenty-five thousand crores of Brahmās,
I shall become a traveler in celestial chariots upon the path of the southern sky."
Whoever performs my worship upon the rising of my celestial chariot shall, in due course,
become the sovereign of the seven worlds. Furthermore,
whoever proclaims this hermitage at Puṣkara by my name shall likewise attain that status.
"Let this very place attain merit; this boon has been chosen by me:

those who shall perform the *śrāddha* ceremony here with devotion, preceded by the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), for them all the hosts of ancestors dwelling in heaven shall remain together with me. (46)
"Let them remain for this period of time; this indeed is my boon.
Having said, "So be it," those gods departed as they had come.
Therefore, the wise should always offer the respectful *arghya* water to Agastya. 47–48.
Bhīṣma said:
O Muni, tell me how the offering of arghya should be made to that Agastya, and what the procedure for his worship is. 49
Pulastya said: At the time of dawn, during its rising at night, the wise man should perform a bath with white sesame seeds; likewise, he should wear white garlands and garments.
One should place an unblemished water-pot adorned with garlands and cloth,
joined with the five precious gems and accompanied by a vessel of ghee;
[and likewise] a golden figure of a man, the size of a thumb, with long, staff-like arms.
Having placed four-armed [images] with their faces toward the pitcher, together with the seven grains and the seven mountains,

one should offer them to an eminent Brahmin along with a bronze vessel, unbroken rice, and white [sandalwood paste], while raising the long-armed [image] over the pitcher, with undistracted mind and facing the east. 52–53.

If one has the means, a man should bow down and give to a brahmin a white cow with silver hooves, a golden face, accompanied by her calf, yielding milk, and adorned with garlands, garments, and bells. O King, all of this must be given by the man at sunrise for seven nights.
Some say that it may last for as long as seventeen years, or even longer than that.
O you who resemble the kāśa flower, born from fire and wind, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from a jar—salutations to you! 55-56.
By performing the abandonment of fruits in this manner every year, a person does not come to grief;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa), he should thereafter offer the fruit. The man who offers the respectful oblation (argha) according to this rite [attains success].
One obtains this world, which bestows the fruits of beauty and health;
by the second [offering], one attains Bhuvarloka, and after that, Svarloka. He who offers seven arghyas attains all seven worlds.
"Thus, whoever recites this, hears it, correctly observes the conduct [prescribed], beholds the worship of Agastya,
or even bestows their thought [upon it], shall, upon reaching the abode of Viṣṇu, be honored by the hosts of gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Great-minded One, tell me that which bestows the fruits of good fortune and health, causes the destruction of enemies, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Pulastya said:
That which the slayer of Andhaka spoke to Umā in the city of Purā, while the righteous and most charming stories were being narrated—
that I shall now proclaim, for it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Gaurī said:
"O Lord of the Gods, a curse has indeed been given to me by Sāvitrī for the sake of Lakṣmī. Tell me how I may attain preeminence over Lakṣmī."
Śaṅkara said:
Listen attentively, O Goddess, to another matter likewise performed by myself—the unsurpassed means of propitiating both men and women. (64)
Either in the month of Nabhasya, or Vaiśākha, or the auspicious Mārgaśīrṣa,
on the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed with white mustard seeds,
[one should apply] yellow pigment (gorocana) along with cow’s urine, cow’s milk, and likewise ghee.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead mixed with *dadhīca* and sandalwood,
for it bestows good fortune and health and is always dear to Lalitā. On the third lunar day of every fortnight, whether a man or a married woman [should do so].
She should wear red garments and white flowers;
a widow, however, should wear only a single white garment,
while a maiden should put on two fine white garments.
Then one should bathe the Goddess with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with pure milk, likewise with honey, and with water scented with flowers.
One should worship her with white flowers and also with various kinds of fruits.
O Goddess, you should always perform worship with parched grain, fried rice, salt, molasses, milk, ghee, white flowers, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds;
O fair-faced one, one should perform the worship of the feet every fortnight. 71–72.
Salutation to Varadā for the feet; likewise, salutation to Śrī for the ankles; salutation to Aśokā for the shanks; and likewise, salutation to Pārvatī for the knees.
Salutation to Māṅgalyakāriṇī for the thighs; and likewise, salutation to Vāmadevī for the hips. (73)
Salutations to Padmodarā for the belly; salutations to Śrī at the throat (74). Salutations to Saubhāgyadāyinī for the hands, and to Sumukhaśrī for the arms;
salutations to Darpavināśinī for the face, and again to Smaradā for the smile (75).
Salutation to Gaurī for this [face], and likewise to Utpalā for the nose; salutation to Tuṣṭi for the forehead and hair, and salutation to Kātyāyanī for the head.
Salutation to Gaurī, salutation to Puṣṭi, salutation to Kānti, and salutation to Śrī.
"Salutations again and again to Raṃbhāyai, Lalitāyai, and Vāmadevyai.
(77) Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should draw a lotus in front, provided with sixteen petals and a pericarp in the proper sequence. (78)
One should place Gaurī in the east, and after that Aparṇā;
likewise, one should place Bhavānī in the south, and after that Rudrāṇī.
One should place Saumyā, the dweller of Madana, in the western part.
Having installed the fierce Pāṭalā in the northwest, likewise Umā in the north (80),
Sādhyā, Pathyā, Saumyā, Maṅgalā, Kumudā, Satī,
Bhadrā, and Lalitā upon the pericarp in the center (81).
One should place [the image] with flowers, unbroken grains, or water, accompanied by a salutation;
and having caused the auspicious sound of songs to be made,
one should worship a married woman (suvāsinī) with red garments, red garlands, and ointments.
One should apply vermilion and bathing powder to their heads;
since vermilion, saffron, and bathing are exceedingly desirable, one should therefore also diligently worship the preceptor who provides the instruction. 83–84.
Where the Guru is not worshipped, all ritual actions there are fruitless.
One should always worship Gaurī with blue lotuses through recitations;
O beloved, she should be worshipped with bandhujīva flowers with great effort during the month of Kārtika.

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Goddess with jasmine flowers; in Pauṣa, with yellow kuraṇṭaka flowers; and in Māgha, one should also worship Her with kunda and water-lily (kumuda) flowers.
In Phālguna as well, a person should honor Her with sinduvāra or jasmine.

One should always worship with *caitra*, *tumullikā*, and *aśoka* flowers in Caitra; with *gandhapāṭala* in Vaiśākha; with *kamala* and *mandāra* in Jyeṣṭha; with water-lilies (*jalāmbuja*) in Āṣāḍha; and with *mandāra* and *mālatī* in Śrāvaṇa.

One should always consume, in due order, cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass (89); as well as water from *bilva* leaves, arka flowers, lotuses, and cow horns, along with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and *bilva* fruit (90).
This consumption [of the offering] is prescribed at the beginning of the month of Bhādrapada; O fair-faced one,
a pair [of man and woman] should be fed on the third lunar day of every fortnight and worshipped with devotion using garments, garlands, and ointments.
One should give yellow garments to the man and silk garments to the woman.
To the woman one should give rice-free of *niṣpāva* beans, cumin, salt, sugarcane, and molasses; to the man, one should give fruit together with a golden lotus.
Just as Lord Anādideva departs after completely abandoning you, so too deliver me from the ocean of saṃsāra with its endless sufferings. 94.
O Kumudā, Vimalā, Ānandā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā, and Śivā!
"Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā, and Pārvatī—
may they be pleased during the months beginning with Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa) for five months"— thus one should utter.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should worship twenty-four couples, or twelve, or eight, or eight again; or alternatively, one should worship them during the four-month period.
Having first given [the offerings] to the Guru, one should afterwards worship the others.
This third [chapter] on infinity has been declared, which always bestows infinite fruit (98).
It is the Goddess who removes all sins and increases good fortune and health; one should never transgress this [instruction], even through stinginess regarding wealth (99).
A man, a woman, or a girl should observe the vow of fasting; however, a pregnant woman, one who has recently given birth, a maiden, or a sick person should do so at night.
When they are impure, they should have it performed by another while remaining themselves pure.
Whoever observes this third [day], which bestows infinite fruit,
shall be honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Even one devoid of wealth should perform the fast for as long as a year.
Even she who performs this rite according to the ritual of the Flower-Mantra shall obtain that same fruit;
or a woman who desires her own welfare may perform it as well. By Gaurī’s grace, she attains the spiritual merit of a birth as a man. 103.

Thus, whether one recites or hears this vow of the Daughter of the Mountain while residing in the world of Indra, he shall attain his desire; and even he who merely possesses faith in it is honored by the gods, the celestial nymphs, and the kinnaras. I shall now describe another third [vow], which destroys all sins.
The wise know this *Rasakalyāṇinī* to have originated in a former kalpa;
having reached the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath in the morning with fragrant water, milk, and sesame seeds. (106)
One should bathe the Goddess with honey and likewise with sugarcane juice (107). Then, with scented water and saffron, one should perform worship;
having worshipped the right limbs, one should thereafter worship the left limbs (108).
One should then worship the two ankles with "Salutation to the Goddess Lalitā," the two shanks with "to Śānti," and likewise the two knees with "to Śrī.
[109] One should worship the waist with "to Madālasā" and the belly with "to Amalā."
I bow to the breasts of Madanavāsinī, to the neck of Eka-mudā, to the tips of the arms of Mādhavī, to the face of Kamalā with her pleasant smile,
to the forehead-brow of Rudrāṇī, and likewise to the locks of hair of Śaṅkarā.
Salutation to Madanāya for the forehead; salutation again to Mūrchhanāya for the eyebrows;
salutation to the bearer of the half-moon for the eyes; and salutation to Tuṣṭi for the face. Salutation to Utkaṇṭhinī for the neck; salutation to Amṛtā for the body.
Salutations to Raṃbhā for the two mighty arms; salutations to Viśokā for the two hands. Salutations to Manmathā for the heart; likewise, to Pāṭalā for the belly.
Salutations to Surativāsinī for the hips; and to Kajaśrī for the thighs. 113–114.
One should worship the knees and shanks with "Oṃ Gaurī," and the ankles with "Oṃ Śānti.
One should worship the feet with "Oṃ Dharādhara" and the head with "Oṃ Viśvakāya, Namaḥ.
[One should worship] with "Oṃ Bhavānī," "Oṃ Kāminī," "Oṃ Vāsudevī," and "Oṃ Jagacchrī. (115)
"Salutations again and again to Ānandā, Nandā, and Subhadrā.
(116) Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites, one who is free from envy should honor a Brahmin couple and feed them with sweet food. (117)

Having given a water-pot filled with water along with a pair of white garments and a golden lotus, one should then worship it with perfumes and garlands, saying: "May Kumuda be pleased here. Then one should undertake the salt-vow (lavaṇavrata).
By this rite, one should always worship the Goddess month after month.
In the month of Māgha, one should avoid salt; in Phālguna, molasses; likewise, fresh butter in Caitra, and honey in Mādava (Vaiśākha). 119–120.

In the month of Jyeṣṭha one should avoid water, and likewise cumin in Āṣāḍha; one should avoid milk in Śrāvaṇa, and similarly curd in Bhādrapada. Likewise, ghee should be avoided in Āśvayuja, and honey in Kārttika.

In Mārgaśīrṣa, coriander (dhānyāka) [should be offered], and in Pauṣa, sugar (śarkarā) is to be avoided. At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot filled with these items month by month at the time of twilight, accompanied by a vessel of food.
Sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas), cakes (sevakas), saṃyāva, pūrikās, nārikās filled with ghee, piṣṭapūrṇas, and naṃdikīs;
as well as milk-vegetables, curd-rice, and piṇḍa-vegetables. 124.
Beginning with the month of Māgha, one should offer these [flowers] in sequence upon the hands:
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Raṃbhā, Subhadrā, Śivā, Jayā, Lalitā, Kamalā, Anaṅgā, Maṅgalā, and Ratilālasā. (125–126)

In the months beginning with Māgha, one should recite "May [the deity] be pleased"; in all cases, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed. One should always observe a fast; however, for those who are unable, eating only at night (nakta) is permitted.

30. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rohiṇī-Candra-Śayana Vrata," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Bhīṣma said: "O Brahmin, tell me the ritual for tanks, groves, wells, ponds, lotus-pools, and likewise for temples."

Who are the officiating priests (ṛtvij) there, O Brahmin? What should the sacrificial invocation (vedī-vāk) be like? What are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), the offerings (bali), the time, the place, and the preceptor (ācārya)? What materials are recommended?
Tell me all this, O observer of noble vows.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the procedure regarding tanks and other such works;
this history is recited in the Purāṇas, O best of kings.
When an auspicious and bright lunar day has arrived during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa),
on a holy day declared by the Brahmins, having performed the *brāhmaṇavācana* rite in a place free from inauspicious things near the lake; 4–5.
The altar (vedi) should be four cubits on each side, square, and have four faces;
likewise, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be sixteen cubits in size and have four faces. Around the altar, there should be pits (garta) one ratni in depth, each having three tiers (mekhalā).
O Prince, there should be nine, seven, or five straight-faced [channels];
the yoni should be one *vitasti* in length and six or seven *aṅgulas* in width;
and the pits (*gartā*) should be one cubit (*hasta*) in measure, with a triple-ringed girdle (*mekhalā*) rising three finger-breadths high.
On all sides, they should be of uniform color and provided with flags and banners;
one should cause these doors to be made for each direction of the pavilion using branches of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
There, eight auspicious *hotṛ* priests and likewise eight gatekeepers should be appointed;
furthermore, eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
who are complete in all auspicious marks, conversant with the mantras, and whose senses are subdued, should be made reciters (*jāpaka*).

One should station the best of the twice-born, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, at each pit; as well as water-pots, sacrificial implements, fans, a bright seat, and a very large copper vessel.
Then, the wise preceptor, having consecrated them with mantras, should scatter oblations of many colors upon the ground for each respective deity.
The sacrificial post (yūpa) should be one cubit (aratni) in length and made from a tree that yields milky sap.

Or, by one desiring prosperity, twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be appointed, equal in stature to the sacrificer; they should be adorned with golden ornaments, including earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
15. And [they should wear] golden earrings, as well as armlets and bracelets.
Likewise, one should give finger-rings, sacred threads, and various garments;
these should be given equally to all, but it is traditionally taught that twice as much should be given to the preceptor (ācārya).
One should also give what is pleasing to oneself, accompanied by a formal declaration (śapatha).

O lord of the people, having first obtained all of this, there was a golden tortoise and crocodile, silver fish and *duṇḍubha* crocodiles, copper jars, frogs, a crow, and a *śiṃśumāra*. 18. Thus, O ruler of the subjects, he secured all of that at the very outset.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
the patron of the sacrifice, together with his wife, sons, and grandsons, was bathed with all medicinal herbs and waters by those who had mastered the Vedas. 19–20.
Having reached the western door, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion; then,
with auspicious sounds and the resonance of kettledrums,
the knower of reality should construct the mandala with five-colored powders.
Then, one should fashion a sixteen-spoked wheel with a lotus at its center and four faces;
it should be square on the outside, circular in the middle, and very beautiful.
Having placed it upon the altar, one should then install the planets and the lords of the worlds.
The wise practitioner, observing all directions, should ritually deposit [the offerings] according to the mantras;
he should place a water-pot (kalaśa) in the center, relying upon the Varuṇa mantra.
Furthermore, the learned one should install Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu in that very same place.
Having installed Vināyaka, as well as Kamalā and Ambikā,
he should then install the host of elemental beings (bhūtagrāma) for the sake of the peace of all worlds.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), it should be provided with flowers, edible offerings, and fruits.
One should wrap those jars containing jewels with cloths,
and having adorned the door-keepers on all sides with flowers and perfumes,
one should say to them, "Perform the sacrifice," and honor the preceptor.

The masters of the Ṛgveda should be stationed to the east; the knowers of the Yajurveda to the south (28); the chanters of the Sāmaveda should be stationed to the west; and the masters of the Atharvaveda to the north.
The sacrificer should sit to the south, facing north (29).

He should say "Sacrifice! to those priests; and to those chanters, he should say, "Remain engaged in the recitation of the most excellent mantras. Having thus instructed them all and kindled the fire, the knower of mantras—
One should offer oblations with mantras, as well as clarified butter and sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh).
The officiating priests (ṛtvij) should likewise offer everywhere with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
having offered according to the rules to the planets, and similarly to Indra and Īśvara.
To the Maruts, the guardians of the world, and to Viśvakarman, he should offer oblations according to the rules;
and he should recite the Śānti-sūkta, the Raudra, the Pāvamāna, and the auspicious hymns.
Furthermore, the Bahvṛca priest should separately recite the Puruṣasūkta in the eastern direction.
Those who know the Yajurveda should recite on the south side the Śākara, Raudra, Saumya, Kauśmāṇḍa, and Jātavedasa hymns, as well as the Saura Sūkta;
and the Vairāja, Pauruṣa, Sauparṇa, and Rudra-saṃhita hymns.
The Śaiśava, the Pañcanidhana, the Gāyatra, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Vāmadevya, the Bṛhatsāman, the Raurava, and the Rathantara;
the Gavāṃvrata, the Vikīrṇa, the Rakṣoghna, and likewise the Yama. 36.
O King, let the Sāmavedins, stationed at the western gate, sing the Sāmans;
and let the Atharvavedins, stationed in the north, mentally recite prayers for peace and prosperity, taking refuge in the Lord Varuṇa. 37–38.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on both nights of the preceding day,
one should take earth from a mountain, a riverbank, a confluence, an anthill, a cow-pen, and a herd of cows, and place it along with medicinal herbs into the water-jars.

One should perform its consecration bath with yellow pigment (rocanā), white mustard seeds (siddhārtha), fragrant substances, and guggulu resin; having first performed this according to the rules with the great mantras, one should provide it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 40–41.
Having thus passed the night with rites performed according to this procedure,
then, when the clear dawn has arisen, one hundred cows—
or alternatively, sixty-eight— should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, either fifty, thirty-six, or again twenty-five [verses were recited].
Thereafter, when the auspicious and pure lagna had arrived,
[the ceremony was performed] with Vedic chants, along with gandharvas and various musical instruments.
Having adorned her with golden ornaments, O lord of the people, one should cause her to descend into the water; while the Sāman hymns are being sung, she should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Taking a golden vessel provided with five gems, [one should perform the rite].

Then, having cast in all manner of sea-monsters, fish, and the like, [the image] was held by four Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; it was filled with the water of a great river and adorned with curd and consecrated rice-grains. 46–47.
One should cause her to place them face down with their openings turned northward in the middle of the water;
then, having bathed well, one should likewise recite the *Punarmā* hymn from the Atharvaveda and, with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," cast [the flowers] and return to the pavilion. 48.
Having honored the members of the assembly, one should offer bali oblations on all sides.

(49) Furthermore, O best of kings, the fire-sacrifice should be performed for four more days; the rite of the fourth day must be performed, and there too, gifts should be given according to one's capacity. (50)

Having prepared the sacrificial vessels and the implements for the sacrifice, he should give them equally to the officiating priests and then distribute the pavilion again. He should also present a golden vessel and a bed to a Brahmin.
Then, one thousand Brahmins, or likewise eight hundred,
or fifty, or twenty, should be fed according to one's capacity;
thus is the rite for a pond described in the Purāṇas.
This same procedure is prescribed for all wells, tanks, and lotus-pools, as well as for their consecrations;
however, there may be a distinction regarding the mantras used for temples, gardens, and grounds.
However, for one who is incapable, the Self-born One has prescribed this rule as being performed with half [the usual materials]:
"In small matters, it should be performed like the *ekāgni* rite by those free from stinginess regarding their wealth;
water remaining during the rainy season is remembered as equal to the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice. (55–56)
That which remains during the autumn season bestows the fruits described;
that which remains in the early winter and late winter is equal to the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices; and they say that which remains during the spring season is equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Even the water that remains during the summer is superior to the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O Great King, he whose intellect is exceedingly pure performs these specific duties on this earth;
being purified, he goes to the abode of Brahmā and rejoices in heaven for many kalpas.
Wandering through many worlds and having enjoyed the pleasures of sound and other senses with celestial nymphs for two *aparārddhas*,
he attains once again that supreme abode of Viṣṇu by the power of yoga.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of a Tank," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahman, describe in detail and according to the rules the ritual for trees.
By what rite should the planting of trees be performed by the wise? And tell me now of those worlds which are said to belong to them.
Pulastya said:
O Lord of the World, having completed everything according to the rules for tanks, I shall now describe the procedure for trees in garden grounds; likewise,
[one should provide] the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the necessary materials, and a preceptor of the same kind.
Likewise, one should honor the Brahmins with gold, garments, and ointments,
having sprinkled them with water containing all medicinal herbs and adorned them with curd and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having decorated the trees with garlands, one should envelop them with cloths.

The piercing of the ears of all [the children] should be performed with a golden needle; likewise, collyrium should be applied with a golden probe. One should cause seven or eight fruits of kāladhauta gold to be fashioned.
One should consecrate each of all those trees upon the altar;
guggulu incense is best here, and they should be placed in copper vessels,
set within seven kinds of grain, and adorned with cloths, perfumes, and ointments.
O Lord of the Earth, having placed water-pots beneath all the trees at the end of the day,
and having performed worship and the offering of oblations according to the prescribed ritual for the world-protectors, Indra and the others, as is appropriate; 8–9.
The twice-born should thus perform the consecration (adhivāsa) of the tree.
Then, [they should give] cows wearing white garments and golden girdles,
possessing brass milking vessels, and most beautiful with their horns adorned in gold.
One should release a milch cow from the midst of the trees, facing northward.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments, auspicious songs,
and the Varuṇa mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, [the rite should be performed] on all sides.
The preeminent brāhmaṇas should perform the ceremonial bath with those very jars;
