having bathed and wearing white garments, the patron (yajamāna) should worship all the composed officiating priests (ṛtvij) with cows according to his means. 13.
With golden threads, bracelets, rings, and purificatory cords (14), with garments, beds, as well as household utensils and sandals,
one should perform the milk-consecration for four days. 15.
A Homa sacrifice should be performed with clarified butter, barley, and black sesame seeds;
sacrificial fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood are recommended on the fourth day, as is a festival.
Furthermore, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should likewise be given there according to one's capacity.
Whatever is most dear to one’s heart, that one should give without envy.
Having given double the amount to the preceptor and prostrating, one should ask for his forgiveness.
The wise person who performs the tree festival according to this rite— 17–18.
O King of kings, the wise man who thus establishes this tree attains all desires and enjoys the infinite state; he too, O King,
shall dwell in heaven for three hundred thousand years of Indra.
He shall deliver from the ocean of worldly existence those men of his past and future who are equal in measure to the sins of a *roma* (hair-pore).
That man who constantly hears this or causes it to be heard attains the supreme perfection, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find. (20–21)
He too is honored by the gods and exalted in the world of Brahmā;
moreover, even trees provide the status of a son to one who has no son.
At sacred fords (tīrthas), they offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and other rites on behalf of those who have planted them.
O Indra among kings, plant an Aśvattha tree with great effort;
it alone shall accomplish for you the task that would otherwise require a thousand sons.
Through the Aśvattha tree, one becomes wealthy; the Aśoka tree is the destroyer of grief.

The *plakṣa* is declared to be the bestower of sacrifice; the milky tree (*kṣīrī*) is remembered as the giver of longevity. The *jaṃbukī* grants daughters, while the pomegranate (*dāḍima*) likewise grants a wife. The *aśvattha* leads to the destruction of disease, and the *palāśa* is the giver of Brahman.
A man who causes a *vibhītaka* tree to be planted will be reborn as a preta.
Through an *aṅkola* tree, there is an increase in one's lineage; through a *khadira* tree, freedom from disease; and the Sun-god is always pleased by those who plant *nimba* saplings. (26–27)
Lord Śaṅkara resides in the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, Pārvatī in the Pāṭalā,
the Apsarases in the Śiṃśapā, and the most excellent Gandharvas in the Kunda.
The hosts of Dāsas dwell in the Tiṃtiḍīka, and likewise the Dasyus in the Vañjula.
The *caṃdana* tree bestows merit and prosperity; the *panasa* likewise does so.
The *campaka* grants good fortune, while the *karīra* leads to adultery.
The *tāla* causes the destruction of offspring, whereas the *kula* tree increases one's lineage.
The coconut tree yields many wives; the sugarcane, a woman beautiful in every limb; the *rati-prada* tree, sexual pleasure; the *kolī*, a daughter; and the *ketakī*, the destroyer of enemies.
Other such trees as these, which have been mentioned, are likewise bestowers of boons.
Those by whom trees have been planted shall attain a firm foundation.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Planting Trees," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-nine.
Pulastya said:
Likewise, I shall explain another [rite] that bestows the fruit of all desires, known by those learned in the Purāṇas as the "Bed of Good Fortune" (saubhāgya-śayana). 1.
Formerly, when these worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, and the others— had been consumed by fire,
the auspiciousness of all beings then became concentrated in one place;
having reached Vaikuṇṭha, it remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
Then, after some time, O King, during another cycle of creation,
when the world was enveloped by egoism and possessed of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
and when the rivalry between the Lotus-seated One and Kṛṣṇa had intensified—
From that [fire] arose a terrifying flame of fire with a tawny appearance;
scorched by it, that which had issued from the chest of Hari—which, resting upon Viṣṇu’s breast, was the very seat of his fortune—[emerged]. 5.
As long as that nectar-like form remained on the surface of the earth, it was not [attained];
however, once it was lifted from the sky by the wise son of Brahmā,
Dakṣa drank it, and it immediately produced beauty of form.
Great power and splendor arose from Dakṣa Parameṣṭhin;
that which remained and fell upon the earth was divided into eight parts, and from them the herbs were born, bestowing sevenfold auspiciousness.
(8) From those [eight parts], the herbs were produced, granting seven kinds of prosperity.

Sugarcane, the king of trees (mango), niṣpāva beans, and śāli rice; likewise cow’s milk along with its product (curd), safflower, its flower, and salt as the eighth—this is called the *saubhāgyāṣṭaka* (the eightfold auspicious set). 9–10.

Because she was formerly drunk by the Son of Brahmā, who was a knower of yoga and knowledge, she became his daughter; she is therefore designated as Satī. Because she transcends the worlds through her grace, she is likewise called Lalitā.
The wielder of the Pināka bow married the goddess Trailokyasundarī, who embodies the auspiciousness of the three worlds and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
What does a man or a woman not attain by worshipping her with devotion? (12-13)
Bhīṣma said: O Muni, tell me how she, Lalitā, is to be propitiated, and what her ritual procedure is that brings peace to the world; please explain this to me. 14.
Pulastya said: Having reached the month of Vaiśākha, on the third day of the bright fortnight, during the forenoon, one who is dear to the people should perform a bath with sesame seeds. 15.
On that day, the goddess Satī,
the excellent lady, was indeed wedded by the Lord of the Universe with the mantras of marriage;
on the third lunar day, one should worship Viśveśvara together with her.

Having bathed the image of Gaurī, who is joined with the Moon-crested Lord, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as well as with scented water, one should worship her with various kinds of fruits, lamps, incense, and offerings of food. 17–18.
Having recited "Obeisance to Pāṭalā," one should worship the two feet of the Goddess and of Śiva; having proclaimed "To Śivā," one should worship the two ankles with "To Jayā.
With "To Tryambaka," one should worship the pair of shanks of Rudra, and with "To Bhavānī," the pair of shanks of the Goddess. 19.

One should worship the head with "Obeisance to Śiva," the two knees for victory with "Obeisance to Harikeśa," the two thighs with "Obeisance to Varada," the waist with "Obeisance to Īśa," and Śaṅkara with "Obeisance to Śaṅkara. (20–21)
Salutations to you, the auspicious one, who holds a trident in both hands and possesses a belly that subdues all; salutations to Rudra, the soul of all, and to Īśānī, the two breasts. 22.
One should worship the single-necked Rudra with the mantra "Śivam vedātmane tadvat" (23). With two hands, one should worship the destroyer of Tripura, the Lord of the Universe, the Infinite,
the Three-eyed One, Hara, and the beloved of Bāhukālānala (24).

One should always worship the ornaments with "To Saubhāgyabhavanā," the face with "To Svāhā and Svadhā," and the wielder of the trident (Śūlin) with "To Īśvara. The two lips, which bestow prosperity, are to be worshipped with "To Aśokavanavāsinī."
To Sthāṇu she offered that [garland], and likewise to the Moon-faced one, O beloved; 26.
"Salutations to Hara, the Lord of Half-Woman," with this she offered her nose; "Salutations to the fierce Ugra," to the Lord of the World; and again, "O Lalitā," she offered her two eyebrows. 27.
One should worship Śarva as the leader of the vanguard, Vāsudeva as Laka, and pay homage to the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha; likewise, one should worship the hair of Śiva with [the mantra]:
"Homage to the one of terrible, fierce, and formidable form; homage to the head, the soul of all. (28)
Having worshipped Hara according to the prescribed rites, one should place before him the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka): glossy flat beans, safflower, milk, cumin,
the king of trees (betel nut), sugarcane, salt, and kustuṃburu as the eighth.
Since it bestows good fortune, one should indeed offer the "Eightfold Good Fortune" (Saubhāgyāṣṭaka);
having thus presented all of that before the two Śivas,
O subduer of enemies, one should eat the *śṛṅgāṭakas* in the month of Caitra and sleep upon the ground.
Again at dawn, having likewise performed his bath and prayers, being pure, he should worship a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
along with two golden images accompanied by the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka).
"May Lalitā be pleased," with these words one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O King, one should always do this on the third lunar day for as long as a year. Now, learn from me this specific distinction regarding the consumption [of the food] and the mantra for the gift.
In Vaiśākha, cow’s horn-water mixed with honey is prescribed; furthermore, in Jyeṣṭha, cow-dung [mixed with honey]; in Āṣāḍha, Mandāra flowers and Bilva leaves are remembered [as the offerings];
in Śrāvaṇa, one should consume curd; and in Bhādrapada, Kuśa-grass water.
In the month of Āśvayuja one should consume milk; in Kārttika, *pṛṣadājya*;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, cow’s urine; and in Pauṣa, one should consume clarified butter (37).
Likewise, in Māgha, black sesame seeds, and in Phālguna, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, Śivā,
Vāsudevī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī,
and Umā— during the time of giving, one should proclaim, "May they be pleased! (38–39).
On the twelfth day of that same month, one should worship Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, one should worship Lakṣmī there along with her husband. Then, on the full moon day, the Grandfather (Brahmā) should be worshipped in the same manner together with his consort.
He is to be worshipped by the wise who desire fearlessness in the hereafter.
Likewise, the eightfold [offering] of auspiciousness should be given by one desiring prosperity: jasmine, *aśoka*, lotus, *kadaṃba*, blue lotus, and *campaka*. 42.
The *kubjaka*, *karavīra*, *bāṇa*, unfading lotus (*amlānapaṅkaja*),
and *siṃduvāra* are remembered as flowers suitable for all months. The *japā*, *kusumbha*, *mālatī*, and *śatapatrikā* [are likewise].
One should always offer whatever is available, as well as the highly praised karavīra flower.
Having thus fasted according to the prescribed rules for the duration of a year, a man, a woman, or a maiden should worship Śiva with devotion at night.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed equipped with all its furnishings,
along with golden images of Umā and Maheśvara, as well as a bull together with a cow;
having thus prepared the bed, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
By worshipping Keśava on the twelfth day for one year,
and by worshipping Brahmā along with Sāvitrī, a man in this world attains all the desires he has mentally longed for. 47–48.

Free from stinginess regarding his wealth and devoid of pride, he should worship other couples as well, according to his ability, with garments and other such gifts, with offerings of grain, ornaments, and cows, and with various other accumulations of riches. 49.
He who thus performs this excellent Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata attains all desires or reaches the eternal state; performing this, one should practice it even while renouncing a single fruit. 50–51.

O lord of men, he who provides a bed of good fortune attains fame and renown month by month, as well as good fortune, health, beauty, clothing, and ornaments; O King, he shall never be separated from these.
But that man who performs the Saubhāgyaśayana vow for twelve,
seven, or eight years is glorified in the world of Brahmā; being duly honored, he shall dwell there for as long as ten thousand kalpas.
Having reached the world of Viṣṇu and likewise attained the world of Śiva,
she acts like a young maiden, O Lord of Monkeys;
cherished by the grace of the Goddess, she obtains that very fruit.

Whoever should even hear this, or bestow it, or even grant their consent, he too shall become a Vidyādhara and dwell for a long time in the heavenly world. This was created here in the past by Madana, and likewise performed by Śatadhanu and Nara. (56–57)
"Would it not have been a great marvel for the Lord of Men if the Wind-god, being delighted, had performed this [act]?
58. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Vows," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty.
Bhīṣma said:
Having reached the Yajñaparvata, for what purpose was this trail of footprints left here by the all-powerful Viṣṇu?
O Great-minded One, tell me that which was done by the God of gods; what gift was given by Viṣṇu here? O Great Sage, tell me that auspicious account of how he made his placement of steps.
The abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu is in Vaikuṇṭha in the heavenly world; how then did he set foot in the world of mortals?
Indeed, in the divine worlds, the gods headed by Indra [reside].
O Brahmin, it is proclaimed that the abode of Śrī Varāha, who is constantly worshipped by those devoted through great austerity, is in Maharloka;
likewise, the abode of the high-souled Nṛsiṃha is said to be in Janaloka.
The abode of Trivikrama is proclaimed to be in the world of Tapas (Tapoloka).
Having abandoned these worlds, how did he place his two feet upon the earth—
at this field of Pitāmaha, in Puṣkara, on the mountain of sacrifice?
"O Brahmin, relate to me in detail how he performed the foot-stroking;
by hearing this, the destruction of all sins will surely come to pass.
Pulastya said:
"You ask rightly, O Lord; listen with a concentrated mind to how the placement of the steps was formerly performed by the divine Viṣṇu,
having reached the Sacrificial Mountain on the slope of the mountain of rocks."

O scorcher of enemies, in a former age, for the sake of accomplishing the divine purpose of Bhīṣma, Viṣṇu previously performed this [deed] for the sake of the earth; all of heaven had been seized by the most powerful Dānavas. (10–11)
Having conquered the three worlds and brought the gods, including Indra, under his control, the Dānavas—
who were the consumers of the sacrificial offerings— became exceedingly powerful there;
all this was accomplished by the mighty Dānava Āṣṭakalī.
When the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, had thus become illuminated, Śakra fell into supreme distress; rendered hopeless for his life,
that lord of the Dānavas, Bāṣkali, thought, "He is invincible to me in battle."
By virtue of Brahmā’s granting of a boon to all the inhabitants of heaven,
I was chosen by all those celestial beings in the world of Brahmā;
I go for refuge to the God, for no other resort is known to exist.
Having reflected thus, the Lord of the Gods, surrounded by all the inhabitants of heaven,
went in haste to where the divine Grandfather Bhīṣma was;
having reached the abode of Brahmā, he was joined by those celestial beings.

He spoke regarding the world's task and the supreme calamity that had arrived: "O Lord, do you not know that a twofold danger has come upon us? For all has been seized by the Daityas through the granting of a boon to you. (18)
"I have indeed related everything concerning the evil-minded Bāṣkali.
O Grandfather, you are our father; therefore, O Lord of Gods, reflect upon this matter here for the sake of the world's peace without delay. (19-20)
While they were watching, even the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis did not proceed; indeed, day after day, we suffered loss at their hands.
For it was as if some common person were speaking solely for his own self-interest.
Thus we should inform him, for we have always rejected his favors:
"If someone has rendered assistance to another, and that person, in turn, does not act to repay that kindness a thousandfold, he is of vain intellect. (22-23)
For that wicked person who has consumed his benefactor and is devoid of shame,
there shall be residence even in the hells; for such an evildoer,
mere repayment for what was done does not constitute goodness.
This [compassion] does not even arise in those whose intellects are solely intent on their own self-interest.
(25) For if there were no place for this world that bestows suffering, his heart would have been rent asunder a hundred times and yet would never have attained satisfaction. (26)
O Lord, lift up those who are submerged here in this world-ocean by means of explaining the skillful methods (*upāya*), through which your splendor shall prevail.
Behold this world situated therein, exactly as it was seen and described by me.
Devoid of Vedic recitation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, with festivals and auspicious rites ceased;
abandoned by the practice of study, freed from news and possessions; deserted by the science of governance, it remained with only its own breath remaining. 28–29.
"The world has fallen into distress and reached an even more painful state;
indeed, during all this time, we ourselves have come to exhaustion.
Brahmā said:
I know him to be arrogant due to the granting of boons;
I consider him invincible to you all, yet he shall be subdued by Viṣṇu.
At that time, Brahmā remained standing, having restrained himself and established his mind in the reality of the essential nature.
As he remained established in samādhi through mere meditation,
the Self-born One, being meditated upon, arrived within a very short time— in a mere moment— while everyone was looking on. 32–33.
Viṣṇu said: "O Brahmin, desist from this meditation; having been requested to do so, I have come before you for the very purpose for which you were meditating. (34)
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of the universe, this is indeed a great favor that the Master has appeared here; for who else could have such a vision as this? 35

My very birth was ordained for the sake of the world; this world exists for your sake, yet in reality it does not exist—how wonderful! (36) You must perform the work of preservation, while Rudra alone shall effect the destruction.
"Since the kingdom of this high-souled Śakra has been seized by Bāṣkali— the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary—
let assistance be rendered to your servant, O Keśava, by providing him with counsel. (37-38)
Vāsudeva said: "By virtue of your boon, this Dānava is currently invincible; however, he can now be overcome by means of intelligence, and his task here is simply to be bound."
"I shall become Vāmana, the destroyer of the Dānavas. Let this Bāṣkali go with me to his abode. Having gone there, let him ask this boon of him for my sake."
"O King, O highly fortunate one, grant three paces of land to this dwarf Brahmin; this is the request I have made.
Thus addressed by Śakra, the lord of the Dānavas replied, "I would give even my own life."

O Grandfather, having bound that wicked-souled donor— who had taken hold of his household— and having diligently cast him down into the netherworld (Pātāla), he assumed the form of a boar for the purpose of slaying him.
"I shall become [the Indra], of this there is no doubt; O Śakra, depart with haste.
Having spoken thus, he ceased and indeed vanished from sight.
Then, after some time, Viṣṇu entered the womb of Aditi.
Extremely terrible omens appeared in great numbers when Viṣṇu, the support of the entire world, had entered the womb; yet, at that time,
an auspicious and powerful omen also arose.
A fragrant and sweet-smelling breeze blew, carrying the scent of *mālatī* flowers.

Then, having performed the prescribed rites and reached the appointed time, the God of gods—compassionate toward all beings and intent on the welfare of the hosts of the thirty deities—assumed the state of the son of Aditi (Viṣṇu), his hair pure and sparse, possessing the splendor of the rising moon and a conch shell. 47–48.

When Viṣṇu descended, the faces of the Siddhas, gods, and asuras—whose eyes were unblinking—became radiant; and due to the winds blowing with dust completely subsided, that day during Viṣṇu’s birth was exceedingly pleasant for the world. Even Aditi, the goddess who bore him in her womb, as she walked, was beautiful in her slow gait, pained by the weight of her heavy hips.
Bearing a pale complexion with a face weary and dejected, she carried a most heavy and deeply advanced pregnancy.
Then, when Nārāyaṇa had indeed entered the womb through the union of the past and the future,
all beings then experienced the fulfillment of their desires without even having undergone hardship.
The wind blew very, very gently; rain fell beautifully upon the mountain-born trees; the paths became secluded, the quarters of the sky were clear, and people had indeed returned to truth.
As the dust was released from the sky, the darkness gradually vanished.
When Viṣṇu had entered within her womb, the thought of a cow arose in her mind.
O Indra among kings, listen to that [thought] of the goddess's mother in its proper sequence:
"What is the use of this mere enumeration? Shall I leap over to heaven? (53–54)
I shall make that Bāṣkali, lord of the Dānavas, a dweller of the netherworld;
for it was beauty and wealth alone that I bestowed upon Śakra. I am the sole power capable of bringing about the destruction of the Dānavas.
I hurl nets of arrows and numerous chariots,
as well as various multitudes of maces, for the destruction of the Dānavas;
[I send] the gods to the celestial realm and the Dānavas to the subterranean world.
"By means of the yoga of the abode (ālayayoga), I shall perform that very task; by my vow, speech has suddenly issued forth and remains established within my mouth.
By this [yoga], that which was previously unthought, unseen, and unheard is now being contemplated. (58)
"Behold, I have bound the leader with my wrath!
(59) Previously, wealth and beauty were given to Kaśyapa;
why is he now devoid of energy, or why are you all so agitated? (60)
"My vision seems to be wandering due to excessive cold; this form has not been properly considered.
Possessed [by delusion], what improper words am I saying? Having fallen under the sway of doubt, I am constantly reflecting thus in my heart. (61)
He bore that divine lord for a thousand divine years.
Then, from her, Vāmana was born as a being of mind-made form (vāmana),
by whose birth the eyes of the Dānavas were truly taken away.
Then, as soon as Janārdana, the god of gods, was born,
the rivers began to flow with clear water and a fragrant breeze blew.
Kaśyapa, too, obtained happiness through that radiant son.
As soon as Janārdana was born from the people, O lord of men, the mental enthusiasm of all those dwelling within the three worlds arose; then,
in the heavenly world, the kettledrums resounded, struck by them.

Due to extreme joy, the delusion and sufferings of the three worlds came to an end; and the hosts of Gandharvas in the world, mingled with their lords, sang with voices full of emotion. Furthermore, the celestial damsels and the throngs of Apsarases danced there, filled with fervent feeling.
In that very way, throngs of *vidyādharas* and *siddhas* wander joyfully through the sky in celestial chariots;

they declare the determination of truth and falsehood, likewise display various wonders, and sing songs free from passion, though they themselves are repeatedly subject to the arising of suffering and happiness. 68–69.
"Those who have gone to heaven indeed dance; they go from here to a heaven earned through dharma.

Thus, in this stainless world of living beings, free from the mass of darkness and devoid of despair, some spoke there on the earth, "Victory! Victory, O Blessed One! while others were exceedingly joyful, and still others followed with constant proclamations and recitations of what had been said. 70.
While others meditated on Him who is hidden for the sake of severing birth, old age, and death, this entire world became completely filled with joy on every side.
Having attained the Supreme Viṣṇu, Brahmā said: "This Vāmana has been born by You for the sake of the world, even though he is the Lord Himself. (71-72)
He is Brahmā and he is Viṣṇu; he alone is Maheśvara.
He is the Vedas and the sacrifices, and he is heaven—of this there is no doubt.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded by Viṣṇu.
The one who is renowned as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū) is known through his distinctness from all else;
just as a crystal gem appears variegated when placed near objects of various colors, so too does that Svayambhū conform to the influence of the qualities (guṇas). || 74–75 ||
Just as the Gārhapatya fire may again assume another name,
so too shall this Blessed One receive names such as Brahmā and others;
in every way, the divine Vāmana will accomplish the work of the gods.
While those celestial beings were thus reflecting and meditating, Indra,
accompanied by Vāṣkala, went to the abode of that lord. From afar, he beheld that city of his, completely surrounded.
It was adorned with preeminent palaces, white and inaccessible to birds, embellished with every kind of gem, featuring well-proportioned great thoroughfares,
and filled with elephants in constant rut that resembled mountains of collyrium.

It was graced by hundreds of horses born from the lineages of gods and *nāgas*, adorned with bodies devoid of flesh, small ears, and the speed of thought; they were further beautified by long necks, prominent brows, and charming features. 80–81.
There were thousands of courtesans there, with complexions like the golden interior of a lotus and faces resembling the full moon, skilled in conversation and playful banter.
There was no merit like theirs, no such knowledge, no such craft, and no such art.
Then he went to the residence of Bāṣkali’s son,
which was crowded with hundreds of gardens and garlanded with social festivals and celebrations; there he was accompanied by all the principal followers of Danu, with the sole exception of Antaka.
Resounding everywhere with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums,
the younger brothers, ever joyful and adorned with many jewels,
were seen sporting like the gods on Mount Meru. 85.
There, a great sound of Vedic chanting was uttered by the elders;
the air was purified of all sins by the smoke of fires fed with clarified butter and made fragrant by the wafting of scented incense. 86–87.
In that city, crowded with fragrant Danujas, the Dānava Bāṣkali,
having brought the three worlds under his control, always dwelt in happiness;
remaining there, he protected the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
He was a knower of dharma, grateful, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses;
he was handsome, an expert in discerning right from wrong conduct among the ancient gods,
devoted to Brahmanas, a protector, and compassionate toward the distressed.
He is not devoted to immoral conduct and is non-violent toward all beings (92).
He honors those worthy of honor, is pure, pleasant-faced, and worships those deserving of worship.
He knows the meaning of all things, is invincible, fortunate, and pleasing to behold (93).
Possessing abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many vehicles, this donor was a constant achiever of the three goals of life (trivarga) and the most excellent man in the three worlds;
dwelling eternally in his own city, he humbled the pride of both gods and demons. 94.
And thus he protected all the subjects in the three worlds. O King, among those Danavas, there was no one who was base,
nor anyone who was miserable, afflicted by disease, short-lived, or suffering.

Whether he be a fool, or ugly in form, or unfortunate, or even one who has been cast out— seeing him thus endowed with a flood of pure virtues, and perceiving that his intellect was firmly settled [in truth],
the high-souled Indra, seeking to propitiate that foremost of Daityas, the chief of Danus, spoke to him.
O King, seeing that lord of the Dānavas endowed with splendor, blazing like the sun,
and capable of sustaining the three worlds, he was then struck with wonder upon seeing Indra arrive before him. 98–99.
Then those Dānavas, intoxicated by war, having arrived, said this:
"O Lord, it is a marvel that Indra approaches your city alone, accompanied only by that foremost of the twice-born, Vāmana! (100)

"O King, tell us now what we must perform; speak to us. He said to all the Dānavas, "While you remain gathered here in the city, let the King of the Gods be ushered in; he is to be honored by me today."
At that very moment, Vāmana and Indra arrived; they were gazed upon with affection by the Lord of Anu,
who considered himself to have achieved his purpose and offered them prostrations.
The king, the leader of the Dānavas, spoke these words:
"Today, indeed, there is no one more fortunate than I in the three worlds,
since I, surrounded by prosperity, behold Śakra come to my home."

If he, out of a desire for my wealth, should come to beg me, I shall certainly give him even my very life when he has arrived at my home; as for my wife, sons, and house, what mention can there be of them in the three worlds? 106.
Having come before him and respectfully brought him onto his lap (107),
she embraced and greeted him, then led him into her own home;
having performed a hospitable reception for him with offerings of water and other honors, she paid him worship with great care (108).

Today the fruit of my first birth is realized; all my desires are fulfilled, since I behold you, O Śakra, who have come to my very home. Having been proclaimed by you as the king of the gods, I am now made the leader of the foremost among the Danus.
"Come to my house, O most meritorious one!
O Purandara, when you are seen by me, you shall obtain that fruit which is gained through the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices properly performed. (110-111)
Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of land, from the gift of cows, or from a sacrifice for a priest— may that fruit be mine today, or even the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O Vāsava, your vision cannot be attained through meager austerity.
"Since my life is thus at your disposal, tell me what must be done that is pleasing to you.
You should not entertain any other hesitation in your heart by any means;
know that it shall be accomplished, even if it should be very difficult to perform. (113-114)

O Destroyer of Enemies, I am fortunate; I have attained merit by beholding you, whose feet are worshipped even by the best of gods. O Lord, tell me everything: what is the purpose of your coming? 115.
"I consider this reason for your arrival to be most wonderful.
Indra said:
"O Bāṣkali, I know you to be the foremost among the leaders of the Danus."

This does not appear at all surprising in you, O best of asuras, once you have been seen: that those who come to your house seeking aid do not depart with their faces turned away. You are a wish-fulfilling tree for supplicants; no other donor exists.
In radiance you are equal to the sun; in profundity you are like the ocean; in forbearance you are indeed like the earth; and in splendor you are comparable to Nārāyaṇa.
O auspicious one, this Vāmana was born as a brahmin in the lineage of Kaśyapa.

"I have been thus entreated by him: 'O Lord, grant me three paces of land, so that I may perform a sacrifice there for the sake of a fire-sanctuary. Having made this his reason for requesting it, O Lord, [grant it] to me. (120-121)
"O Bāṣkala, having displayed your prowess, you have seized the three worlds from me;
I am destitute and without means. Whatever you wish to give, that I do not possess. Therefore, I shall beg of you for the sake of another as well as for my own."
Therefore, perform that which is appropriate for me, who am now a supplicant.
You have been born in the lineage of Kāśyapa as one who increases his family line;
you are born from the womb of Diti, and your father is worshipped by the three worlds.
Knowing you to be such as this, I therefore entreat you:
let three paces of land be given for the sake of a fire-sanctuary for this dwarf, O Dānava, whose body is exceedingly short. 125.
"I do not venture to give away land that belongs to another.
This alone has been given by me, which you have requested from me; provided my elders or my ministers consider these three steps sufficient. (126-127)
"Out of my own need, and for the sake of my kin within my family,
as well as for me who have come to your home—
O hero, O lord of the Dānavas of great luster— perform whatever is appropriate. (128)
"Therefore, let it be given quickly to this high-souled Vāmana.
Bāṣkali said:
"O Lord of the Gods, welcome to you; may you obtain well-being without delay."
Behold yourself as the ultimate refuge of all.
Having entrusted the burden to you, the Grandfather (Brahmā) dwells in happiness,
engaged in meditation and concentration, contemplating the supreme state.
Wearied by many battles, Keśava has cast aside his concern for the world and sleeps happily, having taken refuge on an island in the Ocean of Milk.
And all the other powerful Dānavas, equipped with weapons, [have been slain] by you.
O Śakra, even all of them were struck down by him alone and without assistance:
the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the two Aśvins, the Vasus, and the eternal Dharma. 133–134.
Relying upon the strength of your arms, the gods share in the sacrifices in the third heaven;
you have performed hundreds of sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees,
and by you, O Pākaśāsana, Vṛtra and Namuci were slain.
Formerly, by the powerful Viṣṇu acting according to your command,
even Hiraṇyākṣa, the brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu, was slain; and there,
having placed him upon his thigh, Hiraṇyakaśipu himself was killed.
Seeing you, Vajrapāṇi, approaching upon the head of Airāvaṇa on the field of battle, all the Dānavas shall perish;
even those exceedingly powerful Dānavas who were previously conquered by you.
"I am not equal to even a thousandth part of him in any way. O Lord of the Gods, you are such a person that I do not even count you;
yet, you have come here solely with the desire to extract my flesh. (139-140)
"I shall do it without doubt; I will surely give up even my life.
For what reason, O King of the Gods, have you told me that this land belongs to me?
These wives, sons, cattle, and whatever other wealth exists [are yours]. (141)
"Let the entire sovereignty of the three worlds be given to this Brahmin;
otherwise, there will be infamy for me and my ancestors, without a doubt, that Bāṣkali did not give [the kingdom] to Śakra when he came to his house. (142-143)

"O Indra, even any other seeker who has come here is always as dear to me as you; do not entertain any doubt regarding this at all. O Lord of the Gods, my shame is great that I have only three paces of land."
"O Lord, what has been specifically requested by this Brāhmaṇa shall be granted by you:
excellent villages for him, and for you, the celestial realm; as well as horses, elephants, land, wealth, and women with swelling breasts. (145–146)
O Lord of the Gods, I shall restore to you this earth and these women, by the mere sight of whom even an old man becomes young; please grant me your favor. 147.
When these words had been spoken, O King, Uśanas, the priest, then addressed Bāṣkali, the lord of the Dānavas, with these words:
"You are a king, O lord of the Dānavas, established in sovereignty by the will of Fate. (148–149)
"You do not know what is proper or improper, nor to whom or when anything should be given by me;
yet, after consulting thoroughly with your ministers and examining what is right and wrong,
you have obtained the sovereignty of the three worlds by conquering the gods along with Indra."
"At the conclusion of these words, O King, you shall meet with bondage:
'This Vāmana, O King, is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu;
nothing should have been given by you, for your father has been slain by him himself.'"
This man has arrived as a slayer of your father, a slayer of your mother, and a murderer of your kinsmen; he is one who will destroy your lineage, both in the present and for the future.
Furthermore, devoted to the welfare of Śakra and the other gods, he does not know what is righteous.
By means of his illusory power (*māyā*), he conquered the deceitful Dānavas;
through *māyā*, he manifested the form of a dwarf Brahmin.
What more need be said here? There is nothing whatsoever that should not be given to him. 154–155.
"Even a piece of land the size of a fly's foot is an excessive acceptance for him;
you will quickly meet your destruction—this is the truth, the truth as I have heard it. Though addressed thus by his preceptor, he then spoke these words once more:
"O Guru, all this has been promised by me for the sake of dharma. The fulfillment of one's promise must be performed; it is the eternal dharma of the virtuous.
If this Lord Viṣṇu does not exist, then I am most fortunate. (157-158)
O Guru, if one desires to worship the gods with water accepted according to the *gṛhya* rites, this very Lord has indeed been brought to even greater auspiciousness by you,
for yogis engaged in meditation behold him through constant contemplation. 159.
"O Brahmins, I have not obtained such [merit] as this which has been gained by me today (verse 160).
Those who bestow gifts with their hands holding *kuśa* grass and water,
saying, 'May the blessed Viṣṇu, the supreme self, the eternal one, be pleased' (verse 161)."
When these words regarding the attainment of liberation had been spoken, this doubt arose in me concerning the performance of my duty here:
"I have been instructed by you, yet it was not fully grasped by me in my childhood. (162)
"Even if an enemy comes to my house, there is nothing that should not be given;
having reflected upon this very principle, O Guru, I shall give even my own life-breaths to Vāmana, and even the heaven of Śakra."
"That gift which causes no suffering is the gift bestowed here; however, that gift which causes suffering is considered to be tainted.
Having heard this, the teacher stood there with his face cast down in shame.
Bāṣkali said:
"O Goddess, the entire earth has been requested by me from you;
it would be a cause of shame for me that this [remaining] triple portion of land should belong to him."
Indra said:
"O Lord of the Dānavas, what you have told me is true;
this twice-born man has indeed requested three paces of land from me."
"To this extent, you are indeed a seeker of wealth; for your sake, I too have requested this boon from the son of Danu. Let this be granted.
Bāṣkali said:
"O King of the Gods, accept from me three paces for Vāmana.
"In that place, O Lord of the Suras, may you dwell happily for a very long time.
Having spoken thus, Bāṣkali gave the three paces to Vāmana.

"May Hari himself be pleased with this which has been offered preceded by water. Having abandoned his dwarf form, Hari, the lord of the Dānavas, then traversed the worlds for the sake of the welfare of the gods. 171.
Having reached the mountain of sacrifice and gone there facing north,
the abode of the Dānavas was situated beneath the left foot of the God;
there, the Lord of the World placed his first step upon the Sun.
O King, by that deity of wondrous deeds, the second heaven was struck with his first toe and the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) with his third;
when the egg was pierced by the tip of his big toe, a vast quantity of water gushed forth.
Having flooded all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā in successive order, that stream of water, having washed the abode of Dhruva, the world of the Sun, and that mountain of sacrifice,
entered the Puṣkara lake after purifying the footsteps of Viṣṇu.
The footprints born of Viṣṇu exist upon the surface of the earth;
having gone to that hermitage, one should perform a bath in the pond.
Merely by seeing them, the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice arises for him.
Accompanied by a retinue of twenty-one, he shall attain residence in Vaikuṇṭha (verse 178).
Having enjoyed vast pleasures for three hundred kalpas, at the end of that time, he is born here on earth as a sovereign emperor (sārvabhauma) (verse 179).

That river, which issued from the tip of the big toe of Viṣṇu’s foot amidst a tumultuous downpour of water, is called Vaiṣṇavī; it originated from the foot of Viṣṇu. For this reason, O King, Gaṅgā became known as Viṣṇupadī.

By her, this entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, is pervaded. May that auspicious water which entered the cosmic egg through a wound at the tip of [Brahmā’s] thumb attain the status of a divine river, the river Viṣṇupadī. 181–182.
O highly fortunate one, out of a desire to bestow grace upon all, the universe—including all moving and non-moving beings—is pervaded by the divine river with its various manifestations.
Then Vāmana said to Bāṣkali: "Fill it up step by step."
Then, with his face turned downward, he could find no reply. Seeing him become silent, the priest ran forward and spoke these words:
"The power of generosity is innate; we ourselves are not capable of creating it."
"O Lord, as much of this earth as was given by Sādatta to you, O Viṣṇu, was spoken of by Bāṣkali;
that very extent of the earth which was created by you in the past has not been hidden from me. (186)
"You are of short stature, O Lord, and you are not capable of creating the long-lasting universe; the power of will alone prevails for you, O God, at all times.
Then Viṣṇu, considering him to be a speaker of truth, remained without reply. 187–188.

"Declare your status as the chief of the Dānavas; O Dānava, I shall grant you whatever desire you wish. Since this water has been offered by you into my hand, you are worthy of a boon and a fortunate recipient of blessings. (189)
"I shall grant you whatever desire you seek; choose it. Thus requested by him, Janārdana, the God of gods, replied:
"O Lord of gods, I choose devotion [to you]; let my death be at your hands."
"I am going to Śvetadvīpa, which is difficult even for ascetics to attain.
When he had spoken thus, Viṣṇu said to him: "Wait until the end of the yuga, when I, in the form of a boar, shall enter the depths of the earth."
"Then I shall slay you here, when you come before me. Thus addressed by him, the Dānava retreated from his presence. O King, at that time all the worlds were occupied by Vāmana.
Then, having abandoned that truthful speech of the gods by those Asuras,
the powerful Lord, having seized the three worlds, vanished from sight; and he,
along with Bāṣkali, dwelt happily in his abode in Pātāla.
The wise Śakra protected the three worlds. This manifestation of the Teacher of the World is named Traivikrama;
it is connected with the origin of the Gaṅgā and destroys all impurities.
O King, this origin of the steps of Viṣṇu has been told to you;
having heard it, a person in this world is liberated from all sins, as well as from bad dreams, evil thoughts, difficult tasks, and misdeeds. 198.
Upon seeing the three steps of Viṣṇu, they quickly meet their destruction;
likewise, having seen the sequence of the ages, sinful beings [perish]. Thus, O Bhīṣma, subtlety was demonstrated by Viṣṇu in the manifestation of his footprints.
The man on earth who ascends it while observing silence,
having performed the pilgrimage to the three Puṣkaras, shall attain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
he is liberated from all sins and, upon death, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Origin of Viṣṇu’s Foot," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-one.
Bhīṣma said:

"O Blessed One, it is indeed a great marvel that Bāṣkali was bound when Bali was restrained by you in the form of Trivikrama. This I have heard previously as it was being recounted by the best of the twice-born."
Even today, Bali, the son of Virocana, dwells in Pātāla.
What is the true nature of the Nāga-tīrtha, and how did the Piśācas originate?
How did Śivadūtī come to be here, and by whom was she made auspicious?
"O great sage, by whom was the lotus led into the intermediate space?
Tell me all this, including how Bāṣkali was bound. Previously, the treading upon the earth was performed by the god Viṣṇu."
Furthermore, tell me truly and exactly as it happened what the Lord did for the second reason;
for this account, which destroys sin, should be heard by one who desires prosperity.
Pulastya said:
O King, this burden of questions has been recounted by you out of mere curiosity;
I shall explain all of that to you exactly as it is, O best of monarchs.

O Bhīṣma, you have heard here how Bāṣkali’s bondage was [released] through association with Viṣṇu’s feet; all of that has been recounted by me to you. Furthermore, O Bhīṣma, it shall be attained again by Viṣṇu in the Vaivasvata Manvantara.
The three worlds were seized by the powerful and sovereign Viṣṇu.
Having gone alone to the sacrifice, Bali was likewise bound;
furthermore, the Lord of Gods performed the treading upon the earth.
O lord of men, such was the manifestation of Vāmana;
having again become Trivikrama, he who was already Vāmana became Vāmana once more.
O descendant of Kuru, this entire account of your origin has been told to you.
Listen, O observer of great vows, to how it was for the Nāgas at that sacred ford:
Ananta, Vāsuki, the mighty Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka the lord of Nāgas, and another serpent, Padma. 12–13.
Mahāpadma, as well as Śaṅkha, Kulika, and Aparājita—these are the descendants of Kaśyapa; by them the world is filled. Indeed, by their progeny this world is completely filled.
Crooked in form and fierce in their deeds, with sharp mouths and potent poison,
they would reduce even weak men to ashes in an instant upon biting them;
O lord of men, by the mere sight of them, the destruction of humans would occur.
Day after day, a most terrible destruction occurred;
seeing this depletion of themselves on all sides, all the creatures went for refuge to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, who is the worthy protector.
O Lord of the Earth, with reference to this very matter, all the subjects,
having seen the ancient Brahmā known as the Lotus-born, spoke thus in former times. The subjects said:
O Supreme Lord, Sovereign of the gods of all worlds, protect us!
O God, day after day we miserable ones behold great fear from the high-souled serpents with their sharp fangs. (19-20)
All humans, cattle, birds, and so forth—all this would be reduced to ashes; for though the creation was made by you, O God, it is being destroyed by the serpents.
Having understood this, O Grandfather, do what is appropriate.
Brahmā said:
"I shall provide protection for you, of this there is no doubt. Go now to your own abodes, free from disease and devoid of fear."
Thus all those subjects, having praised the Self-born Brahmā of unmanifest form, returned with supreme joy;
and when the subjects had thus departed, he summoned the serpents and spoke to them.
Then, extremely enraged, Brahmā cursed those led by Vāsuki, saying:
"Day after day, living beings shall be devoured by these evil-minded ones. (25)
"Men and likewise animals bitten by those who have transgressed me perish; for they constantly bring men to destruction because they originate from me.
Therefore, in another birth, may there be [retribution] from my most terrible wrath."
In this terrible Vaivasvata Manvantara,
there will be another king of the Lunar dynasty named Janamejaya,
who will consume you all in a snake-sacrifice within the blazing sacrificial fire. (27–28)
"Tārkṣya will devour the sons of your maternal aunt;
thus shall be the destruction of all you who are evil-minded. Having thus cursed a thousand families, he left until but one family remained.
When they had been addressed thus by Brahmā, those best of serpents trembled; falling at his feet, they then spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, O Creator of beings, our species is crooked."
"O God, you have already brought about his excessive venom, his cruelty, and his very nature as a biting serpent; why do you now curse him?
Brahmā said:
"If indeed you have been created by me with crooked intentions, then what is the use of saying more? Constantly devour those whose limbs are in agony!
(33) The Nāgas said:
"O Lord of Gods, establish boundaries and separate locations for us and for human beings; O God, ordain a covenant between us.
As for the curse that was given, let Janamejaya become a human."
"He will bring about our destruction through a fierce snake-sacrifice.
Brahmā said:
"There shall be one renowned as Jaratkāru, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman."
"From that Jaratkanyā, whom he shall give to him, a son will be born;
that brahmin will be your protector and the purifier of your lineage.
Thus, O Nāgas, I establish an agreement between you and human beings. (36-37)
Therefore, with one-pointed minds, all of you listen to my instruction: Sūtala, Vitala, and the third, Talātala—these three kinds of dwellings have been granted to you; you shall go there.

There, by my command, remain enjoying various kinds of enjoyments for a period lasting until the seventh [Manu], again and again; thereafter, at the beginning of the Vaivasvata [Manvantara], you shall become descendants of Kaśyapa. 39–40.
Suparṇa, the devourer of serpents, shall be the heir of all the gods;
at that time, the progeny of the serpents will be consumed by Vicitrabhānu—
of this there is no doubt for any of you.

Those cruel, voracious, and ill-behaved serpents, whose inner nature has been transformed otherwise, shall devour all living beings pervaded by Time; likewise, when harm is done to a human being, they shall be subdued by men through mantras, medicines, Gāruḍa rites, tantras, and binding spells. 42–43.
"Those who are afraid of them must act accordingly, and no other thought should be entertained by the mind; otherwise, there will be destruction.
When this was said by Brahmā, all those serpents went to the place called Sutala.
They remained there in Rasātala, established in play, enjoying all manner of pleasures.
Having thus received the curse as well as the grace from the Four-faced One,
they remained in their abode in Pātāla with delighted inner souls.
Then, after some time had passed, they reflected once again in this manner.
"The highly illustrious Pāṇḍava will become the king of the Bhāratas;
yet, by some stroke of fate, he shall be the cause of our destruction.
How could he, who is the lord of the three worlds and the grandfather of us all—"
The Creator of the universe, who is worshipped by the world, has bestowed this curse upon us. 48.
Abandoning the god Viriñca, no other refuge is known; the Lord resides there in that most excellent abode of Vairāja. 49.
"The god Sadeva, staying at Puṣkara, is currently performing a sacrifice.
Let us go there and propitiate him; being pleased, he will grant us a boon.
Having reflected thus, all those nāgas went to Puṣkara.
Having reached Yajñaparvata and taken refuge at its rocky slopes, they saw the elephants there, as well as cool streams of water;
facing north, they all emerged, bestowing happiness upon everyone.
From that, O bull of the Bharatas, the Nāgatīrtha was born upon the earth;
some called it Nāgakuṇḍa, while others spoke of it as a river.
It is more meritorious than all other tīrthas and destroys the venom of serpents.
On that occasion of the Āśvina-Śrāvaṇa Pañcamī, these mortals bathe there;
in their families, serpents shall never cause any affliction.
Those men on earth who perform the Śrāddha for the ancestors there [shall also be blessed]. 54–55.
"Brahmā will grant them the supreme abode; of this there is no doubt.
Having recognized the fear of the Nāgas, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then addressed the Nāgas once more with the words previously spoken.

The fifth lunar day (Pañcamī) is auspicious, meritorious, and the destroyer of all sins; for on this very excellent day, the ritual for the Nāgas is performed. On this day, one should completely avoid anything bitter or sour.
One should bathe the nāgas with milk; they will then become friends to him.
Bhīṣma said: How Śivadūtī was born and by whom she was established—[this is told]. 59.
"You ought to explain all of that to me exactly as it is.
Pulastya said:
"Śivā, having reached Mount Nīlagiri, fixed her mind upon ascetic penance. (60)
"Raudrī is the power born from matted hair; hear now her vow, O King:
'Having performed austerities for a long time, I shall devour the entire world. Having thus resolved, the passionate woman practiced the penance of the five fires."
While that goddess was performing supreme penance at another time,
there was a demon named Ruru of great splendor who had received boons from Brahmā;
in the midst of the ocean, he possessed a very wealthy city called Ratna.
There dwelt the lord of the Daityas, who causes fear to all the gods;
honored by many hundreds of thousands of millions upon millions of excellent Asuras, that glorious one was like a second Namuci.

After a long time, he went to the city of the world-protectors (Lokapālas). Desiring victory and surrounded by his army, he set his heart on enmity with the gods. As that great Asura rose up, the water of the ocean surged forward with extreme force.
Filled with many nāgas, grāhas, and fish, flooding the mountain peaks and regions,

and containing within it multitudes of the enemies of the gods adorned with various armors and weapons of wondrous beauty— that vast, formidable, and moving force of excellent warriors emerged from the waters of the Sindhu.
There, elephants approached, accompanied by demon warriors, equipped with bells on their vehicles and endowed with great splendor;
they marched forth, displaying their noble forms as if they were large fish, while horses, bound with golden cords, appeared like Rohita fish at the edge of the water. 68–69.
Stationed together with them, hundreds of thousands and tens of millions [of warriors] quickly marched forth;

likewise, chariots possessing a speed equal to the sun’s chariot, equipped with wheels, poles, axles, and bamboo frames, and with their limbs pressed down by mechanical devices and their banners fluttering, produced a great roar. 70.
In the same way, those foremost warriors, armed with excellent weapons and desiring to cross over, were blocked by the ships;
yet those strikers, having achieved victory in battle after battle, shone brilliantly as they pursued the Asuras,
especially since the gods had fled from them.
The Asuras pursued all the gods here and there; then all the hosts of gods, overwhelmed with fear,
fled toward Mount Nila, the best of mountains, where the Goddess herself was stationed.
Raudrī, endowed with ascetic power, is the supreme Śāmbhavī energy;
she is the goddess who effects destruction, whom they know as Kālarātri. Then, seeing the gods terrified and deprived of their senses, she [acted]. 74–75.

With eyes like full-blown lotuses, the goddess asked in wonder: "I do not see any danger approaching from behind; how is it that all the gods, led by Śakra, have fled? (76) "Why indeed have they all run away?"
The gods said:
"This lord of the Daityas, Ruru of terrible prowess,
is approaching, surrounded by a great fourfold army."
"Therefore, O Goddess, we, being wretched, have come to you for refuge.
Hearing these words of the gods, she laughed loudly; as she laughed, O fair-limbed one, [certain things] issued forth from her mouth. 78-79.
All of them hold nooses and goads, possess full and elevated breasts, are all formidable bearers of tridents, and have faces with fangs like goads;
all of them wear crowns and have their lips bitten in a snarl. 80.

Terrifying all moving and non-moving beings with inauspicious hissing sounds, some were clad in white garments, some in variegated robes, and some in deep blue clothing; others were intensely eager for the drinking of blood. 81–82.

With various forms and faces, and assuming diverse costumes and bodies, the Goddess—who grants fearlessness to the gods—was thus surrounded by them. As the Dānava was speaking, she said: "Do not fear, O gods; may it be well with you."
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he then arrived at that excellent Nīla mountain, which was the path of the gods;
seeing the host of gods before him and the Goddess agitated, he [proceeded]. 84–85.
"Stay! Stay! cried those Daityas as they approached;
then a battle ensued between them and her, one of great terror.
As the Daityas lay on the ground with their bodies pierced by iron arrows, they writhed upon the earth.
Like serpents crawling as they were broken by the staff of his wrath (verse 87), their hearts pierced by spears, their chests crushed by maces,
their heads split by axes, and their skulls smashed by clubs (verse 88).
Pierced in their bellies by the tips of tridents and with their necks severed by excellent swords, the horses, chariots, elephants, and infantrymen fell in battle;
all the Daityas, having reached the field of combat, were slain except for Uru.
Then, seeing his army destroyed, Ruru took recourse to an illusion (māyā).
By that [illusion], the goddesses and even the gods were utterly bewildered on the field of battle;
through that Tāmasī illusion of the goddess, everything became blinding darkness.
Then the goddess Mahāśakrī struck that Daitya;
as he was struck by her, the pervasive darkness of the Daitya departed.
When his illusion had been destroyed and his darkness dispelled, the great Dānava [stood revealed].

The Supreme Goddess quickly entered Pātāla; there, accompanied by the goddesses and filled with wrath, she stood facing him. She blocked the way before the terrified lord of the Dānavas as he was fleeing. 93–94.
Having severed his head with the tip of her claw and taken up his skin, she then rushed out from Pātāla with great speed toward Mount Puṣkara,
accompanied by a vast army of maidens who were multiformed and radiant.
The gods, filled with wonder, beheld the Supreme Goddess seated upon the skin and carrying the skull-bowl of Aruṇa,
established in the place of her own ascetic power; thereafter, the highly fortunate goddesses stood surrounding her.
Hungry, they calmly entreated that goddess:
"O Goddess, we are hungry; grant us the boon of food. Having spoken thus, the goddess then meditated upon their nourishment.
At that time, they did not find that great food which they had been thinking of.
Then they meditated upon Mahādeva, Rudra, Paśupati, the all-pervading Lord;
and through that meditation, the three-eyed Supreme Self arose. 99–100.
Rudra said to that goddess: "What task do you wish to speak of? Tell me, O Goddess of great illusion, what dwells in your mind. (101) Śivadūtī said:
"O God, you dwell here in the midst of the goats in the form of a goat;
these [goats] will devour you with eagerness, for you are their desired food. O Lord of Gods, you ought to give something here for their sake."
"These very powerful ones, desiring food, are making me their stake.
Otherwise, being hungry, they might devour me by force.
Therefore, observing me thus, quickly prepare me as a meal. (103-104)
Rudra said:
O Śivadūtī, I shall tell you one thing that occurred in another age: at Gaṅgādvāra, Dakṣa’s sacrifice was destroyed by my attendants.
There, the sacrifice, having become a deer and possessing great speed, fled;
pierced by me with an arrow, it was drenched in blood.
Then it became a goat-scented being (Ajagandha), and that name was given to it by the gods.
"You alone are Ajagandhā; I shall give you another meal.
"O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, O you of great splendor like the night of universal destruction (Kālarātri), hear from me as I speak of one food that is appropriate for these women. 107-108.
O Lord of Gods, O lady of beautiful hips, if a woman who is pregnant should put on the garment of another woman, or touch it— especially that of a man—
she shall become a sharer [of her fate] upon the surface of the earth for some of those women.
Even if they forcibly seize a child there who is only one year old and remain well-pleased, consuming [the child] for many hundreds of years;
or if others, though uninvited, should seek a vulnerability in the lying-in chamber—[one must protect against them]. 110–111.
O Lord of Devas,
those women who have lost their husbands shall dwell constantly in houses, fields, ponds, tanks, and indeed in gardens, while others stand weeping. 112.
"Among them, some others who had entered their bodies attained satisfaction.
Śivadūtī said: "What you have given is contemptible; it is a source of affliction for living beings."
O Śaṅkara, you do not understand that it is especially improper to give this;
for that which causes shame and brings suffering to living beings is not fit to be given as food to them, O Śaṅkara. (114–115)
Rudra said:
O auspicious lady, formerly when Skanda’s tonsure ceremony had been completed, O beautiful one, that boy was then [attended] by me. 116.
Having arrived, the Mothers prepared an unprecedented feast;
the hosts of gods from the world of Devas came to eat with the Mothers.
When the foremost of the Suras, beginning with Brahmā, were previously in their house—
The Gandharvas and Apsaras, all the Yakṣas and Guhyakas;
the mountain peaks beginning with Meru, as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā; all the Nāgas, elephants, Siddhas, birds, and the destroyers of the Asuras.
Then the ḍākinīs were surrounded by vetālas and all the grahas.

O Goddess, what is the use of saying more? Whatever was created here by Brahmā, all that was given as food, including food according to one's own desire and that which is not obtained from the heavens.
Śivadūtī said:
"O embodied one, prepare for them food that is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds—food seasoned with oil, mixed with jaggery, heart-pleasing, and well-cooked. (121)
"O Supreme Lord, there is nothing that has not been eaten by another; it is unprecedented.
Thus addressed, Maheśvara, the God of gods, then spoke to her for the sake of food in the very presence of Pārvatī.
"I have prepared food of many kinds,
yet all of it has been consumed and nothing else remains here.
Now that you have arrived, tell me what I should give you."
"O ladies, this is unprecedented for you; that which I must especially give has never been tasted by anyone else, and I give it for the sake of food.
These two [testicles] of mine, located at the lower part of Mount Maināka, are round like fruits. (125-126)
"Eat together with me; seize these two testicles, and by this food as well, you shall attain supreme satisfaction.
Having then received that great grace from Śiva, all the goddesses [did so].
Having prostrated and stood before Śarva, he spoke these words:
"Those men who perform auspicious rites without laughter—their wealth, cattle, sons, wives, houses, and so forth [shall belong to me]. (128-129)
Whatever has been given by me in the future, and whatever else remains in my mind, shall be taken away by Dīrghadaśanā through laughter; and they shall become poor.
Therefore, one who possesses discernment must certainly not engage in censure or laughter.
"You shall indeed be known in this world as the Mothers (Mātaraḥ).
Men will offer you oblations during the Kaumudī festival—namely, chickpeas, pūrikās, and cakes together with testicles. (131-132)
Their lineage is not severed by kinsmen or their own people;
one without a son obtains a son, and one seeking wealth obtains wealth.
He becomes handsome, fortunate, an enjoyer of pleasures, and an expert in all the scriptures. (133)
"By means of a vehicle yoked with swans, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
(134) O messenger of Śiva, I too have likewise offered you food;
listen now to what I say regarding why this has become a cause for shame for you. (135)
Victory to you, O Goddess Cāmuṇḍā; victory to you, O remover of spirits!
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess; salutations to you, Kālarātri!
O pure one endowed with the form of the universe, O Virūpākṣī, O three-eyed one!
O Śivā of terrifying form, O Vidyā, O Mahāmāyā, O Mahodarī; O conqueror of the mind, O fortress of the mind, O Bhīmākṣī who destroys the agitated;
O Mahāmārī of variegated limbs, O auspicious one fond of song and dance. 137–138.
O Vikarāli, Mahākālī, you who are beyond the dualities (Alīke), O remover of sins!
O you with noose in hand, staff in hand, with terrifying hands, and fearsome! O Cāmuṇḍā, with blazing face, sharp fangs, and great strength! 139
O Goddess, beloved of Śiva’s vehicle; O auspicious one seated upon the corpse-throne (pretāsana)!
O Goddess with terrifying eyes, who causes fear to all beings! O Karālī, Vikarālī, Mahākālī, and Karālinī! 140–141.
"O Kālikā, Rāla-vikrāntā, O Kālarātri, salutations to you!
O Goddess who wields all weapons, salutations to you, O Goddess who is worshipped by the gods!
(142) Thus was Śivadūtī praised by Rudra, the supreme lord.
The supreme goddess was pleased and spoke these words:
"O Lord of Gods, choose a boon that dwells within your mind.
Rudra said:
O fair-faced one, by means of this hymn, they shall please you;
O Goddess, being omnipresent, you shall become the bestower of boons upon them.
Whoever, having ascended this mountain, worships with devotion— 144–145.
May he who hears with devotion this hymn arising from the Goddess attain prosperity, along with sons, grandsons, and cattle;
and being liberated from all sins, may he reach supreme nirvāṇa. 146.
When a king who has been deprived of his kingdom fasts with self-restraint and purity on the ninth day (Navamī),
and observes a fast on the eighth and fourteenth days (Aṣṭamī and Caturdaśī), O best of men,
he shall regain his kingdom free from all thorns within one year.
This power, endowed with ignorance, is called Śivadūtī;
O King, whoever should constantly hear this with supreme devotion shall be liberated from all sins and attain the highest nirvāṇa.
And whoever recites this with devotion after bathing in the waters of Puṣkara,
having obtained all this fruit, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O King, wherever this remains constantly written in a house, [there it dwells].
O wise ones, for him who worships this with devotion as it resides in a book, there shall be no terrible fear of fire nor any danger arising from thieves and the like;
by him, the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, shall be accomplished.

Many sons are born, as well as wealth, grain, clothing, women, jewels, horses, elephants, and servants; these things quickly come to pass for those in whose house this is written—it shall certainly be so. 153–154.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Deeds of Śivadūtī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Bhīṣma said:
"By what ripening of karma is one born again as a preta, and by what means might one be liberated from this state? Tell me that, O Great-Minded One.
Pulastya said:
O best of kings, I shall explain all this to you in its entirety, so that having heard it, you will not fall into delusion again— namely,
that by which the state of a preta is produced and that by which one is liberated from it. 2.
One reaches a terrible hell that is difficult to cross even for the gods.
However, by conversing with the virtuous and by reciting the praises of holy pilgrimage sites,
men who have fallen into the state of pretas are liberated.
For it is heard, O Bhīṣma, that in ancient times there was a brahmin of strict vows,
widely renowned everywhere as Pṛthu, who was ever established in contentment; devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas at home, he was a knower of yoga and constantly engaged in yogic practice.
He should pass his time engaged in the ritual procedure of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
Endowed with patience and compassion, disciplined by forbearance, and knowing the reality (tattva), he should remain with a mind intent on non-violence and established in gentleness.
He was devoted to the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), endowed with austerity and yoga, intent upon the rites for the ancestors, engaged in Vedic rituals,
possessed of fear regarding the world beyond, and committed to truthful speech.
He was skilled in sweet speech, devoted to honoring guests,
engaged in the performance of sacrifices and charitable works, adept at avoiding the pairs of opposites, intent on the ordinances of his own duty, and dedicated to the practices of Vedic study.
While he was performing such deeds in the house of a Brahmin out of a desire to conquer saṃsāra, many years passed;
then this thought arose in him regarding the visiting of sacred fords (tīrthas).
"May I moisten this body with the meritorious waters of sacred fords.
Having bathed at Puṣkara while self-restrained at the rising of the sun, and having performed his prayers and salutations, he set out upon the road.
In front of him, he saw five extremely terrifying men in a desolate place,
devoid of birds and filled with forest trees laden with thorns.
Seeing them, who were of deformed appearance, most horrific, and of sinful aspect—

With his heart slightly terrified, he stood motionless in form. Then, summoning his courage and casting fear far away, he spoke with sweet words: "Who are you, and from where have you come, appearing so deformed?"
"What action was performed by what speech that this deformity was obtained? How is it that all of you are thus situated, and on what path are you traveling? (17) The pretas said:
Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and overwhelmed by great suffering, our wisdom has been stolen away; we have all lost our sense of direction and are devoid of consciousness.
We do not know even the cardinal directions or any of the intermediate points.
We do not perceive the intermediate space, nor the earth, nor likewise the sky.
This very suffering that has been described would itself become happiness, for this dawn shines forth at the sight of the rising sun. 19–20.
"Ahaṃparyuṣita by name, Sūcīmukha, and another, Śīghraga, Rauhaka, and the fifth was Lekhaka.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"How can there be an origin by name for these pretas born of their own karma?
For what reason, then, do you all possess names?
The pretas replied:

"I would always eat delicious food myself, yet I would give stale food to a twice-born man; having encountered this very reason, my name became 'Paryuṣita' (the Stale One). Many Brahmins seeking food were indicated by me."
With this as my motive,
O best of the twice-born, I was quickly pursued by the one named Sūcīmukha, who had been entreated by a hungry brahmin. It was for this reason, O excellent brāhmaṇa, that I traveled so swiftly.
Out of fear of the twice-born, he ate only what was palatable from atop his house;
with a mind agitated by that [fear], he is remembered as the Āsura Rauhīka.
He remained constantly in silence, and when requested, he would scratch the earth.

Among us, the scribe named Pāpiṣṭha was indeed most wicked. By his own name, this scribe became afflicted with great suffering; he grew excessively thin, his head hung downward, he became lame despite his speed, and his needle became needle-mouthed. 27–28.
"One with a long neck, a protruding belly,
large testicles, and long lips— such was he born from this sin.
Thus has all of my own history been told to you, along with its cause.
"Ask whatever you have faith in; being asked, we shall speak.
The Brahmin said:
"All living beings that exist in this world are rooted in food."
"I also wish to hear from you about your food in its true nature.
The pretas said:
"Listen to our food, which is despised by all living beings."
Having heard this, you revile it repeatedly and constantly.
(32) There, indeed, the deceased eat from houses that have abandoned purity, being defiled by phlegm, urine, feces, and the impurities of women's bodies. (33)
There, the deceased indeed consume food that has been burnt by women, scattered about, strewn with leavings, loathsome due to filth,
devoid of mental modesty, and lacking the fire-oblation (homa). 34.
Indeed, the ancestors eat there those [offerings] that are devoid of vows;
likewise, the ancestors eat there those [offerings] belonging to houses where teachers are not honored and which are dominated by women, being seized by anger and greed. (35-36)
O dear one, as we speak of our own meal, shame arises;
indeed, nothing more than this can even be spoken.
O you of firm vows, we ask you about the cessation of the state of being a ghost.
"O ascetic, tell me how one becomes free from rebirth as a preta.
The Brahmin said:
"By means of the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances performed for one night, two nights, and so forth..."
A man who constantly performs other vows is not born as a preta.
He who daily serves three fires, five fires, or even one fire, and is possessed of compassion for all beings, is not born as a preta. (39–40)
He who is equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward gold and a clod of earth,
and equal toward enemy and friend— that man does not become a ghost after death.
He who is constantly engaged in the worship of deities, guests, and gurus;

A man who performs the ancestral rites (pitr-pūjā) with devotion is not born as a hungry ghost (preta). (42) When the fourth lunar day (caturthī) coincides with a Tuesday (śukla-aṅgāraka), a man who performs the śrāddha ceremony on that day with faith is not born as a hungry ghost. (43)
The man who has conquered anger and doubt, who is free from the attachment of craving,
who is patient, and whose nature is generosity, is not reborn as a preta.
He likewise honors cows, Brahmins, sacred fords, mountains, and rivers.
"And that man who does not honor the gods and those worthy of worship is born as a preta.
The pretas said:
"O Sage, we have heard various dharmas; we, who are suffering, ask you [a question]."
"O Mahāmati, tell us that by which a ghost (preta) is indeed produced.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"By eating the food of a Śūdra, and especially by a Brāhmaṇa..."
Indeed, a man dies because of one residing in his womb; that man becomes a *preta*.
He abandons his mother, father, brothers, sister, and even his son—though they are free from fault—and that man is born as a *preta*. 47–48.
By officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, by abandoning those worthy to sacrifice,
and by serving Śūdras in acts of pleasure, a man is born as a Preta after death.
(49) One who misappropriates deposits, one who betrays friends, and one who is constantly intent on cooking for Śūdras [is likewise born as a Preta].
A man who betrays trust and remains deceitful is born as a preta.
A killer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a cow, a thief, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed, and one who seizes land or a maiden—such a man is born as a preta. 50–51.
"Having received a common sacrificial fee, he who hides it all to himself,
being devoted to atheistic sentiments, is surely reborn as a ghost.
O best of Brahmins, while he was speaking thus, the sound of celestial kettledrums arose in the sky.
A rain of flowers was released by the gods and fell upon the earth by the thousands. Furthermore,
celestial chariots belonging to the departed spirits arrived from all sides due to the conversation with this brahmin and the proclamation of his merit.
Therefore, O son of Gaṅgā, if you desire your own welfare, engage in conversation with the virtuous with every effort;
this story of the five pretas is the tilaka of all dharma. 55.
A man who has been a preta in his previous family becomes a human being after a hundred thousand lifetimes;
or, if he constantly hears this, endowed with supreme faith or even possessed of devotion, he is not born as a preta.
Bhīṣma said:
For what reason is Puṣkara proclaimed to be in the intermediate space, and how indeed is it attained here by sages who are devoted to dharma? 58
"Tell me all of that by which it is obtained, how what has been obtained is secured, and how it yields its fruit; explain it all to me, for I ask out of curiosity.
Pulastya said:
O King, ten million sages residing in the southern region had gathered at Puṣkara for the purpose of bathing; perceiving that Puṣkara had ascended into the sky,
they all became intent on the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, they remained there for twelve years.
Then Brahmā, the great sages, and the gods including Indra assembled there;
the sages, remaining invisible, spoke to them regarding those extremely difficult observances.

O twice-born ones, let the consecration of the lotus be performed with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," using these three Ṛgvedic verses; by this, he will become present. Furthermore, through the recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, it shall indeed become a bestower of fruits.
At the conclusion of the speech by all those Brahmins, it was done accordingly.
By that act, those twice-born ones attained merit through his command;
yet, according to the treatises on dharma, those Brahmins were censured as being "right-lefters" (dakṣiṇottara).
And those others who are mountain-dwellers deserve an invitation for the *śrāddha*;
for this reason,
O King, it is established that one attains purity by bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārtika.
O King, accompanied by Brahmā, it bestows merit upon all.
Whatever castes come there, O King, they all become recipients of merit equal to the twice-born; of this there is no doubt, even without the [Vedic] mantras. 67–68.

When the lunar mansion Āgneya (Kṛttikā) occurs on the full moon day of Kārttika, that lunar day should be known as "Mahatī" (the Great); it is most excellent for bathing and giving gifts. When the lunar mansion Yāmya (Bharaṇī) occurs on that same lunar day at some time, [it is likewise auspicious].
That lunar day (tithi) is proclaimed by the wise to be of great merit;
O lord of men, when the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) coincides with that lunar day,
it is called Mahākārtikī, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
When these three asterisms are respectively on Sundays, Thursdays, and Mondays— these three having been proclaimed by Brahmā himself—
one who bathes here certainly obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Likewise, a gift and the libation for the ancestors become inexhaustible.
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Puṣkara; it is extremely difficult to encounter even at Puṣkara.
Those who perform their ablutions at the auspicious Tīrtha of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which has descended from the intermediate space, shall attain worlds of great splendor;
they have no desire for any other merit, whether performed or unperformed. 75.
"O Great King, this which has been declared is the truth:
it is recited here that among all holy places on earth, this is the most excellent;
O King, no more meritorious holy place than this is recited in the worlds. (76-77)

Especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, that auspicious river, which removes sin and bestows merit, came from that Udumbara forest; by her, that Puṣkara tīrtha, frequented by sages, was filled. 78.
To the south, not far from that mountain, there shines a peak resembling a mass of blue collyrium;
in color it is like dark-green grass, and that peak of his stands like a lotus situated in the sky. 79-80.

In the rainy season, that peak stood as if it were a mass of clouds rising to fill the sky, rich with the fragrance of kadamba flowers and adorned with kuṭaja and arjuna blossoms; it appeared as though it had risen to ascend the path of the sun’s chariot. 81.
