With its well-rounded, downy, and glistening *śrīphala* fruits, it shines on all sides like the breasts of women;
it is graced on every side by swarms of humming bees. 82–83.
In that place, delightful with the sweet warbling of cuckoos and filled with the cries of peacocks,
there rises from the mountain peak this auspicious river, the daughter of Brahmā, endowed with both holy and unholy waters. 84.
Emerging from the bamboo pillar, she flowed forth very extensively toward the north (85).
Having traveled not very far from there, she then turned back;
from that time forward, the goddess remained manifest and gracious (86).
Abandoning her disappearance out of compassion for living beings,
Kanakāsuprabhā, Nandā, Prācī, and Sarasvatī—
these five streams were designated by Brahmā at the Puṣkaras.
On its banks are delightful sacred fords (tīrthas) and shrines (āyatanas), frequented on all sides by sages and perfected beings (siddhas);
in all of them, the Sarasvatī shall be the cause of dharma. 88–89.
At those sacred fords (tīrthas) of Hāṭaka, Kṣiti, and Gaurī,
a gift bestowed by men who have bathed produces inexhaustible fruit of great prosperity.
The lords of sages declare that the gift of grain and likewise the gift of sesame seeds are preeminent.
Whatever is given by men at those sacred fords (tīrthas) is declared to be the most excellent cause for merit.

Whether it be a woman or a man who, being self-restrained and diligent, performs the rite of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśa) at those places—even if he is joined with a wife—he likewise enjoys the fruit as he desires in the abode of Brahmā. 91–92.
Those stationary and moving beings who die in its vicinity due to the exhaustion of their karma—
all of them obtain in its entirety the fruit of sacrifice, which is otherwise difficult to attain. Furthermore,
for those whose minds are afflicted by the sufferings of birth and so forth, it is the source of the fruit of dharma.
This great river, which yields beautiful fruits in every respect and is served by Sarasvatī, is accessible to men without effort.
Those men who constantly drink its pure water are not mere mortals; they are gods dwelling here upon this earth. 94-95.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the twice-born through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, that is attained here by even Śūdras born of their own nature merely by bathing;
and even those who are great sinners [are purified] by the mere sight of Puṣkara. 96.
Being liberated from that very sin, they go to heaven at the dissolution of the body.
There, a man who observes a fast at Puṣkara quickly obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice with little effort. 97-98.
He who, with devotion and according to his capacity, offers sesame seeds to a virtuous Brahmin in the month of Māgha shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
There, he should observe fasting, perform ritual bathing, and likewise consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Whatever man performs [this], he too shall attain heaven at the end of his body (death). Even those classes of thieves who dwell in his vicinity go to heaven by the power of his merit; of this there is no doubt. 100–101.
Furthermore, those men who abide by the conduct of a Śūdra, having fasted for three nights and being endowed with the power of Brahman, bestow wealth upon the twice-born; they,
upon death, ascend a celestial vehicle, possessing four arms and seated upon a lotus throne.
They attain immediate union with Brahman and are not subject to rebirth.
At Gaṅgodbheda, where the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, having emerged from the sky for the sake of seeing the Sarasvatī, arrived [there]. 103–104.

Having gone there, he who has drunk even a single handful of the pure water of the Sarasvatī— which is purified by its very nature, frequented by gods and siddhas, stainless, and worshipped by hosts of vidyādharas— has attained that supreme state. 105.
Looking toward the eastern direction, she said: "O friend Gaṅgā, I am alone, separated from you; I am going forth without any kinsmen.
Then, perceiving her to be thus, Gaṅgā spoke to her as she was emaciated by grief.
Having arrived from the eastern region to see her who was dejected in spirit, and having seen that illustrious lady who was thus afflicted,
Gaṅgā wiped her eyes and then spoke these words.
"Do not weep, O illustrious lady; you have performed a difficult task, my friend.
Indeed, this work of the gods could not have been accomplished by anyone else.
It is for this reason, O illustrious one, that the gods have assembled to see you. (109-110)
Let worship be performed for these [deities] through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
having performed the sequence of rites for Sarasvatī and Surendra,
let there be the recitation of the Brahma-mantra in due order, together with the assembled circle of friends.
The confluence of the Jyeṣṭha and Madhyama rivers in the middle is world-renowned.
Thereafter, the daughter of Brahmā, the Gaṅgā, flows westward while [the other] flows northward;
then all those gods who had gathered at Puṣkara [departed]. 112–113.
Having recognized her difficult feat, they offered her praise:

"You are intelligence, you are intellect, you are fortune, you are knowledge, you are the supreme goal; you are faith, you are the highest steadfastness, you are wisdom, memory, delight, and forbearance. (114)
You are success; you are *svadhā* and *svāhā*; you are considered the great purifier. You are the twilight, night, splendor, being, intelligence, faith, and Sarasvatī;
you are the sacrifice, the great knowledge, and the beautiful secret knowledge. 115–116.
Ānvīkṣikī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti are proclaimed [as your forms].
Salutations to you whose waters are meritorious; salutations to you who flow to the ocean. 117.
Salutations to you who are the liberation from sin; salutations, O Goddess, beloved of the world.
Thus was Goddess Ahisā praised by those devoted to their own divine purposes. Thus did that Goddess Sarasvatī stand there facing the east,
the goddess who embodies all holy fords and is accompanied by all the immortals.
It should be known by the wise as Prācīsītā, for such is the word of Brahmā;
there, the sacred ford named Śuddhāvaṭa is remembered as belonging to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Even those who are great sinners [are purified] by the mere sight of it.

The pure ones enjoy the pleasures of the serpent-king in the presence of Brahmā. Those best of men who perform the vow of fasting unto death there go to heaven by the vehicle of Brahmā, free from all fear.

In that place, even a small gift given by those who know Brahman and have realized the Self results in their giving having been offered for hundreds of future births, provided they are purified in soul. Furthermore, those men who perform the restoration of what is broken or dilapidated there [attain the same merit].
Having reached that world of Brahmā, they rejoice, forever happy.
Whatever worship, recitation, or fire-offering is performed here by embodied beings whose souls are devoted to the love of Brahmā, all of its fruit is infinite. 124–125.
There, by the offering of a lamp, one obtains the eye of knowledge that transcends the senses; by the offering of incense, one attains the station frequented by Brahmā.
Now, what is the use of saying more? Whatever is given at the confluence [of the rivers], [that is the fruit].
That is declared to yield infinite fruit for both the living and the deceased;
through bathing, recitation, and likewise through fire-offerings, it accomplishes infinite results.
Having arrived there, Rāma offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for Daśaratha. 127–128.
The *śrāddha* was offered there by that Mārkaṇḍeya when he showed it;
at that place, which has four-cornered ponds, those who offer funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) all go to the third heaven (*triviṣṭapa*) by means of a vehicle yoked with swans.
In that very pond, Brahmā—
the best among those who know sacrifice— performed the Pitṛmedha sacrifice, completing it with excellent sacrificial fees.
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, and the Rudras as the grandfathers.

The Ādityas are their appointed great-grandfathers; though they are of three kinds, they were called back again by Viriñci. "Remaining here, you must always accept the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites. 132.
Whatever ancestral rite (pitṛkārya) is performed [there], that shall yield infinite fruit.

For those whose livelihood depends on it, their fathers and grandfathers are indeed satisfied; through the offering of libations (tarpaṇa) they obtain satisfaction, and through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna), they attain heaven (triviṣṭapa). 133–134.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should become an offerer of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) even at Prācīna;
having offered it with diligence, the son should satisfy all the ancestors.
[This place] is established in front of the deity Prācīneśvara.
That is called Āditīrtha; it grants liberation even by the mere sight of it. By touching its water there, one is released from the bondage of birth;
by immersing oneself in it, one becomes an eternal attendant of Brahmā. 136–137.
Having bathed at Āditīrtha, the man who, with concentrated mind,
offers even a small amount of food will, for the most part, attain heaven. Furthermore, the man who, having bathed there, gives wealth to those devoted to Brahmā—
Even by giving gold earned through labor, one rejoices happily in heaven.
What else is to be sought there by men from the Prācī Sarasvatī?
For by bathing in her, one attains the fruit characterized by contentment, austerity, sacrifice, and so forth. 139–140.

Those men who drink from the auspicious, divine Sarasvatī flowing toward the east— O Mārkaṇḍeya, the sage declared that those men are not to be known as true kings. Having reached the river Sarasvatī, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding bathing.
Whether one has eaten or not yet eaten, whether by day or by night—142—that sacred ford (tīrtha) is remembered as the most ancient and preeminent among all tīrthas;
it is proclaimed to be the destroyer of sin and the generator of merit for living beings. 143

Furthermore, those who have cultivated their souls, having bathed there and worshipped Janārdana according to their ability, go to the celestial realm (triviṣṭapa). Viṣṇu is the foremost of the gods; therefore, the Sarasvatī flows where he is.
The son of Brahmā spoke to that supreme tīrtha on earth which had been served [by him].
Then, regarding that great tīrtha as one of supreme splendor, Sarasvatī remained there gazing upon the Mandākinī. 145–146.

Svayambhuva declared that sacred ford to be the supreme among all holy sites, for there one attains a merit equal to that of the Mandākinī. In that place, the goddess Sarasvatī resides, praised by the gods.
Perceiving her to be alone, with a dejected face and a distressed mind, Brahmā then created a female companion of pure vision;
and Hari likewise quickly brought forth a doe with lotus-like eyes.
The Lord of Gods, Vajrapāṇi, dispatched even Vajriṇī;
and the three-eyed God, the blue-throated one whose banner is the bull, produced a female companion for Sarasvatī who possessed the luster of a young deer. 150.
O King, being observed by her friends as one who lacked substance, the celestial maiden, delighted, began to depart at the command of the gods;
then, together with her friends, she prepared to go toward the eastern direction. 151-152.

Among all those [rivers] that are identical to Sarasvatī, Prācīsarasvatī is remembered as the most excellent; even those animals on earth that drink her water shall go to heaven, just like the best of the twice-born who do so through sacrifices.

Like a wish-fulfilling gem, this Sarasvatī is to be known here as the Eastern [River]; likewise, she is the cause for the fulfillment of desires, like the river Madānadā. Having looked toward the southern direction, she has turned back again toward the west. 154–155.

"Go now toward the east, to the direction of the Gaṅgā and other such [sacred sites], as previously described. O Goddess, you must not forget me as you return the way you came. (156) Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Descent of the Tīrthas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 32.
Chapter Thirty-Three.
Bhīṣma said:
How was Rāma awakened here by Mārkaṇḍeya?
O Sage, how did their meeting come to pass, at what time, and when?
O great sage, tell us truly according to the facts: whose son was Mārkaṇḍeya, how was that one of great asceticism born, and what is the etymology of his name?
Pulastya said:
Now I shall relate to you once more the origin of Mārkaṇḍeya.
In a former kalpa, there was formerly a renowned sage named Mṛkaṇḍu. 3.

The highly fortunate son of Bhṛgu, together with his wife, performed austerities; while he was dwelling in the forest, a son was born to him. Having reached the age of five, the boy was already preeminent in virtues.
Then, while wandering in the courtyard of that wise man, the boy remained there for a very long time and awakened to his true purpose.
His father then asked him, "How long is the lifespan of my son?"
"Tell me by counting, whether his years are few or many.
Thus addressed by Mṛkaṇḍu, that wise one spoke these words:
"O Lord of Sages, the lifespan of your son has been ordained by the Creator to be six months."
"You must not grieve at all; this truth has been declared by you.
Having heard those words spoken by the wise Bhīṣma, the boy’s father then performed his initiation ceremony.
His father said to him, "Pay homage to the sages.
Thus addressed by his father, he was delighted at the prospect of salutation; for one who pays homage to all castes does not perceive the distinction between caste and non-caste.
Five months and twenty-five days had passed when the seven sages arrived there by way of Mārga;
they were seen by that boy and all were saluted by him.
The venerable ones said to Bhavatri: "He is a boy, wearing a staff and a girdle.
Having spoken thus, they no longer saw the boy, for his life had been exhausted.
O King, knowing that his lifespan was only five days, they became afraid because of him.
Taking that boy with them, they went into the presence of Brahmā. O King, having set him down, they prostrated before the Grandfather;
he was then greeted by Brahmā, who had been informed of the matter by them.
The child was declared long-lived by Brahmā in the presence of the sages;
then those sages were delighted upon hearing these words from the Grandfather.
Seeing the Grandfather and the sages, he spoke, filled with wonder.
"Let it be reported who this boy is and for what purpose he has come.
O King, the sages then informed him of everything: "This is the son of Mṛkaṇḍu whose life is exhausted; please grant longevity to this child."

But because his lifespan was short, the sage tied this girdle upon him, gave him the sacred thread and the staff, and instructed him thus: "O child, whatever person you see wandering upon the earth," His father spoke these words: "Salutation must indeed be offered to him; O Grandfather, this man was seen wandering upon the earth, devoted to the practice of saluting, having arrived here by the turn of fate during his pilgrimage. (20-21)
"How can the word spoken by you— that this boy shall be long-lived— be made true for us?
When they had spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [replied].
"Because of these truthful words, this earth shall remain secure from all fear.
Brahmā said:
"O child, there will arise one Mārkaṇḍeya who shall be equal to me in lifespan."
O best of sages, at the beginning and likewise at the end of a kalpa, this was the thought of that supreme sage.
Thus, O sages, having propitiated Bāla in the world of Brahmā from Pitāmaha, they sent him back once again to the surface of the earth.
When the brāhmaṇas who had gone on the pilgrimage to Tīrthayātrāṅga had departed, Mārkaṇḍeya went to his own father’s house and spoke to him:
"I was led to the world of Brahmā by sages who discourse upon Brahman."
Having granted boons to me, he was dismissed after bestowing upon me long life.
This and other things were given by me; they have passed away and cause you anxiety.
Likewise, at the beginning and at the end of a kalpa, it shall happen immediately thereafter.
"By the grace of that very Brahmā, the creator of the world,
my father, I shall go to Puṣkara, prepared to perform austerities;
there I shall worship the Grandfather, the Lord of the gods."

I shall gratify Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds— the god who grants the attainment of all desires, who destroys all enemies, who bestows all happiness, and who is the supreme refuge of Indra and the other deities. (30–31)
Having heard the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, Amṛkaṇḍu, the best of sages, experienced supreme joy for a single moment as he drew a deep breath; then,
steadying his mind with fortitude, he spoke these words.
Today my fruit of birth and life has become a life well-lived (33), since you,
the creator of all the worlds, the Grandfather, have been seen by me;
through you, a son who sustains the lineage, I am truly possessed of an heir (34).
Go and behold the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā), residing at Puṣkara;
upon seeing that Lord of the Universe, men are freed from old age and death,
and they attain happiness, sovereignty, and imperishable merit from their austerities.
There are three white peaks and three springs;
likewise, there are three Puṣkaras, but we do not know the reason for that: the smallest, the middle one, and the third, the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara.

O Great King, at Puṣkara, where there are auspicious springs designated by the word "Śṛṅga," the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are eternally present; therefore, there is no place on earth more meritorious than this. 38.

The dustless and stainless water of Puṣkara, renowned throughout the three worlds, is the path to the realm of Brahmā; only the fortunate behold it. One who maintains the agnihotra sacrifice for more than a hundred years [attains no such merit as those who behold Puṣkara].
"I was unable to observe even a single Kārttikī at Puṣkara; that deed could not be accomplished by me through my own actions.
Therefore, O Father, Death, the destroyer of all, has been conquered by you effortlessly."
There, the unseen Lord of Gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"No other mortal on the surface of the earth shall be equal to you;
indeed, I have been pleased by him since his birth five years ago."
"By my boon, you shall undoubtedly attain the status of being comparable to those who live for a long time; such is my word of blessing.
Having spoken thus, they all went to the worlds of Brahmā as they desired.
Thus, by that son of Ṛkaṇḍu who had attained such faith, a hermitage was established; it is known as Mārkaṇḍāśrama.
Having bathed there and become pure, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. 45-46.
"A man whose soul is purified of all sins becomes long-lived.
Pulastya said:
"In this manner, I shall further relate another ancient history (itihāsa). 47.
Just as the Tīrtha Puṣkara was established by Rāma, so too,
in ancient times, Rāma— accompanied by Maithilī and Lakṣmaṇa— departed from Citrakūṭa.
Having reached the hermitage of Atri, he questioned that best of sages.
Rāma said:
O great sage, which are the meritorious tīrthas, or what is the sacred field (kṣetra), where, having gone, a yogi may be reunited with his kinsmen? 49
"I do not attain peace at all; O Lord of excellent vows, tell me this:
I am tormented by these three—the dwelling in the forest, the death of the King, and the separation from Bharata. (50–51)
Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, that bull among brahmins then meditated for a very long time and spoke these words.
Atri said:
"Well said, O hero, increaser of the Raghu dynasty!
My father performed the famous pilgrimage site named Puṣkara. There are two mountains renowned as the boundaries, the Yajña and Parvata mountains."
Between those two, there are three sacrificial pits—the eldest, the middle, and the youngest. Having gone there, satisfy Daśaratha with the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas);
it is the most excellent of all holy fords (tīrthas) and the highest of all sacred fields (kṣetras). 54–55.
O descendant of Raghu’s lineage, there is the Aviyoga lake;
O joy of the Raghus, there is another well of good fortune (*saubhāgya-kūpa*) with excellent water.
By offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) at those places as well, the ancestors attain liberation.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) declared that this shall remain so until the time of the dissolution of all beings.
"O Rāghava, go there; you shall make your return again. Having said, "So be it," Rāma also set his mind upon departing.

Having proceeded toward Mount Ṛkṣavat and likewise toward the city of Vaidiśa, and having crossed the river Carmaṇvatī, he reached the Sacrificial Mountain (Yajñaparvata). Having traversed that with speed, he stayed at the middle Puṣkara.
He fully gratified the ancestors and the gods with water offerings. At the conclusion of his bath, the wise Rāma beheld there the eminent sage Mārkaṇḍeya approaching, accompanied by his disciples.
Having gone before him and respectfully prostrated, he asked: "O Lord, in which direction is the pit of sorrow caused by separation? He replied:
"I am the son of Daśaratha, known among people by the name Rāma."
"I have come here at the command of the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva) to behold the Saubhāgyavāpī.
O Blessed One, please tell me about that place and those two wells.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Mārkaṇḍeya replied.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O virtuous descendant of Raghu, may it be well with you; you have performed a meritorious deed, since you have now arrived here in the course of your pilgrimage."
"Come, come and behold that pond which grants freedom from separation;
for here, in this very well, one attains non-separation from all—whether in the next world or this world, whether living or dead. (66)
Having heard these words of the lord of sages, Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, then remembered King Daśaratha, O King,
as well as Bharata along with Śatrughna, his other brothers, and the citizens.
While he was reflecting thus, the time of twilight arrived; having performed the evening twilight rites together with the sages, O Raghava,
he slept there for the night accompanied by his brother and his wife.
At the end of the night, following his dreams,
the joy of the Raghus remained in Ayodhyā with his father, mother,
and others, as well as many kinsmen, once the auspicious marriage ceremony had been completed.
Seated together with his wife and surrounded by the sages,
he was seen in this very same manner by Lakṣmaṇa and likewise by Sītā. At dawn, all of that was recounted to the sages.
The sages replied, "So be it; this is true, O best of the Raghus.
It is recorded in the tradition that a śrāddha must necessarily be performed upon seeing the deceased.
Furthermore, the ancestors desire prosperity and likewise long for food."
O Rāghava, they will grant a vision in a dream to one endowed with devotion;
there shall certainly be no separation for you from your brother, nor from your father, nor from Bharata, throughout the fourteen years, O Rāghava. (75)
Perform the śrāddha for the Kuru king as well as for King Daśaratha, the hero. All these sages are devoted to you and have made themselves available; so too have I, Jamadagni, Bhāradvāja, and Lomaśa.
"Devarāta and Śamīka— these six are the best of the twice-born;
O mighty-armed one, you must procure the necessary provisions for their śrāddha ceremony,
including the primary items of iṅguda flour-cakes along with jujube and āmalaka fruits."

O you of noble vows, grant satisfaction to the Brahmins through this gift of a *śrāddha*, with unripe *śrīphala* fruits, various kinds of roots in great abundance, and by means of meat, grain, and diverse foods along the path. 79–80.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest, he who, being self-restrained and restricted in diet,
offers libations to the ancestors, shall obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
We, however, are going to Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara for the purpose of bathing.
Having spoken thus, O King, all those sages departed from Rāghava. Then the Lord said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Bring me a pure deer, a rabbit with clear eyes, black vegetables, and likewise honey."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, quickly gather for the śrāddha ceremony the foremost jambīra fruits, various roots, ripe kapittha fruits, and whatever other fruits there may be."
Thus, at Rāma’s command, the descendant of Raghu performed everything;
having brought various roots of *badara*, *iṅguda*, and *śāka* trees from there, he constructed a great artificial mound with Rāma. 85–86.
And having learned that Jānakī’s meal was ready, Rāma informed him;
then, having bathed in the Yoga-vāpī, Rāma waited upon those sages while the sun had moved past midday at the time known as Kutapa.
All those sages who had been invited by Rāma arrived;
seeing those lords of munis come, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, feeling ashamed, left Rāma’s side and stood elsewhere. 88–89.
With eyes wide open in amazement and trembling with thought, the Brahmins, having arrived at the time of the śrāddha, reflected:
"The Brahmins have been fed by Rāma according to the rules prescribed in the Smṛtis. (90)
All the Vedic rites have been fully described;
likewise, the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas begins with the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Once the Brahmins have eaten, one should offer the piṇḍas in the proper sequence.
When those foremost of brahmins had been sent away according to their capacity and given their sacrificial fees,
and they had departed, Rāma spoke these words to his beloved:
"O fair-browed one, why were you distressed upon seeing the great sages who had come here?"
Tell me that entire truth and its cause without delay;
there must be a reason for this, so do not conceal it from me. O lady of pure smiles, I adjure you by my life and by that of Lakṣmaṇa.
Having been addressed thus by her husband, she then stood with her face cast down in shame;
shedding a stream of tears, she spoke these words to Rāghava:
"O Lord, hear what kind of wonder I have seen here."
O Indra among kings, Rāma, being thus meditated upon by you, has arrived here;
likewise, two others similar to him, joined with the bodies of Brahmins—these three have come, O descendant of Raghu. (97–98)

"O Raghava, the ancestors were seen by me within the bodies of the Brahmins; having seen them, I was filled with shame and departed from your presence. Indeed, you have fed the Brahmins and performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rites."
Clad in bark and deerskin, how could you have been the one walking before the king? O slayer of enemy heroes, this which you have uttered is the truth;
yet the silken garments were taken away by Kaikeyī.
From that time forward, O Mother, knowing that I had taken refuge in the forest of Cīrinī, I did not think of anything else, so that no sorrow might befall you.
O scorcher of foes, I truly do not remember my mother or my father.
"O Rāghava, when will this forest dwelling end here? O Lord, as I contemplate this very thing again and again incessantly, my days pass away; by your feet I swear. 104.

"How can I, O King, offer this food with my own hand as if it were for a slave? For even among slaves, there is one who is a slave himself who would never consume such a thing. How then could I venture to bestow it upon him? (105)
I, who was seen by the king in the city adorned with every ornament,
fanning the lord of men with a yak-tail whisk in my hand—
how shall I now look upon the ruler of the earth with my limbs smeared with the filth of sweat? (106–107)
"Clearly, having reached heaven through you as his son, he has been delivered;
for seeing me, a young woman suffering in the forest and innocent of any fault, this king’s grief would have arisen—O Rāghava, I would not have perished. (108)
"O Rāma, you are equal to my very life; this is a secret between us here.
By that truth, I shall now touch your feet. Hearing those words of his beloved who spoke so sweetly, Rāghava was pleased.
Having brought him close and embraced him very firmly with great respect, O hero,
he then partook of food, and afterwards Jānakī ate.
Thus they both remained there for that night.

When the thousand-rayed sun had risen, they set their minds on departing. Rāghava went toward the west for a distance of one krośa as far as the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara, remaining there in the eastern part of Puṣkara.
Then he heard these words spoken by the messenger of the gods:
"O Rāghava, may it be well with you! This sacred ford is very difficult to attain.
O hero, remaining in this place, bring about the purification of your own soul."
"The work of the gods must be performed by you; the enemies of the gods must be slain.
Then, with a joyful mind, the hero spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa: "O son of Sumitrā, I have been favored by Brahmā, the God of gods."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, having established a hermitage here, I wish to observe for one month an excellent vow that purifies the body.
When Lakṣmaṇa had replied, "So be it," he completed the vow.
Then, at Puṣkara, Rāma duly gratified his ancestors with offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other gifts, as well as with śrāddha rites.
[There he visited] Kanakā, Suprabhā, Nandā, Prācī, and Sarasvatī.
At Pañcasrotas in Puṣkara, which bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors,
Rāma, having performed that daily worship of the ancestors preceded by the rites for the Pitṛs,
then spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, quickly bring water from the Puṣkara lake;
having performed the washing of my feet, prepare a bed upon the layer of grass. When the night has passed, we shall depart for the southern direction."
Lakṣmaṇa, however, spoke these words: "O Rāma, let water be brought by Sītā; I will never, at any time, assume the state of a slave.
He added, "Furthermore, she is very well-nourished and quite stout."
"What will you do with this wife who is so ill-suited? Or rather, will this beloved go behind you as you depart for the world of the immortals?
You have always nourished her well at all times."
"O best of the Raghus, she, being delighted, constantly causes me distress;
and you too cause me distress, O Rāma, for harm arises elsewhere [from this]. And because of you, I am always afflicted by thirst along with hunger."
Free from doubt, listen further to this:
no one at all is seen following after those who have died—not even their wife, son, or wealth; thus say the wise. 127–128.
Your father, having abandoned the thornless kingdom and sent you away to the forest out of a desire to please Kaikeyī, has died;
yet here remains that Kaikeyī, along with all the wealth and kinsmen.
"O Great King, I believe that Daśaratha alone has attained his final destination; Sītā will certainly not go with you. What will you do with her now, while Rāghava is away? (130-131)
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, which he had never heard before, Rāghava stood despondent, as did the fair-faced Sītā. Then Sītā did everything exactly as Lakṣmaṇa had said.

Having bathed and eaten there at Puṣkara, O hero, those two with lotus-like eyes spent the night and set their minds on departing. "Come, arise, O son of Sumitrā, let us go toward the southern direction. 133-134.
The son of Sumitrā said to the King: "O lotus-eyed one, how can I possibly go? You yourself should go with this wife of yours.
O Raghava, I shall not go to another forest, nor indeed to Ayodhyā."
"I shall dwell in this forest for fourteen years;
if you do not go to Ayodhyā without me,
O King, you must come by this path, O Lord."
"If I survive this time, I shall go again to my father's city; I will perform penance—what will you do with me?
"Go, gentle one; may your path be auspicious; let there be no adversaries on the way."
I see you again, O lotus-eyed one, arrived with your wife in Ayodhyā, the ancestral kingdom of your father and grandfather, O lord of men;
both Śatrughna and Bharata remain intent on carrying out your commands. (139-140)
O scorcher of foes, I am constantly opposed to this dwelling in the forest, both by day and by night; O gentle one, I am unable to perform my duties here, so please go as you please.
To Saumitri, who was speaking thus, the joy of the Raghus replied:
"How is it that you have previously departed from Ayodhyā with me?
O Rāma, I shall dwell in the forest for nine and five years."
"O Raghava, I shall not dwell anywhere even in heaven if I am separated from you;
by that sacrifice, my sin will also become as great as a tiger's.
"Grant me your favor, O Raghava; do not lead me away as well."
"Now, O slayer of enemies, how will you remain on this half-way path?
Lakṣmaṇa replied to Rāma, "I shall not go back to the forest again.
Knowing that Lakṣmaṇa was firmly resolved, Rāma spoke these words.
"Follow me, O son of Sumitrā; I shall go to the forest alone.
When Rāma had spoken thus, Lakṣmaṇa replied, "Let this Sītā be the second [companion].
Then, having accepted Rāma's words, he and Lakṣmaṇa rose up together.
Having reached the boundary mountain, the limit of the sacred field, those two subduers of enemies— Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—
bowed down with the prostration of the eight limbs before the three-eyed Lord of gods, the god of gods who wields the Pināka bow, Ajagandha. 148–149.
Standing with a composed mind, he praised Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī;
with palms joined in reverence and his body covered in horripilation, he was overcome by a state of sattva, having shaken off the qualities of rajas and tamas. 150.
He perceived the Lord, the cause of the worlds, the sovereign of the gods.
Rāma said:
"He who is the creator of this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, and who is likewise the giver of pleasure and pain to what has been created."
I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, who is the cause of dissolution and who, at the time of the end, [protects] him.

(152) I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, who places upon his head the Gaṅgā—whose pure, beautiful, and tossing waters are made turbulent by great waves as she falls from the sky—as if it were a garland of swaying flowers. (153)

I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, by whose lotus feet the peak of Mount Kailāsa was held steady while it was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who himself resembled a peak of Kailāsa;
he by whom the sons of Danu were repeatedly repelled in battle, as well as the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas with all their excellent powers. 154.
I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the bestower of refuge, who was joined by the foremost of sages subsisting on fruits and roots;
who, at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, struck out the eyes of Bhaga and likewise knocked out the row of teeth of Pūṣan;
and who paralyzed Indra’s hand as it was grasped with the thunderbolt. 155–156.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, by taking refuge in whom men become enjoyers of happiness—even those who have committed sins, whose minds are attached to sense objects, and who are not endowed with knowledge, lineage, or learning.
(157) Born of Atri, his splendor is equal to ten million suns; he is the terror of the foremost gods and demons.
I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, who forcibly drank the fiercely blazing Kālakūṭa poison.
(158) The blessed Lord Maheśa bestows many boons upon Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Maruts, and Ṣaṇmukha;
he brought Nandin back from the mouth of Death—I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter. (159)

In a cave of the Himalayas, propitiated by severe penance through the smoke-vow (dhūmavrata) in a manner inaccessible even to others in mind, the Great-Souled One revealed the Saṃjīvanī [mantra] to Bhṛgu; to that Śaṅkara, the granter of refuge, I go for refuge.
(160) [He is served] by various powerful lords of the Gaṇas, whose faces resemble elephants and cats, who shattered the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, who is worshipped by hosts of gods along with the world-protectors.

161 I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, who, having mounted his heroic bull—white as a conch, the moon, and a kunda flower—is followed by the daughter of the lord of mountains and ascends into the sky adorned with clouds of dissolution. 162

I seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the bestower of shelter, who forcibly protected that peaceful sage—who was being led away by those terrifying and most fierce men devoted to the enforcement of restraints—as he remained bowed with devotion and intent on praise;
I seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, whose head is like a young lotus and who has severed [the demon’s] head.

(164) I seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, bowing with devotion to whose feet—the feet of the Giver of Boons—and having praised him with pure words, the sun, his soul unwearied, dispels the darkness with his blazing rays. (165)

"But those men who, being deluded, do not recognize you—the teacher of the supreme gods—possessing the sovereignty over this world of moving and non-moving beings through the authority of the Vedas; later, with their minds unpurified, they undergo torment.
While he was thus praising him, the trident-wielder whose banner is the bull spoke.
Delighted and with a contented mind, Rudra spoke these words to Rāghava: Rudra said:
"O Rāma, I am pleased; may it be well with you. You have been born into a stainless lineage."

And you too, O God who has assumed a human form, are worthy of worship by the worlds. With you as their protector, O Lord, the gods shall remain happy for eternal years, even when the fourteen-year period has long passed.
Those inhabitants of the earth who behold you upon your arrival in Ayodhyā shall enjoy happiness here and imperishable residence in heaven;
having accomplished this great task for the sake of the gods, you may return again to the city.
Having thus bowed to the god, Rāghava quickly departed.
Reaching the river Indramārga and binding his mass of matted hair,
Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Give me this bow."
Having heard those words of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa indeed said to Sītā:
"O Queen, for what reason has Rāma abandoned me without cause? I do not know of any offense for which the mighty-armed one is angry. (173)

"Abandoned by Rāma, I shall undoubtedly give up my life. There is no purpose in living thus; shame, shame on me, a defiler of my lineage, by whom the wrath of the Noble One has been provoked through my sinful deeds. (174-175)
"Which worlds shall I go to, having been ill-disposed toward the Great-Souled One?
Placing both hands to his mouth with a tearful throat, he spoke these words: "I have not offended Rāma in deed, in thought, or in speech. (176)
"O Goddess, if my feet are touched, there shall be no other recourse for me.
Then Sītā said to Rāma: "Why has your younger brother been abandoned?
O child, let this partiality toward Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity, be cast aside."
Rāghava, however, said to Sītā:
"O beloved, I shall never abandon Lakṣmaṇa, even in a dream;
O lady of beautiful hips, you have previously heard of the conduct of this region."
In this land, it is true that all people are solely intent on their own self-interest;
they do not look out for one another, nor do they listen to words beneficial to themselves—neither sons to their father, nor fathers to their sons. (180–181)
"The disciple does not heed the word of the guru, nor does the guru likewise heed the word of the disciple;
affection is what binds one to another's purpose, for no one is dear to anyone by nature.
Even as he was speaking thus, they reached the great river Revā.
Kakutstha, together with his younger brother and Sītā, performed the consecration ceremony;
having gratified his ancestors and the deities with water offerings, he gazed repeatedly at the sun and the gods with a concentrated mind.
Having performed his ablutions, Rāma, the king of kings, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
was like the Blessed Lord Śiva, who has performed his ablutions together with the Daughter of the Mountain and Guha.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Vision of Mārkaṇḍeya’s Hermitage," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Bhīṣma said:
At what time was [this] spoken by the Blessed Brahmā, the creator of the world?
It behoves you to tell me how those worthy of sacrifice began the performance of the rite.
What were the names of those officiating priests appointed by Brahmā, and what sacrificial fee was given to them by that Great-Souled One?
"Proclaim to me the truth of how it truly happened and how it occurred;
great curiosity has arisen regarding the sacrifice of the Grandfather.
Pulastya said:
Previously, I have explained how, after Svāyambhuva Manu had created all the Prajāpatis, he was told: "Indeed, perform the act of creation.
He himself, however, went to Puṣkara and brought back the extensive ritual of sacrifice.
Having assembled all the necessary materials, he took his place in the sacrificial fire-chamber.
Gandharvas sang constantly and throngs of Apsarases danced;
the four priests—Brahman, Udgātṛ, Hotṛ, and Adhvaryu—were the carriers of the sacrifice.
Each of these has three other assistants appointed by himself:
the Brahman, the Brahmaṃśasin, the Potṛ, and the Āgnīdhra.
This fourfold group constitutes the Brāhmī science of Anvīkṣikī, which encompasses all branches of knowledge.
The Udgātṛ, the Pratyudgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya—
this second group of four is proclaimed as belonging to the Udgātṛ.
Furthermore, the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, and the Acchāvāka [form the third group].

O son of Śaṃtanu, this group of four in the third [pressing] consists of the Grāvastut as the fourth; likewise, in the fourth [pressing], there is this group of four consisting of the Adhvaryu, the Pratiṣṭhātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ.
These sixteen are declared by those who contemplate the Vedas to be the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Three hundred and sixty sacrifices were created by the Self-born;
and among all these, they always designate the twice-born as the performers.
Some desired Sadasya as the Udgātṛ, Trisāman as the Adhvaryu, Nārada as the Brahman, Gautama as the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin,
Devagarbha as the Potṛ, and Devala as the Āgnīdhra.
Udgātā was Aṅgiras, and Pratyudgātā was Pulaha;
Nārāyaṇa was the Pratihartṛ, and Atri is called the Subrahmaṇya.
In that sacrifice, Bhṛgu was the Hotṛ, and Vasiṣṭha was the Maitra.
Acchāvāka was declared to be Kratu, and Grāvastut was Cyavana;
Pulastya was the Adhvaryu, and Vaiśaṃbhi was the Pratiṣṭhātṛ. Bṛhaspati was the Neṣṭṛ there, and Śāṃśapāyana was the Unnetṛ.
Dharma was present there as a member of the assembly, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and kinsmen;
likewise were Bharadvāja, Śamīka, Purukutsa, Yugandhara, Enaka, Tīrṇaka, Keśa, and Kutapa. (17–18)
Garga, Vedaśiras, Trisāman, and Adhvaryu were made [his disciples], as were Kaṇva and others, as well as Mārkaṇḍeya and Gaṇḍi;
together with their sons, grandsons, disciples, and kinsmen. (19)
Performing their duties there day and night without weariness,
when the Manvantara had passed, the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice took place;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) was given to the Brahman priest, and the eastern quarter was the fee for the Hotṛ priest.
To the Adhvaryu he gave the western quarter, and likewise to the Udgātṛ the northern;
thus Brahmā gave the entire three worlds as their sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Furthermore, a hundred cows should be given by the wise for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
Twenty-four more than forty—that is, sixty-four—are prescribed for those occupying the second position;
sixteen auspicious bulls should be given to those in the third position. (23–24)
Likewise, one should cause twelve others to be given to the Āgnīdhra and other priests;
by this same number, villages, female slaves, goats, and sheep [should be given].
Having bathed at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice, a feast for a thousand [guests] must be provided.
The Self-born One declared that the sacrificer should give away his entire possessions;
the giving to the Adhvaryus and the Sadasyas is prescribed according to one's own will.
Then, having invoked Viṣṇu, Brahmā, filled with joy, spoke these words: 26–27.
"O you of noble vows, bring Sāvitrī here after she has been propitiated;
for when she sees you, that lady of beautiful countenance will become angry. [Bring her] with affectionate, conciliatory words, and especially those endowed with logical reasoning."
Your speech is always sweet, and from your tongue flows nectar. He who does not heed your words is not seen even in the three worlds.
Go together with the Gandharvas and bring back my beloved. 29-30.
Propitiated by you, she will surely come to this path, being well-pleased; you must not cause delay, but go quickly to Vraja and Mādhava.
Let Lakṣmī go before you, and let the auspicious Sāvitrī go to her own abode.
Go to her place and console my beloved;
O Goddess, he does not wish to do anything unpleasant for you, for he always remains with his face turned toward you, O beautiful one. 32-33.
"Many such sweet words as these should be made to hear by the Goddess, so that she may soon become satisfied.
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, the creator of the world, Viṣṇu then [acted accordingly].
He went with haste to where Sāvitrī was staying.
Seeing Keśava approaching from afar together with his wife, she rose up quickly and was greeted by Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods; salutations to you, the wife of Brahmā.
Indeed, by bowing down to you, every person is liberated from sin.
(37) You are the devoted wife, the highly fortunate one, who dwells within the heart of Brahmā.
Thinking of you day and night, he longs for your favor. Ask this dear friend, the virtuous Lakṣmī, daughter of Bhṛgu;
if you have faith in these words of mine, O fair-eyed one. (38-39)

Having spoken thus, Śauri then touched both feet of Sāvitrī with both his hands and, saying, "O Goddess, salutations to you! O Mother of the World, who are worshipped by the world! he bowed down in reverence.
Having drawn back her feet, the goddess took Hari’s two hands with her own hands and said to Viṣṇu: "O Acyuta, everything has been forgiven by me;
this Lakṣmī shall always dwell within your heart."
Without you, she will never find delight anywhere else;
born as the daughter of Bhṛgu’s wife, this woman of excellent vows is your wife.
Furthermore, through the efforts of the gods and the Dānavas, she was brought forth once more from the ocean.
O Blessed One, wherever she makes her descent—
whether as a goddess in a divine body or as a human woman among men— she will undoubtedly be your companion for a long time, observing the vow of conjugal fidelity.
"O Lord, tell me indeed what must be done by me here.
Viṣṇu said: "The conclusion of the sacrifice has occurred; I have been sent to your presence. (46)
"Bring Sāvitrī quickly so that she may perform her bath with me; let the goddess come swiftly, filled with joy. Having gone there, see your own husband accompanied by all the gods. 47.
Lakṣmī said:
"O Noble One, arise quickly and go to where the Grandfather is;
I will not go without you, for your feet have been touched by me."
Raising her up, he took her right hand with his own right hand.
Knowing that Sāvitrī was delaying, the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) then spoke these words to Mahādeva, who was standing nearby.
"Go with this Pārvatī, O destroyer of asuras;
let Gaurī go before you and you follow behind, O Śaṅkara. Having thus enlightened her, act in such a way that she returns quickly."
When this had been said, Parvati and the Supreme Lord (Shiva) then went and spoke to that couple, the beloved of Brahma: "O devoted wife,
a great task must be performed by you there."
"Ask this fair-hipped Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain;
or ask this large-eyed Lakṣmī, the consort of Indra, O lady of auspicious countenance.
Or ask whichever among them you trust, O Goddess—salutations to you."
The blessing was granted by that Goddess to the trident-bearing God of gods:
"O Śaṅkara, Gaurī shall always abide in half of your body;
O God, most beautiful in the three worlds, you shall shine with her."
"O Slayer of Enemies, let the entire world become partakers of happiness through you, our protector!"—
speaking thus, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā,
was seized by Gaurī with her left hand and Lakṣmī with her right.
Having paid homage to that goddess, Śaṅkara spoke these words: "Come, come, O highly fortunate one, to where your husband resides;
go there, O lady of beautiful hips, for a husband is the supreme refuge for women."
"O Goddess, you should go out of affection for this great undertaking;
O Goddess, here Lakṣmī and Pārvatī stand before you. O fair-faced Goddess, by their word and our own—"
"O beloved of Brahmā, it is fitting to act so as to humble his pride.
O Goddess, requested by us, go there filled with joy.
Gaurī said:
"O Goddess, you yourself have always been my beloved;
Lakṣmī is held in your hand, and Dākṣāyaṇī has been supported by me. Come, come, O illustrious one, to where your husband stands. 63.
The Goddess was placed between Nīta and Sātuta;
Viṣṇu and Rudra were at the front, as were Śakra and the other gods,
along with the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and the entire triple world with its mobile and immobile beings.
Then that goddess Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, arrived there.
Seeing the beautiful-faced Sāvitrī, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, together with Gāyatrī, spoke these words: 65–66.
"This goddess is my servant; I stand under your command. O lady of beautiful hips, command me here as to what task must be performed by me.
Thus addressed by the god Brahmā himself, that goddess—
With her face cast down in shame, the goddess said nothing at all.
68 Urged by Brahmā, Goddess Gāyatrī fell at his feet and said: "O Lord, you have been wronged; please forgive me, O Goddess, salutations to you! 69
Having respectfully embraced her by the neck and clasped her tightly,
he consoled Gāyatrī, saying, "This husband of mine is worthy of honor;
his word must be carried out, for the husband is the lord of the lives of women."
The Blessed One previously stated at the time of creation that Viriñci said:
"There is no separate sacrifice for women, nor a vow, nor even a fast; whatever word her husband speaks, she should do that without disparagement. (71-72)

She who utters censure of her husband, or likewise of her sister, or engages in slander or idle chatter, goes to hell. A woman who observes a vow of fasting while her husband is still living [is likewise doomed].
She robs her husband of his life-span and, upon death, desires hell.
Knowing this, O virtuous lady, you must never do anything displeasing to your husband, nor should you ever serve his right side in any way whatsoever. 74-75.

"In all matters, I shall resort to his right wing, while you, O virtuous one, shall occupy the left; Nārada and Puṣkara shall likewise remain by his side. Furthermore, other stations of Brahmā and various sacred shrines are established there."
"May you obtain splendor as long as creation continues;
both you and I must remain here without a doubt.
At Puṣkara, by the side of Brahmā, take your place on my left. (77-78)
"By this instruction, may you remain at ease, endowed with happiness.
Gāyatrī said: "I shall do exactly as you have directed. (79)
"O friend who is as dear to me as my own life, it was solely due to your own act born of ignorance that this has happened; O Goddess, you are my younger sister, so you ought to protect me always.
Then Brahmā, the God of gods, together with Viṣṇu, [was at] Puṣkara.
At the conclusion of their bath, he granted boons to all the gods:
to Śakra, the lord of the gods; to Divākara (the Sun), the lord of luminaries; likewise to Soma, the lord of the constellations; and to Varuṇa, the lord of fluids. 81-82.
He appointed Dakṣa as the lord of the Prajāpatis, the ocean as the lord of the rivers,
Kubera the overseer of wealth, and likewise the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) as the lord of the Rākṣasas,
of all beings, and of the Gaṇas.
Having likewise assigned Manu to the human beings and Garuḍa to the birds,
Vasiṣṭha to the sages, and the Sun to the planets, the Grandfather, the God of gods, bestowed these and other such offices.
Brahmā spoke respectfully to both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara:
"In all the holy places on earth, you two are the most excellent objects of worship; without you two, a sacred site never attains its state of holiness. (86)

Wherever a liṅga or even an image is seen, that place becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha), becoming holy and bestowing all fruits. And those men who shall perform worship with offerings [will likewise attain such results]. 87–88.
With me placed at your head, how could there be any fear of disease for them?
In those kingdoms where your festivals, worship,
and all such rites shall proceed, hear now what the fruit thereof shall be.
Neither mental anxieties nor physical diseases, nor calamities, nor the fear of hunger; neither separation from loved ones nor association with those who are disliked;
neither eye disease nor headache, nor bile-related ailments, nor colic, nor fistula—none of these shall exist. (89–91)
Therein, there is no fear of malevolent sorcery, nor epilepsy, nor cholera;
there is prosperity according to one's desire, as well as unsurpassed and perfect wisdom, health in every respect, long life, progeny, and wealth. 92.
There shall be no untimely death for cows, nor shall there be clouds that yield little rain;
there shall be no trees bearing fruit out of season, nor even the slightest fear of portents.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu then prepared to praise Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said:

"Homage to the infinite one, whose mind is pure, who is the embodiment of his own essential nature, who possesses a thousand arms, who is the creator originating from a thousand rays, whose body is vast, and whose actions are stainless. (95)

Salutations to Śambhu, the remover of the suffering of the entire world; salutations to the one whose splendor is fiercer than all suns and fires; salutations to the wielder of the discus, whose knowledge is vast; and eternal salutations to the one who has made himself the abode of all intellect. 96.
O Maheśvara, Lord of the past, present, and future beings, Acyuta, the crown-jewel of the beginningless gods!
O Lord of the Great, Lord of All, Lord of the World, Lord of the Earth, Lord of the Universe—constant salutations to You!

O Lord of Sacrifice, Nārāyaṇa, Jiṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Lord of the Earth, Lord of the Universe, Eye of the Universe, Moon, Sun, Acyuta, Hero, You whose form is the source of all activity, You whose form is nectar, the Imperishable! 97–98.

O Nārāyaṇa, whose orb is filled with the flames of a blazing fire, O you who face all directions, O remover of the suffering of all gods, O immortal and imperishable one, protect me, your refugee, O All-pervading Lord! I behold your many faces, O All-pervading One, and you, the ancient goal of sacrifice.
Homage to you, Brahmā, the Lord, the source of the worlds, the great-grandfather!

100 Through many revolutions of the wheel of saṃsāra, at one time you were the supreme god among the best of gods; since you are worshipped by those whose being is purified by all-encompassing knowledge, why do I bow down to you? 101

He who knows You as existing thus prior to primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the most excellent among all knowers; though possessed of a vast form, You are here known by Your subtle form, which forcibly permeates those endowed with qualities. 102.
How indeed are You, O Sugata of auspicious deeds, one whose speech, hands, and feet are devoid of sense organs?
Even though his senses are restrained by the bonds of *saṃsāra*, how can he be known as the supreme Lord?

(103) O God, the formless which is superior to the formed cannot be attained except by those of pure disposition who worship you with the intent to sever the cycle of *saṃsāra*; thus, one may attain the state of the Four-faced One. (104)
O Lord who assumes wondrous forms, even the gods and others do not know Your supreme nature from whence You come;
therefore, O All-pervading One, one should worship that most ancient Being seated upon the lotus-throne during Your descent.
Even the creators of the universe do not know Your true essence, but he alone of pure disposition knows Your single source.
But I know how you, the ancient one, the primordial being purified by austerity, [came to be].
(106) Janaka is indeed well-known as one seated upon a lotus; such is his renown from the Purāṇas.
Even after reflecting deeply, O Lord, he who is devoid of austerity does not truly know you, the all-pervading one, in this way. (107)

Even those like us, the foremost of men, must awaken you; for those fools who, having divided their own intellects, desire to awaken you—though they possess the intelligence of those of noble fame, they are nonetheless deficient in Vedic knowledge.
Whether it be through many lifetimes or through the discerning intellect of the Vedas, there may indeed be illumination.

For one greedy for great gain, neither the lord of gods and gandharvas, Śiva, nor the Lord Viṣṇu in his subtle form can be attained; you, O God, are the manifest form of fulfilled purpose. Though gross, you are subtle and easily accessible; those who perform external rites fall into hell. 109–110.

In this [state], one is liberated or remains established, having expanded one's own nature within the essential form of the Self— consisting of the principles of the moon, fire, sun, wind, and earth— which bear identical forms. O Blessed One, please accept this praise from me, your devotee, especially since you are infinite.

O Lord, for one whose mind is purified through concentration and whose thoughts are solely devoted to the state of being You, You, O Blessed One, eternally abide within the heart. "O Blessed One, O Ancient One, salutations to You"—thus, O All-pervading One, awakened to all states of existence, this hymn to You was proclaimed by me, O Lord. 112–113.

"O Keśava, you who are omniscient and a mass of wisdom, please protect us once more from the fear associated with wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra. Brahmā said: "There is no doubt that you are omniscient, O Lord of the senses."
"You shall always be the foremost among the gods to be worshipped. 115.
After Nārāyaṇa, Rudra, bowing down with devotion, praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus. 116.
Salutations to you whose eyes are like lotus petals; salutations to you who were born from the lotus.
Salutations to the Preceptor of gods and asuras, the Supreme Self who brings about all actions. 117. Salutations to you, Lord of all gods; salutations indeed to the destroyer of delusion.
Salutations to you, who were born from the lotus-seat situated on the navel of Viṣṇu;
salutations to you, who are beautified by hands like sprouts and limbs as red as coral.
I have come to you for refuge; protect me from the cycle of worldly existence.
O Grandfather, having previously seen it with the form of a dark-blue cloud and then as a bud, he again beheld the lotus— red-faced, endowed with petals and filaments,
possessing many edges of petals, innumerable, and stainless.
Remaining there, you indeed set this creation in motion. There is no protection for the world other than you; salutations to you, who are worshipped by the universe!
I have been consumed by the curse of Sāvitrī, and my *liṅga* has fallen to the earth. 121–122.
"Now grant me peace; protect me along with my wife.
May Brahmā indeed protect my feet, and may the lotus-seated one protect my shanks.
May Viriñci, the creator, protect my hips and my private parts."
May the one resembling a lotus protect my navel; may the four-faced one protect my belly. May the creator of the universe protect my chest; may the lotus-born one protect my heart.
May the Lord of Sāvitrī protect my throat; may Hṛṣīkeśa protect my mouth.
"Padmavarṇa is my eye, and the Supreme Self is my head"; having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using the name of his guru, he who was named Śaṅkara became Śaṅkara himself.
Having said, "Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O Brahman," he fell silent.
Then Brahmā, being pleased, spoke these words to Hara:
"What desire of yours shall I fulfill today? Ask me whatever you wish.
Rudra said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Lord, or if you are the granter of boons to me, then tell me one thing, O Vibhu:
in which place do you reside, and in which various places do the twice-born always behold you? (128-129)
"O Lord of All, please tell me how that place on the surface of the earth is made beautiful by the recitation of Your name for one who is devoted to You. Brahmā said:
In Puṣkara he is the best of gods; in Gayā, the four-faced one;
in Kānyakubja, the womb of the gods; and in Bhṛgukakṣa, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha). In the Kāverī he is the creator of the universe, and in Nandipurī, Bṛhaspati.
At Prabhāsa he is Padmajanman; at Vānaryā he is Surapriya (132). At Dvāravatī he is Ṛgvedin; at Vidiśā he is Bhuvanādhipa (Lord of the World);
at Pauṇḍraka he is Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and at Hastināpura he is Piṅgākṣa (133).
I am Vijaya in Jayantī, Jayanta in Puṣkarāvata; I am Padmahasta among the Ugras, and Tamonuda in the Tamonadī.
I am Jayānandin in Ahicchatra and Janapriya in the city of Kāñcī.
I am Brahmā in Pāṭalīputra, and likewise the sage Ṛṣikuṇḍa;
Mukuṇḍa is honored in Mahitāra, Śrīkaṇṭha in Śrīnivāsa, Śubhākāra in Kāmarūpa, and Śivapriya in Vārāṇasī. (135–136)
Viṣṇu is in Mallikākṣa, Bhārgava in Mahendra, the elder in Gonarda, and Pitāmaha in Ujjayinī;
furthermore, Mahābodhi is in Kauśāmbī and Rāghava in Ayodhyā. (137)
The Lord of Sages is at Citrakūṭa; Vārāha is on the Vindhya mountain (138).
Parameṣṭhin is at Gaṅgādvāra, and Śaṅkara is on the Himavat.
Srucāhasta is at Devikā, and Srucihasta is at Caturvaṭa (139).

In Vṛndāvana he is Padmapāṇi, in Naimiṣa he holds kuśa grass in his hand, and in Goplakṣa he is Gopīndra; on the bank of the Yamunā he is Candra, at the Bhāgīrathī he is Padmatanu, and in Jalandhara he is Jalānanda. (140)
In Kauṅkaṇa I am Madrakṣa; in Kāmpilya, I am Kanakapriya (141).
In Veṅkaṭa I am Annadātā; in Kratusthala, I am Śambhu;
in Laṅkā, I am Pulastya; and in Kaśmīra, I am Haṃsavāhana (142).
Vasiṣṭha at Arbuda, Nārada at Utpalāvata, I am Melaka at Śrutidā, and the Lord of the Sea (Varuṇa) at Prapāta;
likewise, I am the Sāmaveda at Yajña and Madhurapriya at Madhura. 143.
In Aṅkoṭa he is Yajñabhoktṛ (the Enjoyer of Sacrifice) and in Brahmavāda he is Surapriya (Beloved of the Gods).
In Gomatī he is Nārāyaṇa, and in Māyāpurī he is Dvijapriya (Beloved of the Twice-born).
In Devā he is Ṛṣivedu (Known by the Sages) and Suramardana (The Destroyer of Demons), who is difficult to overcome.

In Vijayā he is Mahārūpa; in Rāṣṭravardhana he is Svarūpa; in Mālavyā he is Pṛthūdara; in Śākaṃbharī he is Rasapriya (the lover of nectar). 146. In Piṇḍāraka he is Gopāla; in Śaṅkhoddhāra he is Gavarddhana (the nourisher of cattle).
At Kādaṃbaka I am Prajādhyakṣa, and at Samasthala I am Devādhyakṣa; at Bhadrapīṭha I am Gaṅgādhara, and at Arbuda I am Jalaśāyī;
at Tryambaka I am Tripurādhīśa, and at Śrīparvata I am Trilocana.
Mahādeva is in Padmapura, Vaidhasa is in Kāpāla, Śauri is in Śṛṅgiberapura, and Cakrapāṇika is in Naumiṣa. Virūpākṣa is in Daṇḍapurī, and Gautama is in Dhūtapāpaka.
Haṃsanātha is in Mālyavatī; Dvijeṃdra is in Valikā.
Devanātha is in Indrapurī; Purandara is in Dyūtapā.
Haṃsavāha is in Tulambā; Garuḍapriya is in Caṇḍā. 150–151.
At Mahodaya he is Mahāyajña; at Suyajña he is Yajñaketana; at Siddhisvara he is Padmavarṇa; and at Vibhā he is Padmabodhana. At Devadāruvana he is Liṅga; and at Mahāpatti he is Vināyaka.
Tryambaka is in the abode of the Mothers (Mātṛkā), and Kulādhipa is in Alakā;
Gonarda is in Trikūṭa, and likewise Vāsuki is in Pātāla; Padmādhyakṣa is in Kedāra, and Suratapriya is in Kūṣmāṇḍa. 153–154.
In Kuṇḍavāpī he is Śubhāṅga, in Sāraṇī he is Takṣaka, in Akṣoṭa he is Pāpahā, and in Ambikā he is Sudarśana. In Varadā he is Mahāvīra, and in Kāntāra he is Durganāśana.
Ananta is in Parṇāṭa, Divākara in Prakāśā (156); Padmanābha is in Virājā, Svarudra in Vṛkasthala,
Mārkaṇḍeya in Vaṭaka, and Mṛgaketana in Vāhinī (157).

In Padmāvatī, there is the Lotus-House; in the sky, there is the one whose banner is the lotus. O Destroyer of Tripura, I have proclaimed to you these one hundred and eight sacred sites where my presence is manifest during the three junctions of the day. 158.

Whosoever among these, being devoted, beholds even one [of them], having attained a most stainless station, rejoices for eternal years. Whatever evil deed has been committed—whether mental, verbal, or physical—[is thereby purified]. (159–160)
All that goes to destruction; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
But that man who, having gone to all these places, beholds me—he becomes a partaker of liberation wherever I may be stationed. 161.
Through offerings of flowers, incense, and the gratification of Brahmins,
as well as through steady meditation, the Supreme Lord is swiftly attained;
the foremost fruit of his merit is likewise the fruit of liberation at the end.

Having reached the world of Brahmā, he remains there for that duration; then, at the time of renewed creation, he becomes a Vairāja deity of great austerity. Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in this world [are purified].
Whether unintentionally or intentionally, they perish at that very moment.
In this world, one who is poor, or one who has been deprived of his kingdom, having gone to these places, beholds me through meditative absorption (samādhi). 165-166.
Having performed worship and offerings, as well as the ritual bathing and libations for the ancestors,
and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), he shall soon be freed from suffering and become a king with a single umbrella— this is the truth, there is no doubt.
For those by whom the pilgrimage to Puṣkara has been performed, there arise here various royal fortunes, wealth, grain, garments, and women.
Whoever performs this ritual procedure for the pilgrimage, or causes it to be performed, [attains these rewards].

By merely hearing [this], one is liberated from all sins; even that man who has committed incest with those who should not be approached, or who has neglected the performance of Vedic rites for many years, is freed. 170.
By performing this pilgrimage even once, one attains the purificatory refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedas.
What need is there for much speaking on this matter, O Śaṅkara? By this, that which was unattainable here is attained, and even one's sin is destroyed. 171–172.
It is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices, bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and by it,
the completion of all the Vedas is indeed accomplished.
By those who have performed their twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) at Puṣkara, the Sāvitrī has been properly worshipped.
O Śaṅkara, at the close of day, that meritorious water for the twilight worship was brought by his own wife with her own hand in an excellent golden vessel, even though it was made of clay. 174–175.

Listen, O first-born of the day, to the merit that accrues when one has performed that [meditation] preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is to be accomplished through concentration (samādhi) and is free from vital breaths; by that, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) would be saluted for twelve years. 176.

O sinless one, I myself have declared that the fruit of bathing in the Aśvamedha is obtained there, and likewise the merit of giving gifts is tenfold; furthermore, the merit of fasting is infinite for him who provides a meal for a married couple in the presence of Sāvitrī. 177–178.
"Therefore, O venerable one, I have undoubtedly been fed by him here;
he who feeds a second person has, in fact, fed Keśava. Accompanied by Lakṣmī, the Giver of Boons bestows boons upon him. (179)
Accompanied by Umā, he has undoubtedly been fed by you on this third day.
(180) Alternatively, if one should offer food with devotion to young maidens, in her family there shall never be a barren woman nor one who is unfortunate. (181)
Neither is she a mother of daughters, nor is she a beloved wife to her husband;
therefore, by every effort, food should always be placed before Sāvitrī by men who desire either the welfare of the next world or that of this one. 182.
It should always be given, excluding pungent oils such as *abhīṣma* and *kaṭu*. 183.
Food for women should never contain sour substances nor alkaline salts;
it should consist of the five types of edible foods, well-prepared with all flavors. 184.
One should eat well-cooked *ghṛtapūrī* cakes, which are rich in milk, as well as *śikhariṇī*, which is mixed with curd and milk; these bring delight to men and are exceedingly dear to women. 185.
One will possess wealth, grain, and collyrium, and be surrounded by hundreds of women; cakes and fried pastries will be produced there for him—of this there is no doubt.
There shall be no fever, no distress, no suffering, and no separation.
She causes twenty-one generations of her own kin,
along with her relatives, sons, and countless male and female servants, to cross over; indeed, she who bestows this *Pūrikā* fills her entire family.

The entire family of one who bestows a water-pot prospers for a long time, endowed with sons and grandsons; likewise, his daughters become mothers of sons, and his lineage flourishes together with its kinsmen. (189-190)
There is no doubt that the family of young women who give śikhariṇī flourishes, filled with all perfections;
thus has Prajāpati spoken regarding the gift of sweetmeats (modaka). 191.
This alone is the meal for Gaurīs that is praised by Hara. 192.
Blessed with good fortune, sons, virtue, and endowed with wealth and prosperity, she shall become a feeder of thousands in birth after birth, O Śambhu. 193.
And auspicious cakes that are sweet,
primarily consisting of grape juice and combined with jaggery and sugar-candy;
having prepared these with autumnal grain mixed with sugar-candy— 194.

One should provide for women those things that are fit to be drunk and those foods that are fit for the twice-born (195). Furthermore, sheep-skins are suitable for all purposes here during the rainy season; whatever else is fit to be drunk, one should cause that to be provided (196).
Having honored them according to the prescribed rite with gifts of wealth and silk garments, their limbs anointed with saffron and adorned with garlands of flowers,
one should likewise place sandals upon their feet and offer a coconut.
Having applied collyrium to the eyes and vermilion to the head,
and having placed molasses, pleasant fruits, and other soft desired items along with vessels in their hands, one should bow down and bid them farewell.
Only afterwards shall he eat himself, together with his kinsmen and children;
or else, if there is no wealth at the sacred ford for giving or for a recipient, having gone home, I will give it gladly—O God, be gracious to me! 200.
In this very manner, having come to his own home, he should perform the *śrāddha* for the ancestors according to the prescribed rules, preceded by the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
On that day of Brahmā, the ancestors of that person indeed become fully satisfied. (201–202)
O Śiva, for those who give at their own home, the merit is eight times that of giving at a sacred ford (tīrtha);
however, base people do not witness the śrāddha performed by the twice-born.
Indeed, the śrāddha for the ancestors is prescribed to be performed in a secluded and hidden part of the house.
If that [offering] is struck by a downward glance, it does not reach the ancestors at all.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the Śrāddha to be performed in secret;
this is declared by the Self-born One himself to be the means for the satisfaction of the ancestors. 204–205.

Through devotion to Gaurī, let there be an increase; she whose rites are unknown is praised, she who is perceived by the mind as belonging to the *rājasa* quality, and she who bestows fame upon people.
(206) One who desires their own welfare should always give gifts in secret.
Cooked food being given by people on earth becomes visible;
however, that which is visible [to others] never leads to satisfaction here.
When one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed. (207–208)
"There is no doubt regarding this through traditional practice; the word of the Purāṇas is true:
one should never examine a Brāhmaṇa at a sacred ford (tīrtha). Regarding this, Manu has said that one should feed a Brāhmaṇa who arrives seeking alms."

The offering of balls (piṇḍas) should be performed with roasted grain flour (saktu), or with saṃyāva, or with milk-rice (pāyasa); this is what has been seen by the sages. Or it may be offered with oil-cake (piṇyāka) or with inguda; these should always be given by men who are full of devotion. 210–211.
A śrāddha ceremony should be performed there, however, excluding the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana).
Vultures or crows do not take [the offerings] by sight;
that śrāddha is declared to be "pertaining to the sacred ford" (tīrthika), which provides supreme satisfaction to the ancestors.
That must be performed with great effort; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
(213) Through devotion the ancestors are pleased, and being satisfied, they grant all desires: sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and whatever other desires one wishes for in the mind. (214)
The Grandfather (Brahmā), being pleased, bestows [blessings] upon men who have propitiated him through devotion and right conduct.

Whether at an improper time or the proper time, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a Śrāddha should always be performed by men; likewise, as soon as they have arrived, they should always perform ritual bathing and the libation to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa).
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) must be performed, for it is exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
The ancestors, filled with supreme hope, gaze toward a kinsman who has arrived, longing for water as well. (216–217)
One must not cause delay, nor should one create obstacles; for them, their lineage shall remain unbroken at all times. The ancestors desire the giver of a son who performs the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
For they never effect the severance of the continuity [of the lineage].
Therefore, the Śrāddha was proclaimed of old by the Self-born One himself as that which must be performed with superior qualities by the twice-born who are devoted to the ancestors.

At a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a sacred field (kṣetra), or even in one's own home; at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), during an eclipse, at the equinoxes (viṣuva), at the solstices (ayana), or when one’s birth star (janmarkṣa) is afflicted—
these indeed are the times for śrāddha that Svāyambhuva spoke of in ancient times.
When a Śrāddha has been performed for men, bodily affliction ceases;
then, even all the evil deeds committed by one's sons are abandoned,
so that there shall be no suffering from planets, thieves, kings, or the like.

All evil deeds are destroyed, and one attains an auspicious state in the hereafter; there is no doubt in this, according to the word of Prajāpati. In the Kṛta Yuga, Puṣkara is [the foremost], while Naimiṣa is remembered as such in the Tretā Yuga.

In the Dvāpara age one should resort to Kurukṣetra, and in the Kali age one should resort to the Gaṅgā. (225) Dwelling at Puṣkara is difficult to achieve, and performing penance at Puṣkara is difficult; whatever sin has been committed elsewhere attains lightness there at the sacred ford. (226)
Sin committed elsewhere is not removed by visiting other holy places;
however, O Bhārata, he who remembers the Puṣkara lakes with palms joined in reverence at dawn and dusk has effectively performed ablutions in all sacred fords.
Having performed ritual ablutions at dawn and dusk at Puṣkara with his senses restrained, he attains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā;
this applies for twelve years, twelve days, a month, or even half a month.
He who would dwell at Puṣkara constantly shall go to the supreme goal;
the world of Brahmā stands above all other worlds. He who desires to go to Puṣkara should attend upon Puṣkara.
Just as it is with the direct and reverse orders, so it is with the individual and collective [mantras].

One who has bathed properly at Puṣkara enjoys the fruit of ten million [merits]; indeed, whatever fruit is obtained at all sacred fords when they are visited according to the prescribed rites, [that is obtained here].
O joy of the Kurus, by the mere sight of Puṣkara, a human being obtains that same fruit which is found at ten thousand times ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth;
for they all reside together at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day.
As long as the mountains endure and as long as the oceans remain, for that long shall the world of Brahmā belong to those who die at Puṣkara; of this there is no doubt,
even throughout thousands of future births, from birth until the end of death.
Having bathed but once at Puṣkara, one may burn away all evil deeds;
Puṣkara is a field difficult to attain, which destroys every sin. Now listen, O King, to that which destroys the five great sins.
The sacrifice to the God of gods bestows wealth, O son of Brahmā.
Whatever man on earth may be afflicted by poverty, disease, leprosy, and the like in this life, or who is unfortunate and childless— 237–238.
For him, prosperity shall arise immediately, along with full longevity, sons, and happiness— he who,
having fashioned the supreme god Brahmā according to the prescribed rite, beholds him situated within the maṇḍala accompanied by the guardians of the world. 239.
One should worship the mantra-form born of no womb (ayonija), which was honored by Navanābha.
Specifically on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika,
or indeed on all full moon days, one should sacrifice to this deity according to the prescribed rite.
O mighty-armed King, for one who beholds the all-pervading Lord worshipped by his preceptor during a solar transit, or even during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
there shall be immediate satisfaction and the destruction of sins shall occur.
O lord of men, there is also a general examination of the deities here;
however, for the devotees among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the Guru should conduct an examination for one year by means of their caste, purity, ritual actions, and so forth. 243–244.

Knowing that [the initiation] has been successfully conferred, he should take it to heart; they too, having meditated upon the Teacher as the Supreme Lord with devotion, should practice devotion toward the Guru for a year, just as they do toward Viṣṇu. 245.
Then, when a full year has passed, they should propitiate the Guru, saying:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, through the worship of the Supreme Brahman and the propitiation of Viriñci, [we have attained] the crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. (246-247)

"By the recitation of the *Sahasraśīrṣa* and the *Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa*, and likewise through meditation, may such instruction be granted to us; we desire Vedic prosperity—may you be especially gracious. (248)
Then, having been thus requested by them, the wise preceptor should duly worship Brahmā, preceded by Viṣṇu; they,
