with their eyes bound, should sleep on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*),
they should meditate upon their Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*), wearing white garments and a sacred thread,
adorned with white garlands and clothing, and anointed with white sandalwood paste. (251)
Having gone outside, they should perform their daily rites without sloth by the river (252).
The Teacher should cause the tooth-stick to be provided from a milk-tree;
they, having gone to the river that flows to the ocean, should indeed chew it (253).
Alternatively, they may eat from another pond or even from their own house, provided it has been consecrated according to the rules with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin;
that is, consecrated seven times with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā. (254)
Having recited "devasya tvā," he should place [the water] on the hand with "yuje tvā"; 255.
having washed it with "irāvatī," he should eat the *brahmaudana* with "brahmaudane," and after eating, he should throw it far away and observe where it has fallen. 256.
Whether the tooth-stick has fallen facing oneself, toward the east, or even toward an intermediate direction—
when it falls facing oneself, the attainment of the deity and the perfection of the mantra arise.
When the tooth-stick falls with its back turned, all the gods turn their backs [on the practitioner].
If he has gone toward the north, success may or may not occur (verse 258). If he has gone toward the south, there will be death for that Guru; of this there is no doubt.
Having observed an inauspicious sign, he should sleep on the ground in the presence of the God of gods (verse 259).
Having seen dreams, the wise should report them before their guru; then the supreme guru should discern therein what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
Then, having bathed on the full moon day, one should proceed to the temple of the deity.
The Guru should cause the maṇḍala to be drawn upon the ground that has been prepared;
having marked the ground according to the rules with various characteristics,
he should draw a lotus with sixteen petals, or even nine.
Then, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, the wise teacher should show it;
he should carefully bind the eyes of the disciples with a white cloth. He should cause the disciples, holding flowers in their hands, to enter according to the sequence of the castes.
When the wise one has fashioned a nine-naved mandala with colored powders,
he should worship the god Indra preceded by Indrāṇī in the eastern direction;
O King, he should likewise worship Agni surrounded by the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One should assign Agni to the eastern direction, Yama to the southern, Nirṛti to the south-western, Varuṇa to the western quarter, Vāyu to the north-western region,
Dhanada to the north, and Rudra to the north-eastern region.

One should place the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in the east, and likewise the large sacrificial ladle (sruk) in the south; the swan (haṃsa) in the west, and likewise the small sacrificial ladle (sruva) in the north;
one should place the seat (brasi) in the southeast, and likewise the sandals (pādukā) in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should worship the meditation-belt (yogapaṭṭa), and in the northeast, the water-pot (galantikā). Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the east, and Śaṅkara in the south;
the god Sūrya is in the west, and likewise the sages (ṛṣis) in the north.
In the center is Svayaṃpadmajanmā, and likewise Sāvitrī is in the south;
and in the north is the goddess Gāyatrī, whose eyes are like lotus petals.
One should place the Ṛgveda in the east and the Yajurveda in the south.
One should place the Sāmaveda in the west, the Atharvaveda in the north,
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, the Chandas, Jyotiṣa,
the Dharmaśāstras, and other [treatises] in the directions beginning with Indra (the east).
Having worshipped Bala on the eastern petal, one should worship Pradyumna on the southern petal;
Aniruddha on the western, and Vāsudeva on the northern. Then, one should worship Vāmadeva in the east and Sadyojāta in the south.

One should place Īśāna in the western position and Tatpuruṣa in the north; Aghora is to be worshipped everywhere—this is the worship in the maṇḍala. One should worship Bhāskara in the east and Divākara in the south.
Having worshipped Prabhākara in the west and the King of Planets (the Sun) in the north according to the prescribed rite, one should thus worship Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
by placing him within the circle of the directions and arranging eight jars according to the ritual injunctions.
One should arrange the ninth vessel, the Brāhma-kalaśa, in the center;
one who desires liberation should bathe [the deity] with that of Brahmā, while a king who desires prosperity should bathe [him] here with the Vaiṣṇava vessel. 278.
One desiring sovereignty should bathe [the deity] with the water from the vessel of Indra (279).
One desiring wealth and majesty should bathe with the water from the vessel of Agni;
for the ritual of Mṛtyuñjaya, one should bathe the person with the water from the vessel of Yama (280).
The Nairṛta [mantra] is prescribed for the destruction of the wicked;
one should quickly bathe a human being with the Vāruṇa [mantra] for the sake of destroying sin.
However, one who desires health of body should be consecrated with the Vāyavya [mantra].

For one desiring the attainment of wealth, the ritual is prescribed by Kaubera; for one desiring knowledge, it is by Raudra. By bathing in each of these jars of the world-protectors individually, a person becomes freed from all defects.
A king may immediately become like Brahmā, or else he becomes a monkey;
or else, he should worship the Lokapālas in all directions according to their respective order, using jars (kuṃbhas) with their own names according to the prescribed ritual. 284.
Having thus worshipped the gods and the world-protectors with a serene mind,
he should then cause the tested disciples to enter with their eyes bound;
having burned them away by means of the fire-concentration (āgneyī-dhāraṇā), he should then shake them off with the wind [concentration].
Having caused them to be nourished with *soma*, he should then cause them to hear the rules:
"One must not revile Brāhmaṇas, the gods, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā;
nor Indra, Āditya, Agni, the guardians of the world, or the planets. (287)

Having thus announced the rules (samayas) to the Guru, or a Brāhmaṇa, or a lordly sage who has been previously initiated, one should thereafter cause the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed with the mantra:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate brahmaṇe sarvarūpiṇe huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. 288–289.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the sixteen-syllable mantra in the blazing fire;
one should cause all the oblations beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) to be offered. With the three *vyāhṛtis*, however, [one should offer] in the presence of the God of Gods.
At the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice, the initiated disciple should then offer the teacher’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*).
O King, a wise man should give the teacher elephants, horses, vehicles, carts, gold, grain, and so forth; likewise, in a middling initiation, he should give a middling amount. 291–292.
One should cause another pair [of sandals] along with gold to be given to the preceptor;
for when this is done, the great merit that arises cannot be described even in hundreds of years. (293)
If one who has previously been initiated should hear the *Pādma* [Purāṇa], by that [act] the Vedas,
the Purāṇas, and all the mantras along with their compendiums would be as if recited at the holy site of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean. 294–295.
Whatever fruit may accrue to those who recite [mantras] at Devahrada, Kurukṣetra, and especially at Vārāṇasī, during an eclipse or at the equinoxes—
that same fruit becomes a hundredfold when one is present at Pitāmaha located at Puṣkara.

If one who has been initiated hears this after performing the Vedic worship, he obtains various desires whenever he wishes them; even the gods, having performed austerities, meditate upon it and speak of it. (297-298)

O King, when will our birth take place in this land of Bhāratavarṣa? When shall we be initiated, and when shall we hear the Pādma Purāṇa? And when, having entrusted this body to the sixteen-fold self, shall we [attain liberation]? 299.
"We shall go to that supreme state, having gone to which there is no rebirth.
Thus the gods speak and contemplate in their minds:
"O King, when shall we behold the Brahma-sacrifice on the full moon day of Kārttika?"
Thus, O best of the Kurus, this rite has been described by me;
for it is indeed always difficult to obtain even for the gods, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas.
He who knows this in its true essence and he who beholds the maṇḍala [attains the goal].
And whoever should hear this, all are liberated— so says the sacred revelation (śruti).
Hereafter, I shall proclaim this supreme secret by which men may attain fortune, fortitude, contentment, and nourishment.
O King,
by him who first takes up a hand on a Sunday with devotion and casts it with a single handful as many times as seven, all planetary influences always become auspicious.
Then, when the seventh [period] is complete, one should perform a feeding of Brahmins;
and having fashioned an image of the Sun out of gold with effort, a person should clothe it in a pair of red garments, along with a small umbrella and sandals.
One should give a pair of sandals after placing them in a copper vessel;
having performed a ceremonial bath with ghee, one should bestow them upon a twice-born man who has complete limbs, and especially upon a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the ritual procedures. 308.

The fruit of performing it in this manner shall be the attainment of supreme health (309). This ritual prescribed in the Purāṇas ensures the complete acquisition of material wealth; it is unfailing and bestows peace and nourishment upon men (310).
Likewise, the wise man, having carefully observed the Monday,
should diligently consume [the substance] at night for eight Mondays;
on each occasion, he should feed learned Brahmins according to his capacity.
Then, when the ninth [day] is complete, one should perform the feeding of Brahmins;
a pair of garments should be given, and thereafter one should cause Soma to be presented,
placed within a bronze vessel and filled with milk.
Likewise, an umbrella, sandals,
and shoes should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has all his limbs complete, especially on the occasion of a full moon.
Having worshipped Mars under the Svāti constellation, one should observe a fast by eating only at night.
In this manner, one should perform these eight [rites] up until the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, one should cause a golden Aṅgāraka (Mars) placed in a copper vessel to be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is complete in all his limbs. 315–316.
One should offer seven lamps in sequence according to the order of the lunar mansions;
on the eighth, the wise man should cause golden images of the planets to be given,
and he should perform the fire-ritual according to the prescribed injunctions as they have been observed.
O lord of men, understand what occurs when this has been performed:
all malevolent planets become gentle in form, all diseases are destroyed, and the deities attain satisfaction. (318–319)
The Nāgas do not obstruct him, nor do the Pitṛs;
likewise, for those who hear or recite it, there is the destruction of bad dreams.
Even if Mars, Saturn, and the Sun are together with Rāhu...
The fierce planets, which stand at the head of the army and cause great affliction,
[are pacified] by this alone; indeed, O King, he who performs this rite while always endowed with devotion shall become possessed of good fortune.

All of them, being well-disposed toward him, grant peace; it is not otherwise. One should place Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu in vessels made of iron, have these fashioned from iron, and cause them to be given to Brāhmaṇas.
A pair of black garments should indeed be given for their propitiation. Those who desire peace, prosperity, and victory should give golden limbs [to the deities].
O King, at the conclusion of the vow, all these planets should indeed be made of gold.
Those who desire peace should provide a feast for the twice-born at the conclusion of the vow, as well as sacrificial fees according to their capacity for the gratification of the planets;
thus, O Indra among kings, one may attain all desires with little effort. 326.
One should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara, and likewise health from Bhāskara; one should desire wealth from Hutāśana, and the supreme goal from Janārdana;
and one should seek the state of Brahmā, which grants peace to all living beings, from Pitāmaha.
Bhīṣma said:
"As for that sacrifice which you have described as yielding great fruit for sacrificers, it cannot be attained by others due to the brevity of their lifespan. (329)
"O best of sages, tell me of that great fruit which would arise from fasting for a year with very little effort. Pulastya said:
For this purpose, O Great King, the highly illustrious King Śveta, being greatly afflicted by hunger, questioned Vasiṣṭha regarding this inquiry.
There was once a very powerful King Śveta in the region of Ilāvṛta.
He conquered the seven continents along with their cities, together with the entire earth and its mountains.
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, was his priest.
Once, that best of kings, who was supremely righteous, having conquered [his enemies]— 332–333.
Śveta said to his family priest Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers:
"O Blessed One, I desire to perform a thousand horse-sacrifices."

O Guru, O Lord, I have no desire to give gifts of gold, silver, or jewels to the twice-born; rather, I wish to give the gift of food upon this earth. For when food is given to a brahmin, O Master, nothing else remains to be given. (335)

Realizing that nothing at all truly exists, that king never gave anything that was not already given; the highly illustrious King Śveta bestowed red garments, ornaments, villages, and cities upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Never did that king ever fail to provide food and water;
then, O best of men, having performed many horse-sacrifices and having practiced penance for three hundred million years, that performer of sacrifices went to heaven won by his merit.
Having attained the same world as Brahmā, adorned with every ornament, the Apsarases dance there and the wives of the Siddhas sing;
both Tumburu and Nārada are also always present there. 339–340.

The two highly wise ones sang, and the sages endowed with ascetic power praised the performer of many sacrifices with mantras declared in the Vedas; such was the state of that high-souled king, possessed of such splendor. 341.
Thus it was for that great-souled king endowed with such majesty.
His body was afflicted by hunger and especially by thirst.
O best of kings, though he was tormented by that hunger,
he abandoned heaven and went from his celestial chariot to the Rikṣa mountain.
Where his own body had been consumed in the great forest, there the king went from the city; having personally gathered the bones, he remained there licking them.
Then, ascending his celestial chariot once more, the lord of men departed for the sky.

Then, after a long time, the king, firm in his vows, was seen by his domestic priest Vasiṣṭha as he was gnawing on his own bones. The priest said to him: "O Indra among kings, O lord of men, why indeed are you consuming your own bones?"
Having been addressed thus by the great seer Vasiṣṭha, King Śveta then spoke these words to that sage:
"O Blessed One, I am afflicted by thirst and hunger; previously, food was given by me..."
"O tiger among sages, since nothing was given [by me], hunger does not afflict me.
Having been addressed thus, the great sage Vasiṣṭha,
the preeminent among munis, then spoke these words again to the king.
"What shall I do for you, O Indra among kings, especially since you are hungry?
Even for a mere trifle, nothing remains ungiven that presents itself [to me]. By the gift of jewels and gold, a man becomes possessed of enjoyments."
"O King, lord of men, by the giving of food and the granting of all desires, one is fully satisfied;
yet that was not given by you, O King, because you considered it to be a trifle.
Śveta said:
"O Guru Vasiṣṭha, tell me as I ask you how it was that the non-acquisition of what has not been given occurred for me through your grace.
Vasiṣṭha said:
There is one cause by which this is produced; of this there is no doubt.
Listen to that, O tiger among men, as it is being told by me to you: in a former kalpa, there was a king celebrated as Vinītāśva. (353–354)
If the king had indeed begun to perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice,
then at the conclusion of the sacrifice, when cows, horses, and other things were requested from the foremost of the twice-born,
no food whatsoever would have been given by him, as he would have considered it as insignificant as what was given by you.
Then, after a long time, he died on the bank of the Ganges;
in Māyāpurī, Vinītāśva became a sovereign emperor,
and he too, O Lord, went to heaven just as you have become a king.
O King, he too, overcome by hunger, arrived in this very way at the Nīla mountain on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the mortal world,
traveling in a radiant celestial chariot with the color of the sun, like a god.
He beheld his own body as well as himself [as the priest],
a Brāhmaṇa named Hotṛ, performing a sacrifice on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
seeing him, he again questioned that best of the twice-born.
O King, Sahotā told him the cause of his hunger: "O best of men, O ruler of the earth, [give] a sesame-cow, a ghee-cow, a water-cow, and a milk-cow. (361)
"Give it quickly, so that you, freed from thirst and hunger,
may delight in heaven as long as the sun and the moon shine in the sky.
Having been addressed thus, the king then questioned him again.
"Tell me the procedure for the sesame-cow gift; having performed it accordingly, I shall give it.
The priest said:
"O lord of men, listen to that ritual procedure for the sesame-cow. 364.
The cow should consist of sixteen *āḍhakas*, and the calf should be made of four;
its legs should be made of sugarcane, its auspicious teeth of flowers,
its nose of perfume, and its tongue likewise of molasses.
Her tail should be fashioned with a fringe of bells and adorned with ornaments;
having fashioned her in this manner, one should then fashion a cow with golden horns,
silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, according to the previously prescribed ritual for a cow.

O King, having performed this, he should cause that auspicious cow— standing upon a black antelope skin, covered with cloths, strung with thread, and endowed with five jewels— to be given to a Brāhmaṇa according to the mantra. (368)
One should cause [the recipient] to receive that [cow] which is endowed with all medicinal herbs and purified by mantras:
"O sesame-cow offered to the twice-born, may food be produced for me instantly, as well as drink and all flavors; fulfill our desires. (369–370)
"O Goddess, I accept you with devotion, especially for the sake of my family;
salutations to you, the sesame-cow who fulfills all desires pertaining to the body.
O best of kings, in this manner the sesame-cow was then given.

It brings about the fulfillment of all desires; of this there is no doubt. (372) Likewise, a water-cow fashioned with jars, when given according to the prescribed rite, immediately bestows all desired objects. (373)
Likewise, by the observance of the full-moon vow, one hundred cows are effectively given;
such a person becomes like Sāvitrī in heaven, granting all desires. Similarly, a cow made of ghee is given according to the prescribed rites by the wise.
O King,
when the Cow of Taste (Rasadhenu) is thus given in the month of Kārttika,
she fulfills all desires, bestows splendor, grants eternal results, and provides a supreme destination. 375–376.
All this has been told to you in brief, though it is very extensive; the fruit of all actions has been declared by Brahmā to be boundless,
O best of kings, for one who is afflicted by thirst or hunger.
O Lord of Men, that gift should first be given on the day of Kārtika;
it is the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), endowed with all prosperity, filled with living beings, gems, and medicinal herbs, and always accompanied by gods, dānavas, and yakṣas, O Sovereign. (378–379)
Having fashioned this entire [structure] adorned on all sides with silver, enriched with excellent jewels, the sun, and the moon, on the twelfth day of the month of Kārtika,
or else on the fifteenth day of Kārtika itself, and not at any other time.
A devoted man should cause these to be given to his family priest and preceptor.
O King, whatever beings exist within the belly of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), all those are considered as having been given by him; this has been told to you in brief. 381-382.

O King, whatever fruit is obtained by one performing sacrifices with the completion of excellent sacrificial fees— that entire fruit belongs specifically to that region of the universe (Brahmāṇḍa). Furthermore, the man who should bestow this entire Brahmāṇḍa [obtains even greater merit].
Therefore, it becomes as if muttered, offered, recited, and proclaimed. 384.
The King said:
Having performed the ritual for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one shall become a partaker of liberation.
O sinless one, tell me everything regarding the time, the place, and the sacred ford (tīrtha),
by performing which I may become a partaker of the fruit of all [merit], and by which there may be for me soon liberation from this contemptible state of existence. (385–386)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, having heard this, the virtuous Brahmin priest of that king then had a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) fashioned out of all kinds of metals. 387
There he fashioned a lotus adorned with a thousand *niṣkas*; in its center was Brahmā, embellished with rubies,
together with Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, the *ṛṣis*, and the sages.
Nārada and all the others, as well as Indra and all the inhabitants of heaven,
were all golden-bodied and stood before Brahmā;
likewise was the eternal Lord in the form of the Boar, accompanied by Lakṣmī.

One should have blue gems and emeralds fashioned for its ornamentation; the wise man should also provide it with the beauty of *gomeda* stones. Furthermore, one should provide the moon [image] with pearls and the sun with diamonds for their splendor.
One should cause gold to be given for all the planets;

silver is seven times the value of gold, and copper likewise seven times that of silver; then bell-metal should be made seven times the value of copper, and likewise seven times that of the preceding. 392–393.

O lord of men, [the vessel] should be made seven times the size of the bell-metal one; likewise, lead should be seven times the size of tin, and iron should be made seven times the size of lead. The seven continents, the seven oceans, and the seven principal mountain ranges [are thus represented].
Then, having had this performed by skilled artisans through countless repetitions,
one should have the trees and other living beings made of silver,
and the forest-dwelling creatures made of gold.
Having prepared trees, forest lords, shrubs, grasses, leaves, and creepers according to the prescribed rules, everything should be offered at the sacred ford by the wise;
[specifically] at Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Prayāga, and Amarakaṇṭaka.
O Vainya, at these sacred fords— Dvāravatī, Prabhāsa, Gaṅgādvāra, and Puṣkara— one should give gifts during lunar and solar eclipses,
on all the "breaks of the day" (sandhyās), and during the southern and northern solstices.
O King of Kings, this should be given during a Vyatīpāta yoga with great merit, and especially during a Viṣuva; one should not entertain any doubt about this.
Having established a hall for the Agnihotra fire, one should provide a handsome bull endowed with all good qualities.
Having honored him along with his wife and adorned them with ornaments (401),
he made the chief priest the foremost, as well as other twice-born men who were invited together with their wives and endowed with the twenty-four qualities (402).
One should likewise cause rings and earrings to be given;
having honored those who are of such a kind, one stands well-composed before them and bows down again and again with the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta). 403.
Having placed the *vaikarasa* casket before the family priest, [he said:
"O Brahmins, may you be pleased; favor me with a spirit of friendship.
O best of the twice-born, by your gracious countenance, this day shall become even more purified."
Through the bond of your affection, the Grandfather himself was pleased;
and because the Cosmic Egg was offered, Janārdana attained satisfaction.
So too did the Lord who wields the Pināka bow and Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods.
"O best of the twice-born, may you attain satisfaction through this meditation. Having thus praised the Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas,
the king then immediately presented the Brahmāṇḍa to his preceptor according to the prescribed rites.
Then, satisfied by all his desires, that lord of men went to heaven;
and that [wealth] was divided by that very preceptor along with the Brahmins,
and it was given by him as well to others, O lord of men, including the Brahmāṇḍa.
In the gift of the earth as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there should be only one recipient.
By accepting it, he incurs the fault of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
It should indeed be given in the presence of all, after it has been fully proclaimed.
Those who witness this gift being given indeed become purified;
by the mere sight of it, they certainly become liberated—of this there is no doubt.
This is the one called Bhīmadvādaśī, [on which] gold, water, and a deer-skin [are offered].
Having performed these [rites], one sees the fruit of the action through these very things;
it is obtained effortlessly by the doer, as well as co-residence in the same world [as the gods]. O King, cows are always to be saluted with this mantra: 413–414.
Salutations to the cows, the illustrious daughters of Surabhi;
salutations to the daughters of Brahmā, the pure ones—salutations again and again.
By the mere recollection of this mantra, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow at the most excellent holy site of Puṣkara, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika;
whatever sin exists, whether of a woman or a man— [all that shall be removed].

By merely bathing at Puṣkara, all that [sin] perishes without remainder. O Bhārata, whatever holy places there are on earth as far as the ocean, they all come to Puṣkara, especially on the full moon day of Kārtika.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Gift of the Cosmic Egg," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Five.
Bhīṣma said:
The Blessed One has stated that everything was endowed with the basis of the Purāṇas;
likewise, Śveta presented the Brahmāṇḍa to his preceptor.
Having heard this, curiosity arose as to how he performed the licking of bones.
O twice-born one, since the purpose of removing hunger has been accomplished without the gift of food,
I wish to hear about those kings on earth who reached heaven through the gift of food, and how sacrifices are rooted in food.

How was the mind of that great-souled Śveta destroyed, since no gift of food was given by him, nor was it shown to him by the sages? Oh, how great is the majesty of food here, which is the fruit of what is given!
O Brahmins, those who are ever-vigilant proclaim that the gift of food is supreme;
through the gift of food, even the Lord of the Gods enjoys the three worlds here and attains imperishability in the hereafter. 5–6.
"He is proclaimed as Śatakratu by all the best of the twice-born;
because of that, the Lord of the Thirty-three attained a state corresponding to it. "I have heard everything from you regarding the gift that leads to heaven."
Furthermore, O high-minded one, if at any time there has occurred an ancient event that has already transpired which you wish to hear again, tell that to me. Pulastya said:
"O King, this narrative was formerly told to Rāma by the high-souled Agastya; I shall now relate it to you. Bhīṣma said:
In which lineage was that Rāma, the best of kings, born,
for whom this ancient history was told by Agastya?
Pulastya said:
In the lineage of Raghu was born the one named Rāma, possessed of great strength.
He accomplished the work of the gods and slew Rāvaṇa in Laṅkā.
While he was established in the sovereignty of the earth, the sages came to his palace.
Those great-souled ones arrived at the residence of Rāghava;
then, at the word of Agastya, the gatekeeper quickly announced to Rāma that the sages had arrived, accompanied by a smile.
Having seen the garden, which was like the rising full moon, the gatekeeper said:
"O auspicious son of Kausalyā, may you have a blessed day; the night has dawned with a beautiful morning.
O delighter of the Raghus, you have arrived today to behold this splendor."
O King, Agastya stood at the gate together with the sages.
Hearing that the sages, who possessed a splendor equal to the sun, had arrived, Rāma then spoke these words to the one standing at the gate: "Let them enter with haste."
"For what reason were the best of sages obstructed by you from the water?
(17) At Rāma's word, he let those sages enter as they pleased;
seeing that the sages had arrived, he replied with palms joined in reverence. (18)
Rāma, having saluted them as they bowed down, seated them upon their seats;
those bulls among sages sat down on all sides upon comfortable thrones, variegated with gold and well-spread with cushions, and covered with kusha grass.
The family priest offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful arghya offering.
When all those ṛṣis were asked about their welfare by Rāma, those great seers, who were knowers of the Vedas, spoke these words: 20–21.
"May it be well with you, O mighty-armed one; may all be well with you everywhere, O descendant of Raghu!
By good fortune, we behold you safe, having slain your enemies. Sītā was carried away by the evil-minded and most sinful Rāvaṇa."
"O tiger among the Raghus, he was slain by the very power of his wife;
and he has been killed by you alone, without an ally, in the forest of Rāma. There is no one who can perform such a deed as you have done. (23-24)

"O Indra among kings, having come here to converse with you and now beholding you, we have all been purified this very moment; by the sight of you, O Lord of Men, all of us ascetics have become cleansed.
Furthermore, the wiping away of tears was accomplished today through the slaying of Rāvaṇa."
"O Hero, by bestowing this meritorious gift of fearlessness upon the world, you have increased by good fortune, O Kakutstha of immeasurable prowess; through your victory.
You have been seen and spoken with by us, and now we shall depart for our own hermitages. (26-27)
"O scorcher of enemies, when I had entered the forest, I offered you the bow of Indra,
as well as two inexhaustible quivers and armor. O descendant of Raghu, you must come to my hermitage once again."
Having spoken thus, all those sages vanished.
When the foremost of sages had departed, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, reflected upon that task: "What was it that was told to me by the sage? (29–30)
"O descendant of Raghu, you must come again to this hermitage;
I must certainly go into the presence of Agastya. I must hear the secret of the gods, and whatever else he may say regarding my duty."
While Rāma of immeasurable splendor was reflecting thus, he would certainly practice dharma, for dharma is indeed the supreme goal;
he ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years of his sons' lives.
As that high-souled Rāghava gave gifts, performed oblations, and protected his subjects, those years passed as if they were but a single year.
On this very day, an aged twice-born man from the countryside [arrived].
Taking up his dead son, he approached the gate of Rāma and spoke various words filled with affectionate syllables: "O my son, what evil deed was committed by me in a previous life? (35-36)
Since I behold you, my only son— a mere child of five years who has not yet reached youth— passed away with your life cut short, meeting your end prematurely, O dear son, for my sorrow. 37.

"Having failed to perform the funeral rites for his father, he has gone to the abode of Vaivasvata. Clearly, Rāma has committed some evil deed, for by it death has come upon you. Rāghava has perpetrated the murder of a child, the murder of a Brahmin, and the murder of a woman."
"He will enter [the fire] without doubt, along with his wife, once I am dead"—
Rāghava heard all this, filled with pain and grief. Having restrained that brahmin, Rāma spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha.
"What must I do now? What task remains to be done while such a situation persists? Shall I offer my life as an oblation into the fire, or shall I fall from the mountain?
How can I attain purity after hearing the words spoken by the Brahmin? (41-42)

Standing before Vasiṣṭha, Nārada replied to the distressed king: "I have heard the words of the sages in their presence at that time. Listen, O King, for the destruction of the child has indeed arrived at its appointed hour."
O Rāghava, in the former Kṛta-yuga, everywhere the Brāhmaṇas were supreme;
there was not a single non-Brāhmaṇa who performed penance, and all were immortal and long-lived. 44–45.
When the Tretā Yuga arrived again, the unsurpassed Brahmanas and Kshatriyas emerged;
then, in the Dvāpara, unrighteousness entered them as well as the Vaishyas and Shudras. Thus, falsehood was continuously practiced and arose once more.
Three quarters of unrighteousness had arrived, and only one quarter of righteousness remained.
Then, the castes, led by the Brāhmaṇas, became greatly terrified;
subsequently, a second quarter of righteousness was restored.
In that age known as Dvāpara, austerity indeed entered the Vaiśya; thus, the unrighteousness of the three ages establishes itself within Dharma.
Then, when the final age known as Kali arrived, it prevailed.
O bull among men, unrighteousness and falsehood will indeed increase; O King, in the Kali age, there will be the practice of penance even by those born from the womb of a Śūdra,
and that penance will be most intense on the borders of the kingdom.

O tiger among kings, that evil-minded Śūdra, a wicked husband, has committed the murder of a child; for whatever unrighteous act or improper deed a man of base intellect commits within the realm of a king, [it must be punished] in his city.
He goes swiftly to the Sanara hell until the dissolution of all beings.
O tiger among men, the king partakes of one-fourth of that sin; go now to your own kingdom. 53-54.
"Wherever you perceive a misdeed, there you must apply effort;
in this way, O best of men, there will be an increase in your righteousness as well as an increase in your strength, and the life of this child shall be preserved."
Thus addressed by Nārada, the joy of the Raghus was filled with wonder and attained incomparable delight; he then spoke this to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Go, gentle Lakṣmaṇa, and console that best of the twice-born."
"O gentle one, place the body of the child in a vat of oil, and treat it with most excellent perfumes and fragrant oils,
so that the child does not decompose."
"Act in such a way that the body of this boy, whose deeds are untainted, may remain protected,
so that neither calamity nor injury shall befall it.
Having thus instructed Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who is endowed with auspicious marks, [he departed].

He meditated upon the Puṣpaka chariot with his mind, thinking, "May the highly illustrious one come. Having understood that intention, the gold-adorned vehicle that travels at will arrived in the presence of Rāghava within a mere moment.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words: "O lord of men, O mighty-armed one, I stand here before you as your servant.
Having heard what was spoken for a long time from the Puṣpaka, O king, [he replied].
Having paid homage to those great sages, the hero ascended his celestial chariot,
taking with him his bow, two quivers, and a sword of great luster;
he then left both Saumitri and Bharata in the city.
He set out toward the west in haste, searching with great concentration;
thereafter he went to the northern direction situated at the Himavat mountains, and having also gone to the eastern direction, the lord of men searched there as well. 65–66.
Then the joy of the Raghus set out toward the southern direction, which was entirely pure in its conduct and as stainless as a mirror.
On the northern side of the mountain, he beheld a vast lake.

In that place, Rāghava beheld a formidable ascetic performing a most great penance, hanging with his face turned downwards. Approaching that ascetic who was thus practicing austerities, the descendant of Kakutstha [addressed him].
Rāghava spoke these words: "Blessed are you, O one who shines like an immortal!
In what womb was your growth in asceticism nurtured, O man of firm resolve?
I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; I ask you out of curiosity."

"What is it that you have resolved upon—is it the heavenly world or something else? For what purpose do you perform this penance? I wish to hear it, O ascetic. Are you a Brāhmaṇa—blessings be upon you—or are you a Kṣatriya, difficult to conquer? (71-72)
Whether it be a Vaiśya of the third caste or a Śūdra, let it be told truly: austerity, which consists of truth, is eternal for the attainment of the heavenly world;
that austerity consists of truth and is both of the nature of *sattva* and *rajas*.
That which was created by Viriñci for the sake of benefiting the world is indeed called Sāttvika; that which is born from the fiery energy of a Kṣatriya is called Rājasa;
and that which is for the purpose of destroying an enemy is declared to be Āsura.
Or he who conceals his limbs, or those smeared with blood, part by part;
or one who might accomplish the five fires—such a person attains either success or even death.
For this disposition of yours is indeed demonic, and I do not consider you to be a twice-born brahmin.
"Success belongs to those who speak the truth; there is no life for one who speaks falsehood.
Having heard these words of Rāma, whose actions are untainted, he remained with his head bowed down and spoke this speech: 77–78.
"Welcome, O best of kings! It has been a long time since you were last seen, O Rāghava.
You have become my son, and I have become your father, O sinless one. Or rather, it is not even so; for the king is the father of all."
"O King, you are a virtuous and worshipful person; we are performing penance in your territory.
We dwell there because a share was previously ordained for us by the Self-born Creator.
We are not fortunate, O Rāma, but you, O King, are truly fortunate. (80-81)
"O Rāghava, since ascetics desire such perfection even within these very sense-objects,
may you attain perfection through my asceticism. As for what was said by you— 'In which womb shall my asceticism [bear fruit]?'— "
"O King, I was born from a Śūdra womb, yet I have undertaken fierce austerity.
O you of excellent vows, I pray for divinity with this very body. I do not speak falsely, O Lord, out of a desire to conquer the world of the gods. (83-84)
As Śambūka, who was by name a Śūdra,
spoke thus, Rāghava, the descendant of Kakutstha, drew from its scabbard his stainless sword of brilliant luster and severed his head.
When that Śūdra was slain, the gods, led by Agni and headed by Indra, repeatedly praised the descendant of Kakutstha, crying out, "Excellent!
Excellent! And a great, fragrant rain of flowers from the gods fell.
Scattering the dust raised from the earth all around, the gods, freed from their distress, spoke with great joy to Rāma, the best among those skilled in speech:
"O gentle one, O delighter of the Raghus, this task of the gods has been accomplished by you. (88)
"Accept this boon, O Rāma of great vows, for it is on your account that this Śūdra has gone to heaven in his very body.
Having heard the words of the gods, Rāghava remained deeply composed. 89–90.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the thousand-eyed Purandara: "If the gods are indeed pleased with me, or if I am worthy of a boon,
then let this son of a brahmin live, for they are gratified by my deed."
"O Lord, this supreme boon desired by you is highly pleasing to me.
Because of my transgression, this boy—the only son of a brāhmaṇa—was taken prematurely by Time to the abode of Vaivasvata. (92-93)
"Bring him back to life; may it be well with you. I shall not be a liar toward my guru.
For I have heard this promise from the twice-born one: 'I shall restore your son to life by means of my own lifespan—either with half or even with a quarter of it. 94. O Asuras, [bring back] the boy.
"May this best of men live for me, having been granted a boon exceeding ten million boons.
Having heard those words of Rāghava, O best of the wise,
those high-souled ones, filled with joy and affection, replied to him.

O descendant of Kakutstha, at the very moment that the Śūdra was struck down, the Brāhmaṇa’s only son attained peace, regained his life, and was reunited with his kinsmen. 97. In that same moment, O Kakutstha, the Śūdra was slain.
In that very moment, he was suddenly reunited with life.
"May you attain well-being; may it be auspicious for you; we depart, O scorcher of foes," they said, having beheld the great sage in the hermitage of Agastya. 98–99.
Having thus made this vow, the joy of the Raghus ascended that Puṣpaka celestial chariot adorned with gold. 100.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaughter of the Śūdra Ascetic," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 35.
Chapter Thirty-six.
Pulastya said:
Then those gods departed at that time in their great celestial chariots.
Rāma also quickly followed the pitcher-born sage (Agastya) to the penance grove.
The Blessed One had already stated that he would return again; furthermore, he who had previously come to the assembly to see me [had been told the same].
Therefore, by the command of the deity and for the sake of that task, I shall go and see that great sage, who is worshipped by gods and demons;
and being pleased, that most excellent one will himself grant me instruction.
"May I never again become a mortal subject to suffering.
My father is Daśaratha and my mother is Kausalyā; though born into the solar dynasty, I am nonetheless so deeply distressed."
During my time in the kingdom, my forest-dwelling was interrupted by my wife and younger brother;
furthermore, the abduction of my wife was committed by Rāvaṇa.
Yet, without any assistance, I crossed the great ocean.
Having besieged that entire city and brought about the destruction of his lineage,
I beheld Sītā abandoned there in the presence of the gods; they then declared me to be pure, and likewise, "Sītā has been taken home by me."
Having been brought here by one who was displeased with the words of the world and dismissed to dwell in the forest, that queen now dwells as if in her own city;
and I too, born of such a noble lineage, am the foremost among archers.

Having encountered supreme suffering, my heart does not break at all. Surely I was fashioned by the Creator with the very essence of the diamond's core; for now, by the command of a Brahmin, I wander upon the surface of the earth.
While established in austerity, that Śūdra was struck down by a sin arising from Soma;
however, by the word of the gods, my life-breath has once again been established within my heart.
I behold that venerable sage, who is devoted to the welfare of this world.
"By seeing this, my suffering will quickly come to an end;
just as snow melts at the rising of the thousand-rayed sun, so too shall my attainment of misery perish in every way. (13-14)
Seeing that the gods had arrived, the venerable sage Agastya,
being well-pleased, took the guest-offering (arghya) and honored them all. Having accepted that worship and having conversed with the great sage, they [departed].
Then, filled with joy, they went to the heights of heaven along with their followers.
When they had departed, Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, descended from the Puṣpaka chariot and approached the supreme sage Agastya to pay his respects.
The king said: "O best of sages, I am the son of Daśaratha; I have come to pay my respects to you. Behold me with a gracious eye."

"Having seen you, I am now undoubtedly cleansed of all evil. Having said this much, he saluted the sage again and again, and inquired after the welfare of his circle of servants, his deer-children, and himself.
"Desiring a vision of the Blessed One, I have come here after killing a Śūdra.
Agastya said:
"Welcome to you, O best of the Raghus, eternal one worthy of the world's veneration!"
"By the mere sight of you, O descendant of Kakutstha, I have been purified along with the sages.
O tiger among the Raghus, O one of great splendor, accept this water offering (arghya) prepared by me.
Welcome, O tiger among men; it is by good fortune that you have arrived, O slayer of enemies!"

Since you are always highly esteemed for many supreme qualities, you are indeed worthy of worship by me, as you eternally abide within my heart. O gods, they indeed say that you have come as the slayer of a Śūdra.
"By you indeed, O Raghava, has this son been restored to life through the dharma of a Brahmin.
O Blessed One, O high-minded one, please stay here in my presence; at dawn you shall depart for Ayodhya by means of the Puṣpaka chariot."
And accept this ornament, O gentle one, well-crafted by Viśvakarman;
it is divine, shining with its own splendor, and is for you in your divine form. Accept it, O Indra among kings, O descendant of Raghu, and do what is pleasing to me.
It is said that for one who has already received [a gift], giving it away again yields great fruit.
Indeed, you are capable of protecting even the best of the gods, including Indra; therefore, O bull among men, I shall give this to you according to the prescribed rite—please accept it. 27–28.
Then the mighty-armed great chariot-warrior of the Ikṣvākus, with palms joined in reverence and recollecting his own dharma, spoke to the best of sages:
"O Blessed One, the acceptance of gifts from you is indeed censurable."
"How should a Kṣatriya who understands his duty accept gifts from a Brāhmaṇa?
O Great Sage, you should tell me what is given by a Brāhmaṇa; for I have sons, I possess a home, and I am capable. (30–31)
"Overwhelmed by calamity, how may I accept a gift? My wife has been lost for a very long time, and no other woman exists for me. I shall undoubtedly become a partaker of sin alone in this world. (32)

Even a Kṣatriya who accepts gifts when fallen into a difficult situation incurs no fault; Manu himself is the authority on this matter. So too for an aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, or an infant son.
"Even if one has committed a hundred wrongs, she should be maintained," so Manu declared. "O brahmin-sage, I do not accept a gift bestowed by you;
nor, O one worshipped by the gods, should you feel any anger toward me. (35-36)
Agastya said: "O King, there is no fault in accepting gifts when they are offered by sovereign rulers;
for you, O Raghava, are capable of rescuing even the three worlds from the Vaitaraṇī river."
"O Rāma, deliver this Brāhmaṇa, especially this ascetic;
therefore, I shall bestow [this wealth] upon you according to the prescribed rites—accept it, O lord of men.
Rāma said:
"How should a Kṣatriya, who understands what is to be accepted, receive gifts from a Brāhmaṇa?
You ought to tell me that which is given by a Brāhmaṇa.
Agastya said:
In the ancient Kṛta Yuga, purified by Rāma and Brahmā,
all subjects were without a king, as was Indra among the gods.
Those subjects approached the Lord of the God of Gods for the sake of a king.
"Among the gods, there exists a king, the God of Gods, Śatakratu.
O Lord of the World, for our welfare, appoint a terrestrial king now, by honoring whom men may enjoy the earth. (41-42)
Then Brahmā, the best of the gods, having summoned all the world-protectors along with Indra, said to them all: "Let a portion of your splendor be bestowed upon him.
Thereupon, the world-protectors gave a fourth part each of their own splendor.
From him was born Akṣaya, and from Akṣaya was born King Ayuta. Brahmā appointed him as a portion of the world-protectors among men;
thereafter, that king became an expert in ensuring the welfare of those subjects.
Therein, by means of his Aindra portion, the king commands all;
and by means of his Vāruṇa portion, he nourishes all embodied beings.
Likewise, by means of his Kaubera portion, the monarch bestows wealth.
"That portion which belongs to Yama, O King, by that he indeed governs the subjects.
Therefore, O best of men, O Lord, accept this ornament from me as my portion belonging to Indra, for the sake of my deliverance. (47-48)
Then Rāma took from the hand of the high-souled sage a divine and variegated ornament, blazing like the sun;
having received it from Agastya, Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes, [departed].
Having gazed for a very long time and reflected again and again, [he saw] various pearls, equal in size to *dhātrī* fruits, set in gold and adorned with diamonds,
coral, and sapphires.
Seeing it well-fastened with rubies, gomeda stones, lapis lazuli, and topazes, beautifully divided and excellently crafted by Viśvakarman,
he was filled with joy and further reflected thus:
Never before have I seen such jewels as these;
they are so exquisitely fashioned that their value is equal to the earth itself,
yet I have never seen anything like them in Vibhīṣaṇa’s Laṅkā.
Having thus reflected in his mind, Rāghava again approached that Ṛṣi and began to inquire about that divine [vision]:
"O Brahmin, this is most wonderful and unattainable even for kings."
How was it obtained by the Blessed One, or from where was it created?
O Great-minded One, out of curiosity I ask you this: even when resting in the palm of the hand, the many [jewels] shine forth from the center of the hand. 56–57.
O best of sages, know that which illuminates the directions to be the lowest, condemned in all the scriptures;
that which is upward-pointing and three-pronged is declared to be the highest.
"These are indeed the highest births proclaimed by the sages;
for the Blessed One is the treasury of many divine wonders.
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, the sage then spoke these words: 59–60.
Agastya said: Listen, O Rāma, to this great ancient account of what I witnessed in the forest long ago when the Dvāpara age had arrived.
"O mighty-armed descendant of Raghu, listen to this wonder:
in former times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a vast forest extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction, entirely devoid of wild beasts and tigers."
O gentle one, desiring to perform supreme austerity in that uninhabited forest, I have come to enter it;
for the middle of that forest is always well-supplied with roots and fruits.
In the midst of that forest, extending for five yojanas, there was a lake filled with various kinds of vegetables and diverse beautiful groves,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned by ruddy geese.
There, I beheld a most wonderful and exquisitely beautiful lake (66),
crowded with spreading tortoises and filled with flocks of rows of cranes. Long ago, I went there to that lake to perform austerities (67).
Having thus reached that meritorious region entirely free from violence,
O bull among men, I dwelt there for one night during the summer heat. Rising early at dawn, I approached that lake.
Then, O Rāghava, I beheld a corpse somewhere that had not yet touched old age,
standing nearby with supreme splendor and full of life;
reflecting upon its meaning for a moment, as it were, I remained there.
"Is this some creature on the shore, or perhaps a bull among the gods?
Is he a sage, or a king, or is he a sage who has become a king? Or else, has the birth of a king's son been brought about for him? (71)
"Whether it was yesterday, last night, or even this morning, if he has died, I must certainly know the cause of his departure from this lake.
While I remained thus, O best of the Raghus, I was lost in thought. (72-73)
Then, after a mere moment, O King, I beheld a divine and wondrously beautiful celestial chariot, most magnificent, yoked with swans and swift as thought;
and before it, there were thousands of celestial nymphs in their own chariots.
Gandharvas of that same number delighted that excellent man; some sang divine songs while others played instruments. Then they saw the man descending from that celestial chariot.
O descendant of Raghu’s lineage, having bathed after seeing him devouring the flesh of a corpse,
and then having eaten as much fatty meat as he desired,
he quickly descended from the lake and ascended once more to heaven.
To him, who resembled a god and was endowed with supreme splendor, [he said]:
"O fortunate one, O inhabitant of heaven, I ask you this: how is it that your food is so loathsome, yet your destiny is so excellent? (78–79)
If this is a secret that you do not wish to tell me today, I nevertheless desire to hear this supreme speech out of curiosity. Who are you? Speak without hesitation; what is this censurable food?
"O gentle one, why do you eat this? Where have you been?
Whose is this sovereign state that has been reduced to the condition of a corpse?
And how is it that you consume such contemptible food? I wish to hear the truth of these matters."
O best among the virtuous, having heard those words spoken there,
that celestial being, O descendant of Raghu, replied with palms joined in reverence:
"Listen now to this account of mine, arising from both joy and sorrow, exactly as it occurred."
O twice-born one, listen as I relate that which is difficult even for those free from desire to traverse:
in ancient times, there was a king of Vidarbha named Vāsudeva, highly renowned and righteous throughout the three worlds. 84–85.
O Brahman, two sons were born to him from his two wives;
I was known as Śveta, while the younger was Suratha. When that father had passed away, the citizens consecrated me as king.
There, exercising sovereignty with self-conceit and being uncomposed in dharma,
many thousands of years passed for me as I caused the kingdom to be governed and protected the subjects. 87-88.
O best of the twice-born, having set my heart on death due to detachment from some particular object, I came to this penance grove. This delightful forest is utterly devoid of birds.

Having consecrated his brother Suratha as the ruler of the kingdom, he entered and remained near this very lake to perform ascetic penance; having reached this lake, he performed most rigorous austerities.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest,
O Brahmin, I attained the auspicious and painless abode of Brahma’s world;
yet even while I am situated in heaven, O best of the twice-born, hunger and thirst afflict me.
They tormented me intensely, and my senses became deeply distressed.
Then I spoke to the Grandfather, the most excellent in the three worlds: "O Blessed One, this heavenly realm is devoid of hunger and thirst."
"Of what karma is this the fruition, that I have hunger and thirst? What food might I have, O Lord? Tell me this, O Grandfather.
Then, O great sage, the Grandfather meditated thoroughly for a long time.

Then he spoke these words to me: "O sir, there is no food produced from one's own body except for your own flesh; therefore, eat it constantly. By nourishing your own body, you have performed a supreme penance. (96-97)
"O father, look at this white [sandalwood] on the surface of the earth; it was never taken by me in the past when it was begged for with persistence even by a living being seeking alms.
Indeed, out of delusion and confusion, it was not given by me at that time to a guest in my own home."

Therefore, O Indra among kings, even though you have gone to heaven, hunger and thirst now afflict you; eat this excellent body of yours, which has been well-nourished by foods, and through that, satisfaction will arise. 99–100.
Thus addressed, I then spoke to the god Brahmā: "O Lord, even when my own body has been consumed, there is no other food that can truly ward off the hunger of this body without cooked rice."
"O God, as I eat him, he does not diminish; indeed, it becomes my delight.
Then Brahmā spoke again: "Your body has been made imperishable;
day by day, your corpse shall become nourished and white. (102-103)
"O King, eat your own flesh for a full hundred years;
when Agastya, the great ascetic, arrives at Śvetāraṇya, you will then be liberated from this hardship by that most invincible Lord. (104)
He is capable of subduing even the gods and asuras, including Indra;
O royal sage, what then need be said of this contemptible food?
A great task for the gods has been accomplished by that high-souled one through his meritorious deeds. 105–106.
The ocean was rendered waterless and the Dānavas were struck down;
the Vindhya mountain, which had been growing out of its hatred for the Sun, was restrained; and this earth, burdened by its own weight, was made to hang down. 107.
"The southern direction and the heavens have been reached; the three worlds are in a state of turmoil. Having gone there with the Asuras, I have sent you toward the southern direction.
O highly fortunate one, establish me as equal to the world through your status as my preceptor."
Thus, O King of kings, by that sage making the entire earth level, it is seen even today;
and I, having heard this speech of the Blessed One, the God of gods—

I have been consuming loathsome food while my own body remains unsurpassed. For a full hundred years, this loathsome food has not diminished for me, O Brahmin, and yet my satisfaction remains supreme.
Tormented by hardship, I contemplate that sage day and night:
"When will that sage grant me his sight in the forest?
As I was reflecting thus, a hundred years passed here.
"O Brahmin, my destination shall certainly be the realm of Sogastya;
I shall not go to hell after the death of this twice-born Kumbhayoni," he said.
Having heard these words and seeing the loathsome food, Rāma [reflected]. 114–115.

Filled with supreme compassion, Agastya thought, "I shall make that king, who is departing for heaven, a consumer of nectar, and I shall destroy this loathsome [state]," and while reflecting thus, he spoke to him. What will Agastya do?
"O Mahāmati, we consider this [act] contemptible;
therefore, ask us for something desired that will bring supreme joy to your mind. After all, how could the word of Brahmā be otherwise? (117-118)
"O sage, it is impossible for me to do this, nor will anyone else deliver you, except for that one born from the womb of Vaikuṇṭha, who arose from Mitra and Varuṇa.
O Brahmin, even though he had not been asked, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke thus to me.
To Śveta, who was speaking thus, I said:
"I am he; I have come here by your good fortune and have been seen by you—of this there is no doubt.
Then, recognizing me as a celestial being, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
Having raised him up, Rāma then said to him, "What shall I do for you?
The king replied, "O Brāhmaṇa, save me today from this evil deed resulting from my contemptible food. (122)
"By this act performed by you, O my son, the world shall become an inexhaustible heaven for me;
therefore, this gift has indeed been offered by the king, who is adored by the universe. May you show me favor and accept this gift. (123–127)
O descendant of Raghu, when the ornaments were taken by Rāma and came into my hands, my mind was set on crossing over [the ocean] out of greed;
O King, at that moment, your former human body perished.
When his body had perished, that royal sage, filled with supreme joy, was told by me to go once more to heaven by means of a celestial chariot; and by him,
who is equal to Śakra, this auspicious ornament was given to me.
On account of that, by the wondrous deed performed for him by the descendant of Kakutstha,
the King of Vaidarbha became free from all sin.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rāma and Agastya," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Seven. Pulastya said:
Having heard those most wonderful words, the descendant of Raghu...
Out of reverence and wonder, he proceeded to ask further.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, where is that terrible forest in which he performed his austerities?"

How did this wonder come to pass regarding Śveta, the king of Vaidarbha? O great sage, tell me how that king entered that formidable forest— desolate and devoid of wild animals— to practice austerities.
"For a hundred yojanas all around, the region became devoid of humans; how did you enter it? Tell me the purpose for which you went there.
Agastya said:
In a former age, there was a king named Manu, the lord who wielded the rod of punishment.
His son was Ikṣvāku, of immeasurable luster, by name. Having installed that eldest son, who was esteemed by the world, upon the throne, [he departed].
"O Bhavaja, you shall be the king of the royal lineages upon this earth," he said. "So be it," the son promised to his father, O Raghava;
thereupon, exceedingly delighted, the father spoke to him again.
"I am pleased, without a doubt, by that most noble deed of yours;
for you protect the subjects with punishment, yet never inflict punishment without cause.
That punishment which is meted out here by men against offenders—"
When administered according to the rules, the rod of punishment leads the king to heaven.
Therefore, O mighty-armed son, be diligent regarding the rod; in this way, dharma will be fully established for you in the world. 9–10.
Having thus instructed his son extensively with focused concentration, Manu,
being joyful, departed for the celestial realm, the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
He then became absorbed in anxiety, thinking, "How shall I procreate sons?"
Through those various numerous deeds, he became endowed with sons;
together with his sons, who were like the offspring of gods, he gratified the ancestors.
O descendant of Raghu, the youngest among them all was the most excellent.
Then his wise father, seeing that he was brave, accomplished in learning, and honored by the people as a teacher, gave him the name Daṇḍin;
for he foresaw that a staff would one day fall upon his body.
Perceiving that terrible fault of his son, O Raghava, the lord bestowed upon him a kingdom between the Vindhya and Nila mountains; there,
on the delightful mountain peak, he became king with full authority over the rod of punishment.
He then constructed an incomparable city for his residence; he himself gave that city the name Madhumatta. Thus endowed with such a region, the hero established his dwelling there.
Thus the king, together with his priest, ruled that kingdom,
which was filled with joyful subjects like Devarāja in heaven;
meanwhile, Kākutstha, along with Daṇḍa, passed many tens of thousands of years.
The righteous-souled king ruled his kingdom with all thorns removed;
then, at a certain time during the delightful month of Caitra, he proceeded to the beautiful hermitage of Bhārgava.
There, Daṇḍa beheld the daughter of Bhṛgu, peerless on earth in beauty, wandering in a forest region— excellent beyond compare,
with high and full breasts, dark-complexioned, with a face like the moon, and auspicious. (21–22)
Seeing her with a beautiful nose, all limbs lovely, full and elevated breasts, a slender waist, and a broad figure—
wearing but a single garment, alone in the forest, and standing in the prime of youth— he feels great joy. (23)
Having seen her, he was afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god (Kāma) according to the nature of the virtuous;
approaching the maiden who was well-rested, he spoke these words: "From where have you come, O fair-hipped one, and whose are you, O most beautiful lady? (24-25)
"O beautiful one, being tormented by my body, I ask you this:
O lovely lady, from the very moment I saw you, my heart has been stolen by you.
This face of yours is so delightful that it captivates even the minds of sages. (26)
"If I do not obtain food to eat, consider me as dead. O fair-eyed one, restore my life-breaths which have been taken away by you!
O beautiful lady, I am your slave; O auspicious one, favor me, your devotee."
To him who was speaking thus, intoxicated with passion and lustful,
the daughter of Bhṛgu replied with humility to the king:
"Know me to be the daughter of Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, whose actions are effortless."
"O Indra among kings, Arajā is the eldest of those dwelling in the hermitage.
O Indra among kings, Śukra is the father of me, the high-souled one, and you are his disciple according to dharma; and I am your sister, O prince. (30-31)
"O King, you ought not to speak such words; for even from others who are very wicked, I must always be protected by you.
My father is wrathful and fierce; he might reduce you to ashes."

Or else, by the duty of a king, act with force against him who is unrelated to you; entreat your father through actions consistent with dharma, O best of kings, and choose my father of great splendor as your bridegroom.
"Otherwise, a vast and terrible suffering will surely befall you;
my father, when enraged, could utterly consume the three worlds.
Then, having heard those most dreadful and extremely horrific words of punishment, [Daṇḍa...]
Intoxicated with passion, he bowed his head once more and replied:
"O fair-hipped one, show favor to me who am maddened by desire, O lovely woman! My life-breaths are dissolving, obstructed by you, O lady of auspicious countenance. (36–37)

"Having encountered you here, let there be enmity for me, or even a most severe death; accept me as your devotee, O Bhīru, for my devotion to you is supreme. Having spoken thus, he forcibly seized that maiden by the arm.
Another king, with his own hand, stripped her of her garments and treated her in that manner;
embracing her limb by limb and pressing his mouth to her mouth, he proceeded to copulate with her as he desired while she trembled.
Having inflicted that most terrible and dreadful punishment,
Daṇḍa quickly returned to his own city like an elephant intoxicated with rut.
The daughter of Bhṛgu, weeping and miserable, remained not far from the hermitage.
Anxious, he waited upon his father, who was equal to a god.
After a short while, having performed his ablutions, the celestial sage of immeasurable luster,
afflicted by hunger, returned to his own hermitage surrounded by his disciples.
He beheld Arajā and the others overwhelmed by dust, like the moonlight of the moon eclipsed by thick clouds; at that sight, anger arose in that high-souled one who was afflicted by hunger.
As if burning the three worlds, he spoke to those disciples:
"Behold the terrible calamity of this perverse man who lacks foresight—a disaster as fearsome as a blazing crest of fire. (45-46)
He who has touched the flames of a blazing fire in this world will undoubtedly meet his destruction and fall into an evil state along with his followers,
because he has committed such a terrible and dreadful sin.
Therefore, that evil-minded one, joined with the commands of a wicked king and accompanied by his servants, forces, and vehicles, shall obtain an unsurpassed rain of dust;
that fool, whose conduct consists of sinful deeds, shall meet his death. 48–49.
May the Destroyer of Pāka (Indra) shake the territory of this evil-minded one for a hundred yojanas in every direction with a great rain of dust,
and likewise all beings here, whether moving or stationary.
Through a rain of dust, the destruction of all will swiftly come to pass.
As far as the territory of Daṇḍa extends, so far shall a rain of dust fall suddenly for seven nights, affecting the sacrificial grounds and hermitages. 51-52.
Having spoken thus, consumed by anger, he said to that person living in the hermitage,
"Stay at the edge of the countryside.
As soon as Uśanas had spoken, the people residing in the hermitage [departed].

He quickly departed from that region and established his dwelling outside. Having spoken thus to the sage, he said this to Arajas: "O woman of wicked intellect, you must remain here in the hermitage with a concentrated mind."
"O Virajā, remain here for a hundred years, free from passion, as if in a passionless state, in this hermitage of radiant splendor extending for a yojana.
Having heard this command of the brahmin-sage, Virajā, the daughter of Bhṛgu, then [obeyed].
Deeply distressed, she said "So be it" to her father, the descendant of Bhṛgu (57).
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu departed from that place and went elsewhere; within seven days, [the city] was reduced to ashes, exactly as the knower of Brahman had declared (58).

Therefore, the human inhabitants of the Vindhya mountain range became the targets of punishment; for they had been cursed by Uśanas when he was provoked to anger. From that time forward, O descendant of Kakutstha, it has been called the Daṇḍaka forest.
"All this that you asked me, O Rāghava, has been explained to you. For the time for the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) is passing away, O hero.
Here, O Rāma, are the great sages on all sides with their water-pots full."

Having performed the water-libations and worship for the tiger among men, they went to the Sun with hymns composed by Brahmā and others and practiced by all the ṛṣis. When the Sun had set, Rāma went and sipped the ritual water.
Taking the sage’s word to heart, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, proceeded to that holy lake to perform his twilight devotions. Then,
in that delightful forest region adorned with trees—
On that supreme mountain, Nadapunya, adorned with hundreds of cuckoos,
with gardens resounding with the cries of various birds and teeming with diverse animals,
it was crowded with lions and tigers and filled with various twice-born creatures. 65.
The vulture and the owl lived abroad for many groups of years. Then,
having made up his mind to commit a wicked act, the vulture went to the owl's dwelling and,
making that [owl] his enemy, engaged in a quarrel with him.
"Rama, the lotus-eyed one, is the king of the entire world;
let us seek refuge with him quickly—for whose residence could this possibly be?
Thus spoke the vulture and the owl, both filled with anger and indignation.
With their minds agitated by the age of Kali, they both quickly sought refuge in Rāma;
those two, though mutually hostile, likewise touched his feet.
Then, seeing the lord of the Raghus, the vulture spoke these words:
In my view, you are considered the foremost among both the gods and the asuras;
you, O high-minded one, are superior to Bṛhaspati and Śukra.
You are a knower of the higher and lower natures of all beings, like a second Indra in the mortal world.

You are as difficult to gaze upon as the sun, and like the Himalayas in gravity; you are the ocean in depth, and you are the guardian of the world. You are equal to the earth in patience, and indeed comparable to the wind in swiftness.
O Rāghava, you are my guru, endowed with all perfections; you are the very form of Viṣṇu—indignant, invincible, a conqueror, and one who has reached the further shore of the science of all weapons.
O Lord of Gods, O bull among men, listen to what I have to report.
"O Lord, O King, this owl is seizing my dwelling which was built by the strength of my own arms;
he does so especially in your presence. Such is his wicked conduct, O King, that he transgresses your command. (75-76)
"O Rāma, you ought to punish him with the ultimate penalty of death.
When the vulture had spoken thus, the owl addressed these words:
"O lord of men, listen with a focused mind to this instruction of mine."
A king is born from Soma, Śakra, Sūrya, Dhanada, and likewise from Yama;
he is but a mere human being.
But you are the God who consists of all things, whose supreme refuge is Nārāyaṇa.
O King, it is proclaimed that when a matter has been properly deliberated and correctly judged, you,

the slayer of the demon Tāpa, are indeed the one who protects [the people] from the heat [of punishment], since you remove the fear of sin from the subjects through the infliction of punishment for their faults. (80)
As a giver, a striker, and a protector, you are like Indra to us.
You are unassailable among all beings by virtue of your splendor, which is like fire; because you constantly consume the sins of the wicked through your asceticism, O Rāma, you are a sun.
O best of kings, you are directly equal to the Lord of Wealth, or even superior to Dhanada; for your wealth and prosperity are eternally dependent upon your own will,
whereas the treasury of Dhanada and his majesty depend upon him.
O Rāghava, you possess an impartial vision toward all beings, both stationary and moving, as well as toward enemy and friend;
you always govern according to dharma through the established procedures of legal conduct.
O best of kings, that which is the non-human state of yours is declared by this [verse] as the Vairāja; it is celebrated as the "Yama" [state]. 86.
And that which is your human nature, O most excellent of monarchs, is likewise described.
The king was supremely compassionate and filled with mercy toward all.
Indeed, the king became the strength for the weak and the helpless; he was the eye for the sightless and the intellect for those lacking it. 87–88.
"O righteous one, listen to me:
you too must consider that he who is our lord is indeed the king of birds, and he is the one to whom these birds are to be assigned by you. (89)
"O Lord, we have no ownership over this place in your presence.
O King, it was previously created by you alone for the fourfold collection of beings; yet a vulture has entered my abode and is harassing me. (90–91)
"You are the Teacher among gods and men, O bull among men.
Having heard this, the King, his joy having vanished, summoned his ministers himself:
Viṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and Rāṣṭravardhana.
Aśoka, Dharmapāla, Sumantra, and the mighty Mahābala—these were the ministers of King Daśaratha, the son of Rāma;
they were high-souled, endowed with statesmanship, and experts in all the śāstras. (93–94)
Having descended from the Puṣpaka chariot, that righteous-souled one summoned those who were well-composed, of noble birth, and experts in the science of polity;
then the best of the Raghus questioned the vulture and the owl as they were disputing.
"For how many years have you made this abode of yours, O vulture? Tell me this, if you know it according to the truth, for I am curious.
Having heard these words, the vulture spoke to Rāghava as he stood there.
"O Rāma, from that time onwards, this entire earth has been covered with many raised human arms;
it is like a forest adorned with trees," said the owl to Rāma.

"From the very moment the earth was ruled by you, this has been my home. Having heard this, Rāma said to the members of the assembly: "That is no assembly where there are no elders; that is no assembly where the elders do not declare what is dharma."
That is not a court where there is no truth, nor is that truth which is accepted as a pretext;
those members who, having entered the assembly, sit silently reflecting instead of speaking what they have perceived, are all speakers of falsehood. 101.
If one recites the *Navākṣara* [mantra] out of desire, anger, or fear,
a thousand nooses of Varuṇa are cast upon that man;
when a full year has passed, only one of those nooses is released.
"Therefore, one who knows the truth must speak the truth straightforwardly.
Having heard this, the minister Rāma then spoke as follows:
"O King, the owl is beautiful, but not so the vulture, O high-minded one. (104)
"You are the authority, O Great King; you are the king, for the king is the supreme refuge. All subjects have the king as their root; the king is the eternal dharma.
The king is the ruler of those men who do not fall into miserable states. (105-106)
And those who have been released by Vaivasvata become supreme among men.
Having heard the words of his ministers, Rāma spoke these words:
"Listen, for I shall relate that which was declared in the Purāṇa."
The sky with its moon, sun, and stars, along with the mountains, the earth, and the trees—this triple world, including all things moving and unmoving, was then submerged in the ocean of water;
indeed, it all became one, like the single expanse of the sky. (108–109)
Punarbhu entered the womb of Viṣṇu along with Lakṣmī; having restrained her and entered the ocean of waters, he of great splendor,
having composed his self, slept there for many hundreds of years.
Then, when Viṣṇu had fallen asleep, Brahmā entered his belly. Recognizing that it possessed many channels, the great yogi entered it.
From the navel of Viṣṇu, there arose a lotus adorned with gold.
Having emerged from Satī and become a yogi of great power, Brahmā,
desiring to create the earth, the wind, the mountains, and trees,
as well as all intermediate beings, humans, and reptiles, [proceeded]. (113)

The one of great ascetic power created all beings born from wombs and from eggs. From his body arose the two Dānavas, Kaiṭabha and Madhu, who were then of great heroism, terrible, and possessed of boons.
O King, seeing Prajāpati there, both of them, overcome with anger,
rushed with great speed toward the Self-born One to devour him;
and seeing this, all living beings fled away in every direction.
Having slain those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Viṣṇu, who was praised by Brahmā,
caused the earth to expand with their fat for the sake of its preservation; because she bore the scent of that fat, the earth acquired the name Medinī.
Therefore, that wicked-souled vulture, being untruthful and a doer of evil deeds, makes another's abode his own; he is undoubtedly deserving of punishment.
Then, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"Do not kill this vulture; he was previously consumed by the power of asceticism.
O Lord of Creatures, O Sovereign of Men, he was formerly burnt by Gautama.
This one is named Brahmadatta, a hero, pure and devoted to truth. (120-121)
Having returned home, she requested food from the brahmin-sage;
and for a full hundred years, O best of kings, he ate [with her].
Then, he himself offered water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya) to this very Brahmadatta.
O one of great luster, he himself properly prepared food for his own sake;
then, having entered the house of that high-souled man and seen a woman with full breasts, he seized her by the hand. 123–124.

Then, the enraged sage uttered a most terrible curse: "Go, you fool, and become a vulture! Thereupon the king said to the sage, "O illustrious one, show mercy; there will be a release from this curse."
Having heard those words, O lord of men, the compassionate one spoke again:
"In the lineage of the Raghus, there will arise a highly illustrious one named Rāma; he will be a fortunate king of the Ikṣvākus, with eyes like lotuses. (126–127)
"Therefore, O bull among men, you shall not experience the ripening of that [sin] as long as it remains unseen;
