once seen by Rāma, however, it will take effect. Having heard this, the lord of the earth quickly cast off his state as a vulture and became anointed with divine fragrant unguents.
That man of divine form addressed the lord of men:
"O Lord, you are virtuous and a knower of dharma; by your grace, O All-pervading One, I, though a sinner, have been liberated from the terrible hell."
Having dismissed his pride, the lord of the earth in human form spoke to Ulūka:
"O Kauśika, you who know the dharma, enter your own home;
I shall return to where the sage is once I have performed my twilight devotions."
Then, having touched water and performed the evening twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*),
Rāma entered the hermitage of the high-souled Agastya, the "Jar-born" one;
there Agastya respectfully offered him fruit and roots of manifold qualities.
He brought flavorful vegetables for the purpose of a meal;
that tiger among men ate that food, which was like nectar. Delighted and thoroughly satisfied, he spent the night there.
Rising at the break of dawn and performing his daily rites, O subduer of enemies,
the best of the Raghus approached the sage in order to depart. Having paid his respects, Rāma spoke to the great seer born from a jar.
"I take my leave, O Brahmin; may I depart? You ought to grant me permission.
I am blessed and favored by the sight of you, O great sage. By good fortune, I shall become a purified soul through [the grace of] the Great-Souled One."
When the descendant of Kakutstha had spoken these words of wondrous appearance,
the ascetic, his eyes filled with tears, spoke with great joy:
"O Rāma, these most wonderful words of yours, composed of auspicious syllables, are truly marvelous."
"O descendant of Raghu, you have described yourself as the purifier of all beings. O Rāma,
those men who look upon you with a friendly eye for even a single moment are declared by the gods to be purified by all the sacred hymns."
Those living beings on earth who look upon you with terrible eyes are instantly struck by the staff of Brahma and go to hell;
such as you are, O best of the Raghus, the purifier of all embodied beings.
O Raghava, as people speak of you, they shall attain perfection;
go, then, without distress, along a path free from obstacles and fear from any quarter. Rule the kingdom with righteousness, for you are the refuge of the worlds.
Thus addressed by the sage, the king, with palms joined in reverence,
144 set out to pay his respects to Agastya, the best of sages; having saluted that foremost of munis and all those others preeminent in asceticism, 145.
Then, undistracted, he ascended that gold-adorned Puṣpaka chariot;
as it departed, hosts of sages honored that lord of men from all sides with blessings,
just as the immortals honor the thousand-eyed Indra.
Then, on the day of arrival, Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha who is skilled in all matters, reached Ayodhyā and alighted from the sky on foot. Thereupon,
he dismissed the beautiful Puṣpaka chariot that had carried him at will.
Emerging from the inner chamber, the king spoke these words to the gatekeepers:
"Go with swift strides to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata; having informed them of my arrival, bring them here without delay."
Having heard the speech of the gatekeeper Rāma, whose actions are untainted,
they went, summoned the two princes, and reported it to Rāghava.
By the command of Rāghava, the two princes were brought by the gatekeepers.
Seeing that his beloved Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa had arrived,
Rāghava embraced them both and spoke these words:
"I have performed the supreme service for the twice-born exactly as it should be done."
O Raghavas, I desire further to perform that which is rooted in dharma;
together with you two, who are as my very self, I wish to sacrifice in the Rājasūya, the supreme of rituals, wherein eternal dharma resides. (153-154)
Formerly, while residing at Puṣkara, Brahmā, the creator of the world and knower of dharma,
performed three hundred and sixty sacrifices;
having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, Soma likewise offered sacrifice according to dharma.
Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, Mitra, the destroyer of enemies, attained the unsurpassed station of fame in all the worlds;
in a single auspicious moment, he attained the status of Varuṇa. 156–157.
Therefore, having reflected upon this matter, both of you speak what is beneficial.
Bharata said:
"O virtuous one, you are the supreme dharma; the entire earth rests upon you. (158)
O mighty-armed one of immeasurable prowess,
all these great-souled protectors of the earth gaze upon you as they would upon Prajāpati— the gods and we ourselves likewise behold you as the Lord of the World. 159.
O King of great intelligence, the subjects behold you as they would a father; O Raghava, you have become the refuge of living beings here on earth.
O scorcher of foes, it is not fitting that you should perform such a sacrifice.
O tiger among kings, O lord of men, since the destruction of all beings on earth is seen and heard,
there was a great battle of the luminaries in the Tārakāmaya war.

Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, was carried off by Soma out of lust. There, a great battle took place, destroying both gods and Dānavas. In the terrible sacrifice of Varuṇa, there was a conflict involving fish and tortoises.
O tiger among kings, O Raghava, at the conclusion of Hariścandra’s Rājasūya sacrifice, all aquatic creatures perished;
then there occurred the great battle of Āḍībaka, which brought destruction to all the worlds.

"O tiger among men, O King, you have heard that at the Rājasūya sacrifice there is the destruction of all beings on earth, including those of the animal realm, both celestial and terrestrial; therefore, reflect upon this with your intellect, O ruler of the earth. (166–167)
"O gentle one, practice the complete dharma which is beneficial and auspicious for all living beings.
Hearing Bharata's words, Rāghava replied with respect:
"O slayer of enemies, I am pleased by these words of yours, O knower of dharma."
"O lover of dharma, my mind has turned away from the Rājasūya sacrifice.
I shall perform the Pūrṇadharma; and in Kānyakubja, O hero, I shall install Vāmana, whose fame has reached the heavens. (169–170)
"There is no doubt that it will happen, just as [the descent of] the Gaṅgā occurred through Bhagīratha.
(171) Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Prevention of the Sacrifice," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Eight.
Bhīṣma said:
O brahmin-sage, how was Vāmana established by Rāma at Kānyakubja? Where was he obtained? Tell me this in detail.
For indeed, O Blessed One, this sweet voice of mine has been employed in the chanting of Rāma’s glory; it brings pleasure to my ears as I listen.
Out of devotion, people behold that descendant of Raghu with affection.
Knowing the Dharma and grateful, with intellect perfected,
he ruled the entire earth righteously and with great composure.
While he governed the kingdom, the trees bore fruits that fulfilled all desires.
The earth of that great-souled one yields crops without being tilled, and it is abundant with flavorful foods and various garments; moreover, he is without rival.
By him, the work of the gods has been accomplished, for Rāvaṇa was a thorn to the worlds.
Accompanied by his sons and ministers, he was struck down as if in mere play.
O best of the twice-born, O Muni, when that dharma was fulfilled, a realization arose within him;
I truly desire to hear all of his life’s deeds from you.
Pulastya said:
O mighty-armed king, listen with a focused mind to what Rāma, established on the path of dharma, performed at a certain time. 8.
He remembered that lord of the Rākṣasas, thinking:
"How will King Vibhīṣaṇa, remaining in Laṅkā, rule the kingdom as a Rākṣasa?
Hostility toward the gods is a sign of impending destruction."
I have granted him that kingdom, lasting as long as the moon and sun;
through its preservation, his fame shall become firm and eternal.
Rāvaṇa has performed penance here for the sake of his own destruction.
That most wicked one has now been destroyed by me for the sake of the gods' purpose;
therefore, I myself must now go and seek out Vibhīṣaṇa, so that he may be instructed in what is beneficial for him,
whereby he may remain forever.
While Rāma of immeasurable splendor was reflecting thus, Bharata arrived;
seeing Rāma, he spoke these words:
"O Lord, what are you contemplating? Tell me this secret of men."
"O best of men, whether it be for the sake of the gods, for the sake of the earth,
or for your own purpose," Rāghava spoke these words to Bharata, who stood there lost in thought,
"but this is indeed a secret of yours."
"You, O Lakṣmaṇa of great renown, are the vital breath moving outside [the body]. There is nothing unknown to you; do not hold me to a falsehood.
This is my great anxiety: how will Vibhīṣaṇa be dealt with by the gods?"
Since the Ten-necked one was struck down for the sake of what is beneficial,
I shall go to Laṅkā where that Vibhīṣaṇa is;
and having seen him in that city, I will speak to the Rākṣasa regarding our duty.
Having looked upon the entire earth, Sugrīva the lord of monkeys,
the great king Śatrughna, and all his brothers and sons, while the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, Bharata stood before him.
He spoke these words to Rāghava: "I shall go with you;
do so, O mighty-armed one, but let the son of Sumitrā remain here. Having spoken thus to Bharata, Rāma then addressed the son of Sumitrā in the city.
"O hero, you must remain here to guard us until our return. Having thus instructed Lakṣmaṇa and meditated upon the Puṣpaka chariot, the king,
the enhancer of Kausalyā’s joy, ascended that celestial vehicle.
Then the Puṣpaka chariot arrived at the region of Gāndhāra;
there Bharata’s two sons saw it and, observing the conduct of the world,
departed for the eastern direction where Lakṣmaṇa’s two sons resided.
Having stayed for six nights at Puṣkara, the two descendants of Raghu traveled by that celestial chariot toward the southern direction to Prayāga,
the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, frequented by sages.
Having paid homage to Bharadvāja and Atri, they went to their hermitages;
after conversing with the sages there, they arrived at Janasthāna.
Rāma said:
"Here, our beloved Sītā was previously carried away by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa,
after he had slain Jaṭāyu, the vulture who was our father’s friend. Here, too, we had a great battle with the wicked-minded Kabandha."
"Sītā has not been consumed by fire in Rāvaṇa’s abode.
On Ṛṣyamūka, the best of mountains, there is a monkey named Sugrīva; go with your younger brother to Paṃpā, and he will provide you assistance. (29-30)
Having reached Lake Pampā, he went to the female ascetic Śabarī;
thus addressed, the hero stood there in sorrow, despairing of life. "This is that Nalinī," Vīra said, "in which Lakṣmaṇa spoke."
Do not grieve, O tiger among men, O destroyer of enemies;
for when I, your servant, am at your command, you shall recover Maithilī.
These eight months of mine have passed as if they were a hundred years.
"Right here, O scorcher of foes, Vālin was slain for the sake of Sugrīva;
surely this is that Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin, which bears such a resemblance.
For it was there indeed that the righteous Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, [was established]."
Accompanied by the monkeys, the hero remained there for a hundred years.
While Sugrīva remained there together with the monkeys,
the two heroes, Bhārata and Rāghava, arrived at that city.
Seeing that his two brothers had arrived, he prostrated himself and said this:
"O heroes, where have you set out from, and what task will you perform? Then, having seated them both on a throne, he personally offered them the guest-offering (arghya).
While the righteous descendant of Raghu was thus seated in the assembly,
Aṅgada, Hanumān, Nala, Nīla, Pāṭala,
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, and the highly illustrious Panasa [were present].
The family priest, the minister, the astrologer Dadhivakra,
Nīla, Śatabali, Mainda, Dvivida, Gandhamādana,
Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, Vīrasena, and Vināyaka— 40.
Sūryābha, Kumuda, Suṣeṇa the leader of the monkey hosts,
Ṛṣabha, Vinata, Gavākṣa of terrible prowess, and Dhūmra the king of bears, arrived with their armies. 41–42.
All the women of the inner apartments, as well as Ruma and Tārā, and the ladies of Aṅgada’s harem along with other attendants, attained incomparable joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (43).
Then the high-souled monkeys, together with Sugrīva,
and the illustrious female monkeys, headed by Tārā, beheld Rāghava there; with throats choked with tears, they prostrated themselves and spoke as follows.
O Goddess Kausalyā, having conquered Rāvaṇa through your divine power and having established your purity in the fire before your husband, your father,
you have brought Rāma back to the city; behold him now bowing before you.
O descendant of Raghu, you shine precisely because of your youthfulness.
Even without you, that virtuous Jānakī remains steadfast; I know of no other wife for you, and one deprived of his wife does not truly shine.
To Tārā, whose name was equal to the lord of the stars (the moon), who was speaking thus like a pair of krauñca birds or a pair of cakravāka birds, Rāma—
the best of speakers and lotus-eyed— replied.
With beautiful tusks and large eyes, he was difficult to overcome even by the god of death; know that this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is created by Time.
Let all these women go; Sugrīva stands facing him.
Sugrīva said:
"O lords of men, tell me quickly for what purpose you two have come here; for the time for action is at hand."
While Sugrīva was speaking thus, Bharata, urged by Rāma,
announced his departure for Laṅkā;
and Sugrīva said to those two, "I shall go to the city together with you."
"I shall go there to see the Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa, the god among men.
When Sugrīva had spoken thus, Rāghava said, "Go then.
Thus, those three—Sugrīva and the two Rāghavas—remained seated like the three flowers of the tree of love (Puṣpaka).
Having reached the northern shore of the ocean,
Rāma, the lord of the rākṣasas, spoke to Bharata regarding Vibhīṣaṇa, who was there with his four ministers seeking his life. 55-56.
Having arrived there, he was consecrated by Lakṣmaṇa in the kingdom of Laṅkā;
meanwhile, I remained for three days on the further shore of the ocean, thinking, "He will grant me an audience, and the purpose of my kinsmen will be accomplished."
"O slayer of enemies, he granted me the sight of him for only that long;
then, O Raghava, on the fourth day, my anger became exceedingly great.
Drawing my bow with force, I took up a divine weapon in my hand."
Seeing me seeking refuge, he was terrified and took shelter with Lakṣmaṇa;
I was then pacified by Sugrīva, [who said], "O Rāghava, let him be forgiven by you. Thereupon, with an arrow discharged by me, he was driven away to the desert region.
Then, addressed by the king of the ocean, who was exceedingly modest, [he said]:
"O Rāghava,
O tiger among men, having crossed the great ocean filled with water by means of a bridge of stones, you must go to Laṅkā."
This bridge was built by me in the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa;
it was brought to completion in three days by the best of monkeys.
On the first day, fourteen yojanas were constructed.
On the second day there were thirty-six [lakhs], and on the third likewise fifty [lakhs].

This Laṅkā, with its golden ramparts and gateways, was thus made to appear similar [to the original] by the best of monkeys; a great defensive barrier was established here by those foremost of vanaras.
A great battle took place here on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
wherein Rāvaṇa was slain after forty-eight days.
Here, Prahasita, the bull among the Rākṣasas, was killed by Nīla.
Right here, Dhūmrākṣa was struck down by Hanumān; likewise, Mahodara and Atikāya were slain by the high-souled Sugrīva.
And right here, Kumbhakarṇa was killed by Lakṣmaṇa, as was Indrajit.
And here, after I had slain Daśagrīva, that bull among the Rākṣasas,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived to converse with me;
so did the trident-bearing God, whose banner is the bull, accompanied by Pārvatī.
Maheṃdra, the hosts of gods, along with the Gandharvas and Kinnaras,
as well as the Pitāmaha, arrived from the celestial realm, O great king, surrounded by throngs of Apsarases and groups of Vidyādharas.
Desiring the purification of Jānakī in the presence of them all,
Sītā was told by [Rāma] and entered the fire; having attained purity,
she was seen by the lords of Laṅkā and the gods, and was taken away by the command of her father.
Then I was addressed by the king: "Go to Ayodhyā, my son.
O Rāghava, heaven is highly esteemed by you; deprived of you, it would be so.
I have been delivered by you, my son, and I have attained the same world as Indra. (73-74)
And the king said to Lakṣmaṇa, "O son, merit has been earned by you;
together with your brother, you shall attain the highest divine worlds.
Then, having summoned Jānakī, the king spoke these words.
"O lady of virtuous vows, you must not harbor anger toward your husband;
O fair-eyed one, your husband’s fame shall indeed be preeminent.
While Rāma was speaking thus, the Puṣpaka chariot came to a halt.
Thereupon, those foremost of rākṣasas went quickly to Vibhīṣaṇa and said, "Rāma has arrived with Sugrīva; such is the report.
Hearing of Rāma's arrival nearby, Vibhīṣaṇa—
He honored those spies with all desired objects, wealth, and other gifts.
Having adorned that city, he went forth together with his ministers and beheld Rāma seated in the celestial chariot, like the sun upon Mount Meru.

Having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta), he spoke to Rāghava: "Today my birth has become fruitful; all my desires have been attained, since I have beheld your blameless feet, O Lord, which are worthy of worship by the entire world. (81)
"I have been honored by the gods, Śakra and the other denizens of heaven.
Thinking himself superior even to Purandara, the lord of the thirty-three gods,
he remained in Rāvaṇa’s palace, which was ablaze and adorned with every kind of jewel.
When the descendant of Kakutstha had sat down, Vibhīṣaṇa, having offered the guest-offering (arghya), spoke with palms joined in reverence to Sugrīva and Bharata:
"Whatever I may do as a servant for Rāma who has arrived here, that is my duty."
"Having slain this enemy, a thorn to the three worlds and a doer of evil deeds, with the help of my beloved wife, I have given back to you this city which was previously mine;
for this city is mine, these are my wives, these are my sons, and so am I. (85-86)
"May all this be given by me to you, and may it all be inexhaustible for you.
Then all the subjects and those inhabitants of Laṅkā came to see Rāghava, filled with curiosity.
Having been addressed by them thus, O Lord, Vibhīṣaṇa presented Rāma with [the gifts].
All those offerings described by the high-souled Vibhīṣaṇa were accepted by Bharata at the command of Rāma.

The lord of men seized a vast collection of wealth and jewels; thus Rāma dwelt there in the abode of the Rākṣasa for three days. On the arrival of the fourth day, Rāma was seated in the assembly hall.
Kekasī’s son said this to Rāma: "O dear son, I shall show you [him];
by seeing him, great merit is obtained by the best of sages.
This is the illustrious Viṣṇu, the eternal one existing in four forms."
O highly fortunate one, Sītā is Lakṣmī; she was not known before by her elder brother.
Her father previously described this to the gods during their assembly in heaven: "In the lineage of the Raghus, Viṣṇu shall indeed be the son of Daśaratha. (93)
"It shall lead to the destruction of the ten-necked Rākṣasa.
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"O mother, do exactly so; please accept this ninth garment."
A vessel filled with sandalwood paste, along with curds, honey, and parched grain, together with *dūrvā* grass, was offered as an *arghya* oblation upon seeing the son of the Kuru king;
Saramā was placed at the forefront, as were the other daughters of the gods. 95–96.
"Therefore, I shall go ahead to the vicinity of Vraja and Svarāghava. Having spoken thus, he went to where Rāma was stationed,
having driven away all the Dānavas who had come to see Rāma.
Having made the assembly hall pure and having placed Rāma facing him,
Vibhīṣaṇa said:

She also gave birth to the ten-necked Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa while she was begging.
She is that very mother of the gods who now desires to see your feet; therefore, having shown her compassion, you ought to grant her an audience.
Rāma said: "O Lord of Rākṣasas, I shall go into her presence out of a desire to see my mother; you, however, go quickly ahead of me. (101)
Having accepted those words, the Lord rose from his excellent seat;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he offered a salutation. "I greet you, lady; by law you are my mother."
O Goddess, if a human being beholds these two feet through great austerity and various kinds of merit, I shall be fully satisfied; for I am fond of my children, having seen these two. 104.
"Just as Kausalyā was my mother, so too is Kaikeyī; O King, live long and be happy," she said to me. Then Vīravishṇu, who had assumed a human form, spoke to his father.
Having descended into the lineage of Raghu for the sake of the welfare of the gods,
he came to bestow prosperity upon Vibhīṣaṇa, to bring about the destruction of the Ten-necked one,
as well as the slaying of Vālin and the construction of the bridge across the ocean.
"Putra, the son of Daśaratha, will indeed do all this;
now you have been recognized by me through the recollection of that speech of my husband.
Sītā is Lakṣmī, you are Viṣṇu, and likewise the monkeys are the gods."
"I shall go home with my son; may you attain stable fame.
Saramā said:
"Remaining here in the Aśoka grove for a full year..."
"O scorcher of foes, I constantly remember the feet of Sītā, who remains happily serving the god-like Ajaṅka;
when shall I behold that lady, as I contemplate her day and night? (110-111)
For what reason has Jānakī not been brought here by the God of gods?
You do not shine at all when alone, being without that woman.
O scorcher of foes, Sītā shines in your presence, and you in hers.
When she had spoken thus, Bharata asked these words: "Who is this? Then Rāma, perceiving her intention, quickly laughed and said:
"She is indeed the wife of Vibhīṣaṇa, known by the name Saramā."
The noble Sītā, who is considered a very firm friend to her beloved, will see everything as being caused by time; I know not what she will do.
Go, O fortunate one, to your husband's house; protect yourself, O beautiful lady.

"Having abandoned me, who am devoid of fortune, the goddess has departed like a wretched fate (116). Deprived of her, O fair-browed one, I never find any pleasure; as I wander here once again, I see all the directions as utterly empty (117)."
"Let Saramā be released; she is a dear friend of Sītā.

"One must do what is pleasing to the gods; you must not offend the deities."

"O sinless one, you must conduct yourself according to the command of the King of Kings. Whatever human being should ever come to Laṅkā, he must not be slain by the Rākṣasas; rather, he should be regarded by you just as I am."
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"O tiger among men, by your command I shall do everything.

Having understood that intention as proclaimed by Vāyu, [he acted accordingly].
Vibhīṣaṇa, having adorned Vāmana with all kinds of jewels,
brought him and presented him to Rāma, and spoke these words:
"O Rāghava, when Śakra was indeed defeated by Meghanāda..."
"O lotus-eyed one, this Vāmana has been brought here; lead him toward that God of gods and install him.
Saying "So be it," Rāghava did so and ascended the Puṣpaka chariot.
Taking the innumerable wealth and jewels, as well as Vāmana, the best of gods, Sugrīva and Bharata mounted after Vāmana; while proceeding on the path, Rāma said to Vibhīṣaṇa, "Stay here. 126–127.
Having heard the words of Rāghava, he spoke again to Rāghava: "O Lord, I shall indeed do all this that has been commanded by you.
O Indra among kings, by means of this bridge, all human beings on earth—"
"If they come and obstruct you, there will be a violation of your command.
What is your lineage, O Lord? What is this restriction, O God? And what must be done by me?
Having heard these words of Rāghava spoken by the best of the Rākṣasas, [he replied]. 129–130.

Taking his bow in hand, Rāma split the bridge in two; having divided it into three parts with great force, he cut it at the midpoint into sections of ten yojanas each, and then further divided each one into three pieces.
Thus, each was made into three segments of one yojana each.
Having reached Velāvana and performed worship of Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, Rāma named him Rāmeśvara; then,
having consecrated him and taken up Vāmana, the joy of the Raghus departed.
He departed in haste from the southern ocean, and from the sky there arose a voice with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud. 134.
Rudra said:
"O Rāma! May it be well with you. I have now come to stay here for as long as this world exists, O Rāma, and for as long as this earth remains;
until then, O Rāghava, your bridge and sacred ford shall endure."
Having heard those words of the God of gods, which were like nectar,
Rāma said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the lords of gods, the bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees."
Salutations to you, the beloved of Gaurī; salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. 137.
Salutations to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the giver of boons; salutations eternally to the Lord of Creatures, to the fierce one, and to the one with matted hair. 138.
Salutations to Mahādeva, to Bhīma, to Tryambaka, O Lord of the Quarters; salutations to Īśāna, to the slayer of Bhaga, to the destroyer of Andhaka;
salutations to the blue-throated one, to the terrible one, to the Creator praised by the Creator.
Salutations to the slayer of Kumāra’s enemies and to the progenitor of Kumāra;
salutations to the deep-red one, to the smoke-colored one, to Śiva, and to the destroyer; salutations to the blue-crested one, to the wielder of the trident, and to the annihilator of the Daityas.
Salutations to the fierce one, the three-eyed one, whose seed is golden wealth;
to the irreproachable lord of Ambikā, who is praised by all the gods;
to the one who is approachable, who is free from desire, and who is Sadyojāta. 142.
To the one whose banner is the bull, to the shaven-headed, to the one with matted hair, to the celibate student;
to the one performing austerities, to the one who is the austerity itself, to the friend of Brahman, and to the Victorious One;
to the Soul of the Universe, to the Creator of the Universe, who stands pervading the entire universe.

"Salutations, salutations to the Divine One, the remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, the compassionate one toward his devotees, O God, whose mind moves with the splendor of the universe!
(145) Pulastya said:
O King, being thus praised, Hara, the god of gods, spoke these words to Rāghava, who stood before him bowed with devotion. 146.
Rudra said:
"O Raghava, blessings upon you! Speak that which is in your mind.
You are surely Nārāyaṇa himself, descended in secret into human wombs;
and that task of the gods has been accomplished by you, O sinless one."
Now you have accomplished your task, O slayer of enemies; go to your own abode.
O descendant of Raghu, you have established a supreme sacred ford called Setu;
having come here, O King, let men behold it in this ocean.
For those who are burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka), their evil is dissolved;
whatever terrible sins there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, they perish by the mere sight [of this], so there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. 150.
O best of the Raghus, O scorcher of foes, go and establish Vāmana on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
having divided the entire earth into eight portions, depart for your own abode, Śvetadvīpa. Salutations to you, O God! (151-152)
Having prostrated himself, Rāma reached the holy site of Puṣkara;
however, that celestial chariot, O descendant of Raghu, ascended high into the sky while enveloped [in mist].
"What is this veiled vehicle, stationed in the supportless sky? he wondered.
"Something must have happened; look! he said to the monkey. 154.
At Rāma’s command, Sugrīva descended to the surface of the earth and saw Brahmā accompanied by the gods and the Siddhas. 155.
Having arrived and seen him accompanied by the assembly of Brahman-sages and endowed with the four Vedas, the Grandfather of all the worlds spoke to Rāma,
together with the world-protectors, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts.
One must certainly not bypass that very Puṣpaka, the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then Rāma, having descended from the gold-adorned Puṣpaka,
bowed to the god Viriñca, who was seated together with Gāyatrī.
Having prostrated with eight limbs and embraced the earth with five limbs, Rāma, bowing down, praised Viriñca, the God of gods. (159) Rāma said:
I bow to the creator of the worlds, the Lord of Creatures honored by the gods,
the Lord of the Devas, the Protector of the World, the Lord of Creatures, and the Master of the Universe.
Homage to you, O God of Gods, who are saluted by both gods and asuras.
O Lord of the past, the future, and the present; O you with tawny eyes like those of a monkey! You are the child and yet possess the form of an elder; you wear a deer skin as your seat and garment.
You are the Savior, the God, the Sovereign, and the Lord of the three worlds.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Padmagarbha, Vedagarbha, the bestower of memory;
the great Siddha, Mahāpadmī, Mahādaṇḍī, and Mekhalī; Kāla, Kālarūpī, Nīlagrīva, and the best among the wise. 163.
The author of the Vedas, the eternal child, the lord of bound souls (paśus), the imperishable;

he who holds darbha grass in his hand, whose banner is the swan, the creator, the destroyer, Hara, Hari; the one with matted hair, the shaven-headed, the one with a topknot, the bearer of the staff, the bearer of the club, and the one of great fame. 164–165.
The Lord of beings, the presiding deity of the gods, the soul of all, the creator of all, omnipresent, the destroyer of all, the creator, the immutable teacher;
the God who bears the water-pot and likewise the sacrificial ladles, the *sruc* and the *sruva*. 166.
Havanīya, Arcanīya, Oṃkāra, Jyeṣṭhasāmaga; Mṛtyu, Amṛta, Pāriyātra, Suvrata;
Brahmacārī, Vratadhara, Guhāvāsī, Supaṅkaja. 167–168.

He was beautiful to behold, resembling the rising sun; he was attended on both his right and left sides by his two wives. He appeared as a mendicant, yet in the form of a mendicant, possessing three matted locks and having attained firm resolve.
He is the creator of the fluctuations of the mind, as well as Kāma and Madhumadhuka; likewise, he is the forest-dweller, the inhabitant of the hermitage, and the one who is honored;
he is the sustainer of the world, the creator, the eternal and immutable Puruṣa. 170–171.
The overseer of dharma, Virūpākṣa, the possessor of the three dharmas, the creator of beings, the triple Veda, the multiformed one, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns,
the deluder, and especially the binder of the Dānavas. 172.
The god of gods, marked with a lotus, three-eyed, with matted hair born from the lotus,
possessing a tawny beard, wielding a bow, formidable, and of righteous prowess—
thus was Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, praised by Rāma. 173–174.
The Grandfather, taking the prostrate Rāma by the hand, said:
"O Great Lord, you are Viṣṇu who has descended upon the surface of the earth in a human body; that entire task of the gods has been accomplished by you."
Having established the god Vāmana on the southern bank of the Jāhnavī,
and having gone to his own city, Ayodhyā, as well as to the world of the Asuras, Rāma,
being dismissed by Brahmā, prostrated before the Grandfather.
Having ascended the Puṣpaka vehicle and arrived at the city of Mathurā,
the glorious Rāghava beheld Śatrughna, the slayer of enemies, together with his son; and so did Bharata along with the Lord of the Monkeys (Hanumān), and they all rejoiced.
The two brothers, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, arrived like Śakra and Upendra descended from heaven.
Then, having prostrated with their heads and touched the ground with their five limbs,
Rāma quickly raised his brother and placed him upon his lap.
Then Bharata sat down after him, and immediately after that, Sugrīva; then Rāma’s son, taking up the bow, quickly offered the eight-limbed kingdom to the descendant of Raghu.
Then, having heard that Rāma had arrived, all the people of Mathurā—
consisting primarily of the four castes, with Brāhmaṇas being the majority— came together to see him;
and after conversing with all the subjects and the merchants along with the Brāhmaṇas, [he addressed them].
Having stayed there for five days, Rāma set his mind on departing;
then Śatrughna brought horses, elephants,
and gold— both wrought and unwrought— as offerings for Rāma.
Then Rāma, being pleased, said: "O son, all this has been given by me to you; consecrate these two as kings among the people of Mathurā. Having spoken thus, Rāma then reached the midday sun.

Having reached Mahodaya and established Vāmana on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he spoke to the twice-born and likewise to future kings: "This bridge of dharma, which increases prosperity, has been constructed by me."
Once obtained, it must be protected and maintained; it should not be lost under any circumstances.
(188) Thus, with my hands outstretched, I have made this request to you: O kings, since I have petitioned you for this purpose, let what is beneficial be done here. (189)
Daily worship must be performed by all without weariness;
having given villages and whatever wealth had been brought for her adornment, he sent word to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, in Kiṣkindhā. 190.
Having arrived at Ayodhyā, Rāma then spoke to the Puṣpaka:
"You must not come here again; remain wherever the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) resides.
Then, having accomplished his purpose, Rāma considered that there was nothing further to be done.
Pulastya said:
O King, thus has the birth of Vāmana been told to you through the narrative of Bhīṣma and Rāma; what more do you wish to hear? 193.

"I shall tell you all of that about which you have curiosity, O King; I will relate everything to you, O prince, for which you are seeking it. (194) Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Installation of Vāmana," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 38.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Bhīṣma said: Thus has the majesty of Vāmana indeed been told in detail.
Furthermore, tell me another such greatness of Viṣṇu:
how did the lotus arise from the god’s navel, by which the world came into being? And how did the Vaiṣṇava creation formerly occur within the midst of that lotus?

How, in the Padma Mahākalpa, did the world become composed of lotuses? Here, while he was sleeping upon the waters of the ocean, there arose from his navel a lotus that followed the water, manifesting the power of the one whose navel is a lotus.
O Lord of those who know yoga, tell us in its entirety this account of Puṣkara that arose among the gods and the hosts of ṛṣis in ancient times:
how did he create that eternal world there?
How [is it] when the world has become a single ocean, empty, with all moving and stationary beings destroyed;
when the terrestrial globe has been consumed by fire, and the serpents and Rākṣasas have perished;
when fire, wind, and space have vanished, and dharma has been lost from the surface of the earth?
When the great elements had become entirely desolate through their reversal,
did the Lord of the Universe himself— possessed of great energy and great splendor— remain there, established in meditation and following the prescribed method as a knower of yoga? (7–8)
O Brahmin, knower of dharma, you ought to recount this entirely— this glory whose essence is Nārāyaṇa— to me as I listen with supreme devotion.
O Blessed One, you should speak to me, who am full of faith and well-seated.
Pulastya said:
O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, it is fitting for one purified by birth in a noble family to possess such a desire to hear the glory of Nārāyaṇa.
Listen to how it was heard from the gods in the ancient Purāṇas;
and having heard it as it was spoken by the high-souled Brāhmaṇas,
he who possessed a splendor equal to Bṛhaspati beheld it through his ascetic power.
The illustrious preceptor Dvaipāyana, the son of Parāśara, said:
"O best of beings, I shall relate that to you exactly as it was heard and according to my devotion— whatever has been correctly understood by me through the path of the sages."
Who is capable of knowing the Supreme, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa? Even this Brahmā does not know the Sustainer of the universe in its true nature;
His deeds are unknown even to the Viśvedevas, and His secret remains hidden from the great ṛṣis.
He is the essence of all sacrifices for those who perceive reality, the supreme self for those who know the supreme self, hell for those who perform improper actions,
and that divinity known as the presiding deity for the divine realm.
That which is the elemental (adhibhūta) and that which is the supreme (para) for those seeking the ultimate truth—
this is the sacrifice prescribed in the Vedas, and the wise know this to be austerity.
He who is the agent, the doer, the intellect, and from whom the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) arises.
The Praṇava is the Puruṣa, the Teacher, and is perceived as the One;
likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa) is fivefold, as well as the eternal Imperishable (akṣara).
Time, ripening, sacrifice, the sacrificer, and sacred study are also [perceived]. 19.
It is said: "He alone is this very one through various states, yet he is the Supreme (tatparam).
He, the Blessed One, performs everything and yet does not perform anything; he causes all this to be done in him, and the action of those who abide [in him] is accomplished. (20-21)
Let us worship this very primordial one; he alone is satisfied by the act of rising.
He who speaks, that which is to be spoken, and I myself—I shall tell you that. Whatever is heard, whatever is worthy of being heard, and whatever else has been conversed—[all that is he]. 22.

He who is the subject of all discourse and all that is heard, who is devoted to dharma and the essence of dharma; he who is the universe and the Lord of the universe—he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. He who is truth and falsehood, who is the beginning, the middle, and the end, and who is the infinite and the future.
Whatever exists, whether moving or unmoving, and whatever else there may be—all that is the Supreme Person, the primordial source.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga, O descendant of Kuru;
its dawn and twilight are each twice as long as that.
Where dharma has four feet and adharma has its limbs severed;
where men are born peaceful and devoted to their own duty; where the Brahmins are established in dharma as their supreme goal and the kings are established in the conduct of kings.
When Vaiśyas are devoted to agriculture and Śūdras are likewise intent on service,
then truth, goodness, and dharma flourish. This is the dharma practiced by the virtuous, by which the world proceeds.

O King, this was the conduct of all living beings, including men of righteous consciousness and even those of low birth, during the Kṛta Yuga. Three thousand years here are said to constitute the Tretā Yuga.
The twilight period of that [age] is proclaimed to be twice as long;
in it, unrighteousness (adharma) is established with two feet, while righteousness (dharma) is established with three.
Where truth, goodness, and ritual action are prescribed as dharma, [that is the Kṛta age].

In the Tretā age, the social orders (varṇas) undergo transformation, becoming possessed by greed. The degeneration of the fourfold order consists of both patience and weakness; such is the diverse course of the Tretā Yuga ordained by the gods.
The Dvāpara age consists of two thousand years, O descendant of Kuru;
its morning twilight is said to last for as many hundreds of years, and the evening twilight is twice that duration.
Even there, living beings are excessively devoted to material wealth and are overcome by passion (rajas).
O joy of the Kurus, deceitful, ungrateful, and base men are born.
Dharma stands upon two feet, while Adharma has risen upon three;
through hundreds of such reversals, dharma goes to ruin in this Kali age.
In the transition of the Kali age, devotion to Brahman declines, faith is abandoned, and vows and fasts are forsaken;
at that time, [the lifespan] is one thousand years plus two hundred years.
Where unrighteousness has four feet and righteousness is supported by only a single foot; where men are born as lustful ascetics and base individuals;
and where there is no one who is decisive, no one who is virtuous, and no one who speaks the truth. (38–39)

In that age, those men will be known as atheists, devoid of devotion to Brahmins, seized by egoism, and with the bonds of their affection exhausted; indeed, all Brahmins in the Kali Yuga will have the conduct of Śūdras. 40.

In the Kali age, O descendant of Kuru, a reversal of the stages of life (āśramas) now prevails, as does the confusion of the social classes (varṇas) at the end of the yuga. This twelve-thousand-verse account of the yugas was composed in the past. 41–42.
A day of Brahmā is said to consist of a thousand yugas;
when that day has passed, Time, perceiving the dissolution of the bodies of all living beings, forms the intention to withdraw them.
O Lord of the Earth, [he was the foremost] among all the deities and Brāhmaṇas,
O King, as well as among the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, birds, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and serpents. 44–45.

O best of beings, having become fivefold, the Lord of all creatures and the creator of beings [entered] the mountains, the rivers, the domestic animals, those born of the womb of beasts, as well as worms and biting insects. 46.
For the purpose of destroying the world, he indeed wrought a great slaughter:
becoming the sun, he took away the eyes; becoming the wind, he took the life-breath from the collection of living beings;
becoming fire, he consumed all the worlds; and becoming a fierce cloud, he rained down once more. 47–48.
Having become the yogi Nārāyaṇa, the fire that manifests in all forms,
he dries up the oceans with his blazing rays.
Then, having drunk all the oceans, as well as the rivers and wells from every side, he consumes them.
The knower of yoga, having taken all the water of the mountains and becoming possessed of a thousand rays, pierces the earth and delights in the netherworld (Rasātala),
drinking that unsurpassed essence while holding the water.
Whatever exists among living beings— whether manifest, unmanifest, or otherwise— that all the lotus-eyed Puruṣottama withdraws.
And the wind, becoming powerful, shakes the entire world.
Having reached the prāṇa and apāna, Hari proceeds by means of the vital air (vāyu).
Then, all the qualities of the five senses belonging to the hosts of gods and all embodied beings, as well as all the elements that exist— 53–54.

The sense of smell, the object of smell, and the body—these qualities are dependent upon earth; the course of the world has been destroyed by the Blessed One in a mere moment. The tongue, taste, and moisture—these qualities are dependent upon water.
Form, the differentiation of the eye, and the qualities residing in the light of the eye; touch, breath, and movement—the qualities residing in the wind;
sound, the ear, and hearing—the qualities residing in space. (56–57)
Manas, buddhi, citta, and kṣetrajña are dependent upon him;
and beyond them, Parameṣṭhin and Hṛṣīkeśa are likewise dependent.
Then, they were encompassed by the rays of that Blessed One.
Driven by the wind and clinging to the branches of the earth,
the fire produced by their friction blazed in a hundred ways;
that Saṃvartaka fire proceeded, consuming the entire universe.
He utterly consumed the mountains, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and grasses,
as well as the divine celestial chariots and various cities— indeed,
everything that was worth taking refuge in.
Having reduced all those worlds to ashes, the Teacher of the Teacher of the World sustained the manifestation arising at the end of the eon;
becoming a thousandfold rain-cloud and manifesting as a hundredfold, Kṛṣṇa became a great cloud.
Then, with divine water, oblations,
and that most excellent, sweet water resembling milk—
cool and auspicious— the earth attained a state of supreme peace.
The earth, having become one vast ocean of water through its contact with that water due to their shared nature as fluid,
was devoid of all living beings;
even the great beings entered the All-pervading One of immeasurable power.
When the sun, wind, and space have perished, and the world has become subtle and enveloped,
the eternal One, having caused the drying up of the oceans and embodied beings by means of his own self, and having likewise burnt and withdrawn [the universe], sleeps alone.
Assuming his ancient form, he of immeasurable prowess sleeps;
a yogi who has mastered yoga, he moves upon the waters of the single ocean for many thousands of yugas within that solitary expanse of water.

No one at all is able to know the Unmanifest as manifest; who is this so-called Puruṣa? What is yoga, and who is the yogin? Not from behind, nor from all sides, nor from the flank, nor from the front.
Some perceive him as the best of gods;
he is seen as the sky, the earth, the wind, the waters, and the light; as Prajāpati, the sustainer of the world, the lord of the gods, the Grandfather, the abode of the Vedas, the sage, and the Lord.
Having pervaded all, the Sovereign chose to lie down upon the serpent.
Thus, when these three worlds have become a single ocean, the one of great splendor, having covered the earth with his waters, acts as the swan for Nārāyaṇa in the midst of that vast,
great ocean of dust.
The lotus-eyed one of mighty arms [attained] that imperishable Brahman which the wise know;
the Lord, enveloped by darkness in the form of the self,
took up the sattvic mind and entered where that Sattva was established.

Then, the supreme knowledge according to reality regarding the true Brahman was taught as a secret, just as it is remembered in the Upaniṣads; namely, that "the Puruṣa is the sacrifice"— this has been proclaimed as the highest truth.

And whoever else may be designated as a "person" (puruṣa), he alone is Puruṣottama. Furthermore, those Brahmins who perform sacrifices and are known as ṛtvij priests, they too were born from my mouths in the past; so it is heard. 77–78.

From his first mouth, the Lord created Brahmā and the Udgātṛ who chants the Sāmans; likewise, from his two arms, he created the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu. From his [other] mouth, he created the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Stotṛ, and all others in their entirety.
From the penis, he created the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Pratiṣṭhātṛ;
from the belly, O King, the Pratihartṛ and the Potṛ;
and from the two hands, the Āgnīdhra and the Yājuṣa Unnetṛ.
From his two thighs, he created the Acchāvāka and the Sāman-singing Subrahmaṇya priest;
in this very manner, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the World, the Self-Existent One, created these sixteen supreme officiating priests for all sacrifices.

Then that great yogin, known as the Sacrifice, along with all the Vedas—including their auxiliary limbs, Upaniṣads, and ritual procedures—slept upon the single ocean; such was the wonder that occurred in ancient times. 83–84.

Listen then, O Brahmin, out of curiosity: that great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, possessing a lifespan of many thousands of years due to his own ascetic power, was swallowed by the Blessed One and remained within His belly. 85.
Wandering on account of his visits to sacred fords, he traveled across the earth,
visiting holy hermitages and temples of the gods, as well as various regions, kingdoms, and diverse cities. (86–87)
Devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, peaceful, and purified by austerities—thus they are remembered.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya slowly emerged from his mouth;
yet, due to divine illusion, he did not perceive himself as departing.
Emerging from that belly, Mārkaṇḍeya beheld the world as a single ocean, enveloped on all sides by darkness;
intense fear arose within him, and he perceived the reversal of his own life.
Delighted by the sight of the God and filled with supreme wonder, Mārkaṇḍeya, whose soul was unfailing, then became apprehensive and reflected:
"Could this be a delusion of my mind, or am I experiencing a dream?"

"Clearly, one of these two must have perished for me; for this cannot be a dream, as it is consistent with reality. Indeed, it is impossible that the moon and sun should be lost, or that the wind, the mountains, and the earth should vanish."
Thinking, "What is this world of mine? he was overcome with grief;
then he saw a man sleeping like a mountain, submerged in the water like a cloud in the ocean.

"Scorching as if with splendors that surpass the moon and the sun, appearing like the ocean in its profundity through your majesty, who are you that have come here to see the Lord? I am filled with wonder. (95-96)
In that very same way, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya was made to enter the womb once again; having entered the womb once more, he was filled with wonder,
perceiving his own vision exactly as it had been before.
In that very same manner as before, he wandered over the earth and through the forests (98),
visiting sacred fords endowed with holy waters and various hermitages,
as well as those performing sacrifices with the completion of the prescribed priestly fees (99).
He saw hundreds of twice-born ones established in sacrifice within the womb of the Goddess; all the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, were devoted to virtuous conduct.
He beheld the four stages of life (āśramas) clearly present, just as they were in former times.
In this manner, for more than a hundred years, the wise Mārkaṇḍeya wandered over the entire earth while remaining within his [the child’s] belly; indeed, everything was perceived by him there.
Then, at one point, he emerged from the belly once again.
And having beheld a single child sleeping upon the branch of a banyan tree,
[he saw] the world likewise enveloped in mist amidst the waters of the single ocean,
where play was unmanifest and all beings were absent.
Overcome with wonder and filled with curiosity, the sage was unable to gaze upon the child who resembled the sun;
standing aside in a secluded spot near the water, he reflected thus: (104-105)
Thinking, "This is the same Lord seen before," Mārkaṇḍeya, filled with wonder, stood upon that shoreless water;
then, with eyes wide with fear, he went forward to see Him as he had seen Him previously.
To him the Blessed One said, "Welcome, O child," as Puruṣottama spoke with a voice like the clouds:
"Mārkaṇḍeya, you need not fear; come into my presence."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Who is it that proclaims my name while treating me with contempt, even as he continues to defy me for what is known as a thousand divine years? (109)
Indeed, this is not the conduct of the virtuous, nor is it approved even among the gods;
for even Brahmā speaks to me with affection, saying, "May you live long. Who, having undertaken such terrible austerity and renounced their life, would act thus?
"O Mārkaṇḍeya, having spoken thus to me, you ought to behold Death.
Thus provoked by anger, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya [prepared to do so],
whereupon the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana spoke to him once more.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am your father, O Vatsa, your Hṛṣīkeśa, your preceptor, the ancient bestower of life; why do you not approach me? (113)
Desiring a son, your father, the sage Aṅgiras, first propitiated me by undertaking intense austerity.
Seeing him engaged in such formidable penance and endowed with the supreme splendor of the gods, [I appeared].
"I have given you, my son, a great seer of immeasurable splendor.
Who else would venture to behold me—whose self is the soul of all beings and who am composed of yoga—sporting with my yogic power while situated within the single ocean? (115-116)

Then, with a heart full of joy and eyes wide with wonder, Mārkaṇḍeya of great ascetic power— long-lived and honored by the world— placed his joined palms to his head and announced his name and lineage.
Then he offered a salutation with devotion to that Blessed One.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O sinless one, I desire to know this illusion of yours according to its true nature."

O Lord, when you reside in the midst of the single ocean upon Śeṣa in the form of a child, by what name are you known in the world, O Master? I reflect upon this Great-Souled One; for who else could possibly remain there? (119-120)
The Blessed One said: "O Brahman, I am Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all beings; I am the one with a thousand heads and faces, endowed with a thousand feet. (121)
The Person of solar hue is in my mouth, for I am indeed composed of Brahman;
I am Agni, the bearer of oblations, accompanied by the seven horses. I am Indra, the lord of the quarters, Śakra, and the year consisting of the seasons.
Among yogis, I am known as Sāṅkhya, and I am the whirlpool at the end of the age. I am all beings and all deities without exception;
among serpents, I am Śeṣa, and among all birds, I am Tārkṣya.

I am the end-maker of all beings, known by the name of Time; I am the dharma and the austerity of those dwelling in all stages of life. I am the supreme dharma of compassion, and I am the great ocean, the Milky Sea.
That which is true is that supreme one; indeed, I alone am Prajāpati.
I am Sāṃkhya, I am Yoga, for I am that supreme state.
I am the ritual of sacrifice, and I am remembered as the Lord of Knowledge. 126–127.
I am light, I am wind, I am earth, I am water, I am space,
the oceans, the stars, and the ten directions;
I am rain, I am Soma, I am Parjanya, and I am Ravi.
I am the supreme Purāṇa, and likewise I am the ultimate goal. I shall also exist everywhere; I am the future and the synthesis of all that exists.
O Brahmin, whatever you see or whatever you hear—anything at all—I am that.

Whatever you have experienced in this world, remember all that; behold me as the one who previously created the universe and who shall create it again. O Mārkaṇḍeya, in age after age, I protect this entire world.
Markandeya, retain all this that has been told to you. Even while desiring to hear about dharma, I was moving comfortably within my mother’s womb;
there, Brahmā resided in my body along with the gods and the sages.
Know me, the enemy of the serpents, as the union of the manifest and the unmanifest;
I am the single-syllable mantra, the three-syllabled one, and the Grandfather (Brahmā). I am the supreme trivarga, the syllable Om, and the revealer of the Supreme Self.

O high-minded one, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, having entered the mouth of the Blessed One, then entered the belly of the Blessed One; thus does he relate this Purāṇa and other such accounts. (135–136)
Desiring to serve that immutable Swan face-to-face in solitary places,
he took refuge in that which is imperishable and manifold; yet, in that great ocean where both moon and sun have vanished,
the Lord known as the Swan wanders slowly, creating the world as time turns.
Then, having thus become pure,
the lotus-born one performed austerities, covering his body with water;
thereafter, that great-souled and exceedingly powerful being resolved upon the departure from the world of mortals.
And Viśva meditated upon the universe of great beings;
as he was thus reflecting, while the world was in its dissolution, within that subtle, water-filled, spaceless ocean of fixed duration— 140.
The Lord, having entered the waters of the ocean, agitated them.
Then, from within the waters, a subtle aperture first appeared; subsequently, the wind arose from that aperture, following the sound.

Having encountered internal agitation, the wind increased; the ocean, violently stirred by that powerful wind, was tossed about with force. As that ocean was thus agitated, it was churned within those waters.
The great lord Vaiśvānara, whose path is black, indeed became manifest;
then that fire dried up much water, and all the oceans became openings as they spread out into the sky. 144–145.
The waters, which are meritorious and like the essence of nectar, arise from the splendor of the Self;
space arises from apertures, and wind has its origin in space. Then, fire arises from friction, and it too has its origin in him.
Having seen this, the divine Grandfather, the creator of the great elements,
the Blessed One who possesses many forms, beheld all beings and reflected upon the supreme birth of Brahmā for the purpose of creating the worlds.

O best of the twice-born, at the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, Hari— who is called Brahmā— appears on earth as one whose self has been purified through many births and whose soul is refined by austerity. 149.
Having seen that knowledge, the Soul of the Universe attained the state of fitness for yogis.
Recognizing him as one possessed of yoga and endowed with supreme, complete sovereignty, the Knower of Yoga united him with the station of Brahman, the source of the universe.
Then, in that great body of water, Maheśa Hari, the infallible creator of all worlds, performed his aquatic sports according to the prescribed rites; thereafter,
he produced a single lotus born from his navel.
The thousand-petaled lotus, stainless and golden-hued like the sun,
rose up with a brilliance blazing like the cresting flames of a sacrificial fire; it shone with the splendor of the cloudless autumn sun,
possessing noble radiance, while the hair of the Great-Souled One appeared as its beautiful moss.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Lotus," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Forty.
Pulastya said:
Then he created Brahmā, the creator of all worlds, who possesses great splendor, faces in every direction, and is the foremost among those endowed with yoga;
[he was born] upon that golden lotus extending for many yojanas.
Consisting of all qualities of splendor and endowed with the characteristics of the earthly realm,
that lotus which formerly existed as the supreme form of the earth is said by the great seers to have originated from Nārāyaṇa.
That which is called the essence of the lotus is the goddess Earth;
those who know the primary filaments of that lotus to be divine mountains—Himavat, Nīla, Meru, and Niṣadha. 4.
And likewise Mount Kailāsa with its peaks, as well as Mount Gandhamādana;
the holy Triśikhara and the lovely Mandara;
the noble Piñjara, and Mount Vindhya and Mount Asta.
These indeed are the abodes of the hosts of great-souled Siddhas of virtuous conduct, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
Among these, the island known as Jambūdvīpa is situated.
The configuration of Jambudvīpa is such that there, the sacrificial rites are performed. From those [mountains], water flows forth, resembling the taste of divine nectar;
lakes are recorded as existing everywhere, serving as the source for hundreds of divine tirthas.
Those which are the filaments of this lotus here on all sides,
O King, are the innumerable and various mountains upon the earth; and those which are the leaves of the lotus, O Ruler of the People, are the many ancient continents.

Those mountain-filled regions inhabited by Mlecchas are proclaimed to be difficult to traverse. O King, those which have leaves on their lower portions are the respective dwellings of the Daityas, Asuras, and Pannagas.
The space between them is known as Rasātala,
where men who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) sink down.
In the four directions, there are four oceans reckoned to be present.
Thus, for the sake of Nārāyaṇa, this manifestation of the Earth originated from a lotus (puṣkara);
therefore, it is designated by the name Puṣkara.
For this reason, in ancient sacrifices, it was [honored] by the supreme ṛṣis.
By means of sacrifices seen in the Vedas and performed with sacrificial implements, the piling of the sacrificial posts was accomplished;
likewise, by that Blessed One, the earth was covered and pervaded by the universe, and the arrangement of mountains and rivers was likewise created. 16.
He who possesses incomparable power over the universe, who shines like the sun and has the splendor of Varuṇa—
Śanaiḥsvayambhū, whose nature is the world, emitted the sleeping Padmanidhi from the great ocean.
At that time, a great asura named Madhu was born, an obstacle to his ascetic penance.
Simultaneously with that [creation], two demons named Kaitabha and Madhu were born;
having arisen from the qualities of rajas and tamas, they belonged to the class of tamasic beings.
Possessed of great strength, they agitated the entire world, which was then a single ocean.
Wearing divine red garments, with white, blazing, and fierce fangs;
towering with crowns and diadems, radiant with armlets and bracelets; possessing large, wide-open copper-colored eyes, broad chests, and mighty arms. 20–21.
Possessing the strength and firmness of great mountains, they were like two moving peaks; they resembled fresh clouds, their faces were like the sun,
and they were exceedingly terrifying with their massive, expansive armlets upon their arms.
As if tossing the ocean with the placement of their footsteps,
and making the sleeping Madhusūdana tremble as if he were Hari, those two, whose faces are turned in every direction, roamed there in Puṣkara.
Then they beheld that most excellent and intensely radiant one among yogis,
authorized by Nārāyaṇa, creating all beings—
both the deities and the mental sons who are the sages.
Then those two best of asuras, wicked, desirous of combat, and enraged with eyes agitated by fury, spoke there to Brahmā:
"Who are you, standing in the middle of the lotus, white-turbaned and four-armed? (26–27)
Disregarding us both out of delusion, you have become free from desire;
come, O lotus-born one, give battle to us two!
You are unable to remain in the ocean against us two, the supreme lords.
"Who might there be for you, by whom you are appointed here? Who is the creator, who is your protector, and by what name are you designated?
Brahmā said:
"In this world, Viṣṇu, who wields infinite power, is called Īśvara. Know that I was born from him as the creator. Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O great sage, there is nothing superior to us in this world.
By us, indeed, the entire universe is shrouded with darkness and passion; we consist of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), and we transcend even the ṛṣis. (31-32)
Concealing their true nature as destroyers of all embodied beings, we two, who are difficult to overcome in age after age, are joined with virtue, wealth,
"Where there is happiness, where there is majesty, and where there is fame;
whatever is desired by whomsoever—that we two shall bring about.
Brahmā said: [34]
Having seen us two joined together, you were previously defeated by us. Having established that virtuous one, I have taken refuge in him;
he who is the Supreme, whose self is united in yoga, and who is the Imperishable—that is indeed Sattva itself.

He who is the creator of both passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), the source of the universe— from him all beings are born, whether characterized by goodness (sattva) or otherwise. He alone, Vāsudeva, will bring about your destruction.
Then, while still asleep, the god Nārāyaṇa, by means of his own creative power (māyā), fashioned two arms extending for many yojanas; those two long arms were drawn out by the arms of Brahmā,
who was possessed of great strength.
Then those two, fat and resembling two birds that had shed their feathers, went and spoke to the eternal Vāsudeva;
having prostrated themselves, both bowed down before Padmanābha Hṛṣīkeśa.
We know you to be the source of the universe, the one Supreme Person;
we know you to be the cause of us both and the cause of the intellect, for we know you as the eternal, the truthful one whose vision is never in vain. 41-42.
"Therefore, O Lord, we desire to behold you closely;
your vision is never in vain. Salutations to you, O Conqueror of Assemblies!
(43) The Blessed One said:
"For what purpose do you address me, O two best of asuras? Your life has departed; how is it that you both still desire to live?
Madhu and Kaiṭabha replied:
"O Lord, since no one has ever died in this divine place,
we desire both immortality and sonship from you, O you of great ascetic power.
The Blessed One said:
"For you both, this shall indeed come to pass when the Kali age arises;
you will become so, without a doubt. I speak this truth to you.
Having thus granted the boon to the two great asuras, the eternal Viśvadhara, the supreme among gods, [departed].
Then the Lord of the Immortals crushed those two, who resembled collyrium produced from passion and darkness, upon the surface of his thighs.
Standing upon that lotus, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman,
raised his arms and devoted himself to severe austerity.
Blazing as if with splendors and rays, that righteous-souled dispeller of darkness spoke like the thousand-rayed sun with its beams. Then the Lord, the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, assumed another form.

The highly illustrious teacher of Yoga, possessed of great splendor, arrived; as did the wise Kapila, the teacher of Sāṃkhya and the best among Brahmins. Both of these high-souled ones were honored there, being fully devoted to their respective paths.
There, Tvaṣṭṛ and Prāpti spoke to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
who knows the distinction between the higher and the lower, who is honored by the great seers,
and who is fully conversant with the vast expanse of the world.
The leader of all beings, Brahmā, who is worshipped by the three worlds,
having heard those words of the two who had departed after being awakened,
created these three worlds, according to this Vedic revelation of Brahmā.
Then he produced from the earth his own unique son;
and as soon as he was born, that mind-born son approached Brahmā and spoke to him.
"What assistance can we provide for you? Please tell us, O Blessed One.
Brahmā said:
"This one named Kapila is indeed Brahmā and likewise Nārāyaṇa."
"O high-minded one, you must do that which you have spoken.
When he had been addressed thus by Brahmā, the king rose up and said to them with palms joined in reverence: "I am desirous of serving you both; what shall I do?"
The Blessed Lord said: Remember that which is the truth, the imperishable Brahman, which is eighteenfold;
remember that which is the truth, the immortal, the supreme state. 59
Having heard these words, he went toward the northern direction; having gone there, he beheld Brahmā with the eye of knowledge.
Then the Lord Brahmā created the second [being], named Bhuva.

Having formed that very resolve in his mind, he of great intellect [approached Brahmā]. Then he spoke these words: "O Grandfather, what shall I do? Having been thus commanded by the Grandfather, he approached Brahmā.
The Brahmin experienced the taste of nectar; having attained this from him, he reached that supreme state and came into the presence of those two. When he too had departed, the Lord created a third.
The lord Suvarṇābha, who was skilled in the practice for liberation,
also adhered to that same dharma and attained the destination of those two.
Thus, all three of these sons of the high-souled Śambhu have gone [to their respective realms].
Taking those sons of his, the Lord Nārāyaṇa and Kapila, the lord of ascetics, went to that exalted state;
at the very time they departed, O Brahman, Brahmā also departed at that same time.
Furthermore, Brahmā resorted to a most terrible penance for the sake of the supreme state. Yet, while performing that penance alone, he was not able [to create];
therefore, from half of his own body, he produced a beautiful wife.

The Grandfather (Brahmā) created sons resembling himself, from whom the Viśvedevas, the lords of creatures, emerged; first, that Great-Souled One produced through austerity a son who was a lord of the Viśvedevas.
He created the Dharma, which is composed of merit gathered from all sources, under the name Nārāyaṇa. Then he created Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhṛgu, and the sage Aṅgiras.
Those great sages are to be known as most wonderful by virtue of their own deeds;
thus, for the sake of undertaking the thirteen qualities, there were these lineages of great sages:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, and Khasā.
Prācī, Krodhā, Caṃsurā, Vinatā, and Kadrū—
O King, these twelve were the daughters of Dakṣa. Furthermore,
there are twenty-seven powerful constellations belonging to the Moon.
It is said that Kaśyapa was born as the son of Marīci through the power of ascetic penance; Dakṣa gave him twelve daughters,
whom he bestowed upon him, and likewise the sage gave the constellations to Soma.
O descendant of Kuru, all the asterisms beginning with Rohiṇī are meritorious.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sandhyā, and the highly illustrious Viśveśā—these goddesses were created by Brahmā in ancient times. 76–77.
O King, may you have good fortune; these five most excellent daughters, the best among the daughters of the gods, were given by Brahmā, whose deeds are unseen, to Dharmarāja.
She who is the wife of Brahmā, possessing half his form and capable of assuming any shape at will—
Suddenly becoming Surabhi, she approached Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, who is worshipped by the worlds and who knows the cause for the creation of the universe, united with her in sexual intercourse for the sake of the cows, O best of beings.
And he begot eleven sons of great stature, known by the name Dharma,
who resembled the clouds of the crimson twilight, possessed of great size and fierce luster; they cried out, ran about, and went to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Because of weeping (*rodana*) and because of flowing (*dravaṇa*), they are remembered as the Rudras.
Nirhṛti, Saṃdhya, and the third, who is not born from a womb (*ayonija*), as well as Mṛgavyādha, Kapardin, and he who is Mahāviśveśvara—[these are the eleven]. 82–83.
The venerable Ahibudhnya, Kapālī, Piṅgala,
and Senānī of great splendor— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
And from that very Surabhi were born the cows and those who are the gods.

O best of kings, from him were born Aja and Haṃsa; likewise, the most excellent medicinal herbs and Surabhi arose from him. From Dharma, Lakṣmī was born, as well as Kāma and the Sādhyas from the Sādhyā.
Bhava, Prabhava, Kṛśāśva, Suvaha, Aruṇa, Varuṇa, Viśvāmitra, Caladhruva,
Haviṣmat, Tanūja, Vidhāna, and Abhimata. (87)
Vatsara, Bhūti, and Sarvāsuraniṣūdana;
Suparvan, Bṛhatkānti, and Sādhyalokanamaskṛta—the goddess, followed by Vāsava, gave birth to these gods. 88–89.
Dhara is the first deity, Dhruva the immutable is the second,
Viśvāvasu is the third, and Soma the Lord is the fourth;
after that is Anurūpa, and Yama immediately following him.

The seventh was Vāyu, and likewise the eighth was Nirṛti. These were indeed the offspring of Dharma born of Surabhī. And it is remembered that the Viśvedevas were born from Dharma through Viśvā. 91–92.
And Dakṣa, the mighty-armed Puṣkara, Tama, Cākṣuṣa, Atri, and likewise Bhadra and Mahoraga;
Viśvāntaka, Vasu, Bāla, and the highly illustrious Nikumbha.
And Rurudh, possessing the splendor of the sun and the power of the most perfected ones, [was born].
Devamātā gave birth to the Viśvedevas as her sons; Marutvatī gave birth to the Maruts, the gods, as her sons. 94–95.
Agni, Cakṣus, Ravi, Jyotis, Sāvitrī, Mitra, Amara, Śaravṛṣṭi, and the very great Sukarṣa;
Virāja, Rāja, Viśvāyu, and likewise Sumati. 96.
Also Aśvaga, Citrarashmi, and King Niṣadha;
furthermore, Ātmavidhi, Cāritra, Pādamātraga, Bṛhanta, Bṛhadrūpa, and Sanābhiga. 97–98.
From Kaśyapa, Aditi gave birth to the host of Maruts, ending with Jyeṣṭha; indeed, she also gave birth to the twelve Ādityas:
Pūṣan, Mitra, the boon-granting Dhātṛ, and Parjanya—these indeed are the twelve Ādityas, the most excellent among the inhabitants of the third heaven.
Two excellent sons were born to Āditya by Sarasvatī. 100–101.
Diti gave birth to the Dānavas, who were preeminent in austerity, preeminent in virtue, and highly esteemed in the third heaven;
from Kālā she likewise gave birth to those Asuras known as the Kālakeyas, as well as Rākṣasas. 102.
Anāyuṣā’s daughters were diseases of great power.
Siṃhikā was the mother of the grahas; Muni was the mother of the gandharvas; Prācī was the mother of the apsarases; and Bhāratī was the mother of the meritorious ones. 103–104.
O King, lord of the people, from Krodhā were born all the bhūtas, piśācas,
yakṣa hosts, and rākṣasas;
and from Eṇā were born four-footed creatures, as well as goats and cattle.
Thus has been told the Ancient Puruṣa, Viṣṇu, Hari, the Lord,
who was praised by the great seers in former times;
and that man who should always hear this foremost Purāṇa, or should recite it on the festival days (parvan).

Having attained this world, one who is free from passion enjoys the fruits of heaven in the next; he pleases Kṛṣṇa through his fourfold actions—by sight, mind, speech, and deed—and Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with him, grants him a kingdom if he is a king, or supreme wealth if he is destitute. 108–109.
One whose life is exhausted regains life; one desiring a son obtains progeny; likewise, one seeking sacrifice obtains its fruits, as well as various forms of austerity.
Whatever desire one may cherish, that very thing one shall obtain from the Lord of the World.
O best of men, if one should abandon everything else and recite this manifestation of Hari known as Pauṣkara, no misfortune shall ever befall him.
This is the manifestation of the Great-Souled One named Pauṣkara. 111–112.
O Great King, having been celebrated according to the revelation of Vyāsa, hear now of Viṣṇu’s nature as Viṣṇu and his nature as Hari in the Kṛta Yuga;
likewise, his state as Vaikuṇṭha among the gods and his state as Kṛṣṇa among human beings.
Such is the profound course of the actions of the Lord, who is beyond the reach of the senses.
Now, O King, hear exactly as it is concerning the past and the future—that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, who is unmanifest yet resides within the manifest signs. 114–115.
Nārāyaṇa is indeed the infinite Self, the source of origin and dissolution;
having become this Nārāyaṇa, he was the eternal Hari.
He is Brahmā, Vāyu, Soma, Dharma, Śakra, and Bṛhaspati.
O descendant of Kuru, though unborn, he attained the status of being the son of Aditi; this all-pervading Lord, known as Viṣṇu, is the younger brother of Indra,
and his propitiation was the cause for him becoming the son of Aditi.
Then, for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—
he created the gods, Brahmā, and the Prajāpatis in that kalpa;
there he also created the unsurpassed mental lineages of Brahmā.
From those great-souled ones, the eternal Supreme Brahman arose.
Listen to me as I recount this deed of Viṣṇu, who is a source of wonder and is worthy of being praised throughout the worlds. 120–121.
When the Vṛtra-slaying had occurred and the Kṛta-yuga was prevailing,
there took place the battle known throughout the three worlds as Tārakāmaya, wherein all the terrible Dānavas were difficult to conquer in combat. (122)

They slew all the gods, asuras, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas. Being slaughtered in battle, turning their backs with their weapons shattered, they sought in their minds the Lord Nārāyaṇa as their protector.
In the meantime, clouds with the luster of extinguished embers covered the sky along with the sun, moon, and hosts of planets;
accompanied by fierce flashes of lightning, they produced a terrifying roar.
Seven winds blew, striking one another with force;
accompanied by thunderclaps, lightning, fire, and gales, they possessed blazing waters.
With their most terrible roars and portents, they made the sky seem as if it were being consumed by flames.
Thousands of meteors fell, and even celestial beings descended; divine chariots were falling and leaping up, like the terror that arises for all worlds at the end of the four yugas. 128.
In that moment of upheaval, where formless things appeared as if possessed of form,
everything became difficult to discern; nothing at all could be clearly understood, and the ten directions shone forth as if enveloped by a mass of darkness.
Kālī, assuming a physical form and shrouded by dark clouds, entered; the sky did not shine, being overwhelmed and enveloped by a terrible darkness that eclipsed the sun.
The Lord, with his two arms, tore apart that mass of thick clouds and deep gloom.
Hari revealed his own divine form, a body dark as a rain-cloud;
resembling a cloud or collyrium, with hair like a cloud, he was dark in both splendor and physique, like a mountain of black stone.
Wearing blazing yellow garments and adorned with ornaments of refined gold, his body was like smoke-filled darkness, rising up like the fire at the end of an eon;
he had rounded, double-folded, and fleshy shoulders, and his hair was covered by a diadem. 134.
It shone, adorned with weapons resembling molten gold;
it was as lofty as a mountain peak illuminated by the rays of the sun and moon;
its hand was gladdened by the Nandaka sword, and its chest was resplendent with the Kaustubha gem.

Exalted by the variegated fruits of his power, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, he is the mountain of Viṣṇu, whose nature is forbearance, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand;
he bestows the noble fruits of the thirty gods and is the beloved of the beautiful celestial women of heaven. 137.
It is beloved by the minds of all the world and enchanting to the hearts of all beings;
it has the great branches of illusion (māyā) and a luster like a flood of water; it is rich with the pride of learning and ego, and it is the place where the great elements sprout forth. 138–139.

It was covered with special leaves, blossomed with planets and constellations, possessed the great trunk of the world of the Daityas, and was visible to the world of mortals; it had a resonance like the form of the ocean and its roots rested in the netherworld of Rasātala. 140.
It was spread with the nooses of the lords of serpents and filled with birds and creatures; it was a great tree for all the worlds, rich in natural and acquired fragrances;
its waters were the unmanifest bliss, and its foam was the manifest ego. 141–142.
It was a flood of the great elements, with planets and constellations as its bubbles;
it was filled with celestial chariots and vehicles, agitated by the roar of clouds, teeming with swarms of creatures like fish, and abounding with families of mountains like conch shells. 143.

It has the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as its whirlpools and all the worlds as its *timiṃgila* fish; it has heroes as its trees, creepers, and shrubs, and the sloughed skins of serpents as its moss;
it has the twelve suns as its great islands and the eleven Rudras as its cities.
It was endowed with the mountains of the eight treasures, a great ocean for the waters of the three worlds;
it was filled with the waters of the twilight waves and graced by the wind,
