teeming with the villages of hosts of Daityas and Yakṣas, and crowded with the fish that were the hosts of Rākṣasas.
It was filled with the grandfather Brahmā of great heroism and crowded with the jewels of celestial women;
it was teeming with rivers such as Śrī, Kīrti, Kānti, and Lakṣmī,
and it possessed the velocity of the creation and dissolution caused by the great rains of the end of time.
The great ocean of Nārāyaṇa, whose further shore is reached through association with the virtuous;
the god beyond gods, the bestower of boons upon his devotees, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
the gracious deity, the auspicious one who brings about peace. 149.
Adorned with a banner of Suparṇa yoked to a chariot drawn by bay horses (150),
its interior surrounded by noble wheels in the form of the moon and sun, joined with infinite reins, and possessing Mount Meru as its pole— (151).

In the sky, which was adorned with stars as variegated flowers and made beautiful by the planets and constellations, the goddess who grants fearlessness in times of danger remained unconquered by gods or demons; she was endowed with the splendor of pearls joined to the chariot drawn by bay horses.
They beheld the Lord stationed upon a celestial chariot composed of divine worlds.
With palms joined in reverence, all those gods, led by Indra, placed the cry of "Victory! before them and sought refuge with Him, the Protector.
Having heard their words, Viṣṇu, the deity of the gods,
set his mind upon the destruction of the Dānavas in a great battle;
remaining in the sky, Viṣṇu assumed a supreme form.
He spoke these words with a solemn promise to all the deities: "Attain peace; may it be well with you. Do not fear, O hosts of Maruts!
All the Dānavas have been conquered; let the three worlds be taken possession of."
Then, gratified by the words of Viṣṇu, who was true to his promise,
the gods attained supreme joy, as if having consumed the most excellent nectar (amṛta).
Thereupon, the darkness was withdrawn and the clouds vanished.
Auspicious winds blew and the ten directions became serene.
The luminaries, for the most part pure, circumambulated the moon clockwise. The planets did not engage in conflict, and even the oceans became tranquil.

The paths became free from dust, the three heavens and other realms were illuminated, the rivers flowed according to their true nature, and the ocean was not agitated; the senses within the inner selves of men became pure. (161)
The great seers, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud;
and in the sacrifices, the fire-god brought the cooking of the oblations to auspicious completion.
As the path of dharma was established, the worlds became joyful in heart.
Having heard from the mouth of Viṣṇu— the one whose promise is true— words concerning the destruction of their enemies,
the Daityas and Dānavas then made vast preparations for battle and for victory.
Then Māyā created a golden chariot, three *nalva*s in extent and imperishable;
it had four wheels, was exceedingly vast, equipped with great weapons, resounded with the tinkling of a network of small bells, and was adorned with leopard skins. (165–166)
It was beautified by networks of radiant rays and lattices of gold,
crowded with herds of artificial deer and resplendent with flocks of birds;
it was made splendid by divine weapons and missiles, and echoed with the thundering of clouds.
A noble and excellent chariot with good wheels, spacious and like the sky;
filled with maces and iron clubs, it was like the ocean personified; adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, its pole was like the orb of the moon. 168–169.
Adorned with banners and flags, it was like Mount Mandara with the sun;
in some places it had the form of a lordly elephant with a body of coils and the luster of a lion’s mane,
while in others it was joined by a thousand stars and resounded like a rain-cloud pouring down nectar.
Desirous of battle, he ascended a blazing, divine chariot that traveled through the sky and crushed the chariots of his enemies—
just as the radiant sun ascends Mount Meru;
while Tāra occupied a chariot one *krośa* in width and likewise in length.
Resembling a mountain-axle and like a mass of black collyrium, its pole was bound with a collection of jewels made of black iron;
emitting rays like the rising of darkness, it was like a thundering cloud. 173.
It was covered with a great iron net provided with latticed windows,
filled with iron bars and portable mallets,
and strewn with spears, nooses, and unyielding thorns.
Adorned with terrifying javelins and battle-axes,
and raised up for the sake of his enemies like a second Mount Mandara,
he mounted that excellent chariot yoked to a thousand donkeys. 176.
But Virocana, enraged,
stood at the head of that army with mace in hand, like a mountain with blazing peaks;
meanwhile, the Dānava Hayagrīva was mounted upon a thousand horses.
The valiant Śveta, son of Vipracitti, adorned with white earrings, moved through the arrayed host of Dānavas; he,
the crusher of enemy forces, drove his chariot forward.
Stretching his great bow, which was a thousand *kiṣkus* in length,
he stood at the front of the battle like a mountain with its peaks;
Khara, out of rage, shed tears from his eyes as they overflowed.
With his teeth, lips, and eyes quivering, that Dānava, having mounted a chariot drawn by eighteen horses fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, longed for battle and stood facing the fray,
appearing like a divine military array.
Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, most excellent and wielding irresistible weapons, stood facing the battle, making the mountains tremble;
he was urged on by his attendants like young colts out of great excitement. 183–184.
He appeared in the midst of the Daityas like the sun in the midst of the planets;
tall, with the luster of a fresh cloud, and adorned with garments hanging down to his feet,
he shone within the Daitya host like the sun amidst a thick mist.
Then, with his teeth, lips, and eyes as weapons,
he stood laughing in the midst of the Daityas like a cruel great planet; others there were mounted on horses, while others were mounted on lordly elephants in rut.
Others were mounted on lions and tigers, while others were on boars and bears; some rode upon donkeys and camels, and some had clouds as their vehicles.
Other Daityas were foot-soldiers, terrifying and with distorted faces.

Some with one leg and some without legs danced, longing for battle; many slapped their arms, while others roared, and those preeminent among the Dānavas bellowed with the sound of proud tigers. 189–190.
With their arms like iron clubs, those deities, holding stones and mallets in their hands, threatened him with terrible iron bars, spears,
swords, nooses, javelins, goads, and sharp-edged spears. 191.
They sported with *iṣṭaghnīs*, mallets with a hundred edges,
swords, mountain peaks, boulders, and raised iron clubs;
the sky was filled and completely covered on all sides by throngs of clouds.
Thus that army of Dānavas, intoxicated with the pride of all their beings,
stood facing the gods like a massed cloud-bank arisen;
and that dense host of thousands of Daityas, which was like wind, fire, mountains, clouds, and water, was repelled.
Agitated by a flood of forces and surging forth, it appeared like one intoxicated with the desire for battle.
(195) O descendant of Kuru, you have heard the extent of the Daitya army; now hear the extent of the divine army belonging to Viṣṇu. (196)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Daitya Army," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-one.
Pulastya said:
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great strength, together with their armies and followers, equipped themselves in due order;
and Puruhūta, the thousand-eyed guardian of the world, stood at the front.
The leader of all the gods mounted the excellent elephant;
on its left side was his chariot, with its excellent banner resembling a bird's wing,
its wheels shining like the sun, and adorned with a golden parasol.
Followed by thousands of hosts of gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas,
he was praised by radiant brahman-sages dwelling in heaven,
[who were like] flashes of lightning arising from the discharge of Indra’s thunderbolt.
He is joined by hosts of clouds that move at will like mountains;
mounted upon him, the Blessed One traverses the entire world.
Standing at the mouth of the sacrifice, the Brahmins sing praises during the offerings of oblations.
When the sounds of celestial trumpets resound as they have gone to the battle for heaven,
hosts of Apsarases by the hundreds dance before him along with Indra;
he shines with the elephant-king as his banner, like the sun.
Yoked with a thousand horses possessing the speed of thought and the wind,
that excellent chariot shone brilliantly when properly harnessed by Mātali;
it appeared like Mount Meru entirely surrounded by the splendor of the sun.
Raising his staff and a mallet appropriate for the occasion, Yama stood amidst the hosts of the gods, displaying himself before the Daityas;
he was accompanied by the four oceans and by licking serpents.
Wearing conch-shell armlets and bearing a body composed of water,
he brandished the nooses of Time with horses resembling moonbeams,
performing thousands of playful maneuvers that took the form of wind-stirred waves. 11-12.
Wearing pale, fluttering garments and beautiful coral armlets, his excellent body dark with jewels and his chest adorned with a necklace,
Varuṇa stood in the midst of the divine host, holding his noose. 13.
Eager for the hour of battle like the ocean that has overstepped its shore, he was joined by the armies of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas and by the hosts of Guhyakas;
he was the sovereign lord of the treasures, accompanied by the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma. 14–15.
The glorious Lord of Kings was seen with a mace in his hand; the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), fighting from his celestial chariot, stood upon the Puṣpaka vimāna.
Together with that King of Kings, the Lord of Yakṣas, who has men as his vehicle, shone resplendently.
On the eastern wing was the thousand-eyed one (Indra), and on the southern wing was the king of the ancestors (Yama).
On the western wing was Varuṇa, and on the northern wing was he whose vehicle is man (Kubera).
These four world-protectors of great strength possessed four wings each.
As that divine army was moving toward the eastern direction,
the Sun, blazing with splendor and radiant with his glowing rays, arrived on a chariot yoked to seven horses that moved with the speed of the wind. 19.
By means of his asceticism, which followed the path of the wheel of the rising and setting sun as far as the borders of Mount Meru,
he attained the imperishable world through that wheel which is the gateway to heaven,
shining with a brilliance endowed with a thousand rays.
In the midst of the gods, the twelve-fold Divākara moves; the moon, possessing cool rays, shines in his chariot drawn by white horses, gladdening the world with beams filled with frost and water. 22.
[He saw] that lord of the twice-born, followed by the conjunction with the bear (Ursa Major), the cool-rayed one, whose body was marked by the shadow of the hare;
the destroyer of nocturnal darkness, the lord of luminaries, the imperishable master who is the essence of the sky. 23–24.
The Dānavas beheld Soma, the repository of purifying herbs and of nectar, the supreme portion of the world, gentle, and consisting of all essence, standing there with snow as his weapon. 25.
That vital breath (prāṇa) which, existing in all beings among men, is divided fivefold; which, residing in the seven constituents (skandhas), supports and created the three worlds;
whom they call the maker of fire, the source of all, and the Lord. 26–27.
He whose source is proclaimed by words consisting of the seven notes;
whom they call the moving being, and whom they call the bodiless;
whom they say moves through space, travels swiftly, and is born from sound. 28.
Arrogant on account of his own splendor, he, who was the life-force of all beings, blew forth like a cloud against the wind,
causing distress to the Daityas;
while the wind-god [Vāyu] remained there together with the gods, Gandharvas, and hosts of Vidyādharas.

They sported with their bright rays like snakes that had been cast off, while the lords of serpents, creating a fierce poison of wrath, moved through the sky with their mouths wide open as if they had become arrows fixed upon them.
31. They moved through the heavens with gaping maws as if they had become arrows.
The mountains, with their rocky peaks and trees with a hundred branches,
approached the hosts of gods to strike the Dānava army—
that Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Trivikrama, who is the God himself. 32–33.

At the end of the age, he is the black-pathed fire; he is the Lord of the entire universe, the source of all, the destroyer of the demon Madhu, the consumer of oblations, and established in sacrifice.
He is the soul of earth, water, space, and living beings; he is dark-hued and the bringer of peace here on earth.
The wielder of the discus and mace ensured there was no obstacle for the immortals and others;
with his left hand, he grasped the great mace that destroys all weapons—a body like Time itself, bestowing death upon the enemy. 35–36.
With his remaining arms, blazing with splendor, the Lord, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents and who possesses great strength, held a multitude of weapons, such as the Śārṅga bow and others;
he was the twice-born son of Kaśyapa, the devourer of serpents.
It was resplendent with the lord of serpents coiled upon its nine faces;
it rose high like Mount Mandara when joined for the churning of the nectar, having witnessed his prowess many times during the conflicts between the gods and the asuras. 38-39.
On Mount Mahendra, for the sake of the nectar, he was marked with the thunderbolt;
he was like a mountain covered in various leaves and garments, as if filled with mineral ores, possessing a splendor equal to the moon through his support of vast fury. 40.
It was illuminated by a radiant jewel attached to the coils of a serpent;
and it was covered by two wings of beautiful feathers, appearing like the sky at the end of an eon, with clouds and rainbows on either side.
The glorious lord, having mounted his chariot in battle— adorned with blue, red, and yellow banners, drawn by the younger brother of Aruṇa (Garuda),
the best of sky-travelers whose body is golden-hued.
The hosts of gods and the sages, with concentrated minds, followed him;
they praised the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara) with supreme mantras and hymns.
He was embraced by Vaiśravaṇa and preceded by Vaivasvata.

Encircled by the king of waters, adorned by the king of gods, resounding with the roar of the wind, and ablaze with fire; it was pervaded by the splendor of Viṣṇu, the victorious, the patient, and the radiant one. 46.
A battle ensued between the powerful and the more powerful. "May it be well with the gods! Bṛhaspati exclaimed;
"May it be well with the Daityas! Uśanas took up the speech.
From those two powers, a tumultuous conflict then arose between the gods and the asuras, who were each desirous of victory over the other.
The dānavas, with various weapons raised, fought together with the deities.
Fighting like mountains against mountains, they clashed;
that battle between the gods and asuras shone forth as most wonderful,
joined with both righteousness and unrighteousness, and with both pride and humility.
Then, with swift horses and urged elephants leaping into the sky on all sides with swords in hand,
with maces being hurled and arrows falling thick and fast—
With bows being drawn and most dreadful arrows being discharged,
that battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas,
causing terror to the world and resembling the fire at the end of an eon.
In that battle, the Dānavas struck the gods, led by Indra, with iron clubs, mallets, and even mountains hurled from their own hands;
being thus slaughtered by those powerful Dānavas who appeared victorious, they [the gods] were hard-pressed.
From their very dejected faces, they experienced supreme distress in the battle.
Crushed by the tridents of those missiles and their heads split by the iron clubs of the sons of Aditi, their chests pierced, they bled profusely upon the field.
Slain by nets of arrows and rendered motionless by those shafts, they entered into a demonic illusion and were unable to perceive your movements;
they appeared as if paralyzed, their forms resembling those devoid of life.
The strength of the gods was rendered effortless by the Asuras with their weapons;
having cut down those terrible arrows discharged from the bows of the Daityas with his thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed Śakra entered the formidable army of the Daityas. 59–60.
Having slain all the foremost of the Daityas and their great army,
he then rendered them into darkness by means of a web of *tāmasa* weapons; because of that, neither the Daityas nor their mounts could perceive one another.
Overcome by terrible darkness through the splendor of Indra,
yet striving with effort, those best of gods cast down the heads of the hosts of Daityas, which had become like darkness itself.
Overwhelmed and deprived of consciousness by that dark, blue-hued radiance,
the Dānavas instantly fell down like mountains whose wings had been clipped.
There, the space between them was filled with darkness as the lords of the Daityas were utterly defeated.
The body of the Dānava became as if filled with darkness;
then Maya created that great illusion, which was of the nature of darkness and produced a brilliance like that at the end of an eon, having been fashioned by the Aurva fire.
Constantly tormented by the burning rays [of the sun], the Daityas, who were composed of illusion and mental constructs, suddenly rose up in battle with bodies like those of the sun.
Having encountered the illusory bowstring, the inhabitants of heaven were scorched.
They fled toward the region of the moon, a lake of cool-rayed water.
Being scorched by the Aurva fire, their minds bewildered and themselves tormented, those gods sought refuge with the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra). 68–69.
While he was being tormented by Māyāsena and struck down by the Dānavas,
Varuṇa, urged by the King of the Gods, spoke these words:
"O Śakra, in former times a Brahmarṣi performed most formidable austerities."
Urvashī was born first; he was radiant and equal to Brahmā in his qualities.
As he performed undecaying penance like the scorching sun, hosts of sages, gods, and divine seers approached him.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Dānava and lord of the Dānavas,
once petitioned a rishi of supreme splendor;
those brahmin-sages then spoke words consistent with dharma.
"O Blessed One, this lineage of the ṛṣis has its very root severed.
You alone are childless, and no one else remains for this clan; having undertaken a vow of lifelong celibacy, you pursue nothing but hardship. (74–75)
Many lineages of Brahmins, sages of purified souls,
remain as single bodies, secluded and without offspring.
Since all such beings exist in this manner, Menā has no reason for concern regarding sons.
"You are a preeminent ascetic, equal in splendor to Prajāpati.
Therefore, proceed for the sake of your lineage; increase yourself by means of yourself.
Concentrate your powerful energy and create a second body. (77-78)
Thus addressed by the sages, the sage, struck in his mind, censured the assembly of seers and spoke these words:
"For such is the eternal dharma ordained for sages of old. (79)
For a Brāhmaṇa born from the womb of Brahman, who subsists on forest roots and fruits, follows the conduct of the Ṛṣis, and is devoted solely to his own duty,
even a well-practiced life of celibacy might cause Brahmā himself to tremble.
There are three modes of livelihood for people who dwell in the householder stage of life,
and our mode of livelihood is that of those dwelling in the forest hermitage. We subsist on water, subsist on air, and likewise use our teeth as mortars.
There, those such as the stone-grinders and others who perform the penance of the five fires,
remaining steadfast in austerity through vows that are very difficult to practice, place celibacy at the forefront and seek the supreme goal. 83-84.

The Brahminhood of a Brāhmaṇa is ordained through celibacy; thus say those people in the next world who know celibacy. Dharma is established in celibacy, and austerity is established in celibacy. (85)

Those who remain established in celibacy are truly established in the state of Brahman and the like. Without yoga there is no perfection; without yoga there is no fame. In this world, there is no root of fame greater than the austerity of celibacy.
One who restrains the group of sense organs within the womb, as well as the group of five elements,
and practices celibacy— what austerity could be greater than this? (88) Wearing matted hair without yoga and performing vows without mental resolve [are likewise].
The threefold practice of unchastity is known as hypocrisy (dambha).
Where is the wife, where is the union, and where is the perversion of natural state? Indeed, this offspring was created by Brahmā from his own mind. 89–90.

If you possess the power of asceticism, O self-conquered ones, then create mental sons through the rite pertaining to Prajāpati. A womb fashioned by the mind must be established by those practicing austerities.
"Neither noble yoga nor the seed of ascetic vows has been declared by those who practice austerities.
This which you have uttered here, O fearless ones—though it is called the destruction of dharma—is exceedingly like that which is approved by the wicked. (92–93)
Having made my own mind-born self within my radiant body, I shall,
through the yoga of giving, create a son born of my own body even without sexual union;
thus my very self will beget a second self.
As if wishing to consume all creatures by means of the Prajāpati rite,
Varuṇa said: "Urva, being possessed by ascetic fervor, enter into the wide expanse of the sacrificial fire."
With a single piece of wood made of darbha grass, he churned the fire-drill for the sake of producing a son. Suddenly piercing his thigh, that excellent fire arose;
desiring to consume the world, the son became Agni.
Having burst through the thigh of Urvaśī, the fire named Aurva was born, exceedingly wrathful and desiring, as it were, to consume the three worlds;
even as he was being born, he spoke to his father with a piteous voice.

"O Father, do not eat the world; hunger oppresses me!"—thus addressed, he grew like the God of Death, stretching his flames toward the three heavens and devouring the ten directions as he consumed all living beings. 99–100.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived before the sage Urva and said:
"O son, let him be restrained; show compassion for the world. O Brahmin, he shall become his [the world's] protector; I shall provide you with the highest assistance."
"O best among speakers, son, these words of yours are true; listen.
Aurva said:
'I am blessed, I am graced, O Blessed One, since you [have spoken] to me regarding my child.'"
O Supreme Soul, you have indeed granted this thought for our welfare.
(103) Now that the desired time of dawn has arrived for our meeting, O Blessed One, by what offerings will my son be satisfied so that he may attain happiness? (104)
"And where shall his dwelling be? And what shall be the nature of the food that the Blessed One, equal in valor to the Greatly Resplendent One, will provide here? 105.
Brahmā said:

"My womb shall become the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha) dwelling in the ocean; O Brahmin, let this immeasurable water go there, where he, as a thief, will surely drink the water that is my sacrificial oblation. 106.
"O Brahmin, I shall release that expanse of water and its abode.
Then, at the end of the Yuga, O son, this world and I together shall move about here, having destroyed all things."
"This fire, created by me at the time of the end, shall be a consumer of all beings, including gods, asuras, and rakshasas.
"So be it," he said; and that fire, with its circle of flames withdrawn, remained.
Having bowed down to his lordly father Urva, he entered the mouth of the ocean.
Then Brahmā departed, as did all those great sages;
knowing the power of the fire of Aurva, they each returned to their own respective abodes.
Then, having witnessed that great marvel, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
with all his limbs bowed low, spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, this wonder has occurred before the very eyes of the world."

O best of sages, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was well-pleased by your asceticism. "But I must be understood as the servant of both you and your son, O observer of great vows; you are praiseworthy here for your deed. 114
Therefore, look upon me as I am absorbed in meditation, devoted solely to your worship; O best of sages, if I should fail, it would be your own defeat.
Urvaśī said:
"I am blessed and I am graced, since you consider me your guru. O observer of excellent vows, by this austerity of yours, you shall have no fear here at all.
Accept this very illusion (māyā) created by my son."
"Though fuel-less, it is made of fire and is difficult to touch even for fires.
This [missile], being under your control, shall subdue your enemies and protect your own side, while utterly consuming your adversaries. (117-118)
Varuṇa said:
This illusion, which is difficult to withstand and hard even for the gods to overcome, was created in the past by Aurva, the son of Urva, the fire-god. 119
When that Daitya is thus afflicted, she will undoubtedly be rendered powerless;
for this curse was previously given to her by him with his own splendor when she was created.
If she is to be slain, then let the Blessed One act so as to be at ease.
"Let the moon, the source of the waters of Śakra’s treasury, be given to me.
By uniting with it and surrounded by aquatic creatures, I shall destroy this illusion through your grace; of this there is no doubt. (121-122)

Saying "So be it," Śakra, the enhancer of the thirty gods, was filled with joy and commanded Soma, whose weapon is the frost, to go before him for battle: "Go, O Soma, and provide assistance to the wielder of the noose."

For the destruction of the Asuras and for the victory of the inhabitants of heaven, you are considered by me to be the counter-force; you are also the lord of the luminaries. Those who know the Vedas recognize that in all worlds, the essences consist of you.
In this world, there exists no one equal to you, O wielder of the cool weapon (Śiśirāyudha).
Your waning and waxing are unmanifest, like those of the ocean and the sky;
you set in motion day and night, confounding the world with time.

The mark upon you, the body of the hare, is a characteristic consisting of the shadow of the world; those who are born of the stars do not know this illusion of yours. You are situated above the path of the sun and even above the luminaries.
Having suddenly dispelled the darkness, you illuminate the entire world—
the cool-rayed moon, whose body is of frost, the lord of luminaries. Furthermore,
through the conjunction of that time, you are the imperishable sacrificial chariot, the one to be worshipped.

You are the lord of herbs, the source of ritual action, and the source of the waters; you are the cool-rayed one, the repository of nectar, the fickle one, and the one with white steeds. You are the splendor of those with beautiful bodies, and you are the Soma for those who drink the Soma juice.

"You are gentle toward all beings; you are the destroyer of darkness, O King of the Bears. Therefore, O Mahāsena, go with Varuṇa and his host, and subdue the illusory power of the Asuras by which we are being consumed in battle."
Soma said:
"O King of the Gods, O bestower of boons, as you tell me to go for the sake of battle,
I shall rain down this cool mist that dispels the illusions of the Daityas."
"Behold these Daityas, scorched by my fire and enveloped by serpents;
likewise, showers of snakes released by the serpent-king, accompanied by nooses, are encircling those demons as the wind surrounds masses of clouds. (134–135)
Varuṇa and the Moon, the two immensely powerful lords of the waters who wield the noose and the cool-rayed moon,
struck the Dānavas with falls of snow and falls of nooses.
Those two lords of the waters fought in battle, using the noose and snow as their weapons.
Like two great oceans agitated by the waters of the clouds at the end of an aeon,
that entire vast army of Dānavas was completely filled by those two,
appearing as if enveloped by the downpours of the clouds of universal destruction.
Then both Varuṇa and Śaśāṅka, the lords of the waters,
raised their weapons and quelled that illusion created by the lord of the Daityas;
scorched by the net of moonbeams, they were bound with nooses in the battle.
The Daityas were unable to move, like mountains deprived of their peaks.
Struck by the cool-rayed moon, all those Daityas were cast down,
their entire bodies drenched in frost like fires devoid of heat.
Indeed, auspicious and variegated celestial chariots belonging to those gods and Daityas were falling; they fell and rose up again.
Those [beings], bound by nooses held in hands, were covered by the cool-rayed moon.
I beheld the illusory Dānava Dividānava, who possessed a vast expanse of mountains and was laughing with his sword-blade and shield;
he stood upon a heap of fallen trees, surrounded by forests filled with caves. (143–144)

It was crowded with lions, tigers, and herds of animals, and filled with the cries of the leaders of divine hosts; it was thronged with packs of wild beasts, its trees shaken by the wind, and it resounded as it traveled through the sky at will, having been fashioned by her own son.
He created the renowned illusion of Pārvatī on all sides.
With the sounds of swords, showers of stones, and falling trees,
she struck down the hosts of gods and restored those Dānavas to life.
Then, when that illusion had vanished like the moonlight at dawn, the earth became impassable as if covered by mountains;
not a single tree was visible, nor could any deity be seen. 148.
Having abandoned the host of gods— which had its bows cast aside, its weapons shattered and disarrayed,
and was rendered effortless— the glorious Lord, having entered the fray, did not tremble before the wielder of the mace.
Out of forbearance, the Lord of the World, the wielder of the mace, did not become angry;
knowing the proper time and resembling a dark cloud, Hari observed the moment for battle,
desiring then to witness the conflict between the gods and the asuras.
Then, commanded by the Blessed One and urged by the words of Viṣṇu, Aṇi and Pāvaka-Māruta drew forth the Māyā;
having awakened in that great battle, they moved with bewildered speed.

The illusory power of Pārvatī was consumed, her face reduced to ashes; and he, united with the wind, together with the fire, and the fire agitated by the wind—these two, intoxicated as it were, burned the army of the Daityas like at the end of an eon. 154.
There, the wind blew with great speed, and after it, the fire followed from the wind;
the fire and the wind moved about the army of the Dānavas as if playing,
while living beings were being reduced to ashes, falling down and leaping up.

While the celestial chariots of the Dānavas were falling on all sides, scattered by the gusts of wind as their deeds were consumed by the fire, and while the wielder of the mace was being praised as he proceeded to destroy their illusions; 157.
When the Daityas were rendered effortless and the three worlds were freed from bondage (158),
while the gods rejoiced and cried out "Excellent! Excellent!", there was victory for the thousand-eyed Indra and defeat for the Daityas (159).

When all the directions were pure, when the expansion of the Dharma had proceeded, when the path of the moon was unobstructed and the sun remained in its proper station, and when all beings and men were established in virtuous conduct; 160.
While the fire was being offered into the unbroken bond of death,
while the gods were beautifying the sacrifice, and while all the world-protectors were pointing out the path to heaven, they remained stationed in every direction.
When those who have perfected their ascetic practices are absent and evil-doers prevail,
the faction of the gods rejoices while the faction of the Daityas desponds. While Dharma stands with three feet and Adharma possesses but a single foot, [the world prospers].

When the great gates were thrown open, while the path of the righteous remained in existence, when people were engaged in the practice of dharma, when the stages of life (āśramas) had been set in motion,
and when kings shone forth, devoted to the protection of their subjects.

When the worlds had become tranquil and the Dānava’s darkness was stilled, Agni and Māruta engaged in the act of battle; through them, the pure worlds were filled with that [energy], and their deeds were performed for the sake of victory.
Having heard of the great and intense fear caused by Māruta and Agni,
the Dānava renowned as Kālanemi appeared;
his crown was shaped like the sun, and his ornaments and armlets were jingling.
Resembling Mount Mandara, covered in great silver,
formidable with a hundred weapons, possessing a hundred arms, a hundred faces,
and a hundred heads, the glorious one stood like a mountain with a hundred peaks.
Like a fire grown great in the intense heat of summer,
with smoke-colored hair, a tawny beard, protruding teeth, and a formidable face,
he possessed a vast body that filled the interior of the three worlds.
Weighing the sky with his arms, tossing mountains with his feet,
and driving the rain-bearing clouds with the breaths from his mouth—
[he was like] Mandara with its fierce splendor, possessing wide and extended red eyes.
He appeared as if he were coming to incinerate all the hosts of gods in battle;
threatening the throngs of deities and shrouding the ten directions,
he was seen like the enraged Death risen at the time of universal dissolution.
With his right hand raised— its palm broad, its fingers and joints prominent, adorned with hanging ornaments, slightly engaged in action, and beautiful in form— (he stood). 175.
Seeing Kālanemi, who was shouting "Stay! to the Dānavas slain by the gods, all the deities gazed upon him in battle with eyes overwhelmed by fear. 176–177.
The beings beheld him devouring [them], like Kālanemi,
as he strode with the three steps of Trivikrama like another Nārāyaṇa. Having once again attained great height, he caused the sky to whirl with his wind.
Advancing to fight and terrifying all the gods,
the Daitya Kālanemi met with Surendra; embraced by him as he moved through the battle, the Daitya shone like Mount Mandara when it was encircled by Viṣṇu.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, trembled upon seeing Kālanemi approaching like another personified Death; meanwhile,
the great Asura Kālanemi desired to gratify the Dānavas.
Possessed of great splendor, he grew like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat.
Seeing him pervading the interior of the three worlds, those lords of the Dānavas rose up,
unwearied, as if they had drunk the supreme nectar.
Free from fear, terror, and fatigue, led by Tāraka and Maya,
and always appearing victorious in the battle against Maya,
the Dānavas, desiring combat, shone as they entered the field of battle. 184.
As they practiced mantras, as they rushed about in formation,
and as they gazed upon the Dānava Kālanemi, joy arose within them; for those who were there were the foremost leaders, intent on battle.
Casting aside all fear and filled with joy, they stood ready for battle:
Maya, Tāra, Varāha, the Dānava Hayagrīva,
Śveta the son of Vipracitti, and both Khara and Lamba.
Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, and likewise the one named Kiśora;
Surbhānu, who resembles a chowrie, and the great Asura Cakrayodhin—all of these were knowers of the Vedas and were all firmly established in austerity. 188–189.
The skillful Dānavas went toward the arrogant Kālanemi with very heavy clubs, discuses, chariots,
and battle-axes; with maces resembling Time itself, and with slings and mallets.
With stones resembling weapons, as well as with formidable rocks,
with *paṭṭiśas*, *bhiṇḍipālas*, and iron clubs (*parighas*) made of excellent steel,
and likewise with heavy, lethal *śataghnīs*.
With yokes and machines cast off, with ploughs striking fiercely,
with outstretched arms, with nooses, iron clubs, and the like; with arrows having serpent-mouths that were licking and gliding forth.
With blazing thunderbolts and flaming javelins,
with sharp unsheathed swords and bright, stainless spears,
the Daityas shone forth, grasping their bows.
Then, placing Kālanemi at its head in battle, the army of the Daityas shone forth, with their excellent weapons blazing;
by them, whose entire bodies were covered [in armor], they resembled a forest of lotuses at the arrival of the clouds. (196)
The army of the gods, protected by Śakra, rejoiced;
it was accompanied by the cool and warm splendors of the moon and the sun, possessed the speed of the wind, and had the gentle hosts of stars for its banners. 197–198.
Clad in garments of water, laughing with the constellations of the planets,
she was protected by Yama, Indra, Kubera, and the wise Varuṇa;
she was radiant with fire and wind, and was entirely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
That great army, resembling the ocean, blazing,
formidable, equipped with weapons, and graced by yakṣas and gandharvas, shone resplendently; then, at that time, the encounter between those two armies took place.
As the transition between the ages (yugas) occurred, there took place a terrible battle between the gods and the dānavas, involving the union of heaven and earth—
a conflict characterized by patience and prowess, and marked by both pride and humility. 202.
The gods and asuras marched forth with those two formidable armies,
like clouds driven from the eastern and western oceans;
delighted by those two forces, the deities and dānavas moved about.
Just as mountains are struck by two flowering forest trees from the mountains, so too did they strike the kettledrums and blow conch shells many times over,
filling the cosmic egg, the earth, and all the directions.
The sounds of bowstrings striking the palms,
the twanging of bows, and the roar of kettledrums drowned out the voices of the Daityas;
they rushed at one another, seeking to overcome each other.
Desirous of fighting, they grappled with their arms in hand-to-hand combat;
the Dānavas hurled terrible thunderbolts at the gods, as well as iron clubs, excellent weapons, swords, and heavy maces in the battle.
With their limbs shattered by the falling maces and hacked to pieces by arrows,
some fell down violently while others struck back;
then [the battle continued] with chariots, four-horsed steeds, celestial vehicles, and foot-soldiers.
Enraged, they clashed with one another in the combat, meeting in battle with their lips and faces bitten in fury;
chariots fought against chariots, and foot-soldiers against foot-soldiers.
The tumultuous roar of those chariots,
carrying sound through the air, filled the sky like the thundering of clouds in the heavens;
some shattered the chariots, while others were crushed by the chariots themselves.
The chariots, having reached a narrow space, were unable to move;
in the midst of one another in that battle, those clad in armor lifted [their foes] with their arms and struck them there, shouting loudly along with their troops, while wielding swords and shields.
Pierced by various other missiles, they vomited blood, slain in battle; resembling clouds pouring down water,
they met one another, and the sky of the battlefield appeared as a dark storm through the mutual showering of arrows.
In the meantime, the enraged Dānava Kālanemi grew like a cloud being filled by the oceans,
raining down blazing thunderbolts and wreathed in streaks of lightning.
Clouds fell upon his limbs, which resembled mountains and great peaks. As he hissed in anger, with his furrowed brows raining sweat,
flames accompanied by sparks of fire issued forth from his wide-open mouth.
His arms extended horizontally and upwards into the sky like five-mouthed serpents emerging from a mountain;
he was equipped with various nets of missiles, bows, and iron clubs.
He covered the divine sky as if with lofty mountains;
with his garment stirred by the wind, he stood longing for battle like Mount Meru itself, its rocks consumed by the glow of twilight.
With mountain peaks and trees shattered by the force of his thighs,
he struck down the hosts of gods as if with a thunderbolt against great mountains;
and with his sword-bearing arms, he cut and tore their hair and heads.
The gods were unable to move, having been struck down by Kālanemi in battle.
Some were slain by his fists, while others were split asunder—
yakṣas, gandharvas, birds, along with great serpents and kinnaras.
Terrified by him in battle, they fell; though they strove with effort, they were unable to act, being deprived of their senses. By him, the thousand-eyed Śakra was bound with fetters of arrows.
Rendered effortless by the Count, he was unable to move;
like a cloud without water, resembling a waterless ocean,
Varuṇa was made devoid of activity and stripped of his noose in the battle.

In battle, the Lord of the World-protectors, Vaiśravaṇa, surrounded by that one who had assumed the form of Time (Kāla), was made to abandon his function as the Giver of Wealth while lamenting; likewise,
Yama, the Taker of All, whose weapon is Death, [was overcome] by him in the fray.

Abandoning his position in the southern quarter, he fled in fear toward his own direction. Having driven away the world-protectors (lokapālas) and seized their respective functions, he then divided his own body into four parts and placed them in all directions.
Having entered the path of the stars, he seized the divine splendor of Soma as shown by Rāhu, and he even plundered his vast domain; furthermore,
he shook the radiant Sun from the gateway of Dharma.

He took away his [the Sun's] teaching and his domain, as well as his daily activity; having conquered the god Agni, he made him dependent upon his own mouth, and having conquered Vāyu by his power, he brought him under his own control. 233–234.
Having forcibly brought together all the rivers along with the oceans, he made them flow toward him through his heroic power; thus the streams became as if embodied,
bringing under his own control both the celestial waters and those born upon the earth.
He covered the earth, which was well-guarded by mountains;
that great Daitya, who consisted of all the worlds and brought fear to all the worlds, shone like the Great Lord of the elements himself, as if he were Svayambhū. 236–237.
Possessing a single body that shared the domain of the world-protectors, embodying the moon, sun,
and planets, and born from fire and wind, the Dānava Arjuna stood in the supreme station of Parameṣṭhin, which is like the source of all worlds.
The hosts of Daityas praised him, just as the gods praise the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Through his contrary conduct, he turned away from the five things that depend upon Nārāyaṇa: the Vedas, dharma, forbearance, truth, and prosperity.
Because they did not attend upon him, the lord of the Dānavas became enraged;
seeking the station of Viṣṇu, he went from there to the abode of the gods.
There he saw [Viṣṇu], seated upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
He was brandishing a splendid mace for the destruction of the Dānavas;
he resembled a water-laden cloud, his garment was like lightning,
and he was mounted upon a celestial bird of Kaśyapa’s lineage, adorned with golden wings.
Seeing Viṣṇu standing as if suspended in the sky for the sake of destroying the wicked Daityas, the Dānava, his mind agitated, spoke to the unshakeable one:
"This is our enemy, the destroyer of the lives of our ancestors."
"Furthermore, this one who dwells in the ocean—the enemy of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa—is indeed said to be our peerless foe;
by him, in numerous battles, many Dānavas have been slain. (245-246)
This is that merciless one in the world, devoid of shame before women and children,
by whom the breaking of the womb-walls of the wives of the Dānavas was performed.
This is Viṣṇu, the Vaikuṇṭha of the gods and the abode of the dwellers of heaven.
He is the self-born among the self-born and the infinite among the infinite.
This one, the protector of the gods, is being mistreated by us;
having encountered his wrath, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain. 248–249.
Taking refuge in its shadow, the gods stationed at the front of the sacrifice partake of the clarified butter offered in three ways by the great seers.
This [mountain] is the cause of the destruction of all the enemies of the immortals.
"Those clans who have entered his wheel in battle are ours; indeed,
this man, having cast away his life for the sake of the gods in battles,
hurls the wheel— endowed with splendor and accompanied by its lord— at his enemies."
"O Daityas, while I, who am Time itself, stand as the Destroyer of Time, this Keśava shall reap the fruit of the time that has passed. By good fortune, this Viṣṇu has now come before my very eyes."
Crushed by me, he shall perish along with his countless hosts;
by good fortune, I shall today in this battle attain the honor due to my ancestors by slaying this Nārāyaṇa, who brings fear to the Dānavas.
"I shall swiftly slay the hosts of enemies in battle;
for even though he has entered another birth, he continues to harass the Dānavas in combat. This one was formerly Ananta, known as Padmanābha."
In the terrible single ocean, he slew both Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
having divided his body into two parts, half-lion and half-man,
one [form] formerly slew my father, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, bore him as a pure embryo;
he alone, taking three strides, seized the three worlds.
Now, however, that the Tārakāmaya war has arrived once more—
"Having encountered me, he shall perish along with his gods.
Having spoken thus in many ways, he quickly incited Nārāyaṇa to battle alone with harsh words in the fray. 260–261.
Though being hurled by the lord of the asuras, the wielder of the mace did not become angry;
instead, through the power of his great forbearance, he spoke these words with a smile:
"O Daitya, the strength of pride is trivial, whereas the strength born of freedom from anger is stable."
"You have been destroyed by the faults born of pride, you who speak thus to me with such insolence. You are base; fie upon this power of your speech!
Where are those men present where women may roar like this?"
I see you, O Daitya, following the path of those who came before;
who could remain in a state of well-being after abandoning the bridge established by Prajāpati? Today I shall destroy you, the destroyer of the gods' activities.
"I shall establish the deities each in their own respective places.
While the bearer of the Śrīvatsa was speaking these words in the midst of battle,
the Dānava laughed out of rage and, with his discus, severed the hands along with their weapons.
Raising all his hundreds of arms and all his multitudes of weapons in battle,
his eyes red with twice their usual measure of rage, he struck Viṣṇu’s chest; and the Dānavas as well, led by Maya and Tāra, [attacked] in the encounter.
With weapons and swords raised, they rushed toward Viṣṇu in battle. Though struck by the exceedingly powerful Daityas who had raised all their weapons,
he did not waver in the fight, remaining as unshakable as a mountain.
And the great asura Kālanemi, joined with Suparṇa,
raised a massive mace with all his might using his arms and,
filled with fury, hurled that terrible, blazing weapon at Garuḍa.
By that deed of the Daitya, Viṣṇu was filled with wonder.
Then, seeing Suparṇa pained by that mace which had been hurled at his head, and seeing his own body unhurt, [Viṣṇu reflected]. 272–273.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha took up his discus;
the omnipresent one grew in size with great speed, equal to Suparṇa,
and his arms expanded, pervading the ten directions.
Filling the intermediate directions,
the sky, and the earth, he grew once more with his might as if desiring to leap across the worlds, increasing in the firmament for the sake of conquering the lords of the asuras.
The ṛṣis, together with the gandharvas, praised Madhusūdana,
who was instantly scratching his head with his radiant crown,
while treading upon the earth with his feet and covering the quarters with his arms.
It possesses a splendor equal to a thousand suns, has a thousand spokes, and destroys enemies;
it is as fierce as a blazing fire and is beautiful to behold; its rim is like golden dust, its navel is of diamond, and it inspires awe. (278–279)
Sprinkled with the fat, marrow, and blood produced by the Dānavas,
it was an unrivaled weapon with a circular edge like a razor; it was draped with garlands and wreaths, moving at will, and assuming any form at will.

Created by the Self-Existent One himself, it was terrifying to all enemies; filled with wrath and ever-proud in battle, at the mere sight of its hurling, the worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were struck with confusion. (281–282)
In that great battle,

the wielder of the mace, blazing with wrath, raised his discus and [struck] those flesh-eating beings who had attained satisfaction in the great conflict— that one of incomparable deeds, equal to the sun in splendor.
He destroyed the demonic splendor of Kālanemi with his own splendor;
in that very battle, he severed the arms of Kālanemi,
along with those hundred terrible faces that were laughing loudly with fire and ash.
With his discus, Hari forcibly crushed that Daitya;
with his arms severed and his head gone, the Dānava did not tremble, remaining as a headless trunk in battle like a tree without branches.
286. It stood there in the fray like a tree stripped of its boughs.
Having spread his great wings and made his speed equal to that of the wind,
Garuḍa struck Kālanemi with his chest; his body, facing him, spun around in the air with its arms flung out.
Having abandoned heaven, he fell down as if shaking the surface of the earth.
When that Daitya had fallen, the gods, together with the hosts of sages, gathered and honored Vaikuṇṭha, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent! (289).

Then other Daityas, who had witnessed his prowess in battle, rushed forward; but they, being hemmed in by his arms, were unable to move in the fray. Some he seized by the hair, and others he squeezed by the neck.
He severed the face of one and likewise seized another; scorched by maces and discuses, those beings,
their life-force departed, fell from the sky with all their limbs shattered onto the surface of the earth.
When all those Daityas had been slain, the Supreme Person,
the wielder of the mace, having performed what was pleasing to Śakra,
completed his task once that crushing battle for Tārakā had come to an end.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, went quickly to that place together with all the brahmin-sages and hosts of gandharvas and apsaras;
honoring Hari, the God of gods, the Lord spoke these words.
O God, a great deed has been accomplished; the thorn of the gods has been extracted. By the destruction of the Daityas, we too have been fully satisfied.
O Viṣṇu, this great Asura Kālanemi who was slain by you— 296–297.
Indeed, without you, there is no one here who can be his instructor;
he treats even the gods with contempt, as well as the worlds of moving and unmoving beings.
Having brought about the destruction of the sages, he even roars defiance at me.
Therefore, I am well-pleased with this deed of yours, that this Kālanemi, who was like Time itself, has been struck down. Come now; may it be well with you; let us go to the highest heaven.
The Brahman-sages residing there, having gathered in your assembly, await you;
and what boon shall I grant to them, O best of boon-granters,
while the gods remain in their own abodes— you who are the giver of boons to them?
This prosperous triple world has been delivered, its thorns removed.
In this very battle, O Viṣṇu, [the victory belongs] to the great-souled Śakra and the others.
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed Brahmā, the imperishable Hari—
Viṣṇu spoke with auspicious words to all the gods, headed by Śakra: "Listen, O all you thirty deities who have assembled here. (304)
There, accompanied by the Suparṇas and placing Purandara at their head,
we all together struck down the Dānavas led by Kālanemi— beings endowed with great prowess who were even superior to Śakra himself. 305.
In this great battle, only two emerged:
Virocana, the son of Diti, and the mighty Svarbhānu.
Śakra took his own quarter, and Varuṇa likewise took his quarter. (306–307)
May Yama protect the southern quarter, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) the northern;
may the Moon likewise always maintain his conjunction with the constellations, and may the Sun attend upon the commencement of the seasons along with the solstices. 308.
"Let the portions of clarified butter proceed, honored by the members of the assembly;

let the fires be offered oblations by the Brahmins through rites prescribed in the Vedas; and let the gods be worshipped with the offering of bali and the great sages with the study of the sacred texts."
May the ancestors attain satisfaction through the *śrāddha* rite as they please; may the wind move along its proper path, and may the sacrificial fire blaze in its three forms.
May the three social classes satisfy the three worlds with their own inherent virtues.
Let the ritual acts proceed with the twice-born performing the initiatory rites (dīkṣaṇīya); let the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) be duly distributed by the various officiating priests.
Let Sūrya [bestow] cows, Soma [bestow] essences, and Vāyu [bestow] the vital breaths within living beings.
May these rivers, born from the Mahendra and Malaya mountains, flow forth according to their own duties and in due order to satisfy [the world] with their Soma-like waters;
may all these rivers, the mothers of the three worlds, go toward the ocean.
"O deities, let fear of the Daityas be abandoned; attain peace.
May there be well-being for you all, as I shall depart for the eternal world of Brahmā.
Whether in my own home, in the heavenly realm, or especially in battle, there is no difference [in my regard for you]."
One should never trust the Dānavas, for they are indeed base;
they strike at vulnerabilities, and thus their stability is not firm.
O gentle ones, your minds are naturally inclined toward straightforwardness.
Having spoken thus to the hosts of Asuras, the Lord Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth and whose glory is great, departed for the world of Brahmā together with Brahmā,
having generated great joy among the gods.
"This was the wonder that occurred in the Tārakāmaya war between the Dānavas and Viṣṇu, about which you ask me.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Battle between the Gods and Asuras Arising from the Lotus," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The forty-second chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brāhmaṇa, the lotus-born Brahmā has been heard by me as described by you in detail.
O Brahman, I desire to hear in brief the greatness of Bhava and the birth of Guha, how he came to be, and what he accomplished;
and also who this exceedingly powerful Dānava Tāraka was.
O Brahman, how was the great asura destroyed by Kārttikeya?
O sages, how were you sent by Rudra to Mount Mandara? And how was Umā obtained there by Rudra, the supreme lord?
"O Great Sage, relate all of this to me exactly as it happened.
Pulastya said: "In former times, the auspicious Aditi, the source of the Daityas, was addressed by Kaśyapa."
"O Goddess, a son shall be born to you with limbs made of the essence of diamond (vajrasāra).
That son, named Vajrāṅga, shall be a lover of righteousness.
Having obtained her boon, the goddess gave birth to Vajraduśchida."
As soon as he was born, he became one who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures;
with devotion, he said to his mother, "O Mother, what shall I do? Then Aditi, the mother of that lord of the Daityas, spoke to him joyfully.
"O son, many sons were slain by the Thousand-Eyed One;
go now to slay Śakra in order to avenge them.
Having said "So be it" to her, he went by force to the celestial realm.
Having bound the thousand-eyed one with an unerring lasso,
he approached his mother like a hunter approaching a small deer.
In the meantime, Brahmā and Kaśyapa of great asceticism arrived.
Then the mother and son, both fearless, arrived at those three places.
Seeing them, Brahmā and Kaśyapa spoke this: "Release this one, O son, the lord of the gods; what need have you for him?"
"Insult is said to be the equivalent of death for one who is esteemed by his son;
he who was released from your hand at our word is as good as dead.
Released from battle out of respect for another, he remains an enemy to his enemies."
"Though alive, he is as if dead day after day.
Having heard this, Vajrāṅga bowed and spoke these words: "I have no business with him; my mother’s command has been carried out by me."
"O God, you are indeed the lord of the gods and asuras, the venerable great-grandfather;
having been addressed thus, Śatakratu shall carry out your word. O Lord, my delight is in asceticism; may that be accomplished for me without obstacle."
"O Blessed One, by your grace," having said this, he ceased speaking.
(17) When that Daitya remained silent, the Grandfather spoke thus.
Brahmā said:
"Having undertaken this penance, he remains steadfast in my command.
Indeed, through this purity of heart, the fruit of his birth is fully attained.
Having said this, the Lotus-born One created a large-eyed maiden.
The lotus-born god Brahmā gave them to him for the sake of wives;
having bestowed upon her the name Varāṅgī, the destroyer of enemies departed.
Vajrāṅga also went to the forest with her to perform penance.
With his arms raised, that lord of the Daityas practiced for a thousand years;
he, whose eyes were like lotus petals, possessed pure intellect and performed great penance,
remaining with his face turned downward for that same duration and standing amidst five fires for that same duration.
Then, abstaining from food, performing terrible austerities, he became a mass of penance;
thereafter, he made his dwelling within the water for a thousand years. While he had entered the midst of the waters, his wife, who was firm in her great vows—
Standing at the very edge of that lake,
she of great splendor resorted to silence and entered into a terrible austerity without food.
While she was thus engaged in penance, Indra created a terrifying apparition.
Having gone to that great hermitage in the form of a monkey,
the powerful one dragged away the seat and the casket containing perfumes and other articles of worship.
Then, assuming the form of a lion, he terrified the beautiful woman.
Then, even in the form of a serpent, he bit her two feet;
yet by the power of her asceticism, she attained invincibility.
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, continued to afflict her with many terrifying threats.
Then Vajrāṅga’s queen, having pacified her anger, perceived the wickedness of the mountain and prepared to utter a curse.
Seeing her intent on cursing him, the mountain assumed a human form.
The mountain, with eyes fixed upon her, spoke to that woman of beautiful hips and exquisite limbs.
Śaila said:
"O lady of great vows, I am not wicked; I am to be resorted to by all embodied beings."
"Enraged, this subduer of Pāka (Indra) is doing what is displeasing.
In the meantime, a period of a thousand years passed;
and when the Lord born from the lotus recognized that time had arrived, [he acted].
Then, having come to that reservoir of water, the gratified Brahmā spoke to Vajrāṅga.
Brahmā said:
"O son of the gods, arise; I grant you all your desires. (33)
Thus addressed, that lord of the Daityas, a treasure-house of asceticism, rose up and,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the Grandfather of all the worlds.
Vajrāṅga said:

"May I be free from disease and long life; may I have a well-balanced body, freedom from worldly desire, and imperishability; may I be devoted to austerity, and may there be the maintenance of this body.
"So be it," said the god, and he departed for his own abode.
When his penance was completed, Vajrāṅga remained firm in his self-restraint;
desiring to go to his own wife, he did not find her in his hermitage,
and overcome by hunger, he entered the thicket of the mountain.
While he was looking about to gather fruits and roots, he beheld his beloved wife, miserable and weeping, her face hidden by a tree.
Upon seeing her, the Daitya then spoke, consoling her.
Vajrāṅgī said:
"O blessed lady, by whom was this penance performed while intending to go to the world of Yama?
Or what desire shall I grant you? Speak quickly, O proud one. (39)
Varāṅgī said:
"I have been terrified, cast aside, struck,
and oppressed many times by the fierce King of the Gods, like one who has lost her protector."
Seeing no end to her suffering, she resolved to give up her life.
"Grant me a son who shall deliver me from this great ocean of misery.
Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas had his eyes agitated with grief. 41–42.
Although capable of retaliating against the king of the gods, the mighty great asura resolved once again to practice asceticism;
and Brahmā, perceiving his even more cruel intention, [acted].
He arrived with great haste where the son of Aditi was.
Brahmā said: "O son, for what purpose have you again undertaken this religious observance?"
"Therefore, I shall give you back your desired son by my power.
Vajrāṅga said:
"By your command, I have seen [him] upon rising from my state of meditative absorption."
When Indra had been terrified, she, whose limbs were beautiful, spoke with humility, seeking a son:
"O Grandfather, you are pleased; grant me a son who shall be my deliverer.
Brahmā said:
"Enough of this asceticism, O hero; enter into the difficult-to-cross hardship.
There shall be a son named Tāraka, possessed of great strength, who will cause the loosening of the braided hair of the wives of the gods. (47-48)
Having been addressed thus, the lord of the Daityas bowed to the Great-Grandfather and,
having gone there, gladdened his queen whose heart was distressed. Then that couple, their purpose accomplished, departed for their own hermitage.
Then that woman of excellent limbs and beautiful complexion bore the embryo within her womb for a full thousand years;
at the end of those thousand years, that woman of excellent limbs gave birth.
As that Daitya, who was terrifying to the world, was being born,
the entire earth trembled, the great oceans surged,
the mountains shook, and fearsome winds blew.
Even the best of sages ceased their chanting of prayers, and even the serpents and deer became silent.
When that great asura was born, the luster of the moon and sun vanished and all the quarters were shrouded in mist; likewise, all the other great asuras [were filled with joy].
The Asura women arrived there filled with joy;
overcome with delight, they sang and the throngs of Apsaras danced.
Then, O one of great luster, when that great festival of the Dānavas had begun—
Then the gods, including Indra, became despondent in mind (56).
But seeing the son of Varāṅgī, the lord of the Daityas was then filled with joy; he considered that child born by her to be highly significant (57).
O Lord of Daityas, as soon as he was born, Tāraka, of fierce prowess,
was consecrated by the chief Asuras, such as Kujaṃbha, Mahiṣa, and others,
in the great sovereignty over all the Asuras— an office capable of rivaling the entire earth.
Having attained the great sovereignty, Tāraka, the best of kings and the foremost of the Dānavas, spoke these words full of reason. Tāraka said:
"Listen, all you mighty Asuras, to my words: O Dānavas, the gods are the destroyers of our lineage;
for us, according to the law of our birth, this enmity is firmly rooted and inexhaustible."
"We shall practice austerities for the sake of subduing the gods, relying entirely upon the strength of our own arms; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard that and agreed, they went to the Pāriyātra mountain.
Without food, practicing the five-fire penance, eating leaves, or subsisting on water,
he performed these austerities for a hundred years at a time.
Thus, when his body had been emaciated and he had become a mass of asceticism, (63–64)
Brahmā, having arrived, said to the lord of the Daityas: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon;
let there be no death for you from any being whatsoever.
Then Brahmā said to him: "The death of embodied beings is certain."
"Choose a death from that [source] than which you do not fear.

Then I quickly commanded my ministers: "Let my army be mobilized;
if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, the foremost of the gods must be subdued."
"O Asuras, incomparable joy arises when the arrows are restrained.
Having heard these words of Tāraka, the Dānava named Grasana, the commander-in-chief of the Daitya king, prepared that army. 69–70.
Having struck the deep-sounding drum, he quickly summoned the lords of the Daityas,
ten crores in number, who possessed fierce prowess. Jambha was their leader, followed by Kujambha and the asura Antara.
Mahiṣa, Kuñjara, Megha, Kālanemi, Nimi,
Manthana, Jambhaka, and Śumbha— these ten were the leaders of the Daityas;

Fierce, adorned with variegated armor, earrings, and turbans—

In the meantime, Vāyu, the messenger of the gods, having seen that army of the Dānavas in the abode of the Asuras, went to report it to Indra.
Having gone to the divine assembly hall of the high-souled Mahendra, he reported that matter which had arisen in the midst of the gods. Upon hearing that, the king of the gods closed his eyes.
At that time, the mighty-armed Indra spoke these words to Bṛhaspati:
"This conflict between the gods and the Dānavas has arrived. (83)
"What task is there here? Tell me that, along with the means and methods to accomplish it.

Bṛhaspati said: "O best of gods, for those desiring victory, this is the eternal rule: diplomacy preceded by conciliation, followed by intrigue, and then an army consisting of four divisions. (85)
Conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force constitute the fourfold set of expedients.
The greedy do not come within the scope of conciliation; those who share a common purpose cannot be divided; and those who seize by force cannot be won over by bribery. (86–87)
"If this single expedient of punishment pleases you,
O lords," thus addressed, the Thousand-eyed One replied, "So be it. Having reflected upon what ought to be done, he spoke thus in the assembly of the immortals.
Indra said:
"O inhabitants of heaven, listen with full attention to these words of mine; for you are the enjoyers of the sacrifice, divine beings together with your progeny."
"Those who are eternally established in their own majesty and devoted to the protection of the world—
let preparations for battle be made, let my army be assembled, let weapons be brought forth, and let the deities of the weapons be worshipped. (90-91)

"O lords, O dwellers of heaven, having appointed Yama as your general, quickly prepare the mounts and celestial chariots for me! Having been addressed thus, those who were the foremost among the gods equipped themselves for battle.
In battle, he obtained a chariot yoked with ten thousand horses, adorned with golden bells;
it was endowed with various wonderful qualities, difficult for even the gods and dānavas to conquer, and was driven by Mātali, the charioteer of the king of the gods. 93–94.
Mounting his buffalo, Yama advanced at the head of the army, surrounded on all sides by a fierce host of *kiṃkaras*,
filling the expanse of the sky with flames rising like those at the end of an aeon.
Agni, mounted upon a goat and holding a spear in his hand, stood ready. Pavana, with a goad in his hand, possessed of great speed spread abroad, was there.
And the Lord Jaleśa himself was mounted upon the king of serpents. 96–97.
Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, moving through the sky, stood ready for battle on a chariot yoked with men,
formidable and armed with a sharp sword.
On a chariot drawn by great lions stood the god Kubera, the lord of wealth, bearing a mace as his weapon.
The Moon and the Sun, the two Aśvins, accompanied by their fourfold armies—
these generals of the King of the Gods, who are invincible in the three worlds— and thirty-three crores of the hosts of gods [all came]. 99–100.
Seated upon that elephant named Airāvata— whose beautiful trunk was like a lovely celestial golden lotus as white as the Himalayas,
whose lovely cheeks were adorned with charming streaks of bright saffron like a swarm of playful bees,
and who was arrayed in variegated ornaments and garments— the high-minded one shone resplendent. 101.
Adorned with a vast vajra-canopy, his arms encircled by a circle of serpents and armlets;
his sprout-like feet were saluted by the thousand-eyed Indra, and he shone as the subduer of Pāka in the triple heaven.
And [the city] was graced with white parasols and banners, crowded with throngs of horses, elephants, and noble lineages. 102–103.
Then that army of the invincible infantry became difficult to cross due to the warriors shining with various weapons;
thereafter, the Aśvins, the Maruts, along with the Sādhyas and Purandara, arrived,
holding in their hands various divine missiles, as did the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas.
All those of great strength, having united together, struck the lord of the Daityas;
yet they could not discharge their weapons upon his body, which was like a mountain of adamant.
Then Tāraka, the sovereign of the Dānavas, leaped down from his chariot.
He struck the gods by the millions with his palms and the heels of his feet;
the remaining armies of the gods, terrified, fled in all directions, abandoning their equipment for battle. 107.
Seeing those gods fleeing, Tāraka spoke these words:
"O Daityas, do not slay the gods; bring them quickly to the palace of Vajrāṅga and show them to him. Let him see these gods bound."

Then the Daitya, having bound the world-protectors led by Indra along with the Rudras in battle with very firm nooses— like a cowherd binding his cattle— mounted his chariot together with Bhūti and departed for his own abode.
The summit of the vast mountain resounded with the voices of Siddhas and Gandharvas;
he was being praised by the sons of Aditi and well-served by Apsarases.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Tāraka’s Victory in the Battle between Devas and Asuras," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The forty-third chapter.
Pulastya said:
A doorkeeper appeared, dressed in garments of bright Chinese silk.
Falling to the earth upon his knees and covering his face with his hand,
he spoke words that were unconfused and refined with few syllables to the lord of the Daityas, who possessed a radiant body resembling a multitude of suns.
Having bound the gods, Kālanemi presented them and stood at the gate;
he addressed the assembly of bards, "O Lord, where should we stand?
Hearing those words spoken by the doorkeeper, the Daitya replied:
"Stay as you please; these three worlds are my home.
However, let only Indra be released, having had his head shaved, clothed in white garments, and marked with the footprint of a dog."
Having done this, with their minds agitated by distress, they went to see the Preceptor of the World, the lotus-born Brahmā, as their refuge.
Despairing, they approached him and prostrated themselves upon the earth with their heads.
They praised the Lotus-Seated One with words rich in excellent syllables.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, the primordial source from which the sprout of the syllable *Oṃ* first arose, and from whom the infinite variety of the world’s positions emerged."
To you, the embodiment of *sattva*, who immediately after creation desired the withdrawal [of the world] back into the root of *sattva*—salutations to you!

8. Having reflected upon you as the primordial source of all manifest beings by virtue of your majesty, and having considered this very designation, you brought about the division of the worlds above heaven and earth, as well as those below, from this cosmic egg. 9.
It is evident that Mount Meru was the placenta of you who were thus born; we know this, for the space [of the universe] was fashioned by you.
It is evident, O God, that the gods were born from your body, as were all embodied beings who move within the interior of that body.
Heaven is your head, the moon and sun are your eyes, the serpents are your hair, and the quarters of space are the cavities of your ears. (10)
The limbs are the sacrifice, the rivers are the joints, the feet are the earth, and the oceans are their belly.
You are the magician and the cause, renowned by the Vedas as the peaceful light and the sun;
they reveal you through the meaning of the Vedas with their intellect—you who are the ancient one seated within the lotus of the heart.

Those seven subtle principles, well-expounded by the Sāṃkhyas, which they praise as you and as the Self once they have attained yoga—of those, you alone are the eighth, sung as their cause, and you alone exist within them as the individual soul (jīva). Having seen your form, both gross and subtle, some indeed declare that all states of being are caused by you. 13.
They have arisen from you alone at the beginning of creation; at the end of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they shall return unto you.

Your convention is hidden within you; I am Time (*kāla*), whose calculations and conceptualizations have been destroyed, the cause of the manifestation and dissolution of existence and non-existence; that Infinite One is you, its creator and its repository.
The gross is the source of all misfortune, while that which is other than it is the subtle, which is praised even more highly than those [gross things].

Since the absence of the gross is obscured by them, you are proclaimed as the gross among them in the Purāṇa. You unite every being with prosperity, and within every state of being, you cause that which has been cultivated to flourish.
"Again and again, you cast away [the unmanifest] through its manifestation, and in various places you bring about the activity of manifestation.
Thus the gods, having praised the infinite-formed Lord—the refuge, protector, and guardian of those who possess manifestation—ceased; and they praised Brahmā as well, the cause of all. 17–18.
Then they stood with their minds intent on prayers for the attainment of their desired objects.
Thus praised, Viriñci attained supreme grace;
and the Giver of Boons, pointing with his left hand, spoke to the immortals.
Brahmā said:
"O Śakra, why do you not shine? Why is the lotus of your face withered, like a woman whose husband has died and who has suddenly cast off her ornaments?"
Though deprived of fire, you do not shine with smoke; though long dwelling in a forest consumed by fire and covered by a mass of grass,
you do not shine today, afflicted as you are by this body of Yama.
O Lord of the Night-Rangers, why do you speak as if terrified, having been dragged step by step by him with his staff as a mere pretext,

"Your body is parched by Varuṇa as if you were enveloped by fire; moreover, look at your foot from which the blood has been released—you, O Vāyu, are rendered senseless as if cut by the tips of swords. (24-25)
Why have you abandoned the status of Kubera, the Giver of Wealth, and become humble?
Why, though being Rudras armed with tridents, have you displayed such great cowardice? Tell us, by whom has this extreme ferocity of yours been cast aside? 26.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, who abides in the Brahman, the gods—
because speech is the foremost of their powers— urged on the Wind-god.
Then Pavana was impelled by the gods, headed by Śakra.
He spoke thus to the four-faced god: "You know all that moves and is stationary; yet the gods, headed by Indra, along with their hosts, have been forcibly conquered by hundreds of Daityas.
Sacrifices of most wonderful and marvelous qualities were performed by you for the stability of the worlds."
Furthermore, even those sages who had performed sacrifices and desired the fruits of sacred learning stood before you; indeed,
by the power of your command, the abode of the enjoyers of sacrifice was constantly filled with hosts of celestial chariots, which, when seized by the son of Danu, became like a vast field of battle.
You have made this mountain—the abode of the gods, the limit of the suns, and the king of all mountains—possessing every excellence, adorned with sacrifices, and eternally present even in the sky;
its peaks and slopes are graced by the Danujas who are accustomed to dwelling and sporting there. 32.
With its multitude of hanging jeweled caves, it became a refuge for many daityas;

and out of fear of that asura, it was abandoned—though it had long been the object of enjoyment and the cause of bodies filled with despair—and its faces, the quarters of the sky, were once filled with pure luster. 33–34.
In the first age, the excellent thunderbolt, fashioned by you yourself, was hurled at the host of gods;
having struck the body of the son of Diti, it shattered into a hundred fragments like a small amount of knowledge [when confronted with the vast].
And those whose limbs were pierced in battle by arrows were shown by the gatekeepers of the ocean.
Having gained entry with great difficulty into the assembly of that enemy of the gods, we, O Lord, were forcibly seated by those with canes in hand;
remaining silent, we were thus mocked by others.
"O gods, you who possess great purpose, have accomplished all your aims, and are speakers of few words—speak now that which is consistent with the scriptures;
for this assembly belongs to the lion among Daityas, not to Indra, and is unrestrained. (38)
While the messengers of the Daitya laughed much as they spoke thus,
the Seasons in embodied form attend upon him day and night; yet, when an offense has been committed, they do not abandon him despite his terror in any way whatsoever.
In his mansions, songs accompanied by the melodies of stringed instruments are sung with passion by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
meanwhile, the relative importance of friends and others is determined by the services rendered, whether performed or left undone. 41.
"One who abandons those who have come for refuge and has cast aside the shelter of truth"— thus,
whether exhaustively or otherwise, who is able to describe his lack of discipline? In that matter, the Creator alone is the ultimate authority.
Having spoken thus, Vāyu ceased; then the Blessed One, his lotus-face smiling, addressed the gods regarding the actions of the deities. 44.
Brahmā said:

The Daitya Tāraka was invincible even to all the gods and asuras; indeed, not until this day has a man been born in the three worlds who could slay him. Having gratified him with the granting of a boon, I restrained him.
Now, the king of asceticism consists of the burning of the three worlds.
That Daitya requested his death from [the one who is] a seven-day-old infant;
yet that child, being only seven days old, shall become superior even to Śaṅkara.
