The slayer of Tāraka will appear here, radiant as the sun; meanwhile, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara remains without a wife. And the daughter of Himācala shall become his consort.
From her, a son shall be born like fire from the friction-sticks;
upon obtaining him, Tāraka will cease to exist.
I have explained the means by which this shall indeed come to pass.
"And divide his remaining wealth immediately;
wait for a short time with minds free from fear. Having been addressed thus by the Lotus-born One himself, the gods—
Having prostrated before the Lord, those dwellers of heaven departed as was appropriate for each.
Then, after the gods had gone, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
remembered that goddess who had been his consort in a former birth.
Then the blessed Night approached the Grandfather; beholding her in that secluded place, Brahmā spoke to the goddess of night.
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, a great task for the gods has presented itself during this night; you must perform it. Listen to the determination of what must be done:
there is a lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, an unconquered enemy of the gods."
The Blessed Lord Īśvara will bring about his birth; indeed, that son shall be the end-maker of Tāraka. She who was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, became the wife of Śaṅkara. (56–57)
On account of some other cause, that goddess, the daughter of Himavat and the light of the world, became angry with her father;
and because of separation from her, Hara considered the three worlds to be empty.
In a cave of the Satasrhga Himālaya mountain, frequented by siddhas,
he will dwell for some time awaiting their birth;
from those two who have performed intense penance, a great son shall be born.
She will be the destroyer of the Daitya Tāraka;
and as soon as she was born, that beautiful goddess appeared as if her consciousness were slightly diminished,
intensely longing due to separation and yearning for union with Hara.
The union of those two, who have performed intense austerities, shall bring about auspiciousness.
Then, a slight verbal quarrel will arise between them, and subsequently,
a great doubt regarding Tāraka will be seen.
Therefore, when those two are united for the purpose of sexual union, you must create an obstacle for them; listen to how that shall be done by you.
While he is still in his mother's womb, [you shall do so] in your own form and with your own name.
Then Śarva, laughing at her, will reproach that dejected goddess with a jest; thereupon, becoming angry,
she will depart to perform penance, and then, endowed with the power of asceticism, she will [attain her goal].
He shall procreate that son of immeasurable splendor;
he will undoubtedly become the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
You, too, must slay the Dānavas here, who are difficult for the world to conquer.
"As long as the collection of her virtues has not been transferred to the body of Sureśvarī,
you will not be able to slay the Daityas through union with her;
once this has been done, she will accomplish everything for you after performing penance."
When Devī has completed her observances and has finished speaking,
she will then attain a form identical to yours, O Śailajā; at that time,
Bhavānī shall become united with you.
"O Umā, you shall remain joined with a portion of my form;
O bestower of boons, the world shall worship you as Ekānaṃśā.
You, who pervade all and fulfill every desire, shall be worshipped through various distinctions and manifold forms. (71-72)
You are the Gāyatrī with the syllable Oṃ as her mouth, as proclaimed by the exponents of the Veda; you are possessed of a majestic form, worshipped by kings of mighty arms,
and you are honored as "Bhūḥ," the mother of the Vaiśyas, and as "Śivā" by the Śūdras.
You are the unshakeable patience of the sages, even for those self-restrained by compassion;

you are the discernment regarding the application of great means for those who spread through policy; you are the thorough understanding of all objects, and you are the desire dwelling in the hearts of living beings. 74–75.
You are the liberation of all beings, you are the refuge of all embodied souls;

you are the delight of those with passionate hearts, and you are the joy of those who possess firm bodies. You are the true fame of truthful beings, and you are the peace of those who have performed evil deeds.
You are the delusion of all beings; you are the refuge for those who sacrifice with rituals. You are the great tide of the oceans; you are she who sports with playful grace.
You are the night that bestows the joy of embracing the necks of lovers. 77–78.

Thus, O Goddess, you are worshipped in the world through many forms; those who please you, O Giver of Boons, and those who also honor you, shall surely attain all their desires—of this there is no doubt. (79)
Having been addressed thus, the goddess Niśā, saying "So be it," with palms joined in reverence (80),
departed quickly and swiftly to the great abode of Himavat. There she found her seated in a magnificent palace, resting against walls inlaid with jewels (81).
He beheld her, whose lotus-like face was pale in complexion, slightly emaciated, and bent down by the weight of her breasts rising from her face;
she was attended by the king of mantras bound with clusters of great medicinal herbs. 82.
Delightful with life-guards fashioned from raised gold,
it was illuminated by the great light of the radiance from clusters of jewel-lamps,
and attended by many charming servants scattering white mustard seeds.
It was radiant with pure Chinese silk canopies, couches, and bedspreads, delightful with the fragrance of incense, and equipped with everything necessary for use; then,
as the night gradually advanced far into the day...
In this great mansion, where the anticipation of pleasure was fully manifested,
where men were mostly fast asleep and the attendants were overcome by slumber, and where the moon, appearing clearly, acted as a wandering nocturnal bird; (86–87)
Then, while the courtyards were filled with the movements of night-stalkers and the people engaged in auspicious conversation were locked in firm embraces,
Menā’s two lotus-eyes attained a slight state of agitation.
The night of wondrous union entered her mouth with ease;

then, in due order, it entered the interior of the womb of the Mother of the World to bring about intoxication [of joy]. Thinking, "When indeed will another incomparable birth occur? she remained there.
Having delighted the abode of the Goddess in the mountain cave like the night in the forest,
the beloved of the Himālaya, who is the cause of liberation for the world, gave birth to Guhāraṇi during the auspicious Brāhma-muhūrta. 91.
As she was giving birth, all living beings— both stationary and moving— who dwell in all the worlds, became happy.
Even for those in the hells, there was then a great happiness equal to that of heaven.
The minds of cruel beings became peaceful, and the hearts of embodied beings were tranquil; even the brilliance of the luminaries increased exceedingly at that time.
The medicinal herbs and the fruits dwelling in the forests also became sweet.
The garlands became fragrant, and the sky became stainless; the breeze was pleasant to the touch, and the directions were most enchanting.
The fruits produced by the seasons shone with the excellence of their ripeness through the power of yoga. 95–96.
The earth became adorned with rows of rice,
and the long-practiced austerities of the sages of purified souls attained fruition there in the course of time. 97.
Forgotten scriptures reappeared, and at that time, the power of the foremost holy places became most meritorious;
and in the sky, gods by the thousands were present in celestial chariots. 98–99.
Led by Samahendra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Agni,
they released a shower of flowers upon that snowy mountain;
the chief Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
And the great mountains, Meru and the others, having taken on physical forms, were present;
when that great festival had arrived, the divine oceans and rivers came from all directions with their hands outstretched. 101–102.
Then that best of mountains, white as snow, became worthy of service, approachable, and a refuge for all beings, both mobile and immobile in the world;
having experienced this festival, the gods then returned to their own abodes.
Then, by the hosts of gods, lords of nāgas, gandharvas, and playful mountain maidens,
the goddess Himavat’s daughter was brought before me in a competitive rush; subsequently,
she was gradually made to understand through the diligent efforts of wise scholars.
Gradually, through her beauty, grace, and awakening,
she became endowed with all auspicious marks, just like the daughter of Himālaya;
meanwhile, Śakra addressed Nārada, who is honored by the gods.
Then, intent on accomplishing the task, he called to mind the celestial sage (Narada).
Having understood Indra's desire,
the blessed one then arrived at Mahendra’s abode, filled with joy.
Seeing him, the thousand-eyed Vāsava rose from his great throne and honored him with water for the feet as was appropriate.
Having accepted the worship offered by Śakra according to the prescribed rites, [the sage...]
Nārada inquired after the welfare of the god Pākaśāsana.
When his welfare had been asked, the lord Śakra spoke these words.
Indra said:

O Sage, the sprout of virtue has indeed flourished throughout the three worlds; yet, although I already know the perfection of its resulting fruit, you have been questioned by me because you yourself will surely come to know it all. (111–112)

"Let all those on our side quickly exert themselves so that the purpose may be communicated to our friends and they attain supreme bliss— just as the goddess born of the mountain attained union with the wielder of the Pināka bow. (113)
Having understood the entire matter, the venerable Nārada then took his leave and quickly went to the abode on the Himālaya mountains;
there, O best of Brahmins, he arrived at the gate crowded with variegated cane-staffs.
Having been saluted by the Himālaya mountain as he emerged, the sage entered the palace together with him, which had become an ornament of the earth;
and when the vast golden [palace] had been personally presented by the Himālaya, [he sat down].

The mountain offered to that great sage, the best of munis, who sat there with incomparable splendor, the guest-water and water for the feet as was fitting; the sage then accepted that guest-water according to the prescribed rite.

Having accepted the water-offering (arghya), the best of sages was questioned by the Mountain with gentle words; with his lotus-face slowly blossoming, the Mountain inquired after the welfare of his asceticism.
The sage, in turn, then asked the king of mountains about his well-being.
Nārada said:
"O great mountain, oh, this settlement of yours is worthy of your righteousness! O sinless one, the multitude of your caves is equal to the vastness of your mind."
The weight of your multitude of virtues exceeds that of the mountains;
and as for your clarity, O Lord of Mountains, we do not perceive where any lack of discipline resides in you, surpassing even that of the sages. 122

You are eternally purified by various sages who dwell in mountain caves—sages whose splendor is equal to fire and the sun, and who are sanctifiers themselves; they have cast aside celestial chariots, being indifferent to dwelling in heaven. 123.

Even while dwelling in his father’s house, the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras [praised him]. "O Lord of Mountains, how fortunate you are! For Hara, the Lord of the World, intent on meditation, dwells within your cave. 124-125.
When the celestial sage Nārada had spoken thus with respect, Aṅgiras,
followed by Menā, the queen of the Snowy Mountain, who desired to see the sage,
accompanied by her daughter and a small retinue of female attendants, [departed].
With her body bowed low in modesty, she entered the dwelling where the self-controlled and excellent sage sat together with Śaila.
Then, seeing that sage, a mass of splendor, the beloved of Śaila—

Beholding that illustrious lady, who stood with her lotus-like hands folded in salutation before her concealed face, the celestial sage of immeasurable luster honored her with blessings that were like the outpouring of nectar. 129.

Then, her heart filled with wonder, the daughter of the Himavat mountain beheld the divine sage Nārada of wondrous form; and she was addressed by the ṛṣi with affectionate words: "Come here, child! (130–131)
Taking her father by the neck, she sat upon his lap;
he said to her mother, "O daughter, salute this goddess,
for you shall obtain as your husband this blessed lord, rich in asceticism and highly esteemed."
Having been addressed thus, her face then covered by her garment,
she spoke no word at all, her head slightly trembling;
thereupon the mother again spoke these words to her daughter.

"O child, I shall give you that auspicious and beautiful jewel toy which was long ago kept by me; go now to the divine seer Vatsa. Having been addressed thus, she then rose up with speed and [fell at] his feet.

Having joined her lotus-bud hands at her head, she offered salutation. When that salutation was completed, her mother, through the mouth of a female friend, gently urged her to display her auspicious beauty.
Out of curiosity to understand the characteristics of the body,
and out of a woman's nature, he bore deep concern for his daughter in his heart; and the Mountain King, having understood that gesture with his heart, [spoke].
Perceiving that this [opportunity] had arrived in its unmanifest form, the illustrious Nārada, the best of sages, was then urged by the friend of the mountain’s queen;
with a smiling face, he spoke these words. (139–140)

"O blessed lady, her husband is not yet born; he will be devoid of auspicious marks, with palms always turned upward and feet that wander astray. She will possess a beautiful complexion—what more need be said?"
Having heard this, Himavat, overcome with agitation and his composure shattered,
the great mountain, his throat choked with tears, then replied to Nārada.
Himavat said:
Since the course of this world, which is fraught with extreme defects, is difficult to comprehend;
therefore, this [world] of transmigrating beings exists, established within fixed boundaries, created by some extraordinary agent through the process of inevitable creation. (143–144)

It is evident that whatever fruit is produced from a seed accomplishes the purpose of the progenitor, yet there is no one who produces the one already born; thus, the various classes of beings are born solely through their own karma. 145.

An egg-born being is born from an egg-born one; furthermore, a human may be born again as a human. Even among humans, one is born into a superior caste through the excellence of one's dharma. (146–147)
All living beings remain subject to the remainder of birth without a son; among them, human beings are even more so, for they share the same dharma as Naya. 148.
Following the vow of the student (brahmacārin), there is the gradual attainment of the stages of life (āśrama).
By the decree of that Creator, by whom this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) was expanded—(149)—if everyone were to become homeless, there would be no arising of the cycle of existence;
for in the scriptures, the Creator has always praised the attainment of a son. (150)

For the purpose of deluding living beings and as a means of protection from hell, the creation of creatures devoid of women would not be possible. Indeed, the female species is by its very nature wretched and subject to misery. (151)
Because of their capacity for scrutinizing the scriptures, the authors [of those works] have been refuted;
otherwise, the Creator would not have intended for them to attain a superior state.
This has been stated clearly and repeatedly in the scriptures as being of great fruit. (152–153)

Even a maiden who possesses ten sons may be devoid of virtuous conduct; such speech is fruitless for men and brings about the result of exhaustion. For a daughter is indeed wretched and pitiable, increasing the sorrow of her father.
Even she who is endowed with a husband and sons fulfilling all her desires would be [unhappy];
how much more so one who is unfortunate and deprived of husband, sons, wealth, and the like? Furthermore, you have described this collection of defects in the body of a woman. (155–156)
"Alas, O Nārada, I am bewildered, parched, exhausted, and sinking; I am fainting.
Even that which is improper must be spoken, and even that which is currently unattainable must be sought. O Sage, out of compassion, sever this sorrow rooted in my daughter."

Even when [the matter] is determined and beyond doubt, because of the mind's susceptibility to humiliation, and again because of the attachment to the desire for rewards, thirst remains deeply immersed;
for indeed, the supreme birth of women—those who possess both natures—is dependent upon both [lineage and reward]. 158–159.
That which is known as "attaining a virtuous husband" has been declared for the sake of happiness in this world and the next;

for because a virtuous man is difficult to find, it is said that even a husband devoid of qualities cannot be obtained by women without merit. (160) A husband is never obtained by a woman except through her own spiritual merits.
Since dharma is the means of accomplishment, there is delight arising from its transformation;
for noble women, wealth is established in their husband until the end of life.
One who is without wealth is foul-mouthed, foolish, and devoid of all auspicious marks.
"O noble lady, it has always been said that the husband is the supreme deity for a woman; yet you, a celestial sage, have declared that no husband was ever born for her.
This is an incomparable, countless, and unbearable misfortune."

O Sage, having heard that Sanatkumāra was born during the creation of moving and unmoving beings— which is difficult to comprehend and all-pervading— my mind has become agitated by this report concerning the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of the human and divine races. (164–165)
"O bull among sages, it is said that the characteristic [of a woman] was ordained by her hands and feet; thus she was described by you as 'one with upturned hands' (uttānahastā).
That which is called 'upturned-handedness' is indeed that very state which is constant. (166)

"Your feet were described by you as having beautiful soles and as never failing to grant boons to the fortunate who offer gifts; yet even in that regard, no hope for better fortune appears to me through this [present state]. (167–168)
"Furthermore, there are others characterized by bodily marks that indicate various distinct fruits.
Having spoken thus, while the Mountain, who contemplates great sorrow, remained silent, Nārada, honored by the gods, said this with a smile:
Nārada said:
"O great mountain, you speak of sorrow when there is actually a great occasion for joy; with your meaning not fully discerned, you fall into delusion. (170)

Listen to these words of mine, established in secrecy. O Great Mountain, you who have been addressed by me with focused attention, you have not become the husband of this goddess, as I have indeed declared, O Himavat. (171-172)
Mahādeva, the source of the past, the future, and the present,
the refuge, the eternal, the teacher, the benefactor, the supreme lord—
[even] Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the sages are afflicted by birth from a womb, old age, and decay. (173)
O Mountain, all these are but playthings for that Supreme Lord.
By His will, the Lord of the worlds was born from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
O Supporter of the Earth, there is no destruction of the Self even at the end of the stationary world.

For the embodied being born and dying within saṃsāra, it is only the body that perishes here; the destruction of the self is not spoken of. This saṃsāra, which is proclaimed to extend from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects, [is thus characterized].

Afflicted by the suffering of birth and death, he indeed rolls about incessantly. Mahādeva, the immovable Sthāṇu, who was unborn, the progenitor, and ageless, shall become his protector; he is the Lord of the Universe, free from all ailment.
And as for what was said by me, "O Goddess, you are devoid of auspicious marks"—listen now to a thorough investigation of those words.
For an auspicious mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is indeed a divine sign residing in the limbs of the body. (179)
O Mountain, although it reveals the ultimate outcome of life, wealth,
and fortune, the form of the mark of infinite and immeasurable fortune is not actually fashioned upon the body. 180–181.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, there is no mark on her body resembling a mountain;
and as for what I have said regarding her hands always being turned upward—this hand of the Goddess is forever in the boon-granting (varada) gesture, with the palm facing upwards. 182.
"She shall become the bestower of boons upon the hosts of gods, asuras, and sages.
(183) "O best of mountains, listen from me to the explanation of what I have said regarding her feet, which possess a beautiful, unchanging luster. (184)
Her two lotus-like feet were clear and radiant with bright nails;
they cast a beautiful luster as they were reflected by the multicolored rays of the jewels in the crowns of the gods and asuras bowing before her. (185)
O Mountain, this wife of the Lord of the World, whose emblem is the bull, is the mother of all the universe; she has come into being as the source of all that exists and will exist.
This auspicious one, possessing purifying luster, has appeared in your sacred field for the sake of purification.
O best of mountain lords, O Himavat, you must arrange this according to the prescribed rites in such a way that she may quickly enter into union with the wielder of the Pināka bow;
for there is a great task of the gods to be accomplished here.
Having thus heard everything from Nārada, the lord of mountains, the husband of Menā,
then considered himself as if born again;
and Himācala, filled with joy, spoke further to Nārada.
O Lord, I have been rescued by you from that terrible, impassable hell;
having been lifted up from Pātāla, I have been made the sovereign of the seven worlds. O best of sages, I am now renowned as Himācala by you.
"O great sage, I have attained a height of elevation a hundredfold greater than that of the Himalayas. Out of sheer joy, my heart has been carried away;
it no longer deliberates upon the distinctions or the analysis of duties."
O Sage, for those like you, a sight [of you] is inevitably fruitful;
indeed, it was by you yourselves that this was declared as a dwelling place for those who possess your own nature.
I myself am the purifier of the sins of sages and deities.
"Nevertheless, let the command be granted regarding one single matter.
When the Lord of Mountains had spoken thus, Nārada, overflowing with joy, replied to him: "O Lord, everything has been accomplished. 195-196.
"This very same purpose is of even greater importance for you as well in the work of protection.
Having said this, Nārada then quickly departed for the third heaven.
Having gone there, he beheld Mahendra in the abode of the gods.
Then, having sat upon a great throne befitting him,
the Sage was questioned by Śakra and spoke a narrative centered on the Daughter of the Mountain.
Nārada said:
"Whatever was commanded to me has indeed been performed by me;
however, the range of the five-arrowed god's arrows is still required.
Thus was the King of the Gods addressed by the sage who perceives what must be done. 199–200.
The Lord Pākaśāsana (Indra) remembered the mango sprout as his weapon;
thus remembered, it was quickly hurled by the wise thousand-eyed one. Then the fish-bannered god (Kāma), accompanied by Rati, appeared with all his charm.
Seeing him manifested, Śakra spoke to Manmatha.
Śakra said:
"O beloved of Rati, what is the use of much instruction for you?"
"O Manobhava, you know the thoughts within the hearts of all beings;
therefore, O Mind-born One, quickly unite Śaṅkara with the Daughter of the Mountain in such a way that it brings joy to the inhabitants of heaven. (203-204)

"Joined with this honey, go accompanied by Rati"—thus was Madana addressed by Śakra for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. Then the five-arrowed one, being afraid, spoke these words to Śatakratu: 205. "The five-arrowed one, being afraid, spoke these words to Śatakratu."
Kāma said:
"O Lord of the World, do you not know that the god Śaṅkara is difficult to overcome even by this entire assembly, which strikes fear into both sages and dānavas?"
You alone know that cause, the imperishable state of that god;
for generally, whether in favor or in anger, everything belonging to the great is truly great.
Indeed, this celestial beauty, the essence of all enjoyments, has arisen from heaven.
Hearing these words from those who desired a distinction and feared a fall from their status due to the commonality of their fruit, Śakra, accompanied by the immortals, spoke to him.
Śakra said:
"We ourselves are the authority in this matter; there is no doubt that you will find delight there.
However, the capacity of a blacksmith to work with tongs is not expected to exist everywhere. (210) The efficacy of a particular thing is observed in certain instances, but not universally.

Thus addressed, Kāma, accompanied by his friend Madhu, set out; filled with passion, he quickly went to the plateau of the snowy mountain. Having reached it, he reflected upon the means for accomplishing his purpose.
For great-souled ones are indeed unshakable; their mind is difficult to conquer.
Therefore, by first agitating it in this manner, victory over it will be achieved. Furthermore, perfection generally comes to one whose mind has been previously purified.
How can there be such states of being without the pursuit of hatred?
Anger arises from the most cruel attachment; Envy is its terrifying great companion;
and through fickleness, it possesses great strength that destroys the very foundation of fortitude.
Having first closed the doors of my fortitude and drawn away my contentment, I shall not employ this tamasic modification of the mind before me;
for indeed, no wise man here would seek to understand me in that state.
Having entered Virūpākṣa, who is born of the mind and consists of nothing but conceptual construction,
I shall then begin my activity; I will become the one who is difficult to overcome due to the deep whirlpools [of passion] for the sake of Hara, who is established in austerity with a steady soul.
Having thus reflected upon the abode of his lord— a place where the village of the senses is restrained and where the means of pleasure are prepared— Madana then went to that hermitage,
the essence of the world, which possessed platforms made of straight trees.
It was crowded with peaceful beings, motionless, and teeming with living creatures; it possessed networks of various flowering creepers, with the Lord of the Gaṇas situated upon its ridges;
it resounded with the cries of calm bulls, and its slopes were covered with dark-green grass.
There he beheld a certain second companion of the Three-eyed Lord,
Vīraka, the master of the world of heroes, whose splendor was like that of Īśāna;
his mass of matted hair was tawny, like a cluster of filaments from ripe saffron.
He held a cane in his hand, was unperturbed, formidable, and adorned with inauspicious ornaments (223). Then [he saw him] with eyes like lotus petals, half-closed yet wide-awake,
gazing straight ahead at the tip of the bridge of his nose (224).
He has for his upper garment the skin of a most beautiful lordly lion;
he is tawny with the fire of the breath exhaled from the hoods of the serpents on his ears; and the mass of his matted locks hangs down, kissing the edges of his quivering cheeks.

Kāma, having gradually approached his presence, slowly beheld Śaṅkara, whose navel was encircled by the serpent Vāsuki coiled at its base, and who wore the ornaments of serpents fixed upon the tip of his nose while his hands were joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
Then, taking hold of the humming of the bees that followed the trees, the god of love entered the mind of Bhava through the cavity of his ear.
Then Śaṅkara, having heard that sweet sound which had its source in Madana—
With a mind intent on dalliance, he remembered his beloved, the daughter of Dakṣa.
Then, through the power of his meditative absorption, the exceedingly pure Śivā gradually became invisible, yet remained perceptible in a form that was directly manifest to his senses.
Then, having become absorbed in that [state] with his heart obscured by obstacles, the Lord of the Gods entered into a transformation consisting of passion.
Overcome by a slight anger, Dhūrjaṭi resorted to fortitude.
Having cast aside his intoxication and remained there enveloped by his yogic power (yogamāyā), Madana was then possessed by that very māyā and blazed up;
he is the one whose body is will, who is difficult to comprehend, the abode of defects, yet possessed of great resolve.
Then, having emerged from his heart, he whose nature consists of the addiction to latent impressions (vāsanā),
the one who bears the fish-banner (Kāma), reached the external realm and stood before him,
followed by his friend Madhu.
Seeing a cluster of blossoms on a mango tree gently shaken by a mild breeze,
the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) quickly released an arrow named Mohana, which was as beautiful as the chest of Śiva.
Then, with a pure heart, the lofty and harsh great arrow named "Fame" fell upon Śatānīka; it was the bewildering flower-arrow of the God of Love.
Thereafter, when the multitude of his faculties had been pierced in the heart, Bhava [the Lord] appeared.
Though his fortitude was unshakable and he was free from worldly illusions, he became intent upon passion (238).
Then, due to the power of those states of being, he perceived his own possession [by them] and spoke many words consisting of obstacles (239).

Then, from the fierce *huṃkāra* born of the fire of his wrath, a third eye, filled with flames and terrifying, appeared upon the face of Rudra, whose form was fierce and as formidable as the destruction of the world. (240)
Then, standing near him, Dhūrjaṭi unleashed [his power];
by a spark from his eye, while the inhabitants of heaven cried out, Kandarpa—the one who inflames desire—was swiftly reduced to ashes. 241–242.
Having reduced Satī to ashes, the fire born from the eye of Hara expanded,
eager to consume the world, knowing him to be a devourer by his very *huṃ* sound.
Then Bhava, for the sake of the world, divided that fire (*jātavedas*).
In the mango tree, in wine, in the moon, in flowers, in others as well, in bees, and in the mouth of the cuckoo—by means of these distinctions, he pierced the fire of love;
and Hara, both externally and internally, was pierced by the arrows of Smara. 244–245.
Distributed among these various factions, it appears as a great devourer;
divided, it causes the agitation of the world, its expansion being difficult to restrain.
Indeed, it dwells in the heart of one whose desire is filled with the longing for its attainment.

Burning day and night, he fell under the power of terrible suffering. 247. Beholding Smara reduced to ashes by the flame of Hara’s *huṃkāra*, Rati lamented piteously along with her cruel kinsman [Madana]. 248.
Then, having lamented much and now being consoled by her attendants, she went for refuge to the three-eyed God who bears the moon upon his crest;
she took hold of a flowering mango branch followed by bees.

Let her bind her mass of matted hair with her curling locks, and let her smear her body with the charming, white ashes of Smara, which have been produced from the leaves of creepers and trees and are the friend of cuckoos. 250–251.
Falling to the ground on her knees, Rati spoke to the one adorned by the moon:
Rati said: "Salutations to Śiva, who consists of the mind, who pervades the universe; salutations to you whose path is wondrous! (252)
Salutations to Śiva, who is worshipped by the gods, who is ever intent on compassion for his devotees;
salutations to Bhava, the source of worldly existence; salutations to you, the destroyer of Manobhava (the god of love). 253.
Salutations to you, the refuge of Māyā and Madana; salutations to him who is adorned by innate purity.
Salutations to the immeasurable one, the abode of infinite virtues; salutations to the perfected one, the ancient one.
(254) Salutations to the refuge, salutations to the possessor of qualities; salutations to you who are followed by the formidable hosts.
Salutations to the creator of prosperity for the various worlds; salutations to the bestower of the desires of devotees. (255)
Homage to you, whose power is born of action; homage always to you of infinite forms! Homage always to you of irresistible wrath; homage to you who bear the mark of the moon! 256.
Homage to you, whose supreme sport is boundless, who ride upon the king of bulls, and who are the destroyer of the cities!

Homage to the one renowned as the Great Medicine; homage to the one whose form is manifold. Homage to Time; homage to the Artificer; homage to you who transcend both time and its parts. To the Preceptor of the moving and the unmoving, the most excellent object of contemplation, the Teacher who envisioned the creation of all beings. 257–258.
"O Maheśa, I have suddenly sought refuge in You, whose crest is the moon, for the sake of attaining my beloved;

grant me the fulfillment of my sole desire for glory and the husband himself. Without him, O Blessed One, I shall not live. O Lord of Men, what other man in these worlds is as eternally dear to a woman as he is? (259)

The Lord, the powerful, the source of all, the beloved of those who love Him, the skillful, the scorcher of enemies, the one beyond the cycle of birth and death— You alone are the Protector and Guardian of the world, the compassionate one who has uprooted the fear of Your devotees.
Thus praised by Śaṅkara, the bull-bannered Vṛṣākapi, the beloved of Manmatha, [departed].
The bearer of the crescent moon was pleased; looking at her, Śaṅkara spoke these sweet words:
"And this desire shall be fulfilled after a long time, at the end of the age. (262)
"Thus, O Anaṅga, you shall attain great renown throughout the worlds.
Having spoken thus, the beloved of Kāma paid homage to the Lord of the Mountains with her head and departed for another grove on the snowy mountain.
She wept many times, distressed at every step,
until her resolve for death was turned back by the command of Śiva;
then, urged by the words of Nārada, the Himālaya mountain [prepared].

Then the Mountain, having taken his daughter— who had been adorned with ornaments, for whom auspicious marriage rites had been performed, who wore a crest of celestial flowers, and was clothed in garments of white Chinese silk— together with her two female companions, [departed].
Then, his heart’s desire fulfilled, he proceeded through that auspicious region;
having approached the forests, groves, and pleasure gardens, he beheld a woman of inconceivable and great splendor who was weeping. 267–268.
In human form, moved by curiosity as he beheld her weeping upon those lovely mountain slopes in this world,
the Mountain approached her side and questioned her.
Himavat said:
"O auspicious daughter of Kaśika, for what reason do you weep? O beauty of the world, I do not consider this cause to be a trivial one."
Having heard the words of Sātasya, Rati, weeping and sighing, spoke these sorrowful words that increased her wretchedness:
Rati said: [271]
"O you of virtuous vows, know me to be Rati, the beloved wife of Kāma.
And on this mountain, the Lord Giriśa is established in penance;
by him, becoming enraged, the obstacle was created as he opened his eyes in anger. (272–273)
Having escaped the blazing flame of the fire's crest, I was reduced to nothing but ashes;
yet, overwhelmed by fear, I sought refuge in that God and offered praise. Then, being well-pleased, Giriśa spoke to me:

I am pleased; O beloved of desire, the fulfillment of your wish shall come to pass. Furthermore, the man who, taking refuge in me, recites this hymn of praise to you with devotion, shall obtain his desired object even at the point of death.

"O one of great luster, awaiting his words and driven by the force of hope, I shall preserve my body for some time. When she had spoken thus, the mountain, terrifying with agitation, [remained] with Rati.
Desiring to go to her own city by taking him by the hand,
Bhavitrī— whose future was destined to happen because of the inevitability of what was to come— felt ashamed and spoke to her father Giri through the faces of her friends. (278–279)
The Daughter of the Mountain said:
"What is the purpose of this unfortunate body of mine? And how might my husband Śaṅkara come to that same state? (280)
Through austerities, one's desired goal is attained; indeed, nothing is unattainable for one who practices penance, even if misfortune prevails in the world when a means has been undertaken.
Thus, having abandoned all doubt regarding austerity, he acted out of a desire to achieve his own purpose.
To his daughter, who had spoken thus, saying, "I shall perform such penance here," Himavān,
the lord of mountains, spoke with words whose sounds and syllables were faltering.
Himavān said:

"O son of gentle appearance, your body is not capable of enduring the hardships of asceticism that correspond to such fickleness. Furthermore, O one of pleasant looks, there will always be other duties and worldly affairs to attend to. (283-284)
For many destined things come to pass even against one's will;
therefore, O child, there is no purpose whatsoever served by asceticism. I shall go to my own home and reflect upon this matter there.
When the daughter of the Mountain, having been told this, did not follow him home, the Mountain was overcome with anxiety and praised his own daughter; then,
a divine voice arose in the sky throughout the three worlds.
"O daughter, because you have spoken of this fickleness (*umeticāpalam*) to your son, she shall be known by the name Uma throughout the worlds. She,
being success itself personified, will accomplish whatever is desired."
Having heard these words, Śaila then took leave of his daughter in the midst of the sky and quickly departed for his own abode.
Pulastya said:
The daughter of the mountain also went to the mountain, though inaccessible even to the gods;
followed by her two friends, she, the daughter of the king of mountains,
reached the holy peak of Himavat, adorned with various minerals.
It was strewn with divine flowering creepers, its trees resounded with the humming of bees,
endowed with celestial springs, and radiant with hundreds of fulfilled desires;
it was filled with various birds and graced by ruddy geese.
It was adorned with the holy blossoms of both aquatic and terrestrial plants; it concealed wonderful caves, was endowed with celestial dwellings,
resounded with the cries of flocks of birds, and was densely crowded with wish-fulfilling trees.
There he saw a great-branched tree with green foliage, endowed with flowers of all seasons and graced by ruddy geese;
it was strewn with hundreds of various blossoms and possessed many kinds of fruits. (295)
There, having cast off her garments and ornaments— which were like the rays of the sun breaking apart and rejoining the petals of a lotus—
the daughter of the mountain was clothed in divine bark-garments and wore a girdle made of darbha grass. (296–297)
For a hundred autumns she remained bathing three times a day and subsisting on *pāṭala* flowers; then, for another hundred years, she sustained herself with a single withered leaf.
She remained without food for a hundred years, a treasury of asceticism.
Then all living beings were distressed by the fire of his asceticism.
Thereupon, the Lord Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, remembered the seven sages;
they arrived and were all likewise delighted.
Having been honored by Mahendra, they asked him about his purpose:
"O best of gods, for what reason have we been summoned by you?
Śakra replied, "Listen, O venerable ones, to my purpose."
On the Himalaya mountain, the daughter of the Mountain King performs a terrible penance;
for her sake, and for the welfare of the world, you ought to complete your own austerities with haste through union with her who is dear to you. (302–303)
Having said "So be it," the sages then approached that mountain frequented by hosts of Siddhas and spoke to her in sweet-sounding words:
"O lotus-eyed one, what resolve has your heart set upon?"
Then the Goddess spoke to those sages with respect and gravity. The Goddess said:
"O highly fortunate ones, performing penance, you who are like [the sages] should abandon your silence."

Appointed for the purpose of paying homage, you should request [the teacher] without hesitation. Having first taken seats with very serene faces and having sat down, you should then ask him after he has relieved his fatigue. (306–307)
Having been addressed thus, they then took their seats there; and she, having first honored them according to the rules and the prescribed rites,
slowly spoke to the seven sages, those ṛṣis who were radiant like the sun.
Having abandoned her vow of silence and having bowed according to the rules to the sages,
the seven ṛṣis— those venerable ones— then questioned her once more in that same manner, for she had become a vessel of their respect at the conclusion of her silence.
She too, with a mind full of reverence and a beautiful smile, looked at all the sages and, restraining her speech,
spoke: "O Blessed Ones, you know what is desired in the minds of living beings."
Indeed, embodied beings are excessively tormented by their bodies and other such things.
Yet, some who are skillful apply themselves there with various efforts;
through these means, they, being untiring, attain states that are otherwise difficult to reach.

Others, however, having discerned various forms of practice, undertake an exertion for the sake of another body; they resort to that vow adorned with a garland of flowers produced from the sky through the sense of "mine-ness. 314.
Desiring to touch the peak of the Vindhya, her hand repeatedly reaches out.
Indeed, I am intent on attaining the Lord as my husband, who is by his very nature difficult to propitiate and is currently engaged in ascetic penance. (315-316)
Neither gods nor asuras have determined the ultimate reality that is the basis of all action; even now, Madana has been utterly consumed by the one who is free from passion.
How could someone like me hope to propitiate such a Śiva, the Lord?
Having been addressed thus, those sages, their minds having attained steadiness, then spoke in order to understand her words, beginning with the subject at hand. The sages said:
"O daughter, two kinds of happiness are perceived in this world:
the union with this body and the tranquility of the mind.
But by nature he is clad in rags, fearsome, and adorned with ashes and bones. (319-320)
Carrying a skull-bowl, a mendicant, naked, with distorted eyes, unstable in his actions,
having the appearance of one intoxicated or insane, loathsome, and a collector of refuse; he has no purpose other than his master who is bowed down, and he is sought after by embodied misfortune.
If you desire eternal happiness for your own body, how then can you [find it] from Mahādeva, who partakes of living beings, who is loathsome,
and whose ornaments are made of skulls and bones dripping with human fat and marrow?

To him who dwells in the cremation ground, who is adorned with ornaments made from the lordly serpents hissing with fury, who is fierce and followed by the Pramathas— even to him, the slayer of enemies, whose feet are rubbed by the multitude of crowns of the lords of the gods. 324.
Hari exists as the sustainer of the world, the beloved of Śrī, possessing infinite forms; 325.
likewise, there exists the Lord of Sacrifices who is to be recited [in prayer], as well as Indra, the ruler who wields the thunderbolt;
there exists the treasure of the deities, and the Fire-god, the granter of all desires. 326.
There is Vāyu, the sustainer of the world; there is Prāṇa, the life-breath of all embodied beings;
and likewise there is King Vaiśravaṇa, the lord whose majesty consists of all wealth.
Why do you not wish to obtain any one of these?
"Furthermore, whatever other happiness desired by the mind is unattainable here, all that shall be yours—
just so, O daughter, through the power of these worldly riches, for the sake of your attaining auspiciousness in this body or even in the next. (328-329)

Everything that was offered to the gods belongs only to the father; even the hardship endured for the sake of obtaining a bridegroom has become fruitless in this matter. For generally, when a request is made, a capable person is exceedingly difficult to find.
"Because she is assigned to her own place, she is obtained even here as a daughter," so having spoken thus to the excellent sages, the daughter of the mountain,
her eyes red with anger and her lips quivering, spoke.
The Goddess said:
What is the remedy for a false obsession? Where is the restraint for calamity? By what means can those who perceive things in a contrary way be established on the path of the virtuous? (333)

Thus should you know me—one of poor discernment, fond of base and false attachments, and full of egoistic pride; yet for me, there is no further deliberation needed, for you all are like Prajāpati and possessers of all-encompassing vision. (334)
Surely, that God is vast, eternal, the Lord of the world, unborn, sovereign, unmanifest, and the source of immeasurable majesty;
let his true nature as action remain for now, while his consciousness is still veiled.

Even the lords of the gods, headed by Brahmā and Hari, do not know that power of his which arises from himself and expands throughout the worlds; even though it is manifest to all beings, do you not know it as well? 337.
To whom does this sky belong? To whom belongs the form [of the sun]? To whom belongs fire, and to whom the wind?
(338) To whom belongs the earth, and to whom Varuṇa? And to whom do the gods and asuras in the worlds devotedly worship the liṅga, he whose eyes are the moon and the sun? (339)
And as for Brahmā, Īśvara, the gods, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the great sages—
do you not know even their power or their origin?
For the gods, Nārāyaṇa and the others, were born from Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and Aditi was the daughter of Dakṣa. Both Marīci and Dakṣa were indeed the sons of Brahmā;
and Brahmā himself arose from the golden egg, possessing the power of the perfected ones (siddhas).
From whose meditation did the Prākṛta and the Prākṛtāṃśaka manifest? Then, by the very will of Nārāyaṇa himself,
impelled by Him, he entered that birth which was of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
That [action] is also said to belong solely to the deed itself for those whose minds are rendered helpless by the impulse [of karma].
Just as the very mind of one afflicted by madness or similar conditions becomes violent, he perceives even desired objects as indeed contrary [to his will]. (344–345)
"Always laugh at the worldly transactions that are observed;
know Viṣṇu alone as the one who brings about the attainment of the fruits of dharma and adharma.
O sages, thus did I repeatedly utter these words in the presence of the Lord of the Mountain and the Vedas.
Just as farmers on the surface of the earth sow a handful of good seed in excellent fields to obtain a bountiful harvest,

so too those who were renowned as masters of speech, having heard that beneficial and delightful discourse concerning the successive stages of practice, spoke with smiles of beauty upon their faces. (347–348)
The sages said:

"Once the creation of the world has been accomplished, that task is indeed supreme; for the most part, it is a cause for apprehension on the part of the Snowy Mountain, who at that time assumes a form [of a threat]. (349)

It is true that the hearts of all those who are eager and striving for the sake of their duty are in haste; yet, what need is there to mention such great souls? The course of worldly affairs must especially be attended to by those who intend to speak with distinction.
"Since that [Veda] is the source of all dharmas, its authority is upheld by others.
Having said this, the sages departed quickly for the Snowy Mountain (Himalaya).
There, they were honored with great respect by that Lord of the Snow Mountains.
The best of sages, being pleased yet filled with haste, spoke briefly;
the sages said:
"O Goddess, the wielder of the Pināka bow himself seeks you as his daughter."
Therefore, quickly purify yourself by offering yourself as an oblation into the fire;
for that which must be done for the sake of the gods will endure for a very long time.
This effort must be undertaken for the purpose of uplifting the world.
Thus addressed, the mountain, overcome by a surge of joy, became unable to speak a reply as if seeking their permission; then Menā, overwhelmed with affection, spoke to the venerable sages.
Mena herself spoke these meaningful words to her daughter and to those sages:
"I desire that purpose for which the birth of a daughter is sought, even though it is of great fruit."

All that has now presented itself at the proper time through this very process; even for a suitor who is endowed with noble birth, youth, beauty, and power, one's daughter must not be given if he does not ask for her. (358)
"How indeed can he—who is naked, matted-haired, and armed with a trident; who has burnt away desire yet bestows desire;
and who is terrible even to the son of Satī—be worshipped? Thus spoke the sages.
O gods and asuras, understand the sovereignty of Śaṅkara;
with the pair of his lotus-feet being worshipped, they are perfectly at peace.
Whatever form is required for a particular purpose, that very form is long prayed for by him.
"That child, performing terrible penance and delighted by that form,
shall bring those divine vows to their completion; therefore,
remain attentive here, for it will happen right before us."

Having spoken thus, they went together with the Mountain to where the Daughter of the Mountain resides—Umā, who is composed of splendor, whose heat surpasses the flames of the sun and fire, and who is indeed so described by the sages. To that proud woman, he spoke these affectionate and meaningful words: 363–364.

"I do not desire anything from any petty person, except for Śarva, the wielder of the Pināka bow; for he stands as the bestower of supreme prosperity upon all living beings according to their relative gradations, and his courage, sovereignty, deeds, and immeasurable greatness are beyond compare. (365)

I have gone for refuge to Him from whom nothing else exists, and by whom all that proceeds; He whose sovereignty is without beginning or end, who is impartial, resolute, and long-sighted, yet appears otherwise [to the ignorant]. 366–367.
Having heard these words of the goddess, the best of sages,
their eyes filled with tears of joy, then embraced that ascetic woman;
and being exceedingly delighted, they spoke sweet words to the daughter of the mountain.
The sages said:
O daughter, you who are like a stainless embodiment of knowledge, most wonderful and great, you inspire our devotion by taking refuge in the nature of worldly existence. 369.
"Indeed, we do not know the wonderful sovereignty of that god; we have come here to test the firmness of your resolve.
O slender-limbed one, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled before long."
Just as the sun possesses its own radiance distinct from the luster of gems, what meaning can there be for one who has abandoned his own qualities, other than Giriśa? Thus,
by various means, we have sought to entreat him.
This very purpose dwells even more deeply within our hearts as well.
Therefore, you alone are that wisdom, for you alone are indeed policy;
thus, Śaṅkara will undoubtedly bring this task to fruition.
Having spoken thus, all the sages, honored by the Daughter of the Mountain, departed to see Giriśa at the great plateau of the Himavat;
their bodies were bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, and their tawny matted locks were tied in tufts.
With garlands of mandāra flowers held in their hands and followed by bees,
they reached the mountain plateau and beheld Śaṅkara’s hermitage,
where the entire multitude of living beings was profoundly peaceful and the forest was completely still.
There they saw Vīraka at the gate, holding a cane, as he moved through the waters which flowed silently and without agitation in every direction.
Then those venerable sages, being humble out of respect for the gravity of the matter, [approached him].
Those best among the eloquent spoke these words with sweet speech:
"We have come here to see Śaṅkara, the leader of virtues and the three-eyed one; know us to be impelled by the task of the gods. (379-380)
"O Lord, you alone are the one who knows the way; let there be no transgression of the proper time. This request is generally made through the medium of a doorkeeper.
Having been addressed thus by the sages, he then spoke to them out of respect.
"Having gone to the Mandākinī to perform the evening twilight ritual of the sacrifice, O Brahmins,
you shall see the wielder of the trident (Śūlin) in a moment.
Having been told this, the sages, experts in their duties, remained there with diligence.
Just as thirsty cātaka birds [hasten] toward a deep cloud in the rainy season, so too [they approached] him who, in an instant, had completed the ritual procedures of his conduct,
who was seated in the vīrāsana posture, and who was clad in a deer skin.
Then Vīraka, having joyfully knelt down and supported himself upon the earth, spoke with singular devotion to the Lord:
"The seven sages have arrived to behold you, O God of blazing splendor. (385-386)
"O Vibhoṣaṇa, command them to see [me]; then you should practice meditation here.
Having been addressed thus by the great-souled Vīraka, Dhūrjaṭi then gave the order for their entrance with a sign of his knitted brows.
Shaking his head, the great sage Vīrakopa summoned those seven sages,
who were standing nearby, to behold the wielder of the Pināka bow; they quickly tied up their matted locks and donned their flowing black garments.
Then,

having offered handfuls of celestial flowers from heaven with their palms joined together, the inhabitants of the celestial realm entered the divine pavilion of the Lord, the Master of the Mountains, and paid homage to the pair of feet of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then, having been gazed upon affectionately by the wielder of the trident,
those sages, beholding Girīśa, praised him with equal joy. The sages said:
"Ah! Are we now truly ones who have accomplished their purpose, whose sprout-like feet are worshipped by the lords of the gods?
We behold you, who possess the increase of the weight of virtues; please command us regarding the task of protecting all beings without exception.
Then, laughing, the Omniscient One spoke these words to the best of sages:
"Now perform whatever task is in your hearts.
Having been addressed thus, the sages quickly went to where the daughter of the mountain was; those who knew the divisions of time spoke to Girijā in the mountain cave.
"Through your asceticism, you have attained a form that is beautiful, beloved, and captivating;
Śaṅkara is pleased with you and will accept your hand in marriage. We have come here first to request this from your father. (395-396)
"Go home with your father; we shall go to our own abode.
Having been told this, she reflected, "The fruit of asceticism truly exists," and in great haste, she went to her father's divine and beautifully adorned palace.
There, Satī considered that night to be equal to ten thousand years;
meanwhile, O Himādri, intense longing arose in her at the thought of beholding Hara.
Then, at the moment of Brahmā’s day, her friends performed the customary rites for her.

In that most auspicious palace, filled with a multitude of divine blessings, the personified Seasons— gratifiers of all desires— worshipped the Mountain in his embodied form according to the proper sequence of various auspicious rites. 400.
The winds were pleasant during the process of sweeping the mountain;
in the palaces, the Goddess Śrī herself performed various adornments, while Kānti was present in all states of being and Ṛddhi was busy with the task of providing raiment.

The Cintāmaṇi and other jewels approached the mountain from all sides, as did the creepers and great trees such as the Kalpavṛkṣa; and the medicinal herbs, endowed with divine medicines, appeared there in embodied form.
The tastes and the bodily constituents were all servants of that mountain;
the servants of that mountain remained busy dwelling within the hermitage,
as did all the rivers, the oceans, and everything both stationary and moving.
All of them— sages, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras— increased the majesty of Mount Himavat;
even the gods did so for Śaṅkara on Mount Gandhamādana.

Adorned with their collections of ornaments and possessing spotless forms, they stood there. Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), his eyes wide open with noble affection, bound the crescent moon upon the matted locks of Śarva.
Binding a vast garland of skulls upon her head, Kālī said to Giriśa, "O Śaṅkara, beget a son who,
having destroyed the lineage of the lords of the Daityas, shall satiate me with their blood."
Taking the jewel from his ear-ornament, a brilliant necklace,
and a serpent-ornament, Śauri stood ready before Śambhu. Śakra, for his part, presented him with an elephant hide whose fringes were smeared with fat.
The bull, whose broad lotus-face was perspiring with intense exertion,
shone like the sharp peak of the snowy mountain; the winds blew fiercely,
and they adorned that bull, the vehicle of Hari, which was as swift as thought.
The sun, fire, and moon shone within the corners of Śambhu’s eyes;
they bestowed their own luster upon the skull-bowl of the Lord of the World, the witness of the universe’s deeds,
which possessed the radiance of silver mingled with funeral ashes.
The Lord of the Pretas, holding a garland made of human bones in his hand, stood nearby in fear; meanwhile,
Kubera brought various ornaments of great jewels of diverse forms.
Leaving aside his own hand, which was like a circle of blazing lordly serpents,
the Lord himself made the stainless Takṣaka an ear-ornament;
and having completed the ornament, he adorned the Lord with various decorations.
There too, acting without restraint and with bodies full of eagerness, she released all manner of new, delightful trees and medicinal herbs;
yet the Goddess Earth remained distracted by her own nature, which is charming in every way.
Varuṇa himself, having taken various jewels, rich ornaments,
and diverse flowers made of many kinds of gems, stood there adorned with those ornaments— the omniscient god of all embodied beings.
And Jvalana, being self-restrained, presented divine golden ornaments and purifying vessels of refined gold; Vayu blew with a fragrant scent and a pleasant touch toward the Lord.
And the glorious Śatakratu, adorned with the thunderbolt, joyfully took up with his arms the parasol, resplendent as the rays of the moon, and the great smile; meanwhile,
the chief Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang most sweetly while playing their instruments; for a moment, the Seasons themselves sang and danced there,
and the restless hosts stood about, shaking the Himālaya mountain.
Seated in due order, the Creator, the maker of the universe and destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
performed the marriage rites with his wife as prescribed;
he was offered the *arghya* by the King of Mountains and entertained by the hosts of gods.
Then the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), together with his wife who had dwelt there for the duration of the night, was awakened by the songs of the Gandharvas, the dances of the Apsarases,
and the hymns of the gods and Daityas— the Lord of the Immortals.
Having taken leave of the lord of snowy mountains, at dawn he went with his wife to Mount Mandara on the bull-bearer whose speed is like that of the wind.
Then, when the Blessed One Nīlalohita had departed along with Umā, the mountain experienced delight.
For whose mind in this world is there no kinsman? Indeed, for a maiden, it is her father’s lovely palace gardens and secluded forests.
With a heart deeply enamored of the Goddess, the Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes abandoned her.

Then, after a long time had passed, the daughter of the Mountain, accompanied by her friends, played with artificial dolls under the name of "son. Once, the daughter of the Mountain anointed her body with scented oil.

She massaged her body, which was filled with impurity, with powders; taking that powder for the massage, she made a man with the face of an elephant. Playing with that man, the goddess then threw him into the water.
Then, due to his friendship with the auspicious Jāhnavī, he became possessed of a vast body; with that exceedingly expansive form, he filled the world at that time.
The Goddess said to him, "O son," and Jāhnavī also said, "O son."
Gajānana was worshipped by the gods, including Gāṅgeya and others,
and his grandfather bestowed upon him the lordship over the Vināyakas. Then that woman of excellent complexion again began to play, creating a tree.
The lady of beautiful countenance caused that lovely sprout of the *aśoka* tree,
which had already grown and been consecrated with auspicious rites by the brahmins headed by Bṛhaspati— the domestic priests of the Lord of Heaven— to flourish further.
Then the gods and sages spoke these words to the Goddess:
"Now that the path has been shown, you ought to establish the boundaries [of conduct].
O Goddess, what fruit will come from these trees fashioned as sons?"
Having been addressed thus, her limbs filled with joy, she spoke these most auspicious words:
"The wise man who causes a single well to be constructed in a waterless village shall dwell for a year in heaven for every drop of water [provided]. (440-441)
Ten wells are equal to a large pond; ten ponds are equal to a lake;
ten lakes are equal to a maiden; and ten maidens are equal to a tree.
This is indeed the auspicious, established order of things that governs the world.
Having been addressed thus, the brahmins, led by Bṛhaspati, then departed for their own homes after having paid homage to Bhavānī, the Mother.
When they had gone, Lord Śaṅkara [addressed] the Daughter of the Mountain.
Being supported by his hand, he reached his own residence— a palace with pavilions, watchtowers, and gateways that inspired serenity in the mind,
adorned with hanging strings of pearls, and featuring courtyards filled with garlands.
The pleasure-palace was fashioned from refined gold, held within the mind;
it resounded with the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of scattered flowers, and its walls were concealed by the sounds of the singing and music of Kinnaras. (446–447)

A gateway with crystal pillars, adorned by flocks of swans, where a mass of fragrant incense was imperceptibly wafted toward the mind, and where playful peahens were hurriedly presented from all sides. 448.
449–450. There, in that place which was untroubled and free from confusion, though crowded with many kinnaras, walls made of rubies were seen by parrots;
because of their innate confusion, they mistook them for pearls reflected [upon the surface].

There, on a clear ground as dark-blue as Indra’s sapphire, the Lord began to sport with his beloved using dice; established there, they played, their bodies serving as their own assistants, immersed in the bliss of the pleasure of the game. 451.
While Śiva and the Goddess were thus sporting there, a great sound suddenly arose, reaching the very limits of the sky. Hearing it, the Goddess asked Śiva out of curiosity, "What is this? (452–453)

Filled with wonder, he questioned the best of gods, Hara; and the god said: "O lady of pure smiles, this has never been seen by you before. These lords of the Gaṇas, who are always dear to me, are playing upon this mountain."

O lady of auspicious countenance, those best of men by whom I was formerly propitiated through austerity, celibacy, [sacred] names, and the service of sacred fields— they have now arrived in my presence; they are not pleasing to me.

Possessing great enthusiasm for the forms they desire and endowed with the qualities of magnificent beauty, those powerful ones cause wonder by their deeds; they are capable of the creation and destruction of this world through their state of equanimity. 457.
O delightful one, though I am constantly attended by Brahmās, Candra, Indra, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas, I am never separated from these who sport upon the mountain,
their every limb beautiful and heart-pleasing.
When this was said, the goddess, overwhelmed with wonder, left him and,
having reached a window, gazed out with a startled face.
As many as there were— lean, tall, short, stout, or pot-bellied— [she beheld them all].
Some had the faces of tigers and elephants, while others had the forms of rams and goats;
they possessed the forms of various creatures, with flaming mouths, dark-brown in color, both gentle and terrifying, with smiling faces and perpetually dark-brown matted locks. 461–462.

Some had faces like various birds, others had faces like various gods; some were dressed in silk or skins, while others were naked or deformed; some had ears like cows or elephants, and many possessed multiple mouths, eyes, and bellies.
With many feet and many arms, their hands holding various divine weapons; wearing diverse flower-garlands and appearing agitated and terrifying;
bearing various types of armaments and adorned with various kinds of armor.

Having seen those lords of the Gaṇas— possessing divine forms, moving through the sky mounted on various vehicles, resounding with the sound of lutes and musical instruments, and dancing in various postures— the Goddess spoke to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:
"How many are the Gaṇeśas enumerated? What are their names and what is their nature? O Maheśvara, tell me of each one individually, as they are established separately."
Śaṅkara said:
"Countless crores of beings, renowned for their various heroic deeds— these terrifying ones of great strength— have filled the entire world."
In sacred sites of accomplishment, on streets, in ruined gardens, and in houses; in the bodies of Dānavas, among children, and among the insane—
these [beings] enter with joy, partaking of various foods and diversions.
They were drinkers of heat, drinkers of foam, drinkers of smoke, and drinkers of honey;
they fed on fat, drank blood, ate all things, and were even without food;
they were devourers of gods, consumers of ascetics' provisions, and delighted in various musical instruments and pleasures.
"Indeed, it is not possible to describe their hosts individually because of their infinity.
The Goddess said:
"Clad in an elephant hide as an upper garment, with pure limbs and a girdle of muñja grass,"
With his face colored by a paste of red arsenic,
he was of sweet appearance, wearing garlands of blue lotuses bitten by bees;
he played cymbals made of overturned fragments of stone and bell-metal.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, what is the name of this deity who is followed by Kinnaras and who repeatedly lends his ear to the songs of the Gaṇas?
Śarva said:
O Goddess, this very Vīraka is always dear to my heart;
he is the repository of various wonderful qualities and is worshipped by the hosts of Gaṇeśvaras. (476) The Goddess said:
"O Destroyer of Cities, I have such longing for a son like this;
when shall I behold such a son who bestows joy?
Śarva said:

"O slender-waisted one, this very son of yours is the bringer of joy to your eyes; indeed, Vīraka has already fulfilled his purpose through you, O mother. Having said this, she sent off Vijayā, who was eager with joy.
In order to bring Vīraka, the daughter of the mountain descended in haste from her palace that touched the heavens, accompanied by her friend; she beheld Gaṇapa,
who stood in the midst of his host and radiated the brilliance of ten million suns.
Vijayā said:
"Come! By your heroic impetuosity, the Goddess has been propitiated;
she calls for you. Thus addressed, he abandoned the fragment of stone. 481
Accompanied by Vijayā, he slowly approached the presence of the Goddess,
his luster resembling a full-blown red lotus atop a palace spire;
seeing him, she whose breasts were like vast oceans of sweet milk set forth.
Girijā said:
"O child, drink this milk that has been drawn; drink as much as you desire.
Thus the goddess spoke with affection in words of sweet syllables.
"Behold, this son born to me this very instant, Vīraka, has now been given to me by the God of gods.
Having spoken thus, she placed him on her lap and embraced him; the joyful mother kissed him on the cheeks.
Smelling his head, she stroked his limbs and adorned him with divine ornaments herself.
With girdles of tinkling bells, anklets, and armlets and necklaces set with excellent jewels; with priceless virtues,
tender sprouts, and beautiful, auspicious bracelets born of divine mantras— then,
with many pure white mustard seeds mixed together, he performed the rite of personal protection for him.

Having thus taken up his staff and placed a garland upon his head, radiant with streaks of yellow pigment (gorocanā), he wandered slowly through Vraja— careful to avoid its pits— playing with the calves and their keepers;
he passed by mountain peaks and trees thick with swarms of serpents, whose branches had been broken by elephants and which were trembling violently.
Do not enter the region of the Ganges, where the waters are agitated and troubled, like a forest infested with many tigers;
for even a person of pure mind, when dwelling in difficult circumstances as numerous as the years of one's life due to the state of being a son of a hero,
attains what was desired and auspicious, and in the future reaches a state of excellence, having been perfected by all virtues.
Thus addressed, Nayāvirāja, his mind possessed by the power of playfulness, spoke to his mother with a smile:
"O Mother, this bracelet has been made for me by you yourself, decorated with leaf-patterns and painted with pale-red dots;
and this soft garland of lovely *mālatī* flowers has been placed upon my head by you. (490–491)

Thinking with haste, "I shall please the Goddess," Vīraka, filled with joy and accompanied by his own attendants, went outside to play. Moving from the south to the west, from the west to the north, and from the north to the east, he approached; then, from within a window, he beheld Vīraka surrounded by countless [attendants].

He who, out of affection for the world, plays outside with the daughters of the mountains and is greedy for a son, falls into delusion; he is a fool, a mere carrier of a body that is a heap of flesh, feces, and urine, who cannot see the inner chamber when the moon-crested Lord has entered the dwellings of the gods. 493–494.
As they were thus mounting their vehicles, the multitude of weapons belonging to the world-protectors vanished in an instant.

"This swordless, stainless Kṛntaka—tell us, by whom has he been taken? (495) "It could not have been done by the staff-like arms of the gods; what more can we say? O Mountain, there is no task for the host of those with terrifying forms."
"This is a noose; by this, who here shall be bound? O guardians of the world, do not stay here in vain!

(496) "It is even so," they replied. Then, seeing Vīraka, the protector and follower of the gods, the lords of beings spoke to him at the entrance of the sacrificial hall on the ground of the mountain forest, in the presence of the immortals. (497)
Whether plunging into the falling waters of mountain torrents, or within dwellings entwined with clusters of flowers,
or while entering the deep bowers of lofty mountains, or voluntarily seeking protection from the buffeting of the winds;
on the ground at the foot of high golden peaks, his luster became tawny from contact with the masses of golden dust.
In the delightful forests of the sky-dwellers and forest-dwellers, there was a host of beings endowed with beautiful forms who resided there;
and in the caves of Mount Mandara, upon the charming banks of ponds filled with kunda, mandāra, coral, and lotus flowers,
the nectar of their beauty was drunk by the wives of the Siddhas with wide, unblinking eyes.
Desirous of her son and seeking diversion, she remembered Vīraka, Śailaputrī, and Nimeṣa within the blink of an eye;

for he too had attained such a rise of merit at that very moment, since in another birth he would become her own son. How could satisfaction arise for him as he played, even though he was created by the Creator with a splendor like that of clarified butter?

The moment of beholding [the Lord] fallen from the *kalpa* tree; the moment of divine songs; the moment of activity by the hosts of Gaṇas eager for dance; (502) the moment of seeing the great *sāla* and *tāla* trees amidst the blazing clusters of jewels on Mount Gaṇḍaśaila, which resounds with the roar of lions; the moment of seeing the rows of bees upon the various blossoming *tamāla* trees; and the moment of seeing the swaying bees at the roots of the trees. (503)
In a small lotus pond, he whose eyes are like lotuses plays happily on his mother’s lap—free from all blemish, his gaze fixed upon the auspicious one.
Spreading out in the play of a child, the Lord of Ganesha brings joy to the gods.
In the groves, his character is celebrated in song by the Vidyadharas; the wielder of the Pinaka bow sports with playful grace.
When the sun had moved to another region, illuminating the world with its rays,
the mountain situated far away appeared as if it were manifesting a very firm friendship for him within its heart.
The glorious son of Vighanas, though constantly propitiated by the Brahmins, did not provide assistance to the Sun as he was about to fall;
for it is heard that among people this is the established rule: that which has fallen flows downward.
The sun, followed by the day, completely filled his own kin;
meanwhile, the sages, with their palms joined in reverence toward the sun at twilight, quickly withdrew from their seats, overcome by the heat.
Then, in this world, the darkness of night gradually expanded, corrupting the minds of men like the turbidity within the heart of a crooked person;
meanwhile, the walls were illuminated by the lamps of jewels upon the hoods of hissing serpents. 510.
Upon a couch covered with a canopy of various jewels and fine fabrics, shimmering with the brilliance of diverse gems that mocked the rainbow of Indra,
and adorned with a network of tinkling bells and clusters of glistening pearls; 511–512.
On Mount Mandara, whose sky was covered by the lovely, swaying canopy of its playful creepers,
he stood together with the Daughter of the Mountain, moving slowly as she moved, his neck entwined with her vine-like arms.
The moon-crested Lord, whose range of vision was filled by the expansive white moonlight,
and Girijā, whose dark-cornered eyes possessed the luster of blue lotus petals,
appeared exceedingly radiant as they were joined together like the night and the moon.
Then the God spoke to her, who was engaged in the arts of playful sport.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Gaurī’s Marriage," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Four.
Śarva said:
"O slender-limbed one, though you possess a white complexion and white luster,
you appear like a black female serpent clinging to a sandalwood tree that is not white."
"O Moon-like one, joined with Tapana (the Sun), clothed in garments of blood, like the night during the dark fortnight, you cause a defect in my vision.
Having been addressed thus by him, the Daughter of the Mountain spoke to the wielder of the Pināka bow with a loud voice.
With eyes reddened by anger and a face distorted by a frown, she spoke.
The Goddess said:
"Every person is overcome by the dullness resulting from their own actions."
O Moon-Adorned One, one who seeks [you] will inevitably meet with rejection. Since I have sought you through long-practiced austerities, this humiliation is surely destined for me at every step.
I am not crooked like Śarva, nor am I as treacherous as Dhūrjaṭi;
you, however, are known in the world as one who possesses poison and is a refuge for a mine of manifest faults.
For you indeed parch the teeth and are the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes.
"The Lord Āditya, who consists of twelve forms, knows you; yet, by your own faults, you produce a thorn in my head while reviling me. You who call me 'Kṛṣṇa' are yourself renowned as Mahākāla."
"I shall go to the mountain to abandon my life through asceticism, for I have been humiliated by a wretch—
a vile Kāpālika who dwells constantly in cremation grounds. (9)
Having heard his words, which were sharp with anger, Hara— his body smeared with ashes, moving in the midst of the Mothers,
and his moon-crested head trembling— spoke, agitated by the prospect of the undesirable.
Śarva said:
"O daughter of the mountain, I am not intent on censuring you;
rather, under the impression that these were flattering words, I resorted to madness."

If this conceptualization occurs in my mind while it is in its natural state, O Daughter of the Mountain, then if you become angry in this way, I shall never again be afraid of you. O lady of pure smiles, I shall speak only in jest; abandon your anger.
With his head bowed low, he has offered this salutation with joined palms to me.
Indeed, a man who is base and treated with contempt should not undergo such agitation; for it is said that even when his vital spots are touched, a virtuous person does not react like the wicked.
Though the Goddess was entreated with many conciliatory words by the Lord,
she did not abandon her intense anger, for she had been struck at her most sensitive point. Then, the garment held fast by Śaṅkara’s hand was torn away.
Due to the force of her disheveled hair, the daughter of the mountain wished to depart;
as she was going away in anger, the Destroyer of Cities spoke to her again:
"Truly, with all your limbs you bear a resemblance to your father."
His mind was as entangled in a web as the peak of the Himalayas;
likewise, his disposition was more difficult to fathom than the depths of dense forests.
His hardness surpassed that of stone, and his physical stature exceeded that of the great trees in the woods. 19.
"O slender-limbed one, crookedness has been transferred from the rivers and unapproachability even from the snowy mountain; all this has come from the Himavat.
Having been addressed thus, the daughter of the mountain spoke again to the Lord of the Mountain.
With her head trembling in anger and her lips quivering, Umā said:
"By the forceful disparagement of one who possesses virtues, all [of his] merits would be lost. (22)
Indeed, through contact with you who are corrupt, everything has been transferred [to us]:
from the serpents, our multi-tonguedness; from the ashes, our lack of oiliness; from the moon, the turbidity of our hearts; and even from poison, our invincibility. (23)
