Moreover, what is the use of saying more? Enough of this exertion of speech for you.

(24) You have no fear because of your dwelling in the cremation ground; you have no shame because of your nakedness; you have no compassion because of your skull-bowl; and long ago your mercy vanished. (25)
Having spoken thus, she emerged from that temple; as the daughter of the Himālaya was departing with the goddesses of the gods, a tumultuous clamor was raised by her attendants.
"Where are you going, mother? they cried, and running after her, they wept.
Having planted his two feet firmly, the heroic Vīraka, his voice choked with tears, said: "O Mother, what is this? Where are you going, so distressed and angry?
I shall follow you as you depart, devoid of affection. (27-28)
"If not, I shall fall from the peak of this mountain, abandoned by you. Raising her face with her right hand, the goddess said to Vīraka, "O son, do not grieve."
"It is not right for you, my son, to fall from the mountain peak, nor to go away with me. Listen to the purpose for which I am going:
having been addressed as 'Kṛṣṇa' by Hara, I have been paralyzed and insulted."
"I shall perform such penance that I may attain the state of Gaurī. This god is addicted to women; once I have departed, you must constantly guard the door and watch for any vulnerabilities. (32)
"Just as no woman would enter there into the presence of Hara (33), even if you see another woman, O my son, drink [this] poison;
I shall immediately perform what is appropriate thereafter. (34)
"So be it," Vīraka said to the Queen of the Gods at that moment;
his limbs bathed in the nectar of his mother’s command, his fever gone,
he prostrated before his mother and went to see the protection.
The goddess saw her mother’s friend approaching,
adorned and named Kusumāmodinī, the presiding deity of that mountain;
she too, upon seeing the daughter of the mountain, had a mind overwhelmed with affection.
"O daughter, where are you going? the goddess said aloud, embracing her;
she then related to her everything regarding the cause of Śaṅkara’s anger.
Furthermore, the daughter of the mountain spoke again to the goddess, who was like a mother to her.
Uma said:
"O blameless one, you are eternally the presiding deity of the king of mountains;
you are present everywhere, exceedingly affectionate toward him even with your mind."
Therefore, O Ambikā, I shall tell you what must be performed by you:
you must guard against the entry of other women with great effort, and on the mountain, you must constantly practice the secret rites with diligence. 40–41.
"O sinless one, you must tell Pinākin when she has entered;
then I shall thereafter do what is appropriate.
Having been addressed thus, that auspicious woman said "So be it" and went to the mountain.
Then Umā, the daughter of the Mountain, entered her father’s wonderful garden;
having entered the sky, which was obscured by the luster of rows of clouds,
she cast off her ornaments and donned the bark garments of a tree-dweller.

Scorched by the five fires in the summer and dwelling in the water during the rainy season, subsisting on forest fare or fasting entirely, she lay upon a parched earthen platform; thus she remained established there, performing her penance. 45.
In the meantime, the powerful Daitya, the son of Andhaka, having learned that the daughter of the Mountain had arrived, was filled with joy;
remembering the slaughter of his father, he, fierce in battle, conquered all the gods and seized his brother Jambuka. 46-47.

The enemy of the gods, named Āḍi, who was constantly seeking another opportunity against the moon-crested Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, arrived at the city of that slayer of Tripura. Having arrived there, he saw Vīraka stationed at the gate.
Having reflected thus, a boon was granted by the lotus-born Brahmā.
When the Daitya Andhaka had indeed been slain by Giriśa, the enemy of the asuras,
Āḍi performed a vast and most formidable penance.
Having arrived, Brahmā, gratified by his ascetic penance, said:
"O best of Dānavas, what do you desire to obtain through your penance? The Daitya replied to Brahmā: "I choose immortality."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Daityas, for those born here in this saṃsāra, death is inevitable;
therefore, O Lord of Daityas, death must be encountered by all embodied beings."
Thus addressed, the lion among Daityas spoke to the Lotus-born One:
"O Lotus-born One, if my form were to undergo a transformation, then death would come to me; otherwise, I am indeed immortal."
Having been addressed thus, the Lotus-born One then spoke, pleased:
"When you undergo a transformation into a second form, then death shall come to you; otherwise, it shall not happen."
Thus addressed by Amaratāman, the exceedingly powerful son of the Daitya then remembered the means for his own destruction; at that moment,
he came into the range of Vīraka’s vision.
Having avoided Gaṇeśa’s trunk, which was formidable, fierce, and difficult to conquer, he entered the path of vision through a hole in the form of a serpent.
Unobserved by Gaṇeśa, he then entered another body.
Then, casting off his serpent form, the great asura, his mind deluded, assumed the form of Umā in order to delight Giriśa;
he created an illusory form that was inconceivable and enchanting. 59–60.
Having fashioned a firm, adamantine weapon with all its parts complete, augmented by all supernatural powers, and sharp-pointed, the Daitya,
through delusion of intellect, prepared to slay Giriśa by thrusting it into his private parts.
Having assumed the form and appearance of Umā, the Daitya went into the presence of Hara.
Wicked yet possessing a beautiful form, he was adorned with variegated ornaments and garments.
Seeing him, Giriśa was pleased and embraced that great Asura.
Thinking that the daughter of the mountain was perfect in all her limbs,
he asked the daughter of the mountain about her genuine goodness:
"O lady of excellent complexion, you have arrived here having understood my inner intention."
"Deprived of you, my abode and the three worlds are empty; O one of gracious countenance, such a state as this has come upon you is truly improper.
Thus addressed, the lord of the Dānavas spoke these words with a slow smile.
Having recognized the Destroyer of Tripura through his supernormal powers, the Daitya said:
"O Lord, out of desire for ascetic merit, I have gone to the Himālaya mountain to obtain a boon. (67)
"Rati has become distressed by this; therefore, she has come into your presence.
Having been addressed thus, Śaṅkara felt a certain apprehension in his mind and, reflecting upon it, the Lord composed himself within his heart with a smiling face.

Having understood whether she was angry or not, and knowing her to be firm in her vows by nature, Hara—pondering what this might mean and reflecting on her token of recognition—thought thus: "She has not attained her desire, yet she has arrived; how can she be so aware of this? (69–70)
Then the god who wields the Pināka bow did not see that mark of a lotus on his left side, which was formed by the curling of his body hair; thereupon,
realizing it was the illusion of a Dānava, he concealed his true form.
Taking up his penis as a fang-weapon, he struck the Dānava with darkness;
yet the heroic gatekeeper did not perceive that occurrence,
for he saw the lord of the Dānavas in the form of a woman fragrant with the scent of flowers.
Awakened by the messenger Māruta,
the daughter of the snowy mountain heard from the mouth of Vāyu; her eyes turbid with the redness of anger, the goddess beheld her son Vīraka with a grieving heart.
The Goddess said:
"Since you have taken this opportunity for secret union with Śaṅkara, having abandoned me, your mother, who am overwhelmed by affection. (75)
Therefore, this stone mother, devoid of human qualities— harsh, dull, and lacking a heart— will become like the form of Gaṇeśa;
this is the well-known omen of Vīraka’s devotion toward his daughter.
In the context of their origin and the sequence of events, there was doubt regarding the various accounts;
immediately after the daughter of the mountain had thus cast off her curse,
a mighty wrath in the form of a lion emerged from her mouth.
A lion among men, with a neck matted by a mane, his tail raised aloft, his cavernous mouth formidable with fangs, his jaws agape and tongue lolling,
he was emaciated in his belly and limbs.

Then, knowing her mental resolve, the four-faced Lord, the Goddess, remained determined to turn away from him; having understood what was in her mind, the four-faced Lord arrived at the hermitage, which is the refuge of all prosperity.
Having approached, the Lord of Gods spoke to Girijā in clear speech.
Brahmā said: "What do you desire to obtain? What unattainable thing shall I give to you?"
"Desist from this asceticism, which causes such extreme suffering, at my command.
Hearing that, Girijā spoke words constrained by respect for her father-in-law—
words whose desired syllables were released with great effort from her throat.
The Goddess said:
"My husband Śaṅkara was obtained by me through difficult penance; yet he has repeatedly spoken to me in private, saying, 'O dark-complexioned one, you are equal to me. (85)
"Therefore, from this one who has the color of molten gold and whose name is joined with his own,
let there arise from one side of her body a serpent that is free from poison for her husband, the Lord of Beings.
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World replied:
And thus, she became the companion walking by half the body of her husband once more.
Then he cast off that Kṛṣṇā, whose skin was like a blooming blue lotus;
and she too became Bhīmā, three-eyed and holding a bell in her hand.

Then Brahmā spoke to that goddess, who was adorned with various ornaments and wore yellow silk, and who possessed the luster of a blue lotus: "O daughter of the Mountain, by my command, you shall [become] night through contact with his body. 89.
"O you who have attained the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, you shall dwell in the city of Ekānaṃśā.
O fair-faced goddess, this lion that has emerged from the wrath of the Goddess—let him be your vehicle, O goddess, and let him be your banner, for he is possessed of great strength. (90–91)
"Go to the Vindhya mountain; there you shall perform the work of the gods.
This yakṣa named Pañcāla, who has a retinue of a hundred thousand yakṣas, has been given to you as a servant, O Goddess, along with hundreds of my māyās. 92.

Having spoken thus, the goddess Kauśikī departed for the Vindhya mountain. Umā too, her purpose accomplished, went into the presence of Giriśa; but as she was entering, he, being composed, drew her away from the doorway.
Vīraka, holding a golden cane, blocked the goddess;
with great anger, he spoke to her as if she were an adulteress:
"There is no purpose for you here; go before you are devoured."
The Daitya, assuming the form of the Goddess, had come to deceive the Lord;
he entered but was not seen, and was slain by the Lord.
Once he was killed, I was commanded by the enraged Nīlakaṇṭha: "96–97" [This is part of the verse numbering in the source].
"However, because I observe this lack of attention on your part at the gate,
you shall not be my doorkeeper for many successive years;
therefore, I will grant you entrance here— go quickly!"
"Except for the daughter of the mountain, my mother, who is affectionate out of love—
O lotus-eyed one, no other woman shall obtain entrance," having spoken thus, the goddess then reflected in her mind.
Neither the woman nor the Daitya spoke; Vāyu then said to me:
"Vīraka was cursed by me in vain while I was overcome with anger.
Generally, fools who are possessed by anger commit improper acts. (101)
Through anger, one's reputation is destroyed; anger is the slayer of established prosperity.
(102) Having failed to discern the true nature of reality, I have cursed my own son; for those whose intellects perceive things perversely, the arrival of calamity is easy to obtain. (103)
Having reflected thus, the Daughter of the Mountain spoke these words to Vīraka with a face possessing the luster of a lotus, yet manifesting the agitation of modesty. (104) The Goddess said:
"O hero, you are my mother; do not let your mind be deluded.
I am the beloved son of Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Snowy Mountain. O son, do not entertain the suspicion that arises from the confusion regarding the complexion of my body. (105)
When the Lotus-born [Brahmā] was pleased, he granted me immeasurable radiance.
However, you were cursed by me once the events orchestrated by the Daitya were unknown to you; for you entered the woman while Śaṅkara remained in private. (106–107)
"The curse cannot be revoked; however, I tell you this:
you shall soon return from the human state, endowed with all your desires. Then, with his heart's wish fulfilled, he bowed his head to his mother.
Vīraka said to the virtuous daughter of the snowy mountain, who possessed the luster of the full moon:
"O You whose toenails are formidable with the radiance of the finest jewels shimmering on the crowns of the prostrating gods and asuras!"

O Daughter of the Mountain, who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge like a mother to her child; who destroy the suffering of those bowed down in forest fires; whose neck is adorned by the orb of the sun; who steal the splendor of the vast golden mountain—terrified by your formidable and uneven gait, I take refuge in you. 110–111.
O Goddess who grants desires unasked for and bestows instantaneous success upon the world,

I bow to you just as the moon-crested Lord Śiva, the sustainer of the universe, and the sages bow to you; O you who are difficult to conquer due to your pure yoga, and who possess a body like that of your son, you are the sovereign of the circle of great lords.
You, who crushed the host of Andhaka’s kinsmen, were first praised by the foremost of the gods;

you stand upon the dust raised by the great lion-king Bhava, with your neck uplifted by the mass of your white mane, and with the great Asuras pulverized by the flood of your long arms, tawny from the fire of the tip of your stainless spear.
O Mother Caṇḍikā, destroyer of Śumbha and Niśumbha, praised by the worlds,
you who are the sole delight in swiftly subduing the demons who afflict those who bow to you; O Goddess,
your form exists on earth, in the sky, in the path of the wind, and amidst the turmoil of fire.
I bow to you, O matchless Ajitā, the creator of the world, the beloved of Bhava.

116 O you who grant fearlessness, may the oceans with their playful and surging waves, the fire that burns all moving and unmoving things with its brilliance, and the serpents bearing a thousand hoods, leave me unharmed. 117

O Blessed One, refuge for those whose devotion is steadfast, I have come to take shelter at Your feet; may my collection of senses here be rendered submissive through the experience of the bliss of Your playful face.
Then the Goddess, being thus praised by Vīraka, became exceedingly gracious.
The daughter of the mountain entered her husband’s auspicious abode. Vīraka, standing at the door, respectfully sent back even the gods who were desirous of seeing Hara to their own homes.
"There is no time for this; the goddess sports secretly with Vṛṣākapi. Having been told this, they departed as they had come. When a thousand years had passed, the gods became anxious in their minds.
They urged Jvalana (Fire) to learn of Śaṅkara’s actions.
Having entered through a hollow in the wings, Hutāśana (Fire), in the form of a parrot,
saw everything as he lay upon his bed engaged in dalliance with Girijā.
And the Lord of Gods beheld that Fire in the form of a parrot;
Mahādeva, filled with a touch of anger, spoke to him.
124 Śarva said:
"O Śuka, half of my seed has been infused into the Goddess;
because of shame, there was no emission from him. O Pāvaka, you drink the other half! Since this obstacle has occurred on your account, its consequence falls upon you."
Thus addressed, Vahni (Agni), with palms joined in reverence, drank the deposited seed.
Then the gods were drenched by that [seed], for from his mouth the Ṛbhus emerged;
thereafter, the seed of Maheśvara burst open their bellies.

Having emerged from it, a great, pure lake, shining like molten gold, was formed within that vast hermitage of Śaṅkara; it extended for many yojanas and resounded with the songs of various birds amidst its blossoming golden lotuses. 128.
Having heard that, the goddess went to that lake where a great golden lotus had arisen;
filled with curiosity, she entered that lake of golden lotuses,
and having played in the water there, she made a crest-ornament from those lotuses.
Then, seated on its bank surrounded by her companions, the goddess, desiring to drink that water which was sweet and filled with pure lotuses,
beheld those six Kṛttikās, who resembled the splendor of the sun.

Taking that water in a lotus leaf, she set out for her home. Out of joy, she said, "I shall drink the water contained within this lotus leaf. Then all the Kṛttikās spoke to the daughter of the Snowy Mountain: 132-133. Taking that water in a lotus leaf, she set out for her home. Out of joy, she said, "I shall drink the water contained within this lotus leaf. Then all the Kṛttikās spoke to the daughter of the Snowy Mountain:
The Kṛttikās said:
"O beloved, whatever son shall be born when you have conceived, he shall be our son as well—our protector and the one who provides for us. (134)
"O fair-faced one, he shall be renowned throughout all the three worlds. When she was addressed thus, Girijā said: "How can a son be born from you who possesses all limbs produced from my own body?"
Then the Kṛttikās said to her: "We shall indeed provide you with excellent heads, provided that it shall be so. Being thus addressed, the daughter of the Mountain said: "So be it, O blameless ones."
Then, filled with great joy, they gave her water resting upon lotus petals; she too drank that water gradually. And at the very moment that water was drunk, the Supreme Lord [appeared].
Having split open the right side of the goddess’s womb,
a wondrous infant emerged; he was the destroyer of disease and sorrow,
possessing a splendor like a mass of rays from the sun.
Grasping a stainless, fierce trident and a goad, the fire-god, possessing a golden luster, rose up ablaze to slay the Daityas;
for this reason, he also became known as Devakumāra. 141.
Then the infant Skanda emerged again from the left side of the Goddess;
moreover, he appeared here with six faces from the mouth of Agni, and especially from the waters of the Kṛttikās through their branches. 142–143.

The auspicious branches are said to have spread from his six faces; therefore, he is celebrated in the worlds as Viśākha, the Six-faced One (Ṣaṇmukha). He is renowned as Skanda, Viśākha, Ṣaḍvaktra, and Kārttikeya.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, those two of great strength,
resembling the sun, were born in a vast forest of reeds; likewise, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, these two became like fire and flame.
He performed a single *sandhyā* rite for the welfare of the two boys;
then, on that very sixth day, the lord Guha was consecrated by all the hosts of immortals, including Brahmā, Upendra, Indra, and Bhāskara. 147.
With auspicious perfumes, garlands, incenses, and even toys, with umbrellas, fans, nets, ornaments, and ointments,
the Lord Ṣaṇmukha was duly consecrated according to the prescribed rite. 148–149.
Śakra gave him his daughter, renowned as Devasenā; the Lord of the Gods of gods, Viṣṇu, gave him his weapon;
and the Lord of Wealth gave him ten lakhs of Yakṣas. 150.
Agni gave him splendor, and Vāyu gave him a vehicle;
Tvaṣṭṛ gave him a cock as a plaything that could assume any form at will.
Thus all the gods granted him an infinite retinue.

With joyful hearts, the hosts of gods, kneeling upon the earth, gave [offerings] to Skanda, who possessed the splendor of the sun, and praised him with this hymn as the foremost granter of boons. 153.
The principal deities extolled the six-faced one with this prayer.
The gods said:
Salutations to Kumāra of great splendor, to Skanda, by whom the Dānavas were routed;
salutations to you, Guhya, who dwells in the cave, whose radiance is like the orb of the rising sun. 154.

Homage to you, the remover of the world’s fear; homage to you, who are devoted to compassion for the world. (155) Homage to you with your vast and stainless eyes; homage to Viśākha, the observer of the great vow.
Homage, homage to you, fierce in battle; homage to him whose vehicle is the radiant peacock. (156)

"Homage be to you who wear armlets; homage to you who bear a lofty banner. Homage to you who are bowed down by your own majesty; homage be to you, the bearer of the bell, endowed with steadfastness. (157) Kumāra said:
"O Kaṃva, what desire shall I grant? Speak with confidence; even if it be a task impossible for us that has long been contemplated in your heart.
Thus addressed by him, the gods, with their heads bowed in prostration, replied:
All of them, with joyful minds, [approached] the great-souled Guha.
There was a lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, the destroyer of the entire host of the immortals—
powerful, invincible, fierce, of evil conduct, and exceedingly wrathful.
"Abandon that very Daitya, O invincible one, who is the destroyer of all;
for a remaining task has presented itself which brings us great fear.
Moreover, Hiraṇyakaśipu is fierce and cannot be slain by the hosts of gods."
"The destroyer of sacrifices, the performer of evil deeds, Vena, by whom even Brahmā was fathered as a father—seize these two! May prosperity be yours, and may you seize your own great strength.
Thus addressed, he who follows the commands of all the immortals replied, "So be it."
Being praised by the lords of the gods, the Lord of the worlds departed for the sake of slaying Tāraka,
the thorn of the worlds;
then Śakra, resorting to a secret strategy, dispatched him.
Having approached the Daitya, who was harsh of speech and terrifying in appearance, the messenger of the lion among Dānavas spoke these words, granting him fearlessness.
The messenger said:
Śakra, the lord of the gods and master of heaven, says to you:
"O banner of the Daityas, unite with Tārakāsura and his Śakti as you desire; for the world has been set ablaze by the sin committed by you. (166-167)

"Having heard these wonderful words— that I am the slayer of that [Hamsa] and the king of the three worlds— the evil-minded one, whose eyes were bloodshot with anger and whose prosperity was nearly destroyed, spoke to the messenger. (168)
Tāraka said:
"O Śakra, I have witnessed your manliness a hundred times in great battles; yet, O evil-minded Śakra, because of your shamelessness, no peace exists for you."
When the messenger had spoken thus and departed, the Dānava reflected:
"Indra does not deserve to speak in this manner unless he has found a protector; it is now known that Skanda has been born from Indra by virtue of having obtained a refuge."
Then he beheld those evil omens foretelling destruction—
a rain of dust and a fall of blood from the sky onto the surface of the earth—
along with the throbbing of his left eye and a mental sensation of his mouth becoming parched. (172)
He observed the withering of his own lotus-like faces;
he saw wicked and fierce beings speaking evil words.
At that, the son of Diti, his mind fixed upon that unthinkable [event], became despondent in an instant.
It was intense with the deep, resonant ringing of the bells on the herds of elephants,
likewise adorned by the spirited neighing of throngs of horses,
and resplendent with the rows of lofty banners within the various divisions of the army.
With celestial chariots of wondrous form, from which pure chowries were waving;
adorned with ornaments and resounding with the songs of kinnaras;
and bearing garlands made of various blossoming flowers from diverse trees.

Standing in his palace, the Daitya beheld the army of the celestial dwellers, which was free from sorrow, adorned with the brilliance of flashing weapons and shields, possessed a splendor enhanced by lightning, and resounded with the music of various instruments.
Then, with a somewhat bewildered mind, he reflected:
"Who could this unprecedented warrior be, who has not been conquered by me?
While the Daitya was thus overwhelmed with anxiety, he heard words of bitter import.
This heart-rending cry was proclaimed by the Siddhas and Vandin-singers:
"Victory to you, O best of Kumāras, whose fierce and impetuous arms—like a cage of rays from the light of incomparable power—sport in causing the lotus-faces of the gods to bloom! 180–181.

Victory to Mahāsena, who is like a submarine fire to the great ocean of the race of the Daityas, whose sprout-like toenails are curved by the tips of the crowns of the gods, and who possesses a beautiful peacock-chariot;
victory to him who is a formidable forest fire to the lineage of the lords of the Daityas, with the lovely mass of his moving crest appearing like the stalk of a fresh and pure lotus.
"Victory to Viśākha! O Lord, conquer Bāla! O friend of the world, victory to you who pacifies grief! Victory to Skanda, the destroyer of the leader of all the sons of Diti!
(184) Having heard all this proclaimed by the bards of the gods, Tāraka recalled the words of Brahmā regarding his impending death at the hands of a child. (185)
Remembering him who destroys the flood of unrighteousness and always follows the path of the heroic,
[Viṣṇu] quickly emerged from the palace with a mind seized by grief.
(186) The Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, were terrified and their minds were bewildered.
Then, among their own ranks, those whose minds were struck with wonder by the haste cried out.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, the leader of the Dānavas, said: "The flight of this boy would be a cause of shame for me. (187-188)
"If I go to kill him, he too is surely dependent on impurity;
having killed this boy, I would become a causeless object of reproach.
"Go! Run! Seize him! Deploy the army! [189]

Seeing the prince, Tāraka, who possessed a terrifying form, spoke: "O boy, do you desire to fight with the playful ease of a ball? By whom have you been sent forth, O virtuous one, you who speak of the challenge of battle? (190-191)
Then, because of his youth, his intellect was thus limited in its vision;
standing before him, the prince spoke with great joy:
"Listen! The meaning of the scriptures on liberation is not being discerned here at all. (192)
"Even with weapons, riches are not seen in a battle filled with intense fear. Do not despise childhood; even a serpent is dangerous while it is young.
The sun is difficult to look upon when it is a child; likewise, I am a child who is hard to conquer. (193-194)
"What is this mantra with so few syllables that it appears so powerful?"—as Kumāra spoke thus, the Daitya hurled a mallet.
Kumāra warded it off with his discus of unfailing luster. (195)

Then the lord of the Daityas hurled an iron *bhindipāla* weapon; Kārttikeya, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, caught it with his hand. The Daitya then rose up and released a mace that produced a harsh sound.
Struck by her, the Daitya then trembled like the king of mountains;
the Daitya then considered that boy to be invincible and most difficult to withstand.
Reflecting with his intellect, he thought: "Without a doubt, the appointed time has arrived."
Seeing him trembling, all the lords of the Daityas, led by Kālanemi, struck Kumāra, who was fierce in battle;
yet that one of great splendor remained untouched by those blows as well as by afflictions.
In the battle, the lords of the Daityas, who were experts in combat, fought with all their strength and speed against the Dānavas;
then, those thorns of the gods, the Daityas, struck Kumāra in the fray with stone-tipped arrows. 201. The Daityas, destroyers of the strength of the gods, assailed Kumāra in the battle.
Yet Kumāra felt no pain, even though he was struck by the weapons of the Daityas.
The battle between the gods and the Dānavas became life-ending for the gods;
seeing the gods oppressed, Kumāra was overcome with wrath.
Then, with his missiles, he tore apart the army of the Dānavas; struck by those missiles against which there was no defense, all those thorns of the gods,
headed by Kālanemi, turned their backs in flight from the battle.
When the Daityas had fled and were being struck down on all sides,
his consciousness was cast aside by the laughter and the songs sung loudly by the Kinnaras;
he then struck Kumāra with a mace that possessed the luster of refined gold.
With variegated arrows, he turned the peacock away in battle;
seeing the god turned back and his mount covered in blood,
he seized a stainless spear adorned with gold in the fray.
Then the six-faced Mahāsena, with his arm beautiful with golden armlets, spoke to Tāraka, the lord of the Dānavas:
"Stop, stop, O evil-minded one! Behold the world of Yama!"
"You have indeed been struck by my spear; remember now the deeds of the Daityas!
Having spoken thus, he then hurled the spear at the son of Diti. Released from the arm of Kumāra, it resounded with the jingling of his armlets.
His heart shattered like the hard diamond-mountain king,
he fell lifeless upon the earth like a mountain at the time of universal dissolution; his crown and turban were scattered, and all his ornaments were cast aside.
When that Daitya, the leader of the Dānavas, had been slain,
not even a single evildoer among them felt sorrow, even in the hells;
praising the six-faced god, the gods played about with smiles upon their faces.
Full of longing, they returned to their own worlds, leaving him behind;
and all the gods, satisfied and having attained all their goals along with the Siddhas and those whose wealth is penance, granted a boon to the six-faced one.
The gods said:
"That high-minded man who would read this story related to Skanda, or hear it, or cause it to be heard, shall become possessed of fame. (216)

One who recites the life-story of Skanda after performing the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) shall possess long life, good fortune, splendor, fame, and an auspicious appearance; he shall be fearless toward all beings and free from all suffering. 217.
Accompanied by all the Kinnaras, he shall become a lord of great wealth. 218.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Birth of Kumāra and the Slaying of Tāraka," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Bhīṣma said:
Now I wish to hear about the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
as well as the majesty of Narasiṃha, which destroys all sins.
Pulastya said: O King, in a former Kṛta Yuga, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu, the primordial progenitor of the Daityas, performed a very great penance.
For ten thousand years and one thousand years,
he lived in the water, observing the vows of ritual bathing and silence; indeed,
he was endowed with tranquility, self-control, and celibacy.
Brahmā became pleased with his austerity and his disciplined observance.
Then the Lord Svayambhū himself arrived there,
traveling in a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
Together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and deities;
with the Rudras, the Viśvāsahāyas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
and also with the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the rivers, and the oceans.
Together with the constellations, the muhūrtas, the sky-dwelling great planets (7), the gods, the celestial sages (brahmarṣis), the perfected ones (siddhas), the seven ṛṣis,
the meritorious royal sages (rājarṣis), and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases (8).
The glorious Brahmā, the teacher of all moving and unmoving beings, surrounded by all the inhabitants of heaven and the best among those who know Brahman, spoke these words to the Daitya:
"O you of noble vows, I am pleased with this penance of yours, my devotee."
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; obtain whatever desire you wish.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Neither gods, nor asuras, nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, nor uragas, nor rākṣasas [shall be able to slay me]."
"O best of gods, let neither non-humans nor Piśācas slay me;
O Grandfather, let the sages and men not curse me with their curses.
Since the Blessed One is pleased with me, this is the boon I have chosen."
Neither by a weapon nor by a missile, neither by a mountain nor by a tree, neither by anything dry nor by anything wet— nor indeed by any other means— could he be slain.
May I myself become the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire.
The waters, the atmosphere, the stars, and the ten directions;
I am anger and desire, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama; I am the giver of wealth, the lord of riches, the Yakṣas, and the sovereign of the Kiṃpuruṣas.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, this divine and wonderful boon has been granted to you by me;
it shall grant all desires, my child, and you will obtain it without a doubt."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One indeed ascended into the sky to the abode of Brahmā, Vairāja, which is frequented by hosts of brahmin-sages.
Then the gods, gandharvas, and cāraṇas, together with the ṛṣis, [followed].
Having thus heard the granting of the boon, they approached the Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by virtue of this granting of the boon, that asura will slay us."
O Blessed One, let his death also be considered as resulting from Your grace.
The Blessed One is the primordial creator of all beings, the self-effulgent Lord, the creator of the offerings to gods and ancestors, the unmanifested source, and the Supreme. (19-20)
Having heard those words for the benefit of the entire world, the divine Lord of Creatures then comforted him with the cool waters of his speech:
"O gods, the fruit of this asceticism must necessarily be obtained by him."
"At the end of his ascetic penance, Lord Viṣṇu will bring about his destruction.
Having heard those words from the lotus-born Brahmā, all the gods,
filled with joy, departed for their own divine abodes, O Brāhmaṇa.
As soon as he had obtained that boon,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant because of the granting of the boon, oppressed all his subjects;
he harassed the highly fortunate sages of firm vows who dwelt in hermitages.
The Dānava oppressed those who were self-controlled and devoted to the true dharma;
having defeated the gods dwelling in the three worlds, that great Asura brought the three realms under his control and dwelt in heaven.
When he was intoxicated by his own inferior pride and impelled by the law of time,
he made the Daityas worthy of sacrifice and the gods unworthy of sacrifice; likewise, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Vasus were treated in the same way.
The Rudras, the hosts of gods, the Yakṣas, the gods, the twice-born,
and the great sages approached for refuge the mighty Viṣṇu,
the god of gods, who consists of sacrifice, Vāsudeva, the eternal one.
The gods said: "O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, the gods have come to you for refuge; protect us, O Lord, and slay the lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu. (30)
"You alone are our supreme benefactor; you alone are our supreme teacher;
you alone are our supreme deity, the best of gods among Brahmā and the others.
31 Viṣṇu said:
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you freedom from fear.
Likewise, O gods, regain your celestial realm without delay.
For this Daitya, along with his hosts, has become arrogant due to the granting of a boon."
"I shall slay this lord of the Dānavas, who is incapable of being killed even by the lords of the immortals. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the imperishable Viṣṇu,
the Lord Hari, went to the abode of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
With his splendor having the form of the sun, and with another [form] like the moon in its radiance,
he assumed the body of a man for half and likewise the body of a lion for half; then,
with his body in the form of Nārasiṃha, he seized [Hiraṇyakaśipu’s] hand with his own hand.
Then he beheld the vast, divine, delightful, and enchanting assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu, radiant and endowed with every object of desire;
it was a hundred yojanas wide and one hundred and fifty yojanas in length.
It was celestial, capable of moving at will, five yojanas in height, free from old age, grief, and fatigue, unshakable, auspicious, and pleasant;
it possessed beautiful rooms and seats and shone as if ablaze with splendor. 38.
Situated within the waters and fashioned by Viśvakarman,
it was endowed with divine-colored trees that yield fruit and flowers—
blue, yellow, black, dark-green, white, and even red.
He beheld the river Plavanti, resembling a mass of white clouds, with its bright thickets bearing clusters of red blossoms;
it was radiant by nature and delightful with divine fragrances. 41. Raśmimatī, by her very nature, was charming with celestial scents.

Neither experiencing excessive pleasure nor suffering, neither cold nor heat, they do not encounter hunger, thirst, or exhaustion; thus assisted by various, wonderful, and radiant means, they attain that state. 42–43.
Exceeding the moon, the sun, and the splendor of fire, she was self-luminous;
standing upon the surface of the sky, she blazed forth, radiant as if illuminating all.
All beings shone within her, and likewise, human beings were filled with joy.
There was excellent food, both solid and soft, abundant and full of flavor; there were garlands of holy fragrance and trees that bore fruit at all times;
indeed, the waters were cool in the heat and warm in the cold. 45–46.
The Lord beheld kalpa-trees with flowering tops and great branches bearing young shoots and sprouts, covered by canopies of climbing vines;
their flowers were fragrant and their fruits possessed flavor. 47.
In various places there, that lord, the king, saw cool and warm lakes and sacred bathing-places (tīrthas) adorned with fragrant lotuses, white lotuses, and hundred-petaled lilies. 48–49.
With red water-lilies, as well as white and blue lotuses,
and with other very lovely flowers endowed with various wonders,
and also with *kāraṇḍava* ducks, ruddy geese, cranes, and ospreys; 50.
There were birds with white plumage, shining like pure crystal;
there were the songs of many swans and the cries of cranes;
and there were fragrant creepers bearing clusters of blossoms.
The Blessed One, filled with joy, beheld khadira, vetasa, and arjuna trees; mangoes, nimba, nāga trees, kadamba, vakula, and dhava trees (53);
as well as priyaṅgu, those called pāṭala, śālmalī, and haridrava trees.
Śāla, tāla, tamāla, and delightful campaka trees,
as well as other blossoming trees, shone forth in the assembly hall—
elā, kakubha, kaṅkola, lavalī, and karṇapūraka. (54–55)
Madhukas and kovidāras were as tall as many palm trees,
along with numerous añjanas, aśokas, parṇāsas, and citraka trees; there were also varuṇas, palāśas, and apamārgas together with sandalwood trees.
Blue *sumanas* flowers, *nīpa*, *aśvattha*, and *tiṇduka* trees; *pārijāta* trees, *mallikā*, and *bhadradāru*;
*aṭarūṣa*, *pīlū*, and likewise *elavāluka* trees. 57–58.
Mandārakas, kuravakas, punnāgas, and kuṭajas;
likewise red kuravakas and blue ones along with agaru; as well as kiṃśukas, bhavyas, pomegranates, and bījapūrakas.
Kāleyaka, adukūla, hiṅgu, oil-wicks, dates,
coconuts, harītakī, madhūka, saptaparṇa, bilva, barley-gruel, and śarāvatā; 60–61.
There were *asanā* trees and *catamāla* trees, covered with various shrubs,
and creepers of diverse forms laden with flowers, leaves, and fruits;
these and many other forest-born trees were there.
Adorned with various flowers and fruits, they shone brilliantly on all sides.
Cakoras, śatapatras, intoxicated cuckoos,
and śārikas flew toward the great trees that were in full bloom, their tips laden with blossoms.
There, birds of red, yellow, and crimson hues perched upon the tips of the trees,
looking at one another with great joy like jīvajīvika birds;
and there, in that assembly hall, was Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas.
Seated upon a variegated throne measuring ten *nalvas* in extent,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu sat there, blazing with earrings, upon a divine seat spread with celestial coverings that shone like the sun.
Then the great Daityas waited upon Hiraṇyakaśipu,
while the best of the Gandharvas sang divine songs and played musical instruments;
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, and the honored Pramlocā were there as well.
Divyā, Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Puñjikasthalā,
Miśrakeśī, Carambhā, Citrabhā, Śrutivibhramā,
Cārunetrā, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and likewise Urvaśī. (69–70)
Thousands of others, skilled in dance and song,
waited upon the lord King Hiraṇyakaśipu;
likewise, all the sons of Diti, who had obtained boons, attended upon him.
There were Bali, Virocana, Naraka the son of the Earth, Prahlāda, Vipracitti, the great Asura Gaviṣṭha,
Surahantṛ, Duḥkhakartṛ, Sumanas, and likewise Sumati. (72–73)
Ghaṭodara, Mahāpārśva, Krathana, Piṭhara, as well as Viśvarūpa, Svarūpa, Viśvakāya, and the mighty Mahābala;
Daśagrīva, Vālī, and the great asura Meghavāsas.
Ghaṭābha, Viṭarūpa, Jvalana, and Indratāpana—
these hosts of Daityas and Dānavas all wore blazing earrings; they were all adorned with garlands, clad in armor, and all had observed their religious vows.
All of them were heroes who had obtained boons, and all of them had their deaths ordained;
these and many others, all possessing divine accoutrements, waited upon the high-souled lord Hiraṇyakaśipu.
With celestial chariots of various forms, shining as if with fires,
all those sons of Aditi— possessing bodies like that of Mahendra, with arms adorned by variegated armlets and their limbs decorated— waited upon him from every side.
The sovereignty of that great-souled lion among the Daityas has never been heard of nor seen by anyone in the three worlds.
[He was seated] upon a dais variegated with silver and gold, surrounded by pathways inlaid with diverse jewels.
The lord of beasts beheld him in the assembly hall, which was adorned with beautiful latticed windows;
he saw the son of Diti, whose limbs were decorated with golden bracelets and necklaces, blazing with the radiance of the sun’s rays, and being attended by hundreds of thousands of gods. 81–82.
Then, seeing that illustrious one who had arrived like the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra),
his body concealed in the form of a man-lion like fire covered by ashes,
the valiant son of Hiraṇyakaśipu named Prahlāda—
With a divine body, he saw the god arrived in the form of a lion (84). Seeing him, who had assumed that unprecedented form resembling a mountain of gold,
all the Dānavas and Hiraṇyakaśipu himself were struck with amazement (85).
Prahlāda said:
O great king, O mighty-armed one, O first-born of the Daityas, this body of a man-lion has never been heard of nor seen by me. 86
"What is this form that has appeared—unmanifest, supreme, and divine?
It is terrible, bringing about the end of the Daityas, and it seems to proclaim itself to my mind.
Within its body reside the gods, as well as the oceans and the rivers."
Himavat, Pāriyātra, and whatever other principal mountain ranges there are; the Moon together with the constellations, and the Sun together with its rays;
Dhanada, Varuṇa, Yama, and Śakra, the lord of Śacī. 88–89.
The Maruts, gods, Gandharvas, and sages rich in asceticism;
the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess;
Brahmā, the gods, and Paśupati—all these indeed wander about, stationed upon his forehead.
All things stationary as well as all things moving,
and you yourself, surrounded by us and all the hosts of Daityas, [shall enter] your entire assembly hall, which is crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots. 91-92.
O King, the entire three worlds and the eternal law of the world are seen within this Narasiṃha, as is this whole universe;
here also are Prajāpati, the high-souled Manu, the planets, the yogas, the earth, and the sky.
Utpātaka, Kāla, Dhṛti, Mati, Carati, Satya, Tapas, and Dama;
Sanatkumāra of great majesty, all the Viśvedevas, and all the Ṛṣis; as well as Krodha, Kāma, Harṣa, Darpa, Moha, and all the Pitṛs. (94–95)
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu, the leader of the hosts, spoke to all the Dānavas and their attendants:
"Let this lion be seized, for he has assumed an unprecedented form."
Or if there were any doubt, let this forest-dweller be slain!
Then all those hosts of Dānavas, surrounding the lion-king of fearsome prowess, joyfully terrified him with their might. 97–98.
Then, letting out a lion’s roar, the immensely powerful Narasiṃha,
like Death with his mouth wide open, shattered that entire assembly hall.
While the assembly hall was being destroyed, Hiraṇyakaśipu himself—
With eyes agitated by rage, he hurled weapons at Siṃha:
first the most excellent of all weapons, the extremely terrible Daṇḍa-astra, then the fearsome Kālacakra, and furthermore the Viṣṇucakra. 100–101.
The great and most fierce thunderbolt of the Grandfather (Brahmā), fashioned from the three worlds;
the variegated thunderbolt and the two types of dry and wet thunderbolts;
the terrible spear of Rudra, as well as the Kaṅkāla and the mace.
The Brahmaśiras missile, as well as the Brāhma missile;
the Nārāyaṇa missile, the Aindra, the Āgneya, and likewise the Śaiśira;
the Vāyavya, the Mathana, the Kapāla, and the Kiṅkara. (103–104)
Likewise, the Krauñca weapon of unimpeded power, as well as the Mohana, Śoṣaṇa, Saṃtāpana,
Vilāpana, Kaṃpana, Śātana, and the great weapon Rodhana.
Kālamudgara, Akṣobhya, Tāpana, and Mahābala;
Saṃvartana, Mohana, and likewise the excellent Māyādhara; the beloved Gāndharva weapon, and the jewel-like sword Nandaka. 106–107.
The Prasvāpana, the Pramathana, the supreme Vāruṇa weapon,
and the Pāśupata weapon— whose range is unimpeded—
all these divine weapons [were possessed] by Hiraṇyakaśipu at that time. 108.
He offered [his weapons] like an oblation into the blazing fire of Narasiṃha.
With his flaming missiles, that best of Asuras enveloped the Lion, just as Vivasvat covers the Himavat with his rays during the summer season.
The ocean-like army of the Daityas, stirred up by the wind of unbearable fury,
in an instant submerged everything, just as the ocean submerges Mount Maināka;
with spears, nooses, swords, maces, and likewise with clubs.
With thunderbolts and vajras, with great trees having many branches,
with mallets, spiked nooses, rocks, mortars, and mountains,
with blazing *śataghnīs* and also with most dreadful clubs.

Then the demons, equal to Mahendra, with speed like that of the thunderbolt, stood with their hands grasping nooses and their bodies with arms raised on all sides, like young elephants with their trunks upraised.
Their limbs were adorned with garlands of gold, and the hollows of their mouths were filled with very sharp fangs.
With their bodies and horns gleaming with radiant light, they shone like swans clad in silken garments.
That Dānava created the illusion of fire and wind;
against that, the thousand-eyed Indra of great splendor countered it with clouds.
With a great rain of water, he extinguished the fire;
but when that illusion was thwarted, the Dānava in the battle produced a fierce and intense darkness on all sides.
While the world was shrouded in darkness and the Daityas had taken up their weapons,
he appeared like the sun risen with its own radiance;
and during that encounter with the Danavas, they beheld his three-pronged frown.
Then all those sons of Diti, whose lives had been destroyed by Māyā, like the triple-streamed Gaṅgā situated on the forehead of the three-peaked mountain,
went despondent for refuge to the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Then, blazing with rage as if consuming everything with his splendor,
when that lord of the Daityas became enraged, the world became shrouded in darkness;
even the Āvaha, Pravaha, Vivaha, and Samīraṇa winds ceased their flow.
Parāvaha, Saṃvaha, the mighty Udvaha, and likewise the glorious Parivaha—these seven winds that move through the sky were thus agitated, portending fear from calamities.
123. Thus indeed were the seven winds, the roamers of the firmament, thrown into turmoil.
Indeed, all those grahas that appear at the time of the destruction of the entire world roamed joyfully through the sky as they pleased;
and even though it was not the time for union, the night-stalker practiced yoga during the night.

O subduer of enemies, the lord of the stars, together with the planets and the lunar mansions, has turned pale; and the divine sun in the sky has grown dim. At that time, a great black headless trunk (kabandha) was seen in the heavens.
And the sun emitted black rays, while the fire became like smoke;
and the divine sun, situated in the sky, was repeatedly surrounded by seven terrible, smoke-colored rays rising from the sun. 127–128.
The planets remain situated at the tips of the horns of Soma as he stays in the sky;
Venus and Jupiter are positioned on the left and the right respectively, while Saturn and Mars possess a radiance equal to that of the red-bodied one (the sun).
All the sky-dwellers ascended together upon the peaks,
like the terrible planets at the end of an eon; and the moon, the dispeller of darkness, along with the lunar mansions and the planets, slowly climbed upward.

For the destruction of all things moving and unmoving, Rāhu seized the moon, who was not even gladdened by Rohiṇī; the moon was struck by meteors, and blazing meteors moved about the moon as they pleased. 132.
Even the god who is the sovereign lord of the gods rained down blood; meteors fell from the sky with the form of lightning and a great roar,
and all the trees blossomed and bore fruit out of season.
All the creepers bore fruit— those which they say were the destroyers of the Daityas—
and upon every fruit there grew further fruits, and likewise upon every flower there grew further flowers.
They opened and closed their eyes, and they laughed and wept.
The images of all the gods are emitting deep cries, smoking, and blazing, foretelling a great terror;
furthermore, wild and domestic beasts and birds are mingling together. (136–137)
When the hunt was about to begin, they cried out there with terrifying sounds;
the rivers flowed turbid with water in a contrary direction, and the quarters of the sky did not shine, being filled with red dust. 138.
The trees of the forest are never worshipped, even though they are worthy of worship;
they are struck down by the force of the wind, broken, and bow down [in submission].
Likewise, the shadow of all living beings does not turn away from them. 139–140.
When the sun had set and the world was as if at the end of an eon,
Madhu then took up his position above the palace of the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, stationed in its treasury and armory.
For the destruction of the Asuras and for the victory of the Asuras, various portents are seen—terrible and of fearsome appearance;
these and many others of dreadful form have arisen. (142–143)
O Lord of Daityas, as the earth trembled, portents foreboding battle were seen for your destruction;
and as the great-souled one [struck], mountains and hosts of serpents of immeasurable power fell upon the Lord of Daityas. 144.
With mouths filled with the flames of poison, they emitted fire;
there were serpents with four heads, five heads, and seven heads—Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya. 145–146.
Elāmukha, Kāliya, the powerful Mahāpadma, Sahasraśīrṣa, Śuddhāṅga, the lord Hematāladhvaja,
Śeṣa, Ananta, and the great nāga Aprakaṃpya— all were shaken.

The cavities within the earth situated in the waters blazed forth; O Lord of Daityas, they trembled on all sides out of anger. Moreover, those who dwell in the depths of Pātāla possessed various kinds of splendor.
The netherworlds, though normally difficult to shake, were violently agitated and trembled;
then the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu touched the earth,
his lips bitten in rage like the elder brother of Varāha.
The Gaṅgā, Bhāgīrathī, Kauśikī, and Sarayū;
the Yamunā, Kāverī, and the river Kṛṣṇaveṇī;
the Tuṅgabhadrā of great velocity, and likewise the river Godāvarī. 151–152.

The Carmaṇvatī, the Sindhu, as well as the lord of rivers and streams; the Śoṇa, originating from Melaka, with water like jewels; the Narmadā of auspicious currents, and likewise the river Vetravatī. 153.
The Gomatī, crowded with herds of cows, and likewise the eastern Sarasvatī;
the Mahākālī, the Mahī, the Tamasā, and the Puṣpavāhinī—Jambūdvīpa is adorned with all these jewels, like a collection of gems. 154–155.
There is the Suvarṇapuṭaka mountain, adorned with gold mines;
the great river Lauhitya, and the mountain resplendent with gold.
There is also the city of the silk-weavers and Kaśa, a mine of silver.
The great villages of Magadha, as well as the fierce Puṇḍras;
Srughna, Malla, Videha, Mālava, Kāśī, and Kosala—all these trembled at the palace of the son of Vinatā when it was shaken by the lord of the Daityas. (157–158)
The ocean named Lauhitya, which was fashioned by Viśvakarman, has the form of the peak of Kailāsa; it is filled with jewels and waters, and is exceedingly fearsome.
Furthermore, the great mountain Udaya rises for a hundred yojanas.
The glorious mountain has altars of the same color as its rocks and is frequented by rows of clouds;
it shines with flowering trees made of gold resembling the sun—sālas, tālas, tamālas, and karṇikāras. 160–161.
There is the famous Ayomukha, adorned on all sides with minerals;
and there is the auspicious Malaya mountain, which possesses the fragrance of a tamāla forest.
There are also Surāṣṭra, along with Bāhlīka, Śūdra, and likewise Bhīra.
The Bhojas, Pāṇḍyas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Tāmraliptakas;
likewise the Pauṇḍras, Śubhras, Vāmacūḍas, and Keralas—by that Daitya, the gods and the hosts of Apsarases were thus agitated. (163-164)
And there is the abode of Agastya, which was established by Agastya in ancient times;
it is enchanting, crowded with throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, filled with various wonderful birds, and adorned with great trees in full bloom. 165.
With peaks made of gold and frequented by hosts of Apsarases,
Mount Puṣpitaka is indeed auspicious and beautiful to behold;
rising up and piercing the ocean, it serves as a resting place for the moon and the sun.
With its great peaks shining like the rays of the moon and sun and enveloped by the waters of the ocean, it shone as if scraping the sky;
a majestic mountain, possessing lightning, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Where the flashes of lightning are made to descend upon that best of mountains;
there is the mountain Ṛṣabha, the glorious Ṛṣabhasaṃsthita,
and the beautiful mountain Kuñjara, which is the auspicious home of Agastya.

The city of Mālatī, belonging to the serpents known as Vimala and Adurddharṣa, as well as Bhogavatī, were shaken by the lord of the Daityas; likewise, Mount Mahāsena and the Pāriyātra mountain were shaken. 171.
Cakravān, the best of mountains, and the mountain Vārāha;
and also the auspicious city of Prāgjyotiṣa, made of gold, wherein the evil-minded Dānava named Naraka dwelt. 172–173.
O lord of the people, there is the excellent mountain Megha, with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud;
there are sixty thousand mountains there,
and the great mountain Meru, which resembles the rising sun.
Its caves are constantly frequented by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas.
The mountain Hemagarbha, Mahāsena, Meghasakha, and Kailāsa—the lord of mountains—were all shaken by the lord of the dānavas. 175–176.
The lake of the hermits was covered with golden lotuses, its waters were agitated, and it was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks; likewise,
there was Triśṛṅga, the best of mountains, and Kumārī, the most excellent of rivers.
Mount Mandara, covered by masses of snow;
Mount Uśīrabīja; Bhadraprastha, the king of mountains; Prajāpatigiri; and likewise Puṣkaraparvata. 178–179.
Devābha, Parvata, as well as Vālukāgiri, Krauñca, Saptarṣiśaila, and the mountain Dhūmravarṇa—
these and other mountains, as well as regions and provinces. 180.
All the rivers, together with the oceans, were shaken by the Dānava;
Kapila, the son of the Earth, and Vyāghravān were also made to tremble, as were the sky-dwellers, the sons of Night, and those who inhabit the depths of Pātāla. 181–182.
Likewise, another fierce host named Megha, armed with a goad,
and Urdhvaga of terrifying speed— all these were made to tremble;
as were Gadī, Śūlī, Karāla, and Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Resounding like the thunder of a rain-cloud and possessing the speed of a cloud itself, the arrogant demon, the enemy of the gods, rushed toward Nṛsiṃha;
then, by that lion among men with his great, sharp claws, [he was struck]. 184–185.
Then, having been torn asunder and slain in battle by him with the assistance of Oṃkāra,
the earth, time, the moon, the sky, the planets along with the sun, all the directions,
the rivers, the mountains, and the great oceans attained tranquility upon the destruction of the son of Diti.
Then the gods and the sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, were filled with joy and praised the eternal Primordial God with divine names:
"O God, this body of Narasimha has been assumed by you."
Those people who know the higher and the lower will worship this very [form].
Brahmā said:
"You are Brahmā, you are Rudra, and you are Mahendra, the best of gods. (189)
You are the creator and the destroyer, the origin and the dissolution of the worlds;
they call you the supreme perfection, the supreme essence, the supreme secret, and the supreme oblation.
You are the supreme dharma and the supreme glory; they call you the foremost, the supreme, and the ancient one.
They call you the supreme truth and the supreme austerity, the supreme purifier and the supreme path;
they call you the supreme sacrifice and the supreme oblation, the foremost, the supreme, and the ancient;
the supreme body and the supreme Brahman, the supreme yoga and the supreme speech.
They say that you are the supreme secret, the highest goal, the foremost, the ultimate, and the ancient one.
Having spoken thus and having praised the god Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the grandfather of all the worlds, departed for the world of Brahmā.
Then, while the musical instruments resounded and the Apsarases danced,
the Lord Hari,
the radiant deity, having set aside his Nārasiṃha form, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Assuming his ancient form, the Lord whose banner bears the bull departed by means of a radiant,
eight-wheeled vehicle endowed with divine power;
the Lord, whose nature is unmanifest, returned to his own abode.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Narasiṃha," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-six.
Śrī Bhīṣma said:
"The majesty of Narasiṃha has been recounted by you in detail; likewise, let the majesty of Bhava, who is named Bhairava, be told.
Pulastya said:
Listen also to the supreme deed of that God of gods:
there was a Daitya named Andhaka, who resembled a mass of crushed collyrium;
he was endowed with great ascetic power and was indeed invulnerable to the inhabitants of heaven.
Once, having seen the omnipresent Great God sporting together with Pārvatī, he proceeded to abduct the Goddess, thinking:
"I shall carry off this Goddess today; in her separation, he will meet his death."
"Therefore, this Lokasundarī shall become my firm wife;
for if she were not my wife, what purpose would there be in life—she who has lips like the *bimba* fruit, a beautiful face, and a most lovely countenance? (5)
Then, having adopted this resolve and consulted with his ministers,
he made preparations for his army and addressed his general:
"Bring me my victorious chariot, the destroyer of gods."
"I shall conquer all the thirty gods, led by Viṣṇu and Rudra;
I shall seize the daughter of the Mountain, for my mind has been stolen away by her.
This was reported to him, Kanaka’s minister, by the gods regarding the slaying of Kanaka.
Because he was infatuated with the wife of another, he was struck down by the gods together with Indra.
Thereupon, his soul overcome with anger, he said, "I shall slay the gods along with Śaṅkara.
Having slain that Dānava, Śakra, out of fear of Andhāsura, [acted]. 9–10.
Seeking refuge, he went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara;
having seen the Lord of Gods, whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon, he bowed down and,
terrified, addressed Him who holds the thousand-eyed one (Indra).
"O God, grant me fearlessness from the Dānava Andhaka!
I am afraid of his son, who has been struck down in battle by me.
Therefore, as long as that great Asura does not know that his son has been slain—"
"Right there where he stands, let that cruel Dānava— who brings me fear, who is lustful for women, and who abducts the wives of others— be swiftly slain.
O best of Asuras, he must be killed by you in every way."

Having heard these words of Śakra, Śaṅkara, who is the refuge of all, then granted him freedom from fear, saying, "Do not fear," O performer of a hundred sacrifices. Having been granted this assurance, he returned from Kailāsa to Kuśasthalī.
Surrounded by hosts of spirits for the sake of slaying Andhaka, Īśa assumed a massive form, a universal form that was most terrifying;
it was fearsome with blazing serpents darting about like a formidable serpent-king. 17.
With his matted locks and the flames from the jewels on the crests of his hoods, he seemed to burn the sky intensely with his splendors like the fire of time at the end of an aeon;
and with his mouths, marked by sprout-like fangs and radiant as the crescent of the second moon, [he appeared].
With thousands of arms that took the form of the interior of the netherworld (pātāla), which resounded with terrifying roars and were grasping many weapons;
[arms] richly adorned with many ornaments and emitting many fierce sounds.
Clad in a lion’s skin with a tiger’s hide as an upper garment,
assuming the majestic air of an elephant-hide, and filled with the humming of falling bees—
having assumed such a form, the Lord became a source of terror to the demons.
The slayer of the Danavas, Bhima, descended to the earth;
and Andhasura, the younger brother [of Bali], having heard that his son had been slain in battle,
was possessed by the darkness of wrath and sounded the war-trumpets.
Having gathered together and arrived with focused intent at the place where the gods were stationed,
they— along with a vast army equipped with chariots and elephants— beheld those gods and Dānavas who were intent upon the great battle. 24–25.
With their armor fallen away, they sought refuge with Śambhu;
and the three-eyed God, saying "Do not fear" to those gods,
took up his trident and stood there with great fury, baring his fangs.
Then Andhaka, filled with rage, struck the hosts of the gods—who had been joined together as one—with hundreds of millions of arrows;
yet the wielder of the Pināka bow discharged fire with sparks and flames. 27–28.
Then, the chariot-bound Andhaka was completely enveloped by arrows;
thereupon the lord of the Danus, standing on his chariot with his weapons slackened and his strength failing,
summoned all the Dānavas and prepared for battle.
The army of Bāṇa was shattered by many warriors fighting with various weapons;
it was slain in battle by the gods who had formed an alliance with Sthāṇu.
And seeing his host broken by the deities, the Dānava Andhaka [fled].
His body overwhelmed by millions of arrows restrained by Maheśa, he relied solely on his fortitude and,
seizing Rudra’s Pināka bow, struck him.
By the impact of the Pināka, Rudra then fell to the earth;
when the god had been cast down upon the ground, the three worlds trembled, and the oceans overstepped their shores while the mountains shed their peaks.
When the Lord of Gods had fallen to the earth again by Andhaka’s mace, the stars, released in great numbers, departed; then,
filled with rage, Andhaka struck the elephant that had killed [the charioteer] and felled it to the ground.
Having abandoned Śiva, the king of serpents fled and went elsewhere.
After a moment, having regained consciousness, the Supreme Lord rose up; though he took up his divine axe, he did not see the Dānava at all. 36–37.

Having created that tamasic illusion, he who is skilled in hundreds of illusions caused the gods to be utterly deluded by it; then, where could the Dānava go? Then, having encountered fear of Śambhu, what will that sinner do?

As long as they were shrouded in darkness, the gods fell into agitation; with their armies bewildered in mind, they then spoke out due to the gravity of the situation. In that interval, the Sun, whose form is splendor, stood firm.
Arising in the form of a man, he made the quarters free from darkness; when the glow-worm stood revealed with its body thrilled as the darkness was destroyed,
the gods attained joy, their faces and eyes clearly visible.
All the gods were delighted, as were the hosts led by Skanda; they praised with various hymns the Sun-god in human form—
the incomparable, world-pervading Brahman who is beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Seeing him shining with a luster as red as vermilion and possessing the beautiful hue of polished coral, she then touched the ground with her five limbs;
again intent on prostration, she proceeded with focused meditation.
Beholding the God of gods with a tender gaze, the three-eyed Hara,
the Blessed One, slowly spoke to the God in a voice that was both affectionate and deep, filling the three worlds as it were with his splendors.
For living beings who are overwhelmed by the illusions of the Daityas and whose minds are agitated by what they perceive, this alone is the one unfailing deity.
And this alone [is the means] from the entire ocean of saṃsāra.
The Lord, the God, acts as a helmsman for beings, delivering them across [the ocean of existence].
Various living beings, always worshipping this God with devotion, become fit for the supreme good; therefore, bow down to that sovereign Bhāskara. 48–49.
But he who, with his playful rays that possess the brilliance of fresh flowers and serve as crowns for the peak of the mountain of sunrise,
illuminates all the intermediate and cardinal directions with his multitude of beams— that Sun shines in the world for the sake of manifesting his own majesty.
(50) [He is worshipped] by hosts of great sages skilled in the rituals of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Maruts, Acyuta, Vahni, and the Lord of Waters.

Your body is always worshipped by those seeking the highest good, who—like the very limbs of the day with their daily cosmetic ointments—have anointed their entire bodies with divine unguents; and by the gods at the time of universal dissolution, it is worshipped with hymns adorned with circles of diverse words.
But those who praise you while residing in the houses of others, being themselves deprived of a home, shall always remain on this earth with their hands outstretched in begging.

O Lord of Gods, those men whose limbs are afflicted by diseases such as leprosy and eruptions, whose skin is withered, who have deformed nails, and whose hair and noses have fallen away— even they, upon bowing at Your feet, immediately become like those of sixty-four years of age.
The Sāmavedins approach You with the words "Sāma," the Adhvaryus for the sake of the sacrifice with "Tvā," and the assemblies of chief Ṛgvedins with "Ṛk."
Those who know what must be done worship you as the Noble One (Ārya); likewise, the Nāgas and even the Pitṛs worship you;
the Upaniṣads worship you as Māyā; and the six classes of immortal gods worship you as the Sun.
Just as we here worship you, so too do these hosts of Gandharvas and Kinnaras along with the Cāraṇas; and thus, O Blessed One, may you manifest your true form.
Those who constantly worship you, the one worthy of worship, yet are themselves scorched by the heat of their own radiance, stripped of wealth, and clothed only by the sky—
deprived of riches, they wander from house to house with bellies and throats emaciated by hunger, begging for alms with broken shards of pottery in their hands.
(56) [Behold him] whose large eyes are like the interior of a full-blown red lotus, with slightly tremulous, curved, and tawny pupils.

Granted, [this] multitude of noble ladies was delightful with most excellent and beautiful necklaces, yet weary from the weight of their high and full breasts; their thighs were like plantain trees, and their broad, swelling, rounded hips were bound by girdles that jingled with tinkling gems;
their rows of teeth shone brightly, and their faces were adorned with golden hems of garments trailing along the tips of their foreheads. 57–58.

O Blessed One, you who grant liberation from worldly existence—by those women in their lovely homes, whose soft and faltering speech resounds with the tinkling of their anklets, you were worshipped with offerings as radiant as fire and as beautiful as the moon.
You alone are Brahmā; you are Hari; you are Anila; you are Agni; you are Rudra; you are Antaka; you are Varuṇa; and you are the Lord of the Immortals.
"You are the wind, you are life, you are the earth, you are the Lord, you are the sacrifice, you are the lord of wealth, you are the unconquered.
(60) "O seven-horsed one, having been released by the gods from their chariot, you have now crossed over the earth with great speed;
having gone all around this boundless sky, you do not feel even the slightest fatigue. (61)
Delighting in the singular yoga of meditation, through the cultivation of samādhi, those embodied beings who have meditated upon Your fourth state— O Infinite Formed One—
become liberated from fear and are devoted to that eternal Brahman, which is inconceivable, without beginning or end,
free from the diseases of birth and so forth, supreme, ancient, the Lord, and beyond old age, death, sorrow, and fear.
That which is beyond calculation by hosts of those who perceive gross objects is fully esteemed as pure by the exponents of Vedānta.

O You whose form is a mass of fire, the abode of austerities, whose pair of lotus feet are rubbed by the crowns of the multitudes of gods and demons, and whose stainless and beautiful body has been worshipped for a very long time by devotees who have thereby ascended to heaven; [I bow to You]. 63-64.
O Lord of beings, bestower of boons upon beings, you who act without end, whose soul is imperishable, O you whose loud laughter resounds through the sky, O progenitor, sole lamp of the world,
you whose name is the consecration of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur mantras, O cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, O protector of the worlds!
For me, who am wretched, miserable, and submerged in worldly existence, grant beautiful and unimpeded desires.

For one who recites this at dawn, evening, or midday, there shall be no perpetual calamity from the terrible portents of the moon-beams of the Lord of Ascetics, nor the internal afflictions of old age, death, grief,
and disease; such a person attains the same world as the radiant-rayed Sun and achieves virtue, wealth, and desire.
Therefore, that which is eternally manifested from the Sun and from the mind—
to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who grants fearlessness to your devotees, salutations! (68) O Subrahmaṇya, salutations to you, who are worshipped by all the gods!
Salutations to you, O sharp-rayed one; salutations to you, the eye of the world. Salutations to you, O maker of light, O Bhānu, conqueror!
O Lord of the world, I am oppressed by this chief of demons. 69–70.
"O Divākara, what shall I do? How can I slay him?
Sūrya said:
"O most sinful one, conquer this master of a hundred illusions with your trident. 71.
"O Lord of Gods, attain victory by slaying Andhaka with your trident!
Then, seizing the trident and casting it far away, he [Andhaka] struck him with his own splendor.
Thereupon, the evildoer Andhaka struck him with a trident.
In that battle, Rudra, being thus oppressed by Andhaka,
bent his bow Pināka with both arms and himself, as the Lord Śaṅkara, released an exceedingly fierce arrow known as the Pāśupata. (73–74)
From the blood of Andhaka, which issued from his being pierced by Rudra’s arrow,
Andhakas were born by the hundreds and thousands; and as they were being torn apart, yet others arose again from their blood.
The entire world became pervaded by the terrible darkness of Andhaka.
Seeing that Andhaka, the weaver of the thread of illusion (Māyā), the God of gods then created the Mothers for the purpose of drinking Andhaka’s blood.
Likewise, [one may worship] Māheśvarī, Brāhmī, Śaurī, Bāḍavī,
Sauparṇī, Vāyavyā, Śaṅkhinī, Taittirī,
Saurī, Saumyā, Śivadūtī, Cāmuṇḍā, or Vāruṇī. (78)
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vibhāvarī; Śatānandā, Bhagānandā, Picchilā, and Bhagamālinī; Bālā, Atibalā, Raktā, Surabhī, and Mukhamaṇḍitā. (79–80)
The destroyer of Tripura pierced that Daitya with his trident, [striking] Mātṛnaṃdā, Sunaṃdā, Biḍānī, Śakunī, the highly meritorious Revatī, and likewise Śikhipaṭṭikā. 81.
Then his mothers drank the blood that flowed from him.
O King, having become bloodless and red, the Daitya reached a state of withered dryness;
thus impaled upon the stake, the Daitya remained for a thousand divine years.
O observer of noble vows, although he was held fast by the mighty Rudra, the Daitya did not die; rather, at that time, Śambhu was praised with devotion by that Daitya:
"Salutations to Śambhu, the cause of the destruction of worldly existence! Salutations to you, O best of gods; be gracious! (84)
You are the eightfold form consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer—the creator of the world who transcends all.
Having propitiated you with many musical instruments, Bāṇa attained sovereignty over his own city, which is now to be protected by you.
Indeed, the lord of the Rākṣasas, having lifted a mountain with his arms, worshipped you while his form was distressed by your tread.
O Lord who has attained sovereignty over all the hosts of Rākṣasas, whose son is the exceedingly powerful Śakrabandha;
O remover of the fear of worldly existence, O Hara, O Supreme One, O Most Noble One, O Maker of my happiness, O Essence of all the gods!
Your lotus feet—the essence for crossing this ocean of saṃsāra—are the goal of the wind-god (Hanumān), who conquered him and bestowed his desired boons. 87.
O Lord, you who are moved by devotion grant the desired object to that man who places your lotus feet within his heart.
O Lord of Sages, in ancient times, the great sages fulfilled their heart's desires by worshiping you with reverence in your form as a *liṅga*.

O Bhavodbhava, whose sole form is the source of existence, whose manifestation is the fivefold world (*pañcaprapañca*), and who resides in the hollow of the cosmic tree as the life of all living beings—[thus they meditated]. 88–89.
May I, having attained all desires through the contemplation of Your feet, come step by step to the state of being a servant of Yours;
yet I am a fool and do not know how to praise You, O Lover of Your Devotees! May I be pitied even with a gracious mind by that Lord, for I have come as a suppliant. 90.
Thus, O King, Maheśa was praised with devotion and respect by the Daitya;
he granted him the status of Gaṇeśa and the name Bhṛṅgīriṭi.
This, O King, is the majesty of Hara, the remover of worldly existence.
Thus has been told the one called Vighnavighna, who brings happiness to those devoted to him.
Bhīṣma said:
Even for a human being, there is divinity, happiness, sovereignty, wealth, and fame. 93.
"O best of Brahmins, tell me of victory, enjoyment, health, long life, knowledge, prosperity, sons, kinsmen, and all that is auspicious.
Pulastya said:
Endowed with these qualities, the illustrious Brāhmaṇa is always pure in this world; indeed, the divine Brāhmaṇa is ever pure throughout the three worlds in age after age.
Having worshipped the twice-born, the gods enjoy eternal heaven.
The kings of Avanti protected the earth, the worlds, wealth, happiness, and auspiciousness.
(96) In this world, there is no one equal to a Brahmin; he is the deity even of the gods.
He is the very embodiment of Dharma and is truly the bestower of liberation upon the earth. (97)

The teacher of the worlds, worthy of worship, a holy place of pilgrimage, sinless, and the abode of all the gods— this being of pure essence was created by Brahmā in ancient times. In the past, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was questioned regarding this matter by Nārada.
"But by worshipping whom, O Brahman, does Mādhava become gracious?
Brahmā said: "Viṣṇu becomes gracious to him with whom the brāhmaṇas are gracious."
Therefore, by serving Brahmins, one attains the Supreme Brahman.
Viṣṇu always dwells within the bodies of Brahmins and not otherwise;
therefore, through the worship of Brahmins, Viṣṇu is pleased at that very moment.
He who constantly honors Brahmins with gifts, respect, worship, and the like,
has performed a hundred sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas that are accompanied by beloved sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The mouth of a Brahmin is a field that is neither saline nor thorny.

One should sow all kinds of seeds; such cultivation yields results for all time. Whatever is given upon approaching [a worthy recipient] and whatever delightful gift is bestowed—just as there is an end to the ocean, there is no end to giving.
They do not harm even with their minds a Brahmin who is an assailant;
they attain a state of mental favorability that is difficult even for the gods to obtain. When a learned man has come to one's house, he does not depart in despair.
All his sins are destroyed, and he enjoys imperishable heaven.
(106) Whatever wealth a Brahmin may offer at the proper time, place, and to a worthy recipient, know that such wealth remains inexhaustible for him birth after birth. (107)
He shall not fall into poverty, nor shall he be afflicted by illness or cowardice;
having honored a woman who is pleasing to his mind, he shall obtain twice-born brahmins as his reward.
Having performed daring deeds, he shall give them to a brahmin on sacred festival days.

That gift is declared to be of excellent quality, as is the granting of fearlessness and the acquisition of gain. (109) That hand which becomes scarred by being rubbed against the soles of a Brahmin’s feet is called the "hand that brings prosperity" (śrīkara); any other hand is merely a "hand for labor" (karmakara). (110)

Purified by the dust of the brahmins' feet and purified by drops of their water, they are forever freed from calamities and sins and go to the third heaven. Purified by the dust of the brahmins' feet, the courtyards of the houses become pure.
They are like fields of merit and are highly praised for sacrificial rites.
O sinless one, in the beginning, the Brahmin was born from the mouth of Brahmā;
therein the Vedas, which are the cause of the creation and maintenance of the world, were likewise produced.
Therefore, the Vedas were indeed entrusted by the Supreme Being to the mouth of the Brahmin for the sake of honoring all the worlds and certainly for the purpose of all sacrifices—
namely, in the sacrifice to the ancestors, at marriage, in fire-rituals, and in rites for peace.

One should always honor praiseworthy Brahmins during all rites for prosperity. From the mouth of the Brahmin alone, the gods certainly consume the sacrificial offerings (havya), the spirits such as the *balipreta* and others consume the oblations (*bali*), and the ancestors consume the ancestral offerings (*kavya*). (115–116)
Whatever gift, oblation, or offering one may give to the gods and the ancestors during sacrificial rites is fruitless without a Brahmin;
there, the Asuras, Pretas, Daityas, and Rākṣasas consume it. 117.
