Therefore, having invited a Brāhmaṇa, one should have him perform these rites;
performed at the proper time, place, and with a worthy recipient, the merit becomes a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold.
And upon seeing a twice-born man, one should offer a respectful greeting with faith.
By his word, a man becomes long-lived and lives for a long time; however,
through failing to offer salutation, through hatred toward Brahmins, and also through lack of faith,
the lifespan of men is diminished, their prosperity destroyed, and they fall into a miserable state.

By honoring the twice-born, there is an increase in lifespan, an increase in fame, and an increase in the wealth of knowledge; one becomes preeminent—of this there is no doubt. The mud of the water from a Brahmin’s feet is not to be despised, nor are the sounds of the Vedic scriptures to be disregarded. 121–122.
"Those houses which are devoid of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *svasti* are equal to cremation grounds.
Nārada said: "Which brahmin is most worthy of worship, and who indeed is unworthy of worship? (123)
"Tell me the true characteristics of a Brahmin and of a teacher as well.
Brahmā said:
"One who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who is always worthy of worship, and who is endowed with right conduct [is a teacher]. 124
One who is of good conduct, free from impurities, a holy place of pilgrimage for people, and sinless—Nārada said:
"O father, who is born as a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya)—in a noble family or even in an ignoble one? (125)
"Whether he performs good or evil deeds, a Brāhmaṇa is worthy of worship on earth.
Brahmā said:
"Indeed, one born into a family of learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) who is devoid of ritual action is not worshipped at all. (126)
Just as Vyāsa and Vaibhāṇḍaka were honored despite being born in lowly fields and families, so too was Viśvāmitra, who was born in the family of Kṣatriyas; he is my equal.
Vasiṣṭha was the son of a Vaiśya woman, as were other perfected ones (siddhas) and the twice-born.
Therefore, listen to the characteristics of a true learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*) and so forth, O son.

Among those who have become sacred fords (*tīrtha*) on this earth and who remove all sins, one is known as a *brāhmaṇa* by birth, but is called a *dvija* (twice-born) through the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). 128–129.
Through learning, one attains the status of a true Brahmin; this is the threefold characteristic of a Śrotriya.
Purified by knowledge, purified by mantras, and likewise purified by the Vedas, a Brahmin who is pure through bathing at sacred fords and other rites is remembered as most worthy of worship.

He was always devoted to Nārāyaṇa, possessed of a pure inner self, with his senses conquered and his anger subdued, and he was impartial toward all people. He was devoted to his guru, the gods, and guests, and was intent upon serving his parents. (131–132)

He whose mind never delights in another's wife, who is a constant narrator of ancient tales and the exposition of Dharma— by the mere sight of him, one constantly obtains the fruit born of the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices. 133.
Through conversation with him, by bathing in the Bhāgīrathī,
and being purified by various vows, constant ritual ablutions, and the worship of the twice-born,
one should be compassionate toward both friend and foe, and equal toward all people.
That man who does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another, even if it is found in the forest;
who is unsubdued by his senses which are free from desire, anger, and the like; and who does not covet, even in his mind, the wives of others, even when they have come to his home. 136.
Nārada said: What is the characteristic of the Gāyatrī, and what is the merit arising from each of its syllables?
Tell me with certainty regarding her womb, her feet, and her lineage.
Brahmā said:
"The *chaṃdogāyatrī* is [derived] from the *gāyatrī*; its deity is certainly Savitṛ;
it is white in color, has Agni as its mouth, and Viśvāmitra is its seer. (138)
With her head resting on the crown of Brahmā, she resides in the heart of Viṣṇu;
through the rite of initiation, she is bound by the lineage of the Sāṅkhyāyana gotra.
She should be known as having the three worlds as her feet and dwelling within the womb of the Earth.

By performing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-four syllables upon the twenty-four locations beginning from the feet and ending with the head, one attains the world of Brahmā. Having known the deity corresponding to each syllable, one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, I shall declare the fixed characteristics of the Gāyatrī:
it consists of seven, five, and eighteen syllables, beginning with the letter 'ja' and ending with the letter 'ha'. Standing in water, one should recite it a hundred times.
Even those liberated from tens of millions of minor offenses (*upapātaka*), as well as major sins (*atipātaka*) and crimes such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), go to my final abode.
*Oṃ agner vāk puṃsi yajurvedena juṣṭāt somaṃ piba svāhā.*

O son, whether one is born into the family of anyone at all— the Viṣṇu-mantra, the great mantra, as well as those of Maheśvara, Devī, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and the enjoyers of sacrifices— if they possess these qualities, they are indeed virtuous. 145–146.
A Brahmin who is directly composed of Brahman should be worshipped with great effort;
one should always give gifts according to the rules on every sacred occasion (parvan). The giver obtains inexhaustible merit for hundreds of millions of births. 147.
The Brahmin who is devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, who should read and cause others to read [the scriptures],
and who should always proclaim in the world the Dharma, right conduct, the Śrutis, the Smṛtis,
the Purāṇa-saṃhitās, and likewise the Dharma-saṃhitās— [he shall attain success]. 148–149.
Having caused [his fame] to be heard throughout the incomparable worlds and among the twice-born on earth, he, who is equal to Viṣṇu, should be honored by men and gods alike;
for his strength is inexhaustible, and he, O sinless one, has become a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having performed equal worship, a man goes to the abode of Acyuta.
(151) Even if sin is ever committed, the Brahmin is not tainted by those sins, just as the sun and fire remain unsullied even when situated within the house of a Cāṇḍāla. (152)
O twice-born ones, no fault arises for Brahmins from officiating at sacrifices, teaching, marriage, or likewise from accepting improper gifts, for they are equal to fire and the sun;
by remaining established in *prāṇāyāma*, they [purify] those faults born of accepting gifts.
It destroys sins here in this world, just as the wind disperses a cloud in the sky.

(154) One should daily recite the Gāyatrī, accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma), joined with the gods residing in each syllable, and even performed while placing [the mantras] upon one's own limbs. (155)
Freed from all sins, even those committed over ten million lifetimes,
and having attained the state of Brahman, he shall go beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, O Nārada, one should chant the Gāyatrī while performing ten thousand breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).

Nārada said: O Brahman, how are the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) performed? What are the deities for each syllable? Tell me also their ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs in their proper sequence.
Brahmā said:
The apāna wind resides in the region of the anus, while the prāṇa wind resides in the heart of the embodied being.
Therefore, having contracted the anus, one should unite it with the prāṇa.
Then, O son, having performed the supreme *kuṃbhaka* by means of *pūraka*,
and having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, the twice-born man should mutter the *Gāyatrī*.
By this very [method], one who mutters [it] destroys even a great accumulation of sins.
By merely uttering it once, even a minor offense (upapātaka) goes to destruction;
he who, having recognized each phoneme and accent, performs this placement upon the body— that person attains the state of Brahman, and we are unable to describe the extent of that fruit.
Listen, O son, as I declare that which is the divine mantra for each syllable (pratyakṣara).
Having recited this, the twice-born man shall never again drink from his mother’s breast.
The first is to be known as pertaining to Agni, and the second to Vāyu. 162–163.

The third has the Sun as its deity, and the fourth likewise belongs to Vāyu; the fifth has Yama as its deity, and the sixth is said to belong to Varuṇa. The seventh belongs to Bṛhaspati, while they know the eighth to belong to Parjanya.
The ninth is to be known as Aindra, and the tenth likewise as Gāndharva;
know the eleventh to be Pauṣṇa, and the twelfth is remembered as Maitra;
the thirteenth is to be known as Tvāṣṭra, and the fourteenth as Vāsava.
The fifteenth is known as Māruta, the sixteenth as Saumya,
the seventeenth as Āṅgirasa, and after that, the eighteenth as Vaiśvadeva;
the nineteenth is Āśvina, and the twentieth is Prājāpatya.

The twenty-first imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as consisting of all the gods; the twenty-second is to be known as Raudra (belonging to Rudra), and after that, the next is to be known as Brāhma;
the twenty-fourth is Vaiṣṇava—these are the deities of the imperishables.
During the time of recitation, by contemplating [the deity], one shall attain union (*sāyujya*);
having known that deity, his [the practitioner's] speech becomes realized.
Liberated from all sins, he shall go to the state of Brahman. 170.
The wise practitioner should first perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Gāyatrī upon his own body;
the yogi, being discerning, should place the syllable *tat* at twenty-four locations, from the feet up to the head, specifically on the big toes.
One should place the syllable *sa* at the region of the ankles, the syllable *vi* on the two shanks,
the syllable *tu* in the middle of the knees, and the syllable *ka* at the region of the thighs.
One should place the syllable *re* at the region of the private parts and the syllable *ṇi* on the testicles.
One should place the syllable *yaṃ* at the region of the hips, the syllable *bhaṃ* in the circle of the navel (174),
the syllable *go* in the stomach, and one should place the syllable *de* on the breasts;
one should place the syllable *va* in the heart and the syllable *sya* in the region of the hands (175).
Uttering the syllable *dhī*, one should place it on the face;

the syllable *a* should be placed on the palate. One should place the syllable *hi* at the tip of the nose and the syllable *dhi* on the two eyes. Then, one should place the syllable *yo* between the eyebrows and the syllable *yo* on the forehead.
One should place the syllable *na* in the eastern face, the syllable *pra* in the southern face;
one should place the syllable *co* in the western [face] and the syllable *da* in the northern [face]. Having placed the syllable *yāt* upon the head, one becomes established as all-pervading.
Having performed this placement (nyāsa), the righteous soul, who is of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
a great yogi and possessor of great knowledge, shall go to supreme liberation. Now hear again, exactly as it is, the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the time of twilight (saṃdhyā).
One should place "Oṃ bhūḥ" at the heart; one should place "Oṃ bhuvaḥ" at the head.
With "Oṃ svaḥ" [one places it] at the crest-lock (śikhā), and with "tat savitur vareṇyam" upon the body. With "bhargo devasya dhīmahi," one places it on the two eyes. 180–181.
One should place [the mantra] "oṃ dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" upon the hands;
by merely touching water with the mantra "oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ," one becomes purified from sin and shall go to Hari. 182
Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam.
Oṃ, we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects.
Oṃ, water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Oṃ.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, accompanied by twelve Oṃkāras, three times during the twilight (sandhyā) while performing breath-retention (kumbhaka),
and having recited the twenty-four-syllabled Sāvitrī during the worship of the Sun (sūryopasthāna),
one becomes superior in great knowledge (mahāvidyā) and attains the state of Brahman. 183.
Listen with effort to the *Gāyatrī* of six bellies (*ṣaṭkukṣi*) pertaining to the Son (*putra*), knowing which a twice-born man indeed goes to the station of the Supreme Brahman.
(184) Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. (185)
Now, the characteristics of the five-headed Gāyatrī: Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam, Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. 186.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) once again with the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyahṛtis;

thus liberated from all sins, one shall attain union with Viṣṇu. (187) One should place: *oṃ bhūḥ* on the two feet; *oṃ bhuvaḥ* on the knees; *oṃ svaḥ* on the waist; *oṃ mahaḥ* on the navel; *oṃ janaḥ* on the heart; *oṃ tapaḥ* on the hands; and *oṃ satyam* on the forehead.
"Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt"—this [mantra] is for the crest-lock (śikhā).
188. A Brahmin who does not know this is indeed the lowest of Brāhmaṇas.
The sin of one who bows [to this] does not perish; he shall receive abundant gifts.
He who knows this Gāyatrī, endowed with all seeds, knows the four Vedas, the knowledge of Yoga, and the three-fold recitation. 189–190.
He who does not know even this is considered a Śūdra; one should not offer the ancestral *pārvaṇa* rites to such an impure Brāhmaṇa.
No bath yields its fruit for him, and everything becomes fruitless. 191.

Since learning, wealth, birth, and the status of a twice-born are the causes [of merit], all these are fruitless for him, like a flower offered upon an impure place. In ancient times, the four Vedas and the Gāyatrī were weighed by me. (192–193)
The Gāyatrī, which bestows liberation, is remembered as superior to the four Vedas;
it destroys the sin produced by ten births, that committed in a hundred previous lives, and even the sins of three ages when recited a thousand times.
If one recites the Gāyatrī on a rosary both evening and morning,
one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of all four Vedas.
That twice-born man who recites the Gāyatrī daily at the three junctions of the day for a full year [attains the same].
His sin arising from ten million births goes to destruction;
by the mere utterance of the Gāyatrī, he is purified from a mass of evil.
By reciting it daily, the best of the twice-born attains both heaven and liberation.
He who recites the mantras of Vāsudeva day after day and bows at the feet of Hari shall attain liberation (apavargitā). Furthermore,
the hymns of Vāsudeva and the most excellent narratives should be kept in one's mouth.
Even if only a mere fragment of mud from that [river] remains on his body,

he obtains the fruit of bathing in the triple-streamed Ganges through immersion in the Vedas and Shastras; and for those who recite the Dharma in this world, he obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
O best of the twice-born, I am unable to describe such excellent qualities;
for who else is the embodied Viśvarūpa, who is indeed Hari in person, by whose curse one’s life, knowledge, fame, and purity may be destroyed? (201–202)
Through the granting of boons, all prosperities likewise arrive; and through the grace of the Brahmins, Viṣṇu always attains devotion toward the Brahmins. 203.
Salutations to the God who is devoted to the Brahmins and who acts for the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
"Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the benefactor of the world, to Govinda.
(204) That man who constantly worships Hari with this very mantra—Hari becomes gracious toward him, and he shall attain union with Viṣṇu. (205)
Whoever should hear this meritorious narrative, which is the very embodiment of Dharma, their sins— whatever has been committed throughout many lifetimes— shall go to destruction.
Whoever recites it, causes it to be recited, or acts as an instructor for people;
For one who has performed this dance, there is no returning [to rebirth]; he enjoys imperishable heaven.
There he shall obtain wealth, grain, royal enjoyments, and freedom from disease;
he shall have virtuous sons and auspicious fame, and like a god, he rejoices in the celestial realm.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Purificatory Rites of the Brāhmaṇas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Seven.
Nārada said:

"By your grace, O Lord of Gods, I have come to know that most meritorious Brahmin, as well as the lowest of Brahmins, according to my understanding through their actions. Speak quickly, O best of gods, if you desire my pleasure."
Brahmā said:
He who is devoid of the ten kinds of ablutions as well as libations and other rites,
and who is lacking in the twilight prayers and self-restraint— he alone is the lowest of Brahmins.
By means of worshiping the gods, observing vows, as well as the knowledge of the Vedas and so forth,
and by truthfulness, purity, and the like, and by satisfying the fire of yogic knowledge— the great seers have proclaimed these to be the five types of baths for Brahmins.
The baths are those of Agni, Varuṇa, Brahmā, Vāyu, and Divya.
The bath with ashes is called Āgneya; that with water is called Vāruṇa; that with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" is Brāhma; and that with the dust of cows is remembered as Vāyavya.
The divine bath is said to consist of water from the sun's heat and rain.

By performing these baths with mantras, one obtains the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas). Likewise, one gains merit through water that has come into contact with a *tulasī* leaf or a *sālagrāma* stone.
The water from the horns of cows, the water from the feet of Brahmins,
and likewise that from one's principal gurus— this is remembered in the Smṛtis as "the purest of the pure.
(8) Likewise, [purification is attained] through renunciation, pilgrimages, sacrifices, vows, and fire-offerings.
Whatever fruit a wise man obtains through these ritual baths,
that same fruit he attains by constantly performing libations for the ancestors;
yet one who neglects the ancestral rites goes to hell, as does a Brahmin who omits the *saṃdhyā* prayers.
A Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of mantras and vows, even if possessed of the qualities of Vedic knowledge, and who is excluded from sacrifices, gifts, and other such rites, is the lowest of the low.
Those who perform sacrifices for hire, temple-priests, and those who officiate at sacrifices for Kṣatriyas or common villagers [are likewise degraded].
Those who are constantly devoted to the wives of others— these five are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas.
Those devoid of mantras and purificatory rites, lacking purity and self-restraint, eating in vain, and evil-minded— these Brāhmaṇas are the lowest of the low.
Deluded by the desire for gain, devoid of all dharma, and constantly treading upon the wrong path, these Brāhmaṇas are the lowest of the low;
they are bereft of rites such as the Śrāddha and abandoned by service to their gurus. 14.

Those who do not observe the rules of social intercourse and do not respect established boundaries are the lowest of the low. These wicked men are not to be spoken to; they all go to hell. They are impure, of evil conduct, and unworthy of honor in every respect.
Those who subsist by the sword, those who are servants, those twice-born men devoted to riding cattle,

those who live by the work of artisans, those who are usurers for a group, those who trade in children, those who practice sorcery, and those who have taken refuge with outcastes— [these are excluded]. 17.
Those who are ungrateful and those who kill their gurus are remembered as the lowest of all.

Furthermore, those others who are of corrupt conduct, who revile heretical doctrines, who defame the various classes of gods, and who hate the Veda—these twice-born ones are enemies of Brahman. 18–19.
Nevertheless, O best of the twice-born, a Brahmin must never be killed;
by killing him, a man becomes a slayer of a Brahmin and is reborn among the lowest castes, the Mlecchas, and the Cāṇḍāla tribes. 20.

One who has fallen from either food or caste should not be killed under any circumstances. Even after approaching a woman of every caste or eating everything that is forbidden to eat, the status of a twice-born is not destroyed; through merit, a Brahmin may become so again.
Nārada said: "O Grandfather of all the worlds, having committed such an evil deed, if one subsequently performs meritorious acts, what destination does that brāhmaṇa attain? (23)
Brahmā said: "He who, having committed all manner of sins, subsequently conquers his senses, is liberated from all those sins and is worthy once again of the state of Brahman. (24)
Listen to this delightful, wonderful, and ancient tale concerning a certain Brāhmaṇa who had a son endowed with great youthfulness.
Then, due to the perfection of his youth, delusion, and the influence of past karma—

He immediately went to a Cāṇḍālī woman and became more beloved to her than anyone else. Having begotten sons and daughters upon her, he abandoned his own family and remained in her house for a long time.
He did not eat any other forbidden food, and out of revulsion he would avoid liquor.
She said to him, "Always eat one kind of liquor or the other.
He then said to her, "O beloved, you ought not to speak such impurity."
From hearing her [laughter], a belch constantly arose from me.
Once, exhausted from searching for deer, I slept in my house during the day; she took some liquor, laughed, and put it into my mouth. 29–30.

Then, from the mouth of the Brahmin, fire blazed forth on all sides; that flame, together with its family, consumed the house and the wealth. Crying out "Alas! Alas!", the twice-born man rose up and lamented.
At the conclusion of his lamentation, he indeed began an inquiry:
"From where has this fire arisen, and how has my house been consumed by it?
Then the crow spoke these words to him regarding the splendor of that brāhmaṇa: 32-33.

When this account of events as they occurred had been told, the Brāhmaṇa was filled with wonder; reflecting upon its meaning, he spoke these beneficial words to him again in the sky: "O Brāhmaṇa, your great luster has vanished; therefore, become a practitioner of dharma."
Then that twice-born man, having approached the best of sages, asked about his own welfare.
All the sages said to him, "Practice the dharma of giving.
The Ṛṣis said:
The Brāhmaṇas are purified from all sins by means of restraints and vows;
for the sake of purification, he practiced the restraints prescribed in the scriptures, as well as the Cāndrāyaṇa, Kṛcchra, and Taptakṛcchra penances again and again. 36–37.

To quickly dry up your faults, go swiftly to the holy places (tīrthas) belonging to Prajāpati and those that are celestial; perform the worship of Govinda, and your sins will perish from all sides before long. 38.
"By the power of this holy pilgrimage site and by the grace of Govinda,
your sins shall perish and you shall attain the state of Brahman.
Listen, therefore, as we relate the ancient account of how it happened."
Seeking food, the calf, Garuḍa, and the son of Vinatā likewise emerged directly from their eggs like moths;
the young one, hungry, said to his mother, "Give me something to eat. 41.
Then, seeing her son Garuḍa, who was as massive as a mountain and possessed of great strength, the highly fortunate mother was delighted in her heart and said:
"O son, I am not able to satisfy my hunger from all sides."

Your father, the righteous-souled Kaśyapa, who is the grandfather of the worlds in person, is performing austerities on the northern bank of the Lauhitya river; go there and ask him whatever you desire. 44.
Go there and ask your father as you wish.
"By his instruction, father, your hunger and distress will cease.
(45) Then, having heard his mother’s words, the mighty Vainateya, swift as thought, went to his father's presence in a mere moment. (46)
Having seen his father, that best of sages, blazing like a fire,
the bird bowed his head and spoke these words to his father:
"I have come here as a son seeking food for you, O high-souled one."
"O Lord, I am tormented by hunger; let food be given to me.
Then, having entered into meditation and recognized him as the son of Vinatā, that best of sages spoke these words out of affection for his son: 48–49.
"Many hundreds of thousands of most wicked Niṣādas dwell on the shore of the lord of rivers; devour them and become happy.
Those difficult-to-approach 'crows of the sacred ford' (tīrthakākas) are desecrating the holy site."
"Without the Brahmin, eat the Niṣādas unobserved.
Having been told this, the bird then began to devour them;
even the Brahmin, remaining unnoticed, was swallowed by that bird.
Then,
as the bird was firmly caressing his neck with its beak, that best of birds was unable either to swallow it or to vomit it up.
Having gone to his father, he then said, "O Father, what is this?"
"O Meghalaka, I shall not be able to remedy the state of being possessed by the *lagna*.
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa said to him: "O child, you do not understand that this is a Brāhmaṇa whom I previously described to you."
Having spoken thus, the wise and righteous sage laughed at the twice-born man and said, "Come near me; I shall grant you what is for your benefit.
Then the brahmin spoke to Kaśyapa, the bull among sages.

All these relatives of mine are always dear to me—my fathers-in-law, my brothers-in-law, my kinsmen, and others along with their children; shall I go with them to hell or even to the auspicious state? 57-58.
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa was struck with amazement and said:
"Though born in a family of the twice-born, you have fallen among the Cāṇḍālas;
such men certainly dwell in a terrible hell."
For them, there is no atonement whatsoever here in this world by any means.
Even all those of wicked conduct, Cāṇḍālas, and evildoers become happy only after they have abandoned their faults; it cannot be otherwise.
If one has committed a most terrible sin out of ignorance or delusion,
he who subsequently practices dharma shall go to the supreme goal.
A doer of evil should not practice dharma, nor should he again set his mind upon sin.
Just as one who has boarded a boat made of stone sinks in the ocean,
so too, after committing all manner of sins and accumulating a store of miserable rebirths,
he shall later become tranquil and pacify that very fault.
He spoke to that highly wise brahmin, the best among the foremost sages:
"If this bird does not abandon me here, nor all my kinsmen, then I shall give up my life, for this bird strikes at my vital organs."
"Otherwise, let him abandon his kinsmen rather than break the vow of one so firm in soul.
Then, out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the sage said this to Tārkṣya:
"Vomit forth all these Mlecchas along with the Brahmins from every side."
O Lord of Birds, knowing the fault, he then quickly flew up from there through the forests, the mountain slopes, and all directions at his father’s command.
Thereupon, they all became clearly visible, devoid of hair and beards.

Those who resemble Yavanas, who delight in eating forbidden food, and who have some facial hair (69); those who maintain no sacred fire despite being entitled to it due to sin, who are abusive toward the south;
those who are terrible, who delight in the slaughter of living beings, who are evil-minded, and who subsist on the flesh of cows (70).
In the southwest dwell the wicked ones who speak like rākṣasas and are intent on killing cows and brahmins;
in the west reside the terrible kharparas;
and in the northwest are the caturuṣkas, whose faces are covered in beards and who eat cows.
Mounted on the backs of horses, they do not retreat in battle.
In the north, there are mlecchas who dwell in the mountains; they eat all things, are of evil conduct, and are indeed devoted to killing and binding [their enemies]. 72-73.
In the northeast are the hells belonging to those who perform [cruel] deeds, where tree-dwellers reside; these are the Mlecchas situated there, fierce with hunger and with weapons in their hands,
by the mere touch of whom one should enter the water along with one's clothes.
Even in these Kali regions, devoid of righteousness and at improper times,
they will engage in sexual contact on all sides out of greed for wealth;
and having freed those Mlecchas, he (the king) will be utterly tormented by hunger.
The twice-born Tātaka spoke again: "Hunger oppresses me exceedingly.
Thereupon Kaśyapa quickly said to Garuḍa out of compassion:
"The two great ones, the elephant and the tortoise, are standing there, desiring to kill you."
"O immeasurable Great Beings, from one part of the ocean, you two shall quickly drink the water and satisfy your hunger like calves.
Having heard their father's words, they went there and approached it. 78–79.
Having torn apart the great beings, the tortoise and the elephant, with his claws,
that one of great speed and immense strength, possessing the velocity of lightning, seized them both and leapt into the sky;
even the mountains, Mandara and the rest, could not serve as a support for him.
Then, having traveled a hundred thousand yojanas with the speed of the wind, the mighty lord of birds alighted upon a great jambu branch;
that branch suddenly broke as he descended. 81–82.

Terrified by the slaughter of cows and Brahmins, the powerful one seized him with great speed; having caught that exceedingly strong one as he was fleeing with beautiful velocity, Viṣṇu, Hari assuming a human form, approached and spoke this: 83.
"Who are you that wander in the sky, and for what purpose, O Lord of Birds? Why do you carry this great branch along with these two massive elephants and tortoises?
To him, the bird spoke of Hari, who had assumed a human form.
"O mighty-armed one, I am Garuḍa, the son of the sage Kaśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā, having become a bird through my own karma.
Behold these two great beings held by me for the purpose of devouring them."
Neither lower vessels nor trees, nor even mountains could serve as supports;
seeing the Jambū tree rising many yojanas high, they fell upon its branch to eat the golden fruit from above. 87–88.
"What shall I do? How will he endure my speed?
When this was said, Hari then spoke thus to the best of birds:
"Mounting upon my arm, let us devour the elephant and the tortoise."
Garuḍa said:
"The oceans and the best of mountains do not even reach my support;
how then will you sustain such a great being?"
"O Ṛta, who other than Nārāyaṇa is capable of supporting me? What man alone in the three worlds could withstand my force? 93.
Hari said:
"A wise man should accomplish his own task; perform your own task now. O best of birds, once you have performed your duty, you will certainly recognize me. 94.
And having seen that great-souled being, the bird reflected upon it in his mind.
Having said, "So be it," he fell upon the great-armed one; yet the arm of that lord of birds did not waver at the impact. Remaining there, he released his tail-tuft onto the mountain-dweller.

By the mere falling of the branch, the earth with its forests of moving and unmoving beings trembled, and the oceans shook violently. Then, the two creatures, an elephant and a tortoise, were suddenly devoured.
He too did not attain satisfaction, and his hunger was not appeased.
Knowing this, Govinda spoke to that lord of birds: "Eat the flesh from my own arm and be at ease. 98-99.

When he had said this, O son, that man of great wisdom ate the abundant meat before him; indeed, his hunger was not satisfied, yet no wound was found upon him. Then he spoke to Hari, the preceptor of all moving and unmoving beings: 100. "O most wise one, [I have eaten much, yet my hunger remains]. He spoke thus to Hari, the teacher of the animate and inanimate world.
"Who are you, and what is it that you desire? What shall I do for you now?
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Know me to be Nārāyaṇa, who has come here for the sake of your welfare."
To provide proof for him, he indeed revealed his own form:
dark as a rain cloud, wearing yellow garments, four-armed and enchanting,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, the sovereign of all the gods.
And having seen him, Garuḍa bowed his head to Hari and said,
"O Puruṣottama, what pleasing service shall I perform for you?
To him, the Lord of the gods, Hari, endowed with great splendor, replied:
"O hero, you have indeed destroyed existence itself for all time.
To him, the best of birds replied: "O Lord of the gods, I am blessed; O Master, having seen you today, my birth has become fruitful. (105-106)
"Having requested my parents' permission, I shall come to your presence.
Viṣṇu, being pleased, said this: "Become free from old age and death;
you shall be invulnerable to all beings, and your power of action shall be equal to mine."
May there be movement everywhere, and may all happiness be entirely constant. 108.
May everything that dwells in your mind quickly be fulfilled; you shall obtain food according to your desire and to your heart's content, without any hardship. 109.
"You shall immediately deliver your mother from this calamity; it cannot be otherwise. Having spoken thus, Hari vanished on the spot.
Tārkṣya also went to his father and then related everything that had occurred.
Having heard this a hundred times, his soul filled with joy, he spoke again to his son:
"I am blessed, O best of birds; blessed is your auspicious mother; blessed is the field and the lineage in which you, such as this, are the son."
He whose son is born in the family as a supreme Vaiṣṇava shall uplift ten million ancestors and attain union with Viṣṇu;
he who constantly worships Viṣṇu, meditates upon Viṣṇu, and sings [His praises].
One should always recite the mantra of Viṣṇu and shall chant his hymn of praise (114).
One should constantly partake in His grace and observe a fast on the day of Hari;
through the destruction of all sins, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt (115).

Only he who has accumulated a store of virtuous deeds over thousands of millions of births shall, through his merits, attain the servitude of that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), in whose mind Govinda always dwells. 116.
Through the destruction of all sins, one attains the status of a servant of Viṣṇu.
(117) Blessed is that man in the world who attains similarity with Viṣṇu—the eternal Lord of the worlds, the infallible and immutable, who is worshipped by the best of gods. (118)
He with whom [the Lord] is well-pleased is indeed the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Viṣṇu is not attained by the gods even through many austerities, various religious duties, or diverse sacrifices; yet he is easily won over by you.
"Deliver your mother from this terrible calamity caused by her co-wife;
then, having performed the rites for your mother and received your father's command, you shall go to the Lord of Gods after obtaining a great boon from Viṣṇu. (120-121)
Having gone to his mother's side, delighted, he bowed to her and stood before her;
Vinata said:
"O Mother, today you have had food, and your father has also been seen by you. (122)
"O Kīrtimāvatī, why do you delay? I am indeed distressed by anxiety.
Having heard the words of her mother-in-law, Garuḍa spoke of the situation as if laughing;
she, having heard it, was struck with wonder.
"How is it that you have performed such a difficult task since childhood?
Blessed am I and blessed is my lineage, for you have become a friend of Viṣṇu.
Having obtained this boon and having seen the Great-Souled One, my mind rejoices."
"By your manly effort, you have rescued both my lineages.
Suparṇa said:
"O Mother, what shall I do for you? Tell me that which is pleasing to you. (126)
"Having accomplished my task, I shall then go to the side of Nārāyaṇa.
Hearing this, the virtuous Vinatā said to Garuḍa:
"I have great sorrow; O Father, provide a remedy for it."

"Formerly, through my own arrogance, I was sold as a slave by my sister-in-law; who can deliver me from this state? Having made Kṛṣṇa [the target] with poisons, her sons, the great serpents, [have done so]. (128-129)
At dawn she said, "This horse will turn black"; then I spoke there, saying, "He is always dark by his own luster. "Your word is false, Mother," she replied, and then she made a solemn vow.
Then I spoke to Kadrū, the mother of the nāgas, taking an oath:
"If this horse of Hari becomes black, then I shall become your slave"—this is what I said at that time. (131-132)
Then, when Kṛṣṇa had been made a horse for Hari by those artificial [means], she was reduced to slavery at that time by his sons and rogues;
indeed, at whatever time I gave her her desired wealth, [she was thus treated]. 133.
"At that time, you were indeed Adā; I shall go there, O delighter of your lineage.
Garuḍa said:
"O mother, ask her quickly, and I will perform the remedy."
"I shall devour those nāgas; thus let my vow be made true.
Then Vinatā, being distressed, said this to Kadrū: "O auspicious one, tell me what you desire, so that I may be released from this hardship."
That woman of evil conduct said, "Let nectar be given.
Having heard these words, she became lusterless.
Then, approaching her son slowly, she spoke in her distress.
"O sinful one, what will you do by seeking the nectar?
Having heard these words, Garuḍa, filled with great rage, said:
"I shall bring the nectar; O mother, do not turn away from me."
Having spoken thus, he departed with great speed toward his father, thinking,
"O sinless one, I shall now bring nectar for the sake of my mother. To him,
as he was speaking these words, the sage spoke to the Lord of Birds:
Furthermore, above Satyaloka, there exists a city fashioned by Viśvakarman,
a beautiful assembly hall for the benefit of the gods;
it is difficult to reach due to its walls of fire and is unassailable even by the Asuras and the Suras.
A god of great strength was created there by the deities for the sake of protection;
whatever hero he beholds, that very person shall be reduced to ashes.
Suparṇa said:
"O best of sages, a boon was obtained by me from Nārāyaṇa:
'There shall be no fear here for me, even from the hosts of gods and asuras.
Having spoken thus, Garuḍa drew up water from the ocean.
Entering the sky, the bird, swift as thought, flew upward;
yet the abundant dust raised by his very wings did not leave his vicinity, for it followed him closely.
Having gone there, the powerful one extinguished the fire with water from his beak;
yet, with his eyes filled with dust, the asura did not see him.
The powerful one struck down those groups of guards and carried away the nectar.
Having gone to the one who was bringing the bird of nectar, Śatakratu,
mounted upon Airāvata, spoke these words: "Who are you, assuming the form of a bird, that you carry off the nectar by force?"
"Having done what is displeasing to all the gods, how can he live?
With arrows resembling fire, I shall lead him to my abode.
Having heard these words of Hari, that one of great strength spoke out of anger.
"O Unmeasurable One, show your prowess; do not drink [our] nectar.
Having heard this, the mighty-armed one struck with sharp arrows, just as a cloud strikes the peak of Mount Meru with a downpour of rain. 151–152.
With his talons resembling thunderbolts, Garuḍa tore apart the elephant,
as well as Mātali’s chariot wheel and the gods who were leading the way.
Mātali and that preeminent elephant were deeply distressed, O mighty-armed one.
Then all the hosts of gods were turned away by the wind from his wings.
Thereupon, Jishnu became enraged and struck him with his thunderbolt;
yet the great bird was not shaken by the falling of the thunderbolt.
Seeing his own thunderbolt rendered fruitless and shattered, Hari then became afraid;
withdrawing from that battle, he vanished on the spot.
As he was departing with great speed, he reached the surface of the earth.
That best of the asuras spoke in the presence of all the hosts of gods. Śakra said: "O Mother of the Nāgas, if you will now give me the nectar,"
"O sinless one, all the serpents and gods will certainly be made [subservient] by her;
once this vow is undertaken, the fruit of your life will not be lost.
Therefore, with your consent, O blameless one, I shall take her. (158-159)
Garuda said:
"O Hari, at what time will your mother, having been made a slave and being afflicted with grief, become known throughout all the worlds, and you will take away the nectar? (160)
Having spoken thus, the one of great valor went and said to his mother:
"O Mother, let this nectar that has been brought be given to her alone.
Seeing her son together with the nectar, she was filled with joy in her heart.
Having summoned her and given her the nectar, she then became his slave;
at that time, all the gods and great sages were filled with wonder upon seeing the grass, wood, living beings, cattle, and reptiles. 162–163.
Having properly released his mother, Garuḍa departed;
in the meantime, Śakra suddenly carried off the nectar, having placed the poison there unobserved by her. 164.
With a heart full of joy, Kadrū, in great excitement, summoned her sons;
she placed into their mouths the nectar-like *auṣṭra* (camel’s milk), which was characterized by immortality.
Then the mother spoke to her sons: "In your family, this shall always be so."
Then the great sages, the gods, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and humans, their hearts filled with joy, spoke from their mouths: "O Mother, by your grace, may there be offspring for our lineage. 167.
Dismissed by the Nāgas, the gods, along with the Siddhas and sages, departed for their own abodes; the Nāgas remained there, joyful and delighted.
Meanwhile, Garuḍa forcibly devoured the remaining Nāgas.
The remaining ones have fled in all directions; they stay on mountains and in forests, in oceans and in the netherworld,
in caves and in the hollows of trees, or in secluded bowers, while even the serpents remain at ease.
The serpents were ordained by destiny to be his constant food. Having gratified the Nāgas, conversed with his parents,
and honored the gods, he then went to the imperishable Hari.
Whoever should read or even hear this auspicious account of Suparṇa’s deeds shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of the gods. 173.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Birth of Garuḍa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The forty-eighth chapter.
Brahmā said:
O brahmin-sage, beyond this, a twice-born man who has become a Cāṇḍāla or an outcaste—
Having lamented many sorrows, he went to the sage Kaśyapa.
Having approached, he said to the best of sages: "O best of sages, speak words for our benefit; act in such a way that I may be liberated from this sin."
To him, the highly effulgent Kaśyapa spoke with a slight smile on his face from all sides:
"By the mere sight of the Mlecchas, you have indeed become pacified yourself."
By reciting the Gāyatrī, performing fire-offerings (homa), and observing vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa,
while constantly remembering the feet of Hari and fasting on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī); by meditating upon Hari day and night and prostrating before the Lord— 4.
"By bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) with the recitation of mantras, you shall reach the end of the mire.
Then, through the destruction of sin, O twice-born one, you shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa; and by means of vows superior even to bulls, destroying your impurity, you shall attain liberation."
Having heard the words of that sage, he then became one who had accomplished his purpose;
having performed various meritorious deeds, he attained the state of Brahmā once again. Then, having performed intense penance, he went to the heavenly world for a long time.
For one of good conduct, all sin perishes day by day;
for one of evil conduct, merit indeed perishes like collyrium. A Brahmin destroyed by improper conduct may go to the state of a dog through [the lack of] proper conduct. 8–9.

Then, with his life-breaths reaching his throat, the twice-born performed his duties; always practice good conduct through action, mind, and body. By the instruction of Kaśyapa, the twice-born became humble.
But having again practiced right conduct and performed austerities, he went to heaven. A Brahmin who lacks right conduct is slain and despised in the heavenly worlds;
yet, by practicing right conduct once more, he is glorified in the world of the gods.
Nārada said: "O Lord, by honoring the best of the twice-born, people attain their destination; but by causing pain to the twice-born, what destination does one go? (13)
Brahmā said:
That man who does not worship, according to his ability and with devotion, the high-souled brāhmaṇas whose bodies are tormented by hunger, goes to hell. 14.
He who, having reviled another with harsh words, releases them without anger,
shall go to the terrible hell known as Mahāraurava-kṛcchra;
returning from there, he is born among insects and other low-born species.
Therefore, one should not despise a Brahmin who has come to one's house afflicted by hunger, even if that Brahmin is diseased or poor.
He who says "I will not give" to the gods, the sacred fire, or a Brahmin [is a sinner]. 16–17.
Having gone through hundreds of animal births, he enters the state of a Cāṇḍāla; he who, raising his foot, strikes a Brahmin, a cow, his parents,
or his teacher, will certainly dwell in the Raurava hell, for there is no atonement for him.
If, by some merit, he should obtain a birth, he would become lame;
being exceedingly wretched, despondent, and oppressed by pain and grief, having thus experienced three births, there would be his atonement. 19-20.
That man who strikes a Brahmin with his fists, slaps, or blows him on the head, shall dwell for the duration of a kalpa in the terrible Tāpana and Raurava hells.
Then, upon taking birth again, he becomes a fierce and savage dog.
Even if born among the lowest castes, he will be poor and afflicted by abdominal pain and colic.
Furthermore, that man who raises his foot [in disrespect] shall have elephantiasis in his foot, or he shall become lame, or have weak shanks, or have a crippled foot. (22-23)
Indeed, his limbs always tremble from the wind of his own wings;
having killed his mother, father, a brahmin, a snātaka, an ascetic,
or a multitude of elders out of anger, he shall dwell for a long time in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Having lived there, he shall thereafter be born among the species of insects. Furthermore,
O son, for one who speaks words that are hostile and harsh toward the twice-born,
eight types of leprosy will firmly arise upon his body.
Eczema, scabies, ringworm, circular patches, leucoderma, pityriasis versicolor, black leprosy, as well as white leprosy, and the most dreadful early-stage leprosy—
then, through the physician's application [of treatment], merit flees from sin.
Due to a lack of merit, one may meet one's end by this very [disease], like a line drawn upon water.
Among these, three types of mahākuṣṭha are proclaimed: Kālakuṣṭha, Śukla, and the exceedingly terrible Taruṇa. 28–29.
For those who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka), whether through knowledge [of the act] or even through association,
three [defects] indeed arise within their bodies.
Through association and intimate connection, disease spreads among men.
A wise man should avoid these from a distance; having touched them, he should perform a ritual bath.
Having touched one who has fallen from his caste, one afflicted with leprosy, a Cāṇḍāla, a cow-eater, a dog, a woman in her menses, or a Bhilla, he should perform a ritual bath.
In accordance with their sins, those who steal the property of a Brahmin suffer from leprosy manifesting upon their bodies;
there is no doubt that this occurs both in this world and in the next.
(33) He who steals the property of a Brahmin robs his own means of livelihood acquired through righteous means.

Having reached the Akṣaya hell, there is no further rebirth for him. One who is a slanderer of Brahmins, intent on seeking out their faults—upon seeing or even touching such a person, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. 34–35.
Brahmanical property, when consumed out of friendship, burns the family unto the seventh generation;
but one who consumes it by force destroys ten ancestors and ten descendants.
They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison.
Poison kills only one person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys his sons and grandsons.
Having out of delusion approached his mother, a Brahmin woman, or the wife of his teacher, he falls into the terrible Raurava hell, from which rebirth is difficult to obtain. 37–38.
The ancestors of such a person fall into Kumbhīpāka, Tāpana, Avīci, Kālasūtra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava;
indeed, they never consider any atonement for them possible. 39.
By slaying the twice-born, one goes oneself to the state of no-return;
thousands of men fall into that Raurava hell.
Nārada said:
"The sin resulting from the killing of all Brahmins is equal; or how could it be unequal? You ought to tell me this according to the truth.
Brahmā said:

Having killed a Brahmin, one certainly incurs the terrible sin of patricide that has been described; furthermore, listen to what else must be said: he partakes in the slaughter of thousands of millions of Brahmins. 42–43.

Having killed a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is endowed with the knowledge of the Vedas and the scriptures and has his senses subdued, and having killed a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin, one falls ten times further than that. Having caused his own lineage to fall, he does not attain rebirth again.
Having killed a *snātaka* who has mastered the three Vedas, one finds no end to the slaughter.
45. And for one who kills such a Brāhmaṇa—one learned in the scriptures (*śrotriya*), of virtuous conduct, and purified by sacred fords and mantras—there is no end to the sin. 46.
If a twice-born man should give up his life on account of an injury inflicted by another,
that other person is seen to become a slayer of a Brahmin; likewise, if a twice-born man is tormented or struck with harsh words or violent conduct [by another].
"He for whose sake one would give up one's life, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmaghātī).
He shall be put to death here by the sages, the munis, the gods, all those who know Brahman, as well as by the rulers of countries. 48-49.

Even though he has incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin, he is cooked together with his ancestors; therefore, a wise man should certainly honor a Brahmin who has undertaken a fast unto death (prāyopaveśaka), and even if he is free from faults, one should release one's life-breath for his sake. 50.
One should not proclaim those who are associated with terrible, defiled oaths;
nor one who commits suicide, one who climbs trees, or one who subsists on hollows.
He who would commit suicide becomes a slayer of a Brahmin within his own lineage. 51–52.

He who causes the death of a fetus, or an infant, or a sick person, or a guru, shall himself be a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā), and not merely one who is said to have caused it. Furthermore, that lowest of Brahmins who kills a fellow member of his own lineage (sagotra) or another Brahmin [is likewise a slayer of a Brahmin].
That sin would belong to him alone, and not to the one whom he mentions. O Śūdra, having caused pain to a twice-born man, one may accomplish one's own purpose;
even in that case, there is no sin for the Śūdra, nor could it be otherwise. 54-55.
O best of the twice-born, having slain an assassin who intends to kill at that very moment, the killer is not tainted by those sins;
even if he encounters an assassin who has mastered the Vedanta while in battle.
One may strike back against one who seeks to kill, yet by doing so, he does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
An incendiary, a poisoner, a thief of wealth, a stealer of sleep, and a robber of fields or wives— these six are indeed *ātatāyin*s (assassins).
One who strives to kill a chaff-king, one intent on killing his own ancestors,
a king's follower, and a king himself— these four are considered assassins (ātatāyin).
It is not proper to kill again a Brahmin who has already died at that very moment.
By killing a Pūrṇa, one certainly incurs a terrible slaughter through that act of knowledge (60).
In this world, there is no one equal to a Brahmin; he is worthy of worship as the teacher of the universe.
There exists no greater sin than what occurs from killing him (61).
"He is to be worshipped like a god by the hosts of gods and asuras, as well as by men;
it is certain that there is no one equal to a Brāhmaṇa in the three worlds.
Nārada said:
"O best of gods, you ought to tell me in truth: depending upon which mode of livelihood (*vṛtti*) should a twice-born man live?
Brahmā said:
Alms obtained without asking are superior to those obtained by begging; they are praised and not publicly proclaimed.
Better than that is the livelihood of gleaning grains (*uñchavṛtti*), which is most auspicious among all modes of subsistence.
Relying upon this, the best of sages attain the state of Brahman.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to be accepted from the remnants of a sacrifice, for it belongs to one who has participated in the sacrifice.
Having performed teaching or officiating at a sacrifice, wealth should be accepted by the twice-born;
likewise, having taught, having studied, or having performed an auspicious rite for well-being (svastyayana), [wealth may be accepted].
This is the livelihood for Brāhmaṇas: the acceptance of gifts as the subsistence of the learned.

Those who live by the scriptures, those who live by trees—some of whom are auspicious and some inauspicious—and those who live by trees and creepers, as well as those who live by cultivated crops, [are likewise supported].
67. Those who live by trees and creepers, and those who live by garden crops, [are also supported].
There is sin in the killing of creatures born from food; for the pacification of that fault, one should bestow the nine kinds of grain upon Brahmins.
Otherwise, in this world, the lifespan will certainly diminish due to the taking of life. 68–69.
Therefore, one should give abundantly to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born;
for in the absence [of other means], the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is subsisted upon by Brāhmaṇas.
One should fight in righteous wars and practice the auspicious vow of a hero.

Whatever wealth a twice-born man obtains from a king by means of a righteous livelihood is called pure wealth for the purpose of giving at ancestral sacrifices and other rites. O sinless one, he should always practice the science of archery in conjunction with the Vedas.

One should cause a battle to be fought everywhere, employing spears, lances, maces, swords, and iron clubs on all sides, featuring cavalry, elephant-riders, and chariots as numerous as Indra’s illusions, with combatants positioned both on the ground and in chariots. 73.

How can that merit which is surely obtained by heroes through protecting the twice-born, gods, the eternal ones, women, ascetics, virtuous men, virtuous women, gurus, and kings, be attained by those who discourse on Brahman? 74-75.

Having brought about the destruction of all sins, they enjoy the imperishable heaven; even when facing death in a righteous battle, those Brāhmaṇas who fall in the field of battle go to the supreme abode, which is inaccessible even to the exponents of Brahman.
Listen to the meritorious account of that righteous war exactly as it occurred: they fought face-to-face and did not flee out of cowardice;
they did not strike one who was broken, nor one who turned his back, nor one who was unarmed, nor one who had fled.
Those of evil conduct who, desiring victory, kill one who is not fighting, a coward, one who has fallen, one whose sins have been removed,
an unworthy Śūdra, one who is pleased by praise, or one who has sought refuge in battle,
go to hell.
This is declared to be the conduct of a Kṣatriya by those of virtuous behavior;
relying upon it, all the elephants among Kṣatriyas go to heaven.
For a Kṣatriya, death facing the enemy in a righteous war is auspicious.
He shall become free from debt and liberated from all sins;
he shall dwell in the heavenly world, adorned with palaces and jeweled floors, with pillars made of gold and surfaces embellished with gems. 82.
It was perfectly filled with desired objects and adorned with divine articles;
before it, wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) stood at all times, granting everything;
and it was beautified by ponds, wells, lakes, and gardens. 83–84.
The daughters of the city of the gods, rich in youth, serve him;
before him, the hosts of apsarases dance perpetually with joy.
The Gandharvas sing songs, and the gods recite hymns of praise.
In this manner, at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a sovereign king (sārvabhauma), the sole provider of all enjoyments, free from disease, with a body like that of the god of love (Manmatha).
His wives shall be richly endowed with beauty and always possessed of youth. 86-87.
Virtuous, radiant, prosperous, and honored by their fathers—
such Kṣatriyas enjoy [the fruits of their deeds] for seven births in this sequence.
However, those warriors who act unjustly remain in hell for a long time.
In this way, the livelihood of the Kṣatriyas is supported by Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as others, including the lowest castes and Mleccha tribes;
and those warriors who always fight according to righteous warfare. 89–90.
All twice-born castes may attain the highest state through austerity; however,
a twice-born man who is not brave, but timid and devoid of missiles and weapons,
should, in times of distress, adopt the livelihood of a Vaiśya, O best of the twice-born.
He may cause others to perform the livelihood of a Vaiśya, the state of a merchant, and likewise agriculture; however, he must not abandon the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, such as farming and trade.
If a twice-born man speaks falsely regarding his status as a merchant, he shall fall into a miserable state of existence.
Having abandoned moist substances, the Brāhmaṇa attains auspiciousness;

therefore, having provided a means of livelihood, he should give everything to the Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, at the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), the twice-born man should offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rule.
One must not practice falsehood; the balance is established upon the principle of truth.
By practicing deceit with the balance, one falls into hell.
Furthermore, if there is an unequal amount of goods, one should abandon that which is false.
Thus, falsehood must not be committed, for it gives birth to sin; there is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than untruth. Therefore, in all matters, truth alone is preeminent.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once placed upon a scale.
Indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices. He who speaks the truth in all matters and abandons falsehood is truly distinguished. 98–99.
He easily overcomes all difficulties and attains imperishable heaven;
a Brahmin should engage in trade, but must certainly abandon it if it becomes fraudulent.
He should deposit his interest in a sacred place and himself consume the remainder.
It is always a thousand times more difficult than the affliction of the body.
In the pursuit of wealth, mortals enter treacherous waters, as well as desolate forests and wildernesses infested with wild beasts. 102
Out of greed for wealth, they go everywhere— even to mountains, mountain caves, and the formidable fortresses of weapon-wielding mlecchas, or to terrifying dwellings—
abandoning their children and wives and traveling far away. 103.
Others carry burdens on their shoulders, while others bring about downfall through various means;
with great suffering caused by projectiles and even at the cost of life, O son, the accumulation of wealth is held to be greater than one's own life. 104–105.
By these means, wealth acquired through righteous effort is diligently given by the merchant to ancestors, gods, and the twice-born, and he enjoys its inexhaustible fruit.
These two, however, are great defects in the business of trade for the sake of profit.

Not abandoning greed and selling what should not be sold—these two faults a wise man should avoid while acquiring wealth. By giving in charity, he attains inexhaustible merit and is not defiled by the faults of trade. 107–108.
A Brahmin devoted to meritorious deeds should indeed cause cultivation to be performed;
he should yoke four oxen for half a day.
In the absence of four, he may use three, but he must not cause them to work without rest.
One should graze them on uncut grass in a place free from thieves and tigers;
one should provide fodder as desired and personally satisfy them daily.
One should also construct for them a cow-pen that is free from any obstacles.
The wise man should always place pure cow dung and urine, free from food remnants, in the cow-pen, which is the abode of all the gods; he should have it made to resemble his own bed.
One should diligently extinguish [the fires] with cool winds and dust;
one should view the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as being like [the body], and the cow as having a common form.
Thus, whatever pleasure or pain exists in his body is likewise attributed to that [breath]. 113–114.
Whoever causes agricultural work to be performed according to this method shall not be tainted by the faults associated with ox-drawn vehicles, and he shall become wealthy.
Likewise, one who oppresses the weak or those afflicted by disease [incurs similar consequences].
One who [drives] a very young or very old ox incurs a sin equal to the killing of a cow.
He who drives an unbalanced load, whether it be weak or strong, incurs a sin here on earth equal to the killing of a cow; of this there is no doubt.
He who drives away a cow that is about to perish, or who prevents her from eating while she is chewing,
or out of delusion denies her grass or water, shall incur a sin equal to that of killing a cow.
This applies likewise on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the full moon (paurṇamāsī), and on the new moon (amāvāsyā).
The sin incurred from stealing a plow or from killing ten thousand cows is [purified];
that man who worships these [images] with white powders, colorful pigments, collyrium, flowers, and oils, enjoys an imperishable heaven. (119–120)
He who gives a handful of grass daily to another’s cow attains the destruction of all his sins and enjoys an imperishable heaven;
as is the Brahmin, so is the cow—the fruit of honoring both is equal. 121.
"In deliberation, the Brāhmaṇa is the foremost among men; likewise, among animals, the cow is so.
Nārada said:
"O sinless one, you have told me that the Brāhmaṇa was born from the mouth of Brahmā."
"O Lord, how is it that I am certainly not equal to cows? This causes me wonder.
Brahmā said:
"Listen here to the truth regarding how brāhmaṇas and cows [are related]."
In ancient times, the unification into a single mass was fashioned by the Puruṣas.
Formerly, a great peak consisting of radiant energy emerged from the mouth of Brahmā; from that, four parts were produced: the Veda, fire, the cow, and likewise the twice-born.
Before the emergence of light, the Veda and fire existed;
likewise, the cow and the Brahmin were produced separately one after another.
Therein, at the very beginning, the four Vedas were created by me individually.

For the sake of the stability of all worlds and realms on every side, Agni shall consume the oblations for the sake of the gods, and likewise the twice-born [shall consume] the clarified butter produced from the cow; know this, for they were born from one another. 127–128.

If these four great ones did not exist in the worlds, then the entire universe, both stationary and moving, would perish. By them the worlds are always sustained; they remain established by their very nature.
This very nature is of the form of Brahman; therefore, these are remembered as being composed of Brahman.
For this reason, the cow is to be worshipped even by Brahmins, gods, and demons;
she is noble in all undertakings, born of truth, and a mine of virtues. 130–131.

He is the embodiment of all the gods, manifestly compassionate toward all sentient beings; his task regarding their nourishment was created by me long ago. For this very reason, I granted him a most excellent boon.
"It is certain that liberation shall be yours in this very birth. Those who die right here come to my abode; not even a particle of sin remains within their bodies. (133-134)
The goddess Gaurdhenukā and the gods, the primordial goddess Triśaktikā, are indeed established as the source of all sacrifices through His grace. All things sacred to cows purify the entire world.
The urine, dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter of a cow—
by consuming these, sin does not remain within the body;
therefore, the righteous always consume ghee, curd, and milk.
Among all substances, that which comes from the cow is considered the most distinguished, supreme, and auspicious; for one who has no food in their mouth, their very form becomes foul-smelling.
Food [is required] every five nights, and indeed milk every seven nights.
Curd may be used for twenty nights, and ghee for one month.
(139) But for that mortal who eats food not derived from a cow continuously for one month, the pretas indeed devour his meal. (140)
Having eaten supreme, pure, steamed rice made from sun-dried grains,
whatever merit is performed becomes multiplied ten million-fold. Furthermore, whatever sacrificial food (haviṣya) substance is prescribed by the scriptures—
Whatever deed is performed for one who has eaten that [food], it shall all become a hundred-thousandfold.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from any gift that is free of meat, the cow alone is praised for all purposes in every age. 142–143.
He is the giver of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa at all times and for all desires.
Nārada said: By what means or by what application is the highest merit proclaimed? (144)
"Speak, O Lord of all the worlds, so that I may know it according to reality.
Brahmā said:
"Having performed a single circumambulation, one should salute the wealth of cattle. 145
Freed from all sins, he enjoys imperishable heaven; he is as venerable as the preceptor of the gods and as worthy of worship as Mādhava himself.
Having performed seven circumambulations, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, attained sovereign power.
Rising at dawn, the practitioner of yoga should take his vessel along with water into the midst of the cattle and sprinkle it upon the horn;
he should receive that water directly upon his head while fasting—now learn of the merit thereof. 147–148.
O Nārada, those holy fords (tīrthas) that are heard of in the three worlds,
frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and great Ṛṣis—
the bathing in all of them is equal to bathing in the water from the tips of a cow's horns. 149.
The mortal who, having risen at dawn, touches a cow, ghee, honey, mustard seeds, and priyaṅgu grains, is liberated from sin.
Cows are the givers of ghee and milk; they have their origin in ghee and are produced from ghee.
May rivers of clarified butter with whirlpools of clarified butter always flow in my home;
may clarified butter be in all my limbs, and may clarified butter abide in my mind.
May cows be ever before me, and cows even behind me.
"The cows are in all my limbs, and I dwell in the midst of the cows.
Having sipped water (ācamana) thus, one who is pure should mutter this mantra morning and evening;
for him, there is the destruction of all sins, and he shall be honored in the heavenly world. 154
As is the cow, so is the Brahmin; as is the Brahmin, so is Hari;
as is Hari, so is the Gaṅgā. For by this, they are remembered as non-different. Cows are the kinsmen of human beings, and human beings are the kinsmen of cows.
That house in which there is no cow is a house devoid of kinsmen.
The Vedas, along with the six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations, reside in the mouth of the cow;
and Hari and Keśava are eternally stationed upon its two horns. 156–157.
Skanda is always stationed in the abdomen, Brahmā in the head,
the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) on the forehead, and Indra at the tips of the horns.
The two divine Aśvins are in the ears, and the Moon and Sun are in the eyes.
While giving [gifts], Lord Garuḍa resides in the tongue and Sarasvatī in the anus; all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside in the passage of urine, and the Ganges in the excretion of semen;
the sages reside in the pores of the skin, Yama in the mouth, and Yama also at the back.
Dhanada and Varuṇa took their places on his right side,
while on his left side stood the Yakṣas, radiant and possessed of great strength.
The Gandharvas were in the middle of his face, and likewise, the Pannagas were at the tip of his nose.
On the western side of the hooves, the Apsarases are likewise stationed.
Lakṣmī resides in the cow dung, and Sarvamaṅgalā in the cow urine.
At the tips of the feet dwell the Vidyādharas; in the sound "haṃ-bhā," I am Prajāpati.
He who constantly touches the four oceans full of cows and their udders, as well as the earth itself, becomes perpetually purified by his bath; therefore,
such a mortal, being fully nourished, is liberated from all sins.
Whoever should bear upon his head the dust raised by the hooves of cows,
he is as one who has bathed in the waters of all sacred fords and is liberated from all sins.
Nārada said:
"O best of gurus, O beloved of Parameṣṭhin, tell me the truth regarding which of the ten classes of cows yields what fruit when given as a gift, if you are pleased with me.
Brahmā said:
By giving a white-limbed cow to a Brāhmaṇa, a human becomes a lord (Īśvara).
By [giving] a temple, one always becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and prospers in happiness.
But by [giving] a smoke-colored cow, one is liberated from sin in the forest of saṃsāra and attains heaven.
The gift of Kapilā is inexhaustible; by giving Kṛṣṇā, one does not suffer.
In this world, Pāṇḍurā is difficult to obtain, as is Gaurī, who brings joy to the family. Raktākṣī is for one desiring beauty, and Nīlikā is for one desiring wealth.
By giving away a one-eyed tawny cow, one is liberated from all sins.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, or in youth, or in old age; whatever was done by speech, or performed through action, or conceived in the mind—[all that is destroyed]. (170-171)

Whoever bestows a Kapilā cow shall swiftly destroy all such [sins]: approaching those who should not be approached, the sin of betraying a friend, cheating with weights and measures, falsehood regarding a maiden, and falsehood regarding a cow. (172)
A great river ten yojanas wide and of vast extent,
with waters as beautiful as iron arrows, spread out in a sea of water until the two feet and the face of Vatsa were no longer visible.
A cow should be known as the Earth as long as she does not release her calf;
she should have horns of gold, be richly clothed, adorned with all ornaments, have a copper-colored back, silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel. 175.
One should give such a tawny cow (kapilā) to a member of the twice-born who has mastered the Vedas— one whose limbs are adorned with perfumes and flowers and who is decorated with all ornaments.
For him, there is the destruction of all sins, and he shall become imperishable in the world of Viṣṇu.
As that earth is being milked, drops fall upon it;
from them arise gardens with many excellent flowers and fruits.
There, the trees yield fruits according to one's desires, and the rivers have mud made of milk-rice (pāyasa). 178.
Moreover, those who give cows go there to golden palaces.
It has been proclaimed and declared by Brahmā that the fruit for one who gives ten cows and one bull is equal. 179–180.
By [releasing] eleven, one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand;
O Nārada, the fruit should be understood with effort according to that proportion. A son who, on this earth, releases a bull in honor of his ancestors—
The ancestors are highly honored in the worlds of Viṣṇu according to their desires.
O son, four heifers and one bull shall be liberated from all bonds; this is the eternal ordinance.
For as many hairs as there are on his body and on those [cows] in every respect,
for that many thousands of years do humans enjoy heaven.
And whatever water a bull surely splashes up with his tail—
Then that water shall become nectar for the ancestors for a thousand years.
If one scrapes the earth with a hoof, or [offers] a clod of earth or mud there to the ancestors with the utterance "svadhā," it becomes multiplied a hundred thousand crore times.
If the mother perishes while the father is still living, and a cow marked with sandalwood paste is given for her sake, the donor indeed releases his debt to the ancestors.
187. And the giver [is freed]; he indeed releases the debt to the ancestors.
He attains imperishable heaven, honored like Maghavat himself.
A cow endowed with all auspicious marks, young, yielding milk, of uniform color, and gentle—that cow is considered equal to the earth. 188–189.
By the gift of this mantra, one obtains a fruit equal to the gift of the earth; such a mortal becomes equal to Indra (Śatakratu) and uplifts a hundred generations of his lineage.
(190) Having committed the theft of cows, even if the cow, the chariot, or the calf has perished...

He shall remain in a well filled with worms until the dissolution of all beings. Having committed the slaughter of cows, he is cooked together with his ancestors in the terrible Raurava hell for that same duration; such is the retribution.

He who destroyed cow-pastures and obstructed the tethering of the vehicles of the gods went to an inexhaustible hell in birth after birth; whereas he who should hear this most meritorious narrative even once [attains liberation]. 193.
All his sins are destroyed, and he rejoices together with the gods.
Whoever hears this supreme, most meritorious, and great [teaching] is indeed liberated at that very moment from the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes. 194–195.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Cows," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-nine. Nārada said:
"By what conduct does the Brahmanic splendor of a Brahmin increase, and by what conduct is that very Brahmanic splendor destroyed?
Brahmā said:
Rising from his bed during the first watch of the night, that best of the twice-born should constantly remember the gods and, likewise, those who are surely meritorious:
Govinda, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, and Dāmodara.
[Namaskāra] to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading;
to Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas;
to Brahmā, the Sun, the Moon, the Guardians of the Quarters, and likewise the Planets.
Śaṅkara, Śiva, Śambhu, Īśvara, Maheśvara, Gaṇeśa, as well as Skanda, Gaurī, Bhāgīrathī, and Śivā—
King Nala of virtuous fame [worshipped] them, as did Janārdana of virtuous fame.
Vedavatī was the wife of Puṇyaśloka, and Yudhiṣṭhira was Puṇyaśloka.
Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa,
Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma— these seven are long-lived.

A person who, having risen in the morning, constantly remembers these [names] is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter. O dear one, by reciting them even once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
One enjoys the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows. Furthermore, one should void excrement and urine in a clean place;
at night one should face south, and by day one should face north.
He should use another person's tooth-stick, or one made of grass, udumbara wood, or similar materials; thereafter, during the twilight, the twice-born man should remain self-restrained.
In the forenoon, he should contemplate her as red in color, and at midday, as white in color.
In the evening, the twice-born man should meditate upon the dark-colored Sarasvatī according to the prescribed rule. Then, he should diligently perform his bath according to his knowledge;
having washed his limbs, he should thereafter smear them with clay.

In the region of the head, the forehead, the nose, the heart, the eyebrows, the two arms, the sides, the navel, the two knees, and likewise the two feet; one [digit] at the anus, three in the left hand, and ten [in the right]. 14.
One desiring purity for both [the donor and the recipient] should give seven handfuls of earth:
"O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu; O Clay, take away my sin that has been accumulated by me in the past. (15–16)
Whoever applies clay to their body with this very mantra,
all their sins are destroyed and that person becomes pure.
Then, the wise one should perform the ritual bath preceded by the Vedas.

Likewise, at rivers, streams, wells, lotus ponds, and small reservoirs, as well as in a body of water or on a riverbank, a mortal should perform the ritual bath with a jar according to the rules for the sake of the destruction of all sins. 18–19.
The morning bath is of great merit and destroys all sins;
the Brahmin who performs it constantly is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
(20) [It should be performed] near the morning twilight for as long as four daṇḍas.
For that long, the water offered remains as nectar for the ancestors. Beyond that, for two ghaṭikās until the end of one watch (yāma) of the day,
the water is equal to honey and increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Then, for one and a half watches (yāmas), the water is traditionally said to consist of milk;
the water mixed with milk remains so for four daṇḍas.
Beyond that, it becomes plain water for three praharas.
That [water] is declared to be "reddish" (lohitam) until the sun has set.

During the fourth watch of the day, or at night during the ritual bath, one should offer libations to the ancestors; that water is traditionally held to belong exclusively to the Rākṣasas, except when it is taken up [for other purposes]. 24–25.
This water was created by me long ago for the sake of all success;
and the yakṣas are the ones entrusted with the responsibility of guarding that water.
Neither do the ancestors, nor those who have gone to other worlds, obtain it.
Water is difficult for them to obtain, except from their own kinsmen dwelling in the mortal world. Therefore, they should be offered libations by disciples, sons, grandsons, daughters' sons,
and other groups of relatives, as well as by others devoted to the ancestral rites.
Nārada said: "O Lord of Gods, tell me the deity of the water and the procedure for the libation (tarpaṇa); you ought to explain it to me truly, so that I may understand it. (29)
Brahmā said:
Viṣṇu is celebrated in all the worlds as the deity of water; he who is purified by water becomes Viṣṇu, and that Viṣṇu becomes Śaṅkara. 30
By drinking even a mere mouthful of water, a man becomes purified;
especially through contact with kuśa grass, this water is superior to nectar.
This darbha grass, the abode of all the gods, was created by me in ancient times.
