Brahmā resides at the root of the *kuśa* grass, Keśava in its middle, and Śaṅkara at its tip; know that these [deities] are established within the *kuśa*. One who holds *kuśa* in hand is always pure, provided he recites hymns and mantras.
It is said that [the merit] at all [ordinary places] is a hundredfold, while at a sacred ford (tīrtha) it is declared to be a thousandfold.
Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, as well as dūrvā, barley leaves, rice,
balvaja grass, and puṇḍarīka— these seven are proclaimed to be types of kuśa.
Established in this world upon *kuśa* grass, they shall become pure in due succession.
Whatever bath is performed without mantras, all of that becomes fruitless;
yet it attains sweetness surpassing even nectar through contact with sesame seeds.
Therefore, a wise person should always satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds and water;
for with ten sesame seeds, the satisfaction of the ancestors is supreme.
Out of fear of a pillar of fire, the gods do not desire excessive elaboration.
He who, having bathed, daily gratifies the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds; he who, by the release of blue and white [bulls], offers sesame-water on the new moon day;
and he who gives lamps during the rainy season—he becomes free from debt to the ancestors. (38-39)
He who offers libations to the ancestors with sesame seeds on the new moon day for one year attains the status of Vināyaka and is honored by all the gods.
He who offers libations to the ancestors with sesame seeds on all the Yugādi days [attains the same].
Or rather, it has been said that on the day of Māyā, the merit is a hundred times greater than that;
likewise, by satiating the assembly of ancestors during the solstices, the equinoxes, and specifically on the day of Rākā, one is glorified in the heavenly world. 41–42.
Likewise, during the period known as an *manvantara*, or during another auspicious occasion, or at the eclipse of the moon or sun, or at holy pilgrimage sites such as Gayā and others,
one who offers libations to the ancestors goes to the abode of Mādhava.
Therefore, having obtained an auspicious day, one should satisfy the assembly of ancestors (44).
Having first performed the libation for the deities with a concentrated mind,
the wise man subsequently becomes qualified for the libation for the ancestors (45).

At the time of feeding during a *śrāddha*, one should cause [the food] to be given with one hand; for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should give with both hands—this is the eternal rule (verse 46). Having become pure and facing south, one should offer libations to the ancestors.

Furthermore, with the words "May they be satisfied," and by means of their names and lineages, if one out of delusion offers libations to the assembly of ancestors using sesame seeds that are not black,
or if the donor gives water while standing on the ground instead of being situated in water; 47–48.
That gift is given in vain; it does not reach anyone. If a man, standing on dry land, offers water [to those in the water], that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless.

O sinless one, if one who is wearing wet clothes performs the water-libation (tarpaṇa) while still in the water, his ancestors are always satisfied along with the gods. The wise know that a garment washed by washermen is impure. 50–51.
By washing one's hands, the cloth is purified once again;

wearing dry clothes in a clean place, wherever one offers libations to the ancestors, the ancestors will certainly be satisfied tenfold more than that. 52. Then, by doing so, the ancestors are indeed satisfied ten times over.
He who performs his ritual bath, the twilight prayers, and the libations (tarpaṇa)— each exceeding a hundred times— upon a stone, a sword, or even a copper vessel; and he who,
wearing a silver ring on his index finger, offers libations to the ancestors (53–54).
And all of that becomes a hundred-thousandfold, not otherwise;
likewise, having placed a golden ring on the ring finger,
the wise man should offer libations to the multitude of ancestors, and it shall become a million-fold or ten-million-fold.

Holding a sword between the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of his left hand, and grasping a jewel in his cupped right hand with the ring finger, he was going toward the bathing place together with the gods and the hosts of ancestors. 56–57.
Afflicted by thirst and seeking water, they follow after [the water] as it becomes wind; yet, like those who turn back in despair from the wringing out of a cloth, they depart disappointed.
Therefore, one should not wring out the cloth without having performed the libations for the ancestors.
Three and a half crores of hairs on this human body are all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); therefore, one should not cause them pain.
The gods drink from them through their heads, and likewise the ancestors through their beards. (59–60)
Even the Gandharvas, all living beings below,
the gods, the hosts of ancestors, the Gandharvas, and likewise all creatures—
by the mere act of bathing they are satisfied; through bathing, no sin remains.
That man who performs the daily bath is a supreme person;
liberated from all sins, he is glorified in various celestial worlds.
The gods and great sages know the ritual to extend as far as the libations (tarpaṇa).
Beyond this, the wise person should perform the worship of the gods;
he who worships Gaṇeśa encounters no obstacles.
For the sake of health, one should worship Sūrya, and for the sake of dharma and liberation, Mādhava.
One should worship Śiva for the sake of one's duties and desires, and Caṇḍikā for the fulfillment of all desires (verse 65).
Having worshipped the gods, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva bali offering;
then, having performed the fire-ritual, the sacrifice, and the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas (verse 66).
Having made his coming and going firm, he shall go again to the third heaven of the gods and all beings, attaining desire, liberation, happiness, and the celestial realm.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always perform the prescribed rites.
Nārada said: "O father, for what reason do the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, not obtain water, O omniscient one, as human beings do?"
Brahmā said:
"In the past, this water—which consists of all the gods and is nectar—was created by me.
For its protection, and for the sake of guarding it, I created the Yakṣas, who are archers."
"By our word, they shall slay even their father, whether he be a god or not a human (70). Whether they be beasts, birds, insects established in the world of mortals,
or those born as mortals who are gods, as well as humans— of this there is no doubt (71)."
Those who constantly gratify their guru are established in the world of the gods;
however, one who does not bathe eats impurity, and one who does not recite prayers eats pus and blood. By failing to perform the daily libation (tarpaṇa), one becomes a slayer of one's ancestors.
"The sin of failing to worship the gods is equal to the murder of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
Furthermore, the sinner who fails to perform the twilight rites (sandhyākṛtya) slays the Sun.
Nārada said:
"Tell me the sequence of the good conduct of a Brāhmaṇa and his duties; tell me also everything that has been prescribed for the other castes.
Brahmā said:
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains happiness (75).
Through right conduct one attains heaven and liberation; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. Indeed, a man who lacks right conduct becomes censured in the world (76).
A man who lacks proper conduct will always share in suffering, be afflicted by disease, and have a short life; indeed, his dwelling in hell is certain because of his lack of conduct.
Through proper conduct, however, one attains the higher world; therefore, hear the truth regarding conduct.
One should always perform the smearing of the house with cow-dung. Then, one should wash the seat, the wooden plank, the vessel, and the stone slab;
a bell-metal vessel is purified by ash, while copper is purified by acid.
A stone bowl is purified by oil; a plowshare by cow-hair; and bowls made of gold, silver, and so forth, are purified by water alone.
An iron vessel is purified by fire, as well as by heating and washing.

The earth becomes pure from impurity through digging, burning, smearing, and washing, as well as by the falling rain of a cloud. This applies to objects made of metal, gems, and everything made of stone.
In the past, I have declared that purification by means of ashes and earth is prescribed for one's own bed,
wife, child, garment, sacred thread, and water-pot;
these are said to be pure for oneself, but never for others.
One should not eat while wearing only a single garment, nor should one bathe with only a single garment (84). One should never wear another person’s bathing cloth.
One should perform the grooming of the hair and teeth only in the morning (85).
One should always perform salutations to one's gurus;
moreover, one should eat while possessing five moist elements in the hands, feet, and mouth. One who eats while possessing these five moist elements lives for a hundred years.

One should not intentionally step over the shadow of deities, a guru, a *snātaka*, a teacher, or even a Brahmin who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*). One should likewise avoid stepping over a herd of cows, an idol of a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, or a crossroads.
One should perform circumambulation around famous trees,
cows, Brahmins, a Brahmin who maintains a sacred fire, and likewise a couple;
one should not pass between them, for if one does so, one will certainly fall from heaven.

One who is impure from eating (ucchiṣṭa) should never touch fire, a Brāhmaṇa, a deity, or a guru; nor should one touch one's own head, a flowering tree, a sacrificial tree, or an unrighteous person. One who is impure from eating should never look upon these three sources of splendor.
Likewise, he should not look at the sun and the moon, nor at the stars in any direction, nor at a Brahmin, a guru, a deity, a king, or the best of ascetics (92),
nor at a yogi, one who performs divine rites, or a twice-born man who is a narrator of the dharmas.

One should not discard bodily waste on the banks of rivers, nor likewise at the confluence of streams, nor at the foot of a sacrificial tree, nor in a garden or a flower-orchard while still alive. (93–94)
A wise man should never have his hair shaved on a Tuesday, nor in the abode of a Brahmin, in a cow-pen, or on beautiful royal highways;
he should not retain dirt in his teeth, nor cast his fingernails into his mouth.
One should not perform an oil massage on a Sunday or a Tuesday (96).
One should not play musical instruments upon one's own body or seat, nor sit on the same seat as one's teacher.
Furthermore, one should not take away the property of a Śrotriya, nor even that of a deity or a teacher (97).
The way must be yielded to a king, to ascetics, to the lame, to the blind, to women, to a Brāhmaṇa, to cows, and to kings;
as well as to the sick, O Bhārata, to one who is distressed, to a pregnant woman, and to the weak. 98.
One should not engage in disputes with kings, Brahmins, or physicians.
One should avoid from a distance a Brahmin, the wife of a guru, an outcaste, one afflicted with leprosy, a Cāṇḍāla, and one who eats cow-flesh. 99–100.
One should avoid from afar one who is devoid of knowledge and has shaken off virtue;
likewise, one should avoid a wicked woman of evil conduct who spreads slander (101),
who performs evil deeds, is corrupt, and is always fond of quarreling.
One should avoid from afar a woman who is intoxicated, excessively corpulent, shameless, promiscuous,
wasteful, and immoral; one should never salute the wife of a guru while she is soiled.

A wise man should not touch her; having touched her, he becomes pure by bathing. He should always avoid playing with her, and he should certainly never listen to her speech nor look upon the wife of his guru. 104.

One should certainly not look upon one's daughter-in-law, one's son's wife, one's own young daughter, nor any other woman who is the wife of a teacher; nor should one allow physical contact with them.
Likewise, one should avoid conversation with them and even the mere sight of their knitting of eyebrows. (105–106)
One should always avoid quarreling and shameless speech; one should never place one's foot upon husks, charcoal, bones, or ashes (107),
nor upon cotton seeds, discarded flower garlands, wood from a funeral pyre, a cremation ground, or a teacher.

One should not eat dried fish that is foul-smelling or impure. Nor should one eat the remnants of a sacrifice (*vighasa*) or other leavings intended for cooking for another. One should not stand nor walk with a wicked person even for a moment.
A wise man should not stand for even a moment under a tree that provides shade only by its proximity to a lamp,

nor should he engage in conversation with those who are untouchable or with those who have fallen from their status and are enraged; having done so, he would go to the Raurava hell for even a single instant.
One should salute a younger paternal uncle, as well as a maternal uncle, at the navel.
Rising up, one should offer a seat while standing before them with palms joined in reverence.
Likewise, one should avoid one who has been anointed with oil, one who is impure from eating, one with wet clothes, and one who is diseased.
One should not salute one who is distressed while crossing from this shore to the other, nor one who has entered into a sacrifice, nor one who is lost, nor one sporting with women,
nor one engaged in children's play, nor one adorned with flowers or holding *kuśa* grass. (113)
Having covered one's head or both ears, or even having released the topknot from the water;

without performing the worship of the feet; facing south; devoid of the sacred thread (upavīta); naked; or with the lower garment untied—one should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). 114–115.
One who is covered by only a single garment and has not sipped water is certainly not purified;
one should first touch the mouth with three middle fingers,
and immediately thereafter the nose with the thumb and the forefinger.
One should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger (117).
One should touch the two ears with the little finger and the thumb, the navel with the thumb alone, the heart by placing the palm there, and the head above with all the fingers (118).

By touching the tips of his arms [with water], a man then becomes pure; by performing the sipping of water (ācamana) with this, a human being becomes disciplined. Liberated from all sins, he enjoys eternal heaven.
Prāṇa is formed by the three fingers with the tips joined; vyāna and apāna by the mudrā;
samāna by all [the fingers]; and udāna by [all] except the index finger.
Nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—these are the five winds. 120–121.
Those who are pleased by what is given on the ground shall be gratified;
one should offer a bed with wet feet and food with dry feet.
One should never cause a meal or sleep to take place in the dark.

One should never brush one's teeth toward the west or the south. One should never sleep toward the north or the west; from such sleep, one's lifespan diminishes and one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin. 123–124.
One should not sleep facing that direction; however, sleeping toward the east or south is auspicious.
One who eats facing the east gains long life; eating facing the south brings ill repute;
one who eats facing the west gains prosperity; and one who eats facing the north gains fame.
In the east, a man obtains long life; in the south, he attains the state of a ghost (preta).
In the west, he becomes afflicted by disease, while in the north, he gains both longevity and wealth.
Furthermore, the gods eat only once a day, whereas for humans, it is twice a day.

The third portion is for the Pretas and Daityas, while the fourth belongs to the Kauṇapas. Humans offer oblations to the gods consisting of fish, meat, and so forth; others, being unrestrained, consume putrid, stale, and impure food.
Among those residing in heaven and those living here in this world of mortals, these four exist within their hearts:
(129) commendable generosity, sweet speech, worship of the gods, and the satiation of Brahmins;
(130) a spirit of miserliness toward one's own kin, censure of others, wearing tattered clothes, and devotion to low-born people.
Excessive anger and harsh speech are the marks of a man who has come from hell;
speech like fresh butter and a mind tender with compassion—this is the visible characteristic of those born from the seed of Dharma. 131.

A heart impoverished of compassion and speech as harsh as a saw—this is the visible mark of those born from the seed of sin. A person who either recites or even merely hears [this teaching] regarding right conduct and so forth [is purified]. 132–133.
"Having obtained the fruit of right conduct (*ācāra*) and the like, purified from sin, he shall dwell in heaven, unshakable.
(134) Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of Right Conduct," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The Fiftieth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said: O Brahmin,
speak according to your own inclination about that merit which is supreme in the world, always esteemed by all, and which was performed by those of old, one after another.
Pulastya said: Once, O twice-born ones, all the disciples of Vyāsa,
having bowed with reverence to Vyāsa, questioned him regarding dharma, just as you have questioned me.
The twice-born said:
"Tell us what is the most meritorious in the world, the highest among all dharmas;
having performed what do human beings enjoy heaven that is imperishable? (3)
Tell me of a single sacrifice that is free from obstacles, pure, attainable by mortals dwelling on earth— whether they be high-born or low-born—
and which, once performed, makes a man worthy of worship among the gods in heaven. (4)
"O Brahmins, by the power of my grace, let there be speech for each of you.
Vyāsa said:
"I shall tell the five narratives; listen to them from the beginning."
By performing each of these five one by one, one finds liberation, heaven, and fame.
Reverence for one's parents, for the husband, equanimity toward all people, non-malice toward friends, and devotion to Viṣṇu— these are the five great sacrifices (mahāmakhas).
O Brahmins, whatever dharma a man accomplishes before the worship of his parents cannot be attained on earth even by hundreds of sacrifices,
pilgrimages, and other such rites.
The father is dharma, the father is heaven, and the father is indeed the supreme austerity.
When the ancestors have attained satisfaction, all the deities are pleased. For him whose ancestors are gratified by his service and by his virtues,
bathing in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day.
The mother embodies all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and the father embodies all gods; he who performs a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of both his mother and father has, by that act,
circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
When one bows with the head touching the knees of one's parents,
it falls upon the earth, and he attains the imperishable heaven;
as long as the marks of dust from their feet remain upon his head.
A son who drinks the water from the lotus-feet of his parents is purified even if he is attached to mere outward signs;
for him, the sins accumulated over hundreds of millions of births go to destruction. 14.
In the auspicious Manu-epoch, that man is purified from all defilements;
by a single birth, he attains the state of Vināyaka—except for that lowest of men who disregards his parents with his words. 15–16.
That lowest of sons who eats without having honored his parents shall dwell in hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings;
he remains in the Krimikūpa hell until the end of the kalpa.
If one abandons a father who is diseased, elderly, emaciated by lack of livelihood,
or impaired in his eyes and ears,
he shall go to Raurava and be born among the lowest castes, the Mlecchas, or even the Cāṇḍālas.
If one fails to support one's parents, all of one's merit is exhausted;
even if a son worships holy places and deities while neglecting his parents,
he does not obtain the fruit thereof, but dies like a worm upon the earth.
The Brahmins related this ancient account; listen to it with diligence.
Having heard it, you shall not again fall into delusion on this earth.
Formerly, there was a certain twice-born man known as Narottama.
Having departed from his own parents, he went to serve at sacred fords;
as that Brahmin traveled to all the holy sites,
his bathing garments would dry in the air day after day.
And egoism entered the mind of that brahmin:
"There is no one at all equal to me in meritorious deeds or great fame.
When he had spoken thus, the crane then laughed at him. 24–25.
Driven by anger, he cursed the twice-born one, and Baka fell to the earth with his body reduced to ashes. Great fear and delusion entered the lord of the twice-born during that act of destruction.
Then, because of that sin, the garment of the Brahmin did not go into the sky;
he immediately fell into despair and said to Khaṃta: "Go, O Bāḍaba, to the most righteous Cāṇḍāla, Mūka. (27-28)
"There you shall know the Dharma and find peace; let these words of mine be heeded.
Having heard those words from the sky, O gentle one, he went to the abode of Mūka. There he saw his parents attending to all their undertakings.
To those two, he gave warm water at the proper time during the cold season,
as well as oil for warming, betel-leaf, and cotton-lined garments; he also provided daily meals of delicious food, along with milk and sugar-candy.

In the springtime, he caused his parents to wear fragrant honey-garlands and provided them with various other objects of enjoyment and diverse articles of utility; moreover, he constantly fanned them even when it was hot.
Then, having performed the service for those two and having eaten,
he should always prevent their fatigue as well as their distress;
by these meritorious acts, Viṣṇu remains for a long time within his house.
In the atmosphere, devoid of supporting pillars, he sports;
his abode is eternally situated there, O Lord of the Three Worlds.
He is the beloved one who assumes the form of a brahmin, the supreme reality who is not composed of other elements. 35.
Seeing that great being, composed of light, illuminating the temple, the Brahmin was struck with wonder and spoke to Mūka. The Brahmin said:
"I desire that he alone come to me immediately; I wish for what is eternal.
You ought to tell me in truth that which is beneficial for all the worlds.
Mūka said:
"Today I am performing the worship of my parents; how can I come into your presence?
Having first worshipped my parents, I shall indeed perform my duty. Stay at the doorway, and I will attend to you as a guest. (38-39)
When this was said, the Brāhmaṇa then became enraged at the Cāṇḍāla:
"Having abandoned me, a Brāhmaṇa, what further purpose do you have?
Mūka said:
"O Brahmin, why do you rage in vain? I am Nabaka; your anger will succeed against me alone, for there is nothing else here. 41.
In the sky, my bathing-cloth remains hanging and does not dry."

Having heard those words from you, you have come to my house. Stay, stay! I shall speak; otherwise, go away. O best of the twice-born, upon seeing that devoted wife, your beloved desire will be fulfilled.
Then the omnipresent Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a twice-born, emerged from that house and said to the brahmin, "I am going to her home.
Having reflected upon this, that best of brahmins set out together with him.
As Hari was departing, the brahmin, filled with wonder, said this to him:
"O dear one, why do you always remain inside the house of a cāṇḍāla, taking pleasure in the company of women who are despised by people? (45-46)
Hari said:
"At present, your mind has certainly not become purified; however, after seeing my devotion to my husband and other virtues, you will indeed come to know me. 47
The Brahmin said:
"O protector of those devoted to their husbands, what great deed of hers have you heard that I should go there? Tell me the reason, O twice-born one. (48)
Hari said: Among rivers, the Ganges is the most excellent; among women, the devoted wife; among men, the protector of subjects; and among gods, Janārdana. 49

A devoted wife who is always intent on the welfare of her husband shall deliver one hundred and one male descendants of both families; she enjoys heaven for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts. 50.
Or, having fallen from heaven, he shall become a sovereign emperor (sārvabhauma) as her husband;
becoming his queen, she shall experience uninterrupted happiness, and thereafter, there is no doubt that she will repeatedly attain the kingdom of heaven. 51-52.
"Having thus attained a hundred births, liberation will certainly come at the end. The Brahmin said: "Who is a devoted wife (pativratā)? What are her unchanging characteristics? (53)
"Speak to us, O tiger among the twice-born, according to your true knowledge.
Hari said:
"Out of affection for a son it is a hundredfold, and out of fear for a king likewise. (54)

She who beholds Śauri as her husband is a devoted wife (pativratā); she may serve as a maidservant in his work, yet in his pleasure she is like a courtesan, and in feeding him she is equal to a mother.
She is a devoted wife who acts as a counselor for her husband in times of adversity.
She who does not transgress her husband’s command through the actions of mind, speech, or body;
she who always eats only after her husband has eaten—she is a devoted wife (pativratā). On whichever bed her husband sleeps, she attends to him with great care.
And there, she constantly performed worship for her husband;
thus she never fell into envy, nor into wretchedness, nor was she proud. She who regards her husband as equal whether he is honored or dishonored is a devoted wife.
Seeing her husband, brother, father, or son well-attired,
that virtuous wife, devoted to her husband, regards him as a supreme being; O tiger among the twice-born, go to her without passion, just as you have done for me.

He had eight wives; among them was one of excellent complexion, endowed with beauty and youth, compassionate, illustrious, and renowned as Śubhānāmā. Having approached her, he asked for what was beneficial.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there. Seeing him become invisible, the twice-born man was then struck with wonder; he went to the house of his virtuous wife and questioned that devoted spouse.
Having heard the words of the guest, she hurriedly emerged from the house; seeing the twice-born man, the virtuous woman stood there at the entrance.
And seeing her, that best of brahmins spoke these words with joy:
"Speak what is dear and beneficial, exactly as you have seen it. Pativrata said:
"At present, there is worship of the husband; we possess no independence of our own."
"I shall perform my duties later; please accept hospitality today.
The Brahmin said:
"In my body there is no hunger, nor thirst, nor any fatigue."
"If you speak what is undesirable, O inauspicious one, I shall cast a curse upon you.
Then she said to him, "I am not a crane, O best of the twice-born; go to Dharmatulādhāra and ask him what is for your benefit, O brahmin."
Having spoken thus, that illustrious woman departed into the interior of her home;
there the Brahmin saw another Brahmin, just as one might find in the house of a Cāṇḍāla.
Reflecting on this, overcome with wonder, the Brahmin went along with him.
He saw the twice-born one standing there with a joyful mind;
seeing that brahmin and that virtuous woman,
he spoke with delight concerning what had indeed occurred in another land as related by her.
"How does she know my conduct? Even a Cāṇḍāla woman can be devoted to her husband;
therefore, O father, I am filled with wonder—what is this great and supreme marvel?
Hari said:
O father, the cause is known by all beings who contemplate existence,
that you have become filled with wonder because of your exceedingly meritorious and virtuous conduct; O sage, tell me now what was said by her to you.
The Brahmin said:
She instructed me to go and question Dharmatulādhāra regarding meat. Hari said:
"Come, O tiger among sages; I am going toward him.
As Hari was departing, Tulādhāra asked, "Where is he staying? Hari replied: Hari said:
In that place where there was a great multitude of people engaged in the sale of various goods,
the merchant Tulādhāra bought and sold here and there. Whatever person brought oil, fat, or a fraudulent accumulation of food, [he would take it].
He receives everything from the mouth of that [customer] and gives it back as well.

O best among the foremost of men, because he never spoke even a single falsehood— even when his very life was at stake— having abandoned untruth for the sake of truth, he is therefore known as Dharmatulādhara.

When he had spoken thus, they beheld that mortal selling many juices; he was covered in dirt and mud, his sprout-like teeth were stained with grime, and there he uttered various words arising from the wealth of his merchandise. (79)
Surrounded on all sides by many kinds of mortals—both women and men—he spoke to him with a sweet voice, saying: "How, how? Tell me the summary of Dharma, for you have come into my presence. (80-81)
Tulādhāra said:
"O twice-born one, as long as people remain in my presence,
I have no peace for as long as the three watches of the night last."
Taking that instruction, go toward Dharmākara;
there you shall learn everything regarding the fault in the death of the crane and the drying of your own garment. Go, O you who harbor malice toward the virtuous.
"By his instruction there, your desire will bear fruit.
Having said this, Tulādhāra engaged in buying and selling; meanwhile, I shall go toward that virtuous man who is free from malice.
"From the instructions of Tulādhāra, I do not know that abode. Hari said:
"Come, come; I shall go to that house together with you."
Then, as Hari was traveling along the road, a brāhmaṇa spoke to him.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"O Tulādhāra, there is neither ritual bathing nor libations for the gods and ancestors."
"Moreover, my body is smeared with dirt and all my clothes are soiled with grime;
how then could he know my conduct arising from another land?
Therefore, O father, I am filled with wonder; tell me the whole reason for this."
Hari said:
"By truth and by equanimity, he has conquered the three worlds;
by that, the ancestors, along with the gods and hosts of sages, have been satisfied."
By that [truth], the righteous man knows what has occurred and what will occur in the past and the future.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood— especially for a man who is free from fault and possesses an even disposition.
He whose mind proceeds with equanimity toward an enemy, a friend, and a neutral person—
his all sins are destroyed, and he attains union with Viṣṇu. He who conducts himself thus constantly shall deliver ten million members of his lineage.
Truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility, fortitude, stability, freedom from greed,
absence of wonder, and lack of laziness— all these are established in him;
by means of these, he attains both the world of the gods and the world of men in every respect.

The knower of dharma understands his conduct; Hari dwells within his body. There is no one equal to him in the world, nor equal in truthfulness and uprightness. He is truly composed of dharma itself, and by him alone is the universe sustained.
The twice-born said: "Through your grace, I have understood the reason for Tulādhāra's conduct;
now, if you wish, please tell me what happened regarding Adrohaka."
Hari said: Formerly, there was a noble woman of the prince, in the prime of her youth, who was like Śacī to Vāsava, the god of love. 97.
His wife, named Sundarī, was as beautiful as his own life-breath.
Suddenly, he prepared to go on a mission for the king; he reflected in his mind that she was dearer to him than his own life. 98–99.
"Where shall I place him so that his protection may be certain?"—having reflected thus, he suddenly came toward his house.
Having heard such words spoken, he was filled with wonder. (100)

I am neither your brother by marriage nor your brother by blood; I am not a kinsman of yours, nor am I a friend to her father’s or mother’s family. How, then, will you remain at ease staying in my house? 101–102.
In the meantime, he spoke these appropriate words:
"In this world, there is no one like you—one who knows the Dharma and has conquered his senses. You ought not to speak words of censure against the Omniscient One. (103)
"What man is capable of protecting Trailokyamohinī as his wife?
The prince said:
"Having learned of you on earth, I have come into your presence."
"Stay here; I am going to my own home.
When he had spoken thus, she replied again: "In this beautiful city, which is filled with many lustful men, how can there be protection for a woman?"
Saci spoke to him again: "O Kuru, I am going to protect [him]; as a householder, I shall rescue the prince from this peril.
I shall perform an improper act, for service to you is my proper duty and my welfare. (107)
"O father, such a wife must always remain in my house;
protect her who needs protection like a god, and do what is pleasing and desired by me. [She] was sleeping on my bed together with me and my wife."
"If you consider him your own deity, then stay; if not, then depart.
The prince spoke again at that time, "Reflect for a moment. [The other replied,] "Very well, O father; do as you desire."

Then, at his word, he spoke to his wife: "O beautiful one, auspiciousness must be brought about by you; there is no fault in this under my command. Having said this, he too departed by the king's—his father's—command.
Immediately thereafter, during the night, he did exactly as he had been told;
that steadfast man always slept positioned between the two women.
He never wavered from his duty toward either his own wife or the wife of another.
From the touch of his own wife, his mind was filled with desire and longing; yet,
due to contact with her, he felt as if he were a son, and her breasts repeatedly pressed against his back.
Just as an infant longs for its mother’s breast, he yearned for her limbs, and they clung to his own limbs again and again; thus,
day after day, he felt for his mother like a son for his mother.
From that time on, his association with women ceased.
Thus, when half a year had passed, her husband returned to the city; he then inquired among the people regarding her conduct and what had transpired.
Some, wishing him well, spoke to the youths, who were also greatly amazed;
some said, "Because she was given by you, he sleeps together with her. [They asked:
"How can there be peace through the union of a man and a woman? 119.
Whosoever had a longing for her would not speak of it when questioned;
by the power of his merit, he heard the ill-repute concerning her from the people’s talk, and a virtuous resolve arose in him for the sake of liberating her from public scandal. 120–121.
Having himself gathered firewood, he kindled a great fire;
in the meantime, the powerful prince arrived at that house immediately and saw that woman.

Perceiving the state of mind of the woman with her face in full bloom and the man who had fallen into despondency, the prince spoke these words: "O friend, why do you not converse with this woman, who has been here for a long time? 123-124.
That righteous-souled one, his intellect undimmed, spoke to the prince:
"Whatever difficult deed I have performed for the sake of your welfare, I consider it all to be in vain because of the rumors of the people. (125)
"Today I shall go to the fire; let men and gods behold me!
Having said this, O fortunate one, that highly blessed man entered the sacrificial fire.
As he was entering the fire, not even a single flower remained in his mass of hair.
Neither fire consumed her limbs, nor her garments, nor her hair;
the celestial women were filled with joy and all cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
and showers of flowers fell from all sides upon her head. 128.
And against those two who had uttered wicked words, various types of leprosy appeared upon their faces. Then the gods, having arrived there, joyfully drew him [the fire] away from them.
Filled with wonder, the sages worshipped him with exquisite flowers;
at that time, he of great splendor was thus honored by all the best of sages and various men, and he in turn worshipped them all.
The gods, asuras, and men gave him the name Aghahāraka (the Destroyer of Sins).
Purified by the dust of his feet, his wife became free from all sin.
And the gods said to him there, "Accept this woman as your wife."
There has never been his equal in the world, nor will there ever be;
such a man, who has conquered desire and greed, does not exist on earth at present.
[He is superior] to gods, asuras, humans, rākṣasas, beasts, and birds.
This desire is extremely difficult to conquer for all beings, even down to the insects.
From desire, greed, and likewise from anger, it constantly arises among living beings; this desire is the binder of saṃsāra, for there is no such thing as a being devoid of desire. 135–136.
By him alone all fourteen worlds have been conquered; Vāsudeva dwells forever in his heart with joy.
Having thus touched and seen him, men are freed from all impurities.
"Indeed, they shall be purified of sin and attain the imperishable heaven.
Having spoken thus, the gods departed joyfully for heaven in their celestial chariots; the men, being satisfied, likewise returned with the couple to their own home.
Then he possessed divine vision and beheld the gods; he also came to know the news of the three worlds with great ease. Then, on his path, he saw him together with him.
He asked him, "Speak the exalted and beneficial exposition of Dharma.
Sajjanādroha said,
"Go, O knower of Dharma, to the Vaiṣṇava Puruṣottama at Bāḍaba."
"Having seen that which is desired by you, it shall now bear fruit for you—
whether it be the destruction of Baka, or likewise the drying up of the ocean,
or whatever other desire resides within your heart. (142-143)
Having heard these words, he went toward the Vaiṣṇava and joyfully proceeded together with that brahmin who was Viṣṇu himself.
He beheld a pure, blazing Person standing before him.
To him who was radiant with his own splendor and complete in all auspicious marks,
that righteous-souled one spoke while he remained absorbed in meditation— the beloved of Hari—
telling him everything that had occurred and how he had come from afar to see him.
The Vaiṣṇava said:
"O best of gods, O lord of the enemies of the Dānavas, you are always gracious;
and now, O twice-born one, upon seeing you, our minds rejoice."
"Your auspicious and incomparable desire shall bear fruit; otherwise, the garment on the path of the gods would never dry.
Having seen the Lord Hari, the best of deities, staying in my house..."
When this had been said by the Vaiṣṇava, he then spoke to him again:
"Where does that Viṣṇu eternally abide? By your grace, show him to me now. The Vaiṣṇava replied:

"Having entered this beautiful temple of the gods and beheld the Supreme Lord, you shall indeed be liberated from terrible sin and the bondage of birth. Having heard those words of his, he entered the sanctuary. 150–151.
He saw that twice-born one, Viṣṇu, standing upon a lotus-couch; having saluted him with his head, he joyfully grasped his feet. "O Lord of Gods, be gracious! You were not recognized by me before."
"O Lord of gods, O Master, I am your servant both here and in the hereafter.
O Madhusūdana, I have beheld your grace; if you have compassion for me, I wish to behold your form. (153-154)
Viṣṇu said:
"O god among men, it is true that you are always dear to me;
out of affection, I have caused you to behold only those who possess merit. (155)
Through seeing, touching, meditating upon, praising, and conversing with them—
even once— those who possess merit enjoy imperishable heaven;
moreover, through constant association, there occurs the destruction of all sins.
Having enjoyed infinite happiness, it dissolves into my body.
(157) Having bathed in sacred pilgrimage sites and having seen me everywhere, and having seen the lands of the meritorious, it dissolves into my body. (158)
Having always recounted this meritorious narrative before the people,
he indeed dissolves into my body, O tiger among men, provided that he has fasted on our day and heard my life-story with certainty. 159.
Having kept a vigil at night, he dissolves into my body (160).
Constantly making a great clamor with dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the like,
while remembering my name, O best of the twice-born, he dissolves into my body (161).
"You alone have become a sacred ford (tīrtha) by the slaying of Baka; my devotee, for the sake of liberation from whatever sin [remains], spoke while standing there in haste:
'Go to the high-souled Mūka, the best among the meritorious sacred fords.'"
"O father, by seeing the mute man, all those great people were seen;
and from merely seeing them, as well as from conversing with them and through my own association with them, you have come to my house. (163-164)

O knower of Dharma, he for whom the destruction of sin has occurred through thousands of millions of births beholds me with such clarity as you have, O sinless one; it is solely by my grace, my child, that I have been seen by you.
"Therefore, accept as a boon whatever dwells in your heart.
The Brahmin said:
"May your mind remain our protector in every way."
"Except for you, O Lord of all the worlds, nothing ever pleased them.
Mādhava said:
"O sinless one, since such an intellect as this always flashes within you,"
"Therefore, you shall obtain enjoyments similar to mine in my own abode.
However, O sinless one, your parents have not yet received worship from you; only after honoring your parents will you enter my body. (168–169)
By the wind of their sighs and by their intense anger, their ascetic merit (tapas) constantly leaks away; therefore, O twice-born one, honor them both.
That son upon whom the parents' anger constantly falls [is likewise lost].
Neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara can protect you from that hell;
therefore, go to your parents and perform worship for them with great effort. Then, by their very grace, you shall attain my own state.

When this had been said, the best of the twice-born spoke again to the Teacher of the World: "If you are pleased with me, O Acyuta, then show me your own true form. Thereupon, the self-controlled Lord, his heart gladdened by the affection of the twice-born, [revealed it].
The one devoted to Brahman manifested his own form for the sake of the work of Brahman;
he was the Supreme Person, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
the cause of all worlds, who filled the universe with his splendor.
Prostrating himself like a staff, the brahmin spoke again to Acyuta: "Today my birth has become fruitful; today my two eyes have become auspicious;
today my two hands are praiseworthy; I am blessed, O Lord of the Universe. (176)
Today these men go to the eternal world of Brahmā. O Janārdana, by your grace our kinsmen rejoice today; now all my heart's desires have been fulfilled. (177-178)
"O Lord, what is this wonder? How do the wise men, such as Mūka and others, know my conduct so thoroughly, even though it took place in another land?
There dwells a most excellent Brahmin within the space of his house. 179.
Likewise, O Brahmin, you ought to tell me truly how the devoted wife attained the head of Lādhāra, and how Mitrādrohaka came to be in the temple of Viṣṇu through my grace. 180–181.
The Blessed One said:
"He was always devoted to his parents and mute; she was a virtuous and auspicious woman faithful to her husband;
Tulādhāra was a speaker of truth and impartial toward all people. (182)

O best of the twice-born, he who has conquered greed and desire, who is free from malice, and who is devoted to me, is known as a Vaiṣṇava; being well-pleased by their virtues, I dwell joyfully in their abode together with Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī. 183.
The Brahmin said:
"Through association with those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin), men themselves become perpetrators of extreme sins (atipātaka);
thus do those who know the Dharma always declare in the Smṛti scriptures. (184)
"How is it that you remain at home, [disregarding] the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Vedas? (185) The Blessed One said:
"I am the author of all auspicious things, yet I am mute throughout the three worlds."
Even a Cāṇḍāla who abides by his conduct, the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa.
(186) There is no one equal to a mute man in the worlds in terms of meritorious action;
he who is constantly devoted to the service of his parents has conquered the three worlds. (187)
"Delighted by their devotion, I shall remain with all the hosts of gods in the form of a twice-born brahmin within the interior of that man's house and in the sky;
likewise, I shall dwell in the house of the chaste wife and in the palace of Tulādhāra."
I always abide in the abode of Adroha and in the house of Vaiṣṇava;
O knower of dharma, I do not leave that place even for a moment. Therefore, those others who are doers of evil do not see me constantly. 189–190.
"Because of my merit, and because of your grace toward me, I have seen you;
devoted to his parents, pure, and having attained divinity, this Cāṇḍāla has become one with the gods. Therefore, I remain in his house with him out of affection."
O delighter of the twice-born, I engage in conversation with him again and again;
with an unassailable disposition, I always dwell within his mind,
and he as well as those devoted wives know of my conduct toward you.
I shall tell you their history; listen to it in due order, for by hearing it, a mortal is entirely liberated from the bondage of birth.
Among the gods of gods, there is no holy place (tīrtha) superior to father and mother.
He by whom the worship of his parents is performed is indeed the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

The command of one's parents and the command of a deity or a guru yield equal fruit; through the propitiation of the former one attains sovereignty, but through the violation of it, one goes to the Raurava hell. 195–196.
Even though he dwells within my heart, I dwell within his heart; there is no difference between us, and in this world as well as the next, he is equal to me. 197.
In my presence, in my beautiful city, together with all my kinsmen.
He shall enjoy inexhaustible pleasures and at the end he shall merge into me.
For this very reason, O tiger among men, he is mute; he knows the news occurring within the three worlds—wherein lies your wonder? 198–199.
The twice-born said:
"O Lord of the world, whether out of delusion or ignorance I failed to perform the worship of my father, what should be done now, knowing this, for the sake of both the good and the evil? (200)
The Blessed Lord said:
He by whom devotion to his parents has been practiced for even a single day, a month, a fortnight, half a fortnight, or a year, shall go to my abode. 201

Having caused mental distress, one will inevitably go to hell; there is nothing superior to the worship of the parents, whether it has been performed or not performed previously. By performing the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), a man obtains the fruit of devotion to his ancestors.
Food, clothing, as well as cow-products, both with meat and without meat—everything given to one's kinsmen is said to be multiplied a hundred-thousandfold.
By that wise son who performs a śrāddha ceremony even at the cost of his entire wealth, [the ancestors are satisfied]. 203–204.

One attains the memory of past births and receives the fruit of devotion to one's ancestors; indeed, there is no great sacrifice superior to the Śrāddha in the three worlds. Whatever is given here becomes entirely inexhaustible.
Know that in another [place] it is ten thousandfold; for one's kinsmen, it is said to be a hundred thousand.

A single *piṇḍa* is declared to be ten millionfold, and for a twice-born man, it is said to be infinite—whether offered in the waters of the Gaṅgā, at Gayā, at Prayāga, or likewise at Puṣkara. (206–207)
Whoever offers a funeral rice-ball (*annapiṇḍa*) at Siddhakuṇḍa in Vārāṇasī, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, will certainly attain liberation;
his ancestors shall obtain eternal heaven, which is the fruit of their birth. (208)

He who especially offers water with sesame seeds in the Bhāgīrathī attains the path of liberation; what then need be said of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas)? On riverbanks, a thousandfold merit is obtained, and ten thousandfold is desired for offerings made in the water.

Through association with the common fruit, the śrāddha becomes a hundredfold more meritorious on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas, and during solar and lunar eclipses. He who performs the pārvaṇa śrāddha on these occasions attains the imperishable world.
All his ancestors were satisfied for a full year; having bestowed beloved blessings and infinite enjoyments upon their son,
the Pārvaṇa rite should then be joyfully performed by the sons on the auspicious lunar day (parvan).

Having performed this sacrifice for one's parents, one is liberated from the bondage of birth. That śrāddha which is performed day after day is known as the *nitya-śrāddha*. He who performs it with faith attains the imperishable world.
In the same way, having performed the optional *śrāddha* according to the rules during the latter fortnight,
one obtains whatever desire resides in one's mind.
That which is the fifth fortnight, taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as its starting point— 215–216.
In that regard, one should perform the *śrāddha* whether the sun enters the maiden's [sign] or not; for those sixteen days during which the sun has entered the maiden,
they are equal to sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
This highly meritorious *kāmya-śrāddha* has arrived as a source of auspiciousness for him;

due to the absence [of the proper time] during the dark fortnight and so forth, he ought to perform it during the month of Tulā. Once the new moon arrives in the month of Vṛścika, the ancestors fall into despair.
Having uttered a most terrible curse, they returned again to their own abodes;
it is remembered that by the father’s curse, everything belonging to the son—wealth, fame, desired objects, and even life itself—was destroyed. (220)

All these are obtained by human beings birth after birth through the very boon of the ancestors; therefore, one should not abandon this [rite]. Having performed the *nāndīmukha* ceremony at the beginning of a marriage, a vow, a sacrifice, or similar occasions, O twice-born one, [one should proceed]. 221–222.
He obtains inexhaustible merit and his spiritual lineage increases; whereas the man who acts contrary to this goes to hell, his family line perishes, and he remains miserable even while living. 223.
Then one should worship Gaṇeśa, the son of Śambhu, first;
thereafter, the sixteen supreme Mothers; and after that, the assembly of ancestors, beginning with the great-grandfather, for all those who have the "Nāndīmukha" designation.
The wise man should seat all the twice-born at the Nāndīmukha rite facing the east;
he should cause them to utter the word "namaḥ" and employ "svadhā" on other occasions.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, a man, having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water, [attains the fruit].
One obtains inexhaustible heaven, which increases the nourishment of the ancestors.
That man who does not perform a ritual bath there, nor offers funeral cakes and water according to his ability, goes to the state of a Cāṇḍāla for the sake of his ancestors. 227–228.
O twice-born ones, all gifts are equal to [the gift given] on all occasions; all [gifts] are equal to those given during a Vyatīpāta yoga;
and all water is equal to the Ganges when the moon is seized by Rāhu.
It is said that [the merit of a gift] at such a time for the moon is a hundred-thousandfold, while for the sun it is ten millionfold.
When ten million moons and ten million suns have entered the waters of the Gaṅgā,
the fruit that is obtained from the perfect gift of a hundred thousand cows—
that same fruit, they say, is gained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is eclipsed.
One who bathes in the Jāhnavī during an eclipse of the moon or the sun has effectively bathed in all sacred fords; what need is there to wander the earth?
An eclipse of the sun on a Sunday, and likewise an eclipse of the moon on a Monday [is especially meritorious].

It is known as Cūḍāmaṇi; there, it is remembered that the fruit is infinite. Having fasted on the day preceding those two [lunar days] at that holy pilgrimage site (puṇyatīrtha), the man who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa), water, and gifts is established in Satyaloka.
The twice-born one said: "O father, you have thus described the great sacrifice and the śrāddha; but what, O dear one, ought to be performed by a son at the end of the final period? (235)
"What must be done so that the highest good may be attained in birth after birth?
O God, you ought to explain this with effort to me through my wise son. (236) The Blessed Lord said:

When one has reached an advanced age, it is traditionally taught that the father is considered the son; and in later life, the son is considered the father because of his role in providing protection, not because of his being an object of worship.
One should honor the father like a god, yet show affection toward him like a son.
One should never, even in thought, transgress his word.
That son who provides medical treatment for his afflicted father attains imperishable heaven and is forever honored by the gods.
Even for a dying father who beholds the signs of death,
a son who performs the sacrifice attains equality with the gods;
he who grants his father heaven through the rite of fasting according to the prescribed rule.
Listen as I describe the merit of that wise son:
the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices would belong to them, as well as the merit of fasting and ten million-fold the merit of sacred pilgrimage sites. 241–242.

The supreme person who dies in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī shall not drink the milk from a mother’s breast again; he attains liberation. Furthermore, he who voluntarily gives up his life in Vārāṇasī [attains the same].

Having enjoyed the desired fruit, one dissolves into my own body. That same goal which belongs to the sages who are disciplined in yoga and have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), is attained by one who gives up his life-breaths among the seven sons of Brahmā.

O best of the twice-born, he who, relying on the banks of the Lohita river without distinction, gives up his life according to the prescribed rite at that holy ford (Puṇyatīrtha) where Urvaśī’s hair fell, shall attain equality with me. 246.

One who has died and been reborn attains everything and is not defiled by any faults. For one whose departure of life (death) occurs certainly within the interior of a house, as long as the knot remains in the house, so long shall there be bondage for the body. 247–248.
Year after year, even one by one, they are diminished;
for those who witness it, there is no release from this bondage, whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a difficult pass, or in a place devoid of water. 249.
The deceased attains a miserable rebirth and is born again as an insect and the like. If the funeral rites for the deceased are performed on the day after [the death],
he remains in the Kumbhīpāka hell for sixty thousand years.
Merely by touching one who is untouchable, a person becomes impure; having fallen and died, he remains in hell for a very long time and is subsequently born among the mleccha tribes.
Likewise, he is born among various species of insects and other classes of living beings.
Therefore, one should understand merit and demerit within a short time:
for all inhabitants of the mortal world, whatever the destination of men is at death, such will be their state of rebirth through the application of merit and merit. 253–254.
He who dies at a sacred pilgrimage site while contemplating the names of Viṣṇu,
being purified of sin, shall go to heaven and will not be tainted by any defects.
Furthermore, a strong son who carries the body of his deceased father [attains merit].
At every step, he undoubtedly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice (256).
Before the piling of the funeral pyre, the son should cause the sacrificial fire to enter the mouth of his father's body;
then, according to the rite purified by mantras, he should subsequently cremate the body (257).

May I burn all the limbs of one joined with greed and delusion and enveloped by both sin and merit; may he go to the divine worlds. Having burned [the body], even a son should cross over toward the collection of bones.
When the tenth day has arrived, one should discard the wet garment;
having cut away the blood-stained cloth, one should then cast it into fire or water.
Thereafter, on the eleventh day, the wise man should perform the śrāddha rite.
For the sake of nourishing the body of the deceased, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa;
and according to the prescribed rite, one should give gifts such as clothing, a seat, and sandals,
as well as elephants, horses, and land, equal in value to all these other requisites.

One should offer an image of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of liberation from all sins. These sixteen śrāddhas consist of those performed on the fourth lunar day, at the end of three fortnights, six months, and a year, as well as twelve monthly ones.

For one who lacks these [qualities], even if they perform hundreds of *śrāddha* rites with faith according to their ability, their state as a *piśāca* remains firm. One should offer a jar of water and food accompanied by meat for a year.
By rejecting both the permanent and the impermanent due to their non-existence, one should cause the month to pass with patience.
When a year has elapsed, the wise and best of the twice-born should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha according to the rules of the Pārvaṇa rite.
Impurity for a father shall last one year, and for a mother exactly six months;
for a wife, three months; and half of that for a brother and a son. For sapinda relatives, impurity shall last as long as the body remains in the house.
Listen, I shall now tell you that which is forbidden for a son:
a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who follows right conduct must never approach a woman, either after seven ghaṭikās or before nine ghaṭikās [of the day]. 268–269.
The Kutapa period is known as the auspicious time for the ancestors; what is given then becomes inexhaustible.
In the Śrāddha rite, three things are considered purifying: a daughter’s son, the Kutapa period, and sesame seeds.
Furthermore, three qualities are praised here: truthfulness, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.

Having performed a śrāddha, one should avoid the evening twilight prayers, food from others, eating a second time, sexual intercourse, giving gifts, and receiving gifts. Even after performing a hundred improper acts, a wise man should perform a śrāddha.
"That this was to be done was spoken by Viriñci himself;
listen, my son, to an ancient account which I shall relate concerning many.
Having committed the killing of their preceptor's cow, they performed the Śrāddha and went to heaven. (273)
Merely by reciting their names, a Śrāddha becomes inexhaustible.
The seven Brāhmaṇa disciples of the sage Vasiṣṭha were firm in their vows; when the time for the ancestral Śrāddha arrived, [they approached] the sacrificial cow, the beloved of their Guru. 274–275.

Having entreated her and brought her home, the seven brothers joyfully slaughtered that cow for the sake of the sacrificial offering to their ancestors; and after due reflection, they gave the meat to a Brahmin and fed the remaining portions to other Brahmins.
Having completed the ancestral rites and gathered their calf, O twice-born ones, they offered it to their preceptor; however, the cow had been devoured by a tiger.
Then, through the power of their asceticism, he understood the cause of their distress. (277–278)
"Along with the rabbits, you disciples shall become outcasts (cāṇḍālas).
Then the trembling Brahmins stood with their palms joined in reverence, O sinless one, [saying],
"We shall always be the providers of cow-flesh for the ancestral rites."

"Even those who committed thousands of forbidden acts and great sins, having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha), were purified of their evil and went to heaven. O Lord, I have heard from your mouth this ancient account of many kinds. (280–281)
"O knower of dharma, you ought to forgive me; let an end be made to this curse.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Or rather, let the curse be such that it does not afflict you, through the discernment of dharma. (282)

Born among Cāṇḍālas and other such castes, you shall remember your former lives; there shall be no loss of knowledge for you, and the scripture of memory shall not perish. Having emerged from this sinful womb, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
Then, O twice-born ones, having abandoned their lives due to the curse of their preceptor,
they were all born into the Cāṇḍāla caste, yet remained endowed with knowledge;
even as they were suckling at the breast, they did not forget their previous birth.
O highly fortunate one, all the deer born there died and were reborn as cakravāka birds in the forest;
the swans, however, were born white at the Mānasa-tīrtha and became twice-born brahmins again. Desiring death, they perished from that cause of distress.

At that time, the great king known as Dharmaketu went to that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) with his wives and his retinue. Then, out of delusion, three swans [desired] the kingdom, its enjoyments, and the women.
Then, thinking only of edible foods, they went to another world;
having learned the Veda and the Vedāṅgas, they thought, "We shall attain liberation," yet while thus reflecting, they departed from here toward that other world.
Then three kings were born, and four most excellent Brahmins;
in Kurukṣetra, through the power of their asceticism, they thoroughly mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, as well as the knowledge pertaining to this world and the next.

Three kings born in royal families were deluded by pride; due to the loss of their knowledge, they did not understand the welfare or the nature of the next world. Then those brahmins, out of doubt, summoned their own servant.
"O King, go; out of your own miserliness you have given me a leaf in agitation.
(293) "The seven hunters were in Daśārṇa, the deer on Mount Kālañjara, the cakravākas on Śaradvīpa, and the swans in Lake Mānasa. (294)
"O three-born ones, you Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and have set out on the path as messengers to Kurukṣetra—why do you falter?
Having taken the letter, he showed it to the king. (295)
Having seen the letter, the two kings abandoned their kingdoms and went to the twice-born;
having heard their words, those ascetics departed,
and in no long time at all, they attained liberation along with them.
"O twice-born one, whoever hears this account of the seven hunters and others at a śrāddha ceremony,
inexhaustible food and drink shall attend upon the ancestors.
The twice-born said:
"O Keśava, how can the ancestral rite (pitr-kārya) be performed for a Brahmin who is destitute of wealth— a forest-dwelling ascetic as well as a householder? The Blessed One said:
Having gathered grass and wood and having begged for even a single cowrie shell,
one who performs the ancestral rites (pitr-karya) will find that [the merit] becomes a hundred thousandfold. He who performs the ancestral śrāddha after having committed a hundred forbidden acts—

All his sins are destroyed, and that man goes to heaven. (301) Even when nothing else is available, the man who gives fodder to cows on the anniversary of a father’s death or on a lunar festival day obtains a fruit even greater than that of offering the funeral rice-balls. (302)

Formerly, in the region of Vairāṭa, he wept most piteously; now, when his father’s anniversary arrived, he wept because of his total destitution. Having wept for a very long time, he questioned a learned brāhmaṇa.
"O Brahmin, today is the day of the ancestors and the guest; what should I do that would be beneficial?
O best among the knowers of Brahman, I have no wealth, nor even a kingdom; grant me instruction by which I may remain established in dharma. (304-305)
The twice-born said:
"Go quickly now to the forest during this auspicious hour of Kutapa; fetch fodder for my father immediately. (306)
Then, having taken a bundle of fodder according to his instruction and given it to the cow for her nourishment, he was as delighted as if he had seen his own father;
by the grace of this merit, he went to the abode of the gods.

Having enjoyed heaven for a very long time, he was born into a family of wealthy people. On account of his former merit and by reason of performing the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), that man became rich; with all his wealth and property, he offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father.
There, through practice performed over a single birth, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu;
having enjoyed infinite happiness there, he became a sovereign king on earth.
For there is no dharma whatsoever that is superior to the sacrifice for the ancestors.
Therefore, with every effort and according to one's ability, one should act without envy.
That man who recites this lineage of Dharma before people obtains,
in every world, the merit of bathing in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī.
Whatever accumulation of great sins has been committed throughout birth after birth, all of that goes to destruction when [this] is heard and recited even once. 313.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Five Narratives," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 50.
The fifty-first chapter.
Narottama said:
He is the Lord of the world for the thirty gods and for others as well.
He is the Lord, the creator, the destroyer, the protector, the sustainer, the father, and the mother. Our exertion of speech finds its purpose only in narrating the deeds of Viṣṇu;
yet, I have a curiosity, as if from thirst or even hunger.
O beloved Lord, you must indeed tell me that which she asks; for how does that devoted wife know even the past? You ought to describe her power in its entirety.
The Blessed One said:
"O twice-born one, it has been told to me before; yet there is curiosity once more. I shall tell you all of that which dwells in your mind."
Devoted to her husband, regarding him as her very life, and ever intent on her husband's welfare— she who is to be propitiated even by the gods and the sages who discourse upon Brahman,
that woman alone is remembered in the worlds as most worthy of honor.

In that city, which will not suffer disrespect from elders and will remain tranquil, there shall be an exceedingly beautiful ancient capital in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). And in that city, there shall be a woman of Brahmin birth named Sevyā, who is devoted to her husband.

Due to the obstruction caused by his past karma, he became afflicted with leprosy; his mouth was filled with oozing sores. Yet, devoted to her constant service, she would fulfill whatever desire of his she was able to do to the utmost of her power.
He should always worship her like a goddess and show affection without envy.
Once, seeing a most beautiful courtesan walking along the path, his mind became utterly deluded and possessed by the god of love.
Sighing very deeply, he then became exceedingly dejected.
Hearing this, the virtuous woman went out from the house and asked her husband: "O Lord, why are you so distracted? O Master, why do you sigh so?"
"Tell me what ought to be done and what ought not to be done that is pleasing;
I shall do what is dear to you, for you alone are my beloved guru. O Lord, speak what is desired, and I shall carry it out to the best of my ability."
When this was said, he spoke thus to her: "O beloved, why do you speak in vain?
Neither you nor I have the power [to alter destiny]; it is not fitting to speak fruitlessly, nor do you have the authority to ask, just as one cannot obtain the fruit of a distant tree."
Just as a dwarf standing on the ground desires to uproot Mount Meru,
so too, out of delusion and greed for women, he desires that which is difficult even for a husband and wife to accomplish; I shall now describe his retreat.
The devoted wife said:
"O Lord, having understood the state of your mind, I am capable of accomplishing the task. Give me your command; I shall do whatever must be done by any means."
"If I am able to accomplish this task, which is so difficult to achieve, through my efforts,
then, O most auspicious one, your desire will bear fruit hereafter in this world.
When this was said, Parama, being exceedingly pleased, remained there and spoke these words.
It is a settled conclusion that one encounters evil through the habitual practice of sin.
Seeing this most beautiful courtesan, whose limbs are entirely faultless, approaching on this very path, my mind is consumed with distress.
If, through your grace, I obtain one who is in the bloom of youth, then my birth will have borne fruit; O virtuous one, grant this for my sake.
[Otherwise,] if you give me one who is afflicted with leprosy, wretched, foul-smelling, and covered in fresh sores— 21-22.
"O lady of beautiful hips, do not go; death is indeed beneficial for me.
Having heard the words spoken by him, the virtuous woman spoke these words: "O Lord, remain steady now; we shall act according to our ability."
Having reflected thus in her mind,
she quickly took cow dung along with grain at dawn at the end of the night; arriving at the house of the courtesan with joy, she cleaned the courtyard.
With joy, she offered cow dung on the main streets and the alleys;
she quickly returned home out of fear of being seen by the people.
In this manner, that virtuous woman continued her practice for three days.

Then she questioned the chief maidservant, as well as the male and female servants: "Whose works at the crossroads were so beautiful? Even though I did not mention it, who was it that, at the hour of dawn, performed this for the sake of pleasing me? (27-28)
In the act of beautification, the streets, crossroads, and lanes were illuminated; and the chief courtesans, having consulted with one another, said:
"O blessed lady, this work of cleaning was not performed by us."
Then, having been struck with wonder, he reflected at the end of the night;
and she was seen by him, having returned exactly as before.
Having seen that great virtuous woman, the Brahmin lady devoted to her husband, [he was amazed].
Placing her foot upon his head, she said, "Forgive me!
O devoted wife, you have appeared here for the destruction of my life, body, prosperity, wealth, fame, and renown. (32)
"Whatever you desire, O virtuous lady, I shall certainly grant it to you—
be it gold, gems, jewels, or clothing, whatever your heart's wish.
Then that virtuous woman said to him, "I have no need for such things."
"If you would do something for me, I shall tell you what must be done; then there will be satisfaction in my heart, and everything will have been accomplished by you now.
(35) The courtesan said:
"O devoted wife, speak quickly; I shall surely make it true, truly.
O mother, protect me and tell me quickly what my duty is. Out of shame, she spoke words that were censurable, yet they were excellent and pleasing.
Reflecting for a moment, she felt resentment and spoke:
"I am deeply distressed by contact with one who is leprous and foul-smelling; I will allow him to come to my house for only a single day. (37-38)
The devoted wife said: "O beautiful one, I shall come to your house this very night; I will bring my husband back to my home, joyful and having enjoyed his pleasures. (39)
The courtesan said:
"Go quickly, O illustrious lady devoted to your husband, to your own home;
let your husband come to my house at midnight. (40)
"I have many dear kings who are equal to him;
each one of them stays constantly and continuously here in my house. Today, out of fear of you, I shall make my house empty."
"If your husband returns, let him come after he has visited us.
Having heard this, that virtuous woman went to her own home and reported to her husband: "O Lord, the deed you performed has borne fruit."
"Tonight she goes to his house and makes it famous;
there are many suitors for her hand, and no time limit has been set.
The Brahmin said: [44]
"How shall I go to that house? It is not possible for me to go there. Knowing this, how can there be patience? How can the task be accomplished? Thus spoke the devoted wife.
"Having taken him upon my back, I shall carry him toward his home;
once the purpose is accomplished, I shall bring him back again by that very same path.
The twice-born one said:

"O auspicious one, by your very action alone all my business shall be accomplished; for the deed now performed is difficult even for women to endure. And in that beautiful city, there are always wealthy people in their homes."
Then he heard that the king had seized the abundant wealth of the citizens.
Having heard this, the king, filled with rage, summoned all the night-prowlers and said:
"If you desire to live, you must hand over the thief to me today."
Having received the king's command, those spies, agitated by the desire to seize him,
forcibly captured the thief at the king's order in a dense forest at the foot of a tree on the outskirts of the city.
The bull among sages, Māṇḍavya, possessed of great splendor through his concentration in samādhi, stood like a blazing fire— the foremost of yogis—
for whom even the wind moving within the channels (nāḍīs) was no longer perceptible. 51–52.
Seeing that great sage standing there, equal to Brahmā, the wicked ones said, "This is a thief of wondrous appearance; this rogue stands in the forest.
Having spoken thus, those sinners bound that best of sages.
"Those extremely cruel men were neither spoken to nor even looked upon by him.
Then the king said this: 'The thief has been caught by me;
inflict a terrible punishment upon him at the gate of the road.'"
And there the sage Māṇḍavya was impaled upon a stake on the road;
they had driven a stake from his anus up to his head,
yet even with his body pierced by the stake, he felt no pain because of Yama.
The punishment inflicted by others was actually for the benefit of Manu.
In the meantime, during the night when the darkness was thick and dense,
that devoted wife set out, placing her husband behind her.
Due to contact with the body of Māṇḍavya, a leper’s odor reached him;
his meditative absorption was thus certainly broken by that association with the leper. 59.
Māṇḍavya said:
"May he by whom my body was thus subjected to such hardship and pain now be reduced to ashes as soon as the sun has risen.
When Māṇḍavya had spoken thus, he fell to the surface of the earth.

Then the devoted wife said, "O Bradhna, do not rise; certainly for three days you must come to my house. Having brought him from his abode due to her curse, the devoted wife then took him and remained with him as he lay upon a beautiful bed.
Having cursed him, that best of sages departed for his desired destination; meanwhile,
as long as three days passed and the sun did not rise in the world,
he beheld the entire three worlds, including all moving and non-moving beings, to be utterly distressed.
Placing Śatakratu at their head, the gods went to the Grandfather; the inhabitants of heaven reported the entire event to the Lotus-born One, saying,
"We do not know the cause, but you should provide what is appropriate for us."
Brahmā said:
"O Muni, regarding the conduct of the devoted wife and that of Māṇḍavya,
Dhātṛ reported it to the gods just as the sun rises."
Then all the gods, placing Prajāpati at their head, went swiftly from the earth to his presence in their celestial chariots, O Brahmin;
by the splendor of those chariots and likewise by the rays of the sages, [the sky was illuminated]. 67.1–2.

It shone like a hundred suns, yet nowhere else within the interior of the house. "Alas! Woe is me! How has the Sun arrived at my home? [She thought,] while the gods remained invisible by means of celestial chariots resembling swans.
In the meantime, Brahmā spoke to that devoted wife:
"How does the destruction of all the gods, the twice-born, and likewise the cows, appear to you? (70)
"O mother, abandon your anger now, as the sun is about to rise. The devoted wife replied,
"Transcending all worlds, my husband alone is my guru."
"O Sage, when Virocana had risen due to the curse of Asya-mṛtyu, for that very reason I cursed this Sun; it was not out of anger, nor delusion, nor greed, nor lust, nor envy. (72-73)
Brahmā said:
"By the death of just one [of these], the welfare of the three worlds will be secured; therefore, O Mother, even greater merit shall accrue to you in this way. (74)
There, that virtuous woman spoke the truth before the gods, saying: "Having abandoned my husband, Śiva is more pleasing to me than my own life.
Brahmā said:
"When the moon has risen and the sun has been reduced to ashes,
and when the three worlds have become stable, I shall do what you desire.
A man must be manifested from the ashes, possessing a splendor equal to that of Kāmadeva."
Your husband is endowed with all virtues, and you are always like Rati;
just as Hari is worshipped by the gods and Lakṣmī is likewise honored, so too are you two, a divine couple, in heaven—therefore, do as I say. 77–78.
The devoted wife said: "O Brahmin, since my husband has met his death, I am a widow censured by the world; to what worlds shall I go, broken in conduct and defiled? (79)
Brahmā said:
"Therefore, there is indeed no fault in this; he shall now be cured of his leprosy.
By our word alone, let him become a man of passion (Manmatha) and be freed from his leprosy. 80
While he was speaking thus, she reflected for a moment and replied, "So be it. Immediately thereafter, sunrise occurred;
[the king], tormented by the sage’s curse, became like ashes.
Born from the midst of the ashes, that twice-born one was tormented by the god of love;
seeing him, all those city-dwellers were struck with wonder,
the hosts of gods were delighted, and the people became more at ease.
Accompanied by her husband, who had arrived from the heavenly realm in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, that virtuous woman went to heaven along with the gods;
for she was thus devoted to her husband, auspicious, and indeed equal to me. 84.
Therefore, he knows the past, the future, and the unfolding of events.
Whoever causes this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative to be heard in the world,
his sins— whatever has been committed throughout birth after birth— go to destruction.
He attains imperishable heaven and is united with the gods; O Bāḍaba, the Brāhmaṇa obtains the Veda in birth after birth.
He who hears this even once becomes purified and is liberated from the flood of his evil deeds.
"He attains the abode of the gods, and having fallen from heaven, he shall become wealthy.
