(88) Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Devoted Wife," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Two.
The twice-born one said: O Viṣṇu, how did the blow of a stake fall upon the body of the sage Māṇḍavya, and how did leprosy afflict the physical frame of that devoted wife?
Hari said:
"Due to his childhood nature, Māṇḍavya, while lying on a bed of crickets,
placed a blade of grass against his rectum and, out of delusion, released it."
Due to that fault of slander and because he was ignorant of the Dharma,
that twice-born man experienced the agony of a difficult ordeal for a day and night; however, through his meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he did not perceive the origin of the pain.

O best of the twice-born, although that sage performed the *kṛcchra* penance in its entirety and practiced yoga most intensely, leprosy with a foul odor arose upon his body due to the killing of a Brahmin caused by his lack of self-control over the senses.
Formerly, this Brahmin did not give four Gaurīs nor three maidens; yet, because of this [act] of his devoted wife,
he shall attain equality with me.
"Is this not a marvel? Where is the ancient Vedic injunction? He replied: "For him who leads women to their duties, heaven shall certainly be his."
"O Lord, so that this conduct may result in the welfare of all," [he asked].
Hari said:
"There are some women who perform acts of peace even for a man who has given away all his possessions."
Even there, one should not even mentally entertain the thought of protecting her [from others].
No one is truly disliked or beloved by women; like cows in a forest seeking grass, they desire ever-new [lovers]. 9-10.
A woman will certainly resort to a servant who is devoid of consciousness, deformed, lacking in virtues, and of low birth;
she does not seek a husband endowed with virtues, of noble lineage, and possessed of great wealth. 11.

A wife should abandon one who is handsome and skilled in lovemaking if he is base, and instead resort to another; know this, O Brahmin, as the narrative of the dialogue between Umā and Nārada, by which all the various behaviors of women are fully understood. 12–13.

Then the sage Nārada, a brāhmaṇa who desires to know all things by their very nature, reflected within his own mind and went to the supreme mountain Kailāsa, which is firmly established here as the eternal abode of the bull-bannered Lord Śiva.
14. On this mountain, the true narrative of the Bull-bannered One is ever-present.
Having prostrated before the Great-Souled One, the sage questioned Pārvatī:
"O Goddess, I am eager to understand the difficult conduct of women; out of curiosity, you engage in the practice of young brides. (15-16)
"You know the hearts of all women in their true essence;
therefore, tell me about this one who is humble and ignorant among them all. (17) The Goddess said:
The mind of young women undoubtedly dwells upon men,
whether that man is well-attired and seen as a brother or even as a son, and whether he is united with her or not. 18.
"The vulva of women becomes moist, O Nārada; this is indeed the truth, the absolute truth.
There is no fixed place, no fixed moment, and no man who does not seek them;
therefore, O Nārada, the state of chastity arises in women [only by chance]. (19–20)
A woman is like a jar of ghee, and a man is like glowing coals;
therefore, one should not keep ghee and fire in the same place.
Just as one restrains a rutting elephant by means of a goad and a mallet, so too should one control the senses.

O Father, this woman brings even him under her own control; therefore, she must be protected by men. A father protects her in childhood, a husband protects her in youth, and sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
Then, due to her state of independence and by her own will, that wise woman, when solicited by a man, may become one who acts upon his instigation and so forth.
Just as food that is not protected falls under the power of dogs and crows once it has been cooked, [so does she fall]. 24.

In the same way, a young woman may fall into wickedness through her own will; furthermore, her family becomes defiled by association with her. He who is born from another's seed shall be a mixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara).
Born of an adulterer, this sinful *saṃkara* shall certainly dwell in hell;
having passed through the various classes of insects, they are all born again upon the surface of the earth.
Then, O delighter of the twice-born, their lineage will descend to that of a barbarian (*mleccha*).
Since the destruction of the family occurs because of them, one should not support wicked women.
That lowest of men who, knowing the faults of women, nevertheless forgives them,
shall dwell in the terrible Raurava hell together with his ancestors.
One woman brings ruin to a family, while another elevates it;
therefore, a wise man should marry a woman born of a noble lineage with every effort.
A woman of equal status establishes both families in prosperity.
A virtuous wife certainly upholds the lineage, while a wicked one surely causes it to fall.
It is said that in this worldly existence, heaven and hell, family and disgrace, son and daughter, and friend depend upon the wife. 31–32.

Therefore, a wise man should marry one or two wives; however, for the sake of progeny and desire, he should not take many, as that involves many faults. Furthermore, a husband who does not recognize his wife when she has reached her menses [commits a fault].

Even a killer of a Brahmin or a killer of an embryo attains a miserable state; but that sinful man who, out of delusion, abandons a virtuous wife by making her appear ill-favored, shall go to hell after experiencing the sin resulting from not having killed her. 34-35.

By abducting a woman, one enters the lineage of the Cāṇḍālas; likewise, by abandoning a wife, a man becomes fallen. Furthermore, by placing a woman upon his shoulder, he shall dwell in the city of Yama for a long time.

Excrement and urine constantly fall upon his head; thus the evil-minded one carries the burden for thousands of years, and for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall go to the Śaraurava hell.
Then, having passed through the state of insects, he attains humanhood;
thereafter, due to his former impurity, he encounters strife and sorrow. Having thus undergone three births, the man is liberated from that sin.

Having experienced hell for that duration, that solitary deceiver shall become a widow among humans after experiencing the Ucchiṣṭa hell. Furthermore, the man who goes to an outcaste woman, a Mleccha woman, or a Pulkasa woman [shall suffer likewise]. 40–41.
Having enjoyed [the fruit of his merit] there two, three, or four times, the deceiver who has committed [these acts] against his mother, his teacher’s wife, a Brāhmaṇa woman, a queen,
or another husband’s wife, goes to a state from which there is no rebirth.
Having approached a sister, her son’s wife, as well as a daughter or a daughter-in-law (43),
or likewise a paternal uncle’s wife, a maternal uncle’s wife, a father’s sister, a mother’s sister, or any other such woman, there is no atonement. 44.

One who becomes dull-witted by the words of a Brahmin’s laughter, one who becomes deaf in both ears, and one who falls [from his status]—for these there is no atonement, for they have spoken excessive vulgarity on account of women.
45. Indeed, it is all because of women.
The twice-born said:
Having thus incurred such evil karma, how can liberation be attained again?
O Blessed One, explain that to me; I wish to hear it according to the truth.
The Blessed One said:
Having performed obeisance to them, one should embrace a heated iron image and give up one's life; thus purified, one shall go to the other world.

That man who, having abandoned the householder's life, becomes single-minded toward Me, constantly remembers Govinda; for him, there shall be the destruction of all sins, even ten thousand killings of Brahmins or the violation of the preceptor’s wife. 48–49.
By consuming liquor distilled from flour a hundred times a hundred thousand times,
by stealing gold and other precious things, and by long association with such sinners— these and other such sins are great transgressions (mahāpātakas). 50.
Just as dry grass or cotton is utterly destroyed upon reaching fire,
so too a man becomes purified by remembering my name, Govinda; indeed,
he who dwells in the householder’s stage of life should constantly utter the name of Govinda.
Having performed [these rites] and having worshipped, one becomes liberated from sin on the beautiful bank of the Bhāgīrathī during the auspicious eclipse of a planet.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten million cows, [he obtains that same fruit here]. 53.

One obtains that fruit, as well as a thousand times more; having performed the kīrtana of Govinda, one shall dwell eternally in his city. Having resided in that abode according to one's desire, one becomes a sovereign king.
By hearing my stories from the Purāṇas, a person attains similarity with me;
and by narrating the Purāṇa, one attains union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. Therefore, the Purāṇa, which is a storehouse of dharma, should be heard daily.
This should be proclaimed with effort; one shall go to the world of Viṣṇu’s body.
Or rather, when a fault regarding women has been committed, it will certainly result according to its nature; listen, O delighter of the twice-born, as I shall explain this to you in truth.

By giving all kinds of seeds along with a water-pot as a great fruit, one should give them to a Brahmin on an auspicious day; he shall instantly become purified in that very moment. One should give all grains and other seeds to a twice-born man at the proper time.
Having brought about the destruction of all sins, one enjoys an imperishable heaven.
O brahmin-sage, I shall describe the firm virtues of virtuous women as they truly are:
her lineage becomes pure and prosperity perpetually flows for her.
O Brahmin, as you inquire, I have forgotten to mention the quality of devotion to her husband, which secures heaven for both lineages— as well as for the husband and herself.
I shall speak again of that auspicious virtue of women which is beneficial to all the worlds.
Having lived previously with both merit and demerit, those women who later become devoted wives (pativratā) attain my state;
this is praised whether it lasts for six months, a year, or even longer.
She who is devoted to her husband becomes a chaste wife (pativratā) as long as she remains pure and ascends to heaven;
she who follows her husband leads even one who has drunk liquor, killed a Brahmin, or is burdened with every sin,
to heaven, purifying him from his mire.
A husband resembling Kandarpa and exceedingly beautiful—such a man, for as long as he lives in this world, enjoys unsurpassed happiness;
so too does a woman devoted to her husband who, even from afar, brings about the downfall of her master. (66-67)

Having obtained the sign [of her husband's death] from the fire, a woman devoted to her husband rescues her husband from sin; and that woman whose husband has died in a foreign land, having taken the sign of her husband and slept in the fire, shall go to heaven.

If a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste should follow her deceased husband [to death], she does not lead either herself or her husband to heaven by that act of self-destruction; rather, by the command of Brahman, a Brāhmaṇa woman must not die by following him. 69–70.
One who commits suicide attains the state of a renunciant after death; thus spoke the Best of Men. Among all castes, the Brāhmaṇa is considered the most praiseworthy. (71)
"Is there merit for this chief of the twice-born here, or rather the opposite?
The Blessed One said:
"A rash act is never appropriate for a Brahmin woman. (72)
Having committed the slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa without exception, one becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, one born of the Brāhmaṇa caste must perform the vow for a Brāhmaṇa. O Brāhmaṇa, listen as I shall explain this according to the truth and in its true sense.
One should never eat meat from within a marketplace;
by doing so, one obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices for a year.
This is the worship of one's chosen deity, Hari, and is the unsurpassed vow. 74–75.

If the husband also gives water and a funeral ball (piṇḍa) without envy, that virtuous wife shall instantly be united with her husband in the world of Viṣṇu for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of yugas.
Then, having attained the Great Vow (mahāvrata), the Brahmin’s daughter-in-law shall uplift both lineages by the hundreds and thousands; therefore,
she should be honored by her kinsmen, sons, brothers, and other wise ones.
Having restrained herself, she should never cause a lapse in her vow; for if a widow reaches the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) and fails to observe the vow,
she shall become miserable and enter the state of widowhood again in birth after birth.
By failing to observe vows regarding food such as fish and meat,
one certainly reaches hell for a long time and is then born as a female dog.
A corrupt woman who engages in sexual intercourse with a widower brings ruin to her family.
Having experienced the hells, she then becomes a female vulture for ten births,
then a twice-born bird and a jackal, and thereafter she attains human status.
Likewise, due to widowhood in childhood, she falls into the state of a slave.
The twice-born one said:

"O Lord, if you have favor toward me, tell me the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage, as well as the fruit of bestowing her [as a gift], and the prescribed ritual according to the injunctions. (83)
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen to the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage to one who is rich in beauty, endowed with virtues, well-born, possessed of youth, prosperous, and filled with wealth.
And he who gives away a maiden adorned with all ornaments—by that act, the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, becomes his lower lip;
the fruit of giving half the ornaments shall certainly belong to the giver. 85–86.
The fruit of giving even a single foot [of land] to a maiden who is without ornaments shall accrue;
however, that man who consumes the bride-price (śulka) goes to hell.
Furthermore, the fool who sells his own daughter does not return from hell.
He who, out of greed, gives his daughter to an unsuitable man goes to the Raurava hell and attains the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
for this very reason, a bride-price for the groom should never be taken.
The wise man who receives with a focused mind what has been given finds that it becomes inexhaustible for him—
be it land, cows, gold, wealth, clothing, or grain.
By giving all these as a dowry (*yautaka*) to his son-in-law, everything becomes inexhaustible.
Whatever *yautaka* (bridal gift) is given at the time of marriage by those of one's own lineage (*sagotra*) or by those of another lineage (*paragotra*),
all of that becomes inexhaustible;
the giver does not remember the act of giving, nor does the recipient ask for it.
Both go to hell like a water-pot with its rope severed;
indeed, a gift as a dowry must necessarily be given by one who is virtuous. Without having given it, one reaches hell and falls into servitude.

A daughter should not be given to one who is too near, nor to one who is too far away, nor to one who is excessively wealthy, nor to one who is in extreme poverty (94). Nor should she be given to one of low birth, nor to a fool; these six are unfit.
Likewise, not to one who is very old, nor to one who is extremely destitute, nor to a sick man, nor to a resident of a foreign land (95).
Even if they are extremely angry or dissatisfied, a daughter should not be given to these six;
by giving a daughter to them, one goes to hell.
[This occurs] through greed, for the sake of gaining honor, or by the exchange of daughters.
By giving a young woman who is beautiful, adorned with ornaments, and accompanied by a bed—a woman who is the beloved of sages—one obtains the fruit of bowing down.
Furthermore, I shall describe to you the fruit of both these types of women: the young wife and the maiden. 97–98.
One [cow] should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has reached the end of his vows, while another,
purchased from a god, should be given by one who is wise and free from harmful deeds.
(99) By such an act, a king may dwell in heaven for the duration of a Kalpa, or a Brāhmaṇa may become very wealthy.
In every birth, he shall obtain a virtuous wife of excellent complexion.
He who constantly hears this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative shall have all his sins destroyed and shall reach the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures.

He shall obtain imperishable heaven and become beloved by women; furthermore, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious, or he will certainly become a lord of the world. This [text], when heard, removes the sins committed throughout many lifetimes.
She attains good fortune in the world, and likewise becomes an excellent woman.
103. Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Women," within the "Five Narratives" section of the first book, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 52.
The fifty-third chapter. The twice-born said:
O Lord, [I have heard] the life and the incomparable power of Tulādhāra.
"You ought to tell me this in its entirety, if you have favor toward me. The Blessed One said: "He who gives out of sincerity, without greed, and without envy—"
For him, a hundred sacrifices are perpetually accomplished with excellent sacrificial fees.
The sun rises through truth, as does the wind;
likewise, the ocean does not overstep its shore, nor does the tortoise-bearer [the earth] exceed its bounds.
By truth all the worlds and the mountains stand;

but he who has fallen from truth, even if he be a being of strength, will certainly become a dweller in the lower regions. Therefore, let one be devoted to speaking the truth and always intent on truthful action.
Having come to the heavenly world with his physical body, he shall attain the state of the Infallible (Acyuta). By truth, all the sages went to me and attained steadfastness;
by truth, King Yudhiṣṭhira went to heaven with his physical body.

Having conquered all hosts of enemies, he protected the world according to dharma and performed the pure Rājasūya sacrifice, which is very difficult to attain. He constantly provided eighty-four thousand brāhmaṇas [with sustenance].
One should feed [the brahmins] using golden vessels and royal utensils.
Having fed them and given those utensils to them, one should dismiss them;
other than what is desired by the twice-born, one should cause other wealth to be given.
Then, knowing them to be no longer poor, the king, free from envy, should abandon that assembly of twice-born men;
likewise, he should constantly feed sixteen thousand *snātaka*s with truthfulness alone.
Having previously stayed for a long time in his house with the desire to conquer him,
he conquered the entire world by means of favoring the vital breaths (prāṇa).
And by truth, the Asura king Bali shall become Indra.
I remain, as it were, in the very abode of that one who dwells in Pātāla;
I abide constantly within the heart of him whose sole activity is merit.
Or rather, because I was previously bound by him for the sake of liberating him from his birth as a Daitya.
"I shall indeed bestow upon you the earth, immortality, and even the status of Śakra;
for King Hariścandra, by virtue of his truthfulness, has been established in Satyaloka with his own pure body, along with his mounts and retinue. 14.
Many other kings as well as perfected great sages, wise men, and ascetics— all became steadfast in truth. Therefore,
one who delights in truth in this world is capable of being delivered from saṃsāra.

The high-souled Tulādhāra was established in truthful speech; because of his truthful speech, there was no one like him in the world. Truth, when weighed against a thousand horse-sacrifices, outweighed them.
Truth indeed excels even a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Everything can be accomplished through truth, for truth is difficult to transcend. By truthful speech, one attains success and becomes a frequent traveler to heaven. 18–19.
Having entrusted the entire kingdom [to him], it is difficult for one to return again; likewise, this wise man is always a witness and never speaks falsely or like an atheist.
In buying and selling, he is discerning regarding both high and low prices.
Truthful speech is praised, and it is especially so for a witness.
Having spoken the truth, witnesses have gone to imperishable heaven;
a eloquent master of speech, having entered the assembly, speaks the truth.

That which is difficult to attain even through sacrifices and other means is always present in the house of a Brāhmaṇa; whoever speaks the truth in the assembly shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
But having spoken falsely out of greed or hatred, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
One who is a witness to all things, impartial as a scale, and brave among people—especially through the renunciation of greed—shall go to heaven and attain immortality.
A certain highly fortunate Śūdra did not indulge in greed at any time. (24–25)
His livelihood was sustained by vegetables and great hardship; likewise, he subsisted on alms and lived in extreme poverty.
His pair of garments was always tattered, and his hands were his only bowl. Even though he was constantly deprived of gain, he never took the property of others.

Out of a desire to know him, I took a pair of garments and, having respectfully placed them on the bank of the Avakotā river, stood there; yet upon seeing that pair of garments, my mind did not set its heart on greed for them.
Without knowing the other's [intent], he went to his own home out of patience for that; then,
O twice-born one, having reflected in his heart that it was but a small matter, he thought,
"I have dropped a golden-encased udumbara fruit right there."
On the bank of the river Kiṅkarañcana, in a secluded corner devoid of people, he beheld that wonder in the region where he had gone;
it appeared to be an elaborate, artificial arrangement. (30-31)
Now, upon its acquisition, non-attachment is likewise destroyed;
yet this very effort to preserve it is the seat of egoism.
For where there is greed, there is gain; and from gain, greed proceeds.
For a man seized by greed, there shall be eternal hell. If wealth devoid of merit remains in one's house, then madness indeed arises for one's wife and sons. 33–34.
From madness arises the transformation born of desire;
from that confusion comes delusion, and from that, egoism, anger, and greed.
Due to the abundance of these states, his ascetic merit will go to ruin.
When his austerities were exhausted, the muds that delude the mind returned;
bound by those chains of connection, he could not attain liberation.
Having reflected on this, that Śūdra abandoned his home and departed.

While he was still composed, they cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! and, assuming the form of Nirgranthas, they likewise approached his house. Having gone there, I spoke words consistent with fate regarding the course of events.
Then, due to the persistence of his practice and the agitation of the people,
his wife arrived and asked about the cause of the matter; thereupon,
I quickly told her whatever was in my mind.
I have now explained to you in private the cause of my silence; that which was in my heart has been taken from me by fate like one who is ignorant.
O highly fortunate lady, once it is abandoned, that wealth can never be recovered here again.
"As long as he lives, he will undoubtedly experience great misery while consuming it.
Go, O mother, to the empty house; ask him about that which was not obtained. Having heard those auspicious words from her husband, she [went]. 43.
Having gone, he spoke to that wicked man; hearing this, the latter was struck with wonder.
Having reflected, he came into my presence along with her.
He spoke these words to me in secret: "Proclaim your state as a mendicant."
The Jain ascetic said:
"O father, why have you so easily cast away this eye, which has been purified for so long, as if it were a blade of grass? For there is no fortune that remains free from thorns."
Incomparable sovereignty and valor will again perish for you;
you shall witness great suffering among your own kinsmen from birth until death, and you will constantly see with your own eyes the certain destination of those who have died. 46-47.
"Therefore, accept that quickly and enjoy this sovereignty, free from all thorns, incomparable in its power and heroism, and most wonderful to the worlds.
The Śūdra said:

There is a craving for wealth, and wealth is a snare of worldly existence; a mortal fallen into such a trap shall not attain liberation again. Listen now to the faults of wealth, both in this world and in the next.
There is fear from thieves, from kinsmen, from kings, and even from their tax-collectors. All mortals desire to kill one another, just as beasts, fish, and birds prey upon each other.
Thus, for those who possess wealth, how can riches ever bring happiness?
"He is indeed the destroyer of the life-force and the fulfiller of the purpose of the wicked;
he is the beloved abode of Time and the others, and the supreme cause of misfortune. 52.
The Jain mendicant said:
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
Noble lineage, character, scholarship, beauty, enjoyments, fame, and happiness—all these belong to him who possesses wealth.
But for one who is destitute of wealth and abandoned by son and wife, [all these vanish].
How is a friend [to be found], how is the Dharma, and how is birth for the wretched?

(54) The performance of rites such as the *sattva* sacrifice, the construction of lotus ponds, and giving—which serves as a staircase to heaven for the wealthy and a means of success for the destitute—[how do these come about]? (55)
The performance of religious observances (*vrata*), the protection of one's property, and the diligent hearing of the Dharma and other teachings—
these do not succeed for one who lacks wealth;
likewise, the remedy for disease, wholesome diet, and the accumulation of medicine [are not possible].

Protection, as well as conflict, and the certain victory over enemies—these, along with news concerning women, are obtained through the Vasu-yoga. Furthermore, whatever good or evil deeds have been performed in the past or the future [are also known]. 57–58.
"Therefore, whatever belongs to one who possesses great wealth may be enjoyed at will; indeed, through such giving, you shall soon attain heaven.
The Śūdra said:

All vows are fulfilled through freedom from desire; service at sacred fords is perfected through freedom from anger; recitation of prayers is purified by compassion; and contentment is indeed the supreme wealth.
Non-violence is the highest accomplishment, and subsistence on gleaned grains is the most excellent mode of livelihood.

O scorcher of foes, a diet of vegetables is equal to nectar, and fasting is the highest [merit]. Contentment is my great enjoyment, and a single cowrie is my great gift. The wives of others are like one's own mother, and the wealth of others is like a clod of earth.
"O mine in all sacrifices, you who resemble a serpent coveting another's wife;
therefore, I do not accept this—this is the truth, the truth, O mine of virtues.
For it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off."
When this was said, O twice-born one, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of that best of men, impelled by all the gods;
the divine drums resounded and throngs of apsarases danced.

When this was said, he replied to him: "Even by reciting it ten thousand times in a single day, the fruit is indeed eternal; those who know merit understand this as merit."
In this waterless place, a pit for Śiva was dug by me,
and everyone performs their desired rites such as bathing and drinking there at will. Therefore, the daily fruit of my ten thousand coins is expected from that.
Then there was laughter from him as well as from those in the assembly;
yet, overcome with shame, he spoke these words: "This word of ours is true; examine it according to dharma."
Out of envy, he said to his father who was being praised: "Listen to these words of mine, Father!
Having given you ten thousand dīnāras and brought a bundle of straw, I shall cause it to fall into the pit you have dug, so that you may sink in according to your merit."
"At the time when the sacrificial grass (*prastara*) emerges and even floats across [the water], our wealth will go to ruin; otherwise, it shall not, for that is indeed the way of Dharma.
Having said "Certainly," and having taken ten thousand [coins] from him, he went to his own home. (33-34)
In the presence of the witnesses, the thief cast down the clod of earth,
and it was seen by men, gods, and asuras in the great lotus pond.
Then he was weighed upon the scale of Dharma by the witness of righteousness.
The gift of ten thousand *dīnāras* for the water of a lotus pond is not equal, according to the Dharma, to even a single day’s gift of water;
for the wealthy man suffers mental anguish and his wealth becomes futile on the next day.
A mountain of rock emerged like an island upon the water;
then a tumultuous roar arose from the people. Having heard those wonderful words, the two of them arrived there with joy.
Seeing the mountain thus transformed and likewise reduced to ten thousand pieces by him,
the lord of the excavation then hurled the mountain far away; for when the merit of the excavation had been uprooted and destroyed by his son, it was lost.
Having ascended that Sopināka mountain, being utterly liberated birth after birth,
he [attains] inexhaustible fruit by digging wells for the sake of his lineage, groups of mothers, kings, friends, companions, and benefactors. 41.

Especially for ascetics and for Brahmins who are without a protector, one who has caused a tank to be dug enjoys eternal heaven; therefore, O Brahmins, whoever shall perform the digging of a tank and such works according to their ability [attains this merit]. 42–43.
Through the destruction of all sins, he shall attain merit and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
That righteous person who causes this most magnificent narrative of Dharma to be heard in the world enjoys the fruit of giving away all his possessions. 44.
Upon hearing that at the supreme bank of the Bhāgīrathī during an eclipse of the sun,
a man obtains the fruit of giving away ten million cows,
he shall neither encounter poverty, nor sorrow, nor a multitude of diseases.
"One does not incur the great suffering of dishonor for either [party].
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Glorification of Khātā and Others," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Eight.
Vyāsa said:
O highly fortunate ones, I shall describe the specific fruit that accrues from each of all the trees; listen to that, both regarding their individual planting and their separate offerings. 1.
The merit of one who plants sacred trees on all sides along the banks of the Yamunā cannot be known or even described.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by planting trees elsewhere, [that fruit is surpassed here].
Then, near water, it becomes multiplied ten million times;
one who personally stays on the bank of a lotus pond enjoys infinite fruit.
We say that for those who perform meritorious acts under the shade of trees, the merit is a hundred times greater than that.

The fruit that a mortal obtains by planting an *aśvattha* tree near a body of water cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices. Whatever leaves fall into the water on every festival day (parvan), [they become for him as offerings].
Those balls of food, once offered here to the ancestors, became inexhaustible. Birds there certainly ate the fruits at their will;
the merit of that act is equal to eating the food of Brahmā and is likewise inexhaustible.
The fruit that comes from planting an *aśvattha* tree as food for others cannot be attained even by a hundred sacrifices or even by a hundred sons. Cows,
gods, and the twice-born seek its shade when it is hot.
For the performer and for the hosts of his ancestors, heaven becomes imperishable.
Because it is imperishable, no obstacle can arise against one who has planted [it] while established in well-being;
therefore, with every effort, a person should plant a tree dedicated to Mādhava. 9–10.
By planting even a single tree, a man does not fall from heaven;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, plant such great trees near water, in pleasant places, and at sites for the buying and selling of goods. 11.
That noble-minded person who plants trees along the road or by a body of water goes to the delightful heaven after having planted the Aśvattha and other species;
O twice-born ones, I shall now declare the merit that comes from honoring them. 12–13.
He who, having bathed, touches the Aśvattha tree is liberated from all sins;
even a mortal who touches it without bathing obtains the fruit born of bathing. By seeing it, one destroys sin; by touching it, one attains prosperity.

May there be long life through circumambulation; O Ashvattha, salutations to you! (15) To the tree with trembling leaves, in whom Vishnu always dwells, the worthy Bodhisattva—O Ashvattha, salutations to you! (16)
Having offered oblations of horse-gram (*aśvattha*) and milk, as well as food offerings (*naivedya*), flowers, incense, and lamps, one does not fall from heaven;
know that this brings about inexhaustible sons, increase of wealth, and fame. 17.
O Vijaya, Mānada, and Bhaḍra, the worship of the Aśvattha tree is proclaimed to be ten million times more effective than any recitation,
oblation, hymn, yantra, mantra, or the like performed at the root or on its leaves. 18–19.
Who in this world would not worship that [tree] at whose root Viṣṇu resides, at whose middle Śaṅkara stands, and at whose top Brahmā is situated?
That bath which is performed by one observing silence on a Monday or on the new moon day—

The fruit of giving a thousand cows is obtained by worshipping the Aśvattha tree. By performing seven circumambulations, one gains the fruit produced by ten thousand cows; therefore, that [circumambulation] should always be performed extensively, even millions of times.
Whatever is given there—be it fruits, roots, water, or the like—all that yields inexhaustible fruit, arising [in benefit] birth after birth.
Oh! There is no one on earth equal to the Ashvattha tree, for it is Hari in the form of a tree.
Just as the twice-born are worthy of worship in the world, just as cows, and just as the gods, so too is the Lord in the form of the Aśvattha tree considered most worthy of worship—
always during its planting, its protection, its touching, and in the act of its worship. 24–25.
A man who makes even a small cut in the body of an Aśvattha tree gives away his wealth, sons, heaven, and liberation in succession;
however, having suffered in hell for one kalpa, he is reborn as a Cāṇḍāla or similar being.

By cutting it down at the root, he indeed attains non-rebirth; yet men remain in that Raurava hell, which is terrible to behold, for as long as it would take to plant a single *aśvattha* tree and reap its fruit. 27–28.

Likewise, in the case of planting three each of *caṃpaka* and *arka*, as well as eight *bilva* trees and seven *nyagrodha* trees, and ten *nimba* trees— the fruit of these [deeds] shall be equal. (29)

O twice-born ones, the fruit of planting each individual tree has thus been declared. Having understood this, the righteous-souled person who creates an artificial grove [shall dwell] for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Having ascended this thousand-fold [structure] of the mango tree, he goes to the celestial realm (*nāka*);
then, having enjoyed it— whether it be twice or thrice the size, or even less, or not very extensive— the king or the lord should perform it again.
From that very tree, heaven, enjoyments, sovereignty, auspiciousness, prosperity, and well-being arise;
from it is born health and heroism. And thousands of living beings eat its fruits. 33-34.
The birds that dwell upon it, the insects, the winged creatures, the moths,
and other beings that take refuge in its shade— all those ordinary beings,
numbering in the hundreds, become his servants, honored by the gods. (35)
And those great beings who are trees are all of divine form;
they should be honored like fathers with service, water, and funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
And they are the sons of that [tree] in every birth within the mortal world.
Those beings who are handsome, well-disciplined, and always auspicious through meritorious deeds attain the status of a leader of the assembly, like those clinging to the mango tree (38).
[Likewise,] the *dhātrī*, *harītakī*, and others produced from pungent, bitter, and sour substances [attain their respective effects].
All these gardens are pure, always bestowing fruits and granting auspiciousness (39).
There, the palaces are made of gold and adorned with all kinds of jewels;
the celestial chariots (vimānas) are equipped with every ornament and are as swift as the wind (40).

The trees there are made of gold, always and forever giving, providing the pleasures of all seasons; gentle maidens equal to Apsarases, steadfastly devoted to song and dance, dwell there for those who give trees. 41.
There were especially lotus ponds and other excavated pools,
fashioned with pure stones, with rivers whose mud was like milk-porridge (pāyasa), possessing foam like milk, and endowed with food and the six flavors. 42–43.
Just as one enjoys various things in the mortal world, so again in heaven and again on earth; and through that very habit, once more a moat, a garden, and so forth [are produced].
Just as a man, having performed meritorious deeds and the like, becomes a lord of heaven or of mortals.
But one who is unable [to build a large tank] shall obtain the fruit of a lotus-pool by constructing a water-shed (*prapā*).
Herein is the description of the water-shed, which is supreme in removing all sins, bestowing all enjoyments, pure, granting both heaven and liberation, and stable. 45–46.
I shall now describe the characteristics of the water-shed that increases one's fame: having constructed a pavilion at a place on a waterless road frequented by travelers,
when many wayfarers arrive during the summer, the rainy season, or autumn— (47)
Having offered fragrant substances such as agallochum, water, betel nut with camphor, a seat, and betel leaf, one does not fall from heaven;
thus, in just three years, one obtains the fruit of a lotus pond.

A mortal who does not fall from heaven is honored even by the gods; he who provides a water-station for one month during the waterless summer shall dwell in heaven for an entire kalpa, and having descended from heaven, he is glorified on earth.
Those who give lotus ponds have their water-stalls established there. Otherwise, a meritorious "Dharma-pitcher" (dharmaghaṭa) should be given for the destruction of sins;
this Dharma-pitcher is to be known as being identical in essence with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"By your grace, my desires have become fruitful.
As a fee for the water-pot, please accept four gold māṣas as one-fourth part.
In this way, one shall obtain the fruit of providing drinking water within three years alone. (53)

Whoever recites this or causes it to be heard shall obtain the fruit arising from [the construction of] lotus-pools and the like; through its grace, one becomes directly liberated from sin and attains a good rebirth. Whoever causes this auspicious, meritorious narrative to be heard among people [shall likewise attain these fruits].
He shall dwell in the world of the gods for thousands of millions of kalpas.
56. Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Merits of Puṣkariṇī and Other [Tirthas]," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme and auspicious dharma of fame.
The meritorious fruit of building a bridge, as spoken by Brahmā:
Having constructed a bridge across a difficult forest thicket, thick with mud and crowded with stakes, a man becomes purified and attains divinity. 1-2.
He dwells in the divine heaven for a hundred years, equal in duration;
by following this numerical rule, a man does not fall from heaven.
However, at some point, due to contact with impurity, he is born again on earth from that heavenly state.
Then the illustrious Lord, free from disease and sorrow,
having constructed steps and the like upon the mud and other places, does not fall from heaven;
all his sins go to destruction day by day.
Likewise, the fruit of the thirteen transits is proclaimed to be equal;
it is always performed by the wise even at the cost of wealth and life.
Listen now to this ancient narrative, esteemed by the elders.
A certain man, terrified by the great fear of thieves and intent on the act of theft,
placed a cow's head upon a mountain pass and, having committed the robbery,
departed after seizing the wealth of that householder.
Having gone to his own home, people come there on the path;
for all of them, the comfort of Ekapāda is certain.
In the heart of the Durga, the supreme Gośiras is the savior for those with one foot.
And that Cāndrāyaṇa penance was his head situated in the forest.
Then, upon the death of the thief as ordained by Citragupta, there remained for him only the fruit of his dharma. 11.

He did not perform even a single paternal duty—such as visiting a sacred ford, bathing, worshipping Brahmins, giving gifts, honoring his elders, or seeking auspicious knowledge for the benefit of others—not even mentally, let alone through physical action. 12. How much less so by deed?
He committed acts of violence, theft, and the violation of another's wife;
he uttered false accusations against living beings and likewise engaged in the censuring of the virtuous.
In this manner, he committed a hundred thousand offenses, as well as the abduction of cows.
Thereupon, Dharmarāja, whose radiance was like the fire of universal destruction, said: "O Śūra, lead this man to the fruit [of his actions]—to a miserable rebirth from which there is no return.
In the meantime, the compassionate Citragupta spoke.
"O Lord, there remains some merit from his [offering of] cow-heads; may he now obtain it.
O King, let him receive on earth the fruit of twelve years' worth of the arising of merit.
Thus spoke Dharmarāja to him: "Go to the mortal world, O evil-minded one! (16-17)
"Enjoy a kingdom free from thorns for twelve years;
because you were released on account of that very path of the *gośīrṣa* [sandalwood] which was seized, you shall return here once more and attain the state beyond rebirth. 18.
Then, afflicted by grief, he spoke to the god with palms joined in reverence:
"O Dharmarāja, have compassion for me, a doer of evil; O Lord of the Kurus, I know that you are my protector out of affection. (19-20)
The King of Dharma said to him who was thus praised, "Very well, go from here; by my grace, you shall remember your own history even while being deeply distressed.
In that very interval, he was indeed released by the servant.
His birth took place in the house of a certain impoverished merchant.
Due to his past misdeeds, he experienced various kinds of suffering from birth onwards;
having endured great affliction for twenty-one years, [he was born].
In that kingdom, the king died, oppressed by his own past actions;
meanwhile, the ministers and wise counselors, having observed this,
traveled throughout the earth with many investigations.
They immediately surrounded him firmly in front of everyone;
then, free from envy, they performed his royal consecration,
and he accepted the kingdom by the choice of Dharmarāja.
He constructed stone bridges bound with iron, as well as earthen ones; he built causeways across water-fortresses and likewise other crossings (27).
He also constructed ponds, wells, tanks, water-stations, gardens, and trees.
He performed various sacrifices, and thereafter,
for the sake of destroying all his sins, he remembered his past deeds and practiced manifold forms of dharma and diverse vows. (28-29)
Having purified himself from sin by means of satisfying the gods, the Brahmins, and his elders, he went to the abode of the wise Dharmarāja.
Then, seeing him seated upon his vehicle, [Yama] became red-eyed with anger.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke the truth: "O Dharma, perform the protection! (31) Citragupta then addressed these words in the presence of Dharmarāja:
"Purified in deed and in mind, let him go to the world of Viṣṇu. (32)
Having heard this a hundred times and having understood the reason for it, he smiled with joy, his soul serene, and said: "Go, go to the abode of Acyuta!
A celestial chariot, variegated in color and arriving from the world of the gods, awaits you."
Having ascended [that tree], he went to heaven, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, he who in the past gave even a blade of grass (alikam) measuring a cubit (kiṣku) in length,
follows after sovereignty, lineage, and a great heaven.

Likewise, by providing even a cow-pasture of one fathom (vyāma), one does not fall from heaven; that wise person who has provided such a pasture will certainly attain the same destination as a giver of cows. 36. By that wise man, a cow-pasture of one fathom is said to have been granted.

For him, heaven shall be attained; what need is there for other extensive discourses? (37) He who, according to his ability, abandons the grazing ground for cattle for a specific reason, gains a hundredfold more merit than one who feeds Brahmins day after day. (38)
Therefore, one who declares the pasture for cattle does not fall from heaven; however,
he who cuts down a sacred tree or destroys a pasture for cattle—
his twenty-one generations of ancestors are cooked in the Raurava hells.
The village protector, being capable, should recognize and punish one who obstructs the grazing grounds.
He who cuts down the trees of Dharma, especially those that provide grazing for cattle, finds no happiness; therefore, the king should inflict punishment upon him.
That man who constructs a temple for a Viṣṇu-liṅga—
whether it be three-tiered or five-tiered, beautifully adorned and well-provided with water-jars—
or one even greater than this, whether made of clay or stone; 42.
It was filled with the movement of wealth, exceedingly beautiful, and possessed a divine ground (43).
It was perfected through the rite of consecration, surrounded by servants and others, and was especially suitable for the installation of the beloved deity Viṣṇu (44).
Having done this, that best of men attains union with Viṣṇu;
likewise, by making an image of Hari or one of the other [deities],
a man obtains the same fruit as he who has constructed a beautiful temple for the gods.
Not by thousands of sacrifices, nor by gifts on earth, nor by vows and the like;
not for thousands of millions of kalpas, nor for hundreds of millions of kalpas,
[can this be attained] even through palaces endowed with jewels and filled with an abundance of wealth.
He shall dwell in celestial vehicles that move at will and enchant the entire world;
having fallen from heaven, he becomes a sovereign monarch, masterful in his virtues.
(48) Having caused a temple for a Śiva-liṅga to be built according to his own capacity, [he attains this].
That which was described as the *liṅga* of Viṣṇu is to be known as being within the abode of Śiva.
There, the highly fortunate one enjoys supreme bliss for his mind, filled with delightful women and bestowing happiness in every way in heaven. 49–50.

Whether he be a king or a man of great wealth, that person who has fashioned an image of Hara in a temple shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas upon the earth, enjoying inexhaustible pleasures.
(51) Whether it be well-proportioned or beautiful in form, he shall reside in the celestial realm for ten million kalpas.
Whether he be a king fallen from heaven or even one most worthy of honor among the wealthy,
a man who constructs a temple for the Goddess within all her various shrines shall attain the state of a god in the world that originates from all happiness belonging to the Goddess. 52–53.
He attains a state of extreme steadfastness, proceeds to bliss, and reaches a condition free from ailment,
in a palace adorned with jewels upon a floor variegated with gems, where he may enjoy the company of ten thousand women, and which is rendered fearless by the presence of goddesses. (54)

In that house, which was filled with the sounds of dancing and singing, delightful to all the senses and the mind; enriched with jeweled mṛdaṅgas and cymbals, and always resonant with the voices of women; stainless, bliss-bestowing, beautiful, and most auspicious with its jewels.
Likewise, by building an excellent temple for the image of the Goddess,
a person goes to the heavenly world (Svarloka) for ten million billion kalpas;
when he eventually falls from heaven, he becomes a king devoted to the worship of the Goddess.
And thus, for a thousand births, he shall indeed remain mindful on earth.
Having built a temple for Gaṇeśa or for the Goddess with a devoted heart, a man becomes honored by the hosts of gods and is born in heaven.
In that very way, he attains sovereignty and likewise enjoys the pleasures in the city of the Goddess,
always remaining free from obstacles in all his undertakings, just like Gaṇapa himself; for among gods, asuras, and humans, there is no one who can transgress his command.
O best of men, the fruit for one who likewise resides in a temple of the Sun is this:
he becomes free from disease, of a very serene mind, and possesses a splendor equal to that of Kāmadeva;
he is a granter of boons in all worlds, just like the Sun-god himself. 61-62.
Having constructed a stone temple for the peerless Surasā,
one shall enjoy heaven for a hundred crores of kalpas and then become a sovereign of the earth.
The worship of all the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, performed individually [yields great merit].
I shall explain each one for the sake of the welfare of men.
(64) He who offers a lamp of ghee day and night for one month dwells in heaven for ten thousand divine years, honored by the best of gods. (65)
That man who performs a bath with ghee at Āligeya on this earth shall enjoy [the fruit] for thousands of crores of kalpas for every single month;
the fruit of another, such as a lamp of sesame oil, is half of that.
By the fruit of giving water for one month, one shall attain lordship. By the gift of incense, one becomes a Gandharva; by sandalwood, the merit shall be twofold;
and by the gift of musk and agaru-essence, there shall be great fruit.
By the offering of garlands and flowers, a man shall become the lord of the three worlds;
by giving a cotton garment in the cold season, one is liberated from all suffering,
and such a cool garment shall be obtained in every birth during the heat.
One who gives a garment according to their ability shall never fall into ruin. Having given a beautiful covering four cubits in length to wrap around the body,
as well as a covering for the feet, one does not fall from heaven.
By the gift of gold according to his capacity, a man shall become honored in heaven;
he shall possess a pavilion ten yojanas in extent.
By giving gold joined with jewels, one obtains a reward ten times greater.
By giving diamonds, lapis lazuli, emeralds, rubies, and other priceless gems to a brahmin who is learned in the rites of the *ali* [mantra] and is illustrious,
one shall become the sovereign over a mandala extending a hundred yojanas.
Likewise, even having been born on earth, a man who delights all the world, who is eloquent through the gift of fragrant substances, and who is handsome;
and who possesses a beautiful voice like the sound of red nectar— such a man shall become so through the gift of betel nuts (pūga).
By the gift of a boon-granting maidservant, a man shall dwell in heaven for a kalpa.
By the gift of a boon-granting maidservant, one becomes a lord of wealth upon earth;
likewise, by the gift of a servant, one shall have many servants in heaven.
By the gift of all musical instruments, one is born with inexhaustible supernatural power (ṛddhi) on earth in birth after birth; being virtuous, he is honored by the world.
Through mastery of the sciences of dance, song, and so forth, one becomes a lord of the Gandharvas.

Accompanied by male and female servants, and endowed with wealth, women, and excellent things, he dwells in heaven; likewise, by the gift of a cow, he shall dwell in heaven for that same length of time.
Furthermore, by offering milk at a Linga, a man shall dwell in heaven for a kalpa.
By bathing with curd, the merit is doubled; by bathing with ghee, it is increased a hundredfold.
By giving food endowed with the six flavors, one becomes a lord of the earth. Likewise, by giving milk-rice (pāyasa) to the foremost of sages on this earth, [one attains the same].

Having joyfully given sacrificial food (haviṣya), one who has mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras becomes a celibate observer of vows through the gift of meatless food. Through the gift of honey, molasses, and salt, one attains good fortune.

The sweetness [of his speech] is celebrated throughout all the worlds by means of sugar and other such things; having fashioned an image of Śambhu, the Liṅga of the gods, according to the prescribed rite, he shall become the lord of the worlds, beginning with heaven, in due succession. 84.
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, the gods remain present face-to-face [with the devotee].
O best of men, a wise man who performs a single circumambulation around the lingas of Śambhu goes to heaven for a full hundred divine years.
In this very manner, by means of such prostrations to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), one who is revered by the world shall go to heaven; therefore, one should practice this constantly.
(87) That man who steals the wealth of the Lord in the form of the Liṅga—
Having approached a Śiva-linga with arrogance, one shall become a worm due to that act of taking [what belongs to it].
He who takes away the worship offered by a donor for the sake of the Liṅga or for Hari shall not return from hell for thousands of millions of generations.
If one has taken water, flowers, lamps, or other wealth for the sake of a ritual,
but later fails to give it back out of greed, he shall go to the inexhaustible hell.
Having abducted a female servant belonging to another, one does not return from hell.
One afflicted by lust might go to his own mother, but he should never go to a servant girl of Śiva (91). Having gone to a female servant of Śiva, as well as to one who steals the property of Śiva,
and by consuming their food and drink, a man shall fall into a miserable state of existence (92).
Therefore, one does not return from hell after being born as a god or a brahmin;
consequently, for the people of the courtesans' class, wickedness itself is beneficial. Thus, having touched a courtesan, a man becomes pure through bathing.
By resorting to many men, a woman becomes defiled and goes to a miserable state of existence. However, a courtesan who is ascetic, always devoted to the worship of the gods,
and pure through her dedication to her husband's vow, attains imperishable heaven.
He who always regards a courtesan as his mother enjoys every kind of pleasure in the celestial worlds like a god;
indeed, he becomes worthy of veneration by gods, demons, and men, just like Hari. 96.
Likewise, he who is worthy in all the world, the sole purifier of all beings,
who is always a servant of the gods and is devoted to the duties of the gods— he goes to the world of the Lord of the Gods and is glorified there. 97–98.
Having caused pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) to be constructed for these very [deities] according to one's capacity, one attains heaven; hear now the certainty regarding time:
by [offering] grass for one year, or by [offering] a stalk of reed for a hundred years. 99.
Ten thousand [homages] may be performed with other types of wood, a hundred thousand with khādira wood,
and ten million times ten million with very firm stones joined with great effort;
therefore, a wise person should cause a pavilion to be constructed with every possible exertion.
For as long as the builder of a pavilion for people dwells in heaven,
for that same length of time a man shall fall into a miserable state by stealing from it. [This applies to] the lovely accumulation of people and the buying and selling of goods.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by constructing a pavilion for the gods at the confluence of rivers and streams for travelers,
he attains that same fruit, doubled, by staying in the house of a Brahmin. 103–104.
A man who, having caused a beautiful house to be built for one who is destitute, miserable, and especially for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), does not fall from heaven.
Whoever should constantly hear this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative, [shall likewise attain the highest state].
One obtains inexhaustible heaven and gains the fruit of constructing palaces and the like.
Furthermore, by teaching or by reciting [this] for the wealthy, the powerful, and the meritorious, a person does not fall from heaven. 106–107.
That Brahmin who always recites [this] in the temples of the gods, among male and female servants,
and in the presence of kings, lords, the wealthy, and the virtuous, goes upon the path to liberation. 108.
By reciting it, one attains liberation; by hearing it, one obtains that same fruit.
The twice-born said:
"O best of the twice-born, there is one supreme and most meritorious [text] in the world of mortals."
He is easily accessible to mortals and worthy of worship by sages and ascetics;
likewise, he is accessible to men of the four castes and stages of life, whether they possess sin or merit,
whether they possess virtues or lack them, and whether they possess caste or lack it.
Vyāsa said:
Among all living beings, one who is endowed with a rudrākṣa is most excellent;
by the mere sight of it, the mass of sins of people is dissolved. 112
By touching it, one enjoys heaven; by wearing it, one goes to the mountain of Rudra.
He who wears Rudrākṣa on his head, chest, or arms becomes equal to Īśāna in this world, moving everywhere at will in the sacrifice.
Wherever that Brahmin resides, that place becomes meritorious.
By merely seeing or touching him, a man is purified of his sins; likewise, whatever recitation, libation, gift, bath, worship, or circumambulation he performs [becomes infinitely fruitful]. 114–115.
Whatever merit one performs, O twice-born ones, all of that becomes infinite; indeed, the fruit of the rudrākṣa is the greatest among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
By wearing this very [rudrākṣa], an embodied being is purified from sin and becomes a possessor of great merit.
Having taken up the auspicious rosary endowed with the Brahma-knot,
whatever is recited, whatever gift is given, whatever hymn, mantra, or worship of the gods is performed—
all that becomes inexhaustible, and all sin shall go to its destruction. (117-118)
O best of the twice-born, listen as we describe the characteristics of the rosary;
by knowing its characteristics, you shall attain the path of Śiva.
(119) [One should avoid] that which is pierced by insects, lacking a cord, or has a broken bead, in due order.

One should avoid a rosary where the beads are stuck together with one another. One should also avoid a rosary that has been strung by oneself, or one that is loose and where the beads are improperly joined.
One should keep far away from a rosary strung by a Śūdra or others who are impure. 120–121.
The seed-syllable *kaṃ* located in the middle [of the hand] should be recited in due order by means of the movement of the hands, repeatedly touching Mount Meru.
The mantra that one recites should be counted; if it is uncounted, it is fruitless. 122.

By reciting the mantra with one’s own *mālā* before all the gods, while remaining self-restrained, it becomes ten billion times more meritorious than visiting all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*). This should be done on pure ground, in a clean place, or at the foot of a tree.
In a cow-pen, at a crossroads, or in a deserted house, one obtains infinite fruit by reciting the mantra of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, or Sūrya before their respective liṅgas;
likewise in an empty house, before a corpse, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads. 125.
The practitioner who recites the mantra of the Goddess attains success immediately.
Furthermore, every mantra—whether Vedic, Puranic, or derived from the Agamas—bestows one's desired goals when used with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads. 126–127.
One should hold pure water from a *rudrākṣa* on one's head;
purified from all taints, one attains inexhaustible merit.
Furthermore, each individual seed of the *rudrākṣa* is individually immortal.
The mortal who wears this rosary shall become the most excellent among the gods.
The twice-born asked:
"From where did the rudrākṣa originate, and how did it attain its state of purity?"
"For what purpose was he established as an immobile being, and by whom was he set in motion?
Vyāsa said:
"O Brahmins, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a Dānava named Tripura."
Having slain the gods in the city of the intermediate space,
he remained firm there even as all the worlds were perishing, by virtue of a boon from Brahmā;
then Śaṅkara, the Lord, heard the terrifying report presented by the deities.

Then, having fixed upon the Ajagava bow an arrow resembling the God of Death and having seized him with his divine vision, he struck him; he fell upon the surface of the earth like a great meteor fallen from the sky.
From Rudra, agitated by the occurrence [of that event], drops of sweat fell;
from those drops of tears there arose on the earth Mahārudrākṣa.
Living beings do not know the fruit of this very [rudrākṣa] because it is exceedingly secret. 134–135.
Then, on the peak of Kailāsa, having prostrated with his head upon the ground before Maheśvara, the God of gods, Skanda spoke these words: "O Lord,
I desire to know the fruit of the rudrākṣa in its true essence."
It should be recited as a dhāraṇī; indeed, there is merit in seeing it or even in touching it.
The Lord said: "The merit from seeing it is a hundred thousandfold, while by touching it, it is ten millionfold."
By merely retaining it [in memory], a person obtains ten billion-fold merit.
By reciting it a hundred thousand times, ten million times, a thousand times, and even a hundred times ten million times, one obtains such merit; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Whether one is impure from food remnants, engaged in improper actions, or burdened by all manner of sins,
one is indeed liberated from all evils by wearing Rudrākṣa.
If a wild beast dies while wearing a Rudrākṣa around its neck, [it attains liberation].
Even one who has attained the state of Rudra [does so through this]; how much more so then humans and others?
(141) Even one devoid of meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*), if he should wear the Rudrākṣa, being liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal. (142)
Kārttikeya said: [I shall describe those] with one face, and likewise two, three, four, five, and six faces; and those with seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven faces. 143
Tell me also of the deities of those faces: the twelve-faced Rudrākṣa, as well as the thirteen-faced, the fourteen-faced, and that which is self-manifested as Śaṅkara. 144.
And tell me who the presiding deities of those various faces are.
"O Lord of the World, what are their virtues or what are their faults? If there is grace for them, please tell me according to the truth.
The Lord said:
Śiva, who possesses a single face, directly removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Therefore, one should wear [this] upon the body for the destruction of all sins; he shall go to the world of Śiva and rejoice together with Śiva. 146–147.
O Six-faced One, by virtue of great merit and through the grace of Hara, a mortal may obtain Kailāsa with one face; but that man who wears [the Linga] with two faces becomes a god among gods. 148.
Whatever secret sin there may be, such as the killing of a cow, it goes to destruction;
furthermore, by wearing two faces, one attains imperishable heaven. For he in whose body the three-faced Fire himself is established [attains this]. 149–150.
The sin accumulated by him throughout his life is consumed like fire consuming fuel;
whatever sin a mortal incurs through the killing of a woman, the killing of a Brahmin, or the killing of many others,
all of that perishes in that very instant.

The wise man who wears the three-faced [image] obtains that fruit which is gained from the worship of fire, from the fire-ritual, and from oblations of clarified butter; he attains heaven and enjoys it eternally, and he is equal to Brahmā upon this earth.
One shall burn away all accumulated evil deeds performed throughout birth after birth; there shall be no affliction of the stomach, nor shall one fall into physical infirmity.
One shall suffer no defeat, and one's house shall not be consumed by fire.
All these and other [obstacles] are warded off by the vajra;
indeed, nothing inauspicious exists for one who wears the three-faced [liṅga].
Brahmā himself becomes four-faced in whose body it is established. 155–156.

He may become a knower of all scriptures, a twice-born one who is the best among those who know the Vedas, a knower of the true essence of all dharmas and arthas, and one learned in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas.
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a man, or in [the destruction of] dwellings containing many living beings—
All that is quickly burnt away by the retention of the four-faced [mantra].
Maheśa is eternally pleased, and one becomes the lord of all beings. Likewise, Sadyojāta, Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora [are the faces]. 158–159.

The Vāmadeva [mantra] is resorted to by the five faces of the gods; therefore, it is most abundant everywhere on the surface of the earth. Since this [mantra] is the very form of Rudra’s own son, the wise man should maintain it. 160.
For thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, he shall be worshipped by gods and asuras in the presence of Śiva for that long;
possessing the splendor of Śarva, he shall become a sovereign ruler on earth in the abode of Śiva.
Therefore, one should wear the five-faced [liṅga] with every effort;
by wearing the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—of this there is no doubt. (163)
A hero equal to Skanda when the end of the kalpa has arrived, he shall suffer no defeat here;
he is a mine of virtues on this earth and shall attain the status of a Kumāra, just like the son of Gaurī’s Lord. 164–165.

The Brāhmaṇas become honored by kings, the Kṣatriyas attain victory, and the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other castes are always filled with prosperity; Gaurī, the giver of boons, becomes as easily accessible to him as a mother. 166
Then, by the power of his arms alone, that man shall become possessed of universal splendor;
he shall be eloquent, steadfast, and successful in the assembly hall, in the royal palace, and in the council. He shall never fall into despondency, and defeat shall certainly not befall him.
All these and others are obtained solely by wearing [this] six-faced [mantra];
Mahāsena is seven-faced, while the king of serpents is named Ananta. Within each of his faces, however, individual serpents are stationed.
Ananta, Karkaṭa, Puṇḍarīka, Takṣaka,
Viṣolbaṇa, Kārīṣa, and Śaṅkhacūḍa as the seventh— these seven highly powerful serpents are stationed within the seven mouths. 170–171.
Merely by holding this [mantra], poison does not spread through the body,
and Hara becomes supremely pleased, just as he is toward the Lord of Serpents (Nāgeśvara). Through affection for this [mantra], all her sins go to destruction day by day.

Whatever sin a mortal incurs from killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed—all that perishes in an instant; he shall certainly obtain food equal to that of the God himself throughout the three worlds. 173–174.

The eight-faced Mahāsena, the god Vināyaka himself—listen now to the merit that comes from merely holding [this name] in mind. For eight births he shall not be a fool, nor diseased, nor of impaired intellect. (175)
For him, there shall always be freedom from obstacles in all undertakings;
day by day, he shall possess proficiency in the work of writing, skill in great enterprises, and capability in all activities such as those he has begun. 176–177.
Whether it be cheating with half-measures, cheating with scales, or likewise all forms of deception, or if a teacher should touch a woman with his penis, belly, or hand—
all such sins as these he destroys in every way.
Having enjoyed the imperishable third heaven, he is liberated and goes to the supreme goal.
These are all the qualities obtained from wearing the eight faces; indeed, that which is called the Navāsya-Bhairava should be worn on the arm. 179–180.
By wearing the Kapila [amulet], which bestows liberation, one shall become equal to me in strength.
Even he who has committed thousands of millions of Brahman-murders—
by wearing the Navavaktra, all those sins are swiftly consumed.
Just as Maghavat is always worshipped by the gods in the celestial realm, so too is Gaṇeśa, residing in this excellent abode like Hara; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, the serpents perish through the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the ten-faced one. 182–183.
Eleven Rudras are said to reside in the mouth, and eleven are remembered as being in the crest-lock (śikhā). Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who constantly wears [these mantras] there:
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of millions of other sacrifices. 184.

Whatever fruit is obtained from a hundred thousand cows properly given as a gift, that fruit one quickly attains by wearing the eleven faces [of Śiva]. Such a person becomes equal to Hara in this world, and for them, there is no further rebirth. 185–186.
Whoever wears twelve rudrākṣas around the region of the neck,
Āditya is eternally pleased, as he is established within those twelve faces.
One attains that fruit which is gained by performing a horse sacrifice and a human sacrifice.
One quickly attains that fruit, as well as protection from thunderbolts and the like (188).
There is no fear of fire, nor does disease arise;
one enjoys the gain of wealth and happiness, becoming a lord rather than a pauper (189).
Having killed or even caused the death of elephants, horses, men, cats, mice, rabbits, as well as predatory beasts, fanged animals, jackals, and the like—
one is liberated from this without a doubt by wearing [this mantra] on the twelve parts of the face. 190.
If one obtains thirteen beads for the face and eleven for the arms, it is known as the most auspicious Rudrākṣa, which grants the fruit of all desires;
it is indeed an elixir of nectar, a means of alchemy, and a pair of sandals. 191–192.
O Six-faced One, all these succeed for that fortunate person who,
having slain his mother, father, sister, brother, or teacher,
is liberated from all sins by wearing the thirteen-faced [liṅga].
One obtains inexhaustible heaven, just like the god Maheśvara,
O child, if one should constantly wear Rudrākṣa on the head or on the arm, or the Śiva-śakti-piṇḍa, which has fourteen faces. 194–195.
What more need be said, or what need for repeated description?
He is constantly worshipped by the gods and attains [his status] through the weight of his merit. 196. Kārttikeya said:

"O Blessed One, I wish to hear how the ritual placement (*nyāsana*) is performed according to rule when reciting the mantra; tell me, by what mantra is it done, or how is it maintained? (197) The Lord said:
Listen, O Six-faced one, to the truth regarding each and every mouth according to the rule:
these qualities are proclaimed to arise simply from the utterance of the mantra.
Furthermore, that man on earth who wears [this] conjoined with the mantra—

His qualities and his greatness cannot indeed be fully described. (199) Now, the mantras and so forth are taught: *Oṃ rudra* for the one-faced; *Oṃ khaṃ* for the two-faced; *Oṃ vuṃ* for the three-faced.
Oṃ hrīṃ, of the four-faced one; oṃ hrāṃ, of the five-faced one; oṃ hrūṃ, of the six-faced one; oṃ hraḥ, of the seven-faced one;
oṃ kaṃ, of the eight-faced one; oṃ jūṃ, of the nine-faced one.
Oṃ kṣaṃ, of the ten-faced one; oṃ śrīṃ, of the eleven-faced one;
oṃ hrīṃ, of the twelve-faced one; oṃ kṣauṃ, of the thirteen-faced one; oṃ nrāṃ, of the fourteen-faced one.

In this manner, the mantras should be placed in sequence upon the head and the chest; and the garland should be taken. The man who proceeds while holding it obtains, at every step, the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha); it is not otherwise. 200.
One who wears [Rudrākṣas] on all their faces shall become equal to me;
therefore, O son, wear Rudrākṣa with every effort. That man who dies upon the earth after having worn Rudrākṣa [attains the highest state].
O child,

in ancient times, in the Maru country at a place called Vāṇijyaka, a merchant’s son who was traveling there, tormented by a female ghost on the riverbank, [attained] the beautiful city of Sayāti, which is worshipped by all the gods. (202-203)

From that dancing preta, the twice-born man then asked: "Who are you? Why do you dance, being so miserable and shrouded in tattered rags? (204) Then she said to the twice-born man: "I have heard from the messengers of the gods."
"By the fall of a thunderbolt upon this very handsome man,
the death of my husband, O Brahmin, will surely occur right now.
In that interval, a thunderbolt descended from the sky onto his head.
It fell upon the earth with a great roar into a half-fragment of a rudrākṣa;
then my son’s celestial chariot quickly descended from my city. Having ascended it, the illustrious one remained there for a long time.
"O son, having obtained even a fragment of my portion, what wealth could a lord not possess? Thus, for one who has died with even a piece of rudrākṣa, there is a happy rebirth;
we are unable to describe the fruit for a man who wears it with spiritual knowledge."
Whether one belongs to the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Saura tradition,
if they wear a garland made of *mṛta* beads— or even just a single rudrākṣa— once deceased, they shall attain [liberation].
Furthermore, whoever recites this, causes it to be recited, causes it to be heard, or listens to it themselves, [attains the same].
With his soul liberated from all sins, he shall gradually attain the blissful heaven. 211.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty.
Skanda said:
O Lord of the Universe, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, please speak regarding the purity of the fruit of another tree as well.
Īśvara said:
The dhātrī fruit is supremely pure and renowned throughout all the worlds; by planting it, a man or a woman is liberated from the bondage of birth. 2.
The fruit of Vāsudeva is purifying, auspicious, and brings joy;
by the mere eating of it, one is liberated from all impurity. By eating it, longevity is attained, and by drinking it, there is an accumulation of merit.
By bathing, one destroys misfortune and shall attain all sovereignty.
O Mahāsena, in whichever house the Dhātrī fruit always resides,
ghosts, Daityas, and Rākṣasas do not enter that house.
Neither Naga, Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara;
indeed, on the arrival of the day of Hari, the Ekādaśī of both fortnights, the Dhātrī alone is the [true] sacred site for men.
He who performs the bath at the Dhātrī tree on the Ekādaśī of both fortnights—
All their sins are destroyed, and they are glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. The fruit of the *dhātrī* tree should always be used, both for eating and for bathing;
it is essential during the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the day of Viṣṇu, even by merely bathing on that day of Hari. 7–8.
O Six-faced One, that man who, having fasted on both the dark and light Ekādaśīs, eats while his mother is restrained from eating and touches her alone,
is satisfied by that single fast alone.
One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
One attains imperishable heaven and shall attain union with Viṣṇu. Therefore, perform the vow of Dhātrī with every effort. 10–11.
O Six-faced One, no one whose hair is constantly dyed with the juice of the *dhātrī* tree would ever again drink from his mother’s breast;
even by seeing, touching, or merely uttering the name of the *dhātrī*, [one attains such purity]. 12.
Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons, becomes pleased and favorable when facing one. Wherever the *dhātrī* fruit is present, there Keśava resides;
there Brahmā is established upon the lotus, therefore one should place it in the house. 14.
Misfortune perishes wherever the Dhātrī tree stands;
all the gods, being well-pleased, joyfully do not leave that place for even a moment.
He who offers an oblation of Dhātrī fruit as a gift of great wealth [attains prosperity]. 15.

Viṣṇu becomes pleased with him even more than by hundreds of other sacrifices. He who bathes with the juice of the dhātrī fruit and worships Mādhava obtains the desired fruit that resides in his mind.
Having likewise remembered its characteristics and worshipped it with its fruit, O best of men, that fruit is equal to a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
That destination which belongs to the wise, to the sages, and to those who practice yoga— [that is his].
A man who delights in serving the Dhātrī tree attains that same destination.
That goal which is reached by men through visiting sacred fords, undertaking various vows, and so forth, is obtained simply by the excellent service of the Dhātrī fruit. 19–20.
There shall be joy for all the gods, goddesses, and the host of Gaṇas when they perform this bath and use the fruits of the dhātrī tree;
and whatever malevolent planets, fierce Daityas, or Rākṣasas there may be, [they shall be subdued]. 21.
By the excellent use of the dhātrī fruit, all things become free from defects.
The āmalakī fruit is commended for all sacrificial rites and tasks, O son of the Sun, with the exception of the worship of all the gods. 22–23.
Therefore, one should always avoid *dhātrī* fruits from afar, especially on the seventh lunar day and on Sundays. He who bathes with or eats *dhātrī* on a Sunday [incurs misfortune].

His lifespan, wealth, and wife— all of these perish. On the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on a Friday, on the sixth, the first, the ninth, and the new moon day, one should certainly avoid the dhātrī tree from afar.
He in whose nose, ears, mouth,
or hair a *dhātrī* fruit remains at the time of death goes to the abode of Viṣṇu;
by the mere contact of the *dhātrī*, one who dies goes to the residence of Acyuta.
All his sins are destroyed, and he goes to heaven in a chariot.
