That righteous man who, having smeared himself with the juice of the *dhātrī* tree, performs his bath, obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at every step. (28–29)
Merely by the sight of him, even these most wicked creatures, along with all the fierce and malevolent grahas, flee away.
Previously, a certain Pulkasa went to the forest for the purpose of hunting Skanda.
Afflicted by thirst, he killed flocks of deer and birds;
then, seeing an āmalakī tree ahead laden with plump fruits, he climbed it at once and ate the excellent fruit. 31–32.

Then, by fate, he fell from the top of that tree onto the surface of the earth; pierced by intense agony, he then met his death. Thereupon, all the hosts of pretas, as well as the hosts of rakshasas and bhutas, [gathered].

All those attendants of Vaiśravaṇa, though possessed of great strength, were unable to joyfully carry the slender body; even they could not bear to look upon the dead Cāṇḍāla, as they fell into mutual conflict, each saying, "This is mine! (34-35).
They were unable to seize or lead one another away;
then, having looked at each other, they went toward the hosts of sages.
The pretas said:
"For what reason are these wise sages unable even to look upon a Cāṇḍāla who commits evil deeds, nor even upon his servants?
Those who turn their backs in battle die fallen into a pit, even though they are steadfast."
Terrified by violent acts, they are struck down; they are tormented by thunderbolts, fire, and wood.
Mortals are killed by lions and tigers, or by tigers and aquatic creatures, whether staying in water or on land; as ghosts, they are cast down from trees and mountains.
Those killed by beasts or birds, those who died in prison,

those who died by suicide, those for whom rites such as the śrāddha were not performed, rogues who died while their deeds remained hidden, and those who were enemies of their gurus, brahmins, and kings— [these are the ones excluded]. 40.

Heretics, Kaulikas, the cruel, poisoners, and those who give false testimony; those who eat food during periods of ritual impurity—without a doubt, these are the ones whose food is to be enjoyed by the deceased.
Even as they say, "This is mine," we are unable to take him away. 41-42.
"He is as difficult to look upon as the sun; by whose power is this?
The sages said: "O ghosts, he has eaten this ripe *āmalaka* fruit. 43.
They go to his company and obtain his abundant fruits;
for that very reason, he is surely difficult for you to behold. Furthermore, the life-force of one fallen from the top of a tree does not abandon him out of affection.
"Neither by the course of the sun nor by other [means] do evildoers go to heaven purified from sin merely by eating the earth.
The pretas said:
"Indeed, we do not ask out of ignorance, nor are we revilers of you anywhere (verse 46).
Before the celestial chariot from the world of Viṣṇu arrives here,
O tigers among sages, let that which resides in your minds be told quickly (verse 47)."
As far as the sound of the Vedas and the mantras composed therein extends—
wherein the Vedas, various mantras,
Purāṇas, and Smṛtis are proclaimed— we are not able to remain there even for a moment.
"We stand before the rites of sacrifice, oblation, recitation, and the worship of deities; therefore, let our conduct be explained.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, by doing what do men attain birth as ghosts?"
"We wish to hear correctly how his body became transformed.
The twice-born said:
"By the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, and by the particular sufferings of hunger and thirst... (51)
Those false witnesses who were afflicted by other miseries as well, and those who died through execution or imprisonment, have gone to hell as pretas; likewise,
those who were intent on seeking the faults of brahmins and who obstructed their religious duties.
In that very same way, those who have become pretas toward their gurus pierce the donor while he is giving to the foremost of the twice-born;
having long assumed the state of a preta, they do not return from hell. 53-54.
Those fools who, having taken others' or their own cattle, do not protect them from being oppressed or driven away, become preta-born beings on earth due to their karma.
Likewise, those men who are false to their promises, untruthful, and have broken their vows [become so].
Those ghosts born of their own karma on earth eat from the petals of lotuses;
those ghosts born of their own karma on earth sell their pure daughters, their virtuous wives, and their unblemished paternal uncles and maternal uncles.
These and many other pretas were born through their own past actions.
The pretas said: "O twice-born ones, how is it that they do not become pretas? By what action [do they avoid this]? (58)

The twice-born said: "He who, for the welfare of all the world, has quickly spoken these supreme words for the benefit of others—he, the wise one, has indeed performed his bath in the waters of the sacred ford. (59)
A person who has paid homage to the supreme *liṅga* does not become a ghost;
indeed, by fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and especially on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*),
mortals who worship Hari do not enter the state of a ghost at all.
Those who are devoted to the worship of the gods with hymns, mantras, and the like produced from the syllables of the Vedas, indeed become pretas.
Having heard these words of the Purāṇa, which are divine and consistent with dharma, [the sages asked: 61–62.
By teaching and by studying, one does not go to the state of a piśāca;
likewise, those purified by various vows and by wearing lotus seeds (padmākṣa),
and having recited mantras with a rosary of lotus seeds, do not go to the state of a preta at all.
Having bathed with the juices of *dhātrī* fruits and being constantly devoted to eating them, and having thoroughly worshipped Viṣṇu with that [juice], they do not fall into the state of a *piśāca*.
The *pretas* said:
"The seers of the Purāṇas know that merit arises from the sight of the virtuous.
Therefore, since we have obtained the sight of you, you ought to act for our benefit so that the liberation of all of us from the state of being ghosts may occur. (65-66)
"O wise ones, we have come to you for refuge; please instruct us in our vows.
Then all those most excellent of the twice-born, being compassionate, said to them:
"For the sake of your liberation, quickly practice the consumption of *dhātrī* fruits."
The pretas said:
"O Brahmins, we are unable to remain even in the sight of the nurses;
how then could we possibly be capable of eating those fruits now?"
The twice-born said:
"By our word, the eating of these dhātrī fruits here will result in supreme welfare; therefore, you ought to go to the other world."
Then, having obtained a boon from them, the Piśācas climbed a Dhātrī tree and playfully ate its fruit. Thereafter,
they quickly departed from the temple on a stout and very beautiful chariot.
Having ascended that which had arrived, even those who were Cāṇḍālas and Piśācas went to heaven, O son, by means of their vows and sacrifices— a state very difficult to attain.
Skanda said:
"By merely eating the *dhātrī* fruit, they attained merit and went to heaven;
why then do men and others who eat it not go to heaven? 73.
The Lord said:
Due to the loss of their former knowledge, they do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful;
deluded as they are, these ghosts always eat even leavings, things touched by dogs, or phlegm, urine, and excrement, regarding them as excellent food. (74)
The water used for cleansing after defecation, vomit, and offerings made by pigs or cocks;
the food and water of one who has not abandoned recitation during a period of death-impurity or birth-impurity—these the pretas always devour. (75–76)
The wife of such a man is difficult to control, impure, and devoid of self-restraint; having been cast out by her elders, she is wicked, and indeed, pretas dwell there.
Furthermore, those who are not preeminent in their lineage or birth, and are destitute of strength and vigor—[they too shall dwell there]. 77.
Deaf, emaciated, and so forth, these Piśācas are born from their own karma.
For them, there is not even a moment of auspiciousness; being joined with bodies, they are intensely beset by sufferings.
For that very reason, they possess deformed appearances and are utterly deprived of all enjoyments.
Naked, afflicted by disease, parched like nectar, rough, and soiled—
these and other such beings, tormented by suffering, are always born among the classes of pretas due to the ripening of that karma. Thus they are born in such a state as this.
Those who revile their father, mother, and preceptors, those devoted to the censure of the gods, the heretics, the Kaulikas, and the sinful—they become ghosts born of their own actions on earth.
Likewise, those who commit suicide by means of nooses around the neck, water, weapons, or poison [become such ghosts]. 81-82.
In this world, those who are born as pretas, as caṇḍālas and other low-born castes (antyajas), as outcasts (patitas), or those who die of sinful diseases—
these are certainly pretas on earth when they are slain in battle by those of the lowest castes.
Those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka), those excluded from marriage,
those who are reckless due to their valor, these are the pretas born of their actions on earth;
as are those who commit treason against the king and those who cause harm to their ancestors.

Devoid of meditation and study, lacking vows such as the worship of deities, bereft of mantras and ritual bathing, they are intent on approaching the wives of their gurus; likewise, they associate with outcaste women and those in miserable conditions. (86)
Those who die through cruel fasting, those who die while residing in the lands of the Mlecchas, those who speak the Mleccha tongue yet are impure, as well as those who subsist upon the Mlecchas—
those who live off women and wealth and follow after the Mlecchas— [are reborn as such]. 87–88.
Those by whom women are not protected shall undoubtedly become pretas; moreover,
those who abandon a weary brahmin who has come to their home— his body tormented by hunger and possessing the virtues and merit of a guest— go to the state of piśācas.
They sell cows even to Mlecchas and to those who eat beef;
having dwelt happily in the world of the departed (Pretaloka), they go from there to rebirth as animals born during a period of impurity after death. 90–91.

Those who have long been ghosts and piśācas, having died again and again, are those who have been deprived of the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with the birth ceremony (jātakarma). With each individual purificatory rite, their state as a ghost is abandoned.

Those sinners who, from birth, have been devoid of ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, worship of the gods, the Vedas, sacrifices, vows, and sacred syllables, become ghosts (pretas) from whom there is no rebirth.
Their vessels containing the remnants of food and their bodily impurities [become their sustenance]. 93–94.
Those who cause [the ancestors] to fall at a sacred ford (tīrtha) become pretas; of this there is no doubt.
These ancestors and elders, born as pretas due to their past actions, are not at all satisfied on earth by gifts, honors, or worship offered to Brahmins. (95)

That ignoble woman who, having abandoned her husband, dwells with other men, remains for a long time in the world of the departed spirits (preta-loka) and is then born into the lowest wombs. Likewise, those who deceive their husbands, being deluded by the objects of the senses, [meet the same fate]. 96–97.
Those wicked ones who eat sweet food [without offering it] become pretas on earth for a long time;

those who consume excrement and urine, and those who are intent on devouring the property of Brahmins (brahmasva), as well as others who eat what is forbidden to eat, become pretas from whom there is no return to human birth. 98.
Those who seize the property of others by force and do not give even when asked, and who treat guests with contempt, remain in hell as pretas.
Therefore, having eaten an āmalaka fruit and bathed with its juice, [one should perform this rite]. 99–100.
Being completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
therefore, with every effort, one should serve the auspicious Āmalakī tree.
He who would constantly hear this meritorious and auspicious narrative [shall likewise attain such glory].
One whose soul is purified of all sins is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu (102).
He who constantly causes this to be heard in the world, especially among the devotees of Viṣṇu, attains union with Viṣṇu; so the knowers of the Purāṇas declare (103).
Skanda said: "O Lord, the fruit of trees has been known to me as being of two kinds and purifying; now I desire to hear about the leaves and flowers that grant excellent liberation. (104)
Īśvara said:
Among all leaves and flowers, the most excellent is the auspicious Tulasī;
it is pure, the granter of all desires, belonging to Viṣṇu, and very dear to Viṣṇu. 105
The foremost bestower of enjoyment and liberation, auspicious for all the worlds,
and by resorting to which the best of sages have gone to the imperishable heaven—
she was established in ancient times by Viṣṇu for the welfare of all the worlds. 106.
The leaf and flower of Tulasī are established as the foundation of all dharma (107).
Just as Lakṣmī is dear to Viṣṇu and just as I myself am dear, so too is this goddess Tulasī; no fourth [deity] can be found equal to her (108).

A single leaf of Tulasī bestows the fruit of a hundred gold pieces; Viṣṇu, the slayer of Daityas, is not so pleased by other flowers, leaves, perfumes, or ointments as he is by the petals of Tulasī. 109.
By whoever Hari is worshipped daily with supreme devotion,
by that person everything has been given, offered in sacrifice, known, and performed— including sacrifices, vows, and the like;
and throughout birth after birth, they shall possess splendor, happiness, fortune, fame, and prosperity.
Family, character, wife, as well as son and daughter, wealth, kingdom, health, knowledge, and even specialized wisdom;
the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Saṃhitās—[all these are attained through this]. 112.
One who considers everything as being under his control [is surpassed] by the worship of Tulasī for Hari.
Just as the Gaṅgā, whose limbs are purifying, grants liberation in the world of the gods, and just as the Bhāgīrathī is meritorious, so too is the auspicious Tulasī. 113–114.
What is the use of the water of the Gaṅgā, or what is the use of serving at Puṣkara?
One is truly delighted simply by water mixed with a Tulasī leaf for that wise person before whom Mādhava appears face-to-face in birth after birth. 115.
If one hears of the incomparable Tulasī but lacks faith,
yet worships Viṣṇu with the clusters and leaves of that very Tulasī,
O Skanda, it is impossible to describe the fruit of his merit. 116–117.
Wherever there is a grove of *tulasī*, there is the presence of Keśava; there also reside Brahmā and Lakṣmī along with all the hosts of gods.
Therefore, one should always worship that Goddess in close proximity to it.
Whatever hymns, mantras, and so forth [are recited], they all attain infinity.
Furthermore, those who are ghosts (preta), kūśmāṇḍas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, spirits (bhūta), daityas, and the like, always flee from that place indeed. 119–120.

Alakṣmī (misfortune), Ghūrṇā, and all the Mothers such as Ḍākinī and others shrink away upon seeing a *tulasī* leaf. Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as diseases born of sin, [perish]. 121.
Indeed, all those things performed by a wicked minister perish right there;
however, he who has planted a grove of *tulasī* on the earth for the sake of Hari has,
in effect, performed a hundred sacrifices according to the rules with abundant sacrificial fees.
By taking hold of Tulasī at other auspicious objects and at Sālagrāma stones,
one shall attain union with Viṣṇu. Those men rejoice in whose land Tulasī is grown for the sake of Mādhava.

The wise man who plants a *tulasī* tree goes to the abode of Mādhava. Having worshipped the Lord Hari, he who wears the *tulasī* leaf from the sacred remains (*nirmālya*) upon his head becomes purified of sin and shall go to heaven.
In the Kali age, Tulasī destroys sin through worship, chanting, meditation, planting, and wearing; she bestows both heaven and liberation.
(127) One should give instruction regarding her and, moreover, practice it oneself. (128)
The eternal and supreme abode, the residence of Mādhava—
that which is dear to Hari— may it become even more dear to me than all other things. May it be equal to that of all the gods and goddesses in every respect.
O Six-faced One, in ancestral rites and sacrificial ceremonies, a single leaf [is sufficient];
therefore, with every effort, practice the service of Tulasī. By whomsoever Tulasī is served, by him everything has been served.
Therefore, O Six-faced One, serve the guru, the Brahmin, and the deity as a sacred ford (tīrtha). He who,
having placed a tulasī leaf upon his crest, should give up his life,
is liberated from a flood of evil deeds and goes to the stainless heaven.

The destination reached by the wise through sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, through various vows, and through restraints, shall be attained by those who serve Tulasī. By worshipping Hari with even a single leaf of Tulasī, a person [attains that same goal]. 133–134.

One attains the state of being a Vaiṣṇava; what is the use of other extensive scriptures? He who has worshipped Keśava with the tender sprouts of a branch of Tulasī has drunk the milk of ten million mothers. 135.
A mortal man should meditate upon hundreds and thousands of Puruṣas;
by constantly worshipping Hari with tender tulasī leaves, O dear one, the preeminent qualities of tulasī have thus been described by me. 136–137.
We are unable to describe all his qualities even in a vast amount of time;
however, whoever should constantly hear this narrative, which is a collection of merit, is liberated from the sins committed in previous births and from the bondage of rebirth. 138.
By merely reciting it once, one obtains the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice.
(139) He shall never suffer from diseases, nor shall his son ever be dull-witted; he always attains victory and shall never meet with defeat. (140)
In whosever house this letter remains, for that person prosperity prevails;
there is no mental anguish, nor ghosts, nor grief, nor humiliation.
(141) Those [misfortunes] do not stay even for a moment where this script resides. (142)
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-one.
The twice-born said:
O Hari, we have heard from you the auspicious greatness of the Tulasī flower; now we wish to hear the meritorious hymn composed for her. Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, that which I have previously proclaimed in the Skanda Purāṇa,
they shall now recite this Purāṇa before you for the sake of liberation.
All those disciples of the sage Śatānanda were firm in their vows.
Having prostrated before their guru, the brahmins asked about what was beneficial for merit:
"O Lord, O best among the knowers of Brahman, we wish to hear from you that hymn to Lakṣmī which was previously heard by us from the mouth of Brahmā. (3-4)
Śatānanda said:
When her name is uttered, the destroyer of the pride of the asuras is pleased; sins go to destruction and merit becomes inexhaustible. 5.
She is neither worshipped nor saluted by people who speak of her as mere Tulasi;
yet, by the mere sight of her, the merit of giving ten million cows is attained. Blessed are those men in this world in whose house she resides during the Kali age.
For the sake of the Śālagrāma stone, Tulasī should be gathered daily from the earth;
blessed are those hands that pluck Tulasī, and even more blessed are those who plant it here on this earth for the sake of Keśava in the Kali age.
What will this enraged one do, even with his servants?
For by whomsoever the Lord of Gods has been worshipped with a single leaf of *tulasī*, he is the destroyer of suffering.
Is a *kiṃnara* not perfected through the fruits of traveling on pilgrimages and the like?
In bathing, giving gifts, meditation, consuming [food], and in the worship of Keśava, Tulasī destroys sin; in the Kali age, she does so through praise and planting.
O Tulasī, you are born from nectar; you are eternally dear to Keśava.
"O beautiful one, grant me a boon; I gather you for the sake of Keśava.
O you of pure limbs, O destroyer of impurity, act in such a way that I may constantly worship Hari with those parts produced from your body."
Whoever performs the worship of Vāsudeva by plucking a Tulasī leaf with this mantra, it shall become a hundred thousand times ten million times more meritorious.
O Lord of Gods, the best of the deities sing of your power.
The sages, Siddhas, and Gandharvas, as well as the King of the Nagas himself in Patala—
even these deities do not know his power, with the exception of Keshava;
nor can they measure the extent of his qualities even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Lord, in former times, during the effort to churn the ocean of milk, Tulasī was placed upon his head by Viṣṇu;
having now obtained all these limbs of Viṣṇu from you in their entirety, [I am fulfilled]. (16-17)
I bow to you, O Tulasī, whose purity has been attained by you;
act so that I may worship Hari with the leaves produced from your body without obstacle, and thereby attain the supreme goal. 18.
Planted on the banks of the Gomatī by Kṛṣṇa himself and nurtured by him,
Tulasī exists for the welfare of the world and for the benefit of the gopīs;
she was personally served by Viṣṇu while he wandered in Vṛndāvana.

O beloved of the world, at the request of Vasiṣṭha, you were formerly planted by Rāma on the bank of the Sarayū for the sake of increasing Gokula, for the destruction of Kaṃsa, and for the slaying of the Rākṣasas.
I bow to you, O Tulasī, who were planted for the increase of my ascetic merit.
By meditating upon you during her separation from Vāsudeva, the daughter of Janaka was reunited with her beloved in the midst of the Aśoka grove. 22–23.
O Goddess, in ancient times, you were planted by Pārvatī on Himālaya for the sake of Śaṅkara and for the increase of her ascetic merit; I bow to you, O Tulasī.
(24) Even by all the wives of the gods and by the Kinnaras in the Nandana grove, [you are honored].
Salutations to you, who are served for the purpose of destroying evil dreams;
salutations to you, who were personally served by the ancestors at Dharmāraṇya and Gayā, and who were served by the holy Tulasī for one desiring their own welfare. 25–26.
Planted by Rāmācandra and served by Lakṣmaṇa, it was protected with devotion by Sītā in the Daṇḍaka forest;
it is celebrated in the scriptures as the Gaṅgā that pervades the three worlds. 27.
In that very same way, the goddess Tulasī is seen throughout the world of moving and non-moving beings.
On Mount Ṛśyamūka, she was served by the king of monkeys, Vāli, for the sake of obtaining a union with Tārā. 28–29.
Having bowed to the goddess Tulasī, Hanumān crossed the ocean; having accomplished his task and being greatly delighted, he returned. By taking hold of Tulasī, one is liberated from sins.
Alternatively, O tiger among sages, he removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
He who carries on his head the water dripping from a Tulasī leaf obtains the merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā, which yields the fruit of ten cows.
Be gracious, O Goddess of the gods; be gracious, O Beloved of Hari!
I bow down to you, Tulasī, who arose from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
(33) Whoever recites this hymn to Tulasī while keeping a vigil at night on the twelfth lunar day, [attains great merit].
Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses of that person.
Whatever sin was committed in youth, childhood, adolescence, or old age—
all that goes to destruction through the recitation of the Tulasī hymn.
The Lord of Devas, becoming pleased, bestows joy; being satisfied, he grants Lakṣmī, effects the destruction of enemies, and bestows happiness and knowledge.
By the mere mention of the name of Tulasī, the gods grant whatever is desired.
O Lord of Gods, even for those who are censurable, she grants liberation to embodied beings.
Satisfied by the hymn of praise to Tulasī, she bestows happiness and prosperity. Know that she effortlessly destroys the sin that has arisen and stands upon the path.

In whichever house this hymn of praise to Tulasī is found inscribed, no inauspiciousness shall exist there; he certainly attains auspiciousness. (39) Everything therein is auspicious; nothing whatsoever is inauspicious.
For one who gives everything at all times, there shall be abundance of food, and wealth and grain in plenty (40).
His devotion to Keśava is unwavering, and he never suffers separation from his Vaiṣṇava companions;
he lives free from disease, and no thought of unrighteousness arises in his mind (41).
Whoever recites the Tulasī hymn while keeping a vigil on the twelfth lunar day attains that same fruit which is obtained by bathing in thousands of crores and lakhs of sacred fords. 42-43.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Hymn to Tulasī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-Two.
The twice-born said:

By bathing here, all sin undoubtedly goes to destruction—both the great sins (mahāpātaka) and others. Therefore, O Lord, tell me the command regarding this place. Purified from sin, one enjoys the imperishable heaven in the celestial realm like Śakra.

"O Lord of Speech, tell me the instruction whereby there may be no loss of the source of wine; for here on earth everything is merely an object of enjoyment, whereas after death one becomes the best of gods in heaven,
and this [practice] is said to be the staircase to heaven for those struck by the sins of the Kali age."
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmins, for men and women of ordinary birth who are contemplating their destiny, the Gaṅgā swiftly removes sin through the mere sight of her. 4.
By the mere remembrance of the Gaṅgā, sin goes to destruction;
by chanting her name, great evils; by beholding her, heavy impurity;
and likewise by bathing in, drinking from, and offering libations to the ancestors in the Jāhnavī.
The multitude of great sins goes to destruction day by day. Just as cotton or dry grass is consumed by fire in an instant,
so too does contact with the water of the Gaṅgā burn away the sins of men in a moment.
By bathing in the Gaṅgā, one attains imperishable heaven;
one obtains fame, sovereignty, merit, heaven, and in the end, the supreme goal.
He who offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) in the Gaṅgā for the sake of his ancestors [attains the same].

Listen to the fruit of his merit according to the rite preceded by the recitation of the Vākya: one thousand years in the abode of the gods is attained by worshipping with a single grain of rice; know that it is doubled by sesame seeds, and likewise by pure fruits. 9–10.
O Brahmins, by the rite involving cow-products, there is no end to heaven;
likewise, through the constant offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), it becomes as if one has performed a hundred sacrifices.
Blessed indeed are those mortals who dwell on earth while their ancestors remain in hell.
Endowed with wealth and sons, they enjoy health, happiness, honor, and worship.

Whether they have gone to the netherworld, or are insects upon the surface of the earth, or among stationary objects, flocks of birds, and so forth—whether mortals, wealthy men, or kings—they [all attain this]. 12–13.
By their respective sons, grandsons, kinsmen, daughters' sons, as well as by sons-in-law, nephews, friends, allies, and both beloved and disliked ones,
water and funeral cakes (piṇḍas) are offered along with the necessary ritual implements.

In the waters of the Gaṅgā and on its banks, their heaven shall become imperishable. Furthermore, all those ancestors born of one's mother’s lineage who reside above the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) shall all become happy, as shall mortals by the hundreds of thousands.
The beings dwelling in heaven, those situated below, and those residing in the middle—all constantly long for the auspicious Gaṅgā; let them go to the celestial river.
He alone goes to the Gaṅgā by whose [family] members are purified.
This [river], possessing such great merit, carries across and delivers even others.
Even the four-faced Brahmā is not able to describe the entire virtue of the Gaṅgā;
therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall speak here of some of the qualities of Bhāgīrathī.
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and other excellent deities,
having performed austerities on the banks of the Gaṅgā, became imperishable in the heavenly world,
all possessing divine bodies and traveling in chariots that move at will.
Even today they do not turn back from those places filled with jewels that are never exhausted;
there the golden palaces are auspicious, rising above all worlds,
well-filled with desired objects, and where the women are enchanting.
The *pārijāta* trees are equal to flowering trees and comparable to the wish-fulfilling kalpa-tree;
indeed, by performing penance there on the banks of the Gaṅgā, one attains sovereignty through many austerities, sacrifices, and various kinds of vows. (23)
She is the refuge for those who possess many gifts and for those who serve the Gaṅgā.

[She does not accept] one born of an adulterer, an outcaste, a wicked man, an outcaste of the lowest caste, a killer of a guru, one filled with malice toward all, or one burdened with every sin. (24-25)
Sons abandon their father, wives their beloved husbands, groups of friends, and all other kinsmen; yet none would ever forsake the Gaṅgā.
Just as a mother herself performs the purification of her child from the impurities of birth, so does the Gaṅgā. 26.1–27.1.
Embracing them in that way, Gaṅgā washes away their impurity.
Those men by whom Gaṅgā is beheld even once with devotion become highly renowned, honored with enjoyments and ornaments. (27–28)

The auspicious Goddess, who removes the suffering of those who remember her, delivers a hundred thousand generations of their families from the ocean of worldly existence when she is meditated upon, praised, and joyfully celebrated by the virtuous.
Gaṅgā delivers both lineages of men from the ocean of worldly existence.
During the transits of the sun, at the vyatīpāta yoga, and during lunar and solar eclipses—
having bathed in the Gaṅgā on these auspicious occasions— one may deliver ten million members of one’s lineage.
O mortals, during the bright fortnight, by day, and during the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa), [one should likewise bathe] in the Gaṅgā.
Blessed indeed are those who, while Janārdana dwells within their hearts, cast off their bodies here according to this rite in the auspicious waters of the Bhāgīrathī;
having abandoned their vital breaths, they shall go to heaven from which there is no return.
He who is constantly devoted to the limbs of yoga is indeed followed by all the gods.
Since Viṣṇu consists of all the gods and Gaṅgā consists of Viṣṇu, the ancestors are truly satisfied by the offering of rice-balls and water with sesame seeds in the Gaṅgā. 33–34.

Those dwelling in hell go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven attain liberation; for one who harms another’s wife, another’s property, or another’s livelihood, the Gaṅgā alone is the supreme refuge for every human being. 35.

For one who is devoid of the Vedas and Shastras, who is intent on reviling his guru, and who is bereft of the conduct prescribed by the tradition, there is no attainment of the Ganges. What is the use of sacrifices rich in wealth, or of penances that are exceedingly difficult to perform? 36–37.
Ganga, who bestows heaven and liberation, is worshipped for her happiness and good fortune; what need is there for constant supreme restraints or for yogas that restrain the mind?
(38) Ganga, who grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, stands before one's very eyes as happiness and salvation.

The sins accumulated over many births of men are destroyed by merely bathing in the Gaṅgā; a man shall immediately become a partaker of merit at Prabhāsa when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, as if it were the gift of a thousand cows. 39–40.

Whatever fruit one obtains from giving gifts by bathing daily in the Gaṅgā, that very sin is removed by seeing her; by touching her, one attains heaven. Even when encountered incidentally, that Gaṅgā, once plunged into, bestows liberation.
The fickleness of all the senses arising from the power of latent impressions (vāsanā),
as well as cruelty, the longing for another's property, and the desire for another's wife— all these perish upon the sight of the Gaṅgā. 42–43.
Aversion to the dharma of others perishes at the mere sight [of the Gaṅgā];
contentment with whatever is obtained by chance arises, and one proceeds in accordance with one's own duties. Equanimity toward all beings also comes from bathing in the Gaṅgā.

That man who dwells happily having taken refuge in the Gaṅgā is indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta) here; he is the most excellent among all. For one who remains having resorted to the Gaṅgā, there is no further duty to be performed.
That man who has accomplished all that was to be done, who is liberated, and who is liberated while living—
his sacrifice, charity, austerity, recitation, ancestral rites, and worship of the gods,
when performed daily at the Gaṅgā, becomes multiplied by millions upon millions of times.
Sin committed elsewhere perishes on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
sin committed on the banks of the Gaṅgā perishes by bathing in the Gaṅgā, especially on the day of one's own birth-star when it coincides with the day of the Jahnavī’s confluence. 48–49.
A man who bathes in the Gaṅgā shall uplift his entire lineage;
just as a man always praises a wealthy person with great respect,
so too by praising the Gaṅgā even once, he becomes a recipient of heaven.
Even one who, lacking faith, merely utters the name of the Ganges,
that river of merit, becomes a recipient of heaven;
while nourishing mortals on earth, he also delivers the nāgas from the depths below.
The Ganges, which flows through the three paths, is remembered as the divine river that leads one to heaven;
whether by knowledge or ignorance, or whether intentionally or unintentionally,
a mortal who dies in the Ganges attains both heaven and liberation.
The goal attained by a wise man established in *sattva* and disciplined in yoga is the same as the goal attained by an embodied being who gives up their life-breaths at the Gaṅgā,
even if that person were to perform thousands of *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts for the purification of the body.

One may drink as much as one desires; yet the water of the Gaṅgā is superior, for such is the power of sacred fords (tīrthas), and especially that of the gods. Such is the power of the Vedas only so long as one has not reached the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā).
Vāyu declared that there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas);
they exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, O Jāhnavī,
O Gaṅgā who have originated from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, you who travel along the three paths.
O Gaṅgā, renowned as Dharmadravā, take away my sin; you are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, you belong to Viṣṇu, and you are worshipped by Viṣṇu.
Save me from that sin which extends from birth until the end of death.

O Great Goddess Bhāgīrathī, purify me with these three excellent verses— [verses] filled with dharma through faith, endowed with splendor, and consisting of nectar— in the waters of the Jāhnavī. (60–61)
One is liberated from the sins committed over ten million births; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now declare the root mantra spoken by Jāhnavī:
by reciting it even once, a person becomes purified and establishes himself within the body of Viṣṇu.
And this mantra is:
*Oṃ namo gaṅgāyai viśvarūpiṇyai nārāyaṇyai namo namaḥ* (63).
He who bears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Jāhnavī—
A man who is liberated from all sins, even without bathing in the Gaṅgā,
if he touches the wind shaken by the waves of the Gaṅgā’s water,
becomes purified from terrible defilement and attains imperishable heaven.
As long as the bones of a human being remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world—
[this applies] to one's parents, kinsmen, the helpless, and even to one's teacher.
By casting one's bones into the Gaṅgā, a person does not fall from heaven.
That man who carries even a small fragment of bone for his ancestors toward the Gaṅgā obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at every step.

O best of the twice-born, those who have died within the distance of a *krośa* along the banks of the Jahnavī— including the fortunate inhabitants of the countryside, as well as beasts, birds, insects, and other beings, both stationary and moving— [all attain the highest state].
There are other human deities on this earth.
If one dies while traveling on the road to bathe in the Gaṅgā,
he attains heaven and receives the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Those living beings who die on the path while traveling to the waters of the Gaṅgā—
even insects, moths, and locusts crushed under the feet of those going there— go [to heaven].
O twice-born ones, so too do those who point out the direction toward the Gaṅgā to others.
Men who praise her attain supreme merit, the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā (73).
Those whose minds are corrupted by heretics and who revile the Jāhnavī go to a terrible hell from which return is difficult to obtain (74).

Even one who is covered in dust, if they constantly remember and proclaim "Gaṅgā," attains heaven by reciting it; what is the use of much other talk? (75) He who says "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even from a distance of hundreds of yojanas, [attains the same merit].

One is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Those who do not go to the Gaṅgā are born in vain as blind or lame persons, and those men perish through miscarriages in the womb. 76-77.
Those lowest of men who do not glorify the Gaṅgā are equal to the dull-witted; they do not instruct others, being like those driven by wind, their minds deranged.
For those people who do not recite it, the scripture is utterly fruitless.
O Brahmins, those of dull intellect who are fallen and base, yet cause others to recite the fruit of the merit of the Gaṅgā and those who themselves recite it with faith—
those wise ones go to heaven and deliver their ancestors and teachers.
He who provides provisions for those traveling with all his wealth,
and he who travels by means of another's food, shall obtain a bath in the Bhāgīrathī;
one should know that the fruit of the bath belongs twice as much to the instigator as it does to the performer.
Whether by desire, by lack of desire, by compulsion, or by serving another,
one who goes to the meritorious Jāhnavī through yoga shall go to the abode of the gods.
The twice-born said:
"O Vyāsa, I have heard from you the pure glorification of the Gaṅgā. Why is she called Gaṅgā? What is her form, and from where does she come—she who is so exceedingly purifying?
Vyāsa said:
Listen, I shall now relate an ancient and meritorious tale (84),
hearing which the best of men attains the path to liberation.
Formerly, having gone to the world of Brahmā, Nārada, the preeminent among sages (85), [spoke as follows].
Having bowed down, he asked the pure one, the sanctifier of the three worlds:
"O Father, what was created by you that is approved by Śambhu and Kṛṣṇa, intended for the welfare of all the worlds and desired as a place upon the earth? (86)
Whether they be goddesses or non-goddesses, she is the most excellent among them all.
Having approached her, the gods, Daityas, humans, and serpents—the egg-born, the sweat-born, the trees, and others such as those born from sprouts—[attain their goals]. 87–88.
"O Brahman, they all go to the auspicious, eternal, and complete state of supreme power.
Brahmā said:
"In the past, while creating, you spoke of Māyā, whose form is Prakṛti. (89)
"From you, the source of the primordial worlds, I shall create existence.
Having heard this, she then became sevenfold:
Gāyatrī, Vāk, Svar, Lakṣmī, and Sarvasasyavasupradā.
Jñāna, Vidyā, Umādevī, Śakti, Bījā, Tapasvinī, Varṇikā, Dharmadravā—these seven are proclaimed;
the Vedas originate from Gāyatrī, and from the Vedas the entire world exists. 91–92.
*Svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *dīkṣā*—these are remembered as being born from Gāyatrī.
One should always recite Gāyatrī in the sacrifice along with the Mātṛkā syllables and others. By obtaining *svadhā* in the ritual, the gods become free from old age and death.
Then the gods released the essence of nectar upon the surface of the earth.
Thereupon, the earth became rich with crops and an abundance of auspicious medicinal herbs; and by means of fruits, roots, juices, and edible foods, people became much more comfortable.
Bhāratī resides in the mouths and minds of all people;
likewise, she provides the exposition of Dharma in all the scriptures.
She [reveals] higher knowledge, strife, sorrow, delusion, non-delusion, auspiciousness, and inauspiciousness. 96.
Without her, the entire world is considered to have lost its true essence (97).
The lotus-born Brahmā, as well as collections of garments and ornaments, happiness, and sovereignty in the three worlds—all these proceed from her; therefore, she is the beloved of Hari (98).
Through Umā as the cause, Śambhu’s knowledge is perpetually present in the worlds;
she is to be known as the Mother of Knowledge, dwelling in half of Śambhu’s body.
She is the fierce power of the letters (varṇikā-śakti), who utterly deludes all the worlds. 99.
She who effects the maintenance and dissolution of all worlds in all the universes—
by this Goddess, the two Asuras Madhu and Kaiṭabha were formerly slain,
as was the terrible Ruru, renowned throughout all the worlds. 100–101.
She slew Mahiṣāsura, the sole conqueror of all the gods; those foremost of Asuras and Daityas were slain effortlessly by the Goddess.
Thus, she always destroyed the forces of the Daityas with her power.
This entire triple world was indeed protected and gladdened by her;
she, whose form is the very essence of the tree of Dharma and who is established in all righteousness, was beheld by me in her great majesty and held within my water-pot. 103–104.
Born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu and borne upon the head of Śambhu,
she is joined by us three— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— and is renowned as the liquid of Dharma within her water-filled pitcher. 105.
Formerly, at the *bali* sacrifices, Bali—the best among the powerful—was deceived by the almighty Viṣṇu through a stratagem;
thereafter, the entire surface of the earth was traversed by [Viṣṇu] with only two steps. (106–107)
The foot of the Sky, having pierced the cosmic egg, stood before me;
that foot was worshipped by me with the water from my water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Having washed it, the water from that honored foot fell upon Hemakūṭa. 108.
Having reached Śaṅkara from that peak, she remained there amidst his matted locks.
Then, having propitiated Śiva on earth by means of Bhagīratha,
the preeminent elephant was brought down and was constantly worshipped with austerity.
Therefore, having pierced through the mountain with vigor by means of three tusks, she made a hole;
because of those three holes, she became renowned in the world as Trisrotas (the Three-streamed).
Through her union with Hari, Brahmā, and Hara, she is purified and the sanctifier of the world.

Having approached that Goddess, one obtains the fruit of all dharmas. That goal which is not attained by all those devoted to recitation, sacrifice, mantras, fire-offerings, and the worship of gods, is attained through service to the Gaṅgā. 112-113.
Since there is no other means for the accomplishment of Dharma than this,
O Nārada, go to her; for through the union with her, who is the merit of the three worlds,
the bones of Sagara’s sons were joined by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
They went to heaven together with their ancestors and those born before and after them.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of Brahmā, Nārada, the bull among sages,
performed austerities at Gaṅgādvāra and became equal to Brahmā.
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere; however, she is difficult to attain at these three places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. By staying for three nights or even a single night at these sites, a person attains the supreme goal.
Therefore, with every effort, one should contemplate immediate liberation.
Then, O knowers of dharma, go here to the auspicious Bhāgīrathī;
in a very short time, you shall attain heaven and final emancipation.
Especially in the Kali age, for those men who have exhausted their strength through hardship, the Gaṅgā bestows liberation; from her arises an infinite accumulation of merit.
Then those Brāhmaṇas were delighted upon hearing these auspicious words from Vyāsa.
Having performed austerities at the Gaṅgā, they then proceeded upon the path to liberation.
That mortal who hears this unsurpassed and meritorious narrative shall cross over the entire flood of suffering and obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
By reciting it even once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
whoever performs there itself acts of charity, recitation, meditation, hymns, mantras, and the worship of the gods, shall obtain infinite fruit. 123.
Therefore, men should perform recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and other rites in that very place;

it is declared that the fruit thereof is infinite and is obtained birth after birth. Thus ends the [section] titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā" in the first *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-second chapter.
The sixty-third chapter. Pulastya said:
In the meantime, the great sage Saṃjaya, formerly a disciple of Vyāsa, having paid homage to his guru, questioned Bhīṣma:
"Tell me the well-determined method and sequence for the worship of the gods."

Who is the most worthy of worship at the beginning? Who is the one to be worshipped in the middle of the daily ritual? And who is the one to be worshipped at the end? Who is the most powerful? O Brahmin, what fruit does a person obtain after having performed worship?
Vyāsa said:
One should worship Gaṇeśa at the outset for the sake of removing obstacles; indeed, one attains the status of Vināyaka hereafter, just as he did when he was the son of Gaurī. 4.
Formerly, Pārvatī gave birth to these two sons from Maheśvara:
the heroic gods Skanda and Gaṇādhipa, who support all the worlds.
Seeing them, the daughter of the mountain spoke for the sake of her own success.
"O son, this modaka has been given by the gods filled with joy;
it is renowned as 'Mahābuddhi' and is fashioned from nectar (sudhā).
I shall describe its qualities; listen with a concentrated mind. (6–7)
By merely smelling this, one will certainly attain immortality;
one becomes a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures, an expert in all weapons and missiles, skillful in all treatises, a scribe, a painter, and highly intelligent. 8.
One who knows the reality of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*) is omniscient; of this there is no doubt.
O son, he who attains a status superior to that of Dharma shall attain a hundred perfections (*siddhi*);
indeed, I shall grant this which is approved by your father.
Having heard these words from the mouth of his mother himself, Skanda, who is supremely wise, immediately went to every sacred ford situated throughout the three worlds;
mounting his own peacock, he performed his ablutions in an instant.
Having circumambulated his parents, the wise one who bore a protruding belly stood before them with joyful intent; and likewise,
Skanda stood before them, saying, "Give me [the child]."
Then, having beheld him, Pārvatī was struck with wonder and said:
"By ablutions at all sacred fords, by bowing to all the gods,
by all sacrifices, vows, mantras, yogas, and likewise by restraints (yamas)..."
Even a hundredth part of the worship performed for one's parents does not equal a sixteenth part of this [worship]. Therefore, he is a hundred times superior even to a hundred sons;
thus, O Heramba, I give you this modaka fashioned by the gods.
For this very reason, at the beginning of sacrifices and rituals,
in the recitation of the Vedas, scriptures, and hymns, and during the regular rites of worship,
Bhūteśa, together with Pārvatī, granted him a great boon.
By worshipping him alone, may the gods become pleased before me;
and when Gaṇeśvara is worshipped, may there be constant success for all goddesses and ancestors everywhere. 18–19.

Therefore, in all sacrifices, the twice-born should worship Gaṇapa; according to the words of the God of gods and the Goddess, [the merit] in those [sacrifices] is multiplied by millions upon millions.
Having joyfully bestowed all that merit and virtue, the God of gods and the Goddess likewise [bestowed it].
Then, he was granted the leadership of the Gaṇas in the presence of all the gods.
Therefore, in grand sacrifices, in hymns of praise, and in daily worship,
a person who worships Gaṇeśa shall obtain every accomplishment.
Having understood this, all the gods, desiring to attain their beloved and certainly seeking heaven and liberation, worshipped him. Then,
having fasted at night and worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas on the fourth lunar day, they honored him.
If even a deity depicted in a painting or a stone image were to be worthy of worship, [then surely you are so].
Homage to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the pacifier of all obstacles! O wise one, bestower of joy upon Umā, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence. 24–25.
O Lord of the splendor of meditation, knowledge, and discernment that bestows supreme bliss, salutations to you, O King of Obstacles; be gracious at all times.
(26) Whoever, having observed a fast, joyfully worships the Lord of the Gaṇas—
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the gods. (27) I shall proclaim his auspicious hymn of twelve names:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati"—this is the mantra that has been declared. (28)
Gaṇapati, Vighnarāja, Laṃbodaṇḍa, Gajānana,
Dvimātṛja, Heramba, Ekadanta, Gaṇādhipa,
Vināyaka, Cārukarṇa, Paśupāla, and Bhavātmaja. (29)
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites these twelve names,
the entire universe shall be under his control and no obstacle shall arise anywhere;
great spirits shall be pacified, and he shall not be afflicted by diseases.
Completely liberated from all sins, he indeed enjoys imperishable heaven. 31.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-Four.
Vyāsa said: I shall further proclaim another hymn to the Lord of the Gaṇas,
which bestows all perfections, is purifying, and grants the fruit of all desired objects.
I bow to the leader of the Gaṇas, who has a single tusk and a massive body, who resembles molten gold, who has a protruding belly and wide eyes;
who wears a girdle of muñja grass and a black antelope skin, and whose sacred thread is a serpent.
I bow to the Lord Gaṇanāyaka, whose head is adorned with the crescent moon;
the God who removes all obstacles and is himself free from all obstacles, who mounts his excellent mouse in the great battle between the gods and the asuras. 3-4.
I salute the mighty-armed Gaṇanāyaka, who desires to fight,
who delights the heart of Ambikā, and who is surrounded by the Mātṛkās; I salute the Gaṇanāyaka, who is fond of devotion and intoxicated with pride.
I bow to the Lord Gaṇanāyaka, who possesses limbs variegated with diverse jewels, adorned with wonderful garlands, the god who can assume any form at will,
the elephant-faced one, the best among the gods, and whose ears are beautifully adorned. 6–7.
I bow to the Lord Gaṇanāyaka, who holds a noose and a goad;
I bow to that great-bodied Gaṇanāyaka, who is constantly praised by Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas. 8.
The man who recites this meritorious octad of Gaṇas with devotion attains all perfections and is glorified in the world of Rudra; furthermore,
that noble person does not fall into poverty for seven births.
The man who recites this daily shall become a great king;
by reciting or even hearing it, he brings the three worlds under his control.
This is the supreme hymn of great merit dedicated to the high-souled Gaṇeśa. 11.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-Five. Vyāsa said:
In all *nāndīmukha* rites, one should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas;
by that, everyone shall become submissive and merit becomes inexhaustible.
With the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," [one should worship] in all sacrificial jars as well.
A person attains all perfections and shall obtain heaven and liberation.
A wise man should draw the serpent on an earthen image, a painting, a stone, a wooden door, or a vessel.
Moreover, in any other place that is constantly within the range of vision,
a wise person should install the image of Hari according to their ability and worship it;
for him, his cherished undertakings will succeed in every respect.
Nothing whatsoever arises as an obstacle; she brings the three worlds under her control.
A seeker of knowledge obtains the knowledge arising from the Vedas and the Shastras, as well as other arts and crafts, and the victorious [mantra] that bestows heaven.

One seeking wealth shall obtain vast riches; one seeking a daughter shall obtain a virtuous and charming maiden; and one shall attain sovereignty achieved through righteousness and a son who grants liberation to the lineage.
No one is afflicted by diseases, nor by malevolent planets, nor by those born as spirits.
There shall be no danger from horned animals, nor from Rākṣasas, lightning, or forest-thieves; there shall be no king who is prone to anger, nor shall pestilence prevail in the home.
Having worshipped Vināyaka, there shall be neither famine nor weakness.
Salutation to that Lord of the Gaṇas, the destroyer of all obstacles, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing their desired aims.
(10) And this is the mantra: Oṃ namo gaṇapataye.
With flowers dear to Nārāyaṇa and other fragrant ones, with sweetmeats, fruits, and roots, as well as with substances produced in season,
with curds, milk, beloved musical instruments, and fragrant incense.
Whoever worships Gaṇapa shall obtain all supernatural powers (siddhis).
In particular, for one who offers to his liṅga what is dear to the Lord of Wealth—namely, articles for worship and clothing—all of it becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold. 12–13.
In the land of Bhārata-varṣa, in the presence of women,
on the southern bank of the Lauhitya river, there is the Vināyaka in the form of a Liṅga,
by the command of Hara and Gaurī and with the consent of the gods. 14.
He remains established for the sake of the world’s peace by destroying all obstacles.

Having worshipped that deity according to one's ability with collections of materials, one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras attains the state of Vinayaka. 15–16.

Having performed a single circumambulation, seen it, and touched it, a person attains imperishable heaven and is always honored by the gods; this is for the sake of the liberation of even those Mlecchas who associate with it and practice great austerity. 17.
For the sake of obtaining sons for all people, Śambhu, as Vināyaka, performed an ablution there;
whoever touches the Lord of the Gaṇas after that ablution in the Lauhitya river is liberated from the sins committed in seven births—of this there is no doubt. 18-19.

Having approached Vināyaka, one shall not encounter widowhood, nor miserliness, nor grief, nor envy; in every birth, one shall obtain [these]. Again there is success, again enjoyment, again fame, and again strength.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, there is no doubt that one attains everything;
for without performing his worship, all desired objects perish.
Therein, the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—are well-pleased. 21–22.
Then,
in a battle with the highly powerful Asuras led by Hiraṇyākṣa,
Indra was defeated through his prowess by Hiraṇyākṣa himself, who was devoid of worship from the hosts of the Maghons.
Then, for as long as a hundred years in the past, the gods were rendered powerless;
in that great war between the gods and the asuras, the gods suffered defeat. Thereupon, Śiva, the God of Gods, was informed by the deities.
"O Blessed One, our kingdom has been seized by the Asuras and our sacrifices have ceased.
In the meantime, Śambhu spoke these words to the gods:
"O Heraṃba, do not weep; I am pleased with you, and by me [this shall be accomplished]."
"May the supreme accomplishment of the gods and others be attained through worship"— if a person, out of delusion, disregards this on a great festival day,
he shall find no success and shall even suffer defeat at their feet. 27–28.
"By you, the great sacrifice for Gaṇapati was performed with negligence and out of delusion; therefore, defeat has been obtained.
Go quickly to the Puṇyā river of the high-souled Gaṇapati."

"O knowers of Dharma, perform worship; victory will soon be yours. Then, having heard from the mouth of Hara these words which were auspicious and beneficial, all the gods stood before the Lord of the Gaṇas, greatly delighted.
The gods said:
"Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the sole protector of all the gods;
out of affection for the granting of heavenly enjoyments, O Heramba, we bow down to you. (32)
We bow to you, O Heramba, the bestower of victory in all battles, the granter of success in all undertakings, possessed of great illusion and a massive body.
We bow to the one-tusked, highly wise Vināyaka with the long trunk. 33.
"We bow down before the god, the great seer of the gods, and before Indra.
Forgive us for that worship which was previously performed by us with sacrifice. Having heard the words of the gods, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke these words: 34–35.
"O gods, let that which is desired by you be chosen from me.
Then all the gods, headed by Śakra and led by Bṛhaspati, said to Gaṇapati, "May victory be ours!"
Having heard the words of the gods, Gaṇeśa spoke these words:
"Certainly so, O best of gods; may victory be yours quickly!
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, [rejoiced].
They worshipped Gaṇeśa with sandalwood paste and ornaments,
with divine incenses and fine garments, and with flowers born in the Nandana grove— such as Pārijāta and other blossoms that enchant the gods.
Honored by the gods, Gaṇapa spoke to those best of deities:
"Go, O Vibudhas, to the god Viṣṇu, whose valor is marvelous; he will fulfill your desire and whatever you wish for, O Suras. (40-41)

Having mounted their respective chariots and having paid homage to the immutable Hari, who is clad in yellow garments, those hosts of gods departed joyfully. Having reached the son of Hara and having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, they spoke.
"O Great-Souled Keśava, we have indeed come into your presence today.
Having heard these words of the gods, the imperishable Hari spoke this according to the truth: "I shall slay the foremost of the Daityas."
Having heard the nectar of the scriptures fallen from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, the gods were thrilled and filled with great joy; they worshipped Him with their desired offerings.
Then Viṣṇu spoke this again to the gods, headed by Indra.
"Having gathered your respective forces, remain ready and free from anxiety.
I shall seize these men of evil conduct and their army from all sides; meanwhile, you all stand firm and fearless, having taken up your multitude of weapons."
Having heard Mādhava’s words, the preeminent gods departed;
mounting their celestial chariots, they all took up divine weapons.
Indeed, the joyful words of the gods were overheard by the spies of the Daityas.
They spoke to King Hiraṇyākṣa, who possessed great strength.
(49) Having heard that, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas became enraged;
summoning his ministers, he spoke these words in his anger. (50)

Then all the gods, including Indra and others, who were of cruel intent and desiring to seize Mādhava, reported everything to Śambhu. "How shall we obtain victory while this host of Daityas is so formidable? they asked. (51)
Tripurāri said this: "O gods, worship Gaṇeśa! Having worshipped that deity, you shall conquer the asuras and dānavas.
Then the leader of the gaṇas was worshipped by the joyful hosts of gods.
The Gaṇādhipa, being pleased, granted a great boon to Krūra:
"Today you shall conquer all the Asuras. Then the gods, filled with joy, informed Hari that they were desirous of our destruction.
Having heard Hari’s firm command, the chariot-warriors, weapons in hand, stood ready for battle;
O fearless one, let the gods themselves declare here who possesses the power to conquer me. (55-56)
Then, having heard the king's words, Madhu spoke these sweet words:
"O King, I shall conquer Hari; appoint me as your ally. Once Nārāyaṇa is defeated, the thirty gods will certainly be filled with fear."
"Therefore, Nārāyaṇa, the conqueror of all cities, shall be our share. Then, O King, we shall defeat Mādhava along with Dhundhu, Sunda, the mighty Kālakeya, and Madhu as his ally. (58-59)
The four leaders of the entire Daitya host were of firm prowess;
they were heroes equal to Time and Death, having reached the further shore of the knowledge of all weapons.
Among them, Bala spoke these words, in which victory was present:

"And I shall conquer him and Jishnu as well; my vow is firm, O King. (61) Then Namuci and Muci, two brothers arrogant in their strength, said to the king: "We two, being powerful ourselves, shall surely conquer those who are powerful by force. (62)

And Jambha spoke these words to Indra and those led by Indra: "I shall conquer; there is no doubt here. O Daityas, be free from your feverish anxiety. And Tripura spoke these words: "I shall conquer Vināyaka."
Then the commander-in-chief spoke: "By me, the powerful Devāntaka has been dispatched against Kubera and all the Hiraṇyakas along with their rakshasas.
In that interval, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived there.
Having gone there, he said to Hiraṇyākṣa: "I have come as the messenger of Jiṣṇu;
renounce the kingdom, or else, if it is your will, [renounce] your speech and your life-breaths. If you do not, fight me today, or else go to the subterranean realm (rasātala) by force."
Then, out of anger, he spoke these words to Nārada, the best of sages: "O Brāhmaṇa, you are not to be harmed; depart quickly from my presence!
[Tell them] of the calamity, slaughter, and destruction that awaits the gods."
"Behold Hari, Hara, and the others, who have reached their end in an instant.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas said to the commander of the army:
"Prepare the forces and bring all the chariots here quickly."
Having heard the words of the king of the Daityas, the commander-in-chief immediately summoned the forces from all sides; terrified, they arrived quickly—
armies consisting of thousands of millions of akṣauhiṇīs.
And for each hero there were great vehicles— various chariots, as well as elephants, camels, horses, and donkeys;
having mounted lions, tigers, and leopards, they then set forth.
With all kinds of musical instruments and many terrifying lion-roars,
they filled the quarters of the sky, including the oceans, the coastal mountains, and the earth;
all the worlds were struck with fear, and the oceans trembled.
The celestial drums resounded, struck by all the gods,
along with various other musical instruments filled with air and possessing deep, thundering tones;
and those inhabitants of the three worlds who were terrified by the fear of all the worlds [rejoiced].
In that fierce and intense great battle, they fell from their desires into the sky;
with iron clubs, nooses, spears, swords, staffs, axes,
and sharp, terrible arrows, they struck one another in the fray.
With various weapons and missiles discharged in many ways, [the battle] was continuous in all directions—
in the houses, on the earth, on the mountains, and in the waters;
likewise in temples, in the sky, on mountain peaks, and on ridges.
In that vast and dense forest, a battle broke out between the two;
weapons fell upon the armies by the hundreds and thousands, like torrents of water from thick clouds such as Puṣkala and the others.
Some fell upon the earth with their bodies pierced by arrows;
others [fell] by means of spears, maces, umbrellas, tridents, and axes.
These heroes, who had conducted themselves righteously in battles, lay fallen facing the enemy.
Those fearless ones who go to the abodes of the gods for the sake of their master, and those others who are cowardly, sinful, treacherous, or turn their backs in battle—
those warriors who fight through unjust means— they go to the abode of Yama. (82-83)

Those mounted on elephants struck those stationed on chariots; likewise, chariot-warriors struck others, and foot-soldiers struck those on foot—these heroes, longing for battle, slaughtered one another. (84)
Joyful, endowed with virtue, most righteous, and restrained by strength—[such were they]. 85.
But some, their arms severed and their heads split by maces, fell to the surface of the earth with hair, heads, and garments [scattered]. 86.
Thus, those of great strength, cut through the middle and split asunder by the fierce blows of swords and axes, fell to the earth;
though adorned with divine ornaments, they lay there like senseless carcasses.
The surface of the earth became ablaze with heroes, serpents, horses, and chariots;
it was covered with various ornaments, fallen banners, and standards.
Then the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, [was likewise set on fire]. 88–89.
There, in the battle between the gods and the asuras, a great heap of flesh was devoured by many carnivorous beasts amidst the flood of blood;
and copious amounts of that red fluid were drunk by rākṣasas, wolves, and other such creatures. 90.
Meanwhile, other great throngs of jackals and vultures, filled with joy, eagerly devoured the blood mixed with wind. In that interval, the wise Bṛhaspati, honored by the gods, [arrived].
He recited for the gods the Mṛtasaṃjīvanī-vidyā,
the divine Viśalyakaraṇī, and the mighty Brahma-vidyā.
Then the learned Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, who moves with the speed of thought, [appeared].
He wandered joyfully on foot with medicines and their applications.
There, even those who had died in the great battle lived again; free from wounds and endowed with strength, they fought once more with great vigor. 94–95.
Thus, that arrogant host of the Daitya, numbering one hundred thousand,
fell by the power of merit with their necks pierced by arrows. Then, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas rejoiced with shouts of victory.
The sages, the sky-dwellers, and other hosts of Apsarases sang songs;
the Gandharvas and supreme seers offered their praises.
Then, the chief of the Daityas, possessed of great splendor and immense strength, became enraged.
There, the commander-in-chief of the Daitya lord, renowned as Kālakeya,
standing upon his chariot and possessing great prowess, took up his bow and struck those hosts of gods, making them dance upon the earth.
Then the sky was completely covered by a continuous torrent of arrows;
thousands of millions upon millions of arrows fell upon the army,
and from that [shower], the gods who never retreat in battle also descended.
Vomiting blood, all the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
as well as the gods, tormented by his arrows, fell upon the surface of the earth;
some were pierced by hundreds of arrows, and others likewise by thousands and tens of thousands.
The immensely powerful and foremost of gods fell upon the earth in the battle;
all the inhabitants of heaven stationed in their chariots became distressed,
and tormented by his arrows, they were unable to stand before him.
The army, assailed by his arrows which possessed a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt and fire, was plunged into like an elephant plunging into a forest of lotuses;
the gods were unable to stand in battle and then fled toward Indra.
The god known as Citraratha, the best among weapon-bearers and wielder of the bow, mounted his chariot and went forth toward the battle;
he then spoke these words to that great asura general: 106–107.
Just as you, a great hero, joyfully slew the army of the gods, so too are you a praiseworthy and brave warrior esteemed by the asuras;
now, in battle, you have performed a deed dear to Hiraṇyākṣa. (108)
"Now, by means of these arrows, go yourself to my abode. (109) Then Kālakeya, smiling, spoke these words:
"The entire host of gods was already conquered by me with ease. (110)
But now, O bull among the gods, if you have a desire for death here, I shall send you to the abode of Yama with these sharpened arrows, as if in sport, while this entire army stands in battle.
Having spoken thus, the hero, extremely enraged, struck him in battle with an arrow resembling the God of Death; however, he [the opponent] cut those three arrows in mid-air.
Then, quickly joining other arrows in the battle with fury, [he struck again]. (112-113)

He swiftly struck down many daityas and cut them to pieces with agility; thereafter, in that battle, the best of archers forcefully severed one another's bows with sharp arrows possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
That battle between the god and the Daitya was exceedingly righteous.
Sages, gods, celestial musicians, and serpents came to his side, desiring to witness it;
in this manner, hundreds of thousands of arrows were discharged.
Then, for the sake of victory, the two heroes shone resplendent against one another in battle;
thereupon, the highly effulgent lord of the Gandharvas, filled with rage,
pierced him in the forehead with three arrows and in the heart with five.
With seven arrows he struck the navel of Jaṭhara, and with five more he struck Vastu;
thus struck by those arrows, the Daitya became bewildered and fell into a state of stupor. Having slackened his bow, the powerful one regained consciousness only after a long time.
With three arrows, he pierced that best of gods known as Madhu,
and with his weapons, he cut down the bow while the king of the Daityas looked on.
Then, with thousands of arrows possessing a luster like that of Kāla and Antaka, [he struck him].
The most excellent and powerful among the gods pierced the lion-like Daitya. With his consciousness failing, his blood flowing profusely,
and afflicted by many arrows, the Daitya lord became overwhelmed and seized a trident.
Having struck the horses of that very one who held a spear in his hand with four arrows, he caused them to fall;
and with three more, he struck down the charioteer as well. Standing upon the earth, he then slew the excellent Gandharva with his spear.
The powerful Citraratha shattered the trident with three arrows.
Seeing the trident destroyed like a serpent whose coils have been struck down,
the mighty Sura seized a terrible mallet and rushed forward.
Then, with a crescent-shaped arrow, he swiftly severed from the body the head of the commander of the Daitya army, who had arrived with his mallet;
he fell upon the surface of the earth, and the world trembled.
Then all the hosts of Daityas, turning their backs, fled away. 127.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Kālakeyas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-Six.
Vyāsa said:
Seeing his brother slain, the Dānava named Kāleya rushed toward Citraratha, taking up his bow and an arrow.
Seeing the Asura rushing forward with a radiance like that of Time and Death,
the highly heroic Jaya, son of Indra, obstructed him.
Then the one of great splendor, the best of the gods, spoke to the Daitya:
He who strikes down one who is endowed with truth and righteousness, who is certain of benefit in both worlds,
who is afflicted by the pain of weapon wounds, who is dejected, or who is joined with others,
and who is broken or cast out— that man is a fool.
"Having suffered in Raurava for a very long time, one becomes its slave for a long duration;
therefore, do not fight with me, but remain established in the dharma of battle.
Thus spoke Kāleya, overwhelmed with anger, to Jayanta.
"Having slain the killer of my brother, I shall now kill you.
Then Jayanta, the best of the gods, struck that foremost of asuras, who possessed a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction, with his sharpened arrows.
That Asura also pierced Nicakartta with three arrows;
just as a river carrying red minerals flows upon reaching a multitude of raindrops,
so it was with those two of great heroism— neither diminished nor disheartened.
Desiring victory over one another, they both sought to gain the upper hand.
Then, with an arrow, he severed that Daitya’s bow,
and with five shafts, he felled his charioteer to the ground.

With eight sharp arrows, he struck down the four horses; then, standing on the ground and seizing a spear, he struck Kumāra. With his mace, he crushed [the chariot] along with its horses, its fender, and Kubera.
Having cast him down upon the earth, he let out a lion’s roar. Moving with agility across the ground, he stood before him with mace in hand;
the sound was as unbearable to the worlds as the falling of a thunderbolt.
Likewise, the sound of their maces striking each other occurred again and again;
thus did the club-fight between them continue for four years.
When the clubs were shattered, both stood on the ground, wielding swords and shields.
Then, having witnessed that wonderful and hair-raising battle between the two foot-soldiers,
the gods, asuras, and great serpents were filled with amazement;
and at the end of a moment, the armor of both was shattered by the falling of their swords.
A sword-fight then took place between those two who were exceedingly skilled in combat;
Jayanta, of terrible prowess, seized his hair and, having severed his head with a sword, cast it to the ground. 17.
Then all the gods rejoiced with shouts of "Victory!
(jaya), and the hosts of Daityas, utterly broken, fled in all directions.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kāleya," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-seventh chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa, [spoke].
Enraged and with eyes exceedingly copper-red, he commanded the asuras:
"I myself am going to battle with the desire to destroy the gods;
since they neither come nor fight, let them enter here from this path."
Having heard these words, all the remaining lords of the Daitya hosts, highly skilled with spears and nooses, set out for battle;
and their former army was even greater by a hundredfold.
Desiring battle, they proceeded continuously through the sky like that.
Then the Rudras, along with the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas,
and the Vasus, as well as Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and those led by Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu [advanced].
All those warriors went forth, joyful and eager for battle;
in the meantime, a conflict between the gods and the dānavas occurred,
such as had never before been seen or heard of, and which struck fear into all the worlds.
Equipped with many kinds of weapons and missiles, like a forest in winter,
the battle unfolded as they obstructed the earth, heaven,
and the sky; thus they struck one another both in the air and upon the surface of the earth.
With spears, clubs, javelins, and many showers of arrows,
with terrible blows from swords, as well as discuses and battle-axes,
and with various other weapons, they struck one another down.
Terrible forms, as vast as the sky and imperishable, appeared;
with weapons, arrows, and the falling of blood, along with herons, crows, and jackals,
it was like a cloud raining down red iron with showers of clubs.
Likewise, with blood flowing from their own limbs, some gods and dānavas fall down, faint, stumble, and laugh;
they utter cries of distress and repeatedly let out lion-like roars. 12.
The arms of some were severed, and others likewise had their feet cut off;
some, with their sides and bellies mangled, fell by the hundreds upon the earth.
There were thousands of crores of elephants, horses, and asuras.

As the torrents of blood fell in many places upon the surface of the earth, that surface of the earth then became an ocean of blood. Thereupon, rivers flowed there immediately in a reversed direction.
There, grass, wood, and straw became spears; heaps of timber became mallets and clubs; spikes became makaras and other creatures;
and there were jayantikas, banners, fish, tortoises, and leather-bodies. 16–17.
Furthermore, those rivers were obstructed here and there by numerous great camels with arrows and other weapons,
and they were filled with hair, yak-tail whisks,
and moss; likewise, the ocean of blood was formed by others falling in various ways.
Then the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves,
along with a most terrible flood of blood that struck fear into all the worlds,
went to the abode of Yama as Daityas by the stroke of Skanda’s spear.
Bound by the supreme axe itself, by fire with its flames of arrows, and by the noose of Varuṇa, they were submerged in the inexhaustible realm of Yama—
those whose sons, grandsons, leaders, and ministers likewise [fell]. 21.
And the Daityas were struck down by showers of arrows, spears, and double-edged swords;
likewise by the Grahas, the Śvasanas, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
as well as by the wise Kubera with his great mace.
By masses of thick thunderbolts, by frost driven by the moon,
and by the terrible poisons of serpents, the Daityas fell to the surface of the earth,
along with thousands of millions upon millions of other various gods.
Struck down, they all fell to the earth, their life-breaths departed;
some, having abandoned their bodies, went to heaven, while others went to the abode of Yama, and some went to Pātāla, according to the application of their merit and demerit. 25–26.
In the meantime, the supreme sages chanted the Vedas:
"May there be well-being for the Brahmins, for the cows, for women, and for those practicing austerities,
while all other living beings are currently engaged in combat."
Afflicted by the gods, the remaining Daityas, cowardly and terrified of the forest, fled in all directions;
and when the Daitya host was broken, one of great strength named Bala [remained]. 28–29.

He tormented the gods, binding them with arrows equal to fire; many gods, though proud of their strength, were afflicted by his arrows and fell upon the surface of the earth, while some were broken on the field of battle.
Having seen that great, cruel deed, which was terrifying to the world,
the ṛṣis and the gods who remained there praised [him] and cried out in distress;
then the highly effulgent Śatakratu, the subduer of enemies, became enraged.
He struck the army with volleys of arrows, that best among the powerful; and Bala, too, being enraged in battle, assailed Śakra with great haste.
