Those two of mighty strength had their limbs drenched by the flowing blood.
Like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom during the month of Mādhava, that best of asuras,
being impetuous, drove thousands of discuses, spears,
and maces into the ground in the battle against Śakra.
The powerful king of the gods, suddenly whirling about in the battle, effortlessly cut those wheels and spears with his excellent arrows.
Then that Daitya of great splendor struck Purandara with a spear.
She swiftly struck him, who was mounted on an elephant, between the breasts;
struck by her, Śakra wavered upon his elephant.
Regaining consciousness, the victorious Balarāma instantly pierced the demon.
As he stood upon his chariot, the slayer of heroes cut off his bow and hands with a single arrow, and with another sharp shaft, he struck down his shield and standard; then,
with four whetted arrows, he pierced his four horses.
With a single arrow, he severed the charioteer's head at that very moment.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he fell to the earth in a swoon and met his death within a short while.
Then the great Daitya Namuci, enraged and the destroyer of the pride of the gods, suddenly took up a mace and struck the great elephant;
it was as certain as a thunderbolt falling upon a peak of Mount Meru. 42.
And likewise, there arose a great and hair-raising roar;
afflicted by that blow, the lotus-handed one (Padman) trembled, overwhelmed,
his limbs drenched in blood, turning away in agony.

They attacked Śatakratu by the hundreds and thousands; however, Pākaśāsana cut them down with crescent-shaped arrows and iron-tipped shafts. The preeminent gods were tormented by his creatures through his illusory powers.
Some fell to the ground, while others slept upon their chariots.
Seeing that great feat of his, Mādhava then cut with his discus those arrows that had become like living beings and were still clinging to his body.
Then Jishnu felled him to the ground with three arrows;
having fallen upon the earth, the Daitya was unconscious and reeled,
yet he again took up a terrible mallet, intent on killing Shakra.
Then Indra struck the great asura with his thunderbolt;
that immensely powerful one fell upon the surface of the earth with his chest pierced.
"Excellent! Excellent! cried the gods, the siddhas, and the great rishis. 49–50.
Then they honored Śakra with many showers of flowers;
thereafter, all the hosts of Daityas fled from that place in fear, while the Gandharvas sang songs and the throngs of Apsaras danced. 51.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Bala and Namuci," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-Eight. Vyāsa said:
Seeing Bala slain and his own elder brother Namuci also killed, Mucika spoke these words there: "My eldest brother has been destroyed by you;
now, in your absence, I shall send you to the son of the Sun with my arrows."
To him spoke Śakra, of great splendor and worshipped by all the gods:
"Now you shall surely attain the path of righteousness for your brother,
just as a moth, through delusion and unaware of the heat of fire, [flies into it]."
"You wish to fight me just as one might suddenly enter a fire"—
to Indra, who was speaking thus, he struck with three arrows;
Śakra, the conqueror of enemy cities, cut those down with three shafts of his own.
Then he struck Indra with ten arrows and Māra-vaṇa with three;
having cut through Mātali with seven, he roared loudly with fierce sounds.
Then the Daitya, in great agitation, whirled Śakra about once more.
Then Śakra, possessed of great strength and prowess,
out of anger struck that iron armlet with his thunderbolt due to its extreme lightness; by the falling of that bolt, Bhidura fell down lifeless.
At the fall of Danuja, the earth trembled;
the gods broke into dances and the Dānavas fled in all directions.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Muci," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-ninth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Tāreya was endowed with strength and possessed prowess equal to that of Śakra.
He struck Skanda, the slayer of his father, with arrows in the battle.
Then the mighty-armed Skanda, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra,
cut down those various arrows and pierced them with his own excellent shafts.
Then the son of Daitya suddenly covered Skanda with arrows;
undaunted, Viśākha then cut them down with his own shafts.
Tāreya struck Skanda at the head of the battle with fire-arrows.
He discharged an arrow resembling a thunderbolt at Nandana;
meanwhile, Vaiśvānara surrounded the commander of the army.
Then the Daitya again hurled the Raudra weapon against him.
That [arrow] having been warded off by him with his own arrow and struck down,
the Daitya discharged a most dreadful and terrible weapon known as Aghora.
Its arrows were mountain peaks, lions, serpents, and the like.
They rushed toward the son of Pārvatī by the thousands of millions upon millions; but Skanda,
having cut those arrows down, pierced that bull among the Daityas from his feet to the top of his head with shafts resembling fire and the sun.
The gold-feathered arrows lodged deep in the body of the lord of the Daityas shone intensely,
like fragments of gold upon a mountain of black stone. Then, from his body, a great deal of blood flowed forth.
Just as the *puṣpa* tree and the *śamī* tree wither in the month of Caitra,
so too did the horses beneath the chariot lie prostrate, their bodies touching the ground.
Then the great Daitya, filled with rage, took up a terrible and formidable trident.
Having seized that trident, which possessed a radiance equal to the God of Death at the time of universal dissolution,
Pārvatī’s son hurled it at the Lord of the Paśus;
yet it was rendered burnt to ashes by him in an instant upon the field of battle.
Then the Dānava again released his power against Brahmādatta;
he then struck back with a trident possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred peaks, and those two weapons, resembling thunderbolts, clashed even in the sky.
Those two, full of vigor, fell upon the earth;
then the lord of the Daityas suddenly afflicted Skanda with arrows resembling flames of fire, like a rain-cloud drenching a mountain with heavy downpours.
Having rendered them useless, the mighty-armed general indeed cut his bow with a crescent-headed arrow (ardhacandra), and likewise struck off the great head of the charioteer;
furthermore, he felled the horses to the ground with many arrows.

Seizing a mace with great force, that lord of the Daityas struck Guha on his broad chest; by that blow, the peacock of the one whose vehicle is the peacock fell into a swoon and trembled repeatedly. 18.
Then the peacock, having fallen into a stupor, shook again and again.
Then Skanda struck that bull among the asuras once more; with his sword, he swiftly severed the most terrible mace,
and Tāreya, seizing his spear, struck the one who had shattered Krauñca.
Then he too released a spear, unerring and slaying the wicked; having scorched him, that spear, which causes the dissolution of the universe,
pierced Guha— who was like the staff of Yama— and returned to him.
His life departed, he fell upon the earth, shaking the very ground.
Skanda was then worshipped by all the gods with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Tāraka," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventieth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Then the Daitya Devāntaka roared toward the battle.
Biting his lips in rage, the powerful one waged war according to the rules of dharma.
Having approached, he spoke words censured by all the world:
"Out of wicked delusion, you do not know the great dharma in its proper sequence."

Through the application of merit and demerit, you are the lord over punishment and favor; I too have been created by the Creator and carry out your command. Since you do not know dharma, you are like Death with Time at his forefront.
For him there is no disease, nor old age, nor untimely death, nor a servant of Yama.
A doer of deeds who has strayed from Dharma undergoes suffering day and night.
Thus was Vasu, of great prowess, addressed by Yama, whose sole witness is Dharma.
The righteous-souled one severed those [arrows] with three arrows resembling Time and Death in brilliance; he, however, cut them down with another three shafts.
Then, with many lofty arrows possessing a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon, [he struck].
He struck down Yama with countless arrows and cut his shafts asunder with his own.
In the meantime, those two of great strength and prowess, enraged and each desiring victory over the other, struck one another in the battle.
A most terrible battle raged between those two for a day and night;
in the midst of this, the powerful tiger among Daityas, filled with pride and incensed with rage, pierced Praśamana with a spear.
Then, seizing that very spear with his left hand, he quickly struck him violently between the shoulders with it;
his entire body trembled and blood issued from his mouth.
Then, filled with rage, the one of great splendor took up a most terrible and infallible staff and hurled it at the body of that Daitya;
it [struck] his chariot along with the horses, the charioteer, the warrior, and the collection of weapons.
And Śamana, overcome with rage, reduced him to ashes.
When that Daitya had thus fallen, the Dānava named Durdharṣa,
with a trident in hand, rushed forward with the intent to kill Śamana.
As Mṛtyu approached with a trident in his hand, resembling the submarine fire (*baḍavānala*), Raṇa, utterly fearless, confronted him with a spear in his hand.
Seeing Mṛtyu, he immediately struck him with that very trident.
Then, in the field of battle, Mṛtyu hurled a spear;
having suddenly incinerated it with a flame like a peak of fire,
that spear pierced the heart of the Daitya and entered the surface of the earth.

With his chariot and horses fallen upon the earth, his body mangled by the *śakti* spear, another mighty warrior, Durmukha, drew his bow toward Death; bearing sword and shield, he rushed forward like the God of Death himself. 18.
Seeing him, he struck Yama in battle with abundant arrows.
Then that god, leaping from his chariot, suddenly cut off [Yama's] head— complete with earrings— with a sword and cast it to the ground.
All the remaining forces that survived the slaughter fled in the ten directions.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Devāntaka, Durdharṣa, and Durmukha," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
[Chapter Seventy-one]
Vyāsa said:
Then Namuci, enraged and standing upon his chariot,
afflicted the dwellers of heaven with terrible arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, in that battle, the gods, siddhas, kinnaras, and pannagas were unable from all sides to withstand the force of his arrows.
[He saw] a chariot yoked with the horse Uccaiḥśravas, driven by Mātali.
Having mounted [his chariot], Puruhūta advanced toward that one of great strength.
Seeing Śakra of great heroism, Namuci, the bull among the Daityas,
then spoke these words to Vāsava and his followers on the battlefield.
O highly praised one, having destroyed both the natural and the acquired, there is neither infamy nor what is unpleasant; there is neither that which is produced by gain nor victory.
Therefore, when you have struck here, everything becomes eternal.
"I shall obtain the sovereignty of the gods and enjoy happiness in the abode of the immortals.
To him, Śakra of great splendor, the conqueror of enemy cities, replied:
"Bravery is easily attained everywhere by mere words alone."
"O lowest of Dānavas, show your great prowess in battle,
or else I shall lead you to the city of Yama.
Having heard this, the highly effulgent bull among the Daityas was provoked to anger.
With five sharp arrows, he struck the best of the gods;
but Maghavan quickly cut them down with five crescent-headed shafts (kṣuraprās).
Those two of great prowess, seeking the objects of their senses, continued to engage in battle.
With a sudden impulse, they both cut each other's arrows with shafts resembling thunderbolts,
and pierced their bodies with arrows like lightning bolts;
a most unprecedented feat was performed by those two in that fierce encounter.
Seeing his agility, the drawing of the arrow, and the seizing and releasing [of the weapon]— which are so very difficult to achieve—
the hosts of gods and asuras were then filled with wonder.
In that interval, the Daitya unleashed his illusory powers (māyās).
Hundreds of arrows issued forth from there in every direction;
then the powerful Śakra, quickly raising his bow again in anger,
struck him on all his limbs with fierce, flaming shafts.
Then, with eight thousand arrows and more besides,
they pierced and cut each other down;
in that battle, they beheld the sky made continuous by their shafts.
They fell upon the surface of the earth by the thousands from the strokes of his sword;
thus, when that great battle had lasted for a very long time,
Namuci, the doer of cruel deeds, then displayed the weapon of illusion (māyāstra).
In the three worlds, darkness would have become continuous;
the hosts of gods and asuras could not see one another at all, nor could they perceive the sun, the moon, the planets, the fires, or the celestial dwellers.
In that darkness difficult to cross, the sun itself was not visible;
then, by the arrows of the Daitya, which resembled crests of fire,
all the gods were shattered, and Śakra fell before his feet.
With their bodies pierced by arrows, they fell upon the surface of the earth;
others, broken in spirit, fled in the ten directions.
Recognizing his stratagem, Hari, who is worshipped by all the gods, [intervened].

Then he released the Saumya weapon, which possessed the brilliance of a hundred suns in the sky; seeing it delayed, [the opponent] struck the chest of the Daitya with a spear adorned with many bells, and he fell down, overcome with pain.
Having regained consciousness after a long time, the son of Diti, overwhelmed with rage,
rushed impetuously toward Airāvata, the preeminent elephant of the gods, and in his fury, he utterly terrified Indra’s mount.
Having seized the lordly elephant by its shoulder, he cast it down upon the surface of the earth;
then Śakra, having fallen to the ground, was overcome by a moment of fainting. Thereupon, that lord of the Daityas leaped down and stood between the tusks of the elephant.
Desiring to seize Śakra for the sake of slaying that leader of the hosts,
he severed the head of the chief of the Asuras with his sword and cast it down;
all the gods rejoiced, and the Gandharvas sang merrily.
And those sages, filled with joy, praised the best of the gods. 28.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Second Slaying of Namuci," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Seventy-two.
Vyāsa said:
Mounted upon a divine chariot, bow in hand and endowed with great strength,
he went before the hosts of gods and asuras to face Mādhava in battle.
Overcome by great anger, Madhu, the crusher of the ageless, spoke these harsh words to the imperishable Lord Hari: "O Nārāyaṇa, how is it that you do not know the code of combat?"
Having employed an unjust and difficult means of destruction, you have perished and yet you do not grieve.
By this union with the mud, your status as a celestial being, though acquired through worldly conduct, shall be utterly destroyed; I shall now create another creation.
"I shall slay you here along with the hosts of gods," he said;
having spoken thus, he took up his bow and struck the Lord with arrows.
Then Mādhava pierced them with arrows possessing a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt.
Then Madhu struck him on all his limbs with many blows;
O best of gods, that Daitya was concealed by illusion,
as were those heroes— the Rudras and other deities— who possess great strength.
The various goddesses, also equipped with weapons and mounts,
as well as the commanders of the armies, the lords of the hosts, the world-protectors, Śiva, and Viṣṇu—
along with all other deities such as the planets— fought together in unison.
Then the gods were surely destroyed by the illusory power of Madhu;
struck by showers of arrows, spears, and double-edged swords, both from the front and from behind, the gods suddenly fell to the ground, oppressed by weapons. 9–10.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, taking up the Sudarśana discus,
struck down the gods who had become asuras through illusion at the forefront of the battle. Then, having severed their heads by the thousands, he [cut them off].
The Lord of the Gods struck down the Daityas who possessed the nature of Asuras;
thus the All-pervading One caused other Daityas as well to fall from the battle.
Seeing this, all the sages and gods were filled with wonder.
The gods and hosts of sages whisper from ear to ear:
"Hari, the immutable Lord, is the eternal sole protector;
this God is the witness of all, the conqueror of the Daityas in age after age. (14)
"How can he slay all the gods? He will arise at the end of the kalpa.
In that interval, Madhu, having employed his māyā and assumed the form of Hara, spoke to the imperishable Hari. 15-16.
Having slain the gods on all sides in the forefront of the battle against the Daityas, what auspiciousness, virtue, fame, glory, or merit do you possess today?
Due to your state of great madness, you do not distinguish between enemies and your own kin.
"Therefore, I shall send you to the abode of Yama with my sharpened arrows.
Having spoken thus, he struck Keśava in battle with fierce shafts;
but Mādhava cut those arrows down and spoke these words: (18–19)
"I know you, O Daitya, my dear one, who have assumed the form of Hara—
a hero of heroic deeds, Madhu, employed in illusion.
Having struck you down on the field of battle, I shall bestow a false world upon you."
In the meantime, he pierced Maheśvara— the one with matted hair, who has the bull as his emblem, and who is mounted upon a bull— with sharp arrows in the encounter.
At that time, the battle between those two, the god and the dānava, was exceedingly great.
As they were striking one another, cutting down each arrow as it reached them with their own arrows,
the imperishable Hari severed his bow with a razor-edged shaft (kṣurapra).
Then he brought down the horse that was in the form of a bull.
Then the Daitya, with trident in hand, rushed toward the Lord of the World; having whirled his trident, he struck the Supreme Lord,
but [the Lord] cut that trident, which blazed like the fire of time, with three arrows.

Then the cruel, mighty-armed Madhu, a master of supreme illusion, assumed the form of the Goddess; mounted upon a lion, Hari advanced and struck Viṣṇu with various kinds of arrows, yet spoke these words: [26]
"O Lord, O best of Asuras, you alone have struck him down in battle;
I, however, shall slay you and your two sons, Skanda and Vināyaka. When the Daitya had spoken thus, [Skanda] struck him with many arrows. 27–28.

Seeing his two fathers slain upon the surface of the earth, fallen with their lives departed and vomiting blood, Skanda— possessed of great strength and employing his illusory power— took up his spear and advanced to fight Hari.
Then Dhātṛ spoke these words to Skanda, who was afflicted by delusion:
"Behold your two fathers nearby, watching such a battle;
they are wandering through the atmosphere, established as the witnesses of the world."
Having heard this and seen him, he vanished right there;
then the two brothers Dhundhu and Sundhu, exceedingly arrogant,
rushed at Garuḍa in battle for the sake of slaying Hari.
With his sword in hand he cried "Dhūndhuṃ," and with his mace he cried "Suṃdhuma.
With the Nandaka sword he cut down one, and with his mace he struck the other.
Those two great heroes, wounded and bleeding, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then Madhu, having quickly come there shrouded in darkness,
caused a hundred mountains to fall upon Viṣṇu through his illusory power (māyā).
Thereupon, having shattered those mountains in battle, he remained within the darkness.
Out of anger, [the demon] was beheaded and struck down by Sudarśana alone.
Thereupon, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as Śambhu and the thirty deities,
established Viṣṇu’s renown as "Madhusūdana" throughout the worlds.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Madhu," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Seventy-three. Vyāsa said:
Then Vṛtra, of great splendor and the foremost of the Daityas in battle,
mounted upon an elephant as magnificent as a world-elephant, rushed toward the slayer of Bala.
As Vṛtra approached, [Indra struck him] with arrows possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
In that great battle, he pierced the elephant in all its limbs;
then Vṛtra suddenly struck the head of Jiṣṇu himself with a feathered shaft, and the mighty one trembled.
Having encouraged himself and raised his bow,
the valiant one rained a shower of arrows upon the body of that Daitya;
having cut down those arrows, he quickly pierced him with shafts resembling venomous serpents.
Then the one of great prowess pierced Śatakratu, the lord of all the gods, in battle with thousands of arrows;
the arrows flew at one another like the rays of the seven-horsed sun.
Thus, with thousands of arrows, they pierced one another—
arrows as swift as thought, rapid, and firm like mountain peaks;
they were like the touch of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) and were capable of splitting even the thunderbolt (vajra).
In that battle between those two archers, arrows endowed with equal qualities were discharged.
Thus the combat proceeded day and night,
until Mahendra struck down his elephant with his trident.
Having come together upon the surface of the earth, he swiftly drove his chariot forward;
standing in his chariot, he forcefully pierced that god’s elephant Airāvata with a spear,
as one might swiftly split a great mountain with a thunderbolt.
That great elephant, along with Indra, shone even as it trembled.
Then Maghavat, taking up a spear, hurled it at the Asura and pierced the Daitya’s chest; he fell upon his chariot. 11–12.
In an instant, regaining consciousness and crying out,
the winged one pierced Śakra in battle; thereafter, having fallen into a swoon, Indra regained his senses and struck him with sharp arrows.
Afflicted by the pain of being struck by arrows equal in number to a hundred crores,
Vṛtra then hurled a great trident at the Lord of the gods;
the Lord of the gods, in turn, discharged the Vaiṣṇava weapon against it with the Śāmbhava weapon.
In the sky, both [warriors], possessing a brilliance like a mass of fire, struck one another there, emitting sparks;
and by the touch of those sparks, the soldiers of both armies [were scorched]. 16.
Unable to stand before him, like moths before a blazing fire, they were scorched;
they fell to the earth and fled in all directions.
The heroes of both gods and dānavas [perished], and the battlefield there became empty.
Seeing his missile repelled, the Daitya, overwhelmed with rage,
discharged the mountain-mass missile (*śailasaṃdoha-astra*) through his power of illusion (*māyā*). Hari, however, shattered that collection of mountains in battle with floods of arrows.
The Daitya unleashed Aghora against the mighty Puruhūta;
[he created] thousands of millions upon millions of excellent creatures,
including lions, tigers, bears, wolves, leopards, and great elephants.
Beings such as serpents rushed toward the Lord of the Gods with razor-edged arrows, crescent-shaped shafts, bhallas, and śilīmukhas;
but Maghavat, the slayer of enemy heroes, cut them down before they had even reached him.
Then the mighty-armed and valiant Vṛtra, raising his bow,
pierced Śatakratu with thousands of arrows resembling thunderbolts;
and Śakra, having cut those [arrows] with razor-sharp shafts, severed his bow as well.
In that very instant, the best of the asuras struck down the charioteer, the horses, and the earth;
having honored Bhīma with thorny armlets,
he struck Padmin on the head out of delusion, and the elephant fell to the ground.
The Lord of all gods, armed with a mace, descended upon the earth.
Then a mace-duel ensued between them again and again;
as they struck one another, the sound produced by the falling of the maces was indeed constant.
They repeatedly performed whirls and counter-whirls,
as well as downward and upward strikes and most terrifying blows to the sides;
thus did their battle unfold, striking fear into the worlds and the world-borders.

Upon seeing this, the hosts of gods, siddhas, and dānavas were struck with amazement. As those two heroes fought, they fell into a state where death was certain; even the heroic warriors of the gods and dānavas were unable to look upon them.
Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods, stationed in the sky, came to behold that wonder;
yet by the sound of their *huṃ* cries and the roar of the falling mace,
the sound rose higher and higher, like that produced by a thunderbolt.
The two [missiles] broke, and the syllable *eva* was enclosed between them.
Thus, within half a watch (*yāma*), they both fell upon their respective weapons. In the meantime, O hero, those two then took up sword and shield.
To fight back in that most terrible battle, they both advanced; their swords were like lightning and meteors, and their shields were like fire.
Their agility was beheld by all the worlds, who were filled with wonder.
They both cut each other’s many-colored shields;
thus did their battle with formidable blankets proceed,
displaying circular maneuvers, the use of discus and bow, agility, and leaping.
Like the battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava,
Maghavan, leaping up and seizing Vṛtra by the hair,
swiftly and suddenly severed his head with a sword upon the head of the elephant.
Then the cry of "Victory! arose from all sides among the gods;
with their hearts blossoming with joy, the gods worshipped Maghavan.
The celestial drums resounded and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The Gandharvas sang songs, and the sages recited hymns of praise; all the Daityas, terrified, fled in every direction, casting away their weapons. 40.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Vṛtra," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 73.
The seventy-fourth chapter. Vyāsa said:
[He saw] a chariot endowed with four horses, possessing a splendor equal to the sun.
Then Traipuri ascended and spoke these words to the Lord of the Gaṇas:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, since my father was slain by your father here,
therefore today I shall send you to the abode of Yama with my arrows."
Then the god Gaṇeśa said to that son of Tripura:
"In former times, a great and sinful deed was committed by your wicked father, who acted as an enemy to the gods; indeed, we have heard of it from our own progenitor."

Knowing him to be wicked and devoted to evil deeds, he killed that father with a single arrow by the power of his knowledge and strength. Having been rescued from the mire through delusion, he was sent to the abode of Yama.
"O Daitya, I have repeatedly sent you along that path here," he said to the highly wise leader of the hosts of gods;
[the Daitya] then pierced him with ten sharp arrows, blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then, with thousands of arrows, he impetuously pierced the Daitya— using shafts resembling the staff of Yama, including razor-headed arrows (kṣurapras), stone-tipped arrows (śilīmukhas),
heron-feathered arrows, and those exceedingly sharp ones possessing a brilliance like the fire of a thunderbolt.
Lambodara, who is worshipped by the gods, cut his arrows asunder;
then, suddenly, he pierced him with shafts resembling thunderbolts. With all his limbs tormented by those arrows, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then Bhadra, Saubhadra, Bhīṣaṇa, and Nirjarāntaka,
each seizing their own mace, rushed toward that Vināyaka;
simultaneously, with the blows of their maces, they struck the leader of the Gaṇas.
Then, with great agility, that one of immense strength rendered their maces useless and struck Bhadraka on the head with an axe. He then felled the head of Saubhadra with the edge of his sword.
Then, having struck down Bhīṣaṇa with his axe and Nirjarāntaka with his sword, Heramba felled four other leaders of the Gaṇas and other enemies, who were as massive as great mountains. 13–14.
Then, regaining his senses, Traipura, the best of asuras,
mounted his own chariot and struck that foremost of gods with arrows,
crescent-shaped shafts, kṣurapras, and bhallas.
The righteous-souled one cut those arrows down and pierced them in return with his own shafts;
with four arrows he struck the Saindhavas, and with one, the charioteer,
causing the leaders of the hosts to fall to the earth.
Moving with agility to another chariot, the son of Tripura pierced the lord of the Gaṇas with arrows resembling thunderbolts;
his limbs drenched in blood, he became terrible to behold like the wrathful Yama. 18.
With three arrows in the forehead, seven in the space between the breasts,
four in the region of the navel, and five in the crown of the head, the son of Śambhu, filled with great wrath, pierced the powerful one. 19–20.
With all his limbs afflicted by arrows, that Daitya, having fallen into a state of extreme dejection at the front of the battlefield, collapsed upon his chariot. Then,
he was removed from the arena of battle by his steadfast charioteer.
The brave leader, honored by the gods, did not turn his face away from the battle.
Having regained consciousness after a long time, he spoke these words to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, go toward the fearless leader, the son of Hara."
Then the charioteer spoke these words—truthful, beneficial, and gentle:
"Who on the field of battle is capable of withstanding the arrows of Hara’s son?
Therefore, O son of Prabhā, you have fallen into delusion and have been brought here by me."
"Knowing this, let that which is appropriate now be performed.
In the meantime, urged by the king, the best of poets restored the elephant to consciousness through the application of medicinal herbs and other remedies. 25-26.
He caused a hundredfold increase in his vital strength and commanded victory;
first, having given water consecrated with mantras, he healed the wounds on his limbs and ascended.
Then, along with his elephant, he shattered the mountain with its very tusks.

In this manner, that most invincible elephant, standing upon the back of the Daitya, struck down hundreds of thousands of troops and their commanders in battle with arrows possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction. 28–29.
Having struck down the foremost of the lords of the gods upon the earth with arrows then possessing a luster like the rod of Yama,
those of great heroism fell, drenched in streams of blood.
On whichever path that great Daitya went with his elephant,
there he created a terrifying and accumulated heap of corpses with his arrows;
some were struck down by the elephant, and others by the elephant-rider.
Some gods were scorched by the very force of his whirling;
thus the leaders of the hosts of gods, fearless in battle, struck him along with his elephant with many arrows using various weapons and missiles.
Nevertheless, those mighty warriors were unable to fight that elephant.
Then the elephant of Tripura struck them down with its tusks and with arrows;
those gods whose bodies were mangled fell from the mountain to the earth.
Afflicted by pain and terrified, they sought refuge with Gaṇeśa;
seeing the slaughter of the gods, the powerful Lord of the Gaṇas struck them along with their elephant with arrows equal to the fire of the thunderbolt.
Obstructed by the force of the elephant's speed and then launched upward by the arrow,
the two of them then pierced each other with arrows;
both roaring, they each desired victory over the other.
Then the two foremost heroes, the Asura and the Asura, their entire limbs smeared with blood, [fought]; meanwhile, the intoxicated elephant was pierced by the mouse with its own teeth.
Thus, the elephant being pursued by the mouse, there ensued a most terrible battle between the two.
Then, in the distribution of blows above and below, a wondrous battle took place with four [warriors].
That battle was noisy and tumultuous, terrifying to all the worlds; it was fought with teeth against teeth alone, and with arrows against the finest of arrows. 40–41.
That battle between the gods and the dānavas became terrible; there,
Ākhuka split the mighty Mahānāṅga,
and standing upon the tip of his backbone, he struck him again with a spear.
Through the Daitya’s mouth, heart, and shoulder, he [the elephant] fell swiftly to the earth with his rider, vomiting blood and deprived of life;
the sages and gods proclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (43-44).
There, with other unfailing weapons, they struck the Daityas in battle until neither army could bring the fight to a conclusion through victory.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Tripura," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-fifth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words from Maheśvara, the gods, led by Śakra, [acted].
All those hosts of Daityas fled in every direction.
Then the mighty-armed great Asura named Kumbha arrived; he, a Nairṛta, struck the king of the Yakṣas violently with his mace.
The Lord of the Guhyakas struck that supreme being violently with blows from his mace;
thereafter, a terrifying club-fight ensued between the two.
It involved the *cakrabandha*, the *mahābandha*, and the *purovadhyanibandhana* [bindings].
His vehicle was exceedingly terrifying, filled with explosives and oil.
Having engaged in a great battle with it, at the conclusion, the Lord of Wealth caused that explosive device to fall upon the chest of that Kumbha.
Then Kumbha, his tusks shattered, fell to the surface of the earth; meanwhile,
the immensely powerful Jambha, standing upon his chariot,
then struck Airāvata and Indra’s horse severely with volleys of arrows.
Vāsava pierced that best of asuras with a thunderbolt;
drenched in blood and deprived of life, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Thus did the most terrible forest become both non-terrible and indeed terrible.
With agility, he pierced the leaders of the four divisions in battle according to his power, and he struck down each of the generals individually;
with volleys of arrows, Jayanta brought Saurabha under his control.
Having slain Śaktihasta, Saṃhrāda, Yamadaṇḍa, and Narāntaka, he cast them down with their bodies reduced to ashes; and by the stroke of his sword,
he struck down Kāla and Bābhrava.
Śakti killed Amṛtyu, and Aśva likewise killed Nighṛṇa in battle;
these seven of great strength were then consumed by Agni. Bhadrabāhu, Mahābāhu, Sugandha, and Gandha—these were they.
Bhaurika, Vallika, and Bhīma—these were the leaders at the front of the army.
Their bodies consumed by the fire of battle, they fell lifeless upon the earth;
likewise, the mighty ones bound by the nooses of the high-souled Varuṇa also fell. 13–14.
The five Dānavas— Turu, Tumburu, Durmedhas, Sādhaka, and Asādhaka— mighty beings who were heroes terrifying to other heroes, fell upon the earth, struck down by the network of Śūra’s rays. 15.15–16a.
The Daityas Krūra, Krauñca, Raṇeśāna, Moda, Saṃmoda, and Ṣaṇmukha were struck down in battle by Śara with his arrows, like trees felled by the wind;
and Nairṛta, with his mace, cast Bhīma to the ground.

By the falling of spears from the Rudras, hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas fell in battle, terrified, though they were experts in the art of combat. And by the falling of arrows from the Vasus, those heroes garlanded with rays [were struck down].
By the hailstones from the clouds and by most dreadful thunderbolts,
hundreds of powerful Daityas were struck down on the battlefield;
by the blows of Kubera’s mace, they fell by the thousands.
The foremost of the Daityas were split asunder by Śakra’s thunderbolt alone;
likewise, struck by Skanda’s spear, they fell upon the earth in countless numbers. By the blow of Gaṇeśa’s axe, the most prominent leaders fell.
By the fierce discus released from the hand of Vaikuṇṭha,
the heads of the foremost Daityas fell by the thousands upon thousands of crores, as if struck by the staff of Yama, the god of death.
Then Kāla struck down the Dānavas upon the earth with his sword;
Mṛtyu [struck] the Daityas with his spear, as did Pāśin with his noose, and others with the falling of Takṣaka and the rest, and with the cool rays of the moon. 24.
Then, with a noose that struck down the pride of horsemen and donkeys,
he likewise destroyed the elephants of the Daityas by splitting their frontal globes with his iron club;
thus, with great agility, he felled both horses and elephants.
Thus, by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases of great power,
as well as by other deities and the leaders of the hosts of Mothers,
these most terrible Dānavas of the dissolution have been struck down.
With arrows, blows from swords, spears, javelins, and battle-axes (28), as well as with clubs, maces, and lances, the gods struck down the asuras.
As they were thus being destroyed, the king of the daityas arrived. (29)
Resembling the chariot of the Sun, adorned with a jewel-encrusted chariot, made of refined gold,
divine, and decorated with bells and chowries;
it was filled with banners and flags, beautiful, and comparable to the chariot of Śakra.
Having mounted [his chariot], the great hero Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the asuras,
who was difficult for gods and asuras alike to resist, struck with nets of arrows the elephants along with their troops, the heroes, and the chariots with their thousands of horses. 31–32.
He struck them down upon the earth by the hundreds and thousands;
thus, as he moved through all the hosts of the gods,
O Lord of Daityas, he rained down showers of arrows resembling Death itself.
Then, in due course, he churned the divine armies in battle,
just as an elephant in a cluster of lotus ponds crushes a thicket of lotuses with its sharp tusks;
thereafter, with the force of his speed, he repeatedly let out lion-like roars.
Then, from the force of falling upon the earth, he struck Jayanta with ten very sharp-pointed arrows;
he struck Remanta with five arrows, and Śakra with fifteen.
He struck Citraratha with twenty arrows and Guha with twenty-five; Heraṃba with thirty shafts, Yama with forty,
and likewise Kāla and Mṛtyu each with twice that number in his hand.
He pierced Guhyakeśa, the life-breath of the world, with ten arrows each;
he pierced all the Rudras individually with six and seven arrows each,
and all the Vasus along with the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas with his arrows.
With ten, eighteen, and six arrows, he pierced the gods. Due to the flood of his vigor, his extreme heroism, and his swift and light-handed striking,
the gods, having encountered this calamity, were unable to retaliate out of fear.
Struck in battle by arrows resembling the trident of Maheśa that pierced their vital organs, the immortals fell to the earth in a swoon;
even the foremost of the gods were unable to stand before him.

Then the gods, driven away and joined by the Lord of the Three Heavens, went for refuge to Hari, the protector, having been struck down there. In the meantime, Viṣṇu spoke to Jiṣṇu, the lord of birds.
Now, at the forefront of the battle, he went quickly and with speed to the presence of the Daitya to destroy him;
having pierced his chariot with arrows, he obstructed Viṣṇu’s rapid advance.
Standing before the chariot, the two Daityas spoke to the imperishable Viṣṇu:
"Having slain you along with the gods, we shall today create another creation.
Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to that roaring bull among Daityas.
"O sinful one, if you are capable, stand firm in battle to contend with me!
Then he struck the imperishable Viṣṇu with hundreds of arrows.
Undisturbed, [Viṣṇu] cut down those arrows which resembled the staff of Yama.
Again, he discharged thousands of arrows at him in the battle. Śauri, having cut those down with his own arrows,
pierced him in turn with shafts that were difficult to withstand due to their great weight and whose touch was like the submarine fire.
With sharp, piercing arrows that flew like birds and were as swift as thought, which— due to the lightness of Keśava’s missiles— were like cotton or dry grass,
that bull among the Daityas was struck by thousands of golden shafts.
Afflicted by that oppression and filled with rage, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa seized a mountain peak in battle and struck Mādhava with force;
but Hari effortlessly crushed it with his mace.
In this manner, a thousand mountains were indeed struck down one after another;
likewise, by the monkey’s agility, they were reduced to powder by the water from his mouth.
Then that best of Dānavas again assumed a thousand arms.
With arrows, extremely fierce spears, tridents, axes, and other weapons,
he rained down many upon Viṣṇu with a mind possessed by anger;
but that best of gods cut them down as they were hurled by him.
With blazing, most terrible arrows that struck fear into the asuras—
arrows resembling the trident of Śambhu— he pierced [the enemy] in all his limbs; for the lord Hari, the imperishable master of the Dānavas, was present in that battle.

Having become possessed by foul impurity, she swiftly rushed toward Hari’s broad chest and cast down that supreme, all-powerful [mace], which was as terrible as the tongue of Time and adorned with eight bells.
That best of asuras shone like a dense cloud accompanied by lightning;
then the Daityas cried out, "Victory!", uttering words of praise.
Thereupon, the enemy of the Dānavas discharged his discus at the Daitya army.
Having severed their heads, he returned again to Mādhava;
with a discharge of his spear, he struck down the Daitya in battle.
After regaining consciousness after a long time, [the Daitya] [assailed] Keśava with a fire-arrow.
Enraged in battle, Hari struck down the son of Kubera and repelled him;
then he unleashed a most terrible *māyā-astra* and an *āsura-astra*.
Likewise, he [discharged] lions, tigers, hyenas, elephants, and reptiles.
In that battle, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa struck Viṣṇu.
Then, in the fray, Hari cut down the floods of weapons and missiles produced by his illusory power (māyā) with arrows alone,
and likewise struck him with his spear.
At that moment, his entire body trembling and drenched in blood,
Viṣṇu, his form overflowing with gore, dragged it away; then the lord of the gods pierced that trident with three arrows.

With ten arrows, Hari cut down the fender, the standard, the banner, the chariot itself, the parasol, and the charioteer. When the chariot had been struck down, the Daitya leaped up and mounted another chariot.
The powerful lord of the Daityas ascended [the mountain] and turned his face toward him;
then a most terrible battle, hair-raising and great, took place between Hiraṇyākṣa and Hari, causing amazement to the worlds. 69.
Then there was a battle with missiles between them, involving mutual attacks and counter-attacks. Thereafter, as they engaged in constant hand-to-hand combat, a hundred divine years passed;
then the Daitya of great prowess grew like Vāmana.
In his rage, he seized the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, with his mouth; having lifted up the circle of the earth, he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
The remaining Daityas, filled with joy, followed him and entered as well.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, perceiving the vast power of the Daitya,
assumed the form of a boar with the intent to slay the king of the Daityas;
having taken on the body of a hog, Viṣṇu pursued and entered after him.
Having gone there, he saw the earth situated at the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala) and, with his tusks, he took up the Vasundharā, the support of the worlds.
The lord of the Daityas arrived, taunting him with bold words.
Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a boar through his illusory power, endured those harsh words with anger and, like a mountain, held up this earth upon the waters.
Then,
while she was performing her own ritual there, the king of the Daityas arrived;
possessed by great anger, he struck Hari with his mace.
Through his illusory power (māyā), Viṣṇu became a boar and deceived him with that mace;
then, as one endowed with yoga, he struck Mṛtyu with the Kaumodakī.
Thereupon, the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa was again overcome with rage.
He struck the Lord with his fist on the right arm;
thus the battle was most terrible, with movements to the left and right,
advancing and retreating, as well as whirling, hurling, and imitative maneuvers.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, standing in the sky, watched the battle;
they cried out, "May it be well with the subjects, the gods, and the sages!
and they spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods, who was in the form of a boar.
"Do not play like a child; abandon this thorn in the side of the gods.
Then Viṣṇu, endowed with great splendor and assuming the form of a Māyā-boar, obtained the consent of Brahmā and others and hurled his fierce discus.
Resembling a thousand suns, possessing a thousand spokes, and of great luster;
fierce, the bringer of destruction to the Daityas, and equal in brilliance to the fire of universal dissolution—that discus was released by Viṣṇu against the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa. (85-86)
While Brahmā and the others looked on, he instantly reduced [the demon] to ashes; then the fierce discus, the destroyer of Daityas, returned to Acyuta.
Thereupon, the gods led by Brahmā, along with Indra and the other world-protectors, [approached].

Having seen the victory of Viṣṇu, they gathered together and offered praise. The gods said: "We bow down to Viṣṇu, who is the primordial source of the universe, the lord of gods and asuras, and the protector of the worlds."
We have indeed gone for refuge to Him from whose navel-lotus, it is said, the Lotus-born Brahmā emerged.

(89) Salutations again and again to You who assumed the form of a fish; salutations to You who bore the body of a tortoise; we offer our salutations to You in the form of the Man-Lion, and likewise salutations to You in the form of Vāmana. (90)

Salutations to You, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, Rāma; salutations to Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa; salutations to the slayer of Pralamba, Śitikaṇṭha (the blue-throated one). Salutations to the Buddha, the deluder of the Daityas.
Salutations again to the one named Kalki, the ender of the Mlecchas, who assumes the form of a boar.
For the sake of the welfare of the world, you assume a form in age after age for the destruction of the asuras.
Indeed, this very arrogant Daitya named Hiraṇyākṣa has now been slain by you—he who, with utter contempt, held even the world-protectors headed by Indra in low esteem. (92–93)
"O God, know that he was struck down by you solely for the sake of the world's welfare;
be gracious, O God of gods, for you are the creator of this universe through your form as Brahmā. You alone are its protector in age after age, assuming most enchanting forms."

Becoming the fire of time and Hara, you alone shall bring the universe to destruction at the time of the end. Therefore, O Lord, you alone are the cause of the universe; there is nothing else—neither the living nor the non-living, whatever has been, whatever will be in form, and likewise whatever is currently existing.
You alone are everything known as the moving and the unmoving; apart from you, nothing in the universe appears at all.
Whether it be "it exists" or "it does not exist," that which is based on duality—the nature of both being and non-being—appears in you alone.
Therefore, O Lord, no one whose intellect is immature is able to know you.
"Except for a person who has taken refuge at your feet, we have come to you, the worthy refuge, for protection.
Vyāsa said:
Thereupon, Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, spoke to the inhabitants of heaven.

"O gods, I am pleased; may it be well with you through this hymn of praise to you now. O gods, for whoever shall recite this *Vijaya-stotra* with devotion and respect, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds will be difficult for them to attain."

Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of one hundred thousand cows, a person attains that same fruit by reciting or hearing [this account]. The constant glorification of the God of gods always grants all desires. 101.
Beyond this, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a greater knowledge. 102.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Hymn of Victory," at the conclusion of the battle between the gods and the asuras, in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Six.
Saṃjaya said:
O Brahmin, I desire to hear from you in truth the destiny of those Asuras who were slain in battle, whether they were facing the enemy or turning away.
"O venerable teacher, where have those innumerable Daityas gone, who were still present today in the three worlds with all their moving and non-moving beings? Please tell me this.
Vyāsa said:
Those who have died as heroes in the presence of the foremost Daityas in battle,
having themselves attained divinity, enjoy eternal pleasures. There, the palaces are made of gold and adorned with various jewels.
There were trees that grant all desires, joined by the waters of the celestial river;
and there was an auspicious lotus pond filled with fragrant lotuses, blue water-lilies, white lilies, and other flowers, as well as curds, milk, ghee, and sugar-candy.
Endowed with exceeding beauty and always remaining in the prime of youth,
they exercise sovereignty there as well as upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, having obtained eight births, they become wealthy, presiding officers, and ministers.
With half their bodies facing forward, they enjoy the celestial realm eternally. Those who turn their backs, those who are cowardly, fearful, deceitful in battle,
and those who hate the gods and the twice-born, go to a terrible hell.
Those who kill an opponent in battle who has fallen, fainted, or been broken, as well as Mlecchas and those who speak evil, go to hell; likewise,
those who steal the deposits of others are in truth turned away from the higher realms.
At night, thieves who act with violence disappear into the forest;
those who eat everything, the deluded barbarians (mlecchas), the killers of cows and Brahmins, and other wicked speakers—these are the barbarians who are of deceitful origin. 10–11.

For them, there is the speech of the Piśācas, and no worldly conduct exists; there is no purity, no austerity, no knowledge, no libations to the gods or ancestors, no giving, no śrāddha rites, no sacrifice, and no worship of the deities. 12.
They fail to serve their ancestors, the twice-born, the gods, and ascetics (13).
Due to the loss of knowledge, they possess neither purity nor spiritual cleansing; they lust after their mother, their sister, and other women, including their own wives (14).
Every form of perversion from the world is stained by improper conduct,
as is the case with the descendants of Tārkṣya and other inhabitants of the lineage;
for those Daityas born into such families, merit is never a motive.

Those who kill Brahmins, women, or children go to a miserable state after death. Wicked-souled men who eat beef and are addicted to consuming forbidden food go to the womb of insects, or become trees and ants.
Those enemies of the gods are not fit for the *namaḥ* mantras nor for the gods;

they are their elder brothers and co-born, similar to them, yet fierce and of vulgar conduct. They are the ones who cause hair and body hair to grow on the earth, and they delight in consuming raw flesh.

Whatever [merit] comes from vows of self-restraint, giving, ritual bathing, sacrifice, and so forth—[all that is lost by those who] take pleasure in fish, meat, and the like; who speak untruths; and who are always full of lust, always full of greed, and always possessed by anger and pride. (19–20)
Delighting in killing, binding, and agitation, fond of gambling and music, having wicked servants, taking pleasure in base people, and devoted to foul odors—
such are those men who find no joy in the gods, nor in the wise, nor in the hearing of the Dharma. 21.
In meritorious acts such as hymns and mantras, they lack determination regarding what ought to be done;
they are afflicted by many diseases and intense anger, and possess various forms and retinues—
these are the signs of Daityas among the human species on this earth.

They do not know the next world, nor their own guru, nor anyone else; they desire only the filling of their wombs, and not guests, gurus, or the twice-born (dvijas). They care neither for God, nor for a son, nor for their lineage, nor for a friend, nor for kinsmen.
They do not know of giving in dreams, nor of food, nor of household goods;
because they guard their wealth, these yakṣas in human form will not give away even a little wealth, O King, even at the end of their lives. (25-26)

Listen with a single-minded focus to the characteristics of those who dwell in the miserable states of yakṣas, who carry the burdens of others for their own sake, and of pretas, which are despised by the entire world— both for women and for men. (27)

Constantly bearing the mire of impurity and devoid of truth and purity, they accumulate filth upon their teeth, hair, garments, and bodies; even the occasional cleansing of their houses, seats, vessels, and other belongings is no longer pleasing to them. (28–29)
Not seeing any happiness in women, they quickly enter the forest;
on this earth, they take delight in consuming the remnants of offerings, leavings, and putrid things, and food, drink, and rest are pleasing to them only in the darkness. 30.
Sometimes there is health and sometimes impurity in their bodies;
such indeed is the characteristic of ghosts in the world of men.
They do not know what is beneficial or harmful, nor friend or foe, nor virtue or vice.

Those who dwell in the mortal realm are like beasts; they do not, by their very nature, perceive the states of sin and merit, nor bathing, nor the worship of gods and brahmins, nor even recognize enemy, friend, or neutral party—though they are known as such by those possessed of discerning intellect. 33.
Due to the diversity of their intellects, they wander falsely upon this earth (34). These men are of the nature of Yakṣas, excluded from all sacred rites;
I shall now describe their distinctions and characteristics on the surface of the earth (35).

The wise call him a crow who, though born in the immortal worlds, stands upon the defiled earth as a city-dweller in disguise, acting in accordance with his very sin, and consuming the remnants of offerings and the like.

Devoted to forbidden food, sinful, and fond of putrid things, he becomes a dog; engaged in all domestic affairs, he lives by means of both edible and inedible substances. Having attained birth in various species of animals on earth, he is born into such lineages.
With hands like those of dogs, they are fond of devouring mlecchas, especially pigs and those who fight with their feet;
they take pleasure in nourishing and eating things that are foul, contemptible, and unholy. 39.
Because they make mountains out of fire and gather heaps of wood, those Mlecchas should always be known as being agitated by fear of the Kṣatriyas,
while the world’s dharma has perished and it is forever devoid of purity.
Then even those of noble birth will become barbarians and thieves;
through association with them, and by connection, eating their food,
42 and through sexual union with their women, others likewise will attain that same state.
At that time, all people were tormented by suffering and disease;
they were utterly bewildered by famine and lack of food, and constantly oppressed by kings.
There, mortals took delight in falsehood and were devoid of all purity.
People will no longer listen to the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Saṃhitās;
they will be sinful, fond of liquor and meat, eaters of all things, and most cruel.
They will be devoted to harsh conduct and constantly intent on deception.
Sons do not nourish their father, nor do they support their mothers-in-law;
servants do not serve their virtuous masters, and some women do not honor their husbands, nor their fathers-in-law, nor their own mothers. (46-47)
There, men will be perpetually distressed and there will be quarrels in every house;
the kings will be mlecchas and drunkards, as will the ministers and priests (48).
And Bali will be worshipped by men with fish and meat, while [the true devotees] will be without meat.
The surface of the earth was pervaded by heretics, those exhausted by yoga, and by the primary movements of the guṇas;
it was filled with wealthy men, cuckoos, and the dull-witted, both in the forests and in the cities, where lovers and brides were mutually infatuated. 49-50.

Men eat both what is fit and unfit to be eaten, such as fish, meat, and so forth; yet other twice-born ones in the forest consume only that which is blameless. Furthermore, all other devoted animals go to the state of non-rebirth.
All those former gods, being sinful, cause their ancestors to fall;
they are indeed Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Murtyakas, and Guhyakas—those who delight in immodesty, neither gods nor humans. 52-53.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Lord, how do those who possess the truth recognize the *lakṣya* amidst mortal states? Therefore, please dispel this doubt of mine from its very root. (54)
Vyāsa said:
Whether among the twice-born or other castes, Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Pretas take on forms corresponding to the sins they have committed; yet, they do not abandon their own inherent nature. 55
Those born among asuras and mortals who are always eager for quarrel,
deceitful, treacherous, and cruel, should be recognized as rākṣasas on this earth.
(56) Furthermore, on this earth, there is the giving of gifts that causes distress to people, as well as the worship of deities [performed with such motives].
Having obtained wealth through their fierce nature, they enjoy sovereignty eternally (57).

Through victory, valor, and other merits, they shall again proceed to the destruction of their sins; thus it is on earth, as well as in heaven, in the world of the Nāgas, and in the abode of Yama (58).
By means of fierce austerity, someone attains the state of a god in heaven; having propitiated Vāsudeva, Prahlāda became honored by the gods.
Likewise, the Daitya Andhaka, by praising Hara, became a member of his assembly.
The mighty Bhṛṅgī obtained the leadership of that very gaṇa. These and many others, such as Bali and Indra, O dear one, always attain the state of the virtuous both in this world and the next.
Some of the best of gods, born on earth in the lineage of Daityas,
nourish all their ancestors by the hundreds and thousands; yet even with a single wise son, the protection of the entire lineage is secured.
Even a single son devoted to Viṣṇu may uplift ten million ancestors; even one who has conquered his senses, whose soul is righteous, and who is intent on the worship of Brahmins and gods,
shall cause dharma to flourish in the city, the countryside, and throughout the remaining Kali age.
The righteous-souled Ekorakṣa protected the city, the village, the people, and the clans; and there was a great city of Brāhmaṇas that was full of learned men.
There, all the twice-born were constantly devoted to the performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
Devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, wise, honoring guests and the twice-born,
performing sacrifices, vows, and fire-rites, and firmly resolved in the six duties— yet even for them, their minds dwell upon sin during times of extreme hardship. (66–67)
The heroes constantly perform the eternal vow of sacrifice; once, by the turn of fate, a wise householder,
a brahmin seer who was learned in the mantras, offered clarified butter into the fire with the appropriate mantra.
At that time, he suffered from such extremely severe dysuria; having gone there to relieve himself, he stationed a maidservant for protection,
but due to her negligence, a dog ate the clarified butter.

Then, out of haste, that brahmin quickly offered into the fire his own vessel, which was filled with his own urine and had been hidden from view. Immediately thereafter, he perceived that miracle within the fire.
Taking that very peak made of gold, shining like the Jāmbūnada gold, the Brahmin joyfully formed a sinful intent;
out of astonishment, he asked the maidservant, "Tell me, my dear, how did this come to be? (72-73)
O twice-born one, she then related everything exactly as it had occurred;
thereafter, that [practice] was performed by him constantly and at the proper time.
A wonderful prosperity arose in his house, causing amazement to the world.

Then, having heard of one another's deeds within that city, all those wicked men committed such evil acts out of greed; and because of their excessive greed, a great amount of impurity entered even into their own hearts.
Then, due to that mire, fear, and delusion, a derangement of the intellect occurred;
consequently, that entire city was utterly consumed by a mass of sins.
At that time, all the women were wicked and all the people were corrupt through the power of their evil deeds.
The aged and wise Brahmin then set his mind upon that task.
At that time, his virtuous wife, overcome with great sorrow and tormented by distress, spoke to her husband regarding the improper deed.
The Brahmin woman said:
"O Lord, it is truly painful for me to see you thus joined with sorrow; whether this be the custom of the village or otherwise, you ought to do something else. (80)
Then, the one who knew the faults therein smiled and spoke these words:
"O highly fortunate lady, he who lives by sin, having abandoned dharma which is the supreme benefit, is indeed controllable; he goes to a new body."
These Brahmins, who were of improper conduct, along with their wives and attendants—

due to their association with heinous crimes (atipātaka)— were considered equal to those guilty of the great sins (mahāpātaka); accompanied by that great sin, they shall go to the netherworld (rasātala).
"Even after attaining non-rebirth at the end, no end to offenses is found;

I alone remain here for the sake of protecting my own merit. Then she spoke these words to him, which were laughable to the world: "84" [Note: This is verse number 84]. Then she spoke this to him, speech that was a source of laughter for the world.
"You ought to speak before me, and not of anyone else.
The twice-born one said:
"O beloved, if I were to go elsewhere from here, at that very moment—"
"Accompanied by his own people and kinsmen, he shall go to the city and then attain a low state.
Having spoken thus, that twice-born man, being exceedingly pleased, took his own wealth and quickly went with her to the border of the kingdom.
Standing within the pericardium, she beheld him; he remained as steady as before.
"This virtuous wife has not abandoned her husband, and this city shall not perish," said the excellent Brahmin, who was greatly amazed, after reflecting thus. 88. He spoke these words.
"What indeed is that substance remaining right there outside our house?
Having reflected thus, the virtuous one said: "I have brought the sandals by mistake; while you two remain there, what indeed shall I do with them? 90.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous wife took her husband and approached; she saw that the city had become free from distress and had departed from her husband's vicinity.
Then the Brahmins and the other castes, the spies, and the city-dwellers—

They remain in a terrible hell, suffering and subject to no rebirth [from that state]. They go to the city of Yama with great difficulty, and there is no atonement for them. Therefore, that which has a foul odor and is impure is declared to be avoidable. 92–93.
Delighting in eating as before, yet committing sin today, one who is habitually thievish, a night-walker, and a deceiver should be known by the wise as such (94).
He is unwise in all undertakings and ignorant in all actions.
One who is devoid of the conduct of the *samaya* is merely a beast, as ignorant as a child.
(95) Thus there are those such as camels and others, and those such as mongooses that eat [their own kin];
they are violent, causing distress to their own relatives, and cowardly in battle. (96)
A man who always delights in eating the remnants of others' meals and so forth is called a dog by the wise;
one who is constantly devoted to the act of theft and deceives many friends is proclaimed by mortals as a donkey. (97) A man who is always engaged in quarreling is proclaimed a monkey. (98)

By nature always fickle and constantly restless for food, the man on earth who is a monkey delights in the forest; he is a "branch-eater" (śākhāmṛga) among men, and by his speech and intellect, he is a backbiter toward both his own kin and strangers. 98–99.

Because he causes agitation, that man is known as *anuraga*; he is powerful, of a wandering disposition, and always devoid of shame. He is fond of putrid meat and a seeker of enjoyments; such a person is declared to be a *nṛsiṃha*.
From its very sound, other beings such as wolves and the like become terrified and flee;
likewise, elephants, men, and others who are known to be far-sighted—thus one should understand the matter among human beings as well, in this same sequence. 101–102.
We shall describe the characteristics of the gods as they abide in human form:

[those who are] constantly devoted to the worship of the twice-born, the gods, guests, teachers, the virtuous, and ascetics, and who are dedicated to penance, the treatises on dharma, and ethics. (103)
He was patient, having conquered anger; truthful, with his senses subdued (104). Compassionate and kind toward the world, handsome, and sweet-voiced;
a master of speech, virtuous in all undertakings, skillful, and possessed of great strength (105).

He was learned in the sacred syllables (sākṣara), a scholar, and one who knew the true principles of song and dance; he was proficient in the works of spiritual science (ātmavidyā) and in all the notes of the lute (sarvatantrīsvara).
He was also skilled in all sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), in products of the cow (gavya), and in meatless fare (nirāmiṣa). 106.
He was delighted by the immediate taste of substances, and by things that were fresh and exceedingly beautiful—
by perfumes, garlands, garments, scriptures, and ornaments;
he was likewise pleased with guests, with giving, and with rites such as the pārvaṇa śrāddha.

Time passes through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts, as well as through vows, sacrifices, worship of the gods, and recitations; thus, a day should not be spent like a eunuch. This indeed is the constant conduct for human beings.
Like a god, he is sung of by the best of sages with human speech.
However, a god is preeminent in *sattva* while a human is subject to fear;
a god is always profound, whereas a human is always gentle.
Indeed, through the praise of these two, there arises great joy even among the Daityas and others;
for it brings about a state of supreme affection, happiness, friendship, merit, and auspiciousness, both among gods and humans, as well as among Daityas and Rākṣasas. 112.
Pretas and others find pleasure among pretas, and animals likewise among animals;
crows and others find pleasure among their own kind, as do others among their own species. Their states of being pleased or displeased are known through their characteristics. 113–114.
Thus, by the distinction of merit, one may discern the pleasant and unpleasant among various births, as well as virtue and vice, and excellence and defect.
On this earth, there is no happiness for a husband and wife when there is a difference in their birth.
One may find joy among one's own kind, whether liberated or even in hell.
Those who perform meritorious deeds obtain a long life through great merit; whereas sinful souls, such as Daityas and other men, meet their end. 116–117.
In the Kṛta age, the gods, Daityas, and other species were born on the earth;

in the Tretā age, they were one-footed; in the Dvāpara age, two-footed; and in the Kali age, during its transitional period (saṃdhyā), they are all crowded together, possessing only a quarter-part [of their former nature].
O Bhārata, that which was set in motion became manifest as the birth of the gods and others;
those who were the warriors and armies of Duryodhana, as well as all those who were Daityas and others on earth, such as Karṇa and his ilk—[all these arose]. 119–120.
Gāṅgeya was the chief of the Vasus, Droṇa was the lordly celestial sage, Aśvatthāman was directly Hari himself, and Nakula was born from the Kula of Hari.
The five Pāṇḍavas were born as the five Indras, and Vidura was Dharma himself.
Gāndhārī, Draupadī, and Kuntī—these queens shall remain on the surface of the earth.
During the middle of the Kali age, gods and Daityas will appear; the Daityas, as well as humans, ghosts, carnivorous beasts, and birds, shall always be born. 122–123.
Among them was a paramour’s servant girl, most wretched and exceedingly weak,
who, out of constant affection for their mutual quarrels, spoke of their conduct in all their sins, disputes, and unjust deeds. (124)
"Those such as the Daityas who are addicted [to vice] all go to hell.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Because of the false nature of the Daityas and others, they do not possess divinity nor the abode of the gods."
How is there enjoyment, how is there happiness, health, and the accumulation of strength?
(126) How is there sovereignty, longevity, fame, desired things, beloved power, the science of ethics and so forth, and the eternal growth of one's birth? (127)
"O Lord, you should tell this to me, your worthy disciple: how are the acts of giving, study, and sacrifice performed? O Bhava, you ought to speak this to me. Vyāsa said:
It is certain that for the Daityas, penance consists of audacity,
as do their vows, sacrifices, and the like, as well as affection for their own kin.
He who is self-controlled, free from vices, and has grasped the true meaning of the treatises on ethics— (129)
Purified by these various means, he becomes possessed of the characteristics of a god.
O twice-born one, he who personally performs meritorious deeds according to the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and rituals— both here and in the celestial realms— is capable of uplifting the world.
He who, out of particular devotion, beholds a Vaiṣṇava and honors him,
is liberated from all sins and is capable of uplifting the virtuous. Such a Brāhmaṇa is constantly devoted to the six duties and always intent upon all sacrifices.
Those men who always delight in the proclamation of the Dharma and are capable of upholding the Dharma,
as well as those who betray trust, are ungrateful, violate their vows,
hate the twice-born and the gods— they cause the earth to perish. 133–134.
Those men who are addicted to liquor, who are sinful, who are devoted to gambling, who converse with heretics and the fallen, and who destroy the earth;
those who are devoid of virtuous deeds, who are constantly anxious, and who are fearless—[these cause the destruction of the world]. 135.
Those men who, agitated by the pursuit of wealth contrary to the meaning of the Smṛti scriptures, cause the earth to waste away;

those base men who, abandoning their own proper livelihood, engage in inferior occupations; and those men who, out of hatred and intent on reviling their gurus, cause the earth to waste away—[these destroy it]. 136–137.
Those men who obstruct the giver, incite others toward sinful deeds,
oppress the wretched and the helpless, and devastate the earth—
these and many other such men are doers of evil karma. 138.

Men who cause others to fall cast them down to the earth. (139) He who hears this beautiful account—the most secret of secrets, which is supremely beneficial—shall have no misfortune, suffering, ill-fortune, or wretchedness upon this earth. (140)
In the state of being a Nāda and so forth, there arises birth in the heavenly world and eternal happiness;
for him there is no untimely death, nor is he defiled by sins.
In this world he is the overseer of all people, and in the third heaven he is the lord of the heavens.
Having enjoyed heaven for kalpa after kalpa, he proceeds upon the path to liberation. 142.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Merit," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Seven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord, best of the twice-born, this sky exists eternally; who is he, what is his power, and from where was this compassionate lord born?
What task indeed does he perform, being so intensely composed of rays,
who is always worshipped by the gods, the best of sages, the siddhas, the cāraṇas, the daityas, the rākṣasas, and by all humans, beginning with the brāhmaṇas? 2.
Vyāsa said:
Know that the supreme splendor of Brahman has issued forth from the body of Brahmā;
it is directly composed of Brahman and bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Seeing the peak, which was exceedingly fierce and difficult to endure due to its stainless rays,
the people fled, tormented by those harsh beams;
thereafter, all the oceans, excellent rivers, streams, and so forth [were likewise affected].
Living beings there were withering away, and the sick people were dying;
then Śakra and the other gods approached Brahmā, and at that time they spoke of this matter, to which the Creator replied.
O gods, he is the primordial source of the body of Brahmā, the progenitor of the world, and the Lord who dwells within the quality of sattva.
This very one, consisting of rajas, is the moon itself situated within the body;
by these two, the worlds in the three realms, including all things moving and unmoving, are protected.
The gods who are born by divine apparition, as well as those here who are born from a womb,
born from eggs, born from sweat, and those born from sprouts and so forth— all these [originate] right here.
Indeed, we are not able to describe the full power of this Sun.
By him the worlds were certainly protected, generated,
and nurtured; there is no one equal to him among all beings because of his universal protection,
seeing whom even at the break of dawn a heap of sins dissolves away.
Having propitiated him, the twice-born attain liberation;
indeed, at the time of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), the Brahmins who know the Veda raise their arms, for they are worshipped by the gods.
12. They truly become those honored by the deities.

By worshipping this very goddess, who resides within the maṇḍala and whose nature is the twilight (sandhyā), all twice-born ones attain both heaven and liberation; even those on earth who have fallen or are defiled by remnants of food become purified by her rays.
By the mere performance of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), one attains purification from defilement—
even upon seeing a caṇḍāla, a killer of cows, an outcaste, one afflicted with leprosy,
one burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka), or one enveloped in minor sins (upapātaka). 15.

Those men who behold the Sun are purified from heavy sins. By the mere act of worshipping him, one is liberated from all diseases; there shall be no blindness, nor poverty, nor suffering, nor cause for lamentation.
By worshipping Virocana here and hereafter, one attains [the goal];
for even the gods such as Hari, Hara, and others are not seen by the worlds, whereas this God is remembered as being accessible through the form of meditation. 18.
The gods said:
"O Brahman, let him be propitiated for the sake of grace; let there be service and worship of him. Indeed, the sight of him alone is equal to the fire of universal dissolution."
All beings, beginning with men, have attained the state of immortality on earth;
by the power of his splendor, the oceans and other elements have been destroyed. We ourselves are not capable of enduring this—how much less so other ordinary people? (20-21)
"Therefore, by your grace, let that means be ordained so that we may worship the Sun as men do with devotion.
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā went to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
Having gone there, he began to offer praise for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds:
"O God, you who have become the eye of the entire world, free from ailment;
you who directly assume the form of Brahmā, yet are as difficult to behold as the fire of universal dissolution."
For you abide within all gods, and you are always the friend of Vāyu within their bodies;
from you comes the digestion of food and the like, and life itself is certain.
You alone are the Lord of the world, the cause of both creation and dissolution.
Without you, there is not even a single day of life for all the worlds.
You are the Lord of all the worlds, the savior, the protector, the father, and the mother;
by your grace, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.
O Blessed One, there is no one equal to you among the gods, nor indeed among all beings;
the true nature of everything in the world is sustained by you alone. You are the creator of form, fragrance, and the like, and the sweetness of tastes is produced by you.
Thus, the Sun-god is the Lord of the Universe and the cause of all existence;
O Lord of the world, you alone are the pure cause of holy fords, sacred fields, and sacrifices, the witness of all, and the mine of virtues. 29–30.

He is the omniscient one, the creator of all, the sustainer, and the protector, ever intent on his task; he is the destroyer of darkness, the mire of sin, and the disease, and the annihilator of poverty and suffering.
He is the supreme kinsman both in this world and the next, the omniscient one, and the eye of all.
"Except for you, there is no one who benefits all the worlds.
Āditya said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O Indra of the universe, O creator of the universe!"
"Speak quickly, O Ordainer; whatever you desire, I shall do for you.
Brahmā said:
"Your rays are exceedingly fierce and utterly unbearable for the worlds."
"O Lord of the Gods, act in such a way that these rays become as soft as this.
Āditya said:
"These supreme rays, numbering millions upon millions, are capable of destroying the worlds."
"O Lord, they were not severed by the application of that which is desired in this world.
Then, by the power of the Sun's words, Viśvakarman was quickly summoned by Viriñci and, having fashioned a whirling disk made of adamant, [the task was undertaken]. (35–36)

He cut off the suns of the enemy's army, which resembled the fire of universal dissolution; by those very [rays], Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus was fashioned there, as well as the infallible staff of Yama and the trident of Paśupati.

By the command of Brahmā, Viśvakarman quickly fashioned for Kāla a supreme sword and for Caṇḍikā a spear that brings great joy to her preceptor, as well as a supreme weapon, a variegated trident (38–39).
O Sage, that which remained as the thousand-rayed one was further diminished by Aja; then, through the agency of Upāya, he was born again from Kaśyapa and Aditi,
and is thus remembered as Āditya.
This [wind] moves within the interior of the universe and even whirls around the peak of Mount Meru (41).
