Constantly above the earth, at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas, it moves day and night;
there, the planets, beginning with the moon, move as impelled by fate (42).
The Sun, consisting of twelve aspects, traverses the twelve months;
his transition from one sign to another is perceived by everyone as a *saṃkrānti*. O Sage, I shall now describe the entire fruit that accrues to people during those transitions.
In the signs of Sagittarius, Gemini, Pisces, and Virgo, there are the six Aṣṭakās;
in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo, Viṣṇupadī is traditionally taught.
Know that libations, gifts, and likewise the worship of the gods performed during these times yield inexhaustible merit.
The fruit of [giving] during the sixty-eight [periods] is eighty-six thousandfold;
at Viṣṇupadī it is a hundred thousandfold, and during the solstices (ayana) it is ten million times ten millionfold.
Indeed, whatever gift is given at Viṣṇupadī is proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
I declare that for the donor, there is always my presence in birth after birth.
(47) From the gift of a cotton garment in the cold season, no suffering arises in the body;
from the gift of a balance-scale and from the gift of a couch, the fruit of both is indeed inexhaustible. (48)

He who, free from envy, gives all kinds of utensils and a bed to a Brahmin of excellent complexion, shall obtain the rank of a king. Likewise, by offering fire and water at the riverbank or on a path at dawn, [he attains the same]. 49.

By giving oil and betel-leaf, one shall become a sovereign on earth. By bowing to a Brahmin with a disposition of truthfulness, one shall become wealthy and attain imperishability. On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, at the break of dawn— (50–51)
Having gratified the ancestors with sesame seeds and water alone, which yields inexhaustible merit in heaven,
and having given a cow of auspicious marks, with horns adorned with gold, radiant with jewels,
silver hooves, and accompanied by a bronze milking vessel; 52.

By giving this to the most eminent of the twice-born, a king shall become a sovereign ruler of the entire earth (sārvabhauma). By giving food and ornaments, a king becomes a lord of a province (maṇḍaleśa) and a master of wealth.
Furthermore, he who gives a sesame-cow (tiladhenu) equipped with all its necessary utensils [attains great merit]. 53–54.
One who gives food to a Brāhmaṇa is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven births and becomes imperishable in heaven; by giving such food, one enjoys eternal heaven.
[Likewise, one should give] grain, clothing, servants, as well as houses, seats, and so forth.
Prosperity never abandons that foremost of the twice-born who gives gifts;
(56) whatever gift is given, whether it be small or great, becomes inexhaustible in the other worlds, as does that given on the anniversaries of the Yugas. (57)
Alternatively, the worship of the gods, hymns of praise, and the listening to religious narratives purify one from all sins; such a person becomes worthy of honor in heaven.
The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is remembered as Anvantarā.
Whatever gift is given on that [day] is said to be entirely inexhaustible. Wealth, enjoyments, as well as sovereignty and a stay in heaven lasting for the duration of a kalpa—
therefore, giving and the honoring of the virtuous bestow infinite fruit in the life hereafter.
In the Manvantara, the seventh lunar day (saptamī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha is declared by the Purāṇas to be the most meritorious, protected by the Sun;
in the month of Māgha, during the dark fortnight, that saptamī is known as Koṭibhāskara.
A person who fasts on that meritorious day is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing at the time of dawn on that day yields great fruit.
Whatever sin has been committed by me there during seven previous births— may the Sun-god, through this Saptamī, destroy that for me, along with my disease and grief.
O Saptamī, you who possess seven times seven powers, you are the mother of all beings.
On the seventh day, when the sun has risen in the circle of the divine master, the solar orb,
one should bring together arka leaves, barley, fragrant flowers, jujube fruit, and rice grains, which are placed in a copper vessel or upon its leaf. 65–66.
Having offered a beautiful *argha* along with a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) and vermilion (*sindūra*), whatever sins have been committed throughout seven lifetimes go to destruction;
[otherwise], one is tormented by hells, diseases, and sinful miseries. 67.
One should feed sacrificial food that is pure, prepared with sun-dried rice;
one should avoid food ground on a stone, ginger as a vegetable,
the leaves of the *koradūṣaka*, plantain, and goat's ghee.
One should avoid hair, insects, and the like, as well as bathing with hot water;
during the vow, one should avoid all small seeds and similar items. Furthermore, while observing the vow, one should not engage in any other activity except for reflection on dharma.
The Saura-vrata is of great merit and is praised by the Purāṇas;
for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of years,
one obtains eternal enjoyment in heaven equal to that of Āditya.
Thus, after the exhaustion of his merit in heaven, he becomes a king on earth and a man of great wealth;
through former practice, he performs the Bhāskara-vrata in the mortal world,
and likewise obtains for himself eternal happiness to be enjoyed in heaven.

Through the grace of the Sun, those born [on this day] attain the perfection of health. (74) That which occurs on a Sunday coinciding with the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is renowned as Mahājaya; elsewhere, it is remembered as Vijayā. (75)

A crore of *vijayā* [leaves] would be infinite; such is *mahājayā*. By this single vow alone, one is liberated from the bondage of birth. [One should offer] a precious horse, gold, red cloth, and grain.
The Lord of Heaven and Earth grants these [rewards] in succession out of affection for Bhāskara.
O Brahmin, listen as I explain their distinctions according to the truth:
he who gives here a fine horse adorned with excellent ornaments [attains the highest reward]. 77–78.
Having reached the earth graced by the seven oceans and freed from enemies,
that mortal shall become a sole sovereign within a single birth-cycle. Furthermore,
he shall obtain a vehicle drawn by horses, or one with winged limbs, or even one adorned with bulls.
A wise person should prescribe a dakṣiṇā of one or two gold māṣas.
Having given a vessel of jewels of great value, or whatever is made of gold, or even pure gold alone, one becomes a lord of wealth in the third heaven.
Whoever offers red cloth and grain along with water according to their ability attains lordship over heaven and earth; Fortune never forsakes such a person.
He shall be free from disease, of a very serene mind, a conqueror, and possessed of great majesty.
As long as the sun shines, he is indeed most worthy of worship. He who observes the twelfth, the eighth, or the seventh lunar day in the month of Māgha and other such times,
having enjoyed his desired fruits here, is honored by the gods themselves.
Having performed the Arkāṅga-saptamī vow according to the prescribed rules, a wise man,
purified from sin, shall obtain his desired objects here and attain liberation.
(85) I shall now describe its characteristics and the specific procedure for each month.
And by the grace of this vow, one shall be honored among the gods in heaven (86).
When the bright fortnight has begun, on a Sunday during the northern solstice,
under a lunar mansion with a masculine name, one should undertake the Saptamī vow (87).
Hasta, Anurādhā, Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Punarvasu—
these are called the male-named constellations by the wise.
On the fifth day, one meal is prescribed, while on the sixth, eating only at night is proclaimed.

On the seventh day there should be fasting, and on the eighth day the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place. Having performed the fast according to the rules, one should consume the tip of an arka plant, pure cow dung, fine black pepper, water, and fruit; likewise, one should observe eating only at night (nakta), fasting, and eating only once a day (ekabhakta).

Having performed the *Vāsara-saptamī* in this sequence— offering milk or food smeared with ghee— one obtains the desired fruit from the Sun-god. "The tip of the *arka*" refers to the tip of the branch of an *arka* tree situated to the northeast of the village.
One should drink two distinguished, fine leaves along with water, without touching them with the teeth.

Pure cow dung that has not fallen on the ground, measuring one *pala* with both thumbs, should be drunk along with water, without touching it with the teeth. A single whole black pepper—excellent, unblemished, not old, large, and not dried out—should be drunk along with water, without touching it with the teeth.

Water should be drunk as it flows from the base of the ring finger; fruit—any one of the dates or coconuts—should be eaten without being touched by the teeth; and food smeared with ghee should be consumed in the quantity of a peacock’s chick, and the ghee itself should be of that same measure.
When the sun casts a shadow twice the length of one's own body, [one should fast].
Then one should understand that *anaktam* does not mean eating at night;
rather, one should first worship the deity with fruits, flowers, and mantras,
and thereafter perform the gift of food in the quantity prescribed by the rules.
Then, one should meditate on [the deity] who is complete with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments,
two-armed, red in color, and holding a red lotus in his hand. 94.

At the time of worship, especially, one should meditate upon the god Āditya as a radiant orb situated in the midst of abundant water, accompanied by his retinue, seated upon a lotus throne, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents. 95.
Now, this mantra is:
"We know the Sun; we meditate upon the thousand-rayed one; may Sūrya impel us. (96) This supreme mantra is declared to be recited on the seventh lunar day as bringing victory.

One should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) afterwards with Karavīra and Karañja flowers, which resemble red saffron, especially on the eighth day. The breaking of the fast must be performed on the eighth day itself; it should never be done on the ninth day.

If the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is performed on the ninth day, one does not obtain the fruit of the vow; therefore, the breaking of the fast should take place in the afternoon, consisting of food free from pungent, bitter, and sour flavors. One should carefully clean the rice, discarding grass, seeds, and other such impurities.
One should avoid mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and the like, as well as ghee.
One who is capable should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas with offerings such as milk, according to one's ability, providing food, drinks, and vegetarian side dishes. 100–101.

A man who performs this Saptamī vow, which yields infinite fruit, which pacifies all sins, and which increases wealth and progeny, should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins after distributing them according to their merit. 102.
O best of the twice-born, he who performs this vow month after month for the gratification of the Sun and concludes it with devotion, goes to the world of the Sun;
he shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas and thereafter attain the supreme goal.
This supreme secret was spoken by Śambhu in the past;
it is proclaimed that the fruit for one who constantly hears it or upholds its vow is equal to that of one who causes others to hear it as well. 105
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Arkāṅga-Saptamī Vow," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Eight. Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Blessed One, through your grace I have heard of this purifying vow;
now I wish to hear of another that is dear to the Sun.
Vyāsa said:
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground before Maheśvara, who was seated comfortably on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, Skanda spoke these words:
"The ritual procedure known as Arkāṅga has been heard by me from you in such detail."
"O Lord, I wish to hear in truth the fruit that comes from the day of the week (vāra) and so forth. The Lord said:
"On the day of the Sun, the man observing the vow should offer an arghya with red flowers."
By eating only at night and consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one does not fall from heaven.
For one who always performs every virtuous practice on the seventh lunar day, which is the day of the Sun, the Supreme Lord, together with his retinue, becomes pleased.
By observing the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāra) in a manner consistent with a hero,
one attains the status of a Gaṇapati as long as the sun remains in the sky;
it is meritorious, grants all desires, bestows sovereignty, and destroys disease.

This meritorious vow of the Sun, which bestows heaven and liberation, is beneficial; O Śivā, when performed on a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on the seventh lunar day (saptamī), or even on that very day,
all acts such as the vow and worship shall attain inexhaustibility.
On a bright Sunday, one should perform the worship of the Lord of Planets;
having drawn him out with the breath through the mouth of the fire, one should place him within the mandala.
He has two arms, stands upon a red lotus, possesses a beautiful neck, and is clothed in red garments.
Having visualized [the deity] adorned with all red ornaments, one should hold a flower with both hands, smell it, and cast it toward the northeast.
We know Aditya; we meditate upon Bhaskara; may that Bhānu inspire us. (11)

Then, according to the procedure taught by the Guru, one should perform the anointing; at the conclusion of the anointing, the incense; at the conclusion of the incense, the lamp; at the conclusion of the lamp, the food offering (naivedya); and thereafter, one should offer water.
Then one should perform the recitation, praise, mudrās, and prostration.
The first mudrā is the añjali; the second is known as the dhenu.
He who worships the Sun in this manner shall attain union with the Sun.
"By the grace of that Sun, this terrible Brahman-slaughter with a skull held in my hand has been released on the bank of Vārāṇasī.
There is no deity higher than the Sun to be found in the three worlds."
"By whose grace I have been liberated from terrible and heavy sin.
Skanda said:
"O Lord, O Master, having heard these words from you, wonder has arisen within me."
"O God, there is no one other than you; how could the murder of a Brahmin be committed against you?
You are the wise one, the Lord, the yogi, the enjoyer in the world, the imperishable and immutable. You alone are the preceptor of the gods, the pervasive form, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). (17-18)
"The Omniscient One, the Giver of Boons, is eternally the Lord of all living beings; O Protector, whence could there be any evil deed in you, and especially anger? Śiva said:

"For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, we— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— manifest separately in age after age and perform everything, O son. For us, there is neither bondage nor liberation, nor is there anything that is not to be done or that ought to be done."
Likewise, for the sake of protecting the world, Rāma performed [this] according to the prescribed rites;
it is supreme in every respect, the destroyer of all obstacles,
the pacifier of all diseases, and the accomplisher of all goals.

Becoming manifold through the divisions of time, the blameless one performs penance month after month; thus, the one becomes twelvefold. In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa he is Mitra, and in Pauṣa he is the eternal Viṣṇu.
Varuṇa shall scorch [the world] in the month of Māgha, and likewise Sūrya in Phālguna; the Sun shall scorch in Caitra, and Tāpana is remembered [as the one who does so] in Vaiśākha;
Indra shall scorch in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and Ravi shall scorch in Āṣāḍha.
Gabhastiman is in the month of Śrāvaṇa, Yama in Bhādrapada,
Hiraṇyaretas in Āśvayuja, and Divākara in Kārttika; thus these twelve Ādityas are proclaimed for each respective month.
Possessing vast forms and great splendor, with a brilliance like the fire at the end of an eon—
those who recite this daily find no sin remaining; they shall have neither disease nor poverty, nor shall they ever be subject to contempt.
One obtains inexhaustible heaven, happiness, sovereignty, and fame in succession.
I shall now proclaim the supreme Great Mantra that brings delight to all:
*Ūṃ, obeisance to the thousand-armed one; obeisance, obeisance to Āditya.* (29)
Salutations to you who hold a lotus in your hand; salutations again and again to Varuṇa.
(30) Salutations to the destroyer of darkness; salutations again and again to Śrī Sūrya. Salutations to the thousand-tongued one; salutations again and again to Bhānu. (31)
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Rudra; salutations, salutations to you!
You are Agni within all beings, and you are Vāyu; salutations, salutations to you!
You are omnipresent within all beings; indeed, nothing exists apart from you.
Established within every body in this world of moving and non-moving beings—having thus recited this, one shall obtain desires such as the enjoyments of heaven in due order.
Āditya, Bhāskara, Sūrya, Arka, Bhānu, Divākara. (33–34)
Suvarṇaretas, Amitra, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ— these ten, along with Svayambhū and Timirāśa, are proclaimed as the twelve [names].
Whatever man recites these names of the Sun, which are pure, [attains merit].
Freed from all sins and all diseases, he attains the supreme goal.
(36) Furthermore, I shall describe another [aspect] of the Great-Souled Bhāskara:
those known as Raktas, who resemble blood in color, with bodies as red as vermilion. (37)
O Six-faced One, listen to those names which are the foremost:
Tapanas, Tāpanas, Kartā, Hartā, Graheśvara, Lokasākṣī, Trilokeṣu, Vyomādhipa, and Divākara. (38)

The great sage Agnigarbha, Heaven whose vehicle is the seven horses, the lotus-handed one, the dispeller of darkness, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the singer of the Sāmaveda; Kālapriya, Puṇḍarīka, and the meditated-upon Mūlasthāna. 39–40.
For one who always remembers [him] with devotion, whence can there be fear of disease?
O Kārtika, listen with diligence to this auspicious [account] which removes all sins;
O high-minded one, not even the slightest doubt should be entertained regarding the Sun-god. 41.
"Ūm̐ indrāya namaḥ, Ūm̐ viṣṇave namaḥ.
(42) This recitation, this fire-offering, and likewise this ritual worship at the twilights, brings about all peace and destroys all obstacles. (43)
It destroys all diseases, such as cutaneous eruptions (lūtā) and boils (visphoṭaka),
as well as jaundice (kāmalā) and other ailments, even those that are most terrible.
It likewise cures fevers occurring every day, every third day, and every fourth day.

Leprosy, consumption, diseases of the abdomen, and likewise fever; urinary stones, dysuria, and various other ailments and maladies; whatever diseases arise from wind (vāta), and whatever diseases are born of the womb (garbha-sambhava). 45–46.
Crushing the great diseases and consisting of the pain of those who are afflicted,
all these go to dissolution simply by the utterance of "Āditya.
O Lord of the gods of gods, protect me from the fears of planetary influences and diseases.
When the sun has been praised, they all attain tranquility.
(48) I shall now proclaim the root mantra of the great-souled Bhāskara, which accomplishes all desires and goals, and which eternally bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (49)
And this mantra is: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ*.
By means of this mantra, all success will certainly be attained at all times. Diseases do not afflict one, nor does any undesirable fear arise.
He who takes the water from the *sūryāvarta* [plant] in the proper sequence is liberated from disease merely by drinking it;
it must not be given away, it must not be disclosed, and it must be recited over with great effort. 51–52.
To those who are non-devotees, childless, heretics, or worldly-minded,
one should administer a mixture of pungent oil as both nasal drops and a drink.
O son, by drinking the water of *sūryāvarta*, one is liberated from all diseases.
The root mantra should be recited during the twilight prayers and in fire-offering rituals (homa). While it is being recited, diseases as well as malevolent planets are destroyed.
What need is there for many other scriptures or for mantras of great length? 54–55.
"O child, this *Sarvaśānti* is the accomplisher of all aims;
it must not be given to an atheist, nor to one who reviles the gods or Brahmins. It should be given to one devoted to the guru, and never to anyone else. (56)
The person who, having risen early in the morning, shall constantly recite this,
is released from all sins— even the killer of a cow and the ungrateful man.
It bestows physical health, increases wealth, and brings about fame.
There is no doubt that he with whom the Sun is pleased shall attain his desired fruit,
whether he recites [this] once, twice, thrice, or always at all times;
such a person shall obtain the presence of Brahmā.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter. One desiring knowledge obtains knowledge; one desiring wealth obtains wealth.
He who listens with devotion, endowed with pure conduct, [attains these fruits]. 60-61.
One who is completely liberated from all sins goes even to the world of the Sun; furthermore,
whatever Vrata-conduct or sacrifices are performed during the vow of Bhāskara, if one recites [this] in sacred places and at holy fords (tīrthas), it shall become ten millionfold in merit.
If a wise Brahmin recites this in the presence of the planets during a planetary feast, in the presence of the foremost of the twice-born during a Brahmin feast,
before ascetics, or in the presence of the gods, his merit shall be infinite. (63-64)
Whoever recites this, or causes it to be recited, is glorified in the world of the gods.
65. Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Peace of the Sun," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter Seventy-Nine.
Vyāsa said: In the Middle Country, O auspicious lady, there was a sovereign emperor known as Svarāṭsamrāṭ,
who was purified by many austerities and various kinds of vows.
He indeed constantly worshipped the gods with a pure disposition; however, leprosy eventually appeared on his left hand, and it became white.
Then, through the application of medical treatment, the symptoms were seen as they were before.
Having summoned the foremost of the twice-born and his ministers, he spoke these words.
The King said:
"O Brahmins, I have committed a sin that is unbearable and censured by the world."
Therefore, this is a great field of merit where I shall cast off my body.
O heroes who know the dharma, command me for the sake of my welfare in the next world— whatever benefit there may be for me after death, since I am now without a lineage.
"Therefore, O twice-born ones, speak with full confidence regarding that which I have declared and what I shall do.
The brahmins said:
"The kingdom has been abandoned by you, who are wise and of virtuous character."
"O King, this world is ruined; therefore, you ought not to speak [otherwise].
Indeed, we perceive this remedy for it:
O Lord, worship Mahādeva with mantras and with great effort."
The king said:
"O best of Brahmins, by what means shall I propitiate the Sun,
who is afflicted with foul leprosy and despised by the world?"
"Unseen by all beings, I am despised, O twice-born ones.
What shall I do with a kingdom, and what would be the use of performing worship?
The twice-born replied:
"By staying here in your own kingdom and worshipping Virocana,
you shall be liberated from terrible sin and attain both heaven and liberation.
Having heard this, O Indra among kings, he prostrated before those best of the twice-born.
He performed the supreme propitiation of that Sun-god through daily worship with mantras, offerings, ointments,
various kinds of fruits, water-libations, and unbroken grains of rice.
With hibiscus flowers, arka leaves, karavīra, and karañja;
with red saffron, vermilion, and vāsantika flowers and the like;
and with fragrant plantain leaves and their most charming fruits.

Having prepared the *arghya* offering in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, the king, always facing the sun, offered it together with his ministers and domestic priests; likewise, the queens and the noble ladies offered the *arghya* from all sides. 15.
By all those residing in the inner apartments, along with their wives and guards,
as well as by the groups of servants and others, offerings are made day after day through extremely fierce solar propitiations (*arka-śānti*) and other supreme hymns and mantras.
With the root mantra and other mantras, they worshipped the Sun; likewise, another vow known as Arkāṅga was performed by them with great concentration.
Gradually, having reached the end of the year, the king attained freedom from disease.
When the terrible disease had been suppressed, the King caused the entire world to perform auspicious sacrifices and vows; likewise, [he offered] fragrant *japā* flowers and plantain fruits. 19–20.

Having performed this great merit, which is dear to all people, a person— abstaining from food and subsisting on sacrificial grain (*haviṣyānna*)— should worship the Sun with *arka* leaves that have no flowers, using arrows as the sacrificial offerings. 21.
In this very way, Vibhākara, honored by those three groups, was deeply gratified; approaching the king, he spoke these words out of compassion:
"Choose a boon, whatever is desired that dwells in your heart."
For the benefit of all the city-dwellers and his own followers,
the king said:
"If you wish to grant me a boon that is pleasing to the eyes of all."
"May the supreme heaven be ours all together in your presence," they said.
Sūrya replied:
"Those ministers of yours—twice-born brahmins along with their wives and their retinues—" (25)
Possessing fresh youthfulness, pure, and free from disease, they shall dwell in my beautiful city until the dissolution of all beings, provided with every enjoyment.
It is filled with celestial trees and palaces that grant all desires like the kalpa-tree.

"O highly fortunate one, through the means of women, dance, song, and other such [pleasures], you shall become King Manu after five kalpas have passed. These men standing before you are kings and these are the household priests. (27-28)
"Likewise, you learned and wealthy men who dwell in the countryside shall obtain happiness there by receiving boons from me, and you will attain heaven.
Having spoken thus, the Eye of the World vanished right then and there.
Then, O Bhadrā, King Saporu rejoiced in heaven.
There, those insects and others who had been consumed there, along with their sons and so forth, experienced great and wonderful enjoyments under the celestial trees in the heavenly realm. 30–31.
In this very manner, O King, Brahmins, sages of celebrated vows,
and those of the Kshatriya and other castes, quickly went to the sun-like heaven. Some requested wealth, while others asked for sons and wives.
Through the grace of the Sun-god, one attains happiness, heaven, and likewise health. O auspicious one,
that pure person who recites this "Puṇyakūṭa" shall have all their sins destroyed and be honored on earth like Rudra himself.
He becomes a witness for all in heaven, a bestower of boons, and dear to the Sun;
that mortal who listens with self-restraint shall obtain his desired fruit, having crossed over all sins in the very assembly of the Sun. 35.
One shall always become eloquent, meritorious through hearing this, and wealthy.
This most secret of secrets was proclaimed by Bhāskara; it was told to Yama and celebrated on earth by Vyāsa. 36–37.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Bhadreśvara," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty. Vaiśampāyana said:
"O twice-born one, by your grace, this power of Śrutagraheśvara has been attained; now tell us the means for propitiating the planets, beginning with the Sun.
Who are Ketu, Rāhu, and the others? How are they pleased, and what is pleasing to them?"
"When the proper time and place have arrived, that vision [of the Lord] is both auspicious and inauspicious.
Vyāsa said:
"In this world, the planets and other celestial bodies experience the fruits of merit and sin."

They perform auspicious and inauspicious acts for the sake of the destruction of all karma; Sūrya is to be known as Time and the Ender among the planets and among people, for he is the lord of restraint and favor through his fierce and gentle conjunctions. 3–4.

I shall now describe the propitiation of that very planet from its state; he who offers oblations with the sprouts of the *udumbara* and *palāśa* trees, using the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena," and also with radish for the sake of pacification.
One should offer oblations with [the two ladles] filled with clarified butter for the sake of obtaining desired fruits;
for the pacification of all diseases and for liberation from killing and bondage,
one hundred oblations should be offered with each individual mantra.
On a Sunday, one should give a goat cooked with ghee to the Sun,

and feed Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability with delightful offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya). This should be done on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, and likewise on the fifteenth.
The sick shall be freed from disease, and one shall emerge from hardship unharmed.
He shall be honored as a hero throughout the entire cosmic egg— from the highest immortality down to a mere blade of grass, and from the vastness of the universe down to the size of an atom.
Through the sequence ending in withdrawal, he is the cause of the origin and maintenance of all;
at the time of the emission of breath for living beings, he moves through the body as far as the soles of the feet.
At the time of death, he departs from the midst of the body along with the vital breath.
The moon, always situated within the head and endowed with sixteen digits (kalās),
rains down a shower of nectar day and night with its face turned downward. By that [nectar],
all living beings, from the great creatures down to the minute ones, sustain their lives.
The broad-shouldered [Viṣṇu] nourishes the stationary and moving beings;
by these two, who possess flowers, the world is both sustained and produced.
Through the propitiation of those two, there is always auspicious nourishment that leads to the higher realm.
The practitioner, remaining always pure, shall accomplish all his undertakings.
That lowest of men who, out of delusion, does not worship the Moon—his life-span comes to an end and he goes to hell. 15–16.

O Gaṅgādhara, crest-jewel who bears the stainless digits, O Jagannātha, salutations to you, the Moon, on the second lunar day; likewise, salutations to the Moon upon reaching any other lunar day as well. 17.
The person who performs [this rite] shall obtain his desired fruit.
O glorious Moon, born from the eye of Atri, arisen from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, and residing upon the crown of Maheśa—salutations to you! 18–19.
"Obeisance to you of divine form, O Lord of the World who is like the moon;
the wise know [you] in the bright fortnight as well as in the dark, during the three watches of the night.
(20) "Ūṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Soma"—this is the mantra to be recited.
He who thus worships Soma at dawn, or causes others to hear it, or listens to it himself, shall become like nectar in this world in birth after birth. 21.
He who thus praises and worships [the deity] on earth with these thousand names attains imperishable heaven, from which return is difficult to achieve. 22.
Thus ends the worship of Soma.

In a vessel of bell-metal, brass, bronze, or iron, filled with ghee, O Auspicious One, one who is free from envy regarding the ritual act—whether it be deficient or excessive due to one's wealth—hears [the teaching] in gold or silver; in the case of Mercury, it occurs in a vessel of white metal, and in the case of Budha (Mercury), in a black vessel. 23.
Having established [the deity] in all its forms, one should give it to one who has many sons.
Supreme good fortune arises, far exceeding even nectar;
for both women and men, there shall never be misfortune.

Desiring beauty and good fortune, a man free from envy should first speak these words and give to a twice-born man a vessel full of curd placed within a bronze bowl: "I give this; grant me beauty and good fortune. (26)
According to one's capacity, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, as well as new garments and so forth; 27.
One should offer food that is complete in all its qualities and very pleasing betel-leaf, along with flower garlands and the like, for the sake of attaining beauty and good fortune. 28.
Thus, he who bestows this gift upon a twice-born person dedicated to Soma shall enjoy beauty and good fortune in both the heavenly world and the world of men. 29.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Worship of Soma," in the first section, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 80.
The eighty-first chapter.
Vaiśampāyana said: [He described] the origin of Lohitāṅga and his gratification among the people.
"I wish to hear in truth about his power, majesty, and splendor. Vyāsa said:
"The god born from a portion of Hara was born of low birth as the son of the Earth."
Established in goodness, complete in being, a hero on earth who wields power;
sharp, a cruel planet, the deity with the red body, full of majesty;
a youth endowed with beauty, the lord consisting of lightning strikes.
By this [fire], the Daityas were roasted; the flesh-eaters, the Asuras, and their enemies, as well as humans, plants, beasts, and birds, were likewise consumed through the ten conjunctions.
Vaiśampāyana said:
How was this [Graha] born from Śambhu, and how was the son of Mahī born?
How is it that the god is cruel? I wish to know this. (5) How may he always be propitious toward all the worlds?
When the guru speaks with a sense of full confidence regarding me, there is no doubt [of his realization].
Vyāsa said: O King, in the lineage of Hiraṇyākṣa, there was a wise ruler of the asuras.
A Daitya known as Andhaka, the destroyer of all the gods,
was born by virtue of a boon from Viṣṇu; having acquired the prowess of Viṣṇu,
he gradually conquered the gods, including Indra and the drinkers of Soma.
Then the gods, having approached Vidhi, spoke these words:
"Our kingdom, our happiness, and our sacrifices have been seized by Andhaka alone;
therefore, let a means for his slaughter be told and let it be carried out."

Then Dhātṛ spoke these words to the gods: "He has no wealth other than this; there is nothing for him from the drinking of the nectar due to Viṣṇu’s boon, O gods. However, his status as an asura will surely result in his humiliation. (10-11)
For the sake of the welfare of the world, he entered into all the women there who were endowed with faith and desire, yet filled with doubt; indeed,
his mind was not steady toward any woman except for Pārvatī Durgā, whom he had left behind.
Then the Lord of the World, becoming enraged, shall bring him to deformity.
Thereupon, abandoning his state as an Asura, he will become a Gaṇa of His.
Having spoken thus to Śraddhā, who was filled with desire, the Lord of Creatures— 13–14.
He sent Vicikitsā and Svamāyā toward him; thereupon, agitated by desire and intent on seeking women,
he did not perceive the difference between his own wife and the wives of others because of his state of doubt.
Then, impelled by Māyā, he wandered through the three worlds. On the slopes of the Himavat, he beheld a most beautiful jewel of a woman;
having seen Pārvatī, the Daitya fell under the sway of desire.
If he desires to seize her who is difficult to capture due to the loss of his knowledge, Umā, assuming the form of a *kākoṭavī* through her own body,
stands near the Lord; and he, full of passion, seeks to seize her.
Then, his mind agitated by desire and his consciousness rendered insane,
that bull among the Daityas did not leave Pārvatī, the mother Śivā.
Thereupon, having returned from meditation, the husband of Pārvatī joined him.
Having seen him, O lord of Daityas, he returned to his own abode,
eager to conquer Śambhu after having prepared his warriors; driven by lust and delusion, he was senseless in his desire to bring back Gaurī alone.
Having heard this, the gods, urged by Nandin,
went there and engaged in a great, terrible battle that struck fear into the worlds;
the preceptor of the Daityas then restored those Daityas who had died in the fight back to life.
Having reported this entire event on Kailāsa,
Śambhu, out of anger, then spoke these words to Nandin:
"O hero, go quickly to the abode of the Daityas by my command."
While all the Daityas and the lord of the Daityas looked on in their assembly, [he] seized that evil-minded descendant of Bhṛgu by his hair and,
having brought him from our presence, quickly led him away while he was utterly distraught.
Then the glorious Nandīśvara, commanded by the Lord of Pārvatī,
took Kāvya by the hair with force in front of the Daityas;
and as he was leading him away, the Daityas struck him with weapons and arrows.
They were unable to cause pain to the powerful Nandin;
taking him by the hair, Nandi went joyfully before the gods and arrived in the presence of Hara along with him. 28–29.
Seizing Bhārgava, the preceptor of the asuras, with fury,
that lord, equal to Kāla and Antaka, swallowed him whole while remaining in his mountain-like form.
Then the powerful lord of the Daityas, surrounded by his entire army, became enraged.
Then he rushed toward Vaśaṅkara with terrible weapons and other implements. Likewise, the gods, the Vidyādharas,
and others, being greatly enraged, proceeded to the battle there against the Daityas.

In the meantime, a terrible battle arose against Bhīṣma, like that between the gods and the Dānavas, causing fear to all the worlds. Then, with their weapons fully trusted [in their power], the gods struck down the Dānavas.
In that great battle, the son of Danu struck down the gods, and they [the gods] struck him;
desiring victory over one another, they pierced each other with arrows made of gold, resembling thunderbolts, and adorned with jeweled feathers. 34–35.

The powerful and great Daityas intensely illuminated his limbs and the very heavens with their lovely forms, while the best of the Kāśyapa gods, possessing heroic might, struck them down with collections of unfailing weapons. 36. Having slain them, those foremost of the gods caused them to fall.
The great army, which had pervaded the world and was well-protected by Bala and Āyudha,
was brought to destruction in an instant by all the gods with their trusted weapons, while Mahādeva himself fought with great effort. 37–38.

O twice-born one, although he had been extracted from the trident and remained undecayed for a long time, Andhaka— being of humble intellect— was made into Bhṛṅgiriṭi by being led into the state of a Gaṇa.
Then, having addressed the gods, Śiva vomited forth Śukra.
The embryo then fell upon the earth; therefore, he is remembered as Bhauma (the Earth-born).
Śukra, having addressed Śiva, departed for the Daityas filled with joy.
Thus was Bhauma born, an emanation of Hara produced from the earth.
On the fourth lunar day, on a Tuesday, those of virtuous vows should perform his worship during a planetary affliction such as *daśā* or *ariṣṭa*, or when [Mars] is in an unfavorable sign,
in a trine (*trikoṇa*) or a mandala, using red flowers and unguents.
Thus worshipped, Bhauma bestows intelligence, wealth, sons, happiness, and fame. What more do you wish to hear?
Vyāsa said:

O disciples, this auspicious narrative of Dharma has been told to you; having heard it, one is no longer born or even dies again. It bestows merit upon the twice-born and should be cultivated by those who desire well-being. 44–45.
"Go as you please, having accomplished your purpose by my command.
Brahmā said: Having thus addressed them, the blessed Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, [departed]. 46.
Having determined the various aspects of dharma through the *śamyā* and *prāsa*, O son, you too, having understood the truth with faith,
may you dwell at ease according to the time, joyfully singing the praises of Hari. 47.
Instructing the worlds in dharma and gladdening the Teacher of the World,
Pulastya said:
"Thus addressed, O King, Nārada departed for Gandhamādana."
To see Nārāyaṇa, the best of sages, at the hermitage of Badarī. 49.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Origin and Worship of Bhauma," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-two.
Bhīṣma said: The worship of the Sun, the Moon, and Mars has been heard; now tell me the worship of Mercury, the son of the Moon. 1.
Pulastya said:
Born from the womb of Tārā, Budha is the son of Candra;
he is to be known as a gentle yet cruel planet, bestowing both auspicious and inauspicious results upon men. 2.
The mandala of Budha is proclaimed to be arrow-shaped;
one should construct that mandala with powders having colors like emeralds.
There, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings, flowers, and beautiful incenses.
One should perform the ritual gift-giving according to the rules when the Moon is in its tenth *ariṣṭa* period or its *gocara*.
For the sake of awakening and satisfaction, one should give camphor, mung beans, yellow cloth, an emerald, and gold, according to one's capacity.
"O son of Soma, O one of great wisdom, O you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
salutations to you! O you who dwell among the planets, be forever gracious toward me.
Having thus praised Budha with devotion and a concentrated mind, O Great King.
One shall obtain all desires through the grace of the Son of Soma (Budha).
O King, the worship of the Guru is prescribed within a circular maṇḍala fashioned with well-prepared,
beautiful powders of yellow color.
One should worship with yellow flowers, perfumes, garments, and gold;
and if there is malefic influence from the *daśā* or *gocara*, one should give gifts according to one's capacity.
[The gifts include] chickpeas, split pulses, yellow cloth, and gold.
One should give a Puṣyarāga gem to a Brāhmaṇa for the pacification of misfortune.
O Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods and expert in all scriptures,
be gracious to me now and be satisfied with this gift.
O Indra among kings, when one acts in this manner, the Guru becomes favorable; through the proper worship of the Guru, a person attains all desires.
Now, O King, I shall describe the worship of Bhārgava as well.

By performing which, the attainment of all desires arises perfectly for men. The mandala of Bhārgava is prescribed as five-cornered; it should be constructed according to the rules by a wise person using white-colored powders.
A man endowed with faith and devotion should worship Bhārgava with white perfumes, flowers, and likewise white garments;
the offering of silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed according to one's capacity. 15.
When the first of the ten [types of] misfortunes (ariṣṭa) has arisen, one should cause a white horse to be given as a gift.
Rice, a white cloth, silver, sandalwood, camphor, and richly fragrant substances should be given as a donation to a twice-born man. 16–17.
"O son of Bhṛgu, O highly fortunate one, O priest of the Dānavas,
be satisfied by this gift, you who are worshipped by all the Asuras. Having recited this mantra, one should give the gift as prescribed.

O descendant of Kuru, Śukra Āśubhārgava becomes pleased with him. Having fashioned a human-shaped mandala for the purpose of worshipping Śanaiścara using black-colored powders, one should worship there with devotion.
With black perfumes, flowers, and likewise with garments of that same color,
iron, the gift of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), oil-cake, and sesame seeds—
these are the gifts for the misfortune caused by Saturn; [one should also give] a black cow and black clothing.
O highly fortunate son of the Sun, O mighty Chāyā-putra, one should give gold and likewise a sapphire according to one’s ability. O Śani, look downward; I am pleased with this gift. 22–23.
Having thus praised Śani with devotion, whoever gives [these offerings] to a twice-born man, Śani will become favorable to him even when he is in a malefic transit (gocara).
All the characteristics of Rāhu, such as his color and so forth, as well as his maṇḍala, are like those of Śani.
The form of the Sun is prescribed there; the worship is like that for the Son of the Sun (Saturn). 25.
Gomedaka stone, mustard seeds, black sesame, black beans, a buffalo, and likewise a goat—this is proclaimed as the gift for Rāhu. 26.
O Lord of Daityas, son of Siṃhikā, O Rāhu who crushes the moon and sun,
O you of excellent vows, may you be pleased by this gift of great fortune;
one should fashion for Ketu a beautiful orb in the shape of a banner.
O King, the entire worship, including the colors and other details, should be understood as being performed on a Saturday.
Seven types of grain along with gold are prescribed for the gift of the Ketu.
When this is done, O King, the two [the Sun and Ketu] become favorable to men.

They should bestow wealth, sons, happiness, and good fortune; one should likewise recite the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena" for the Sun, and that same mantra for the Moon. For Mars, the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā" is to be chanted as well as the hymn of praise.
"Udbudhyasva" is for the son of the Moon (Budha); "Bṛhaspate" is likewise for Guru (Jupiter).
"Annāt pari" is for Śukra; "Śanno devīḥ" is for Śani (Saturn).
"Kayā naḥ" is for Rāhu, and "Ketuṃ kṛṇvan" is prescribed for Ketu. 31–32.
Thus have these mantras been declared for the worship and recitation of the planets;
when performed in this manner, O best of kings, all the planets become perpetually favorable to men and bestow abundant prosperity.
O Great King, this entire [account] has been related to you here in due order.
Having heard it, a person attains the essence of the meaning of all that has been heard and reaches the very presence of the Lord.
This is purifying, a treasury of glory, and it shall be exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
"This [account] serves as nectar for the gods and brings merit even to sinful men.

He who recites this glorious account with devotion, or hears it here, or beholds the worship of the Enemy of Madhu and Mura, shall dwell in the world of Indra for one kalpa, honored by Brahmā, Śiva, and the lords of the gods. Furthermore, he who bestows even a thought [of this] upon people is likewise honored there.
Whoever should constantly hear this auspicious account of the sages' conduct is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
They praise austerity in the Kṛta age, and knowledge alone in the Tretā age.
They say that sacrifice is the duty in the Dvāpara age, while in the Kali age, charity alone is the duty;
among all forms of giving, this one alone is the most excellent. There is no gift higher than the granting of fearlessness to all living beings.
The Lord, the Master, declared that for a Śūdra, charity is the primary duty.
Through charity, he attains all his desires; it is austerity, merit, purifying, life-prolonging, and the destroyer of all sins. 40–41.
This ancient account, which describes the performance of *śrāddha* at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), has been told;
whoever hears it or even reads it becomes a fortunate man.
Liberated from all sins, he shall attain Hari together with Lakṣmī.
"O Great King, this meritorious account, which destroys even great sins, has been told to you.
It is well-honored by Brahmā, Arka, and Rudra; those who know the truth declare that it must be heard.
O King, this Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa has been proclaimed by me to you. (43-44)
The wise man who causes the Brahmins to hear, or who himself hears or recites, this Pauṣkara— the primordial source of the Purāṇa consisting of ninefold creation—
rejoices in the world of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas. 45
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Planets," in the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, within the section on the Manifestation of the Purāṇas.
The *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* is complete.
May there be auspiciousness.
